## What the chapter is doing
- "Satan stood up against Israel and incited David to number Israel." David orders a census. Joab objects, does it anyway, and leaves out Levi and Benjamin.
- God is displeased and strikes Israel. David confesses. Through the seer Gad, God offers three punishments: three years of famine, three months of defeat, or three days of plague with the angel of Yahweh destroying. David chooses to fall into God's hands.
- 70,000 die. The angel heads for Jerusalem, and Yahweh says, "It is enough!" The angel stops at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
- David sees the angel standing between earth and heaven with a drawn sword over Jerusalem. He begs God to punish him, not the sheep.
- David buys Ornan's threshing floor at full price, "I will not... offer a burnt offering which costs me nothing," builds an altar, and God answers with fire from heaven. The angel sheathes his sword.

## Pay attention to this
- **Two tellings of one story.** 2 Samuel 24:1 says Yahweh's anger "incited David" to count Israel. 1 Chronicles 21:1 says a *satan* did. Same event, two ways of telling who moved David. 🔴
- **No "the" in front of satan (21:1).** In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 the figure is *ha-satan*, "the satan," a title: the adversary, the accuser. Here the word stands bare. It's the one place in the Old Testament where it might work as a proper name. The LSB prints "Satan." 🔴 for the grammar, ⬜ for what it means.
- **"Stood up against Israel" (21:1).** Standing is what an accuser does in court. In Zechariah 3:1 the satan stands at the high priest's right hand to accuse him. 🔴 for both texts, 🟡 for the courtroom picture.
- **Joab sees it (21:3, 6).** David's hard-edged general calls the census a cause of guilt and finds the order "abominable." When Joab is the conscience in the room, something's wrong. 🔴
- **David owns it (21:8, 17).** "I have sinned greatly." "Is it not I who commanded...? These sheep, what have they done?" 🔴
- **"Fall into the hand of Yahweh" (21:13).** David picks the punishment that leaves Israel in God's hands, because God's mercies are great. 🔴
- **"It is enough!" (21:15).** God stops the angel himself, at the edge of Jerusalem. 🔴
- **The angel between earth and heaven (21:16).** Chronicles shows him, huge, with a drawn sword stretched over the city. Samuel doesn't describe him this way. 🔴
- **Full price (21:24).** "I will not... offer a burnt offering which costs me nothing." 🔴
- **Fire from heaven (21:26).** God answers David's sacrifice the way he answered at the tabernacle's first offering (Leviticus 9:24) and at Carmel (1 Kings 18:38). That marks the spot. 🔴
- **This is the temple site.** The next chapter has David say "this is the house of Yahweh God" (22:1), and Solomon builds the temple on Ornan's threshing floor on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1). 🔴

## Read it like 400 BC, not 2026
- **Chronicles was written for people back from exile.** It retells Samuel and Kings for a community rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, roughly the 400s BC. So the Chronicler cares most about where the temple came from. This chapter is its origin story. 🔴 for the audience, 🟡 for the date.
- **Why a census was dangerous.** Counting your fighting men meant planning for war on your own strength, and it treated Yahweh's people as the king's property. The law tied every census to a ransom payment "so that there will be no plague among them" (Exodus 30:12). 🔴 for Exodus 30, 🟡 for the reasons.
- **The satan as a role.** In the Old Testament, *satan* is first a job: adversary, opponent, accuser. In Numbers 22:22 the angel of Yahweh himself stands in the road "as a satan" against Balaam. Peggy Day's study argued that any member of the council could serve as "a satan" on a given occasion. 🔴 for Numbers 22, 🟡 for Day's reading.
- **Heiser's answer to the two tellings.** Numbers 22:22 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 are the only two places where a bare *satan* names a divine adversary, and Numbers names its satan as the angel of Yahweh. And only three times does the Old Testament put a drawn sword in a heavenly figure's hand: Numbers 22:23, Joshua 5:13 and 1 Chronicles 21:16, all the angel of Yahweh. So Heiser reads the satan of 21:1 as the angel acting as adversary, God in angel form. On that reading Samuel and Chronicles never disagreed. 🟡
- **The critical model is different.** Scholars like Newsom (*New Interpreter's Bible*) read the same data as God's anger being pushed off onto a separate figure, who only later hardens into the devil. Same Hebrew evidence, a different frame. 🔴 that they read it that way.
- **"Satan" as a name came later.** The earliest texts that use Satan clearly as a personal name are centuries later, like the Assumption of Moses and Jubilees (DDD). 🔴
- **The Destroyer.** The killing angel is a known figure: the destroyer at the first Passover (Exodus 12:23), the angel at Araunah's floor (2 Samuel 24:16), and Paul's "destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10). DDD notes he kills in numbers, always on Yahweh's direct order, and is always stopped by a sacred act. Here the act is David's altar. 🔴
- **Threshing floors were holy spots.** Open, high, flat ground where grain was separated, and in the ANE often a place where the divine met the human. A threshing floor becoming the temple site fits that world. 🟡
- **The numbers differ.** 2 Samuel 24:9 gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah. Chronicles gives 1,100,000 and 470,000. The price differs too: 50 shekels of silver in Samuel (for the floor and oxen), 600 shekels of gold here (for "the site"). Chronicles may be counting differently or pricing the whole area. 🔴 for the differences, ⬜ for the fix.

## My notes
- I worked this chapter through Unseen Realm 101, Session 6, "the satan problem," alongside Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3.
- **No article.** In Job and Zechariah it's *ha-satan*, a title. Here *satan* has no article, the one place it plausibly works as a proper name. 🔴 on the article data. My memory hook: "the satan" is a role, like "the prosecutor." You don't name your kid Prosecutor. The name comes later.
- **Two frames, same data.** Newsom (NIB 4:348) and Merrill (*Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi*, 120) read the missing article as the function turning into a name, God's anger pushed onto a lower figure that only later hardens into a dualistic enemy. That's a history-of-religions projection model. Heiser's frame is revelation unfolding about a real being. I don't want to teach the critical model as if it were Heiser's.
- **Later than it looks.** DDD notes the earliest texts that use Satan clearly as a name (Assumption of Moses 10:1; Jubilees 23:29) come centuries later.
- **The Destroyer (21:12, 15–16, 27, 30).** From my Fact Book entry: Chronicles gives the destroying angel a visible, giant form with a drawn sword he sheathes when Yahweh calls him off, matching "the angel who was destroying" in 2 Samuel 24:16.
- My Fact Book entry for the satan also records Heiser's case that the satan of 21:1 is the angel of Yahweh, and that his argument rests on the angel-of-Yahweh material, not on the missing article alone. If someone hasn't worked through the visible-Yahweh texts first, the census reading looks like a dodge. 🟡
- **Divine council:** yes. The satan as an adversary role in God's court, the angel of Yahweh with a drawn sword, and the Destroyer.

## Open threads
- Who incited David, Yahweh (2 Samuel 24:1) or a satan (1 Chronicles 21:1)? I flagged it and haven't worked it. Genuinely debated. ⬜
- Is the satan of 21:1 a human adversary (an enemy nation stirring David to count troops), the angel of Yahweh, or the figure later called Satan? ⬜
- Why exactly was this census a sin, when Numbers has God order censuses? ⬜
- How to fit the different numbers and the different price. ⬜

## Worth reading
All of these are in my Logos library. The ones marked (vault) are also in my vault books.
- **Michael Heiser, *The Unseen Realm*.** (vault) Chapter 8 on the satan and the angel-of-Yahweh case. On Audible too.
- **Michael Heiser, *Demons*.** The short treatment of 1 Chronicles 21:1. On Audible too.
- ***Bible Study Magazine*, July–August 2010.** Heiser's short article on the census and who authorized it, God or Satan.
- **Van der Toorn, Becking and van der Horst, eds., *Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible*.** (vault) The "Satan" and "Destroyer" articles.
- **John Walton, ed., *Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, OT vol. 3*.** Censuses, threshing floors, the temple site.
- **Michael Wilcock, *The Message of Chronicles* (BST).** How the Chronicler retells David for the returned exiles.
- **John Thompson, *1, 2 Chronicles* (NAC).** The main commentary for the book.

## Quiz
Take it before you read and again after.

1. According to 1 Chronicles 21:1, who incited David to count Israel?
2. In 2 Samuel 24:1, the same story says what moved David?
   a) His generals
   b) The anger of Yahweh
   c) A prophet
   d) The Philistines
3. Which of David's men objected to the census?
4. True or false: in Job 1–2 the Hebrew has "the satan," with "the" in front of it.
5. What three punishments did Gad offer David?
6. Which did David choose, and why?
7. What did Yahweh say to the destroying angel at Jerusalem?
8. What did David see standing between earth and heaven?
9. Why did David refuse to take Ornan's threshing floor for free?
10. How did Yahweh answer David's offering?

### Answer key
1. Satan (21:1).
2. b. The anger of Yahweh.
3. Joab (21:3).
4. True (Job 1:6).
5. Three years of famine, three months of defeat by enemies, or three days of plague with the angel of Yahweh destroying (21:12).
6. The plague, to fall into Yahweh's hand, because his compassions are great (21:13).
7. "It is enough! Now relax your hand" (21:15).
8. The angel of Yahweh with a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem (21:16).
9. He would not offer a burnt offering that cost him nothing (21:24).
10. With fire from heaven on the altar (21:26).

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul warns from Israel's wilderness story. They were all under the cloud, all through the sea, all fed and watered by God, and most of them still died in the desert for idolatry, sexual sin, testing God and grumbling. "Let him who thinks he stands take heed that he does not fall."
- So flee idolatry. The Lord's Supper is a sharing in Christ's blood and body, the way Israel's sacrifices made people sharers in the altar.
- An idol is nothing, but what the nations sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God. You can't drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.
- Marketplace meat is different: eat it and don't ask. If someone at a dinner points out it was offered to an idol, skip it for his sake. Do everything to the glory of God.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Our fathers" (10:1).** Paul calls the wilderness generation the fathers of a mostly Gentile church. Israel's story is now their story. 🔴
- **"Baptized into Moses" (10:2).** The cloud and the sea as a baptism, the manna and water as a meal. Israel had their own "sacraments" and fell anyway. 🔴
- **"The rock was Christ" (10:4).** Paul puts Christ in the wilderness with Israel. 🔴
- **Five sins, five falls (10:6–10).** Craving, idolatry, sexual immorality, testing, grumbling. 🔴
- **"Put Christ to the test" (10:9).** Some manuscripts read "the Lord." If "Christ" is right, Paul says Israel tested Christ in the desert. 🔴 for the variant.
- **"The ends of the ages have arrived" (10:11).** Paul's readers live where the ages meet. 🔴
- **The way of escape (10:13).** A promise in the middle of a warning. God doesn't leave you without a door. 🔴
- **"Sharers" (10:16, 18, 20).** *Koinōnia*: partnership, participation. Eating at a table makes you a partner with whoever the table belongs to. 🔴
- **"An idol is anything?" No... but (10:19–20).** The same "nothing" from 8:4, now with the second half: the sacrifices go to demons. 🔴
- **Two tables (10:21).** Cup of the Lord, cup of demons. You can't sit at both. 🔴
- **"Provoke the Lord to jealousy" (10:22).** Straight from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21). 🔴
- **The market is fine (10:25–26).** "The earth is the Lord's, as well as its fullness" (Psalm 24:1). Food is food. 🔴

## Read it like AD 54, not 2026
- **Deuteronomy 32:17 is the bridge.** "They sacrificed to demons who were not God, to gods whom they have not known." The Hebrew word is *shedim*. Paul's "they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (10:20) follows that verse almost word for word in the Greek Old Testament. 🔴
- **The Greek Old Testament made the gods "demons."** It translates *shedim* as *daimonia*, and Psalm 96:5 in the Greek reads "all the gods of the nations are demons." Isaiah 65:11 condemns people who set "a table" for Gad, the god of fortune; the Greek has "the demon." By Paul's day, a Jew reading his Greek Bible saw pagan gods as *daimonia*. 🔴
- ***Daimon* used to be neutral.** In classical Greek a *daimon* was an in-between spiritual being, good or bad. The New Testament only uses the word negatively. 🔴
- **The rock that followed.** Jewish tradition told of a well or rock that went with Israel through the desert (Pseudo-Philo, *Biblical Antiquities* 10:7; later rabbinic texts). Paul takes the legend his readers knew and says the real provider was Christ. 🔴 for the tradition; 🟡 that Paul is playing off it.
- **"Sat down to eat and drink, and stood up to play" (10:7).** Exodus 32:6, the golden calf party. Feasting before an idol was exactly what a Corinthian temple banquet was. 🔴
- **The destroyer (10:10).** The destroying angel of the Passover (Exodus 12:23) and the angel of judgment in 1 Chronicles 21. God's judgment carried out by a heavenly agent. 🔴
- **The cup of blessing (10:16).** At a Jewish meal, and especially Passover, a cup was blessed with thanks to God. Paul's readers knew the Lord's Supper came from that table. 🔴
- **Temple meals made you a guest of the god.** Invitations to dine "at the table of the lord Sarapis" survive on papyrus. The god was treated as the host. That's why Paul calls it "the table of demons." 🔴
- **Grace before meals.** Jews blessed God before eating, and later rabbis used Psalm 24:1, the verse Paul quotes in 10:26, to say everything belongs to God and must be received with a blessing. 🔴 for the rabbinic use; 🟡 that the custom was this settled by Paul's day.

## My notes
- **The bridge text is Deuteronomy 32:17.** "They sacrificed to demons who were not God" (*shedim*). Paul's 10:20 follows that verse's logic almost directly. Same word-world as Psalm 82: real *elohim* of the nations, created, rebellious, under sentence ("you will die like men," Psalm 82:7), with no right to worship. 🔴
- **The two questions behind the "contradiction" with 8:4:** Does a god live in this statue? No. Is there a real rebel spirit exploiting this worship? Yes.
- **The meat line is about relationship, not what the meat is.** Bought in the market with no rite attached, it's just food (10:25). Eaten as a participant in the temple rite, you've joined the demons' table. That's the line Paul won't let anyone cross. 🔴
- **Fact Book work (Heiser, DDD).** The Greek Old Testament renders *shedim* as *daimonia*, and that's how the categories connect. Heiser reads 32:17 against 32:8–9: the *shedim* are the same allotted *elohim*, indicted for abusing their guardianship. Paul's warning in 10:20–21 shows he accepted the Deuteronomy 32 framework and didn't treat "demon" as empty superstition. Revelation 9:20 keeps the idol-equals-demon equation. 🔴 that the sources say it.
- **10:20 is one of the passages that carries the divine council load,** with Deuteronomy 32:8–9 and Psalm 82. 8:5 only gestures. 🔴
- **Divine council:** this is the load-bearing chapter for Paul and the gods of the nations.

## Open threads
- A Logos pull on Deuteronomy 32:17 to 1 Corinthians 10:20 was offered and not run.
- How do chapters 8 and 10 fit? Does 10:21 forbid all temple dining, or only eating during the rite? ⬜
- 10:9, "Christ" or "the Lord"? It changes how strongly Paul puts Christ in Israel's history. ⬜
- 10:8 says 23,000 fell; Numbers 25:9 says 24,000. Paul may be blending Numbers 25 with Exodus 32:28, or counting differently. Not run down. ⬜

## Worth reading
Where each one is: Logos, my vault library, or both.
- **Bob Becking, Pieter van der Horst and Karel van der Toorn, eds., *Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible*.** (Logos) The "Demon" article behind my Fact Book entries.
- **Michael Heiser, *Demons*.** (Logos) Deuteronomy 32:17, *shedim*, and how Paul uses them.
- **Michael Heiser, *The Unseen Realm*.** (Logos, vault) The allotted *elohim* and the table of demons.
- **Kenneth Bailey, *Paul through Mediterranean Eyes*.** (Logos, vault) The cultural read of chapters 8–10.
- **Anthony Thiselton, *First Corinthians: A Shorter Exegetical and Pastoral Commentary*.** (Logos) How chapters 8 and 10 fit together.
- **N. T. Wright, *Paul for Everyone: 1 Corinthians*.** (Logos, vault) The wilderness story as the church's story.
- **Clinton Arnold, *Powers of Darkness: Principalities and Powers in Paul's Letters*.** (vault) Paul's demons and powers against their Greek and Jewish background.

## Quiz
Take it before you read and again after.

1. Which Old Testament story does Paul use as a warning in 10:1–11?
2. What does Paul say the rock in the wilderness was?
3. Name two of the sins Paul lists from Israel's history.
4. Finish 10:12: "Therefore let him who thinks he stands..."
5. What does God promise along with every temptation (10:13)?
6. True or false: Paul says an idol is something powerful in itself.
7. According to 10:20, to whom do the nations really sacrifice?
   a) To God
   b) To nothing
   c) To demons
   d) To the emperor
8. What two things does Paul say you can't share in at the same time?
9. What does Paul say about meat sold in the market?
10. Finish 10:31: "Whether, then, you eat or drink or whatever you do..."

### Answer key
1. Israel in the wilderness after leaving Egypt (10:1–11).
2. Christ (10:4).
3. Any two: craving evil, idolatry, sexual immorality, testing Christ, grumbling (10:6–10).
4. "...take heed that he does not fall" (10:12).
5. The way of escape, so you can endure it (10:13).
6. False (10:19).
7. c. To demons (10:20).
8. The cup and table of the Lord and the cup and table of demons (10:21).
9. Eat it without asking questions for conscience' sake (10:25).
10. "...do all to the glory of God" (10:31).

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul turns to "spiritual gifts." As pagans they were led around by mute idols. Now the test of the Spirit is simple: nobody speaking by God's Spirit says "Jesus is accursed," and nobody can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit.
- There are many gifts, ministries and workings, but one Spirit, one Lord, one God. Each believer gets a showing of the Spirit for the good of all, given as the Spirit decides.
- The church is one body with many members. The foot can't quit because it isn't a hand, and the eye can't tell the hand "I have no need of you." God placed every member, and the weaker-looking parts are necessary.
- "Now you are Christ's body." God appointed different roles, and not everyone has every gift. Then Paul promises "a more excellent way," which is chapter 13, love.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Led astray to the mute idols" (12:2).** Before Christ they were being *led*. Someone or something was doing the leading. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for the reading.
- **The test is about Jesus (12:3).** Not how dramatic the experience is, but whether it confesses Jesus as Lord. 🔴
- **Spirit, Lord, God (12:4–6).** Three in a row, each tied to the gifts. Paul's language is already Trinitarian in shape. 🔴
- **"For what is profitable" (12:7).** Gifts are for the body, not for the one who has them. 🔴
- **"Just as He wills" (12:11).** The Spirit decides who gets what. 🔴
- **Jews or Greeks, slaves or free (12:13).** All baptized by one Spirit into one body. The church's oldest dividing lines are gone at the door. 🔴
- **The foot and the ear (12:15–16).** Members talking themselves out of the body. Paul says the feeling is wrong: "it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body." 🔴
- **"God has appointed the members... just as He desired" (12:18).** You don't audition for your part. 🔴
- **The weaker parts are necessary (12:22–24).** Paul turns the ranking upside down: God gives more honor to the part that lacked it. 🔴
- **"Do all speak with tongues?" (12:30).** In Greek the question is built to expect "no." 🔴

## Read it like AD 54, not 2026
- **The body was a political picture.** The Roman story of Menenius Agrippa (Livy 2.32) has the body's members rebel against the belly; the moral was that the lower classes should keep serving the upper ones. Stoics like Seneca also called humanity one body. Paul uses the same picture and flips it: the "weaker" and "less honorable" parts get the honor. 🔴
- **Corinth's healing temple had body parts on the walls.** At the Asclepius sanctuary archaeologists found clay hands, feet, eyes, ears and other body parts left by people asking the god for healing. Corinthians knew bodies broken into pieces and handed to a god. Paul's body is whole and belongs to Christ. 🔴 for the finds; 🔵 that Paul had them in mind.
- **Honor and shame ran everything.** Who sat where, who spoke, who wore what. "Less presentable members" are the parts we cover with clothes, and covering is honoring. Corinth's church brought those rankings in the door (1:26–29, 11:21–22). 🔴
- **Religious frenzy was familiar.** Greek cults, especially of Dionysus, prized ecstatic, out-of-control experience. Paul says being "led" around by forces you don't control was the old life. The Spirit's mark is confessing Jesus as Lord, not losing yourself. 🔴 for the cults; 🟡 for the contrast in 12:2.
- **"Jesus is accursed" (12:3).** Deuteronomy 21:23 says anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Some Jews could say a crucified Jesus was cursed, and under pressure Roman courts later made Christians curse Christ. 🔴 for the texts; ⬜ for who in Corinth said it.
- **Distinguishing spirits (12:10).** In a city full of gods and spirits, the church needed people who could tell where a message came from. Paul assumes there are other spirits to tell apart. 🔴 for the gift; 🟡 for the reading.
- **One body under one head.** In Ephesians and Colossians Christ is the head the whole body grows from and toward (Ephesians 4:15–16; Colossians 2:19), and he's seated "far above all rule and authority" (Ephesians 1:21–23). The body belongs to the King who outranks the powers. 🟡

## My notes
- **My question:** "The body of the church, who we are, what part am I, real definition."
- **The answer I got to:** Paul's body language is a hard structural argument against anxious self-ranking, not a warm picture. God arranged the members as he chose (12:18), so parts are assigned, not auditioned for. The lesser-looking parts are declared necessary (12:22), which flips the Corinthians' honor ranking. The member who says "because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body" (12:15) is told that reasoning is false. 🔴
- **So "what part am I?" is the wrong first question.** The body works because every member is necessary whether or not it can name its function.
- **Christ is the head as source and goal** (Ephesians 4:15–16; Colossians 2:19), the ongoing presence of the risen King. That ties to Wright's "how God became king."
- **Myth-buster:** "find your spiritual gift and plug in" turns Paul's anti-anxiety, anti-hierarchy argument into a personality test.
- **Symbolic vs. diabolic.** *Symbolon* is from *syn* + *ballō*, "thrown together"; *diabolos* is from *dia* + *ballō*, "thrown apart." That root is fact. My reading of it: a member who builds up the body serves the whole, and a member who makes himself the most important is making the diabolic move, the part exalting itself over the whole. Scholars hold the same application, but it's theology, not dictionary. 🔴 for the etymology; 🟡 for the application.
- **I'm not anti-church.** I believe the church is incomplete, not unnecessary.
- **12:30 and tongues.** In my tongues research, 12:30 is the grammatical wall against "everyone filled with the Spirit speaks in tongues." 🔴
- **Divine council:** none named here. The hooks are the "mute idols" that led them (12:2) and the gift of distinguishing spirits (12:10). The idols and demons chapters are 8 and 10.

## Open threads
- Offered and not run: a side-by-side study of 1 Corinthians 12, Romans 12 and Ephesians 4 with Bailey's honor and shame reading and the Greek. ⬜
- Is the "first apostles, second prophets, third teachers" list (12:28) a ranking or a sequence of how the church got founded? ⬜
- "Earnestly desire the greater gifts" (12:31): a command, or Paul describing what they were already chasing? The Greek form allows both. ⬜

## Worth reading
Where each one is: Logos, my vault library, or both.
- **Kenneth Bailey, *Paul through Mediterranean Eyes*.** (Logos, vault) Honor and shame in the body argument. The one I wanted for the side-by-side study.
- **Anthony Thiselton, *First Corinthians: A Shorter Exegetical and Pastoral Commentary*.** (Logos) The gifts and the body, carefully.
- **N. T. Wright, *Paul for Everyone: 1 Corinthians*.** (Logos, vault) Short and clear on the body.
- **Clinton Arnold, ed., *Zondervan Illustrated Bible Backgrounds Commentary, vol. 3*.** (Logos) Asclepius, the body-politic fable, Corinthian status.
- **Mark Taylor, *1 Corinthians* (NAC).** (Logos) Steady verse-by-verse help.

## Quiz
Take it before you read and again after.

1. What topic does Paul start in 12:1?
2. What can no one say except by the Holy Spirit?
3. True or false: Paul says there are many different Spirits giving different gifts.
4. Why is each believer given a showing of the Spirit (12:7)?
5. Who decides which gifts each person gets?
6. Into what were Jews, Greeks, slaves and free all baptized?
7. What does the foot say in 12:15?
8. Who placed the members in the body?
   a) The apostles
   b) The members themselves
   c) God
   d) The elders
9. What does Paul say about the parts of the body that seem weaker?
10. True or false: According to 12:29–30, everyone has every gift.

### Answer key
1. Spiritual gifts (12:1).
2. "Jesus is Lord" (12:3).
3. False. Varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit (12:4).
4. For what is profitable, the common good (12:7).
5. The Spirit, just as he wills (12:11).
6. One body, by one Spirit (12:13).
7. "Because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body" (12:15).
8. c. God (12:18).
9. They are necessary (12:22).
10. False (12:29–30).

## What the chapter is doing
- The Corinthians wrote Paul about food sacrificed to idols. Some of them said, "We all have knowledge." Paul answers that knowledge puffs up and love builds up.
- He agrees an idol is nothing in the world and there's no God but one. There are many so-called gods and lords, but for us there's one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
- Not everyone has that knowledge. For a believer who used to worship idols, eating that meat still feels like worship, and his conscience gets hurt.
- So use your freedom with your brother in mind. If you wreck a weak brother's conscience you sin against Christ. Paul says he'd give up meat for good before he'd do that.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Now concerning" (8:1).** Paul is answering their letter point by point (7:1, 8:1, 12:1). He may be quoting their slogans back to them: "we all have knowledge," "an idol is nothing." 🔴 for the letter; 🟡 for the slogans.
- **Knowledge vs. love (8:1–3).** The point isn't being right; it's what being right does to your brother. And the one who loves God "has been known by Him." 🔴
- **"An idol is nothing in the world" (8:4).** The carved thing isn't a god. Paul agrees. Hold this next to 10:19–20 before you decide what he means. 🔴
- **"So-called gods... many gods and many lords" (8:5).** Paul doesn't say these are imaginary. He says "so-called" and "as indeed there are." 🔴 for the wording; ⬜ for how much weight it carries.
- **The Shema rewritten (8:6).** Israel's prayer is "Yahweh our God, Yahweh is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Paul splits it: "one God, the Father" and "one Lord, Jesus Christ," and puts Jesus inside the one God as the one "by whom are all things." 🔴 for the Shema echo; 🟡 for how strong a statement about Christ it is.
- **"Accustomed to the idol until now" (8:7).** The weak brother isn't silly. He spent his life worshiping at those tables. 🔴
- **"Dining in an idol's temple" (8:10).** Paul isn't only talking about meat at home. Some of the "knowers" were eating in temple dining rooms. 🔴
- **"The brother for whose sake Christ died" (8:11).** That's Paul's measure of another believer's worth. 🔴
- **Sin against the brother is sin against Christ (8:12).** 🔴

## Read it like AD 54, not 2026
- **Corinth was a Roman city.** Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC. Rich, mixed, full of freed slaves and traders, with temples to Apollo, Aphrodite, Asclepius, Demeter and the emperor. 🔴
- **Temples were restaurants.** Temple complexes had dining rooms. Archaeologists found them at the Asclepius sanctuary in Corinth. Papyrus invitations survive from Egypt asking guests to dine "at the table of the lord Sarapis." Birthdays, guild meetings and business deals happened there. Saying no could cost you your place in the city. 🔴
- **Most meat started on an altar.** Animals were often sacrificed before the meat went on sale. Corinth had a meat market (*macellum*), and leftover sacrificial meat could end up there. 🔴
- **"Gods in heaven or on earth" (8:5).** Greeks and Romans had sky gods, earth gods, household gods, city gods and deified emperors, and called many of them "lord." 🔴
- **The Old Testament said it first.** Deuteronomy 10:17 calls Yahweh "God of gods and Lord of lords." Psalm 82:1 has God judging "in the midst of gods." Israel never denied the other beings existed; it denied they were Yahweh's equals. 🔴
- **Deuteronomy 32 behind both chapters.** The nations were handed to other gods (32:8), and when Israel worshiped them they "sacrificed to demons who were not God" (32:17). Paul quotes that line in 10:20. 🔴
- **Knowledge was a status badge.** In Corinth "knowledge" and "wisdom" marked the spiritual elite (1:18–31). Paul turns it: knowledge without love is just inflation. 🟡

## My notes
- **My question:** if the Psalm 82 worldview is right and lesser gods are real, does Paul's "an idol has no real existence" (8:4) contradict it?
- **No contradiction.** Paul makes two claims on two levels. The carved object is nothing; no god lives in the statue. The spiritual being receiving the worship is real, but demoted: a *daimonion*, not a *theos* worth the name. He finishes the thought in 10:19–20. 🔴
- The two questions behind the "contradiction": Does a god live in this statue? No. Is there a real rebel spirit exploiting this worship? Yes.
- **8:5, "many gods and many lords,"** in the Corinthians' world, before "for us there is one God and one Lord" (8:6).
- **Method: not every verse carries the same weight.** Deuteronomy 32:8–9, Psalm 82 and 1 Corinthians 10:20 carry the divine council load. 1 Corinthians 8:5 and Ephesians 6:12 only point toward it. Pushing one verse past its grammar costs you credibility with exactly the readers who'd otherwise be persuaded. 🔴
- **Reading mythology isn't worship.** Paul's line is allegiance at the table, not familiarity with the stories. He quotes pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), and Tolkien and Lewis used pagan furniture. The category is a rebel spiritual being getting worship it has no right to through a cultural form, not "demon number 47 named Zeus." 🟡
- **Divine council:** the "so-called gods" of 8:5. It's a gesture here. The load-bearing verse is 10:20.

## What the chapter is doing
- After three years of peace with Aram, Ahab king of Israel wants Ramoth-gilead back. Jehoshaphat king of Judah agrees to join him but asks for a word from Yahweh first.
- Ahab's 400 prophets all say go. Zedekiah even makes iron horns: you'll gore the Arameans. Jehoshaphat asks if there's another prophet of Yahweh. There's one, Micaiah, and Ahab hates him because he never says anything good.
- Micaiah first parrots the others, then tells the truth: Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd. Then he tells what he saw: Yahweh on his throne, the host of heaven around him, asking who will entice Ahab to fall. A spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets, and Yahweh sends him.
- Zedekiah slaps Micaiah. Ahab throws Micaiah in prison until he comes home safe. Micaiah: if you come back, Yahweh hasn't spoken by me.
- Ahab goes into battle in disguise. A random arrow finds the gap in his armor. He dies propped up in his chariot, and dogs lick his blood. Jehoshaphat's reign in Judah and Ahaziah's in Israel close the book.

## Pay attention to this
- **Jehoshaphat wants Yahweh's word (22:5, 7).** Four hundred prophets aren't enough for him. He can tell the difference between a crowd and a prophet of Yahweh. 🔴
- **"The Lord" vs. "Yahweh" (22:6, 12).** The 400 first say "the Lord (*Adonai*) will give it." Jehoshaphat then asks for "a prophet of Yahweh." Once pressed, they start using the name. 🔴 for the wording, 🟡 for reading it as a tell.
- **"I hate him" (22:8).** Ahab knows which prophet tells him the truth. That's why he hates him. 🔴
- **Micaiah's first answer is a parrot (22:15).** Word for word what the 400 said. Ahab can tell it's mocking and demands the truth. 🔴
- **Sheep with no shepherd (22:17).** The shepherd is the king. Micaiah is telling Ahab he'll die. 🔴
- **The throne room (22:19).** "I saw Yahweh sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left." A prophet reports what he saw in God's council. 🔴
- **A real discussion (22:20).** "One said this while another said that." The council members offer ideas. 🔴
- **"How?" (22:22).** Yahweh asks the spirit for his plan, approves it and sends him. 🔴
- **The deception is announced (22:23).** Micaiah tells Ahab, in front of everyone, that his prophets have a lying spirit. Ahab is warned and goes anyway. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for weighing that in the God-and-lying question.
- **"How did the Spirit of Yahweh pass from me to speak to you?" (22:24).** Zedekiah honestly thinks he has the Spirit. 🔴
- **An arrow "at random" (22:34).** Literally "in his innocence." A man shooting with no target hits the one man God targeted. The disguise doesn't help. 🔴
- **Dogs lick his blood (22:38).** "According to the word of Yahweh which He spoke." Elijah had said it (21:19). 🔴

## Read it like 853 BC, not 2026
- **Ahab was a major king.** An Assyrian inscription of Shalmaneser III (the Kurkh Monolith) lists "Ahab the Israelite" with 2,000 chariots at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC. His "ivory house" (22:39) fits the carved ivories found at Samaria. 🔴
- **Kings kept prophets on staff.** In Mari, Assyria and elsewhere, kings consulted groups of prophets and diviners before war, and checked one against another. A court with 400 prophets who say what the king wants is a familiar ANE picture. 🔴
- **The threshing floor at the gate (22:10).** City gates and threshing floors were open public places where kings judged and decisions were made. In the Ugaritic Aqhat story, the king Danel sits judging at the threshing floor by the gate. 🔴
- **Iron horns (22:11).** Horns stood for strength. Prophets often acted out their message. Zedekiah's prop was standard prophetic theater. 🔴
- **The council of the gods was a known picture.** Ugaritic texts show El enthroned with the assembly of the gods. Heiser points out that "standing by Him" is a technical phrase paralleled in those council scenes, and that Yahweh's question has a form paralleled at Ugarit. 🔴 for Ugarit's council, 🟡 for the specific parallels.
- **But Yahweh presides.** In the Balaam text from Deir Alla, the gods debate with nobody in charge. In 1 Kings 22:19 Yahweh sits on the throne, asks the question and makes the call. Brueggemann and Walton both make that point. 🔴
- **A prophet who stood in the council.** Jeremiah 23:18, 22 says a true prophet is one who has "stood in the council of Yahweh." Micaiah's vision is his credential. 🔴
- **Evil spirits in the ANE.** Mesopotamia blamed misfortune on the "evil wind" and the seven evil spirits. Israel puts even a lying spirit under Yahweh's command. 🔴
- **Isaiah's matching scene.** "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" (Isaiah 6:8). Same throne, same question to the council, a volunteer. 🔴

## My notes
- In my prophets list I flagged Micaiah's vision as one of the clearest divine council scenes in the whole Old Testament, and put it on my close-reading list with Zechariah's night visions and Ezekiel 1.
- From the Unseen Realm 101 prework (Session 4): the divine council, the host of heaven, sons of God, rulers and authorities, is invited to take part in decisions. 1 Kings 22 is the Ahab example. God doesn't need a team. He wants to share authority. That's the BibleProject cut of Heiser's frame.
- From my Revelation 4 study: Kensky's point that the divine courtroom shows up all over the Hebrew Bible, Micaiah's vision included. And the participatory point, which Heiser stresses isn't just him: Ahab's death is already decided, God convenes the council and asks how, a spirit volunteers, God approves. Mullen's study of the assembly of the gods backs up the council setting.
- **The lying spirit (Fact Book entry).** McCarter in DDD treats the spirit of 22:21 as a rare personal, semi-independent council member. That's different from the "evil spirit" that troubles Saul (1 Samuel 16–19), which reads more like a narrative device than an individual being. The closest parallel is Eliphaz's night spirit in Job 4:12–21. The parallel account is 2 Chronicles 18:18–22.
- **ANE background.** The Mesopotamian "good wind" and "evil wind" with the seven evil spirits. No exact Mesopotamian match for a spirit volunteering inside a convened council in what DDD surveys.
- **Governance.** From my Numbers 22 work: at Deir Alla the gods negotiate with no one presiding; in 1 Kings 22:19 Yahweh presides. Same furniture, different governance. Use the parallel to flatten the difference and you've skipped Brueggemann. Deny the parallel and you've skipped Heiser's own dictionary article. Both moves are wrong.
- My work on this chapter is through the dataset entry and course material, not a dedicated chapter study. The rest of the chapter I haven't worked.

## What the chapter is doing
- Wives with unbelieving husbands can win them over without a word by how they live. Real beauty is the hidden person of the heart. Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding and honor them as fellow heirs of grace.
- Everyone: be humble and kind, and bless people who insult you. If you suffer for doing right, you're blessed. Don't fear what they fear. Set Christ apart as Lord in your heart and be ready to give a defense of your hope, with gentleness and respect.
- Christ suffered once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Put to death in the flesh, made alive in the spirit, he went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah's day.
- Noah's eight were brought through the water, and baptism now saves you, not by washing dirt but as an appeal to God from a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus, who is at God's right hand with angels, authorities and powers subjected to him.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Without a word" (3:1).** Peter expects some believing wives to have unbelieving husbands, and the strategy is conduct, not argument. 🔴
- **"Fellow heir of the grace of life" (3:7).** In a world that ranked wives below husbands, Peter makes them equal heirs before God, and ties a husband's prayers to how he treats her. 🔴
- **Blessing for insult (3:9).** Peter quotes Psalm 34 right after (3:10–12). 🔴
- **"Do not fear their fear" (3:14).** Peter is quoting Isaiah 8:12–13, where the next line is "It is Yahweh of hosts whom you should regard as holy." Peter puts Christ in that slot: "sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts." 🔴
- **"Always being ready to make a defense" (3:15).** *Apologia*, a courtroom word for a legal defense. It's where "apologetics" comes from. 🔴
- **"With gentleness and fear" (3:15).** How you answer counts as much as the answer. 🔴
- **"Once for all" (3:18).** One death, never repeated. 🔴
- **"Made alive in the spirit; in which also He went" (3:18–19).** Whatever the proclamation was, it happened in connection with his death, resurrection and going up (3:22 uses the same "having gone"). 🔴
- **"Spirits now in prison... who once were disobedient... in the days of Noah" (3:19–20).** Peter ties these spirits to the time of the flood. 🔴
- **Baptism corresponds to the flood (3:21).** Water that judged the world carried Noah's family through. 🔴
- **The chapter ends on a throne (3:22).** Angels, authorities and powers subjected to the risen Christ. 🔴

## Read it like AD 62, not 2026
- **Peter's readers were "exiles."** The letter goes to scattered believers in five provinces of what is now Turkey (1:1), mostly Gentile converts who had walked away from their old gods and were slandered for it (4:3–4). 🔴
- **A wife was expected to share her husband's gods.** Plutarch's advice to a bride says a wife should worship only her husband's gods and shut the door on strange religions. A Christian wife of a pagan husband was already defying the household. Peter's advice is how to do that without giving needless offense. 🔴
- **Braided hair and gold (3:3).** Elaborate hairstyles and jewelry marked wealth and status in Roman society. 🔴
- **"Calling him lord" (3:6).** In Genesis 18:12 Sarah calls Abraham "my lord" in her own thoughts. Peter makes Gentile women Sarah's daughters. 🔴
- **The Watchers in prison.** 1 Enoch tells of the angels who sinned before the flood (the "sons of God" of Genesis 6) bound under the earth until judgment, and of Enoch going to announce their sentence to them (1 Enoch 10, 12–16). Peter's readers knew that story. "Spirits in prison" from "the days of Noah" fits it closely. 🔴 for 1 Enoch; 🟡 for reading 3:19 through it.
- **Proclamation, not a second chance.** The verb is *kēryssō*, to announce like a herald. Heiser reads it as Christ announcing his victory to the imprisoned Watchers, the way Enoch announced their doom. Older readings say Christ preached through Noah to the people of Noah's day, or preached to the dead in Hades. 🟡 for Heiser's reading; ⬜ which is right.
- **"Spirits" usually means non-human beings.** In the New Testament "spirits" on their own nearly always means spiritual beings, not dead humans (Hebrews 12:23 is an exception). 🟡
- **Baptism as a pledge.** The word in 3:21, *eperōtēma*, was used for a formal pledge or answer in a contract. Heiser reads baptism here as a loyalty oath: the believer declares allegiance to the risen King over the powers. 🔴 for the contract usage; 🟡 for Heiser's reading.
- **Angels, authorities and powers (3:22).** Same family of words Paul uses for the spiritual rulers (Romans 8:38; Ephesians 1:21). Psalm 110 again: Christ at the right hand with enemies under his feet. 🔴

## My notes
- **3:15 and Luke 21:14 (Miller).** Two verbal links. Luke's verb *apologeomai* and Peter's noun *apologia*, deliberate courtroom language. And the shared phrase "in your hearts": Luke 21:14, "set in your hearts not to prepare beforehand to defend yourselves"; 1 Peter 3:15, "sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts, always being ready." Same phrase, same slot, opposite instruction. 🔴
- **Miller's reconciliation:** Jesus forbade memorizing a precise speech, not thinking about what you'd say.
- **The settings differ, and that makes the case stronger.** Luke is about formal state persecution; 1 Peter is mostly about verbal abuse from individuals (Miller; Horrell and Williams in the ICC allow legal settings too). Peter takes Jesus' saying out of the courtroom.
- **The line I keep:** the apostle who was in the room when Jesus said it is the one who takes the saying out of the courtroom, and the moment he does, he attaches a command to be ready. The folk use makes the same move and lands on "don't prepare." 🔴
- **My standing rule:** "the Spirit will give you the words" doesn't mean you shouldn't study. It means you don't have to write your argument.
- **3:18–22.** Heiser reads Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison, tied to the days of Noah, as a victory announcement to the Watchers. I hold it at 🟡 in both my framework summary and my book club prep table.
- **Enoch is a lens for the New Testament, not for Genesis.** It shows what Peter and his readers assumed. Influence isn't inspiration.
- **Divine council:** heavy here. The Watchers, the spirits in prison, and angels, authorities and powers under Christ's feet.

## META: the book of Samuel
- **Where it sits.** The hinge between Judges ("there was no king in Israel") and the kings. Three men carry it: Samuel (last judge, first great prophet), Saul (the king Israel asked for), David (the king God picks, still not crowned when 1 Samuel ends).
- **The question the whole book is asking:** what kind of king does the covenant God want?
- **One book, not two.** Hebrew Samuel is one scroll. The Greek translation needed two scrolls, so it got cut in half. The split isn't thematic. 🔴
- **Who wrote it.** Nobody knows. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) says Samuel, then Nathan and Gad, but Samuel dies in chapter 25, so he can't have written all of it. Best read: unknown writers working from older stories, records and poems, finished around or after the exile. ⬜
- **When.** Late 11th century BC, roughly 1050–1010. Israel is moving from loose tribes to a monarchy, and the Philistines (iron, five organized cities) are the pressure that makes Israel want a warrior-king. 🔴
- **The text is messy.** The Hebrew (MT), the Greek (LXX) and the Dead Sea Scroll 4QSamᵃ disagree more in Samuel than almost anywhere in the Old Testament, sometimes by whole sentences. 4QSamᵃ often sides with the Greek, so the Greek was translating a different Hebrew text, not making things up. When translations split in Samuel, that's usually why. 🔴
- **Three movements:** chs. 1–7/8 Samuel and the ark, chs. 8/9–15 Saul rises and is rejected, chs. 16–31 David rises while Saul falls. Chapter 8 is the seam.
- **Three things to track the whole way through:**
  - The Hannah reversal: God brings down the proud and lifts the low (her song in ch. 2 runs the whole book).
  - The word of the LORD as the real power. Prophets speak and it happens.
  - A presence nobody controls (the ark, chs. 4–6).

## What the chapter is doing
- Elkanah has two wives. Hannah is loved and has no children. Peninnah has children and torments her for it, every year, at Shiloh.
- Hannah breaks, prays silently, and vows that if God gives her a son she'll give him back for life.
- Eli the priest thinks she's drunk. She sets him straight, he blesses her, and she goes home at peace.
- She has a son, names him Samuel ("I asked him of the LORD"), weans him, and hands him over at Shiloh. She kept the vow.

## Pay attention to this
- **A barren woman means someone is about to be sent.** Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, later Elizabeth. This child anoints Israel's first two kings, so the monarchy starts with a woman crying in a sanctuary, not in a palace. 🔴
- **Peninnah is an adversary.** "Rival" in 1:6 has teeth. A woman's standing ran through her sons, so this is an attack on Hannah's place, and it happens on the trip that was supposed to be worship. 🔴
- **"Am I not better to you than ten sons?" (1:8).** Kind, and it misses. Elkanah measures her worth by his love. She's carrying something he can't reach. 🔴
- **Shiloh, not Jerusalem.** No temple yet. Eli's family runs the sanctuary. Before the kings, end of the judges. 🔴
- **Eli can't tell prayer from drunkenness (1:12–14).** He's watching her mouth and still gets it wrong. Hold it against 3:1, "the word of the LORD was rare." 🟡
- **No razor on his head (1:11).** Nazirite language (*nazir*). She isn't asking for a child to keep. 🔴
- **Her face changes first (1:18).** She eats and her face is no longer sad, before she's pregnant. 🔴 for the line, 🟡 for reading it as the turn of the chapter.
- **Count the asking.** *Sha'al* runs all the way through: Eli's blessing (1:17), the name (1:20), "my petition which I asked" (1:27), and twice in 1:28, where "dedicated" is the same verb. The last words of her speech are literally "he is *sha'ul* to Yahweh." *Sha'ul* is Saul's name. 🔴
- **The bull in 1:24.** Hebrew has "three bulls." The Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek have "a three-year-old bull," which fits "they slaughtered the bull" in 1:25. LSB and ESV go with the scroll. A small example of why Samuel's text is messy. 🔴

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **"Yahweh of hosts" (1:3, 1:11).** First time that title shows up in the Bible, and Hannah is the first person to pray it. *Tseva'ot* means armies, and most of the time it's the heavenly army. In Heiser's frame that's the council around God's throne. So the first person to call on the God of the armies of heaven is a woman nobody listens to, and the title comes back on the ark in 4:4. 🔴 for where it shows up first; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Who closes a womb.** Around Israel, fertility had its own gods. Mesopotamian prayers ask Ishtar to "open the womb," and Canaan had Asherah and Ashtaroth (Israel is still putting the Ashtaroth away in 7:3–4). The narrator says twice that *Yahweh* closed Hannah's womb (1:5, 1:6), and she goes to no one else. A 2026 reader sees a medical problem. An Israelite reader saw a question about which god runs the house. 🔴 for the ANE background, 🟡 for reading it as a quiet polemic.
- **Barren meant shamed.** In that world a childless wife had no security, no heir and no standing, and people read it as God's disfavor. That's why Peninnah's needling works and why "ten sons" lands so flat. 🔴
- **Two wives was legal.** Hammurabi's laws regulate first and second wives. Scripture never bans it, but every time it shows up (Sarah and Hagar, Rachel and Leah, Hannah and Peninnah) it brings a fight. 🔴
- **The sacrifice meal is a seating chart.** The fellowship offering was eaten as a household meal before God (Lev 7:11–34), and the portions showed rank. Hannah's double portion was public honor in front of everyone, and her refusing to eat (1:7) was her walking away from the table. 🟡
- **Praying silently looked strange.** Prayer was normally spoken out loud, which is part of why Eli gets it wrong. The rabbis later made Hannah the model for how to pray: lips moving, voice not heard, and never drunk (Talmud, Berakhot 31a–b). 🔴 for the Talmud; 🟡 for the out-loud norm.
- **Her vow wasn't only hers.** Under Numbers 30 a husband could cancel his wife's vow the day he heard it. In 1:23 Elkanah lets it stand: "may Yahweh establish his word." In 2026 we'd call it her promise. In 1050 BC it was a family decision, and he signed off. 🔴
- **Weaned means a toddler.** Women nursed two to four years (2 Maccabees 7:27 says three). Hannah hands over a little boy, not a teenager. 🔴
- **"Daughter of Belial" (1:16).** Hannah begs Eli not to count her a worthless woman. *Belial* means worthlessness here, but by the time of Paul it's a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). 🔴
- **Elkanah the Levite.** 1:1 calls him an Ephraimite, which is where he lives. 1 Chronicles 6 puts him in the line of Levi (Kohath). That helps explain how his son ends up serving at the sanctuary. 🔴 for what Chronicles says; ⬜ for how the two fit.
- **Shiloh doesn't last.** Jeremiah later tells Jerusalem to "go to Shiloh" and see what God did to it (Jeremiah 7:12). The place where this chapter happens is a warning by the time the Bible is finished. 🔴

## My notes
- I see the first part of Samuel as ways to use God. One right one and a few bad ones:
  - Hannah asks for a child and gives it back to God. The good one.
  - The elders (ch. 4) try to force God to be their weapon. Wrong.
  - The people (ch. 8) ask for a king and get what they asked for, not realizing they lose what they had.
- That frame holds up. The guild pairs ch. 1 and ch. 8 by the same verb: VanGemeren calls *sha'al* a Leitmotif with 31 uses, and Longman/Dillard read Hannah's naming speech as "ironically anticipating Saul." 🔴 Chapter 4 as the place where nobody asks at all, they just fetch the ark, is my piece. 🟡
- *Sha'al* is also oracle language, the verb for asking God through the ephod for a yes or no. So the elders in ch. 4 skip the very thing the verb names.
- Where that goes: in 28:6 Saul, the asked-for king, asks the LORD and gets no answer, "by dreams or Urim or prophets." The verb that names him is the verb that leaves him. It starts in Hannah's mouth.
- **The name Samuel.** I first took the older line that Hannah's naming speech really belonged to a Saul birth story and got moved over. I dropped that. ❌ Hoffner (EEC 1:163): rearrange the consonants of *Shemu'el* and you get *sha'ul me-*, "asked from" Yahweh. The pun is in the name, just scrambled. 🔴 O'Connor calls it a loose pun, normal in any literature, no redaction theory needed. 🟡
- **Open hands.** Hannah is the anti-Saul before Saul exists. She begs for the one thing she wants and lets it go. Saul grabs a throne and hangs on after God has taken it.
- **Divine council:** no council scene here. It's a ground-level story, and the one hook is "Yahweh of hosts." The council scenes come in ch. 5 (Dagon), 16:14 (the evil spirit) and 28 (Endor).

## Open threads
- Where *sha'al* lands in 28:6. I haven't studied the Saul arc yet.
- 1:5, Hannah's "double portion." The Hebrew is hard to read here and the Greek says something different. I haven't run it down. ⬜
- How hard "Yahweh of hosts" should be pushed in a chapter with no council scene. Is it just the Shiloh name for God, or is the narrator setting something up for the ark chapters, where it's "Yahweh of hosts, enthroned on the cherubim" (4:4)? ⬜
- 1:22, "stay there forever." Is Hannah making Samuel a permanent Nazirite (like Samson) or just giving him to the sanctuary? The Dead Sea Scroll adds a line calling him a Nazirite outright. ⬜

# 1 Samuel 10: Pay Attention to This

Read all of chapter 10 in one sitting. Verse 1 repeats the end of the last reading, so you pick up at the anointing itself. The chapter has two scenes: a private one on the road home with three signs and the Spirit (10:1–16), and a public one at Mizpah where Israel is told who its king is (10:17–27). The last verse is tied to a textual problem that carries into chapter 11 (point 15).

The colored markers show how firm each claim is:

🔴 the text plainly says it, or the sources agree
🟡 a strong reading the text supports, but an inference
🔵 possible, worth knowing, not settled
⬜ open question

---

## 1. The oil comes from a flask, not a horn

Samuel pours oil on Saul's head from a flask (*pak*) and kisses him (10:1). David is anointed from a horn (*qeren*, 16:1, 13), and so is Solomon (1 Kings 1:39). Jehu gets a flask like Saul (2 Kings 9:1, 3).

The text doesn't say why. One literary reading notes that *pak* is used only for Saul and Jehu, while *qeren* is the word in Hannah's song, "the horn of his anointed" (2:10). Others say it is just the container. 🔴 for the vessels, 🔵 for any meaning attached to them.

## 2. Verse 1 is longer in the Greek than in the Hebrew

The ESV footnote says the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, adds a line after "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel?" It says Saul will reign and "save them from the hand of their surrounding enemies," and it names the sign that follows. The ESV and NET Bible print the longer text. The NKJV prints the shorter Hebrew.

The NET Bible thinks a scribe's eye jumped from the first "the LORD has anointed you" to the second and skipped what sat between. 🔴 for the difference, 🟡 for the longer text being the original.

## 3. Three signs for a man who doesn't believe it yet

Samuel gives Saul three signs for the road home (10:2–6). Two men near Rachel's tomb will say the donkeys are found and his father is anxious about him, which is almost what Saul told his servant in 9:5. Three men at the oak of Tabor will give him two loaves. A band of prophets will meet him at Gibeath-elohim, and the Spirit will come on him.

The narrator says all three came true that day (10:9) but describes only the third. They are for a man who called his own tribe the smallest in Israel (9:21). 🔴 for the signs, 🟡 for their purpose.

## 4. Rachel's tomb is where Genesis doesn't put it

Genesis 35:19–20 buries Rachel on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem in Judah. Here the tomb is "in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah" (10:2), and Jeremiah 31:15 puts Rachel weeping at Ramah. Some readers take 10:2 as Benjamin's southern edge, near Bethlehem. Others look north toward Ramah. Nobody has settled it. 🔴 for the three texts, ⬜ for the location.

## 5. A Philistine post sits on the hill of God

The third sign is at Gibeath-elohim, "where there is a garrison of the Philistines" (10:5). The Hebrew *netsiv* can mean garrison, outpost, or officials, and it is the word in 13:3. That sits badly with 7:13, which says the Philistines stayed out "all the days of Samuel." Gill reads 7:13 as no more invasions during Samuel's sole judgeship, which leaves room for small posts. 🔴 for the tension, 🟡 for that way out.

## 6. A band of prophets, and the Spirit rushes

The prophets come down with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre, "prophesying" (10:5). The Hebrew doesn't say what that looked like. Music and prophecy go together elsewhere (2 Kings 3:15, 1 Chronicles 25:1). 🔴 for the instruments, ⬜ for how it looked.

Then "the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you" (10:6). The verb *tsalach* is also used for Samson (Judges 14:6), Saul in 11:6, David in 16:13, and the harmful spirit on Saul in 18:10. In this period the Spirit usually comes for a task. He leaves Saul (16:14) and stays on David (16:13). 🔴

## 7. Do what your hand finds, then wait seven days

Samuel says, "do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you" (10:7). Then he sends Saul to Gilgal to wait "seven days" until Samuel comes (10:8).

The seven days return in 13:8, where Saul waits and then offers the sacrifice himself. Commentators split on whether 13:8 is the same wait as 10:8 or a fresh appointment, since the events from 10:9 to 13:7 can't fit inside one week. Hoffner reads 10:8 as a standing order. Bergen and Keil and Delitzsch read 13:8 as the test Samuel set in 10:8. 🔴 for the command, ⬜ for whether they are the same appointment.

## 8. Another man, and another heart

Samuel says Saul will be "turned into another man" (10:6), and "God gave him another heart" (10:9). The verb in both is *haphak*, "turn, change." In Hebrew the heart is the center of thought and decision, so this is a change in how he will think and choose. The rest of Saul's story shows it did not keep him obedient. Matthew Henry's line: Saul became another man, but it may be doubted that he became a new one. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for reading it as fitness for the job.

## 9. "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

When people see Saul prophesying they ask, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" A man answers, "And who is their father?" and it becomes a saying (10:11–12). It can mean the prophets have no family line, so anyone can join, or that their father is God, who raises up whom he likes. The Targum reads it as "who is their teacher." ⬜

The saying returns in 19:24, when Saul prophesies and lies naked all day and night before Samuel. The book gives it two settings. 🔴

## 10. The king is announced inside a rebuke

At Mizpah Samuel speaks for Yahweh: I brought you out of Egypt and saved you from every kingdom that oppressed you, "But today you have rejected your God, who saves you" (10:18–19). That is 8:7 again, said to the whole nation just before the king is named. Israel gets what it asked for and hears what the asking meant at the same gathering. 🔴

## 11. The lot narrows to one man, and he is hiding

The lot goes from tribe to clan to person, Benjamin, the Matrites, then Saul son of Kish, the same steps as Joshua 7:16–18, where it finds Achan. "When they sought him, he could not be found" (10:21). Whether the narrator wants Achan in your ear isn't stated. 🔴 for the match, 🔵 for any intent.

They "inquired again of the LORD," and he says Saul "has hidden himself among the baggage." The verb *sha'al* is the one behind Saul's name, *Sha'ul*, "asked for." It is also in 10:4, where the Hebrew for "greet" is literally "ask you for peace." So the asked-for man is found by asking. 🔴 Why he hid isn't said. Humility, fear, and not wanting the job all fit. ⬜

## 12. Taller than anyone, and the shout

Saul "was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward" (10:23), the same line as 9:2. Samuel says, "Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen?" and the people shout, "Long live the king!" That is the coronation formula for Absalom, Solomon, and Joash (2 Samuel 16:16, 1 Kings 1:39, 2 Kings 11:12). The proof offered is what the crowd can see, which 16:7 later sets aside. 🔴 for the formula, 🟡 for the link to 16:7.

## 13. A written charter, laid up before Yahweh

Samuel tells the people "the rights and duties of the kingship," writes them in a book, and lays it up before the LORD (10:25). What it held is open. Some say the royal takings of 8:11–17. Others say the king law of Deuteronomy 17:14–20, or a new charter limiting the king. Gordon notes the difference between 8:9, which describes how a king will act, and 10:25, which sets out what the kingship allows and requires. ⬜ for the contents.

Walton says "before Yahweh" most likely means a sanctuary, and compares Hittite vassal treaties, which could be read publicly and deposited in a sanctuary. See also Deuteronomy 31:26 and Joshua 24:26. 🟡 for the place.

## 14. Men whose hearts God touched, and men who despised him

"Men of valor whose hearts God had touched" go with Saul (10:26), another place where God acts on hearts, as in 10:9. But "worthless fellows," literally "sons of *beliya'al*" (the label for Eli's sons in 2:12), ask, "How can this man save us?" and bring him no present (10:27).

"Save" is *yasha*, the same verb as 10:19 and 9:16. In 11:13 Saul says, "today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel." The chapter asks who saves, and Saul's answer in chapter 11 gives it to Yahweh. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for reading them as one thread.

## 15. "He held his peace," or "about a month later"

The Hebrew ends the chapter with Saul saying nothing: "and he was like one keeping silent." The Greek and a Qumran manuscript (4QSama) read "about a month later" there and join it to chapter 11. The two Hebrew phrases look almost alike, and a mix-up of the letters *dalet* and *resh* may explain it. 🔴 for the two readings, ⬜ for which is right.

4QSama and Josephus also have a paragraph here: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had been gouging out the right eye of the Gadites and Reubenites, and 7,000 men had escaped to Jabesh-gilead. It explains Nahash's demand in 11:2. The NRSV, NLT, NAB, NEB, and ISV print it. The NIV, ESV, and NET Bible put it in a note. McCarter and Cross treat it as original text a scribe skipped. Auld calls it a later expansion built on a real tradition. 🔴 for the manuscripts, ⬜ for whether it was original.

## What the chapter is doing
- Hannah prays a song: God breaks the mighty and lifts the weak, the barren has seven children, and he will give strength to "His king" and exalt the horn of "His anointed" (2:1–10).
- Then the chapter cuts back and forth. The boy Samuel serves before Yahweh. Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, take the sacrifices by force and sleep with the women who serve at the tent (2:11–26).
- Eli scolds his sons and they don't listen. Samuel keeps growing "in favor both with Yahweh and with men" (2:26).
- A man of God comes to Eli: his house will be cut off, both sons will die on the same day, and God will raise up a faithful priest (2:27–36).

## Pay attention to this
- **The chapter is braided.** Song (1–10), Samuel (11), Eli's sons (12–17), Samuel (18–21), the sons (22–25), Samuel (26), the oracle (27–36). A rising boy and a rotting house, side by side, over and over. The alternation is the argument. 🔴 for the structure, 🟡 for reading it as deliberate.
- **Hannah's song is the plan for the whole book.** The proud brought down, the low lifted up. Eli's house falls while Samuel rises; later Saul falls while David rises. 🔴
- **A king before there is a king (2:10).** "He will give strength to His king, and He will exalt the horn of His anointed." Israel has no king yet. "Anointed" is *mashiach*, the word that becomes "messiah." 🔴
- **Mary's song is built on this one.** Luke 1:46–55 follows Hannah almost line for line: the proud scattered, the humble lifted, the hungry filled. 🔴
- **"Vile men" (2:12).** In Hebrew they are "sons of Belial," worthlessness. In 1:16 Hannah begged Eli not to count her a "daughter of Belial." The woman he thought was worthless wasn't; his own sons were. 🔴
- **"They did not know Yahweh" (2:12).** Priests at Israel's central sanctuary, and that's the narrator's flat verdict. 🔴
- **Fat first (2:15–16).** The worshiper says, "They must surely offer up the fat in smoke first." The servant says, "No, you shall give it now; and if not, I will take it by force." The order was the offense. 🔴
- **"They spurned the offering of Yahweh" (2:17).** 🔴
- **Samuel grows (2:26).** "In favor both with Yahweh and with men." Luke uses nearly the same words for the boy Jesus (Luke 2:52). 🔴
- **Hannah gets five more children (2:21).** She gave her only son away and gets three sons and two daughters. 🔴
- **A hard line (2:25).** The sons wouldn't listen "for Yahweh desired to put them to death." The chapter doesn't explain it. ⬜
- **"Making yourselves fat" (2:29).** The man of God charges Eli too, not just his sons. Hold it for 4:18. 🟡

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **The fellowship meal was the one shared offering.** The peace offering (*shelamim*, related to *shalom*) split three ways: the fat burned for God, the breast and right thigh to the priest (Leviticus 7:31–34), the rest eaten by the family. It was the closest thing in the system to sitting down to eat with God, and Eli's sons turned it into a shakedown. 🔴
- **The fat was God's (Leviticus 3:16–17).** *Chelev*, the hard fat around the kidneys and liver, was the best part of the animal. It burned first, and eating it got a person cut off. God gets the best, and gets it first. 🔴
- **The fork was real equipment.** Bronze forks belonged to the altar tools, and three-pronged forks have turned up in temple sites at Gezer and Lachish (Hoffner). The sin wasn't the tool. The law set the priest's portion; the fork method said "whatever I spear, I keep." 🔴
- **Commentators split on 2:13–14.** Some read it as a custom that had already gone bad, with 2:15–16 as the sons pushing it further. Others read the narrator condemning both. ⬜
- **"Horn" means strength.** A raised horn was the picture of a strong animal, and of a strong person or king. Hannah's horn is raised (2:1), and so will be the anointed one's (2:10). 🔴
- **"The pillars of the earth are Yahweh's" (2:8).** Hannah's world rests on pillars God set. Her song lifts the poor because the God who holds up the world says so. 🔴
- **Divine council: none here.** The song names Yahweh as the one who brings down to Sheol and raises up (2:6) and thunders from heaven (2:10), but there's no council scene. Those come in ch. 5 (Dagon), 16:14 and 28.

## My notes
- **The open-hands contrast.** Same sanctuary, opposite people. Hannah gives God her best and her first, the son she begged for. Eli's sons take God's best and first for themselves, by force, before he's honored. 🟡
- **The Magnificat.** I worked Mary from the Luke side first. This chapter is where Mary's song was quarried. 🔴
- **I asked who the prophet was.** When the voice says Eli's sons will die, who is speaking? The text doesn't tell us. He's an unnamed "man of God," and the narrator leaves him nameless because the message matters, not the messenger. An old rabbinic guess says Elkanah. That's tradition, not text. ⬜
- **I asked for the details on the fat and the fork.** All three points checked out in Logos: the *shelamim* as the shared meal, the fat as God's portion that burns first, and the fork as a legitimate tool misused. 🔴
- **2:29 feeds chapter 4.** The charge against Eli's house, "making yourselves fat with the choicest of every offering," is where the *kaved* thread starts.
- **The man of God's oracle widens the problem.** It isn't only that Israel has no king. The priesthood is rotten too, and God is restarting Israel's whole leadership through a child a praying woman lent to him. The "faithful priest" (2:35) points past Samuel toward the line of Zadok. 🟡

- Was the fork custom in 2:13–14 already a corruption, or was only 2:15–16 the abuse? ⬜
- Who is the faithful priest of 2:35: Samuel, Zadok, or someone further on? ⬜

## What the chapter is doing
- "Word from Yahweh was rare in those days; visions were infrequent" (3:1). Eli's eyes are failing. The boy Samuel sleeps in the temple where the ark is, before the lamp of God goes out.
- Yahweh calls Samuel three times, and three times Samuel runs to Eli. The third time Eli understands and tells him to answer, "Speak, Yahweh, for Your slave is listening" (3:9).
- Yahweh's first message to Samuel is judgment on Eli's house: Eli knew his sons were bringing a curse on themselves and didn't rebuke them, and no sacrifice will ever atone for it (3:11–14).
- Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli presses, hears it all, and says, "It is Yahweh; let Him do what seems good in His eyes" (3:18). Samuel grows, none of his words fall to the ground, and all Israel knows he's a prophet (3:19–21).

## Pay attention to this
- **The first verse diagnoses the era (3:1).** Revelation had gone quiet. After chapter 2 it isn't hard to see why: the men running the sanctuary had stopped listening. 🔴 for the verse, 🟡 for the link to ch. 2.
- **Eli's eyes are going dim (3:2).** The same priest who couldn't tell prayer from drunkenness in ch. 1 now can't see well either. 🟡
- **"The lamp of God had not yet gone out" (3:3).** The lamp burned through the night, so this is before dawn. It also reads as Israel's light being low but not quite dead. 🔴 for the time, 🟡 for the second sense.
- **"Samuel did not yet know Yahweh" (3:7).** The boy doesn't recognize the voice, and the priest is slow to work it out. 🔴
- **Eli's last good act (3:9).** He teaches the boy how to answer God. 🟡
- **"Yahweh came and stood" (3:10).** This isn't only a voice. Yahweh stands there, and 3:15 calls it a "vision." 🔴
- **The sin is named (3:13).** Eli knew and "did not rebuke them." His failure was not knowing and not acting. 🔴
- **No sacrifice can fix it (3:14).** "Shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever." 🔴
- **Two witnesses (2:27–36 and 3:11–14).** An unnamed man of God and then Samuel give the same verdict. The law settled a matter on two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). 🔴
- **"It is Yahweh" (3:18).** Eli failed as a father and as a priest, and he still bows to God at the end. The narrator won't turn him into a villain. 🟡
- **The last verses answer the first (3:19–21).** "None of his words fall to the ground." Yahweh "appeared again at Shiloh." The word that was rare is flowing. 🔴

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **"Word" and "vision."** In that world a god's will came through dreams, omens and temple incubation, sleeping in a sanctuary to receive a message. Samuel is lying in the temple when God speaks, but he isn't looking for an omen. He gets words. 🟡
- **Sleeping near the ark.** The ark was the footstool of the invisible King's throne. Samuel lies down "where the ark of God was" (3:3). The boy who will speak for the King sleeps at his feet. 🔴 for the place, 🟡 for the picture.
- **The prophet as a new office.** After this, Israel has a voice that can stand outside the priesthood and later outside the palace. Samuel's line runs through Nathan and Elijah, the men who confront kings. 🟡
- **"From Dan to Beersheba" (3:20).** The standard way of saying the whole land, from the far north to the far south. 🔴
- **Divine council: Yahweh who stands.** In 3:10 Yahweh "came and stood," and 3:15 calls it a vision. This is the visible Yahweh, the kind of appearance the Old Testament also tells of with Abraham and Moses. Heiser reads these appearances as Yahweh present in a form people can see. 🔴 for the text, 🔵 for how far to push it here.

## My notes
- I read chapters 2 and 3 together and asked for the breakdown of both. The chapter is short, and the last three verses answer the first one.
- **The judgment is told twice on purpose.** The unnamed man of God and then Samuel deliver the same verdict on Eli's house. Two witnesses. 🔴
- **I asked who the first prophet was.** The text doesn't name him. An old rabbinic tradition guesses Elkanah, Samuel's father. Tradition, not text. ⬜
- **A falling house and a rising boy.** Hannah sang that God brings down the proud and raises the low. Chapter 3 finishes that handoff. The word Eli's sons treated with contempt goes to a boy who doesn't let any of it fall to the ground. 🟡
- **Divine council:** no council scene here. The hook is Yahweh coming and standing in 3:10. The council scenes come in ch. 5 (Dagon), 16:14 and 28.

## What the chapter is doing
- Israel camps at Ebenezer, fights the Philistines and loses about four thousand men. The elders ask, "Why has Yahweh defeated us today?" and then send to Shiloh for the ark, "that it may come among us and save us" (4:1–4).
- The camp shouts so loud the earth shakes. The Philistines panic, "God has come into the camp," then rally and win. Thirty thousand fall, the ark is taken, and Hophni and Phinehas die (4:5–11).
- A runner from Benjamin reaches Shiloh. Eli, ninety-eight and blind, hears that Israel fled, his sons are dead, and the ark is taken. At the word "ark" he falls backward off his seat, breaks his neck and dies, "for the man was old and heavy" (4:12–18).
- Phinehas's wife goes into labor at the news and, dying, names her son Ichabod: "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God was taken" (4:19–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **The right question, the wrong answer (4:3).** The elders ask why Yahweh let them lose, which is exactly right. Then they skip asking him and go get the box. 🔴
- **They "sent" and "carried" (4:3–4).** No inquiring of God, no prayer, no prophet. Nobody asks. 🔴 for what the text says, 🟡 for reading the silence as the point.
- **The ark's full title (4:4).** "Yahweh of hosts who sits above the cherubim." The ark is the footstool of an invisible King's throne, and Israel treats it like a lucky charm. 🔴
- **Joshua asked; the elders didn't.** After Ai, Joshua fell on his face before the ark and asked God what went wrong (Joshua 7:6–10). 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for reading it as a contrast.
- **The Philistines take Yahweh's history more seriously than Israel does (4:7–8).** They remember the plagues on Egypt, garbled, and still win. 🔴
- **The prophecy lands (4:11).** Both sons die the same day, as 2:34 and 3:11–14 said. 🔴
- **What kills Eli (4:18).** He takes the rout and his sons' deaths. It's the ark that drops him. His heart "was trembling for the ark of God" (4:13). 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for reading his heart.
- **"Old and heavy" (4:18).** The word is *kaved*. Here it means plain body weight, the reason the fall killed him. 🔴
- **Ichabod (4:21).** "No glory," or "where is the glory?" *Kavod*, glory, comes from the same root as *kaved*, heavy. The heavy priest dies as the glory leaves. 🔴 for the shared root, 🟡 for reading the two together.
- **"Departed" is the exile word.** The verb is *galah*, to go into exile. The glory has gone into exile. 🔴
- **Remember Ebenezer (4:1).** Israel loses here. In 7:12 Samuel sets up a stone with the same name after a victory. 🔴 for the name, 🟡 for the loop.

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **A god went where his object went.** Across the ancient Near East a god was tied to his cult object. Have the god's statue or chest, have the god's power. Carrying the ark into battle was meant to force Yahweh to fight. 🔴
- **The ark as a throne footstool.** Winged creatures flanking a seated king match royal furniture from the region. The carved throne on the Ahiram sarcophagus from Byblos is the well-known example. 🔴
- **Divine council: "Yahweh of hosts."** *Tseva'ot* is the heavenly army. The ark belongs to the King of the armies of heaven, enthroned above cherubim, the throne guardians. The Philistines hear it as "these mighty gods" (4:8), plural. They are right that this is a power from the unseen world and wrong about how many. 🔴 for the title, 🟡 for the council read.
- **Gods were captured in war.** Taking an enemy's god statues was standard practice. Sargon II carried off the gods of Urartu; Tiglath-pileser I gave captured gods to Assyrian temples. Losing the ark looked, to everyone watching, like Yahweh losing. Chapter 5 answers that. 🔴
- **The numbers.** About 4,000 and then 30,000 dead (4:2, 10). Hebrew *eleph*, "thousand," may also name a military unit, so many commentators think the figures were smaller. The scale of the disaster isn't in doubt; the arithmetic is. ⬜
- **Dust and torn robes (4:12).** The runner arrives in the signs of mourning. Everyone at the gate knew the news was bad before he spoke. 🔴

## My notes
- I see the first part of Samuel as ways to use God. Chapter 4 is the elders trying to force God to be their weapon. They don't *sha'al*, ask. They send and fetch. The pulls confirmed it: they act "without any indication of seeking divine guidance first." 🔴 for that. Chapter 4 as the place where the asking verb is missing is my piece. 🟡
- **You cannot weaponize the presence of God.** That became a field note. Same instinct as Eli's sons in ch. 2: take what belongs to God instead of bowing to him.
- **Eli was fat.** My first thought: "So Eli was fat. I am sure that shows how he stole meat too and ate while others starved?" Then I pushed: "I have to think *kaved* means both fat and heavy hearted, double duty, he just lost his sons." And I tied it to the famine we just read in Ruth.
- **The pulls ruled.** 4:18 is one of only two places in the Hebrew Bible where *kaved* is purely physical weight (Renn; Oswalt, TWOT 426). The clause explains a fatal fall, not a mood. ❌ for my double-duty reading. And there's no famine in 1 Samuel 1–4; Ruth's famine is about 150 years earlier. ❌ for the hoarding reading.
- **What survived is better.** 2:29 charges Eli's house with "making yourselves fat with the choicest of every offering." He didn't have to swing the fork to be guilty. He got heavy on a corruption he had the power to stop, in a time of plenty. The heavy priest dies at the moment the glory, *kavod*, leaves. False weight against true weight. No commentator I've seen calls it deliberate wordplay, so I don't claim they do. 🟡
- **The Raiders of the Lost Ark article** starts here. The ark in that film is a weapon; in this chapter, treating it like one is the sin.
