## What the chapter is doing
- The Philistines carry the ark to Ashdod and set it in the house of Dagon, beside his statue (5:1–2).
- Next morning Dagon is on his face before the ark. They stand him back up. The morning after, he's on his face again, and his head and both hands are cut off on the threshold, with only the trunk left (5:3–4).
- The hand of Yahweh comes down on Ashdod with tumors. "His hand is severe on us and on Dagon our god" (5:6–7).
- They pass the ark to Gath, then to Ekron, and every city is struck. Ekron cries out that it's been brought to kill them, and the lords agree to send it back (5:8–12).

## Pay attention to this
- **Two thrones in one room (5:2).** The ark is Yahweh's throne; the statue is where Dagon was thought to be present. Chapter 4 could look like Yahweh lost. Chapter 5 says he left, and now he defends his own name in enemy territory with no army. 🔴
- **Face down, twice (5:3–4).** Falling on your face is the posture of worship and surrender. The same construction is used elsewhere for men who have fallen slain. Either way, Dagon is a defeated power, not furniture that tipped over. 🔴
- **Head and hands (5:4).** The second morning his head and "both the palms of his hands" lie on the threshold. Cutting off head and hands was proof of conquest (compare Adoni-bezek in Judges 1:6–7). 🔴
- **A handless god and a heavy hand.** Dagon just lost his hands, and "the hand of Yahweh" comes down. The hand is named four times in this stretch. 🔴
- **LSB shows you the wordplay (5:6, 11).** "The hand of Yahweh was glorious against the Ashdodites." The word is *kaved*, heavy, the same root as *kavod*, glory. The glory that left Israel in 4:21 shows up here as weight on Israel's enemies. 🔴
- **"On us and on Dagon our god" (5:7).** The Philistines themselves say Yahweh's hand is on their god. 🔴
- **The threshold custom (5:5).** Dagon's priests don't step on his threshold "to this day." A note explaining a practice the readers knew. 🔴
- **Pass the ark (5:8–10).** Ashdod, Gath, Ekron. Each city tries to hand the problem to someone else. 🔴
- **Nobody owns this God (5:11).** The people who took the ark as a trophy beg to send it home. 🔴

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **Captured gods went to the winner's temple.** Putting the ark in Dagon's house was a thank-offering for the victory: the Philistines were crediting Dagon with the win (Hoffner; McCarter). 🔴
- **Or the god had defected.** Another ancient reading of a captured god: he was angry with his own people and switched sides. Set against ch. 4 that's half right, and the half that kills them. Yahweh had turned against Israel's sin; he had not changed sides. 🟡
- **Dagon was no minor god.** Chief god of the Philistines, but worshiped across the ancient Near East from the Early Bronze Age to the Roman period. At Ugarit he's the father of Baal. 🔴
- **The name is unresolved.** Fish (*dag*), grain (*dagan*), or a root meaning cloudy or stormy. "Fish god" is the popular one, not the proven one. It traces to Wellhausen's emendation of 5:4 (*dago*, "his fish part"), hinted at by Jerome and since dropped from the critical Hebrew Bible. DDD calls all three etymologies doubtful. ⬜
- **Divine council: Dagon is a real defeated power.** This is the first council scene in Samuel. In Heiser's frame Dagon is one of the rebel *elohim* over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8), and the ark narrative is a contest between gods, fought in Dagon's own house, which was understood as a cosmic center. The ANE category is a "struggle for rule among the gods" (Miglio; Gordon). 🔴 for the ANE category, 🟡 for the council read.
- **What were the tumors?** *Ophalim*. The mainstream reading since Luther is bubonic plague: swellings, port cities, and the gold mice in ch. 6. 🔴 as the standard view. Heiser points to bronze phallus-shaped objects found at Ashkelon in the 1990s, Aegean-style fertility items, and reads *ophalim* as a strike on Philistine fertility and harvest, Dagon's own business (*The Bible Unfiltered*, 97–99). 🟡. Two live readings; I'm not forcing one.
- **Thresholds were charged places.** Zephaniah 1:9 mentions people who leap over the threshold. 🔴

## My notes
- I see the first part of Samuel as ways to use God. Israel tried to use him in ch. 4. Here the Philistines captured him and learn they caught something they can't hold.
- **My first take:** "Dagon seems to fall into a real lesser god, and his name still is used today in Lovecraft being a fish god." I'd already pulled the three proposed meanings of the name.
- **The question I actually wanted answered:** "if these are real lesser gods, are they completely helpless today? Or are they still trying to manipulate the world today, trying to insert themselves into pop culture or into the thinking of man?" I said it was just an observation. Heiser's framework says the powers of Deuteronomy 32 are not inert until the final reclaiming. Lovecraft borrowed the name and the fish reading for his Deep Ones, and real occult groups later formed around the fiction. Whether Dagon himself is behind that can't be proven. The category fits the model. 🔵, and I keep the seam visible between the Bible's Dagon and Lovecraft's.
- **Why spell these out:** "if I am seeing it, I'm sure others are too, and they need to be fully spelled out." There are videos out there saying the same things, half-baked.
- **Head and hands to Saul.** Saul's head ends up fastened in the temple of Dagon (1 Chronicles 10:10). The god who couldn't keep his own head ends up displaying the head of Israel's failed king. David takes Goliath's head in ch. 17. 🟡
- **Dead statue or real power?** I left this for a pull. The text holds both readings, bowing or slain, and both assume Dagon is real. My trusted sources split on how far to push it. ⬜

## What the chapter is doing
- After seven months the Philistines call their priests and diviners. Don't send the ark back empty, they say: send a guilt offering of five gold tumors and five gold mice, one for each lord, and "give glory to the God of Israel" (6:1–6).
- They set the ark on a new cart pulled by two milk cows that have never been yoked, with their calves shut up at home. If the cows head for Beth-shemesh, it was Yahweh; if not, it was chance (6:7–9).
- The cows go straight up the road, lowing the whole way, and don't turn aside. The people of Beth-shemesh, reaping wheat, rejoice. They burn the cart and sacrifice the cows (6:10–18).
- Then Yahweh strikes men of Beth-shemesh "because they had looked into the ark of Yahweh." They ask, "Who is able to stand before Yahweh, this holy God?" and send for Kiriath-jearim to take it (6:19–21).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Do not send it empty" (6:3).** The Philistines pay to give the ark back. A guilt offering, not dumping it in the sea. 🔴
- **Five and five (6:4, 17–18).** One gold tumor for each lord: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, Ekron. Everybody implicated, everybody paying. 🔴
- **"Give glory to the God of Israel" (6:5).** *Kavod* again. Israel lost the glory in 4:21; now the Philistines are sending glory back. 🔴
- **"Ease His hand from you, your gods, and your land" (6:5).** The priests say Yahweh's hand is on their gods too. 🔴
- **They remember Pharaoh (6:6).** "Why then do you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts?" Pagans quoting the exodus. 🔴
- **The cows test is rigged against the ark (6:7–9).** Untrained animals don't pull straight, mothers turn back to their calves, and nobody drives. If they go straight to Israel, it wasn't chance. 🔴
- **"Lowing as they went" (6:12).** Crying for their calves and still not turning aside. Instinct overridden. 🔴
- **Careful pagans, careless Israelites.** The Philistines consult priests, build a new cart, send a gift, and survive seven months. Beth-shemesh gets casual on home ground and dies. 🔴
- **"Looked into" (6:19).** LSB says "looked into the ark." The Hebrew is *ra'ah* with the preposition *be*, which can mean a foolish, gawking stare. It doesn't require prying the lid off, which is how it's usually preached. ⬜ for what exactly they did.
- **The question the whole ark story was asking (6:20).** "Who is able to stand before Yahweh, this holy God?" 🔴

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **Images of the trouble, sent away.** Making gold images of the disease and the pest, so the trouble passes into them and leaves with them, was a known ANE practice. A Hittite ritual (Ambazzi) sends an animal off carrying the disease. 🔴
- **Divination with animals.** The Philistine priests and diviners (6:2) build a test the way diviners did: set up a sign and read the result. Their own method convicts them. 🟡
- **The ark had to be covered.** Numbers 4:5–6 has the priests cover the ark before it moves, and Numbers 4:20 makes looking on the holy things a death penalty. 🔴
- **The number (6:19).** The Hebrew reads oddly, "seventy men, fifty thousand men," in a strange order with no "and." Fifty thousand is impossible for a town that size and is widely taken as a note that slipped into the text. Josephus gives the smaller number, and many translations follow him. LSB prints 50,070; check your footnote. Don't build on it. ⬜
- **The Hebrew and Greek tell the offense differently.** The Hebrew points to looking into the ark; the Greek frames it as disrespect by one family, the sons of Jeconiah. ⬜
- **Divine council: the Philistines' gods under Yahweh's hand.** The priests ask for relief for "you, your gods, and your land" (6:5). Chapter 5's contest is still on their minds: Yahweh's hand is on Dagon and the rest. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for the council read.

## My notes
- **The radiation analogy, my point.** The tumors, the priests' clothing, the distance rules all made me think of radiation coming from the ark. I wasn't saying the ark held uranium. I was pointing out how the effects look alike, and that God usually works through the world he made: "God uses what's in the physical world today to his will. This is what he's created and this is what he uses."
- **Where it holds and where it breaks.** It fits the half about concentrated, invisible power that needs protection and rules. It breaks on selectivity. The same ark strikes the Philistines and Beth-shemesh and blesses Obed-edom's house (2 Samuel 6:11). That's holiness with a covenant switch on it, not dosage. 🔴 that the danger runs on covenant standing (Duvall and Hays; Vannoy; Bergen). 🟡 for the analogy as a teaching tool.
- **The arc of 4:1b–7:1.** Israel presumes and loses the ark. The Philistines seize it and can't survive it. They send it back with reverence. Israel presumes again and dies. 🔴
- **This chapter anchors the Raiders article.** The Philistines handled the holy thing with protocol and lived. Beth-shemesh handled it with familiarity and died. Nobody controls this presence.

## What the chapter is doing
- The ark goes to the house of Abinadab at Kiriath-jearim and stays twenty years, and "all the house of Israel lamented after Yahweh" (7:1–2).
- Samuel tells them: if you're coming back with all your heart, put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth and serve him alone. They do (7:3–4).
- At Mizpah they pour out water before Yahweh, fast, and say, "We have sinned against Yahweh." The Philistines attack. Israel begs Samuel not to stop crying out, Samuel offers a lamb, and "Yahweh thundered with a great thunder" and threw the Philistines into confusion (7:5–11).
- Samuel sets up a stone and names it Ebenezer, "Thus far Yahweh has helped us." The Philistines stay out all his days, and Samuel judges Israel on a yearly circuit from his home at Ramah (7:12–17).

## Pay attention to this
- **Twenty years of waiting (7:2).** The people who tried to use God in chs. 4–6 now grieve for him. That's where repentance starts. 🔴 for the time and the lament, 🟡 for reading it as a change of heart.
- **"Serve Him alone" (7:3–4).** They hadn't stopped worshiping Yahweh. They'd been worshiping him alongside the Baals and Ashtaroth. The problem was divided loyalty, and they actually put the others away. 🔴
- **Water poured out (7:6).** The Law never commands it and the text doesn't explain it. A poured-out heart, contrition, how fragile life is: nobody has settled it. The posture is clear: a nation emptying itself. ⬜ for the meaning, 🔴 for the confession.
- **Same enemy, opposite response (7:8).** In ch. 4 they carried the ark into battle like a charm and lost. Here they ask the prophet to keep praying, and they win. Presumption then, dependence now. 🔴
- **"Yahweh answered him" (7:9).** Crying out works. Hold this for 8:18. 🔴
- **Yahweh thunders (7:10).** Hannah sang it in 2:10: "Against them He will thunder in the heavens." Here it happens. Israel barely fights. 🔴
- **Ebenezer (7:12).** *Even ha-ezer*, "stone of help." Israel camped at a place called Ebenezer when it lost the ark (4:1). The ark story starts with disaster at Ebenezer and ends with victory at an Ebenezer. 🔴 for the name, 🟡 for how close the two places are.
- **"Thus far Yahweh has helped us."** If you've sung "Here I raise my Ebenezer" in "Come Thou Fount," this is the stone. 🔴
- **Peace with no king (7:13–17).** No king, no standing army. Israel repents, the prophet prays, God fights, the land has peace. 🔴

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **Baal and Ashtaroth.** Baal was the storm god; Ashtaroth (plural of Ashtoreth, Astarte) the goddess paired with fertility and war. Israel's neighbors credited them with rain and harvest. 🔴
- **Thunder was Baal's weapon.** The storm was supposed to be his. Israel has just put Baal away, and the first thing Yahweh does is take the thunder Baal got credit for. 🟡, and I haven't run it against the commentaries yet.
- **Divine council: whose storm?** Under the Deuteronomy 32 picture, the gods of the nations are real powers that took credit for what Yahweh does. Yahweh thundering at Mizpah is him showing whose weather it is. 🟡
- **Standing stones marked what God did.** Jacob set one at Bethel; Joshua set twelve at the Jordan and one at Shechem. A named stone was a witness for the next generation. 🔴
- **A judge on circuit (7:16).** Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah were old holy places, and Ramah was home. Samuel went to the people instead of making them come to him. 🔴 for the circuit, 🟡 for the rest.
- **Fasting and confession together (7:6).** Fasting was a public sign of mourning and repentance across the ancient world. Here it comes with words: "We have sinned." 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Samuel grows old and makes his sons judges at Beersheba. They take bribes and pervert justice (8:1–3).
- The elders come to Ramah: "Appoint a king for us to judge us like all the nations." Samuel takes it badly and prays. Yahweh says, "they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me from being king over them" (8:4–8).
- God tells Samuel to give them what they ask, but warn them first. Samuel lays out "the custom of the king": he will take your sons, your daughters, your best fields, a tenth of your grain and flocks, and you'll be his slaves. "Yahweh will not answer you in that day" (8:9–18).
- The people refuse: "No, but there shall be a king over us," one who will "go out before us and fight our battles." Yahweh says, "Listen to their voice and appoint them a king" (8:19–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **Samuel's sons repeat Eli's house (8:1–3).** The judges had no way to guarantee faithful heirs. The complaint is real. A real problem, the wrong answer. 🔴 for the sons, 🟡 for the parallel.
- **"Like all the nations" (8:5, 20).** Israel was called to be different, a people whose King was Yahweh. Asking for a king like everyone else's is asking to give that up. 🔴
- **"They have rejected Me" (8:7).** God tells Samuel it isn't about him, and that Israel has done this since Egypt (8:8). 🔴
- **"The people who had asked of him a king" (8:10).** The verb is *sha'al*, the same verb Hannah used for Samuel in ch. 1. And the king they get is *Sha'ul*, Saul, "asked for." 🔴
- **"The custom of the king" (8:9, 11).** The word is *mishpat*. In 2:13 the same word described the "legal judgment" Eli's sons made up for grabbing meat. A *mishpat* that takes, twice. 🔴 for the word, 🟡 for the link.
- **Take, take, take (8:11–17).** Sons, daughters, fields, vineyards, olive groves, servants, donkeys, a tenth. Yahweh has been the God who gives. The king they want takes. 🔴
- **The king's "tenth" (8:15, 17).** *Ma'aser*, the same word as the tithe Israel already owed God. 🔴
- **"Yahweh will not answer you in that day" (8:18).** In ch. 7 they cried out and God answered with thunder. Hold this for 28:6. 🔴
- **"Fight our battles" (8:20).** One chapter earlier Yahweh fought their battle with thunder. They watched that and asked for a man with a sword. 🔴 for their words, 🟡 for the link to ch. 7.
- **God says yes (8:22).** Not approval. Sometimes the answered prayer is the discipline. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for reading it as judgment.

## Read it like 1050 BC, not 2026
- **Samuel describes real kings.** Drafted labor, taxes, land seizures, palace staff: these were the normal rights of Egyptian, Hittite, Assyrian and Canaanite kings (Hoffner). He isn't exaggerating. 🔴
- **A ten-percent royal tax was normal.** Ugaritic economic texts show kings taking about a tenth, and in that world the line between temple tithe and royal tax was blurry; both were stored in temple complexes. A tenth by itself isn't shocking. 🔴
- **The tithe was Yahweh's tax as King.** It supplied his palace, the tabernacle, and his officials, the Levites. Paying it was how Israel said in grain that God ruled them. The king's tenth puts him in that slot. 🟡 (VanGemeren and Novick read it this way.)
- **Deuteronomy already described a king (17:14–20).** One God chooses, one of their own brothers, who doesn't pile up horses, wives or gold, who writes out his own copy of the law and reads it all his life, and doesn't lift himself above his brothers. Monarchy wasn't banned. The trouble is the kind of king and the reason. 🔴
- **A king was a warrior first.** Ancient kings were expected to lead the army in person. "Go out before us and fight our battles" is the job description of every king around them. 🔴
- **How Samuel hears God.** He prays and Yahweh speaks (8:6–7, 21–22). No ark, no altar, no ephod. Priests asked God through objects like the Urim and Thummim, which gave yes or no. A prophet got a message with content. Commentators call the exchange conversational (Chapman; Wilson). 🔴 What it was like for Samuel, the text never says. ⬜
- **Divine council: none here.** The council material in Samuel sits in ch. 5 (Dagon), 16:14 (the evil spirit) and 28 (Endor).

## My notes

They trade a King who answers for a king who takes. 🟡 for my frame; the ch. 1 and ch. 8 pairing on *sha'al* is the guild's reading. 🔴
- **The seam.** I asked whether to cut the first part of 1 Samuel here, and the answer was yes. Chapter 8 closes the Samuel and ark movement. Chapter 9 opens fresh with Kish, Saul and the lost donkeys.

1 Samuel 9: Pay Attention to This
Read 9:1 through 10:1 in one sitting. The chapter break falls in the middle of a scene: Samuel tells Saul to stand still so he can hear the word of God (9:27), and the anointing that word leads to is in 10:1. The signs and the public choosing at Mizpah (the rest of chapter 10) are the next reading.
The colored markers show how firm each claim is:
🔴 the text plainly says it, or the sources agree 🟡 a strong reading the text supports, but an inference 🔵 possible, worth knowing, not settled ⬜ open question
1. Saul is introduced like a hero
Kish gets a five-generation pedigree and the title gibbor chayil, a man of wealth and standing (the same phrase can mean a mighty warrior). His son Saul is described as choice and handsome, the best-looking man in Israel, and taller than everyone from the shoulders up.
Hold 9:2 next to 16:7, where God tells Samuel not to look at appearance or height when the next king is chosen. The second verse is aimed back at this one. Hannah sang in chapter 2 that God brings down the mighty and raises the lowly, and here the book starts acting it out. 🔴
2. The future king's first job is finding donkeys, and he can't
Kish sends Saul out to look for lost donkeys. Saul crosses four regions and finds nothing, then wants to go home before his father starts worrying about him instead of the animals. The story keeps going only because someone else won't let it stop. 🟡
3. Watch the servant
The servant, who never gets a name, knows a man of God lives in the town and that everything he says comes true. He also has the silver to pay him, a quarter shekel. Saul doesn't know who Samuel is, though Samuel is the best-known man in Israel. Ask who in this scene actually knows how to find God. 🟡
4. The narrator stops to explain a word
Verse 9 breaks the story to tell us that what people now call a prophet (navi) used to be called a seer (ro'eh). It's a note added for later readers who no longer knew the old word, which tells us the book was put into its final form well after these events. 🔴 for the note itself, 🟡 for what it says about dating.
The verb in that note is darash, "inquire, seek," the ordinary word for asking God something the right way, through a prophet or by lot. Keep it in mind. It comes back at the end of Saul's life.
5. Young women at a well
As Saul climbs toward the town he meets young women coming out to draw water (9:11). An Israelite reader knew what happens when a man meets a young woman at a well: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah, Jacob finds Rachel, Moses finds Zipporah, and each time a marriage follows.
This time nothing happens. The women give directions and Saul walks on. Scholars call this an aborted type-scene. Where the reader expects a betrothal feast, Saul gets a sacrificial meal with a prophet instead. Robert Alter read the broken pattern as an early warning: a king whose courtship scene never finishes is a king who won't found a dynasty. 🔴 for the pattern, 🟡 for the foreshadowing.
6. God told Samuel the day before
"Yahweh had revealed this in Samuel's hearing" (9:15) is literally "uncovered his ear," a Hebrew idiom for telling someone something privately. God names the man before Saul ever arrives. The donkeys were never the point. 🔴
7. God calls Saul nagid, not king
In 9:16 Saul is to be nagid over Israel. English Bibles render it "ruler," "prince," or "leader." The people asked for a melek, a king, in chapter 8. The word God uses comes from a root meaning "to declare" or "to designate," so a nagid is the one God has designated.
That doesn't deny that Saul is a king; he's called melek soon enough, and nagid is used for good rulers and bad ones alike. What the word puts in front of you is who did the choosing. Israel asked for a king like the nations had, and God's answer names the man He appointed. 🔴 for the word's range, 🟡 for the reason it's used here.
8. Exodus is in God's mouth
"I have regarded My people because their cry has come to Me" (9:16). Put it beside Exodus 3:7–9, where God tells Moses at the burning bush that He has seen His people's misery and heard their cry. Saul's commission is framed as deliverance: save My people from the Philistines. That's the standard he will be measured against. 🔴 for the verbal parallel.
9. A verb that cuts two ways
In 9:17 God tells Samuel, "This one shall restrict My people" (LSB). Many translations soften it to "rule" or "govern." The Hebrew verb, 'atsar, appears 46 times in the Old Testament, and nearly everywhere else it means shut up, hold back, imprison, or make barren. This is the only place it could even be read as "rule."
Coming right after chapter 8, where Samuel warned that a king would take sons, daughters, fields, and flocks, the word sounds like a warning folded into the commission. Robert Bergen goes further and reads Saul's reign as a discipline on the nation: he will fight Israel's battles and also hem Israel in. 🔴 for how the verb is used, 🟡 for reading it as judgment.
10. "Tell me" and the one who is told
The verb higgid, "tell, declare," runs through these chapters. The servant hopes the man of God can tell them their way (9:6, 8). Saul asks Samuel to tell him where the seer's house is (9:18). Samuel says he will tell Saul everything on his heart (9:19). Back home, Saul's uncle presses him to tell what Samuel said (10:15–16).
Higgid most likely comes from the same root as nagid. Saul keeps asking to be told things, and what he's told is that he is the designated one. Tony Cartledge suggests the wordplay may be deliberate. 🟡
Then in 10:16 Saul tells his uncle about the donkeys and doesn't tell him about the kingship. Reading that silence as the end of the wordplay is my inference, not a sourced claim. 🔵
11. The least tribe and a bad hometown
"Am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel?" (9:21). Benjamin is the tribe Israel nearly wiped out in Judges 19–21, and Gibeah, Saul's hometown (10:26), is the town where that civil war started. Israel's first king comes from the tribe whose last major story was the nation's worst moment. 🔴 for the background, 🟡 for how much the narrator intends it.
12. The reserved portion
At the high place, Samuel seats Saul at the head of about thirty invited guests and has the cook bring out a leg portion he had set aside for him before Saul arrived (9:22–24). Samuel planned the honor in advance, which fits verse 15: God had already named the guest.
The thigh was the priest's portion in Leviticus 7:32–33, and readers have wondered whether Saul being handed it carries meaning. 🔵 Note too that worship at a high place (bamah) is legitimate here; there's no temple yet, and the ark is out of commission after chapters 4–6.
13. Saul's name, and the seeking verbs that frame his life
Saul's name, Sha'ul, means "asked for," from the verb sha'al, "to ask." Chapter 1 played on that verb with Samuel's birth, and chapter 8 has the people asking for a king. The verb doesn't show up in chapter 9. It returns in 10:22, where the people ask (sha'al) Yahweh where Saul is, and the asked-for one is found hiding among the baggage. 🔴
Two other verbs do appear in chapter 9, and they come back at the end of Saul's story in 28:6–7, at Endor:
9:3: Kish tells Saul to go seek (baqqesh) the donkeys.
9:9: going to a seer is how a person inquires (darash) of God.
28:6: Saul asks (sha'al) Yahweh, and Yahweh doesn't answer him.
28:7: Saul tells his servants to seek (baqqesh) a medium, so he can inquire (darash) of her.
Saul's first scene and his last both open with servants sent to seek something: lost donkeys at the start, a medium at the end. The man who first came to Samuel by the right road for inquiring of God ends up using the same verb for consulting the dead. The verbs in the Hebrew are 🔴. Reading them as a deliberate frame around Saul's life is 🟡.
1 Chronicles 10:13–14 gives the verdict on Saul's death with darash twice: he sought a medium and did not seek Yahweh. That's a different book, written centuries later, so it can't be part of the Samuel author's design, but a reader of the whole Bible hears it. 🔵 as an echo.

## What the chapter is doing
- After the Lord's coming in chapter 4, Paul turns to timing. They don't need dates. The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, right when people are saying "Peace and safety!"
- But believers are sons of light and sons of day. So stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God appointed us for salvation, not wrath.
- A run of short commands for church life: respect your leaders, warn the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, don't pay back evil. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. Don't quench the Spirit or despise prophecy; test everything.
- Paul prays that God would make them holy through and through, spirit, soul and body, and closes: faithful is he who calls you, who also will do it.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Like a thief in the night" (5:2).** Jesus' own picture (Matthew 24:43). The point is surprise, not secrecy: a thief doesn't call ahead. 🔴
- **"Peace and safety!" (5:3).** The slogan people are repeating right before the floor drops. 🔴
- **Labor pains (5:3).** Sudden, sure, and you can't stop them once they start. 🔴
- **Sons of light, sons of day (5:5).** Who you are decides how you live: awake and sober. 🔴
- **Armor (5:8).** Faith, love and hope worn like a soldier's gear. Paul builds this out later in Ephesians 6. 🔴
- **"Not appointed us for wrath" (5:9).** The chapter that opens with destruction lands on salvation. 🔴
- **The short commands come in a row (5:16–22).** Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. They're for a whole church, not a monk. 🔴
- **"Pray without ceasing" (5:17).** Three words in English, two in Greek. The adverb is *adialeiptōs*. 🔴
- **Don't quench, don't despise, but test (5:19–21).** Paul wants prophecy taken seriously and checked. Both halves. 🔴
- **Spirit and soul and body (5:23).** The one verse where Paul lists all three. 🔴
- **"Have this letter read to all the brothers" (5:27).** Letters were read out loud to the whole church. Most people heard Scripture before they ever read it. 🔴

## Read it like AD 50, not 2026
- **Thessalonica was a Roman showpiece.** Capital of Macedonia, on the main Roman road (the Via Egnatia), a free city loyal to Rome. Inscriptions there name city officials called *politarchs*, the same title Luke uses in Acts 17:6. 🔴
- **Paul left in a hurry.** He was there a short time before a mob accused the believers of saying "there is another king, Jesus" (Acts 17:7). He wrote this letter not long after, to a young, harassed church. 🔴
- **"Peace and safety" sounds like Rome.** Roman coins and slogans praised *pax* and *securitas*, peace and security, as the empire's gift. People who trusted that slogan would be caught off guard. 🔴 for the slogans; 🟡 that Paul is aiming at them.
- **Sons of light and sons of darkness.** The Dead Sea Scrolls have a whole War Scroll about the final battle between "the sons of light" and "the sons of darkness," with angels and Belial's spirits fighting on each side. Paul uses the same language. The night isn't only bad behavior; it's the domain of the powers. 🔴 for the Scrolls; 🟡 for the divine council read of 5:4–8.
- **The armor is God's armor.** Isaiah 59:17 has God himself putting on righteousness as a breastplate and the helmet of salvation. Paul hands God's own armor to the church. 🔴
- **Jews prayed set times.** Psalm 55:17 has evening, morning and noon; Daniel prayed three times a day; Acts shows the third, sixth and ninth hours (2:15, 10:9, 3:1). The first believers didn't invent a prayer habit. They already had one. 🔴
- **"Without ceasing" in ordinary Greek.** The word was used for things that keep recurring: a cough that keeps coming back, steady payments, repeated attacks. Josephus uses it for the Romans' attacks on a city and the battering ram against Jerusalem's walls. Those happen again and again, not in one unbroken moment. 🔴 for Josephus and the general usage; ⬜ for the cough example (I haven't checked it in the papyri).
- **Prophets in the church.** Greek cities had oracles and people who spoke for gods. The church had prophecy too, and Paul's "test everything" is the safeguard. 🔴

## My notes
- **My question:** Psalm 1 tells me to meditate on the Torah day and night, Paul tells me to pray without ceasing. How can I do this and not live a life as a monk?
- ***Adialeiptōs* means recurring, not literally nonstop.** Paul uses it of never leaving the Thessalonians out of his prayers (1:2–3), not of hitting a quota. The same apostle told the same church to work with their hands (4:11). 🟡
- **I had to pull one claim back.** I first said flatly that the word "does not mean uninterrupted." That's too strong. It literally means "without leaving a gap," and the recurring sense comes from how people used it, not from the word's parts. ❌ the flat version.
- **Psalm 1's *hagah* is out loud.** Muttering, growling, saying it under your breath (Isaiah 31:4 uses it of a lion over its kill). Joshua 1:8 has the Torah not leaving your *mouth*. And "day and night" is a merism, two ends standing for the whole. Both commands assume a daily practice, not quitting your job. 🔴
- **The New Testament assumes a practice it never installs.** The Didache supplied the rule as soon as Gentile converts couldn't inherit it: pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. Psalm 55:17, Daniel, and Acts' third, sixth and ninth hours. Deuteronomy 6:7 adds rising and lying down; meals add three more. Under seven minutes a day, built in stages. 🔴 for the Didache.
- **Where I pushed back.** A list of things to notice with no set times leaves you feeling hopeless. If there's no guide, there's nothing to build on. The specific rule existed and had been buried.
- **My thesis:** You have to have the structure without thinking the structure has any power. Like training: fixed times, volume, rest. No starting weight means nothing gets lifted.
- **Today's church** is so afraid of legalism it forgets the New Testament was written when Jews were already keeping a strict daily routine. Jesus says "whenever you pray," not "if" (Matthew 6:5).
- **The Lord's Prayer my way.** I used to pray it every time in my own words, line by line ("Father God, who lives outside of space and time, creator of everything..."), and I fell out of the routine. That's Luther's method in *A Simple Way to Pray* (1535).

- **My theology framework:** 5:17 with Colossians 3:2 under constant awareness; 5:21 (test everything) under discerning what's preached.
- **Divine council:** sons of light against the night. The War Scroll background is the hook. Chapter 4's archangel and trumpet carry the heavenly side of the Lord's coming.

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul is boasting because the Corinthians forced him to. Rival "most-eminent apostles" have been impressing them, so Paul plays the fool on purpose.
- He tells of "a man in Christ" caught up to the third heaven, into Paradise, who heard words no one is permitted to repeat. It's Paul, but he talks about it in the third person and refuses to build his ministry on it.
- To keep him from exalting himself he was given "a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me." He begged three times for it to go. The Lord said, "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness."
- So Paul boasts in weakness: "when I am weak, then I am strong." He reminds them he never took their money, says he's coming a third time like a parent, and admits he's afraid of what he'll find.

## Pay attention to this
- **"It is necessary to boast, though it is not profitable" (12:1).** Paul hates doing this. The whole section from 11:16 is a "fool's speech." 🔴
- **"I know a man in Christ" (12:2).** He keeps his own vision at arm's length. The most spectacular thing that ever happened to him, and he won't put his name on it. 🔴
- **"Whether in the body... or out of the body I do not know" (12:2–3).** Said twice. Paul admits what he doesn't know about his own experience. 🔴
- **Third heaven and Paradise (12:2, 4).** Same trip described two ways. Paul puts Paradise up in the heavens. 🔴
- **The thorn was given (12:7).** Passive: "there was given me." God allowed it for a purpose, even though it's "a messenger of Satan." 🔴
- **"Messenger" is *angelos*.** The same word as "angel." 🔴
- **Three times (12:8).** Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane. Paul's prayer gets a "no," and the "no" comes with a promise. 🔴 for the count; 🟡 for the echo.
- **"My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9).** The Lord didn't remove it. He told Paul what would carry him through it. 🔴
- **"So that the power of Christ may dwell in me" (12:9).** "Dwell" is a tent word, *episkēnoō*, like God's presence pitching its tent in the tabernacle. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for the tabernacle echo.
- **"When I am weak, then I am strong" (12:10).** The verse everybody knows, and it sits at the end of a list of insults, distresses and persecutions. 🔴

## Read it like AD 56, not 2026
- **Corinth loved a winner.** Speakers were judged by presence, polish and status. The rival teachers had letters of recommendation, impressive speech and probably visions to talk about. Paul's opponents said his letters were weighty but in person he was unimpressive and his speaking poor (10:10). 🔴
- **Self-praise had rules.** Plutarch wrote a whole essay on how to praise yourself without being offensive. Boasting about your weaknesses, as Paul does, turns the custom upside down. 🔴
- **Heavenly journeys were a known genre.** Jewish writings described righteous men carried up through layered heavens: 1 Enoch 14, the Testament of Levi, 2 Enoch. 2 Enoch 8 puts Paradise in the third heaven, which is Paul's exact map. 🔴
- **"Four entered Paradise."** A later rabbinic story (Tosefta Hagigah 2:3) says four sages "entered *pardes*" and only one came out unharmed. Heavenly ascent was treated as dangerous. 🔴 for the story; 🔵 for how early it goes.
- **Paradise is a Persian word.** *Paradeisos* came from Persian for a walled garden, a king's park. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Eden. Paradise is the garden of the King, which is where his throne is. 🔴
- **Words not permitted (12:4).** Mystery religions bound initiates not to repeat what they saw, using the same kind of word, *arrhēta*. Paul's point is the opposite: what he heard wasn't his to use for status. 🔴 for the term; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **A thorn or a stake.** *Skolops* can mean a thorn or a pointed stake. "Thorns in your sides" in the Old Testament are people, the Canaanites left in the land (Numbers 33:55; Joshua 23:13). 🔴
- **An angel of Satan.** In the Old Testament the satan works inside God's permission (Job 1–2). Paul's thorn comes from Satan's side and is still "given" for God's purpose. 🔴 for Job; 🟡 for the parallel.
- **"To torment me."** The verb (*kolaphizō*) means to strike with the fist, the word for the guards hitting Jesus (Mark 14:65). 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Elijah knows Yahweh is about to take him. He tries three times to leave Elisha behind, at Gilgal, Bethel and Jericho. Three times Elisha says, "I will not forsake you."
- At the Jordan, Elijah rolls up his cloak, strikes the water, and they cross on dry ground. Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit.
- A chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, and Elijah goes up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha cries "My father, my father," tears his clothes and picks up the fallen cloak.
- Elisha strikes the Jordan with the cloak, "Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?", and the water parts for him too. The prophets at Jericho bow to him.
- He heals Jericho's bad water with a new jar of salt. On the road to Bethel a crowd of youths mocks him, "Go up, you baldhead." He curses them in Yahweh's name and two she-bears maul forty-two of them.

## Pay attention to this
- **"I will not forsake you" (2:2, 4, 6).** Three tries to send Elisha away, three refusals. Elisha passes the test by not leaving. 🔴
- **Everybody knows (2:3, 5).** The prophet groups at Bethel and Jericho both ask, "Do you know Yahweh will take your master today?" Elisha: "Yes, I know; be silent." 🔴
- **The route runs backward.** Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho, across the Jordan to the east. That's Joshua's way into the land, walked in reverse. Elijah leaves from the side where Moses died. 🔴 for the places, 🟡 for the reverse-conquest reading.
- **Water parts twice (2:8, 14).** Elijah parts the Jordan like Moses parted the sea. Then Elisha parts it like Joshua parted the Jordan. The successor does what the first leader did. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the Moses and Joshua pattern.
- **"A double portion" (2:9).** Not twice as much power as Elijah. It's the firstborn son's share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha is asking to be Elijah's heir. 🔴
- **"If you see me when I am taken" (2:10).** The sign is whether Elisha can see into the unseen. He does. 🔴
- **Chariot of fire (2:11).** Note it's the whirlwind that takes Elijah up. The chariot and horses separate the two men. 🔴
- **"The chariots of Israel and its horsemen" (2:12).** Elisha calls Elijah Israel's real army. When Elisha dies, King Joash says the same words over him (13:14). 🔴
- **"Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?" (2:14).** Elisha's first act is a question to God, and God answers by parting the water. 🔴
- **Jericho healed (2:19–22).** Joshua put a curse on anyone who rebuilt Jericho (Joshua 6:26), and it came true in Ahab's day (1 Kings 16:34). Now Elisha heals the cursed city's water. "Death or barrenness" ends. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the link.
- **"Go up, you baldhead" (2:23).** Elijah just "went up" (2:11). The taunt says: you go up too, disappear like your master. 🟡
- **They came from Bethel (2:23).** Bethel was one of Jeroboam's two calf shrines (1 Kings 12:28–29), a center of state religion opposed to Yahweh's prophets. 🔴

## Read it like 850 BC, not 2026
- **The sons of the prophets.** Groups of prophets lived and trained together at places like Bethel, Jericho and Gilgal, with a leader they called "father" or "master." Elijah was theirs. Now it's Elisha. 🔴
- **The firstborn's double share.** Under Israel's inheritance law the firstborn got two shares of the father's estate (Deuteronomy 21:17). Asking for a double portion of a master's spirit was asking to be named the heir among the prophets. 🔴
- **Fire and horses are the host of heaven.** Later, when Aramean troops surround Elisha, his servant's eyes are opened and he sees the hills "full of horses and chariots of fire" (6:17). These are Yahweh's armies, the host of heaven at war. In Heiser's frame that's the council's military side. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the frame.
- **The storm belongs to Yahweh.** Elijah's whole career was a fight with Baal, the storm god who rode the clouds (1 Kings 18). He leaves in a whirlwind, Yahweh's own storm. 🔴 for Baal's role, 🟡 for reading it as a last word against Baal.
- **Taken without dying.** Only Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah leave this way in the Bible. In Mesopotamia, Utnapishtim, the flood hero, gets immortality and is moved to a far-off place. Being taken meant being removed from the human world. Malachi 4:5 says Elijah will come back. 🔴
- **Baldness was shame.** A shaved or bald head went with mourning and disgrace (Isaiah 3:24; Amos 8:10). Israel's priests were forbidden to shave their heads because it was a pagan mourning rite (Leviticus 21:5). "Baldhead" was an insult with teeth. 🔴
- **"Young boys" isn't little kids.** The Hebrew *ne'arim qetanim* uses a word (*na'ar*) that covers anyone from a baby to a young man of fighting age. Joseph is a *na'ar* at seventeen. A crowd big enough that forty-two get mauled is a mob of youths, not toddlers. 🔴 for the word's range, 🟡 for the reading.
- **Curses in Yahweh's name.** A prophet's curse wasn't a temper tantrum. It was a word in God's name that God either backed or didn't. The bears say he backed it. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the reading.
- **Salt cleans.** Salt was used in purification and covenant rites (Leviticus 2:13; Ezekiel 16:4). A new jar, never used, is a clean vessel. 🔴

## My notes
- My question on the bears was simple: doesn't "baldhead" mean something besides having no hair?
- The answer had three layers. A bald or shaved head in the ANE meant mourning, disgrace or uncleanness, which is why Leviticus 21 bans priests from shaving their heads. "Go up," read next to 2:11, means: you go up too, vanish like your master. And possibly "baldhead" was a slur for a prophet, if traveling prophets shaved as a mark of office (some scholars).
- So this isn't some kids laughing at a bald man. It's a crowd mocking the new successor to Elijah on the road to Bethel, a center of calf worship and anti-prophet feeling in the north. *Ne'arim qetanim* is debated but most likely means young men, not small children.
- **2:19.** From my tree-of-knowledge work: Jericho's *ra'* water is a clean example of *ra'* as harmful, life-diminishing, here causing barrenness. *Ra'* isn't just moral evil. It's whatever damages life.
- **2:11.** From my Eden-as-divine-space notes: a human taken into the divine realm (Enoch, Elijah, Utnapishtim) has to leave the human world behind. Alive, but removed.
- That's all my notes cover: one exchange and two side uses. The rest of the chapter I haven't studied.
- **Divine council:** the chariot and horses of fire, the heavenly army, and the Spirit of Yahweh carrying a prophet away (2:16).

## What the chapter is doing
- Just as false prophets rose up in Israel, false teachers will slip in among believers, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit people out of greed. Their judgment isn't asleep.
- Peter's proof is three old judgments: God didn't spare the angels who sinned, the world of Noah's day, or Sodom and Gomorrah. And he rescued Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and hold the wicked for judgment.
- The false teachers despise authority and slander "glorious ones," something even angels won't do. They're like animals, feasting with the church, eyes full of adultery, following the way of Balaam.
- They promise freedom and are slaves themselves. For people who knew the way and turned back, the last state is worse than the first: a dog back to its vomit.

## Pay attention to this
- **False prophets then, false teachers now (2:1).** Peter reads the church's problem through Israel's history. 🔴
- **"Denying the Master who bought them" (2:1).** *Despotēs*, the owner of slaves. They're running from the one who paid for them. 🔴
- **Greed is the motive (2:3, 14, 15).** Said three times. 🔴
- **Three examples, in Genesis order (2:4–6).** Angels (Genesis 6), the flood (Genesis 6–9), Sodom (Genesis 19). 🔴
- **Rescue sits next to judgment (2:5, 7, 9).** Noah and Lot. The point isn't only that God judges; he knows how to get his people out. 🔴
- **"Angels who sinned... cast them into the pit" (2:4).** The Greek verb is *tartaroō*, "to put in Tartarus." This is the only place in the Bible it appears. 🔴
- **"Glorious ones" (2:10).** Most take these as angelic beings. The false teachers mock spiritual powers they don't understand. 🟡
- **Angels won't do it (2:11).** Even greater angels don't bring a slanderous charge "before the Lord." Jude 9 tells the specific story behind this. 🔴
- **Balaam (2:15–16).** A prophet for hire, corrected by his own donkey. 🔴
- **"Slaves of corruption" (2:19).** "By what a man is overcome, by this he is enslaved." 🔴
- **Better never to have known (2:21).** A hard warning for people who heard the truth and walked away. 🔴

## Read it like AD 65, not 2026
- **The angels who sinned are the Watchers.** Peter puts the sinning angels right before the flood, in Genesis order. In 1 Enoch the Watchers come down, take human wives, father the giants, and God has them bound in darkness until the day of judgment (1 Enoch 10). Peter's "chains of darkness, being kept for judgment" lines up with it. 🔴 for 1 Enoch 10; 🟡 that Peter means exactly this.
- **Tartarus.** In Greek myth (Hesiod), Tartarus was the deepest prison under the underworld, where the Titans, the older rebel gods, were locked away. The Greek text of 1 Enoch 20:2 uses the word too, naming the angel set over Tartarus. Peter reaches for the word a Greek reader knew for imprisoned divine rebels. 🔴
- **Noah "a preacher of righteousness" (2:5).** Genesis never shows Noah preaching. Jewish tradition did: Josephus and later writers have Noah warning his generation, and 1 Clement 7:6 says he preached repentance. Peter uses the tradition his readers knew. 🔴
- **Balaam the greedy prophet.** In Numbers 22–24 Balaam blesses Israel, but Numbers 31:16 blames him for Israel's sin at Peor. By Peter's day Jewish tradition remembered him as the prophet who sold out for money. 🔴
- **Love feasts (2:13).** The church ate together, and these teachers were at the table. "Feast with you" is the shared church meal. 🔴
- **The proverbs (2:22).** "A dog returns to its own vomit" is Proverbs 26:11. The sow story is a saying known from other ancient sources. 🔴
- **Jude and 2 Peter overlap.** Much of this chapter runs parallel to Jude 4–18: the angels, Sodom, slandering glorious ones, Balaam, waterless springs, black darkness. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude and handled the Enoch material more carefully. 🟡
- **The letter was disputed early.** Eusebius lists 2 Peter among the books spoken against (*Ecclesiastical History* 3.25). Questions about who wrote it go back to the early church. 🔴 for Eusebius; ⬜ on authorship.

## My notes
- **2:4–5 is evidence for Genesis 6.** "God did not spare angels who sinned, but cast them into the pit," with "chains of darkness," tied to the flood generation. Heiser: this matches 1 Enoch 10's sentence on the Watchers. With Jude 6, it's his anchor that the New Testament itself chose the supernatural reading of Genesis 6:1–4. 🔴
- **Influence isn't inspiration.** My rule from the book club prep: Peter and Jude show what they assumed their readers knew, not that 1 Enoch is Scripture.
- **Don't read Genesis through Enoch.** Enoch serves best to understand the mindset of the New Testament authors. It's not the context of Genesis. What it shows is a continuity between the Genesis context and the Second Temple context.
- ***Tartaroō.*** My Logos pull came back empty on the word. Heiser answers it in the video: sent to Tartarus, Peter reaching into the Greek Titans material where divine beings are imprisoned in the underworld. 🔴
- **Supernatural reading, yes; same story, no.** All pre-New Testament Jewish traditions took Genesis 6:1–4 supernaturally. They didn't all agree on the details: Jubilees keeps the angels but changes the teaching part to put the blame on humans. 🔴
- **2:21** (better not to have known the way than to turn back) is used by Blomberg next to the tower-builder and warring-king parables.
- **Jude and 2 Peter.** The majority view is that 2 Peter used Jude and handled the Enoch material more cautiously. That's a judgment about direction, not a settled fact. 🟡
- **Divine council:** heavy. The angels who sinned, Tartarus, the "glorious ones" and the angels who won't slander them.

## META: the book of Acts
- **Where it sits.** Volume two of one work. Luke wrote the gospel and then Acts for the same man, Theophilus, and Acts 1:1 points straight back at "the first account." Luke and Acts together are the longest single work in the New Testament, more words than all of Paul's letters. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** what does the risen and enthroned Jesus do next, and who gets let in?
- **Who wrote it.** Luke, the doctor who travelled with Paul. The tradition is early and it doesn't waver (Irenaeus, the Muratorian list, the old prologue to Luke). The "we" passages (16, 20–21, 27–28) put the writer on the boat with Paul. 🔴 for the tradition; 🟡 for the identification.
- **When.** Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, alive, teaching "with all boldness and without hindrance" (28:31). No trial result, no execution under Nero, no fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. The simplest reading is that Luke stopped where the story was when he wrote, around AD 62, with the gospel a little before. The standard critical date is AD 80–85. 🟡 for the early date; ⬜ as a settled question.
- **The text has two shapes.** Acts survives in the main text and a "Western" text (Codex Bezae and its relatives) that runs close to a tenth longer, with added details and smoothed seams. When a translation footnotes Acts more than usual, that's why. 🔴
- **Structure comes from 1:8:** Jerusalem (chs. 1–7), Judea and Samaria (chs. 8–12), then out toward the end of the earth (chs. 13–28). Peter carries the first half, Paul the second.
- **Things to track the whole way through:**
  - The temple to Rome. Acts opens with the believers in the temple (2:46, 3:1, 5:42) and ends in the capital of the empire.
  - The Spirit driving the mission, and Jesus still acting through it. "All that Jesus *began* to do and teach" (1:1) means the rest of the book is what he keeps doing.
  - Roman officials who look at the movement and find nothing to charge it with (Gallio, Festus, Agrippa).
  - Gentiles getting in, and how hard that was for the first believers to accept (chs. 10, 11, 15).

## What the chapter is doing
- Luke recaps volume one, then shows the risen Jesus teaching about the kingdom for forty days and telling the disciples to wait in Jerusalem for the Spirit.
- They ask if he's restoring the kingdom to Israel now. He tells them the timing isn't theirs and gives them the job instead: witnesses from Jerusalem to the end of the earth.
- He's taken up in a cloud. Two men in white tell them he'll come back the same way.
- In the upper room, about 120 people pray. Peter explains Judas's end from the Psalms, they set two men in front of God, cast lots, and Matthias makes the Twelve whole again.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Began to do and teach" (1:1).** Luke counts the whole gospel as the beginning. Acts is the risen Jesus still at work, now through the Spirit and his people. 🔴
- **The ascension happens twice.** Luke 24 closes on it and Acts 1:9–11 replays it with more detail: the cloud, the two men, the promise of return. The seam between the books is on purpose. 🔴
- **The disciples' question (1:6).** "Is it at this time You are restoring the kingdom to Israel?" Jesus doesn't call the hope wrong. He takes the clock away from them and hands them a mission. 🟡
- **1:8 is the table of contents.** Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the end of the earth. Read the rest of Acts and check off the places. 🔴
- **"His brothers" are in the room (1:14).** The same brothers who didn't believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5) are now praying with the apostles. One of them, Jude, will write a letter. 🔴
- **The Judas aside (1:18–19).** It's in parentheses in most Bibles because Luke breaks out of Peter's speech to explain for his readers, down to translating "Hakeldama" from "their own language." 🔴
- **Two death accounts.** Matthew 27:5 says Judas hanged himself. Acts 1:18 says "falling headlong, he burst open in the middle." Both agree a field was bought with the money and got a name tied to blood. 🔴
- **"Headlong" may not be the word.** The Greek *prēnēs* is usually read as "headlong." A minority argue it can mean "swelling up," and a few later versions read *prēstheis*, "becoming swollen." If "swollen" is right, Matthew, Acts and the later Papias story move closer together. 🟡 that the question is real; ⬜ on the answer.
- **The job description (1:21–22).** An apostle here has to have been with them from John's baptism to the ascension and become "a witness with us of His resurrection." The office is tied to being an eyewitness. 🔴
- **The last lots in the Bible (1:26).** After Pentecost nobody in the New Testament decides anything this way again. The Spirit comes in the next chapter. 🔴 for the fact; 🟡 for the reason.

## Read it like AD 62, not 2026
- **Theophilus was a real reader.** In Luke 1:3 Luke calls him *kratistos*, "most excellent," the same title he uses for the governors Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26, 24:3, 26:25). A man of rank, already taught, being handed the solid version. Two long scrolls cost real money, so a patron like him likely paid for the copying. 🔴 for the title; 🟡 for the patron.
- **Forty days.** Israel heard that number and thought of Moses on the mountain and the wilderness years. Jesus teaches "the kingdom of God" for forty days before the next stage starts. 🟡
- **"Restoring the kingdom to Israel" was the hope in the air.** Jews under Rome were praying for God to gather the tribes, throw off the empire and set things right. The disciples are asking the question every faithful Jew in the room would ask. 🔴
- **A cloud means God is there.** The cloud led Israel, filled the tabernacle and the temple, and in Daniel 7:13 one "like a Son of Man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and gets a kingdom. Jesus going up in a cloud reads as being taken into God's presence and enthroned. 🔴 for the background; 🟡 for reading the ascension through Daniel 7.
- **Enthroned over the powers.** Peter's sermon in the next chapter puts Jesus "at the right hand of God" with Psalm 110 (2:33–35). Later letters say what that seat means: "far above all rule and authority and power and dominion" (Ephesians 1:20–21), with "angels and authorities and powers" put under him (1 Peter 3:22). The ascension is a throne room event, and the throne room has other beings in it. 🟡 for the divine council read.
- **"Two men in white clothing" (1:10).** That's how angels show up in Luke (24:4). They're God's messengers announcing the return. 🔴
- **A Sabbath day's journey (1:12).** About 2,000 cubits, a little over half a mile, the distance rabbis allowed on the Sabbath. Olivet was that close. 🔴
- **Twelve means Israel.** Twelve apostles for twelve tribes (Luke 22:30). With Judas gone, the number has to be fixed before the Spirit comes on renewed Israel. 🔴 for Luke 22:30; 🟡 for why the gap had to be filled now.
- **Casting lots was how Israel asked God.** The Urim and Thummim, the land divided by lot, the priests' turns chosen by lot (Zechariah in Luke 1:9). "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from Yahweh" (Proverbs 16:33). Nobody in 1:26 thought they were gambling. 🔴
- **The way a wicked man dies.** Ancient writers told the deaths of tyrants and traitors with swelling, bursting and worms: Antiochus IV in 2 Maccabees 9, Herod in Josephus, and Herod Agrippa in Acts 12:23, "eaten by worms." Wisdom of Solomon 4:19 has the ungodly burst open, "speechless, headlong," with both words Luke uses for Judas. A first reader knew this kind of death. 🔴 for the pattern and the overlap; 🟡 that Luke is echoing Wisdom on purpose.
- **Hakeldama is a real place.** The traditional site is in the Hinnom valley south of Jerusalem, and first-century tombs there have been dug (Avni and Greenhut, 1996). The catch: they're mostly family tombs of the well-off, not a burial ground for strangers. 🔴

## My notes
- I see Acts 1 as a "Previously on" card. If Luke-Acts were a limited series on HBO Max, Acts would open with a recap of the disciples worshiping in the temple and go from there. Luke does it: 1:1–2 recaps volume one and 1:9–11 replays the ascension with more detail. 🔴 that Luke recaps; the TV framing is mine.
- The early date was my call before I looked it up. If Paul dies under Nero in the mid-60s and Acts ends with him still alive under house arrest, the simplest answer is Luke wrote when the story ended where it ended. Which also means the gospel came first. The post-70 date leans on Jesus not being able to predict the temple's fall, and that's a philosophical move, not a historical one. 🟡
- **Two deaths.** Matthew has a hanging, Acts has a fall and a burst body. The usual harmonization (he hanged, the rope or branch gave, he fell) is a third account built to hold the other two. I can present it, but only as interpretation, not as what the text says. 🟡
- **Papias.** There's a third account from Papias where Judas doesn't die by hanging at all. He swells so badly he can't pass where a wagon passes. Moss (2019) reads it as dropsy, the disease ancient writers gave to the greedy. Papias isn't writing a coroner's report; he's writing a body that means something. 🔴
- **I had to fix my own post.** It credited Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 3.39, for Papias on Judas. That chapter is about Papias but has nothing on Judas. The fragment survives through Apollinaris of Laodicea. ❌ the Eusebius citation.
- **"Iscariot means liar" is a lexicon mistake.** No Aramaic word like that is attested. It comes from an error in Jastrow's dictionary that got copied forward. The *sicarius* (dagger-man) theory has its own problem: John 6:71 calls his father Simon Iscariot, and assassin isn't a family trade. 🔴
- **Luke's restraint.** Luke gives Herod Agrippa the worms (12:23) and doesn't give them to Judas. 🟡
- **Matthias.** The bar was presence: from John's baptism to the ascension. He had to be a witness of the resurrection. Being a good man wasn't enough.
- **Divine council:** no council scene in Acts 1. The hook is the ascension itself, Jesus taken into the cloud and seated (2:33–35). The big council chapter is next: Pentecost as Babel turned around.

## What the chapter is doing
- Cornelius, a Roman centurion in Caesarea who fears God, prays and gives alms. An angel tells him to send to Joppa for Simon Peter.
- The next day at noon Peter, hungry on a rooftop, sees a sheet let down from heaven full of every kind of animal. A voice says "slaughter and eat." He refuses three times. "What God has cleansed, no longer consider defiled."
- While he's puzzling over it, Cornelius's men arrive and the Spirit tells Peter to go with them. In Caesarea Peter says God has shown him "that I should not call any man defiled or unclean" (10:28).
- Peter preaches Jesus. While he's still talking, the Spirit falls on the Gentiles, they speak in tongues, and Peter has them baptized.

## Pay attention to this
- **Cornelius is already a God-fearer (10:2).** Devout, praying, giving to Jewish people, "well spoken of by the entire nation of the Jews" (10:22). He's as close as a Gentile could get without becoming a Jew. 🔴
- **Two visions, timed to meet.** God works on the Gentile and the Jew at the same time, a day apart, and the messengers arrive while Peter is still perplexed (10:17). 🔴
- **"By no means, Lord" (10:14).** Peter calls him Lord and says no in the same breath. And he says it three times (10:16). 🔴
- **Peter sees animals and concludes people (10:28).** He doesn't walk out saying pork is fine now. He walks into a Gentile's house and says God showed him not to call any *man* defiled or unclean. 🔴
- **"You yourselves know how unlawful it is" (10:28).** The problem was going into the house and eating at the table. That's what Jerusalem complains about in 11:3: "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them." 🔴
- **"God is not one to show partiality" (10:34).** Peter says he "most truly" comprehends it now. He'd heard Jesus for three years and needed a rooftop and a sheet to get here. 🔴
- **"Healing all who were oppressed by the devil" (10:38).** Peter's short version of Jesus' ministry for Gentiles puts the devil in it. 🔴
- **The Spirit doesn't wait (10:44).** Peter is still talking. No laying on of hands, no baptism first. God settles the question before anyone can vote on it. 🔴
- **"Just as we did" (10:47).** Peter's argument for baptizing them is that God already gave them what he gave the Jewish believers at Pentecost. He tells it again in 11:15–17 and 15:8–9. 🔴

## Read it like AD 38, not 2026
- **Caesarea was Rome's town.** Herod the Great built Caesarea Maritima as a harbor city with a temple to Augustus. It was the Roman governor's seat. A centurion there commanded around 80 men and represented the empire. 🔴
- **God-fearers.** Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God, went to synagogue, gave alms and prayed at Jewish hours, without circumcision or full conversion. Luke notices them more than any other New Testament writer. 🔴
- **The hours are prayer hours.** Cornelius prays at the ninth hour (3 p.m., 10:3, 30), the time of the afternoon offering (3:1). Peter goes up at the sixth hour, noon. Jews prayed set times through the day (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10). 🔴
- **"Ascended as a memorial before God" (10:4).** That's sacrifice language. The grain offering had a "memorial portion" burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:2). A Gentile's prayers and alms are described like an offering God accepts. 🔴
- **Joppa.** The same port Jonah ran to when he fled from preaching to Gentiles (Jonah 1:3). Now the reluctant prophet from Joppa is Simon son of John (the Aramaic "Jonah"), and this time he goes. 🔴 for Joppa and the name; 🟡 for the echo being Luke's design.
- **A tanner's house (10:6).** Tanning meant handling dead animals, and tanners were looked down on. Peter is already staying with one. 🔴 for the trade; 🟡 for the purity point.
- **The food laws were a wall.** Leviticus 11 sorted clean and unclean animals, and Leviticus 20:24–26 ties it straight to Israel being separated from the peoples. Jubilees 22:16 says it outright: separate from the nations and don't eat with them. No law in the Torah forbade a Jew to eat with a Gentile, but the social taboo was strong. 🔴
- **Peter talks like a prophet.** "I have never eaten anything defiled" is close to Ezekiel 4:14, where the prophet protests to God that he has never eaten unclean meat. 🔴
- **The nations coming home.** Under Deuteronomy 32 the nations were handed off to other gods while Israel was God's portion. In this chapter God himself sends an angel to a Roman officer and pours his Spirit on a Roman household. Peter: "in every nation the one who fears Him and does righteousness is welcome to Him" (10:35). 🟡 for the Deuteronomy 32 frame.

## My notes
- **He saw animals. He concluded people.** Peter doesn't conclude pork is safe now or that God updated the nutrition guidelines. He concludes no *person* is common or unclean. The clean and unclean animal list was a working model of the clean and unclean people list. Peter got it right away because the type finally met the thing it was typing. 🔴 for 10:28; 🟡 for the typing.
- **The wall.** I read the food laws as a boundary marker for a people who had to stay distinct until the Messiah came through them. The pressure on Israel wasn't only persecution; it was the pressure of dinner. "Come eat with us. It's just food." A people who can't eat at your table can't be absorbed by you. Once the Messiah came and the mission turned outward, a wall that kept the nations out worked against the thing Israel existed for. Ephesians 2:14 says the wall came down. Mark 7:19: "thus he declared all foods clean." 🟡
- **Blood stays.** Acts 15 keeps the ban on blood because blood was never the wall. It goes back to Noah (Genesis 9:4), before Israel existed. 🔴
- **Table fellowship is the offense, not the food law.** 11:3 says so. No purity law forbade eating with Gentiles; social taboo did (Blue). 🔴
- **Threefold refusal, threefold denial.** Peter refuses three times like he denied Jesus three times (Williams and Dinkler). Luke writes Peter's habit of failing a second time, in the same number of beats, and then has God override it. Witherup reads the retellings in 10, 11 and 15 as teaching the reader, and this as Peter's own conversion. 🔴 that the sources say it.
- **The Spirit as interpreter.** Tyson: Scripture and divine intervention working together, the Spirit opening texts that were already there. That's where my Luke 5 piece should land.
- **Luke 5.** Holtzmann read the deep water in Luke 5 as the Gentile world and built Acts 10 into the symbol. Peter's resistance here is the objection my Luke 5 reading has to survive, and the threefold pattern changes what that objection is.
- **The surprise matters.** It took a vision and a defense in Jerusalem to authorize this. That shows Gentiles getting in was exceptional at first, not normal.
- **Divine council:** an angel of God, the devil's oppression in 10:38, and the nations being welcomed back. No throne-room scene.

## What the chapter is doing
- On the day of Pentecost the believers are together. A sound like wind fills the house, tongues like fire rest on each of them, and they speak in other tongues.
- Jews from all over the known world, in Jerusalem for the feast, each hear "the mighty deeds of God" in their own language. Some are amazed, some say they're drunk.
- Peter stands up with the Eleven and preaches: this is Joel's "last days" Spirit, Jesus was killed by lawless hands and raised by God, David saw it coming, and Jesus now sits at God's right hand and has poured out the Spirit.
- The crowd is cut to the heart. Peter tells them to repent and be baptized, about 3,000 are added, and the new community devotes itself to teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer, meeting in the temple and in homes.

## Pay attention to this
- **These are real languages.** "Other tongues" (*heterais glōssais*, 2:4), and each hearer says "in our own language in which we were born" (2:8). Luke names the regions. Whatever else happens, he presents it as known human languages people understood. 🔴
- **The miracle is in the hearing too.** Galileans speaking, and Parthians, Egyptians and Romans understanding. Luke makes a point of the speakers' accent (2:7). 🔴
- **"Devout men from every nation under heaven" (2:5) are Jews.** Diaspora Jews and proselytes (2:10) home for the feast. The first church is overwhelmingly Jewish. Not entirely, but close. 🔴
- **The list of places runs in a circle** from the east (Parthia, Media, Elam) through the middle (Judea, Asia Minor) to Egypt, Rome, Crete and Arabia. It reads like a map of the world from Jerusalem. 🔴 for the list; 🟡 for reading it as a world map on purpose.
- **"Last days" (2:17).** Peter changes Joel's "afterward" to "in the last days." For Peter, the last days started that morning. 🔴
- **"All mankind," sons and daughters, slaves male and female (2:17–18).** The Spirit isn't only for prophets, kings and priests anymore. 🔴
- **Both sides of the cross in one verse (2:23).** "Delivered over by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God" and "you nailed to a cross by the hands of lawless men." Peter holds God's plan and human guilt together and doesn't explain the seam. 🔴
- **Psalm 110 is the hinge (2:34–35).** David didn't go up to heaven; his Lord did. The ascension in chapter 1 becomes the coronation here: "God has made Him both Lord and Christ." 🔴
- **"Be saved from this crooked generation!" (2:40).** That phrase comes from the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32:5. Keep that song in mind for this whole chapter. 🔴 for the wording.
- **They stayed in the temple (2:46).** Acts opens in the temple, the same place the gospel of Luke ends. These are Jews who now know who the Messiah is. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Pentecost is Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks.** Fifty days after Passover, the wheat-harvest firstfruits (Leviticus 23:15–21). It was one of the three feasts when Jews came to Jerusalem, so the city was packed with pilgrims from the diaspora. That's why the crowd is from "every nation." 🔴
- **The feast tied to Sinai.** Later Jewish tradition connected Shavuot with the giving of the law at Sinai. Fire, a loud sound and God coming down (Exodus 19) sit behind the wind and fire here, and the God who gave the law on stone now gives his Spirit. 🔴 for the Exodus imagery; 🟡 that a first-century reader already linked this feast to Sinai.
- **Babel turned around.** At Babel, God "confused" the languages (Genesis 11:7, 9). The Greek Old Testament uses *syncheō*, and Luke uses the same verb for the crowd being "bewildered" (2:6). One language split into many at Babel; at Pentecost many languages carry one message. 🔴 for the shared verb; 🟡 for the reversal as Luke's design.
- **Deuteronomy 32 is the background.** "When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when He separated the sons of man, He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel" (Deuteronomy 32:8). That's the LSB following the later Hebrew text. The Dead Sea Scroll (4QDeut) reads "sons of God," and the Greek reads "angels of God." After Babel, God handed the nations over to lesser divine beings and took Israel for himself (32:9). Those beings went bad (Psalm 82), and Psalm 82 ends with "Arise, O God... For it is You who will inherit all the nations." 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for Heiser's reading of how it all fits.
- **"Distributing themselves" (2:3).** The tongues of fire are *diamerizomenai*, divided out. The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:8 uses the same verb for the Most High dividing the nations. Heiser reads Pentecost as God starting to take the nations back from the gods they were given to. 🟡
- **The table of nations.** Genesis 10 lists the nations born after the flood (seventy in Hebrew, seventy-two in the Greek), right before Babel. Luke's list of peoples in 2:9–11 sounds like it. 🟡
- **Jesus is enthroned over the powers.** "Sit at My right hand, until I put Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet" (2:34–35, Psalm 110:1). In the Deuteronomy 32 world, the nations' gods are part of what goes under those feet. 🟡
- **A crooked generation.** Deuteronomy 32:5 calls Israel "a perverse and crooked generation" in the same song that tells about the nations being split up. Peter borrows the line (2:40). The whole chapter is Deuteronomy 32 played backwards. 🔴 for the quotation; 🟡 for how far to push it.
- **The third hour (2:15).** Nine in the morning, the time of morning prayer and sacrifice. Nobody is drunk at nine on a feast day. 🔴
- **David's tomb was a landmark (2:29).** People in Jerusalem could point to it, and Josephus says later kings broke into it. Peter's argument works because everyone knew where David's body was. 🔴
- **Bread from house to house (2:46).** The Lord's Supper was a real meal in a home, not a token. Groups were small. *Koinōnia* (fellowship, 2:42) meant sharing money and food, not only friendship. 🔴

## My notes
- I came at this chapter through the tongues question. It's one of the things that has split the Church into two groups, people who believe it and people who don't, and I wanted the history from the early church to today.
- **Acts 2 is real human languages.** That's a fact from the text, not a position. The trouble is the words: xenolalia (a real language you never learned), glossolalia (language-like speech that isn't a known language) and angelic speech get thrown together, and the New Testament doesn't have a technical term for any of them. Using the modern words on the old text is its own distortion. 🔴
- **Babel reversal.** The list of nations sounds like the table of nations, and under Deuteronomy 32 this is the disinherited nations being called back in their own tongues. I hold it as a strong inference, not a fact. 🟡
- **Church as the continuation of Israel.** Pentecost reverses the Deuteronomy 32 / Babel disinheritance through the people of the Messiah. Incorporation, not substitution. The Church doesn't replace Israel; it's where Israel's story was going. 🟡
- **Are Acts tongues and Corinthian tongues the same thing?** Unresolved. Luke describes languages people understood. Paul describes speech nobody understands without an interpreter. Nothing in Scripture closes that gap and both camps fill it from their systems. ⬜
- **2:5.** Overwhelmingly Jewish, not entirely. I picked those words on purpose in the church history paper. Gentiles coming in was exceptional enough that it took a vision and a council (Acts 10, 15).
- **2:46.** Acts opens in the temple. Luke ends his gospel with the disciples in the temple and opens volume two right back there.
