## What the chapter is doing
- The church is growing, and the Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily food.
- The Twelve won't leave the word of God to run the tables, so the congregation picks seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom. The apostles pray and lay hands on them.
- The word keeps spreading, and "a great many of the priests" come to the faith (6:7).
- Stephen, one of the seven, does wonders and signs. Men from the Synagogue of the Freedmen argue with him, can't stand against him, and bring false witnesses to the Sanhedrin. While they stare at him, his face looks like the face of an angel.

## Pay attention to this
- **The first church fight is about food and fairness (6:1).** Not doctrine. Widows from one group were being missed. The apostles take it seriously enough to reorganize the church over it. 🔴
- **The congregation chooses, the apostles appoint (6:3, 6).** The people pick the seven; the Twelve pray and lay on hands. 🔴
- **All seven have Greek names.** Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, Nicolas. The men picked to fix the Hellenist widows' problem seem to come from the Hellenist side. 🔴 for the names; 🟡 for what it means.
- **Nicolas is "a proselyte from Antioch" (6:5).** A Gentile who had converted to Judaism, now one of the seven. Antioch comes back big in chapter 11. 🔴
- **The table servers don't stay at the tables.** Stephen does "great wonders and signs" and argues in the synagogues. Philip preaches in Samaria in chapter 8. The job description didn't box them in. 🔴
- **"Unable to oppose the wisdom and the Spirit by whom he was speaking" (6:10).** Jesus promised this in Luke 21:15: "a mouth and wisdom which none of your opponents will be able to resist or refute." Luke uses the same verb in both places. 🔴
- **The charges sound familiar (6:13–14).** Speaking against "this holy place and the Law," and saying Jesus will destroy the temple. These are the charges at Jesus' own trial (Mark 14:58), with false witnesses again. 🔴
- **His face (6:15).** The council stares at the accused and sees an angel's face. Luke ends the chapter there and lets Stephen speak in chapter 7. 🔴

## Read it like AD 34, not 2026
- **Hellenists and Hebrews.** Both groups are Jewish believers. "Hellenists" spoke Greek as their first language, mostly diaspora Jews who had moved to Jerusalem. "Hebrews" spoke Aramaic and were rooted in the land. Language, synagogue and culture split them before the church did. 🔴
- **Widows were the test case.** The Law names the widow, the orphan and the stranger again and again as the people God watches over (Deuteronomy 10:18, 24:17–21). A widow with no son had no income. Diaspora Jews often came to Jerusalem to die near the temple, which may have left more widows on that side. 🔴 for the Law; 🔵 for the extra widows.
- **Laying on of hands.** Moses laid his hands on Joshua to pass on his authority in front of the congregation (Numbers 27:18–23). The apostles do the same thing with the seven. 🔴
- **The Synagogue of the Freedmen (6:9).** Freedmen were former slaves or their descendants, likely Jews taken to Rome as captives and later freed. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem (the Theodotus inscription) records a synagogue built for reading the Law and for housing visitors from abroad. That's the world of 6:9: Greek-speaking Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia. Cilicia's main city was Tarsus, Saul's hometown. 🔴 for the inscription and the places; 🟡 that Saul was in that synagogue.
- **Priests joining (6:7).** Thousands of ordinary priests served the temple in rotation and were not the same people as the high-priestly families running the Sanhedrin. Some of them believing doesn't conflict with the leaders' hostility. 🔴
- **The temple and the Law were the two things you could not touch.** For a Jew in Jerusalem, saying the temple would fall or the customs of Moses would change sounded like an attack on God. 🔴
- **A face like an angel.** Moses came down from the mountain with his face shining because he had been with God (Exodus 34:29–35). The council that accuses Stephen of speaking against Moses sees Moses' kind of face on him. Angels belong to God's throne room, the court above the court. 🟡

## My notes
- I only worked 6:10 so far, as the promise of Luke 21:15 paid out. Luke writes the promise in volume one and shows it paid in volume two. Same verb (*antistēnai*), on purpose. 🔴
- Where this came from: I asked about the verse that says don't worry what to say on trial, the Holy Spirit will tell you. I thought it was Acts or Paul. It's Jesus, four times in the Gospels, and Acts 6:10 is where Luke shows it happening.
- My first read on it: that itself doesn't mean you shouldn't study. It means you don't have to write your argument. The promise covers what you say under interrogation, not the knowledge you bring into the room.
- Standing rule I hold: we will never say something was "just for the Twelve." If it were, why record it? Stephen fits that: he isn't one of the Twelve, and the promise is paid to him. 🟡
- **Divine council:** no council scene in chapter 6 itself. The angel's face is a hint. The court above the court opens in chapter 7, when Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand.

## What the chapter is doing
- The high priest asks Stephen if the charges are true. Stephen answers with Israel's history: Abraham, Joseph, Moses, the wilderness, the tabernacle, David and Solomon's temple.
- The story keeps landing in the same place. Israel rejected Joseph, rejected Moses, made a calf, and resisted the prophets God sent.
- He ends by turning the charge around: "You men... are always resisting the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you" (7:51). They killed the prophets and now the Righteous One.
- They rage. Stephen looks up and sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They drag him out and stone him. He prays for them and "fell asleep." A young man named Saul holds the coats.

## Pay attention to this
- **God shows up outside the land.** Abraham hears God in Mesopotamia, Joseph has God with him in Egypt, Moses meets him at a bush in Midian. The charge was about "this holy place." Stephen's history keeps putting God somewhere else. 🔴 for the details; 🟡 for reading it as his point.
- **The rejection pattern.** Joseph's brothers sold him. Israel said to Moses, "Who made you a ruler and a judge?" (7:27, 35). Then "This Moses whom they disowned" is the one God sent as ruler and deliverer. Put "this Jesus whom you crucified" next to it. 🔴
- **7:37 is the key line.** "God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers" (Deuteronomy 18:15). Israel rejected Moses and his kind of prophet; now they've rejected the last one. 🔴
- **Moses was powerful in words and deeds (7:22).** Luke says the same of Jesus in Luke 24:19. The parallel is built at word level. 🔴
- **"The Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands" (7:48).** Stephen quotes Isaiah 66: "Heaven is My throne, and earth is the footstool of My feet." He isn't against the temple; he's against thinking God can be held in it. 🔴 for the quote; 🟡 for the balance.
- **The speech turns into an accusation.** Stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears (7:51). Those are Moses' and the prophets' words for Israel, used on the council. 🔴
- **Jesus is standing (7:55–56).** Everywhere else in the New Testament the risen Christ is seated at God's right hand. Here he stands. 🔴
- **Stephen dies like Jesus.** "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" and "Lord, do not hold this sin against them" (7:59–60) mirror Jesus' prayers on the cross (Luke 23:34, 46). 🔴
- **Saul (7:58).** The witnesses lay their garments at his feet. The man who will carry the gospel to the nations is introduced holding coats at the first martyr's death. 🔴

## Read it like AD 34, not 2026
- **A Sanhedrin hearing.** The council was the highest Jewish court in Jerusalem, led by the high priest. Under Rome it couldn't legally carry out a death sentence on its own (John 18:31). What happens to Stephen looks more like a mob than a ruling. 🔴 for the limit; 🟡 for this being a mob action.
- **Stoning had rules.** The guilty was taken outside the camp or city (Leviticus 24:14), and the witnesses threw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:7). They took off their outer cloaks to throw, which is why Saul is holding garments. 🔴
- **The Law came through angels (7:38, 53).** Stephen says Moses was "with the angel who was speaking to him on Mount Sinai" and that Israel "received the Law as ordained by angels." Paul (Galatians 3:19) and Hebrews (2:2) say the same thing. Deuteronomy 33:2 has God coming from Sinai with his holy ones. The giving of the Law was a divine council event. 🔴
- **"Delivered them up to serve the host of heaven" (7:42).** Stephen reads the golden calf as the moment God handed Israel over to the star-gods. Deuteronomy 4:19 says the sun, moon and stars, "all the host of heaven," were allotted to the other nations. Israel chose the gods of the nations, and God let them have what they chose. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the Deuteronomy 4 and 32 frame.
- **Moloch and Rompha (7:43).** Stephen quotes Amos 5:25–27 from the Greek Old Testament. Moloch was the god child sacrifice was offered to. Rompha (Kiyyun in the Hebrew) is usually taken as the planet Saturn, a star-god. These are the real gods of Israel's neighbors, not cartoon idols. 🔴 for the quotation; 🟡 for identifying Rompha.
- **The court above the court.** In the Old Testament, God holds court with his heavenly council: Satan accuses Job "among the sons of God" (Job 1:6) and Joshua the high priest (Zechariah 3:1). The accused has an accuser and no advocate; God defends him himself. The New Testament adds an advocate, Jesus (1 John 2:1). 🔴
- **Daniel 7 behind "Son of Man."** In Daniel 7, thrones are set, the court sits, and one like a Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days. Outside the Gospels, Stephen is the only one in the New Testament who uses "the Son of Man" as a title for Jesus. He's naming the figure from that heavenly courtroom. 🔴 for the usage; 🟡 for reading the scene through Daniel 7.
- **Why standing?** Three readings: he stands as Stephen's advocate before the Father; he rises to welcome the first martyr; or he stands as judge over the men killing him (Daniel 7). F. F. Bruce ties it to Luke 12:8, the Son of Man acknowledging before God those who acknowledged him before men. 🟡 for each; ⬜ on which.
- **Rhetoric was a trained skill.** Educated men in the Greek world learned how to build a defense speech: opening, story, argument, conclusion. Stephen's speech has that shape. 🔴

## My notes
- **The speech is formal rhetoric.** Humphrey lays it out: exordium, narratio, argumentatio, peroratio. By 7:51 he's at the conclusion and has turned the blasphemy charges back on his accusers. 🔴
- **Deuteronomy 18:15 at 7:37 is the interpretive key** (Tuckett). As Israel rejected Joseph and Moses, they reject the prophet like Moses. 🔴
- **None of it was improvised.** The Spirit supplied the wisdom his accusers couldn't withstand. Stephen supplied Genesis, Exodus, Amos and Isaiah, and the training to arrange them. The promise means you don't have to write your argument. It doesn't mean you shouldn't study. 🔴
- **I withdrew one claim.** In an earlier draft I said Stephen cites the "words in your mouth" promise while he's inside its fulfillment. He doesn't. 7:37 quotes Deuteronomy 18:15, a prophet like me, not 18:18's words in his mouth. ❌
- **Two courtrooms.** I read Luke 12:8–12 as one unit about two rooms: the heavenly court where the Son of Man speaks for you (vv. 8–9) and the earthly court where the Spirit teaches you what to say (vv. 11–12). That started as my own 🟡 and came back sourced, with Bruce making the connection to Stephen. 🔴
- **Old Testament courts have an accuser and no advocate.** The New Testament brings one in (1 John 2:1).
- **Stephen lost. The Son of Man stood up.** The promise was never that you win the earthly case. The verdict that counts is given in a different room, where for the first time the accused has someone on his feet speaking for him.
- **Aftermath.** Saul holds the coats. The persecution that follows scatters the church and spreads the gospel (8:1–4).
- **Divine council:** heavy here. Angels at Sinai, the host of heaven in 7:42, and the heavenly court in 7:55–56.

## What the chapter is doing
- God speaks against the whole family he brought out of Egypt: "You only have I known among all the families of the earth; Therefore I will punish you" (3:1–2).
- A chain of questions: do two walk together without meeting, does a lion roar with no prey, does a trap spring with nothing in it? Nothing happens without a cause, and when Yahweh speaks, a prophet has to prophesy (3:3–8).
- Philistia and Egypt are called in as witnesses to look at the oppression in Samaria (3:9–10).
- An enemy will surround the land and plunder its fortresses. Israel will be "rescued" like the scraps a shepherd pulls from a lion's mouth (3:11–12).
- God will smash the altars of Bethel and the rich men's winter houses, summer houses and ivory houses (3:13–15).

## Pay attention to this
- **"You only have I known... Therefore I will punish you" (3:2).** Being chosen doesn't mean being exempt. It means being held to account. 🔴
- **"Known."** *Yada'*, the covenant word for a close, chosen relationship (Genesis 18:19). 🔴
- **The questions build (3:3–6).** Each one is "of course not." The last is the one that bites: if disaster comes on a city, hasn't Yahweh done it? 🔴
- **"His secret counsel" (3:7).** The Hebrew is *sod*, the word for a council or the private talk of a council. Yahweh does nothing without telling his prophets what was decided. 🔴
- **The lion has roared (3:8).** Yahweh is the lion. Amos opened the book the same way: "Yahweh roars from Zion" (1:2). 🔴
- **Foreign witnesses (3:9).** Ashdod (Philistines) and Egypt are invited to come look. Even the pagans would be shocked. 🔴
- **"They do not know how to do what is right" (3:10).** They store up violence and robbery in their fortresses. 🔴
- **Read 3:12 all the way through.** "Just as the shepherd delivers from the lion's mouth a couple of legs or a piece of an ear, So will the sons of Israel inhabiting Samaria be delivered, With the corner of a bed and the cover of a couch!" The "delivered" pieces are leftovers of something already eaten. 🔴
- **Bethel's altar horns (3:14).** The horns of an altar were where a fugitive grabbed for sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50). God cuts them off. No place left to run. 🔴
- **Winter house, summer house, ivory (3:15).** Second homes for the rich. 🔴

## Read it like 760 BC, not 2026
- **A boom time.** Amos preached under Jeroboam II (about 786–746 BC), when the northern kingdom was rich and secure. Within forty years Assyria destroyed Samaria (722 BC). 🔴
- **The shepherd's proof.** Under Exodus 22:13, a shepherd whose animal was killed by a wild beast brought back what was left as evidence, so he wouldn't have to pay for it. Two legs or a piece of an ear was the legal proof that the animal was dead. Amos's audience knew that law. The "rescue" in 3:12 is the evidence of a death. 🔴
- **Amos was a herdsman (1:1; 7:14).** He knew sheep and lions. 🔴
- **Samaria's ivories are real.** Excavators at Samaria found hundreds of carved ivory pieces, inlays for furniture, from this period. The "houses of ivory" (3:15) and beds of ivory (6:4) are what they dug up. 🔴
- **Bethel was the king's sanctuary.** Jeroboam I set up a golden calf there (1 Kings 12:28–29), and it stayed the north's royal shrine (Amos 7:13). Judgment starts at the altar. 🔴
- **The prophet in the council (3:7).** A true prophet was one who had stood in Yahweh's *sod*, his council, and heard what was decided (Jeremiah 23:18, 22; 1 Kings 22:19–23). Amos 3:7 says the same thing in one line: the decision is made in God's council, then the prophet is told. 🔴 for the word *sod*; 🟡 for reading it as the heavenly council here.
- **"The God of hosts" (3:13).** *Elohe ha-tseva'ot*, God of the armies of heaven. The one judging Bethel commands the heavenly host. 🔴

## My notes
- I logged this one from a sermon. The preacher built the sermon's climax on 3:12 as a rescue text: the shepherd reaches into the lion's mouth and saves two legs and a piece of an ear, so God restores the remnant and builds a church out of it.
- **What the verse says.** It's a judgment oracle, and the picture is grim. Two legs and a piece of an ear are the scraps a shepherd brings back as legal proof the animal is already eaten. Nothing is left to save. Verse 11 sets it up and verse 15 finishes with the houses destroyed.
- **My assessment.** The pastoral instinct was good. The verse says the opposite. I logged it among the main findings of my sermon analysis, and it's one of the errors a single lookup would have caught.
- **Divine council:** no council scene, but 3:7 uses *sod*, the council word. The prophet hears what God's council decided before it happens.

## What the chapter is doing
- In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel dreams. The four winds stir up the great sea and four beasts come out: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear with three ribs in its mouth, a four-headed leopard with wings, and a fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns (7:1–7).
- A little horn comes up among the ten, with human eyes and a mouth speaking great boasts (7:8).
- Thrones are set up, the Ancient of Days takes his seat, the court sits and the books are opened. The fourth beast is killed and burned (7:9–12).
- One like a Son of Man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given an everlasting kingdom that all peoples serve (7:13–14).
- An attendant explains: four kings, and the saints of the Highest One will receive the kingdom. The horn wars against the saints for a time, times and half a time, then the court sits and his dominion is taken away (7:15–28).

## Pay attention to this
- **Daniel 7 is in Aramaic.** Daniel 2:4b–7:28 is written in Aramaic, the language of the empire. The rest of the book is Hebrew. 🔴
- **The sea (7:2–3).** The beasts come out of the great sea stirred by the four winds. In the Bible the sea is the home of chaos. 🔴
- **The lion with eagle's wings (7:4).** Its wings are plucked, it's made to stand like a man, and it's given a human heart. That's a humbling. 🔴
- **"Thrones were set up" (7:9).** Plural. More than one throne in God's court. 🔴
- **The Ancient of Days (7:9).** White clothing, hair like pure wool, a throne of fire with burning wheels. 🔴
- **"The court sat, And the books were opened" (7:10).** A courtroom, with records. 🔴
- **"With the clouds of heaven" (7:13).** The Son of Man arrives riding the clouds. 🔴
- **"One like a Son of Man."** Aramaic *bar enash*, "a human one." He looks human, and he's given what only God holds. 🔴
- **"Might serve Him" (7:14).** The Aramaic verb is *pelach*. In Daniel it's used for serving a god (3:12, 14, 17, 18, 28; 6:16, 20). 🔴
- **The saints of the Highest One (7:18, 22, 27).** The kingdom is given to the Son of Man (7:14) and to the saints (7:27). Who the "holy ones" are is argued: God's people, angels, or both. 🔴 for the text; 🔵 on who.
- **"A time, times, and half a time" (7:25).** Three and a half. Revelation picks it up (12:14). 🔴

## Read it like 550 BC, not 2026
- **This is a council scene, and a judgment.** Thrones set, the high God seated, thousands attending and myriads standing before him, the court sitting, books opened. It's the same divine court as 1 Kings 22, Psalm 82 and Job 1, now sitting to judge the empires. Heiser connects the books of 7:10 to the heavenly record in Malachi 3:16. 🔴
- **Who sits on the other thrones?** The text doesn't say. Council members, the saints, or the Son of Man. Rabbi Akiva reportedly said one throne was for God and one for David, and was rebuked for it (Talmud, Hagigah 14a). 🔴 for the Talmud; ⬜ for who sits.
- **Riding the clouds is God's title.** In Canaan "rider of the clouds" was Baal's title. The Hebrew Bible takes it for Yahweh: Deuteronomy 33:26; Psalm 68:4, 33; Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1. Daniel 7:13 is the one time the cloud rider is not the God on the throne. 🔴 (Heiser, *Unseen Realm* 249–250).
- **Two powers in heaven.** So the throne room has two divine figures: the Ancient of Days and the one like a Son of Man, who rides the clouds like Yahweh and gets worship-language service. Jewish readers before Jesus wrestled with this. The rabbis later called the view "two powers in heaven" and banned it (Alan Segal's study is the classic). Compare Genesis 19:24, Psalm 110:1, and the angel of Yahweh in Zechariah 3. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 the further you push it.
- **Ancient of Days and El.** Ugaritic texts picture El as the aged, gray-bearded father of the gods who sits enthroned, and Baal as the younger rider of the clouds who receives kingship. Daniel 7 uses that court shape and fills both seats with Israel's God. 🔴 for the Ugaritic pattern; 🟡 for direct use.
- **Beasts from the sea were empires.** The chaos sea and its monsters (Leviathan, Rahab) were old symbols for powers set against God. Daniel uses them for kingdoms. 🔴
- **The lion with eagle's wings is Babylon.** Winged lions guarded Babylonian and Assyrian palaces, and lions lined the Ishtar Gate's processional way. The plucked wings and human heart echo Nebuchadnezzar's humbling and restoration in Daniel 4. It fits the four-kingdom sequence of Daniel 2. 🔴 for the Babylonian imagery; 🟡 for the Daniel 4 link.
- **Nations had their princes.** Later in Daniel the angelic "prince of Persia" and "prince of Greece" fight Michael, "your prince" (10:13, 20–21; 12:1). The empires on earth have powers behind them in heaven, the Deuteronomy 32:8 worldview. Daniel 7's court is where those powers lose. 🔴 for Daniel 10; 🟡 for linking it to chapter 7.
- **Jesus took the title.** "Son of Man" is the name Jesus uses for himself most. At his trial he says they'll see the Son of Man "coming with the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62), and the high priest tears his robes and calls it blasphemy. 🔴

## My notes
- **The cloud rider.** Riding the clouds is a deity title, Baal's in the ANE and Yahweh's in the Hebrew Bible: four times of Yahweh, and a fifth time at 7:13, given not to the seated God but to the Son of Man (*Unseen Realm* 249–250). 🔴 This was the thing Heiser pointed out that most readers miss because of translation and familiarity.
- **Two Yahweh figures.** The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man, two divine figures in one throne room. Heiser's "Two Powers in Heaven," a Jewish category before Christianity that the rabbis later forbade (Segal is the foundational academic work). 🔴 to 🟡 depending on how far you push it.
- **"Serve" in 7:14.** *Pelach*, used in Daniel only for service given to a god (compare 3:17). The Son of Man receives worship language.
- **Jesus at his trial.** Claiming the cloud-rider role is why the high priest cries blasphemy. The category was familiar. The claimant was what they disputed.
- **Revelation 1 blurs the two.** The white hair of 7:9 belongs to the Ancient of Days. Revelation 1:14 gives it to Jesus, the Son of Man. That's early high Christology.
- **7:4, the lion with eagle's wings.** I'd heard it read as America breaking off from Britain, so I asked where it comes from. The grounded reading is Babylon (the Ishtar Gate lions), with the plucked wings and human heart as Nebuchadnezzar's humbling in Daniel 4, inside the four-empire sequence of Daniel 2. The America reading comes from British-Israelism and Armstrongism, with a 7/4 = July 4 flourish. It's theory bordering on eisegesis, and it turns a humbling into a coronation.
- **My own test:** if I use an eagle as a symbol, I could put the same emphasis on Nazi Germany or the Roman Empire. A symbol that fits everything specifies nothing.
- I held that apart from the America-as-Babylon reading of Revelation 17–18. I'm not saying America is Babylon, but I could go along with that one on my reading. I need to understand what both sides are saying, then do my own work on what Jesus says.

## What the chapter is doing
- In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel reads in Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem will last seventy years (9:1–2).
- He fasts in sackcloth and ashes and prays a long confession: we sinned, we didn't listen to the prophets, the curse of the law of Moses has come on us, you are righteous. He asks God to act for his own name's sake (9:3–19).
- While he's still praying, Gabriel arrives about the time of the evening offering. The answer was issued the moment Daniel started praying (9:20–23).
- Gabriel gives the seventy weeks: seventy "sevens" decreed for Daniel's people and city to end sin and bring in everlasting righteousness (9:24).
- Seven weeks and sixty-two weeks to an anointed prince; the anointed one cut off; the city and sanctuary destroyed; a covenant for one week, with sacrifice stopped halfway and the abomination that makes desolate (9:25–27).

## Pay attention to this
- **Daniel reads Scripture (9:2).** He finds the seventy years in "the books," in Jeremiah (25:11–12; 29:10). The prophecy starts with a man reading the prophets. 🔴
- **He prays "we," not "they" (9:5–15).** Daniel confesses the nation's sin as his own. 🔴
- **"For Your own sake" (9:17–19).** He asks on the basis of God's name and compassion, "not on account of any righteousness of our own." 🔴
- **"The man Gabriel" (9:21).** Gabriel looks like a man. He is the same messenger from 8:16. 🔴
- **The evening offering (9:21).** There's no temple, but Daniel still keeps time by the hour of the sacrifice. 🔴
- **"Seventy weeks" (9:24).** The Hebrew is *shavu'im shiv'im*, "seventy sevens." The text doesn't say sevens of what. Most read it as sevens of years: 490 years. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for years.
- **Six goals (9:24).** Finish transgression, end sin, atone for iniquity, bring everlasting righteousness, seal vision and prophecy, anoint the most holy. 🔴
- **Where the punctuation goes (9:25).** LSB follows one reading: "until Messiah the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks." The Hebrew accents put a break after "seven weeks," which some translations (ESV, RSV) follow: an anointed one after seven weeks, then sixty-two weeks of rebuilding. 🔴 that the versions differ; ⬜ on which is right.
- **"The Messiah will be cut off and have nothing" (9:26).** *Mashiach*, an anointed one. Christians have read it as Jesus. Others read it as a high priest such as Onias III (killed 171 BC). 🔴 for the word; ⬜ on who.
- **"He will make a firm covenant" (9:27).** Who "he" is, the coming prince of 9:26 or the Messiah, is one of the hardest calls in the Old Testament. ⬜
- **The abomination that makes desolate (9:27).** It returns in 11:31 and 12:11, and Jesus quotes it (Matthew 24:15). 🔴

## Read it like 539 BC, not 2026
- **Babylon has just fallen.** "The first year of Darius" is right after Persia took Babylon in 539 BC. Seventy years from the first deportation (605 BC) is close. Daniel is asking whether the time is up. 🔴 for the date; who "Darius the Mede" was is debated. ⬜
- **Seventy years from Jeremiah, sevenfold from Leviticus.** Chronicles reads the seventy years as the land getting its missed Sabbaths back (2 Chronicles 36:21; Leviticus 26:34–35). Leviticus 26 also threatens punishment "seven times" for sin (26:18, 21, 24, 28). Seventy years times seven gives seventy sevens. A first reader would hear Sabbath years and Jubilees in it. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the link.
- **A messenger from the council.** "The word was issued" (9:23) at the start of Daniel's prayer. A decree goes out from God's court and a messenger carries it, the way 7:10 and 10:12–13 picture the heavenly court and its servants. In the next chapter the messenger is held up 21 days by "the prince of the kingdom of Persia," until Michael helps (10:13). 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for reading 9:23 as a council decree.
- **Angels with names.** Gabriel (here and 8:16) and Michael (10:13, 21; 12:1) are the only angels named in the Old Testament. Naming angels grows in Second Temple Judaism (1 Enoch 9; 20). 🔴
- **Prayer at the hour of offering.** Praying at the time of the evening sacrifice, toward Jerusalem (6:10), kept temple time without a temple. Later Jewish practice built daily prayer on the same hours. 🔴
- **Second Temple readers had their own counts.** The Qumran community and others used seventy-sevens schemes to date the end. The Maccabean crisis (Antiochus IV stopping sacrifice and setting up an altar in the temple, 167 BC; 1 Maccabees 1:54) is how many read 9:27. 🔴 for 1 Maccabees; 🟡 for that reading.

## My notes
- I came to Daniel 9 by way of the rapture. When I separated the modern definition of the rapture from what Scripture says, Daniel's seventieth week turned out to be the gap the whole system needs.

- **The other case.** Nothing in the text says there's a gap of thousands of years. The gap is brought in to fit a framework, which strains a claim to read literally. - **Sparring use.** I once compared Daniel's weeks to Genesis 1's days: if weeks aren't literal in Daniel, why would days have to be literal in Genesis? The young-earth counter held: Daniel 9 marks itself as non-literal, Genesis 1 doesn't. I accepted that. The stronger answer for Genesis is inside Genesis, where 2:4 uses *yom* for the whole creation week, so the Daniel comparison isn't needed.
- **Divine council:** Gabriel and the word "issued" from heaven are the hooks. The full picture of heavenly princes behind nations comes in Daniel 10.

## What the chapter is doing
- It opens with "you are sons of Yahweh your God": no cutting yourselves or shaving your foreheads for the dead, because you are a holy people (14:1–2).
- Then the food list, the same rules as Leviticus 11, with a named list of clean animals: ox, sheep, goat, deer, gazelle, roebuck, wild goat, ibex, antelope, mountain sheep (14:4–5).
- An animal that dies of itself can't be eaten by Israel, but it can be given to the sojourner or sold to a foreigner. And don't boil a young goat in its mother's milk (14:21).
- Then the tithe: a tenth of the crops, eaten before Yahweh at the place he chooses, turned into money if the trip is too far, and every third year stored in town for the Levite, the sojourner, the orphan and the widow (14:22–29).

## Pay attention to this
- **14:21 gives the game away.** The animal that died of itself can go to the sojourner to eat or be sold to a foreigner. You don't hand poison to your neighbor and call it holy. The meat is fine. The rule is about Israel. 🔴
- **The reason is in the same verse.** "For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God." 🔴
- **The kid in its mother's milk, third time.** Also Exodus 23:19 and 34:26. Goat is clean and milk is clean. Only the combination is banned, so no health reason can explain it. 🔴
- **It sits next to firstfruits and the tithe every time.** God gets the first and the best, and you don't boil the young one in the milk that was meant to keep it alive. 🟡
- **The tithe is eaten, by you, before God (14:23).** "So that you may learn to fear Yahweh your God." The tenth is a meal at God's table, not only a payment. 🔴
- **The third-year tithe feeds people with no land (14:28–29).** The Levite, the sojourner, the orphan, the widow. 🔴
- **The word for tithe is *ma'aser*.** Hold it. In 1 Samuel 8 the king will take "a tenth" with the same word. 🔴
- **Mourning rules come first (14:1).** Cutting and shaving for the dead were how neighbors mourned. Israel's family identity, "sons of Yahweh," rules it out. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Pork was normal next door.** At Philistine sites pig bones run up to about a quarter of the animal remains; Israelite hill sites have almost none. The food line was visible in every village. 🔴
- **The Ugaritic "kid in milk" ritual is a myth.** For years study Bibles said Canaanites boiled a kid in its mother's milk as a fertility rite. The broken Ugaritic line behind that turned out to read closer to "coriander with milk." Scholars have dropped it; older reference works still carry it. 🔴
- **The real cluster is mother and young.** Don't take the mother bird with her young (22:6–7). Don't kill an animal and its young on the same day (Leviticus 22:28). Don't offer one before it's eight days with its mother (22:27). The bond between mother and young is protected even inside the killing. 🟡
- **Kosher meat and dairy comes from these three verses.** The rabbis read them three ways (don't eat, don't use, don't cook meat and milk together), and the whole system of separate dishes grew from that. That's later reading, not the original meaning. 🔴
- **Tithes were common, and so was the blur between tax and offering.** Around Israel tenths went to temples and kings, stored in temple complexes. In Deuteronomy the tenth goes to God's table and to the poor. 🔴
- **Mourning rites for the dead.** Cutting the skin and shaving the head were ordinary mourning rites in the region. Israel is told its identity as Yahweh's children rules them out. 🔴 No divine council scene in this chapter; the council texts in Deuteronomy are 4:19 and 32:8–9.

## What the chapter is doing
- The Levites get no land. Yahweh is their inheritance, and they live from the offerings (18:1–8).
- When Israel enters the land it must not copy the nations' ways of getting answers from the unseen world: passing a child through the fire, divination, omens, sorcery, spells, mediums, spiritists, calling up the dead (18:9–14).
- Instead Yahweh will raise up "a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; you shall listen to him" (18:15). God will put his words in that prophet's mouth (18:18).
- A prophet who speaks in God's name what God didn't say, or speaks for other gods, dies. The test: if what he says doesn't happen, God didn't say it (18:20–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **The prophet is God's answer to the forbidden list.** The nations listen to diviners and the dead; "but as for you, Yahweh your God has not allowed you to do so" (18:14). The prophet comes right after. 🔴
- **"A prophet like me" (18:15).** Moses promises someone like himself, from among their own people. 🔴
- **It goes back to Horeb (18:16–17).** The people asked not to hear God's voice out of the fire again, and God said "they have spoken well." The prophet is the go-between they asked for. 🔴
- **"I will put My words in his mouth" (18:18).** Not impressions or omens. Words. 🔴
- **Whoever won't listen, God will require it of him (18:19).** The prophet carries God's own authority. 🔴
- **The test is whether it happens (18:22).** And if it doesn't, "you shall not be afraid of him." 🔴
- **The promise stays open to the end of the Torah.** Deuteronomy 34:10: "there has not yet arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses." 🔴
- **The New Testament says who it is.** Peter quotes 18:15 in Acts 3:22–23, and Stephen in Acts 7:37. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Divination was normal religion.** Around Israel you learned the gods' will by reading sheep livers, stars, oil on water, and the flight of birds. Kings kept staffs of experts for it. Israel bans all of it. 🔴
- **Prophecy replaces the toolkit.** Diviners read signs and guessed. A prophet received words. That's why accuracy is the test: if he claims God's own words, they have to come true. 🔴
- **Calling up the dead was real practice.** The *'ov* (medium) was tied to the spirits of the ancestors. Consulting the dead meant going around Yahweh to another source of knowledge. Saul does exactly this at Endor in 1 Samuel 28. 🔴
- **"Passing a son or daughter through the fire" (18:10).** Child sacrifice, tied to Molech worship. It heads the list. 🔴
- **Divine council: other voices from the unseen realm.** The banned practices are ways of getting knowledge from spirits and the dead. Deuteronomy wants Israel listening to one voice only. In Heiser's frame this is Israel staying out of other powers' territory. 🟡 for that frame; the owned sources frame it as ancestor cult and covenant betrayal.

## What the chapter is doing
- A covenant is made in the land of Moab, "besides the covenant which He had cut with them at Horeb" (29:1).
- Moses goes over what they've seen: Egypt, forty years in which their clothes and sandals didn't wear out. "Yet to this day Yahweh has not given you a heart to know" (29:4).
- Everyone stands in the covenant, from leaders to woodcutters and water-drawers, and also "those who are not with us here today" (29:14–15). He warns against the man who blesses himself and says he'll be fine while he walks in his own stubborn heart (29:19).
- He pictures the land burned like Sodom and the nations asking why. The answer: they forsook the covenant and served gods God never gave them. The chapter ends: "The secret things belong to Yahweh our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our sons forever, that we may do all the words of this law" (29:29).

## Pay attention to this
- **Hidden and revealed (29:29).** The Hebrew sets *hannistarot*, "the hidden things," against *hanniglot*, "the revealed things." The line is hidden versus revealed, not earthly versus heavenly. 🔴
- **What's revealed is for doing.** The revealed things are given "that we may do all the words of this law." 🔴
- **"Not given you a heart to know" (29:4).** They saw everything and still didn't understand. Paul quotes this in Romans 11:8. 🔴
- **The covenant reaches people not born yet (29:14–15).** "Those who are not with us here today." 🔴
- **The man who blesses himself (29:19).** "I have peace though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart." The danger is a quiet one, a root that grows poison. 🔴
- **Gods "He had not apportioned to them" (29:26).** The same verb as 4:19, where the host of heaven was apportioned to the other nations. Israel's sin is going after gods that were never theirs. 🔴 for the verb, 🟡 for reading it with 4:19 and 32:8–9.
- **Exile is foreseen before they enter (29:28).** "He cast them into another land, as it is this day." 🔴
- **Numbering.** In the Hebrew Bible 29:1 is 28:69, so 29:29 is 29:28. Check the footnote if your Bible's numbers don't match. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Covenant renewal was a ceremony.** Treaties were renewed when a new generation or a new vassal ruler came in, with the terms read again and curses named. This is the new generation standing before the King. 🔴
- **Curses were part of the deal.** Ancient treaties ended with curses on the vassal who broke faith. The burned land in 29:23 is the curse clause turned into a picture. 🔴
- **The nations as witnesses (29:24).** In that world a ruined land told everyone that its people had broken faith with their god. Here the nations themselves give the answer. 🟡
- **Divine council: gods not allotted to Israel (29:26).** In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview the nations were given to other *elohim*, and Israel was kept as Yahweh's own portion (32:8–9). Serving those gods is a vassal running to another lord's territory. 🟡
- **"Secret things" isn't a two-tier cosmos.** It's easy to read 29:29 with a council or Second Temple lens as "God told Moses only the things of earth." The verse is about the limits of what people know before God, tied to obeying the law. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- The Song of Moses: heaven and earth are called to listen, and Yahweh is "the Rock," perfect and just, while his people are crooked (32:1–6).
- The Most High divided the nations and set their boundaries, and kept Jacob as Yahweh's own portion. He found Israel in a howling waste and carried it like an eagle carries its young (32:8–14).
- Israel grew fat and kicked, and went after strange gods, "demons who were not God," new gods their fathers never feared (32:15–18). So God hides his face, sends judgment, and still won't let the enemy boast (32:19–35).
- God will vindicate his people: "See now that I, I am He, and there is no god besides Me" (32:39). Then Moses is told to go up Mount Nebo and see the land he won't enter (32:48–52).

## Pay attention to this
- **Check your Bible at 32:8.** Most translations, LSB included, read "according to the number of the sons of Israel." The Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut^j reads "sons of God," and the Greek reads "angels of God." ESV follows the scroll. Your footnote will show it. 🔴
- **"Sons of Israel" doesn't fit the scene.** The verse is about the nations being divided, which points back to Babel (Genesis 10–11). Israel didn't exist yet. 🔴 for the timing, 🟡 for using it as an argument.
- **Yahweh keeps one nation for himself (32:9).** "Yahweh's portion is His people; Jacob is the allotment of His inheritance." The other nations went to someone else. 🔴
- **"Demons who were not God" (32:17).** The Hebrew is *shedim*, the same word Psalm 106:37 uses. The gods Israel ran after are real beings, just not God. 🔴
- **Found in *tohu* (32:10).** "A howling waste" uses *tohu*, the "formless" of Genesis 1:2. 🔴
- **The eagle that "hovers" (32:11).** The verb is *rachaph*. In this stem it shows up only twice in the Bible: here, and Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit hovers over the waters. 🔴
- **"Yahweh alone guided him, and there was no foreign god with him" (32:12).** Israel got out of the wilderness with one God, no others. 🔴
- **"There is no god besides Me" (32:39).** Read next to 32:8 and 32:17, it means none compare with him, not that the others don't exist. 🟡

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **A god for every nation.** Everyone around Israel assumed each people had its own god. At Ugarit the high god El had seventy sons, the *bn 'il*, "sons of El." Genesis 10 lists about seventy nations (by some counts), and later Judaism spoke of seventy angels over seventy nations. 🔴 for Ugarit, 🟡 for the seventy.
- **Divine council: the disinheritance.** Read with "sons of God," 32:8–9 says that at Babel the Most High handed the nations to lesser *elohim* and kept Israel as his own. Psalm 82 judges those gods for ruling badly. Genesis 12, Abraham, is God starting to take the nations back. 🔴 for the text variant, 🟡 for the disinheritance reading.
- **Deuteronomy 4:19–20 is the other side of the same deal.** There God apportions the host of heaven to the nations and takes Israel as his inheritance. 🔴
- **Why the Hebrew changed.** Emanuel Tov calls the Masoretic "sons of Israel" an anti-polytheistic alteration: a scribe smoothing out a reading that sounded like many gods. The change likely came after AD 100, when the Hebrew text was standardized. 🔴 for Tov's label, 🟡 for the date.
- **The Rock.** Other nations called their gods mountains and rocks. Moses keeps calling Yahweh "the Rock" and mocks "their rock" as no match (32:31). 🔴
- **The eagle is a known image.** The Ugaritic Aqhat legend uses the same verb, *rhp*, for eagles in flight. The verb describes motion over a nest. 🔴
- **Michael over Israel.** Daniel 10:13 shows the same picture later: princes over Persia and Greece, and Michael as Israel's prince. 🔴 for the principle.

## My notes
- **The manuscript case is the foundation stone for me.** Three witnesses: the Dead Sea Scroll (about 2nd century BC) has "sons of God," the Greek has "angels of God," the Masoretic text (about AD 1000) has "sons of Israel." The harder reading wins, because scribes smooth problems out, they don't make them up. Nobody invents "sons of God" from "sons of Israel." 🔴 for the variant.
- **My framework from the Heiser critique study:** *elohim* is a description, Yahweh is the Name. Other *elohim* are real (you can't hand nations to nobody), they're created and lower (the Most High hands out, they receive), and Yahweh stands apart. That isn't polytheism. 🟡
- **What the worldview can and can't do.** In the drmsh Deuteronomy 32 Worldview community I pushed back: "This is the problem that I have with a lot of this DCW, we forget to look at Christ." It's a reading tool for hearing what the biblical writers assumed. It isn't an ethical system or a war ethic. When Hunter asked whether it gives moral guidance on warfare, my answer was that it doesn't. It should make the cross bigger, not compete with it.
- **Why I trust Heiser.** "I thought he refused to try to draw lines to connect dots" where there weren't any. He'd lay out the options and say this one explains the most. Not 100% settled law.
- **Talking past each other.** With Natalie on X my point was about the manuscripts. She heard it as a claim about what God can or can't do. I agreed with her that God knows the end and sits outside of time, and restated that my point was about the text.
- **The eagle (32:10–11).** Two rare words, *tohu* and *rachaph*, sit in both Genesis 1:2 and here. Fesko pointed me to the *tohu* link. So Moses tells you how to read Genesis 1:2, and he tells you with a bird. The affection preachers find in "brooding" isn't in the verb; it's in the eagle. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Moses climbs Mount Nebo to the top of Pisgah, and Yahweh shows him the whole land, from Gilead to Dan to the western sea. "I have let you see it with your eyes, but you shall not cross over there" (34:4).
- Moses dies in Moab "according to the command of Yahweh," and Yahweh buries him in a valley opposite Beth-peor. Nobody knows the place "to this day" (34:5–6).
- He is 120, with his eyes still clear and his strength still there. Israel weeps for thirty days, and Joshua, full of the spirit of wisdom because Moses laid hands on him, takes over (34:7–9).
- The Torah ends: "there has not yet arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face" (34:10–12).

## Pay attention to this
- **"He buried him" (34:6).** God himself buries Moses. 🔴
- **"To this day" (34:6).** Somebody writing this is looking back across time. 🔴
- **Moses in the third person.** The whole chapter talks about Moses, never as Moses. 🔴
- **"Not yet arisen" (34:10).** This answers Deuteronomy 18:15, "a prophet like me." The Torah closes with the promise still open. 🔴
- **Face to face.** What made Moses different was the way God knew him, not his miracles alone (34:10; Numbers 12:8). 🔴
- **The hands on Joshua (34:9).** Moses laid his hands on him (Numbers 27:18–23), and the people listen to Joshua. The handoff happens before the funeral is over. 🔴
- **Beth-peor (34:6).** Moses is buried across from the place where Israel fell into the worship of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25). 🔴 for the place, 🟡 for reading meaning into it.
- **He sees the land and doesn't enter it.** It goes back to the water from the rock at Meribah (32:51; Numbers 20:12). 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Writing your own death.** If Moses wrote Deuteronomy, how did he write this? The rabbis argued it: Joshua wrote the last verses, or Moses wrote them ahead of time, weeping. The plain answer from the text is a later editor finished the account. That's evidence of how Scripture was put together, not a threat to inspiration. 🔴 for the rabbinic debate, 🟡 for the editor.
- **How the Torah grew (Mackie).** Moses writes at key moments (Exodus 17:14; 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9, 24–26). Joshua writes "the law" on stones (Joshua 8:32), so the early Torah was short. Old place names got updated for later readers, like "Dan" in Genesis 14:14, a name the city only got in Judges 18:29. The final form came late in the monarchy to after the exile, about 700–400 BC. 🟡
- **Divine council: the body of Moses.** Jude 9 says Michael the archangel disputed with the devil over Moses' body, a story from a lost Second Temple work, probably the Assumption of Moses. The hidden grave in 34:6 is the gap that story grew in. 🔴 for Jude, 🔵 for any link back to Deuteronomy's intent.

## My notes
- I came to this chapter through the How We Got the Bible class, building from Mackie's BibleProject classroom sessions 7–9.
- **How did Moses write his own death?** Third person, "to this day," and "not yet arisen" all point to a later inspired editor. Not a problem for inspiration. It's how Scripture was compiled. 🟡
- **Seam One.** 34:10 answers back to 18:15 and hands off straight to Joshua 1:1–9. The Torah ends waiting for the prophet like Moses, and the Prophets open with Joshua as a partial answer. 🟡
- **Stained glass.** The light is the divine word; the glass is human culture and craft. The Bible's human side is a feature, not a flaw.
- **My own side link.** Socrates' complaint that writing weakens memory, and *Fahrenheit 451*'s people who become the books. Scripture survived because a community took it in so deep that burning the copies wouldn't have killed it. Isaiah sealing the teaching among his disciples (Isaiah 8:16) is that picture.

## What the chapter is doing
- Moses, on the plains of Moab, tells Israel to listen to the statutes and keep them, without adding or taking anything away (4:1–2). Their wisdom will be how the nations see them.
- He takes them back to Horeb: they heard God's voice out of the fire but saw no form (4:12, 15). So no images of any kind, and no worshiping the sun, moon and stars.
- He warns that if they make idols in the land they will be scattered among the nations, and that if they seek Yahweh there with all their heart they will find him (4:25–31).
- He closes on what no other people has had: God speaking out of the fire, a nation taken out of another nation. "Yahweh, He is God; there is no other besides Him" (4:35). Then three cities of refuge are set apart east of the Jordan.

## Pay attention to this
- **"You saw no form" (4:12, 15).** The ban on images rests on what happened at Horeb. They heard words. They didn't see a shape. 🔴
- **The host of heaven is "apportioned" to the peoples (4:19).** Yahweh gave the sun, moon and stars to all the nations under heaven. Israel is not to be drawn away to them. 🔴
- **"But Yahweh has taken you" (4:20).** Out of the "iron furnace," Egypt, to be "a people for His own inheritance." The nations got the host of heaven. Israel got Yahweh. 🔴
- **This is Deuteronomy 32:8–9 from the other side.** There God divides the nations by the number of the sons of God and keeps Jacob as his own portion. Here God allots the host of heaven to the nations and takes Israel as his inheritance. Same transaction, two angles. 🔴
- **"A consuming fire, a jealous God" (4:24).** Hebrews 12:29 quotes the first half. 🔴
- **Exile is in the plan before they cross the river (4:25–31).** Moses already sees them scattered and then seeking God from there. 🔴
- **"There is no other besides Him" (4:35, 39).** Read next to 4:19, it's a claim about who is God over all, not a claim that the host of heaven isn't there. 🟡

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Images were how gods were present.** Around Israel a statue was washed and "opened" in a ritual so the god would live in it. People didn't worship the wood. They worshiped the god they believed was in it. Israel's no-image rule says no image can hold Yahweh, and making one is an attempt to control him. 🔴
- **The sky was full of gods.** Sun, moon and stars were worshiped across the ancient Near East as divine powers. Calling them "the host of heaven" puts them in God's army, not on his throne. 🔴
- **Divine council: the allotment.** In Heiser's frame the nations were handed over to lesser *elohim* at Babel (Deuteronomy 32:8–9), and the "host of heaven" in 4:19 is the visible side of those powers. Israel alone is Yahweh's own portion. 🟡 for the frame, 🔴 for the two texts pairing up.
- **Deuteronomy reads like a treaty.** Hittite suzerain treaties have the same shape: history, terms, witnesses, blessings and curses. "No other gods" is a Great King demanding exclusive loyalty from his vassal. 🔴
- **Heaven and earth as witnesses (4:26).** Treaties called the gods as witnesses. Moses calls heaven and earth. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Moses gathers all Israel and reminds them that the covenant at Horeb was made "with us, all of us who are alive here today," not only with their fathers (5:3).
- He repeats the ten words that Yahweh spoke "face to face" out of the fire (5:4, 6–21).
- He tells how the people, terrified of the fire and the voice, asked him to go near and hear for them, and Yahweh said they had spoken well (5:23–28).
- So Moses stays to receive the rest of the commands, and the chapter ends with: walk in all the way Yahweh has commanded, so that you may live (5:32–33).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Not with our fathers ... but with us" (5:3).** This is a new generation, forty years later, most of whom were children or unborn at Horeb. Moses tells them the covenant is theirs, today. 🔴
- **"Face to face" (5:4).** The whole nation heard God's voice. That takes away the out of "Moses just said God said so." 🔴
- **The Sabbath reason changes.** In Exodus 20:11 you rest because God rested after creation. In Deuteronomy 5:15 you rest because "you were a slave in the land of Egypt" and Yahweh brought you out. Same command, two reasons. 🔴
- **Your slaves rest too (5:14).** "So that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you." The people who were slaves give rest to their own servants. 🔴
- **The tenth word is ordered differently.** Exodus puts "house" first in the coveting command. Deuteronomy puts "wife" first and adds "field" (5:21). 🔴
- **"And He added no more" (5:22).** These ten were spoken aloud to the whole assembly and written on two stone tablets. Everything after comes through Moses. 🔴
- **The people asked for a go-between (5:27).** "Go near and hear all that Yahweh our God says." God says they spoke well, and wishes "that they had such a heart" to fear him always (5:29). 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Covenant was a known form.** Treaties between a great king and a lesser one opened with who the king was and what he'd done for the vassal, then gave the terms. "I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out" (5:6) works the same way: rescue first, then the rules. The covenant framework is treaty-shaped. The ten themselves don't match any treaty list. 🟡
- **Rescue first, then law.** The ten are the house rules for people already in the house, not a test to get in. 🔴
- **Moral law was everywhere; this God wasn't.** Don't murder, don't steal, don't lie in court: Hammurabi and other codes cover the same ground. The first four words (one God, no images, the Name, the Sabbath) have no real parallel. 🔴
- **A whole nation hearing a god was unheard of.** In the ancient world gods spoke to kings, priests and diviners. Deuteronomy 4:33 asks whether any people ever heard a god's voice out of fire and lived. 🔴
- **Slaves and rest.** Slaves in that world didn't get a day off by law. Israel's Sabbath ties rest to memory of Egypt. 🟡
- **No council scene here.** The divine council material sits close by in 4:19 and 32:8–9. See My notes.

## META: the book of Exodus
- **Where it sits.** Second book of the Torah. Genesis ends with Jacob's family welcomed into Egypt; Exodus opens with their descendants enslaved there. It takes Israel from Egypt to Sinai and ends with God's glory filling the tabernacle. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** who is Israel's real master, Pharaoh or Yahweh, and what does it look like for God to live among his people?
- **Who wrote it.** Jewish and Christian tradition says Moses. The book shows him writing some of it himself: the Amalek record (17:14), "all the words of Yahweh" (24:4), and the covenant terms (34:27). Moses as the source with later shaping is the common conservative view. 🟡
- **When.** Two main dates for the exodus. Early: about 1446 BC, from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, under an 18th-dynasty (Thutmosid) pharaoh. Late: the 13th century BC under Ramesses II, from the city name "Raamses" in 1:11. I hold the early date. ⬜
- **Text issues that are real.** Jacob's family is "seventy" in the Hebrew of 1:5, but "seventy-five" in the Greek and a Dead Sea Scroll, which is the number Stephen uses in Acts 7:14. The 430 years in 12:40 cover Egypt only in the Hebrew; the Greek and Samaritan texts count Canaan and Egypt together. And "Red Sea" is *yam suph*, literally "Sea of Reeds." 🔴
- **Movements:** chs. 1–18 deliverance from Egypt; chs. 19–24 the covenant at Sinai; chs. 25–40 the tabernacle (instructions, the golden calf crisis in 32–34, and the building).
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - Whose servant Israel is. The same Hebrew root (*'avad*) covers slaving for Pharaoh and serving Yahweh in worship.
  - The plagues as judgment "on all the gods of Egypt" (12:12), Yahweh against the gods behind Pharaoh.
  - The name. "I AM WHO I AM" (3:14), "that you may know that I am Yahweh," again and again.
  - God's presence: the bush, the pillar of cloud and fire, the mountain, the tabernacle.
  - Protection marks: the blood on the doorposts, the line between Goshen and Egypt.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jacob's seventy descendants have become a people so large "the land was filled with them" (1:1–7).
- A new king "who did not know Joseph" sees them as a threat and puts them to forced labor building the storage cities Pithom and Raamses (1:8–14).
- The harder Egypt pushes, the more Israel grows (1:12).
- Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill the baby boys. They fear God and refuse (1:15–21).
- Pharaoh orders all his people to throw every Hebrew son into the Nile (1:22).

## Pay attention to this
- **Genesis 1 language (1:7).** "Fruitful," "multiplied," "filled" the land. God's creation blessing is working in Egypt. 🔴
- **"Did not know Joseph" (1:8).** The man who saved Egypt is forgotten. 🔴
- **"Let us deal wisely with them" (1:10).** Pharaoh's plan is called wisdom. It's fear: they might join Egypt's enemies and leave. 🔴
- **The more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied (1:12).** Pharaoh's plan backfires every time. 🔴
- **Five times "slave labor" (1:13–14).** The verb and noun pile up: *'avad*, *'avodah*. Later God will say "let My people go, that they may serve (*'avad*) Me." 🔴
- **The midwives have names; Pharaoh doesn't.** Shiphrah and Puah get named. The king of Egypt stays "Pharaoh." 🔴
- **They feared God (1:17, 21).** Fear of God beats fear of the king. 🔴
- **Their answer to Pharaoh (1:19).** "The Hebrew women are vigorous." Whether that's a cover story or true, the text praises them and God rewards them with households. 🔴
- **Into the Nile (1:22).** The river that gave Egypt life is ordered to swallow Hebrew boys. The first plague will turn that river to blood (7:20). 🟡

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Pharaoh was a god.** Egyptians saw the king as the son of Ra and the living Horus, keeper of *ma'at*, the order of the world. A first reader wouldn't hear a politician picking on immigrants. They'd hear a god-king setting himself against the God of Israel. 🔴
- **Divine council:** Heiser reads the whole exodus as Yahweh against the gods of Egypt, and 12:12 says it outright: "on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments." Pharaoh's war on the Hebrew boys is the opening move on the human level of a fight that's bigger than Egypt. The same pattern shows up when Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16). 🔴 for 12:12; 🟡 for reading ch. 1 that way.
- **Forced labor was state labor.** Egypt drafted foreigners and its own peasants for building projects (corvée). Brick-making with quotas is shown in Egyptian tomb paintings (the tomb of Rekhmire shows foreign workers making bricks). Brutal, but a different thing from American chattel slavery, where people were owned as property. 🔴
- **Storage cities.** Pithom and Raamses held grain and supplies for the army and the crown. 🔴
- **A new dynasty.** "A new king" fits a change of ruling house, like the native Egyptian kings who drove out the Semitic Hyksos rulers (around 1550 BC) and then distrusted Semitic people in the Delta. 🔵
- **Midwives and the birthstool.** Women gave birth squatting on a pair of bricks or stones (the "birthstool," 1:16). Egyptian texts mention birth bricks. 🔴
- **The Nile was a god's gift.** The flood that watered Egypt was worshiped as Hapi. Pharaoh uses the sacred river to kill. 🔴

## My notes
- **"A new king who did not know Joseph."** I think about 400 years is the timeline. America, 250 years in, already fights over what it was built on. Over 400 years, without our kind of record-keeping, and with Egyptians recording only the winning memories, of course Joseph got forgotten. A regime change (Hyksos out, native kings in) could add to it. 🟡
- **The date.** I hold the earlier biblical chronology: 1 Kings 6:1's 480 years puts the exodus around 1446 BC, under a Thutmosid pharaoh. I treat the Bible as a reliable historical record: more than once we thought it didn't line up, and later archaeology showed it did (the Tel Dan inscription, the Pilate stone, the Pool of Bethesda). Heiser doesn't argue it hard, but he leans away from Ramesses II toward an earlier Thutmosid king (Thutmose IV's Dream Stele comes up). And we say BC, not BCE.
- **What kind of slavery.** It was state-imposed forced labor (*'eved*), not ownership of people as property. Different mechanism, still brutal. Harsh labor and brick quotas were how labor worked in a lot of places, even in America into the 20th century. Chattel slavery is defined by legal ownership of persons.
- **Why Pharaoh did it.** Fear of the numbers, wanting the free labor, and plain paranoia about losing control.
- **The council frame.** Pharaoh killing the Hebrew boys and Herod killing the boys of Bethlehem line up: earthly rulers acting as instruments of a cosmic hostility, with Christ as the new Moses who survives it.
- **A thought experiment, not a sermon.** I pushed the thread forward to abortion in America today: sexual freedom with no consequences treated as an idol, and children sacrificed to it, like the children sacrificed to Molech. I'm keeping that as a thought experiment.
- **Separate by choice.** I think the Hebrews kept themselves apart, not because of an Egyptian law, but because Genesis made a big deal of staying separate from the nations. Joseph and Moses were exceptions with unusual stories.
- **The midwives.** I half-remember a sermon detail about midwives in general doing something to protect baby boys. I haven't found a source for it.

## What the chapter is doing
- God resets Israel's calendar: this month is now the first month (12:1–2).
- Passover is set up before the rescue happens: a spotless year-old lamb per household, killed at twilight, its blood on the doorposts, eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed to leave (12:3–11).
- God will pass through Egypt, strike the firstborn, and judge "all the gods of Egypt." Where he sees the blood, he passes over (12:12–13, 21–23).
- Seven days of unleavened bread are made a permanent feast, and parents are told what to say when their children ask (12:14–20, 24–28).
- At midnight every firstborn in Egypt dies. Pharaoh drives Israel out. They leave with unrisen dough, Egyptian silver and gold, and a mixed crowd, after 430 years (12:29–42).
- The rules for who may eat it: circumcised members of the household, native or foreigner (12:43–51).

## Pay attention to this
- **The meal comes before the rescue (12:1–28).** Israel keeps Passover in faith, the night before anything happens. 🔴
- **"Against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments; I am Yahweh" (12:12).** The plagues were never only about Pharaoh. 🔴
- **The blood is a sign "for you" (12:13).** God sees the blood and passes over. 🔴
- **The destroyer (12:23).** Yahweh passes through, and he will "not allow the destroyer to come into your houses." 🔴
- **Dressed to run (12:11).** Belt on, sandals on, staff in hand, eating fast. 🔴
- **"When your children say to you" (12:26).** The feast is built to be asked about and explained. 🔴
- **"This new slavery" (12:25–26).** The Hebrew word for the Passover service is *'avodah*, the same word used for their slave labor in 1:14. LSB keeps the echo. They're trading one service for another, Pharaoh's for Yahweh's. 🔴
- **No home without someone dead (12:30).** The great cry of 11:6 comes true. 🔴
- **"Bless me also" (12:32).** Pharaoh's last words to Moses. 🔴
- **Plundering with favor (12:35–36).** They asked, and the Egyptians gave. "Thus they plundered the Egyptians." 🔴
- **A mixed multitude (12:38).** Non-Israelites leave with them. 🔴
- **"Not break any bone of it" (12:46).** John 19:36 applies this to Jesus on the cross. 🔴
- **One law for native and foreigner (12:48–49).** A circumcised foreigner eats like a native. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Pharaoh's firstborn was a god's heir.** Pharaoh claimed to be the son of Ra and the living Horus. His firstborn's death strikes the divine claim and the line of succession on the same night. 🔴 for the claim; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Divine council: the gods of Egypt are judged.** 12:12 says out loud what the plagues were doing. Numbers 33:4 looks back on the same night: "on their gods also Yahweh executed judgments." Heiser reads this as Yahweh's victory over the gods of Egypt, not only over a human king. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **The Destroyer.** The Hebrew is *mashchit*, from a root meaning "ruin" or "spoil." The same figure shows up later with a drawn sword over Jerusalem (2 Samuel 24:16; 1 Chronicles 21:15), and Paul names him as known (1 Corinthians 10:10). The Dictionary of Deities and Demons files him separately from an "angel of death" who takes people at their natural end: the Destroyer kills in numbers, only on Yahweh's order, and is stopped by a ritual act like the blood. 🔴
- **Blood on the door.** Doorways were where households were thought to be most open to harm, and protective rites at thresholds show up across the ANE. Israel's mark at the door isn't magic: God names it as the sign he will see. 🟡
- **A calendar of their own (12:2).** Egypt's year was tied to the Nile and Egypt's gods. Israel's new year starts with the night God brought them out. 🟡
- **Leaven.** Yeast was kept going from batch to batch, so getting rid of all of it meant a clean start. 🔴
- **"Six hundred thousand men" (12:37).** The Hebrew word for "thousand" (*'eleph*) can also mean a clan or military unit, and scholars argue over the size of the exodus because of it. 🔵

## My notes
- **12:12 is the key verse of my plagues post.** The climax is a public judgment on the whole pantheon.
- **The protection motif starts here.** Passover blood heads my list: the marked household is protected while judgment falls outside. Same covenant logic with Noah's ark, Rahab's cord, the mark of Cain, Gideon's fleece, and the veil and Christ's body (see Exodus 8).
- **The Destroyer.** In the entry I validated for my Fact Book, *mashchit* passes through Egypt, is held back by the blood, kills in numbers and only on Yahweh's order, and is always checked by a cultic act. The Dictionary of Deities and Demons separates it from the angel of death. 🔴
- **12:35–36, the plundering.** Spoils of war and a founding endowment, not reparations. My three challenges to the reparations reading: forced labor, not chattel slavery; spoils from God's victory, not back wages; a one-time gift to that generation, not a claim passed down (see Exodus 3). 🟡
- **The food law in the chapter.** No leaven for seven days (12:15–20). The lamb roasted, nothing left till morning, no bone broken (12:8–10, 46). The uncircumcised may not eat Passover (12:43–48). These laws didn't come out of nowhere: I see Leviticus as putting into one formal document commands God had already been giving since Noah and Abraham.

- **Grace, then the ask (19:4–5).** "You have seen what I did," then "if you will listen." Rescue comes first. 🔴
- **"Treasured possession" (19:5).** *Segullah*, a king's personal treasure. 🔴
- **"For all the earth is Mine" (19:5).** Israel is chosen out of a world that already belongs to God. 🔴
- **A kingdom of priests (19:6).** The whole nation is to stand between God and the nations like priests. Peter applies it to the church (1 Peter 2:9). 🔴
- **The fence (19:12–13).** Touch the mountain and die, and no one may touch the person who did. 🔴
- **Graded access (19:20–24).** Moses goes up; Aaron may come; the priests and people stay back. 🔴
- **"The third day" (19:11, 16).** God comes down on the third day. 🔴
- **"Lest He break out against them" (19:22, 24).** Holiness is dangerous, not decorative. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **The mountain where heaven meets earth.** In the ANE, gods lived on and met people at sacred mountains. Sinai is that place: God comes down, the people stay at the foot, and only the mediator goes up. Eden was a mountain garden (Ezekiel 28:13–14), and Zion becomes the next one. 🔴 for the ANE belief; 🟡 for the chain.
- **A king's treasure.** *Segullah* matches an Akkadian word for a king's own private property, set apart from the rest of the realm. 🔴
- **Treaty language.** "You have seen what I did... so now, if you will listen... then you shall be" matches the shape of ANE covenant treaties: the great king's past help, then the terms, then the blessing. 🟡
- **Storm language.** Thunder, cloud, fire and a shaking mountain were the marks of a storm god's arrival (like Baal at Ugarit). Yahweh comes to Sinai in the full storm. 🔴
- **Divine council: the holy ones at Sinai.** Later texts say God came from Sinai "with ten thousand holy ones" (Deuteronomy 33:2) and that the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). Exodus 19 shows only fire and cloud, but Israel remembered a crowded mountain. 🔴 for the texts.
- **Laundry and abstinence (19:10, 15).** Getting ready to meet a god meant ritual purity: clean clothes, and no sex, which made a person ritually unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:18). 🔴

## My notes
- **The barrier.** A boundary around the mountain that even priests can't cross, violators killed from a distance, and levels of access (Moses, Aaron, the priests, the elders, the people). Holiness is tied to priestly status (Babcock, *Trajectories*, 4; Rosemann; Harris, "Priest," DNTUOT 626). 🔴
- **What Sinai does to the "visitor model."** In the Eden discussion, someone offered Sinai as proof that humans don't belong in divine space at all. The barrier checks out as described, but it points somewhere else: Sinai sits on the far side of Genesis 3. The research classified Sinai as a place where heaven and earth intersect, not divine territory proper. There's no pre-fall evidence for the danger. 🟡

- **The eagle.** Here God carries Israel on eagles' wings. In Deuteronomy 32:11 the eagle hovers over its nest, and that's the same verb as the Spirit hovering over the waters in Genesis 1:2. The love is in the eagle, and it shows up again here.

## What the chapter is doing
- A Levite couple has a son. His mother hides him three months, then puts him in a waterproofed papyrus basket among the reeds of the Nile while his sister watches (2:1–4).
- Pharaoh's daughter finds him, knows he's a Hebrew baby, and pays his own mother to nurse him. She names him Moses (2:5–10).
- Grown up, Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, kills the Egyptian and hides the body. The next day a Hebrew throws it back at him: "Who made you a ruler or a judge over us?" (2:11–14).
- Pharaoh tries to kill him. Moses runs to Midian, rescues seven sisters at a well, marries Zipporah and has a son, Gershom, "a sojourner in a foreign land" (2:15–22).
- Back in Egypt the king dies, Israel cries out, and God hears, remembers his covenant, sees and knows (2:23–25).

## Pay attention to this
- **"He was beautiful" (2:2).** The Hebrew is *tov*, "good," the word of Genesis 1: "God saw that it was good." 🔴
- **"Ark" (2:3).** *Tevah*, the same word as Noah's ark. It's used only for these two in the whole Bible, and both are sealed with pitch. A rescue through water, again. 🔴
- **Pharaoh's daughter undoes Pharaoh's order.** He said throw the boys into the Nile. His own daughter pulls one out of it. 🔴
- **His mother gets paid to nurse him (2:9).** 🔴
- **The name (2:10).** "Because I drew him out of the water." 🔴
- **"His brothers" (2:11).** Twice in one verse. Raised Egyptian, Moses still calls the Hebrews his brothers. 🔴
- **"He turned this way and that" (2:12).** He checks for witnesses before he kills. 🔴
- **"Who made you a ruler or a judge over us?" (2:14).** Israel rejects him before God sends him. Stephen makes the point in Acts 7:25–27, 35. 🔴
- **A well and a wife (2:15–21).** Abraham's servant found Rebekah at a well, Jacob met Rachel at a well, Moses meets Zipporah at a well. 🔴
- **"An Egyptian delivered us" (2:19).** That's how the Midianite girls see him. 🔴
- **Four verbs for God (2:24–25).** He heard, remembered, saw, knew. God hasn't been mentioned since the midwives in ch. 1. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Sargon's basket.** A Mesopotamian legend says Sargon of Akkad's mother put him in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and set him in the river, where he was found and raised to become king. A first reader might know the type: a baby saved from the water grows up to lead. 🔴 for the legend; 🟡 that the audience would hear the echo.
- **"Moses" sounds Egyptian.** *Mose* is an Egyptian word for "born of" or "son," the same piece in names like Thutmose and Ramesses. The Hebrew explanation plays on *mashah*, "to draw out." An Egyptian princess gives an Egyptian name that turns out to say something in Hebrew. 🔴
- **Raised in the palace.** Egyptian royal households raised foreign children with princes and trained them in the court. Acts 7:22 says Moses was "educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians." 🔴
- **The Nile was divine.** The river was tied to the god Hapi and fed the whole country. The river Pharaoh used to kill the boys is where God saves this one. 🔴
- **Midian.** A desert people east of the Gulf of Aqaba, descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2). Moses runs to distant family. 🔴
- **Divine council:** no council scene here. It's a ground-level story where God is silent until the last two verses. The confrontation with Egypt's gods starts in ch. 7 and is named in 12:12.

## My notes
- **Moses is impulsive, not instantly righteous.** The killing and the run for his life show it.
- **When did Moses learn he was Hebrew?** The text doesn't say. His mother nursed him, so he likely knew from early on, but that's an inference.
- **How did he know the man was Hebrew?** There wasn't much physical difference between Egyptians and Hebrews. The markers were dress, religion and grooming: Hebrews likely wore beards, Egyptians were clean-shaven. 🟡
- **2:21, Zipporah.** She enters here, and that sets up the circumcision crisis of 4:24–26.
