## What the chapter is doing
- God speaks the Ten Commandments to the whole nation. He opens with who he is and what he did: "I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" (20:1–2).
- The first group is about God: no other gods, no idols, don't misuse his name, keep the Sabbath (20:3–11).
- The second group is about neighbors: honor parents, don't murder, commit adultery, steal, lie in court or covet (20:12–17).
- The people are terrified by the thunder and smoke and beg Moses to speak to them instead of God (20:18–21).
- God gives the first instructions about altars: no gods of silver or gold, an altar of earth or uncut stone, no steps (20:22–26).

## Pay attention to this
- **"The ten words."** The Bible itself calls them *'aseret haddevarim*, "the ten words" (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13). "Commandments" is the English tradition. 🔴
- **Rescue before rules (20:2).** God says who he is and what he's already done before he asks anything. 🔴
- **"Yahweh your God."** LSB keeps the personal name where most English Bibles print "the LORD." 🔴
- **"No other gods before Me" (20:3).** It doesn't say other gods don't exist. It says Israel gets none of them. 🔴
- **Jealous (20:5).** God's jealousy is a husband's, not a rival's: he won't share his people. 🔴
- **Three or four generations, then thousands (20:5–6).** Judgment is short; lovingkindness (*chesed*) runs to thousands. 🔴
- **The Sabbath rests everyone (20:10).** Sons, daughters, slaves, animals, foreigners. 🔴
- **The Sabbath points back to creation (20:11).** In Deuteronomy 5:15 the reason given is the exodus instead. 🔴
- **Spoken to everyone (20:18–19; Deuteronomy 5:22–27).** The only law the whole nation hears God speak. After this they ask for a mediator. 🔴
- **Coveting (20:17).** The last one is about desire, not action. 🔴
- **Moses goes into the "dense gloom where God was" (20:21).** The people back away; the mediator walks in. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Law codes were common. This one is different.** Hammurabi's laws (around 1750 BC) and older codes from Ur and Eshnunna also ban murder, theft and adultery. What they don't have is a god speaking directly to the whole people, a ban on images, a weekly rest for slaves, or a law against wanting what's not yours. 🔴 for the codes; 🟡 for the contrast on coveting.
- **The shape of a covenant.** ANE treaties opened with the great king's name and past help, then gave the terms. The covenant around the Ten Commandments has that shape. The ten themselves don't match a treaty, though: there's no treaty with a numbered list of ten, and the opening is a self-introduction, not a history. 🟡
- **Images were how gods lived among people.** In Egypt and Mesopotamia a god's statue was where the god dwelt, fed and dressed by priests. Israel isn't allowed to make one. The only image of God on earth is the human being (Genesis 1:27). 🔴
- **The name was a tool in Egypt.** Egyptian magic used divine names to compel the gods. "Don't take the name in vain" rules out using Yahweh's name as a lever, along with false oaths. 🔴 for Egyptian name-magic; 🟡 for this being the main point of the third commandment.
- **A week with no omens.** Other peoples had unlucky days tied to the moon and omens. Israel's Sabbath is a weekly holy day tied to creation and freedom. 🔴
- **Divine council:** "no other gods before Me" assumes there are other *elohim* in the picture. The Old Testament treats them as real, created beings who rebelled (Deuteronomy 32:17 calls them demons), not as nothing. The command is loyalty to Israel's God over all of them. 🟡

## My notes
- **What I wanted to know.** Why did the Ten Commandments need to be given at all, why do Christians honor these ten and ignore the other 613 laws, and why was this so important that it had to be spoken out loud to the whole nation, when a lot of it (don't kill, don't cheat on your wife, don't lie) is already written on the heart?
- **How they're counted.** Three traditions. Jewish (20:2 as the first word), Augustinian (Catholic and Lutheran: 1 and 2 merged, coveting split in two), and Reformed, Orthodox and Anglican (following Philo and Josephus: no other gods and no images separate, coveting one). Keil and Delitzsch: Scripture gives no guidance on how to divide them. 🔴 for the history.
- **The treaty correction.** I first had the treaty parallel as settled. Corrected to 🟡: the covenant framework is treaty-shaped (Mendenhall), but the ten themselves aren't (Blenkinsopp). The same form also shows up in Assyrian treaties from Jeremiah's time, so it doesn't prove an early date. ❌ for the 🔴.
- **The prologue.** Rescue first, then the rules. The law is the household code for people already in the house, not an entrance exam. The verb is *hotzetikha*, "I caused you to go out," and the Greek has *exegagon*. They were *'eved* (slaves) in Egypt.
- **Why these ten hold their place.** Not the moral, civil and ceremonial grid. The Torah doesn't draw that line; it's a later Christian tool (Walton's critique, carried over from my capital-offenses study). The text itself sets these ten apart: the only law spoken aloud to the whole nation (20:18–19; Deuteronomy 5:22–27), written by God's finger (31:18; 32:16), the only text put in the ark, and given twice.
- **The package deal.** Commandments 6–10 are open to conscience and match ANE law codes. Commandments 1–4 can't be reached by natural reason. The ten weld Israel's covenant distinctives to the moral floor, so you can't take one table without the other. That's a jayms.com post: "Why You Can't Keep the Second Table Without the First." 🟡
- **The law diagnoses; it doesn't cure.** Galatians 3:19; Romans 7:7. The heart-writing of Jeremiah 31:33 is the new covenant's difference: stone first, hearts later.
- **The Egypt mirror.** Where the anti-Egyptian reading holds (commandments 1–4) and where it breaks (6–10). 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- The Book of the Covenant (chs. 21–23) opens. The first law after the Ten Commandments is about Hebrew servants: six years of service, free in the seventh, with no payment (21:1–4).
- A servant who loves his master and family can choose to stay for life. His ear is pierced at the doorpost (21:5–6).
- Protections for a daughter sold as a servant-wife: she can be redeemed, can't be sold to foreigners, and can't be shortchanged on food, clothing or marriage rights (21:7–11).
- Laws on killing and injury: murder, manslaughter and a place of refuge, striking or cursing parents, kidnapping, fights, and "eye for eye" (21:12–27).
- Laws on goring oxen and open pits: who's responsible when an animal or a hole kills or injures (21:28–36).

## Pay attention to this
- **The first law is about slaves (21:2).** God's first ruling for a people just freed from slavery limits servitude. 🔴
- **Six years, then free "without payment" (21:2).** It echoes the six-and-seven rhythm of the Sabbath. 🔴
- **"I love my master" (21:5).** The lifelong option is the servant's choice, out of love for the household. 🔴
- **"Bring him to God" (21:6).** The Hebrew is *ha'elohim*. Some translations say "to the judges." 🔴 for the wording; ⬜ for what it means.
- **The doorpost (21:6).** The same kind of doorpost that held the Passover blood. 🟡
- **Kidnapping is a capital crime (21:16).** Stealing a person to sell or keep gets the death penalty. 🔴
- **A slave's eye or tooth sets him free (21:26–27).** A master who injures a slave loses the slave. 🔴
- **"He is his property" (21:21).** Literally "he is his silver." The text says it plainly, and there's no softening it. 🔴
- **Eye for eye (21:23–25).** A rule for judges to fit the penalty to the harm, not a license for personal revenge. 🔴 for its place in a law code; 🟡 for the limiting purpose.
- **Responsibility for what you own (21:28–36).** An owner who knew his ox gored and didn't pen it is liable. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Debt slavery was how the poor survived.** Across the ANE, people sold themselves or their children into service to pay debts. Hammurabi's laws release debt slaves after three years. Israel's law limits it to six and frees them with nothing owed. 🔴
- **Eye for eye was a known rule.** Hammurabi has it too, but there the penalty depends on class: injure a noble and you lose your eye, injure a commoner and you pay silver. Exodus applies it the same to everyone except the slave, who walks free instead (21:26–27). 🔴 for Hammurabi; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **The goring ox.** The goring ox shows up in Hammurabi and the laws of Eshnunna too. Israel's version adds that the ox is stoned and not eaten: a human life is on it. 🔴
- **Ear piercing.** Marking a lifelong servant at the household's door made him part of the house. Deuteronomy 15:17 repeats the rite. 🔴
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. "Bring him to God (*ha'elohim*)" in 21:6 (and again in 22:8–9) is the one place *elohim* language shows up. It could mean God at the sanctuary, judges acting for God, or household gods in older custom. ⬜

## My notes
- These are my notes on Wes Huff's sermon on Exodus 21 (March 2026). They're thin as exegesis: a sermon, not my own study of the chapter's Hebrew.
- **Context.** These laws were given to a people just freed from 400 years in Egypt. The seventh-year release was revolutionary in the ANE.
- **Choosing to stay.** The awl through the ear marks a servant choosing to stay out of love for his master and family.
- **Owning people fights the image of God.** Gregory of Nyssa: humans are owners of the earth by God's decree, and putting them under the yoke fights God's order. Because people are *tselem*, God's image, they can't be priced like property. 🔴 for Gregory.
- **Allowed is not approved.** The "hardness of hearts" principle from Matthew 19: God regulates broken systems to limit cruelty while pointing to something higher. 🟡
- **The abolitionists.** Wilberforce argued from equal, intrinsic human value. 🔴
- **What kind of service.** From my reparations work and my Paul *doulos* post: Hebrew service was closer to indentured service with release protections (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15; Leviticus 25), different from Roman and American chattel slavery, where people were owned as property for life. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Laws for honest courts: no false reports, no following the crowd, no bribes, no favoritism to rich or poor (23:1–3, 6–8).
- Help your enemy's lost or fallen animal (23:4–5). Don't oppress the foreigner, "for you also were sojourners in the land of Egypt" (23:9).
- A seventh-year rest for the land, so the poor and the wild animals can eat, and a seventh-day rest for workers and animals (23:10–12).
- Three yearly feasts: Unleavened Bread, Harvest and Ingathering. Bring the first fruits to God's house. "You shall not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother" (23:14–19).
- God will send his angel ahead of Israel, with God's name in him, to bring them into the land. No covenants with the peoples there or their gods (23:20–33).

## Pay attention to this
- **Help the enemy's donkey (23:4–5).** The law reaches into how you treat someone who hates you. 🔴
- **No favoritism either way (23:3, 6).** Don't tilt for the poor man just because he's poor, and don't twist justice against him. 🔴
- **"You know the soul of a sojourner" (23:9).** Israel's own memory of Egypt is the reason. 🔴
- **The land rests too (23:10–11).** The seventh year's leftovers belong to the poor and the animals. 🔴
- **"Do not mention the name of other gods" (23:13).** Not even in your mouth. 🔴
- **"None shall appear before Me empty-handed" (23:15).** 🔴
- **Firstfruits and the goat in one verse (23:19).** "Bring the choice first fruits... You shall not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother." The two are placed side by side here, at 34:26, and near the tithe law in Deuteronomy 14:21. 🔴
- **"My name is in him" (23:20–21).** The angel who leads Israel carries God's own name and can pardon or refuse to pardon sin. 🔴
- **Little by little (23:29–30).** God won't clear the land in one year, so it doesn't go wild. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Courts ran on witnesses.** With no forensic evidence, a case lived or died on testimony. A false witness or a bribe could kill an innocent man (23:7). 🔴
- **Three pilgrim feasts.** Barley harvest in spring (Unleavened Bread), wheat harvest in early summer (Harvest, later Pentecost) and the fall fruit harvest (Ingathering, later Booths). Neighboring peoples tied harvest feasts to fertility gods. Israel ties them to Yahweh and the exodus. 🔴
- **The Ugaritic "kid in milk" ritual is a myth.** For a long time study Bibles said 23:19 banned a Canaanite fertility rite from Ugarit. The broken Ugaritic line that was supposed to prove it reads closer to "coriander with milk." Scholars have dropped it (Branch, *Dictionary of Daily Life*, 1:227–228). Older references like Unger's still carry it. 🔴 that the parallel is dead.
- **Divine council: the angel with God's name.** In Heiser's frame this is the angel of Yahweh, Yahweh himself in visible form: he has God's name "in him" and can forgive or refuse to forgive. It's a key text for what Heiser calls Israel's "two Yahwehs," one invisible and one visible. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for Heiser's reading.
- **Sacred pillars (23:24).** Standing stones (*matsevot*) marked Canaanite shrines and stood for gods. Israel is told to smash them. 🔴
- **Hornets (23:28).** It may be literal, or a figure for panic. Some have suggested it's a symbol for Egypt's power, since a bee was an Egyptian royal emblem. 🔵

## My notes
- **The law that breaks the "arbitrary list."** I singled this one out. Goat is clean. Milk is clean. Nobody is banned from eating either one. The ban is entirely about the combination, so there's no possible health angle.
- **Myth Busters: the Ugaritic ritual.** The story everybody tells is that it was a Canaanite fertility ritual and God banned it to keep Israel from copying it. The Ugaritic text doesn't say that. The parallel rested on a misread broken text and scholars have abandoned it. Nobody's lying; everybody's standing downstream of a mistake nobody went back to check. 🔴 dead.
- **Read the cluster.** With Deuteronomy 22:6–7 (let the mother bird go), Leviticus 22:28 (not mother and young on the same day) and 22:27 (eight days with the mother first), it's one shape: the bond between mother and young is protected, even inside the killing. That milk existed to make the kid live. Turning it into the thing you cook the kid in runs creation backwards. A man who'd do that has stopped noticing, and that's exactly what this whole system exists to prevent. 🟡, my preferred reading.
- **Where it sits.** All three times it's bolted onto firstfruits and the firstborn. God gets the firstborn, and you don't boil the firstborn in the milk that made him. 🟡
- **Other readings.** Revowel *chalav* (milk) as *chelev* (fat): 🔵. The rabbinic threefold reading (don't eat, use or cook meat with dairy) is where kosher meat-and-dairy separation comes from, but that's how the verse was received later, not what it meant first (Carasik, 308).

## What the chapter is doing
- Moses tells the people all God's words and judgments. They answer with one voice, "All the words which Yahweh has spoken we will do!" (24:1–3).
- Moses writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, and sacrifices are offered (24:4–5).
- He reads the book of the covenant, the people promise again, and he throws half the blood on the altar and half on the people: "the blood of the covenant" (24:6–8).
- Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders go up, see the God of Israel standing on what looks like a sapphire pavement, and eat and drink. God doesn't strike them (24:9–11).
- Moses goes up into the cloud for the stone tablets. The glory sits on the mountain like a consuming fire, and Moses stays forty days and forty nights (24:12–18).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Moses wrote down all the words of Yahweh" (24:4).** One of the few places the Torah shows Moses writing. 🔴
- **Twelve pillars (24:4).** The whole people is represented at the altar. 🔴
- **Blood on the altar and on the people (24:6–8).** Half to God's side, half to the people's: both parties bound by the same blood. 🔴
- **"The blood of the covenant" (24:8).** Jesus uses these words at the Last Supper: "this is My blood of the covenant" (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28). 🔴
- **The promise twice (24:3, 7).** "We will do," then "we will do, and we will be obedient." Within weeks they make the golden calf (ch. 32). 🔴
- **"They saw the God of Israel" (24:10).** The text says it plainly, then only describes what was under his feet. 🔴
- **"He did not stretch out His hand against" them (24:11).** Seeing God should have been fatal. It wasn't. 🔴
- **"They ate and drank" (24:11).** The covenant ends in a meal in God's presence. 🔴
- **Six days, then the seventh (24:16).** The cloud covers the mountain six days, and God calls on the seventh. Genesis 1's rhythm. 🔴
- **Forty days and forty nights (24:18).** 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Covenants were cut with blood.** "Cut a covenant" (24:8) was the ordinary phrase, because treaties were sealed by killing an animal; the parties took on its fate if they broke faith (compare Genesis 15; Jeremiah 34:18). 🔴
- **Covenants were written down.** ANE treaties were put in writing and read to the people. Moses writes and reads "the book of the covenant." 🔴
- **A meal sealed the deal.** Eating together finished an agreement and showed peace between the parties. Here Israel's leaders eat in God's own presence. 🔴
- **The sapphire floor.** Probably lapis lazuli, the deep blue stone tied to heaven in Mesopotamia and used in temple decoration. The elders see the floor of heaven. Ezekiel 1:26 sees the same blue stone under God's throne. 🔴 for lapis; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Divine council: seventy elders.** At Ugarit, the high god El had seventy sons, and Genesis 10 lists seventy nations. Here seventy elders sit with the God of Israel on his mountain and eat. Heiser reads Israel's leadership here as an earthly picture of God's council. 🟡

## My notes
- **24:9–11.** Seventy elders with Moses, Aaron, Nadab and Abihu see God and live. God "did not lay his hand on them." The line assumes that seeing God could normally kill you, and "they ate and drank" may mark that they survived (Collins, *Introduction to the Hebrew Bible*, 136). 🟡
- **What it does to the "visitor model."** This was offered as proof that humans don't belong in divine space. Like Sinai in ch. 19, it sits after Genesis 3, and it fits the model where heaven and earth intersect, not divine territory closed to people.
- **24:4, Moses writes the terms.** One of three moments the Torah shows Moses writing (with Exodus 17:14 and Deuteronomy 31:9, 24–26). Scripture as the written authority of the relationship, "like marriage vows committed to writing" (Mackie, BibleProject classroom). That's part of my How We Got the Bible work. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Moses, now a shepherd for his father-in-law Jethro, comes to Horeb, "the mountain of God," and sees a bush burning that doesn't burn up (3:1–3).
- God calls him by name, tells him to take off his sandals on holy ground, and names himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (3:4–6).
- God has seen, heard and known Israel's suffering, has "come down" to rescue them, and is sending Moses to Pharaoh (3:7–10).
- Moses objects: "Who am I?" God answers, "I will be with you," and gives his name: "I AM WHO I AM," Yahweh (3:11–15).
- God lays out the plan: gather the elders, ask Pharaoh for a three-day trip to sacrifice, expect a refusal, expect wonders, and Israel won't leave empty-handed (3:16–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **The angel of Yahweh in the fire, then God speaks (3:2–4).** The angel appears; Yahweh sees; God calls from the bush. The text moves between them as if they're the same. 🔴
- **Holy ground (3:5).** The ground is holy because God is there. It's the same mountain where Israel will meet him in ch. 19. 🔴
- **Moses hides his face (3:6).** He's afraid to look at God. 🔴
- **Seen, heard, know, come down (3:7–8).** The verbs from 2:24–25 come back, and now God acts. "Come down" is the verb of Babel (Genesis 11:5). 🔴
- **"Who am I?" (3:11).** God doesn't answer the question about Moses. He answers with himself: "I will be with you" (3:12). 🔴
- **"I will be" and "I AM" (3:12, 14).** The same Hebrew verb, *'ehyeh*. "I will be with you" and "I AM WHO I AM" (*'ehyeh 'asher 'ehyeh*) are tied together in the Hebrew. 🔴
- **The name (3:15).** Yahweh, built on the verb "to be," is "My name forever." 🔴
- **The sign comes after (3:12).** Proof Moses was sent: they'll worship at this mountain. He has to go before he gets it. 🔴
- **"A three days' journey" (3:18).** The first request is to go worship, not to leave for good. 🔴
- **"You will not go empty" (3:21–22).** The women ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver, gold and clothing. "Thus you will plunder the Egyptians." 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **Names carried power.** In Egypt, knowing a god's secret name gave you a hold on it (there's a story of Isis tricking Ra into telling his). Moses asks for God's name, and God gives one that can't be used as a handle: "I AM WHO I AM." 🔴 for the Egyptian belief; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **Mountains were where gods lived.** Horeb is "the mountain of God" before Moses arrives. Across the ANE, sacred mountains were the meeting point of heaven and earth. 🔴
- **Bare feet in holy places.** Priests served barefoot in sanctuaries, in Israel and elsewhere. Taking off your sandals marked the place as belonging to the god. 🔴
- **Divine council: the angel of Yahweh.** The angel appears in the fire, and then Yahweh speaks from the same fire. In Heiser's frame he's Yahweh in visible form, the second figure who is Yahweh and is sent by Yahweh. It's the same angel who later goes before Israel with God's name "in him" (23:20–21). 🟡
- **"The God of the Hebrews" (3:18).** Pharaoh would hear a tribal god of a slave people, one god among Egypt's many. The plagues answer that. 🔴
- **The Canaanite list (3:8, 17).** Six peoples in the land: the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite and Jebusite. A first reader knew that land wasn't empty. 🔴

## My notes
- **The plundering (3:21–22).** I've heard this used as a biblical case for reparations to Black Americans. I tested it on three points and each held up:
  - The bondage was state-imposed forced labor, closer to corvée than to chattel slavery as a legal system. Harsh labor and brick quotas were how labor worked in a lot of places, even in America until the 20th century.
  - The silver and gold read as the spoils of war. There was a battle between God and Pharaoh, God won, and took the spoils. It isn't back wages.
  - It was a one-time thing for that generation, to start their new nation. It isn't a payment passed down four generations or made for the rest of their lives.
- **Where that leaves it.** Real theological echo between liberation and provision. Not a structural precedent for modern policy. The parallel verses are 11:2–3 and 12:35–36. 🟡
- **3:14.** "I AM WHO I AM" is Yahweh declaring absolute existence and authority at the head of the council. My category frame: *elohim* is what a spiritual being is, but the Name is who God alone is. Only Yahweh is un-originated. Jesus reaches for the Name, not the category, in John 8:58: "before Abraham was, I am."
- **3:18.** The original demand was a three-day trip to worship, not freedom outright. That shapes how the whole negotiation with Pharaoh plays out.

## What the chapter is doing
- Moses keeps objecting. God gives him three signs: the staff that becomes a serpent, the hand that turns leprous and back, and Nile water that turns to blood (4:1–9).
- Moses says he can't speak. God says he made man's mouth. Moses says "send someone else," God gets angry, and Aaron is named as his spokesman (4:10–17).
- Moses heads back to Egypt with his family and the staff of God. God tells him to warn Pharaoh: "Israel is My son, My firstborn... I will kill your son, your firstborn" (4:18–23).
- On the road, Yahweh seeks to kill Moses. Zipporah circumcises their son with a flint, touches his feet with the foreskin, and says, "You are a bridegroom of blood to me." God lets him go (4:24–26).
- Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of God. They gather the elders, do the signs, and the people believe and worship (4:27–31).

## Pay attention to this
- **The staff becomes a serpent (4:3).** Moses runs from it. Then he grabs it by the tail, which is how you get bitten. 🔴
- **"Who has made man's mouth?" (4:11).** God answers Moses's weakness by pointing to himself, again. 🔴
- **God's anger (4:14).** "Send someone else" is the objection that crosses the line. God still gives him Aaron. 🔴
- **"You will become as God to him" (4:16).** Moses will be to Aaron what God is to a prophet. 🔴
- **The first hardening (4:21).** God says "I will harden his heart" before anything has happened. 🔴
- **"Israel is My son, My firstborn" (4:22–23).** The tenth plague is announced here, before the first one. Pharaoh's firstborn for God's firstborn. 🔴
- **The strangest three verses in Exodus (4:24–26).** God has just sent Moses, and now seeks to kill him. 🔴
- **Zipporah acts.** A Midianite woman knows what to do and does it fast. 🔴
- **"Bridegroom of blood" (4:25–26).** *Chatan damim*. The phrase shows up only here. 🔴
- **Flint (4:25).** Joshua uses flint knives for the circumcision at Gilgal too (Joshua 5:2–3). 🔴
- **Whose feet?** "His feet" could mean Moses or the boy, and "feet" (*raglayim*) is sometimes a polite word for genitals in Hebrew. 🔴 that the Hebrew is open.

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **The serpent was Pharaoh's symbol.** The cobra (uraeus) reared up on the front of Pharaoh's crown as a sign of his power and his gods' protection. A shepherd's staff that becomes a serpent, controlled by a man who grabs it by the tail, says something about who really holds Pharaoh's power. 🔴 for the uraeus; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Egyptians practiced circumcision.** Egyptian priests and some men were circumcised, likely at puberty or before marriage, and Egyptian art shows it. In Israel it was done to baby boys, as the sign of Abraham's covenant (Genesis 17). 🔴
- **Genesis 17:14.** An uncircumcised male "shall be cut off from his people; he has broken My covenant." Moses's own son is outside the covenant he's about to bring to a nation. 🔴
- **The firstborn was the heir.** In an ANE household the firstborn son carried the family name and the double share. Calling Israel God's firstborn is a claim of household: these people belong to my house, not Pharaoh's. 🔴
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. The confrontation with Egypt's gods starts in ch. 7 and is named in 12:12. In my post I frame 4:24–26 as Yahweh asserting authority over his appointed servant's household at the threshold of the mission. 🟡

## My notes
- **The weird stuff is where the theology is.** Churches skip passages like this one. The weird stuff is usually where the deepest theology lives.
- **Moses wasn't careless. He was hedging.** I don't think it was an accident his son wasn't circumcised. He'd had the burning bush, he knew what he was called to do, but he hadn't fully committed. An uncircumcised son kept an exit ramp open in Egypt: citizenship, inheritance. Yahweh's response was immediate and severe: you don't get to do this halfway. 🔵 (this is my inference; I have no source for the citizenship angle)
- **You can't be called and then do it your way.** The calling was real. Being called doesn't mean you execute it on your own terms. You can't serve Yahweh with one foot out the door.
- **Zipporah's act is Moses's act.** Genesis 2:24: the two become one flesh. When she circumcises the son and touches Moses with the blood, that isn't a third party covering for him. It's Moses doing it through her, because they're covenantally one. Her faithfulness is his.
- **The household is the covenant unit.** Moses can't mediate a covenant to a nation while his own house sits outside it. Passover marks households together (12:3–4), and "as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh" (Joshua 24:15). A Midianite woman does the covenant work the called man failed to do.
- **The honest limit.** In May I added a line to my post: this household-authority reading follows the divine council framework, it isn't proven from three verses alone, and it isn't the only reading available.

## Pay attention to this
- **"I set you as God to Pharaoh" (7:1).** The word is *elohim*. Pharaoh claimed to be a god; God makes Moses one to him. 🔴
- **"My hosts" (7:4).** God calls Israel his *tseva'ot*, his armies. The slaves are an army in God's eyes. 🔴
- **"That the Egyptians shall know that I am Yahweh" (7:5, 17).** The point of the plagues is stated over and over: knowing who Yahweh is. 🔴
- **A different serpent (7:9–12).** In 4:3 the staff became a *nachash*. Here it becomes a *tannin*, the word for a sea monster or dragon. 🔴
- **Aaron's staff swallows theirs (7:12).** The magicians can match the trick, not the outcome. 🔴
- **The hardening verbs.** Exodus uses three different Hebrew words for Pharaoh's heart: "strong" (*chazaq*), "heavy" (*kaved*) and "hard" (*qashah*). English Bibles often flatten them all to "hardened." 🔴
- **Pharaoh "went into his house" (7:23).** He doesn't even take it to heart. 🔴
- **The magicians copy, they can't undo (7:22).** They make more blood. They can't make clean water. 🔴
- **Seven days (7:25).** The first plague lasts a full week. 🔴

## Read it like 1446 BC, not 2026
- **The Nile was a god's gift.** The yearly flood that made Egypt possible was worshiped as Hapi, and Khnum was said to guard the Nile's source. Turning the river to blood hits the center of Egypt's life and religion. 🔴 for the gods; 🔵 for matching this plague to one god in particular.
- **Pharaoh going out to the water (7:15).** Pharaoh's morning trip to the Nile may have been a ritual, the god-king at the sacred river. 🔵
- **A heavy heart.** In the Egyptian Book of the Dead, a dead person's heart is weighed against the feather of *ma'at*. A heavy heart failed and was devoured. Exodus keeps saying Pharaoh's heart was "heavy" (*kaved*). A first reader who knew that picture would hear Pharaoh failing the judgment while he's still alive. 🔴 for the weighing; 🟡 for the link.
- **Serpents and staffs.** Egyptian magicians were known for handling snakes, and the cobra was Pharaoh's royal emblem. Aaron's serpent eating theirs is a power statement in Egypt's own symbols. 🔴 for the background; 🟡 for the reading.
- **The *chartummim* were scholars.** The word for the magicians is borrowed from Egyptian and means something like a lector-priest, the learned men who read the sacred and ritual texts. 🔴
- **Divine council: the gods of Egypt.** In Heiser's frame the plagues dismantle Egypt's pantheon domain by domain before Egypt and before the heavenly council, and 12:12 names it: judgment "on all the gods of Egypt." 🔴 for 12:12; 🟡 for the domain-by-domain frame.

- **Two units, two titles.** The "ruler" (*nagid*) of Tyre in 28:1–10, the "king" (*melek*) of Tyre in 28:11–19. Both target a human ruler. 🔴
- **"I am a god" against "you are a man" (28:2, 9).** The prophet repeats it so nobody misses it. 🔴
- **"Wiser than Daniel" (28:3).** Ezekiel also names Daniel with Noah and Job (14:14, 20). The spelling is *Dan'el*. 🔴
- **"You were in Eden, the garden of God" (28:13).** Eden is called God's garden, not Adam's. 🔴
- **Nine stones (28:13).** Ruby, topaz, diamond, beryl, onyx, jasper, lapis lazuli, turquoise, emerald. All nine are among the twelve on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17–20). The Greek translation lists all twelve. 🔴
- **"The anointed cherub who covers" (28:14).** A cherub is a throne guardian, like the ones at Eden's gate (Genesis 3:24) and over the ark. 🔴
- **The Greek reads 28:14 differently.** The Septuagint has "with the cherub I placed you," which makes the figure a companion of the cherub, not the cherub itself. 🔴 that the versions differ.
- **"The holy mountain of God" (28:14, 16).** Eden is a garden on a mountain. 🔴
- **"Stones of fire" (28:14, 16).** The phrase only appears here. What they are is argued. ⬜
- **"Created" (28:13, 15).** *Bara'*, the Genesis 1 verb. This being was made. 🔴
- **"Until unrighteousness was found in you" (28:15).** Blameless first, then a fall. 🔴

## Read it like 586 BC, not 2026
- **Tyre was the richest port in the world.** An island city off the Phoenician coast, it ran sea trade across the Mediterranean (chapter 27 lists its cargo). It held out against Nebuchadnezzar for thirteen years (about 585–572 BC). "In the heart of the seas" is literal. 🔴
- **"I sit in the seat of gods" is council language.** "Seat of the gods" (*moshab elohim*) and the god's home "in the heart of the seas" echo Ugaritic descriptions of El's dwelling at the source of the rivers, where the council met. The king's boast puts him in the divine assembly from the first lines. 🔴 for the Ugaritic parallels (Heiser, Naked Bible 143; *Unseen Realm*).
- **Eden is God's dwelling.** In the ancient Near East a god lived in a garden on a mountain, with water flowing out. Ezekiel 28:13–14 and 31:8–9 call Eden the garden of God on the holy mountain, with a cherub as its keeper. That makes Eden divine space first and human space second. 🔴 (Dumbrell; Hendel; my Unseen Realm 101 Session 5 notes).
- **Wise Dan'el was famous before the book of Daniel.** Ugaritic texts tell of Dan'el, a just king and judge, father of Aqhat. Ezekiel's "Daniel" next to Noah and Job (14:14) may be that ancient figure, which would fit a Phoenician audience. 🟡
- **Two readings of the comparison.** Everyone agrees the target is the human king. The fight is over who he's being compared to:
  - **Adam in Eden.** The first human in God's garden. Dumbrell points out the stones match the high priest's breastpiece, which gives the garden's first resident a priestly and royal character. Walton and Walton (*Demons and Spirits* 218) lean cautiously this way. Heiser's own *Demons* (71) takes it seriously. 🟡
  - **A divine rebel.** Heiser: Eden on the mountain of God, a guardian cherub (a divine category, never used of Adam), the stones of fire as the council's setting, and a boast lifted from Ugaritic council language. 🟡, and Heiser calls it his own minority view.
- **Heiser's sharpest argument.** Adam was already on earth, so he couldn't be thrown down to it. Being cast to the ground and sentenced to the pit fits a heavenly being expelled, not a human (*Unseen Realm* 93). It rests on the story's logic, not on a word. 🟡
- **Van Dijk's proposal.** Read "the seal" (*chotem*, 28:12) as a word for "serpent." Suggestive, not settled. 🔵
- **The serpent and the rebel.** The figure wouldn't live under God's wisdom and wanted to be God, the same temptation the serpent offers in Genesis 3:5. 🟡
- **"Ezekiel 28 is about Satan" came later.** Bullinger says Ezekiel 28 describes Satan in Eden, and the *Bible Knowledge Commentary* (Dyer 1:1283) says Satan is the true king behind Tyre. Both mix up "about" and "behind." The chapter is about a king. 🔴 for what the text names.

- I laid out both readings side by side. Adam in Eden: many commentators, Dumbrell on the breastpiece stones, Walton and Walton cautious, and Heiser's own *Demons* grants it as serious. Divine rebel: Heiser, on the cherub, the mountain, the stones of fire and the Ugaritic boast.
- **The sharpest argument is Heiser's in *Unseen Realm* 93.** Adam was already on earth and couldn't be sentenced to the underworld by being thrown down. That fits a heavenly being. It's from the story, not from wordplay, so it doesn't depend on a pun. I also noted van Dijk's "serpent" reading of 28:12.

## META: the book of Genesis
- **Where it sits.** First book of the Torah and the foundation for everything after it. It starts with the whole world and ends with one family living in Egypt, which is exactly where Exodus picks up. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** the world God made went wrong, so what is he going to do about it, and through whom?
- **Two halves.** Chapters 1–11 are about all of humanity (creation, the fall, the flood, Babel). Chapters 12–50 narrow to one family (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph). The seam is 11 into 12: God scatters the nations at Babel, and the very next thing he does is call Abram. 🔴
- **Narrowing so it can widen.** God goes from the world to one man, but the reason he gives is the world: "in you all the families of the earth will be blessed" (12:3). 🔴
- **The chapter headings are built in.** The phrase "these are the generations of" (*toledot*) shows up ten times (eleven if you count Esau's twice in ch. 36) and divides the book into sections: 2:4, 5:1, 6:9, 10:1, 11:10, 11:27, 25:12, 25:19, 36:1, 37:2. 🔴
- **Who wrote it.** Jewish and Christian tradition says Moses. The book itself never names its author. Moses could have shaped older material, and a later hand updated some place names ("Dan" in 14:14 is named after a tribe that didn't exist yet). ⬜
- **When.** The stories run from creation to roughly the 1800s–1600s BC (Joseph in Egypt). If Moses is behind it, the book took shape around the exodus, which I put in the 1400s BC. 🟡
- **The text issue that's real.** The ages in the family trees of chs. 5 and 11 differ between the Hebrew (MT), the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek (LXX). The Greek adds centuries. Anyone building a date for creation out of those numbers has to pick a text first. 🔴
- **Movements:** chs. 1–11 the primeval story, 12–25 Abraham, 25–36 Jacob, 37–50 Joseph.
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - Three rebellions, each answered by God: Eden (ch. 3, answered by the promise in 3:15), the sons of God (ch. 6, answered by Noah), Babel (ch. 11, answered by Abram).
  - The seed: who carries the promise, and how often it looks like it will die out (barren wives, younger sons, a brother sold into slavery).
  - The heavenly host: "Let Us" (1:26), "like one of Us" (3:22), the sons of God (6:2), "let Us go down" (11:7), the angels on the ladder (28:12).
  - Genesis and Revelation mirror each other: tree of life, river, God dwelling with people, Babylon founded and Babylon destroyed.

## What the chapter is doing
- God speaks a dark, watery, empty world into order in six days and rests on the seventh.
- Two panels. Days 1–3 make the spaces (light and dark, sky and sea, dry land). Days 4–6 fill them (lights, birds and fish, animals and people). Day 7 stands outside the pattern.
- That explains why light comes before the sun and why people come last.
- Humans are made "in Our image," male and female, blessed, and given a job: fill the earth, subdue it, rule over the creatures.
- God looks at the whole thing and calls it "very good."

## Pay attention to this
- **Nothing fights God.** The deep and the waters are just there in 1:2. Nobody resists, there's no battle, and God orders everything by talking. 🔴
- **"Formless and void" (1:2).** *Tohu wabohu*. The words mean empty, useless, nothing working yet, more than "shapeless." Isaiah 45:18 uses *tohu* the same way: God did not make the earth to be empty, he formed it to be lived in. 🔴
- **The Spirit "hovering" (1:2).** The verb is *rachaph*. In this form it shows up only here and in Deuteronomy 32:11, where an eagle hovers over its young. 🔴
- **God names things (1:5, 8, 10).** Day, night, heaven, earth, seas. Naming is ruling. Later God brings the animals to Adam to name. 🔴
- **"Great sea monsters" (1:21).** *Tanninim*, the same word other texts use for chaos dragons. Here they're just one more thing God made, and he calls them good. 🔴 for the word, 🟡 for reading it as a jab at the dragon myths.
- **The sun and moon have no names (1:16).** "The greater light" and "the lesser light." Israel's neighbors worshiped them as gods. Genesis gives them a job: lamps, and markers for "signs and seasons." 🟡
- **"Let Us" (1:26), then "He created" (1:27).** Plural when God speaks, singular when God acts. 🔴
- **Image and rule come together (1:26–28).** Being made in God's image comes packaged with the job of ruling and filling the earth. 🔴
- **"Very good" (1:31).** Six times "good," then once "very good" when people are in it. The word is *tov me'od*, not *tamim* (flawless). The command to subdue the earth assumes there's work left to do. 🔴
- **Plants only (1:29–30).** People and animals get plants for food. Meat comes after the flood (9:3). 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **Everybody had a creation story.** Babylon had *Enuma Elish*: Marduk kills the sea goddess Tiamat and builds the world out of her body. Egypt had its own. Genesis uses the same furniture (waters, a dome, lights) and refuses the fight. 🔴
- **"The deep" (*tehom*).** Older scholars tied the word to Tiamat. Ugaritic texts took most of that apart. The contrast still holds either way: in Genesis the waters are not a rival god. 🔴 for the no-combat contrast, 🟡 for the exact word history.
- **Existing meant having a job.** Walton's point: in the ancient world a thing existed when it had a function in an ordered system. A 2026 reader asks "what is it made of and how long did it take?" The first reader asked "who put this in order, and what is it for?" Walton reads Day 1 as God making time (a period of light called "day"), which is why light can come before the sun. 🟡
- **The sky is a solid dome.** The "expanse" (*raqia*, 1:6–8) holds back the waters above. Israel shared that picture with its neighbors, and God didn't stop to correct it. Genesis is teaching who runs the cosmos, not its physics. 🔴
- **The sun and moon were gods next door.** Shamash in Babylon, Ra in Egypt. Calling them "lights" and putting them to work is a demotion. 🟡
- **Only kings were images.** In Egypt and Mesopotamia the king was the image of a god. Genesis gives that title to every human, male and female. 🔴
- **Idols needed a mouth opened.** In the "washing of the mouth" ritual priests opened an idol's mouth so the god could come in and live in it. In Genesis the living God makes his own image out of dust and breathes into it (2:7). He doesn't need a wooden one. 🔴 for the ritual; 🟡 for the polemic.
- **Rest means rule.** When an ANE god "rested," he moved into his finished temple and took the throne. Day 7 is God taking his seat over a finished world, not God tired out. 🟡
- **Divine council: "Let Us make man" (1:26).** God is speaking to the heavenly host around his throne (Heiser). The plural is not the Trinity (it switches straight back to singular in 1:27, and 11:5–7 has Yahweh already down when he says "let Us go down"), and it's not a "plural of majesty," which Hebrew uses on nouns but never on verbs or pronouns like this. The host hears the announcement. God alone creates. 🟡 for the council reading; 🔴 that the grammar rules out majesty.

## My notes
- **Two panels.** That's how I see the chapter: form the spaces, fill the spaces, then God rests over it. Walton pushed me further. The chapter is mostly about giving everything its job and its place, not a manufacturing report.
- **1:2, "hovering."** I asked whether *rachaph* also means love. It doesn't, by itself. The "brooding" idea comes from a Syriac word, and John Day shows that sense is secondary even in Syriac; every ancient translation read motion. Leupold: how the Bible uses a word outranks what a cousin language does with it. The tenderness is real, and it arrives through the eagle in Deuteronomy 32:11, which also shares the word *tohu* with 1:2 (Deut 32:10). The love is in the eagle, not the verb. That became my jayms.com post "The Eagle Over the Nest." 🔴
- ***Rachaph* and *racham*.** One letter apart, and *racham* is womb and compassion. Tempting. The roots aren't related. 🔴
- **The rabbis saw the eagle too.** Ben Zoma (Tosefta Hagigah 2) ties 1:2 to the eagle of Deut 32:11, "touching and not touching." The dove version only turns up in the Babylonian Talmud (Hagigah 15a), so the eagle looks earlier. 🔴
- **1:26, "Let Us."** I follow Heiser: God is talking to his council. Does that mean the council helped create? No. Deuteronomy 13:1–3 has a "let us" where the people addressed aren't told to do anything. God announces, God creates.
- **Image of God.** Read the little Hebrew preposition as "make humankind *as* our image." The image is something we are, not something we have. Any definition has to fit all of it: men and women equally, only humans, passed to Seth (5:3), still there after the flood (9:6), and never partial.
- **The idols are backwards.** The other nations made idols and opened their mouths so a god could come live in them. Yahweh doesn't need wooden idols. We are the image he placed on earth, and his breath is in us. The idol ritual is a copy and a perversion of God breathing life into man.
- **Ambassador, not "image."** The English word "image" kept confusing me, so I use ambassador. When an ancient king sent someone out as his representative, that person carried the king's power whether he did the job well or badly.
- **Two layers, and the Windex.** The office (being God's image) survives the Fall intact. The ambassadorship, actually representing him well, got distorted. It's a smudged mirror. You don't replace the mirror, you Windex it so it shows the King better. That's what Christ does.
- **Romans 1:19–20 finally made sense.** I used to read it as "look at all this, it couldn't come from chance." Reading Lewis on God's likeness spread through creation, I saw it differently: God put pieces of his own likeness into different things, so people should know him from what he made.
- **How long were the days?** I believe the earth is far older than 6,000 years and that Genesis 1–3 is true and in order. I read "day" (*yom*) as a period of time, not 24 hours. There's no sun until Day 4, so how are we counting days?
- **We're still in the seventh day.** Days 1–6 close with "evening and morning." Day 7 doesn't. I read that as still open, with John 5:17 and Hebrews 3–4: God looking at his creation and saying it's enough, not God tired out.
- **Where I got pushed back, and took it.** I argued that if Daniel's "seventy weeks" aren't literal weeks, Genesis days don't have to be literal either. The counter: Daniel 9 marks itself as non-literal and Genesis 1 doesn't. So my honest claim is that the text *allows* an old earth, not that it *requires* one. I can't prove it from the Hebrew alone, or the young-earth side would have nothing to stand on.
- **Science.** I keep notes on the day-age lineup (a beginning, an early water-covered earth), but Genesis isn't written as a science book. ⬜
- **Divine council:** the hook here is "Let Us" in 1:26. The full scenes come in 3:22, 6:1–4 and 11:7.

## What the chapter is doing
- The Table of Nations: the families that came from Noah's three sons after the flood (10:1, 32).
- Japheth's line spreads to the coastlands and the north (10:2–5).
- Ham's line includes Cush, Egypt (Mizraim), Put and Canaan, and the empire-builder Nimrod (10:6–20).
- Shem's line runs through Eber, the name behind "Hebrew," and splits at Peleg, "for in his days the earth was divided" (10:21–31).
- Each section closes the same way: by families, by languages, by lands, by nations.

## Pay attention to this
- **Languages already split (10:5, 20, 31).** Every section says "according to their tongues." The Babel story in ch. 11, where everyone speaks one language, explains how that happened. Chapter 10 is the result; chapter 11 is the cause. 🔴
- **"The earth was divided" (10:25).** In Peleg's day. *Peleg* sounds like the Hebrew for "divide." It points ahead to the scattering at Babel. 🔴 for the wordplay; 🟡 for the Babel link.
- **Nimrod (10:8–12).** Son of Cush, "a mighty one on the earth," "a mighty hunter before Yahweh." His kingdom starts at Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in Shinar, then he builds Nineveh and Calah in Assyria. Babylon and Assyria, Israel's two great enemies, both start with him. 🔴
- **"Mighty one" (10:8).** *Gibbor*, the same word used for the "mighty men" of 6:4. 🔴 for the word; 🔵 for reading Nimrod as one of them.
- **Canaan's families (10:15–19).** Sidon, Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite and the rest: the peoples Israel would face, with Canaan's borders drawn out. 🔴
- **The Philistines come from Egypt's line (10:14).** 🔴
- **Eber (10:21, 24–25).** Shem is called "the father of all the children of Eber." The line narrows toward Abram (11:10–26). 🔴
- **Names that came back.** Havilah, Cush and Asshur were in the Eden description (2:11–14). They show up here as names on the post-flood map. 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **A nation was a people, not a country.** *Goy* here means a people group tied together by ancestry, language, land and culture. It doesn't mean a modern nation-state with borders and a government. 🔴
- **Seventy nations.** Count the names in the Hebrew text and you get about seventy (the Greek has seventy-two). Seventy was the number of a complete family: Jacob's household that went to Egypt was seventy (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5). 🔴 for the count, with "by some counts."
- **Seventy sons of God.** At Ugarit, the god El and his wife Asherah had seventy sons, the *bn 'il*. Later Jewish tradition gave each of the seventy nations an angel over it. 🔴 for Ugarit and the later tradition.
- **Divine council: Deuteronomy 32:8–9.** When the Most High divided up the nations, he set their boundaries by the number of the sons of God. That's the reading in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4QDeut) and the Greek; the later Hebrew text, and most English Bibles, have "sons of Israel." Israel didn't exist yet. Heiser reads Genesis 10 as the list of nations and Babel (ch. 11) as the moment they're handed to the sons of God, with Israel kept as Yahweh's own portion. 🔴 for the manuscript reading; 🟡 for tying it to Genesis 10–11.
- **Babylon and Nineveh were the big cities.** Babel, Erech (Uruk) and Accad were ancient and famous centers in southern Mesopotamia; Nineveh and Calah became Assyria's capitals. A first reader heard Israel's greatest enemies traced back to one rebel's kingdom. 🔴

## My notes
- **What a "nation" means.** I asked what "nation" refers to in Genesis 10–11. It's an ethnolinguistic people group: ancestry, language, land, culture. Not a nation-state. 🔴
- **Why chapter 10 comes before chapter 11.** I asked why they're in reverse order. Genesis groups things by theme, the same way it sets 1 and 2 side by side. Chapter 10 gives the result (nations spread by language) and then ch. 11 goes back and tells how it happened. The technical name is *Wiederaufnahme*, resuming an earlier story. 🔴
- **The seventy.** The Ugaritic seventy sons of El (Day, *From Creation to Babel*, 79), the later seventy angels over seventy nations (Hess, 147), and Smith's "seventy gods over seventy countries" all line up. The only hedge left is the arithmetic: Genesis 10 reaches seventy "by some counts." 🟡
- **Nimrod.** His name likely comes from *marad*, "to rebel." The hunter line gets read three ways: a literal hunter, a warrior-king, or a hunter of men. Jewish tradition (Josephus, the Midrash) makes him Babel's leader and Abraham's persecutor. The Bible doesn't say either one. 🔴 that the Bible doesn't say it.
- **The rivers.** Havilah, Cush and Asshur are on this map after the flood. That cuts against the claim that the flood relocated Eden's rivers past recognition: the writer is using a map his readers knew.

## What the chapter is doing
- Everyone speaks one language. They settle on a plain in Shinar and decide to build a city and a tower "whose top will reach into heaven," to make a name for themselves and not be scattered (11:1–4).
- Yahweh comes down, says "let Us go down" and confuse their language, and scatters them. The place is called Babel (11:5–9).
- The family line runs from Shem down ten generations to Terah, with lifespans getting shorter (11:10–26).
- Terah's family: Abram, Sarai who is barren, Lot. They leave Ur for Canaan but stop at Haran, and Terah dies there (11:27–32).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Lest we be scattered" (11:4).** God told Noah's family to fill the earth (9:1). Babel is a refusal of that command, and God's answer is the very thing they tried to avoid. 🔴
- **"Make for ourselves a name" (11:4).** In 12:2 God tells Abram, "I will make your name great." What Babel grabbed, God gives. 🔴
- **The name is *shem*.** The mighty men of 6:4 were "men of renown," literally men of the name (*shem*). The builders want a *shem*. And the next family line is Shem's (11:10). 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for reading it as deliberate.
- **Yahweh "came down" (11:5).** The tower meant to reach heaven is so small God has to come down to see it. 🔴
- **Already down, then "let Us go down" (11:5–7).** Yahweh has come down in 11:5, then in 11:7 says "Come, let Us go down." He's speaking to someone. 🔴
- **Babel and *balal* (11:9).** "Babel" sounds like *balal*, "confuse." The Babylonians said their city's name meant "gate of the god." Genesis makes it "confusion." 🔴
- **Brick for stone, tar for mortar (11:3).** The narrator explains Mesopotamian building to readers who built with stone. 🔴
- **Sarai is barren (11:30).** The chapter that ends the primeval history ends on a family with no child, right before God promises Abram a great nation. 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **The tower was a ziggurat.** Mesopotamian temple towers were stepped artificial mountains of fired brick. They weren't for climbing into heaven. They were where the god was believed to come down to meet people, with a temple on top or beside. Babylon's great ziggurat was called Etemenanki, "house of the foundation of heaven and earth." 🔴
- **So the project was about control.** Building a home for a god at a place of your choosing, on your terms, so heaven comes down where you want it. 🟡
- **Divine council: "let Us" (11:7).** God is speaking to his council, as in 1:26 and 3:22. Heiser uses this verse against the Trinity reading of 1:26: Yahweh is already present and still summons someone else to go down with him. 🟡
- **Babel is where the nations get handed over.** Deuteronomy 32:8–9: when the Most High divided the nations, he set their borders by the number of the sons of God (the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek reading), and kept Jacob as his own portion. Israel didn't exist at Babel, so "sons of Israel" in the later Hebrew text doesn't fit. Deuteronomy 4:19–20 is the same deal from the other side: God allotted the sun, moon and stars to the nations and took Israel for himself. 🔴 for the manuscripts; 🟡 for placing it at Babel.
- **Then Abram.** God gives up on the nations for now and starts over with one man from Ur, a city that worshiped the moon god Sin. Terah's family "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2). 🔴
- **Long lives getting shorter.** Shem lives 600 years, Terah 205. Mesopotamian king lists also have enormous reigns before the flood that shrink after it. 🔴 for the king lists.

## My notes
- **Three rebellions.** Eden (a human crossing, bringing death and exile), Genesis 6 (from above, bringing the flood), Babel (a whole human society, bringing the division of the nations). Each one gets an answer: 3:15, Noah, Abram. 🟡
- **The tell is "lest we be scattered."** It refuses the command to fill the earth.
- **11:5–7 and the plural.** Heiser reads it like God summoning someone not yet there, which hurts the Trinity reading of "Let Us" in 1:26.
- **Elohim is a category, not a rival.** *Elohim* names where a being lives (the spiritual realm), not its rank. God is *elohim* by category, but when he says who he is he gives the Name or lifts the category up: El Most High, El Almighty. You can't be "Most High" in a set of one. The other *elohim* are real, created and rebellious, not nothing: Deuteronomy 32:17 calls them demons, and you can't sacrifice to a nobody and have God name it that.
- **Not polytheism.** Nothing was created except by God. When I sat in a group where people talked loosely about "other gods," I heard a near-heresy. *Elohim* doesn't mean there are other gods like God Most High. They're heavenly beings he made.
- **Chapters 10 and 11.** Babel is told after the Table of Nations. Genesis groups by theme and then goes back (see Genesis 10).
- **Nimrod.** Later Jewish tradition links him to Babel. The text doesn't.
- My first chat on this ("Michael Eisner on the Tower of Babel," which was Heiser misheard) only got as far as naming Heiser's argument.

## What the chapter is doing
- Four kings from the east crush a revolt by five kings around the Dead Sea, including Sodom and Gomorrah, and carry off Lot, who's living in Sodom (14:1–12).
- Abram takes 318 trained men from his own household, attacks at night, chases the raiders past Damascus and brings back Lot, the people and the goods (14:13–16).
- On the way home Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram. Abram gives him a tenth of everything (14:17–20).
- The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods. Abram refuses to take so much as a thread, so nobody can say Sodom made him rich (14:21–24).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Abram the Hebrew" (14:13).** The first time anyone in the Bible is called a Hebrew. 🔴
- **Giant clans in the battle list (14:5).** The eastern kings strike the Rephaim, the Zuzim and the Emim. Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 20 calls the Emim and the Zamzummim (likely the Zuzim) Rephaim, tall like the Anakim. 🔴
- **318 men born in his house (14:14).** Abram is a wealthy clan chief with his own fighting force, not a lone wanderer. 🔴
- **Melchizedek shows up from nowhere (14:18).** No family, no introduction, no exit. Three verses. 🔴
- **His name and city.** *Melek* (king) plus *tzedek* (righteousness): king of righteousness. Salem, "peace." Psalm 76:2 uses Salem for Jerusalem. 🔴
- **King and priest at once (14:18).** In Israel those offices were later kept apart. 🔴
- **"God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth" (14:19).** *El Elyon*. Then Abram swears by "Yahweh God Most High" (14:22), putting the covenant name on the same God. 🔴
- **A tenth (14:20).** The first tithe in the Bible. 🔴
- **Two kings, two offers.** Melchizedek gives bread and wine and a blessing. The king of Sodom offers loot. Abram takes the blessing and refuses the loot. 🔴

## Read it like 1900 BC, not 2026
- **Eastern kings raiding west was real.** Coalitions of Mesopotamian and Elamite kings did march west to control trade routes and collect tribute. The names Arioch, Tidal (like the Hittite name Tudhaliya) and Chedorlaomer (an Elamite-style name) fit that world, though none of the four has been matched to a known king for sure. 🔴 for the name types; ⬜ for identifying them.
- **The King's Highway.** The raid runs down the old trade route east of the Jordan, through Ashtaroth, Ham, Kadesh and back. 🔴
- ***El Elyon* was a known divine title.** "Most High" (*Elyon*) shows up for the high god in West Semitic texts, and "creator of earth" is a title of the god El at Ugarit. Melchizedek uses the language of his world, and Abram claims it for Yahweh. 🔴 for the titles; 🟡 for reading Abram's oath as claiming them.
- **Divine council:** "Most High" is a ranking word. It means nothing unless there are lower ones. Deuteronomy 32:8 uses the same title for the God who divided the nations among the sons of God. 🔴
- **The Rephaim were the giant clans.** For a first reader, the Rephaim, Emim and Zuzim were the giant peoples tied back to the Nephilim. They're already in the land in Abram's day. 🟡
- **Bread and wine were a covenant meal.** Sharing a meal sealed peace and alliance. 🔴
- **The tithe was common.** Giving a tenth to a god or king shows up across the ANE. Abram gives his to God Most High's priest. 🔴
- **Melchizedek in the Dead Sea Scrolls.** A Qumran text (11QMelchizedek) pictures him as a heavenly figure who brings liberation and judgment and applies "God (*elohim*) stands in the divine council" (Psalm 82:1) to him. 🔴 that the text says it.

## My notes
- **Priest before Levi.** Hebrews' argument: Abraham tithed to Melchizedek, Melchizedek blessed Abraham, and Levi was "in Abraham," so Melchizedek's order is greater than the Levitical one (Hebrews 7). 🔴
- **Who was he?** The options I gathered: a real historical king (most common), a Christophany (weakened by Hebrews 7:3, "made like the Son of God," which means he isn't the Son), an angelic being or Michael, or Shem (Jewish tradition). ⬜
- **Bread and wine.** Read toward communion, as a type. 🟡
- **Heiser.** My chat asked what Heiser would say. The answer: Psalm 110:4 puts Melchizedek beyond normal categories, 11QMelchizedek presents him as an *elohim*-level heavenly figure in a priestly and judging role in the divine council, scholars debate whether that text means Michael, and Hebrews is working with a known Second Temple tradition and applying it to Christ. I haven't checked that against Heiser's own books yet. 🔵
- **Status.** The Melchizedek study is still open and the scope isn't decided. I gathered the Heiser and 11QMelchizedek material in April and haven't packaged it.

## What the chapter is doing
- God finishes, rests on the seventh day, and blesses it (2:1–3).
- The camera comes down from the whole cosmos to one man. Yahweh God forms him from dust and breathes life into him (2:7).
- God plants a garden in Eden, in the east, with real rivers and real lands, puts the man in it to work it and keep it, and gives one command: don't eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (2:8–17).
- "It is not good for the man to be alone." The man names the animals, finds no partner among them, and God builds the woman from his side (2:18–23).
- Marriage is set out (2:24). They're naked and not ashamed (2:25).

## Pay attention to this
- **The name changes.** Chapter 1 says "God" (*Elohim*). From 2:4 on it's "Yahweh God," the covenant name. Same God, closer up. 🔴
- **No evening and morning on day seven (2:1–3).** Every other day closes with it. This one doesn't. 🔴
- **"Formed" and "breathed" (2:7).** A potter's verb and then God's own breath. Man is dust plus breath, and the breath is what makes him a "living being." 🔴
- **Eden has an address (2:10–14).** Four named rivers (Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, Euphrates) and named lands (Havilah, Cush, Asshur). It's a place on the earth, not the whole earth. 🔴
- **The garden is *in* Eden (2:8).** Eden is the bigger place; the garden is planted inside it. 🔴
- **Gold and onyx (2:11–12).** The same materials later dress the tabernacle and the high priest (Exodus 25; 28:9–20). 🔴
- **"Cultivate it and keep it" (2:15).** The verbs *'avad* and *shamar* are the pair used for the Levites' service at the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7–8; 8:26; 18:5–6). 🔴 for the word pair, 🟡 for reading Adam as a priest from it.
- **Two trees (2:9).** The tree of life in the middle, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The grammar names two, and 3:22 needs two. 🔴
- **"Not good" (2:18).** The first thing in the Bible called not good is a man alone. 🔴
- **Helper (2:18).** *'Ezer* is a word the Bible uses for God himself helping Israel (Psalm 121:1–2). It doesn't mean lesser. 🔴
- **The man names, then says "Woman" (2:19–23).** *Ishshah* from *ish*. 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **A garden was where a god lived.** In the ANE, gods had gardens at their temples and on their sacred mountains, and kings planted royal gardens. A first reader hearing "Yahweh God planted a garden" heard "God set up his home." Ezekiel 28:13–14 puts "Eden, the garden of God" on "the holy mountain of God." 🔴
- **Eden is the first temple.** East-facing like the later tabernacle (2:8), rivers flowing out like the temple river in Ezekiel 47, gold and onyx like the tabernacle, and a man set there to serve and guard. Jubilees 8:19 calls Eden the holy of holies. 🔴 that the parallels are there; 🟡 for how far to push them.
- **The mountain where heaven meets earth.** ANE peoples put the meeting place of gods and men on a cosmic mountain, where rivers start. Eden's one river splitting into four fits that picture, and the Bible keeps coming back to mountains (Sinai, Zion). 🟡
- **Work was not slavery.** In Babylon's *Atrahasis* story, humans are made because the lesser gods got tired of digging canals: people exist to do the gods' labor. In Genesis, God plants the garden himself and gives the man a job in it. Work is a calling, not a punishment. 🔴 for Atrahasis; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **Rest means rule.** When an ANE god rested, he took his seat in his finished temple. The seventh day is God enthroned over his world, not God catching his breath. 🟡
- **Clay and breath.** Egyptian art shows the god Khnum shaping people on a potter's wheel, and Mesopotamian stories mix clay with a god's blood. Genesis uses the potter picture and gives the breath straight from God. 🔴 for the parallels.
- **The rivers were the writer's map.** "East of Asshur" (2:14) orients readers by places they knew. Havilah, Cush and Asshur show up again in Genesis 10 as names on the post-flood map. 🔴
- **Divine council:** Eden is God's home, and in Heiser's frame his home is where his council meets. The garden is where heaven and earth overlap. The council itself steps into view in 3:5 and 3:22. 🟡

## My notes
- **Eden is not the whole world.** The four rivers and named lands give it latitude and longitude. When people teach that Eden was the whole pre-fall earth, I sorted out who says what: Eden as a starting point God meant to spread outward is mainstream (Beale, Walton, Heiser and others). The whole pre-fall earth as Eden comes from LDS and young-earth teaching, and it's doctrine, not exegesis. 🔴
- **Garden as temple.** East-facing, rivers flowing out, gold and onyx, *'avad* and *shamar* in 2:15. Adam is set there as priest-king: work and keep as priestly service, rule as God's vice-regent. 🟡
- **Two trees.** In the Discord exchange somebody argued it's really one tree. I checked ESV 2:9 myself. I can't see it as one tree. The "one tree" reading has to explain away the grammar and 3:22. 🔴
- **2:14 and the flood-moved rivers.** Answers in Genesis and Apologetics Press claim the flood relocated Eden's rivers. I asked for the evidence and there isn't any independent geology behind it. What actually changed the region was sea-level rise after the last ice age: the Persian Gulf was dry land at the glacial peak and filled in around 6,000 years ago. Zarins identifies the Gihon with the Karun and the Pishon with the Wadi al-Batin. 🟡 for Zarins; 🔴 that the flood-moved claim has no geology behind it.
- **Visitors or residents?** One reading (J. Harvey Walton, through Carey G.) says Eden is divine space where humans never belonged. My pushback: God installs the man and gives him a job. Nobody guards anything until 3:24, after the rupture. 🔴 that the guarding is post-fall.
- **The seventh day is still open.** No evening and morning. I read it with John 5:17 and Hebrews 3–4. The honest version: the text allows it.
- **2:7 and the image.** God shapes the man and breathes into him. The idol rituals around Israel opened a statue's mouth for a god to move in; Yahweh made his own living image and breathed into it himself (see Genesis 1).
- **Lewis helped me here.** C.S. Lewis's Space Trilogy is what really helped me understand the Eden story.

## What the chapter is doing
- God tests Abraham: take Isaac, "your only one, whom you love," to Moriah and offer him as a burnt offering (22:1–2).
- Abraham goes early the next morning. Three days' walk. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. "God will provide for Himself the lamb" (22:3–8).
- Abraham binds Isaac on the altar and raises the knife. The angel of Yahweh stops him. A ram caught in a thicket takes Isaac's place (22:9–13).
- Abraham names the place "Yahweh Will Provide," and God swears by himself to bless Abraham and bless all nations through his seed (22:14–18).
- News of Nahor's family closes the chapter, introducing Rebekah, Isaac's future wife (22:20–24).

## Pay attention to this
- **"God tested Abraham" (22:1).** The reader is told up front it's a test. Abraham isn't. 🔴
- **"Here I am" three times (22:1, 7, 11).** To God, to Isaac, to the angel. 🔴
- **Three ways of naming Isaac (22:2).** "Your son, your only one, whom you love." Each phrase tightens. It's the first time the Bible uses the word "love." 🔴
- **"We will return to you" (22:5).** Abraham tells the servants both of them will come back. Hebrews 11:17–19 says he reasoned God could raise the dead. 🔴
- **Isaac carries the wood (22:6).** The father carries the fire and the knife. 🔴
- **"God will provide for Himself the lamb" (22:8).** Abraham's answer, and then a ram shows up, not a lamb. The lamb is still waiting. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for reading it forward to Christ (John 1:29).
- **The angel of Yahweh speaks as God (22:11–12, 15–16).** "You have not withheld your son... from Me." Then "By Myself I have sworn, declares Yahweh." The angel speaks in God's own first person. 🔴
- **"In the place of his son" (22:13).** Substitution in plain words. 🔴
- **Moriah.** 2 Chronicles 3:1 puts Solomon's temple on Mount Moriah. 🔴
- **The promise widens (22:18).** "In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed," the 12:3 promise again, now sworn by oath. 🔴

## Read it like 1900 BC, not 2026
- **Child sacrifice was real in that world.** Canaanite and later Phoenician religion offered children to gods in crisis. The king of Moab sacrifices his son on the wall in 2 Kings 3:27, and Israel's law bans giving children to Molech (Leviticus 18:21). A first reader wouldn't have found the command unthinkable. What would stun them is that God stops it and provides the offering himself. 🔴 for the practice; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **The firstborn belonged to God.** Israel's law claims every firstborn and has them redeemed (Exodus 13:2, 13). Genesis 22 is the story behind that. 🟡
- **The angel of Yahweh.** In Heiser's frame he's Yahweh present in visible form, the "second Yahweh figure" who speaks as God and is God, and who Christians later saw as the Son. 🟡
- **Divine council: the test in Jubilees.** Second Temple Judaism retold this chapter with a heavenly accuser. In Jubilees 17:16 the prince Mastema proposes the test, like the satan in Job 1. Genesis has no accuser at all: God tests. 🔴 for what both texts say.
- **The Akedah.** Jewish tradition calls this "the binding" (*akedah*, from "bound" in 22:9) and reads it in the synagogue at Rosh Hashanah. 🔴

## My notes
- **Jubilees reframes the test.** Jubilees (around the 160s BC) has Mastema, an adversary figure, propose the test (17:16), mirroring the satan's challenge in Job 1. It counts ten trials of Abraham (17:17; 19:8) and stresses that he obeyed out of love. The effect is to keep God from being the one who starts the test. 🔴 for Jubilees.
- **Teaching hook.** In my mentoring outline: father takes his son up a mountain to die, God provides a substitute. Sound familiar? That's not an accident. Watch for that pattern. 22:13–14 is the reading.
- **Divine council:** the chapter has no council scene, only the angel of Yahweh. The heavenly accuser is something Jubilees adds, not Genesis.
- My notes on this chapter are thin. I've worked on how it was read later more than on the chapter itself.
