## What the chapter is doing
- The serpent questions God's word to the woman, then flatly contradicts it: "You surely will not die!" (3:1–5).
- She eats, gives to her husband "with her," and he eats. Their eyes open and they know they're naked (3:6–7).
- God comes walking in the garden, asks "Where are you?", and gets a chain of blame: the woman, the serpent (3:8–13).
- God pronounces on the serpent, the woman and the man, and inside the curse on the serpent is a promise: her seed will crush his head (3:14–19).
- God clothes them, says the man has become "like one of Us," sends them out, and posts cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life (3:20–24).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Indeed, has God said...?" (3:1).** The first words out of the serpent's mouth are a question about what God said. 🔴
- **The woman adds a line (3:3).** God said don't eat. She says don't eat "and you shall not touch it." 🔴
- **"You will be like God, knowing good and evil" (3:5).** The "knowing" is plural in Hebrew, which fits "like gods" or "like divine beings." 🔴 for the grammar.
- **"Her husband with her" (3:6).** Adam was standing right there. 🔴
- **Only two changes are reported.** Their eyes open and they know they're naked (3:7), and God says the man has become "like one of Us" (3:22). The text is quiet about anything else the tree did. 🔴
- **"Knowing good and evil" is an idiom.** *Yada' tov wara'* means being able to tell good from bad: a child too young to know good and evil (Deuteronomy 1:39), a king who can discern (2 Samuel 14:17; 1 Kings 3:9). It doesn't mean knowing everything. 🔴
- ***Ra'* is wider than "evil."** It covers the whole range of what works against life: bad, harmful, ruinous. Hebrew doesn't split "bad" from "evil" the way English does. 🔴
- **"Walking" in the garden (3:8).** The same verb form describes God walking among Israel in the tabernacle camp (Leviticus 26:12; Deuteronomy 23:14; 2 Samuel 7:6–7). 🔴
- **The blame chain (3:12–13).** "The woman whom You gave to be with me." Then "the serpent deceived me." 🔴
- **The fruit is never named.** Fig leaves show up afterward to cover them (3:7). The apple came much later. 🔴
- **3:15, the seed promise.** Enmity between the serpent's seed and hers; he crushes the head, the serpent strikes the heel. The church has read it as the first promise of Christ since the second century. 🔴 for the reception; 🟡 for the messianic reading in the verse itself.
- **God makes the clothes (3:21).** No animal killing is narrated. God makes and clothes. 🔴
- **The guard comes after (3:24).** Cherubim and a flaming sword at the east of the garden. Nobody guarded anything before the rupture. 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **The serpent was not just a snake to them.** Serpents were divine symbols all over the ANE: the cobra (uraeus) on Pharaoh's crown, serpent figures guarding thrones and temples. A talking serpent in God's garden would read as a divine being, not a zoo animal. 🔴 for the iconography; 🟡 for the reading.
- ***Nachash* has three senses.** Heiser: "serpent" (noun), "diviner" or one who gives omens (the verb *nachash* is divination, and Duane Smith ties serpents to omen-reading), and "shining one" (the bronze-like shine of the root). A word that can hold all three fits a bright divine being who deceives. 🟡
- **Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 tell the back story.** "Shining one, son of the dawn" wants to set his throne above the stars of God (Isaiah 14:12–14). The king of Tyre is pictured as a cherub in "Eden, the garden of God" on God's mountain, cast down for pride (Ezekiel 28:13–17). Both are aimed at human kings, using a story about a divine rebel the audience already knew. 🟡
- **Seraphim were winged serpents.** Isaiah's *seraphim* (6:2) share the word used for the "fiery serpents" of Numbers 21. The Dictionary of Deities and Demons (Mettinger) says scholars now generally picture them as winged serpents with some human features, drawn from the Egyptian uraeus. 🟡
- **Divine council: "like one of Us" (3:22).** God speaks to his council again, like 1:26. That reading stands even if you reject the divine-being serpent. 🔴 for the plural; 🟡 for the council reading.
- **Cherubim guard holy places.** Winged guardian creatures flanked thrones and temple doors across the ANE (the Assyrian *lamassu*, for one). The cherubim at the east gate of Eden turn the garden into a guarded sanctuary, and cherubim show up again on the ark and woven into the tabernacle curtains. 🔴
- **Gilgamesh lost his plant to a snake.** In the Gilgamesh epic a plant that restores youth gets stolen by a serpent. So the tree of life has background furniture. The tree of knowledge doesn't: there's no ANE parallel to it (Mark S. Smith). Its exact symbolism can't be decoded from the background. 🔴
- **Death was a known threat.** The serpent's "you surely will not die" only works as a temptation if death means something to her. 🔴

## My notes
- **The serpent was more than a snake.** I don't like using "Satan" here, because the word gets misunderstood. *Satan* means the adversary or accuser, and in the Old Testament it's mostly a title with "the" in front of it (Job 1–2). Was the serpent *the* satan or *a* satan? I don't know. Was he the tempter? Yes. A plain snake? No. He's crafty above every other creature, he talks (no other animal in the Old Testament talks except Balaam's donkey, and she speaks for God), and the word carries cunning, shining and serpent. To a Hebrew reader he's a divine council being, maybe taking on a serpent form.
- **Adam and Eve weren't surprised.** They were used to seeing heavenly beings in the garden. They walked with God.
- **God did not make the snake lie.** The snake took God's own words and twisted them. God tests people, but he doesn't tempt them or twist his own words, and he can't lie. So the speech came from a rebellious being, not from God using an animal.
- **The satan in Job is not the *nachash* cast down.** That's the point. Different figure, different job.
- **Eve was deceived, Adam chose.** God gave the command to Adam before Eve was made (2:16–17). Eve was deceived by the serpent (3:13); Adam, standing right there, disobeyed (compare 1 Timothy 2:14). 🟡
- **Heiser and Walton disagree, and I flag it.** Heiser reads the *nachash* as a divine rebel. Walton reads the serpent as a catalyst, a chaos creature, not Satan. When I teach it I say so.
- **The seraphim reversal.** One Logos pull said the seraph root means "burn," not snake, and I nearly dropped the serpent link. ❌ for that drop. One source disagreeing isn't proof. Heiser and BibleProject get held to the highest standard and need real proof before I dismiss them, and the Dictionary of Deities and Demons backed them up.
- **What did the tree add?** This is the one I still can't fully close. The version I grew up with was perfect world, perfect people, fruit ruins everything, Jesus restores it to perfect. The world was called "very good," not perfect. Adam and Eve already bore God's image, made choices, named animals. The text only reports shame and a real likeness to God. It's interested in the fallout and quiet about the mechanics. The "they weren't ready" angle is probably closest to where I land. I just don't know what they weren't ready for. ⬜
- **What I sorted as fiction.** The fruit was a fig: no support. The forbidden act was really killing an animal: my own session guess, no textual hook, marked fiction. "They had no idea what death was": corrected, since 3:4 only works if death is a known threat. ❌
- **"Autonomy" is benched.** I stopped using it as a teaching word because it hides the gap in what we actually know.
- **The dominion chain.** Given (1:26–28; Psalm 8), lost (3:17–19; Romans 8:19–22), claimed by the enemy (Luke 4:5–8; John 12:31; 2 Corinthians 4:4), recovered at the cross and resurrection (Colossians 2:15; Matthew 28:18), keys held (Revelation 1:18), finished (Revelation 11:15). Heiser (*Unseen Realm*, 340) backs Luke 4:6: the authority offered was real. He routes it through Babel and Deuteronomy 32, though, not mainly through Eden. 🔴 for the chain.
- **The keys were collected, not won.** The victory was finished at the cross. If there's any descent, it isn't combat. It's John Wick walking in to collect what's already his. Revelation 1:18 says "I have the keys," not "I fought for them." Making the descent the climax weakens the cross.
- **My own framework.** Eating the fruit was enthroning the serpent's word over God's, which handed over the keys. That goes past where Heiser and Walton stop, and I teach it as mine. The part that's grounded: obeying is allegiance in the Old Testament, so trusting the serpent's word over God's was shifting allegiance away from God (Middleton). 🟡
- **Luke 4:6, "selective correction."** Jesus rebuts the devil's other temptations but not the claim that the world's authority was handed to him. Silence from someone correcting everything else means something. Refusing the deal isn't the same as conceding the title, but it's the better reading. 🟡
- **3:21.** God makes the clothes. Walton rejects reading a sacrifice into it and rejects investiture too; he lands on grace, God covering them for a harder world. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- On his way home after twenty years with Laban, Jacob meets the angels of God and calls the place "God's camp," Mahanaim (32:1–2).
- He hears Esau is coming with 400 men. Terrified, he splits his people into two camps, prays, and sends wave after wave of animals ahead as a gift (32:3–21).
- He sends his family across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles him until dawn, puts his hip out of joint, and Jacob won't let go without a blessing (32:22–26).
- He gets a new name, Israel. He names the place Peniel, "I have seen God face to face," and walks away limping (32:27–31).
- That's why Israel doesn't eat the hip sinew (32:32).

## Pay attention to this
- **Angels at both ends.** Jacob met angels at Bethel on the way out (28:12) and meets them again on the way back (32:1–2). 🔴
- **"Two camps" (32:7, 10).** Jacob splits into two camps out of fear, then thanks God that he crossed the Jordan with only a staff and has "become two camps." Same word, *machaneh*, as "God's camp" in 32:2. 🔴
- **Faces everywhere.** "I will appease his face... I will see his face; perhaps he will lift up my face" (32:20). Then Peniel, "face of God" (32:30). In 33:10 Jacob tells Esau, "I see your face as one sees the face of God." 🔴
- **Wordplay at the river.** Jabbok, "wrestled" (*ye'abeq*) and Jacob (*Ya'aqov*) all sound alike in Hebrew. 🔴
- **"A man" (32:24).** The text says a man. Jacob says he saw God (32:30). Hosea 12:3–4 says he wrestled with "the angel." 🔴
- **The touch (32:25).** One touch dislocates the hip. 🔴
- **"Let me go, for the dawn is breaking" (32:26).** The one who could end the fight with a touch asks to be let go. 🔴
- **The name exchange (32:27–29).** Jacob has to say his own name, "heel-grabber," before he gets a new one. When he asks the man's name, he doesn't get it. 🔴
- **Israel (32:28).** "You have striven with God and with men and have prevailed." 🔴
- **The sun rises and he's limping (32:31).** 🔴

## Read it like 1800 BC, not 2026
- **Nobody sees God's face and lives.** That conviction runs through the Old Testament (Exodus 33:20; Judges 13:22). Jacob's surprise at Peniel is that he's still alive. A first reader would hear "the dawn is breaking" against that: daylight would mean seeing the face. 🔴 for the conviction; 🟡 for reading the dawn this way.
- **Names were identity.** Knowing someone's name meant having some hold on them. Jacob has to give his; the man won't give his. Compare Judges 13:17–18, where the angel of Yahweh refuses to give his name too. 🔴
- **A blessing was a real transfer.** Jacob already stole one blessing from his father (ch. 27). Now he fights for one face to face. 🔴
- **River crossings at night.** Some scholars see an old folk motif behind the story: a river spirit guarding a ford that has to leave by daybreak. Genesis turns it into an encounter with God. 🔵
- **Divine council: the camps of God.** "God's camp" in 32:2 is the heavenly host, and Jacob's "two camps" sit next to it. The "man" at the Jabbok is the angel who is also God (Hosea 12:3–5 calls him the angel and then Yahweh, God of hosts). In Heiser's frame he's the angel of Yahweh, Yahweh in visible human form. 🟡
- **A food law from a story.** "To this day the sons of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip" (32:32). Every other food rule comes as a command. This one comes from a memory. 🔴

## My notes
- **My question was simple.** Jacob wrestled with God and wouldn't let go. Why did God tell him to let go, and why does he limp the rest of his life? And what limp do I have?
- **"Let me go" isn't God getting tired.** It reads as a theophany, most likely the angel of Yahweh. The danger was seeing God's face at daybreak. Jacob names the place Peniel and is amazed he lived. 🟡
- **The limp is the wound and the credential.** The touch that put his hip out showed who held the power the whole time. The blessing and the wound are one event. The heel-grabber now walks dependent. 🟡
- **What limp do I have.** I turned the question on myself. I'm keeping it as a meditation, not something to diagnose.
- **32:32, *gid hanasheh*.** The sciatic sinew is the only food law grounded in a story instead of a command, and it was never applied outside Israel. It's a story, and it isn't the Gentiles' story. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Outside Eden, Adam and Eve have two sons. Cain farms, Abel keeps flocks. Both bring offerings; God accepts Abel's and not Cain's (4:1–5).
- God warns Cain that sin is crouching at the door. Cain kills Abel in the field anyway (4:6–8).
- God confronts him, curses him from the ground, and sends him out as a wanderer, but puts a sign on him so no one kills him (4:9–16).
- Cain builds a city. His line produces herding, music and metalwork, and ends with Lamech bragging about killing a man (4:17–24).
- Seth is born in Abel's place, and "men began to call upon the name of Yahweh" (4:25–26).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Where is Abel your brother?" (4:9).** It echoes "Where are you?" in 3:9. Same God, same kind of question, one generation later. 🔴
- **Abel brought the firstborn and the fat portions (4:4).** Cain brought "of the fruit of the ground." The text marks the difference in what was brought, and Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered "by faith." 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for why God rejected Cain's.
- **Sin crouching at the door (4:7).** Sin is pictured like an animal waiting to pounce, and "its desire is for you, but you must rule over it" uses the same words as 3:16. 🔴
- **Blood has a voice (4:10).** "The voice of your brother's blood is crying out to Me from the ground." 🔴
- **The sign on Cain (4:15) is protection.** It keeps others from killing him. It isn't a mark of shame. 🔴
- **East of Eden (4:16).** Cain moves further east, further from the presence. 🔴
- **The arts come from Cain's line (4:20–22).** Jabal: tents and livestock. Jubal: lyre and pipe. Tubal-cain: bronze and iron. 🔴
- **Lamech turns sevenfold into seventy-sevenfold (4:23–24).** God's protection of Cain becomes Lamech's license for revenge. Jesus flips the same number into forgiveness (Matthew 18:22). 🔴
- **Two lines.** Cain's line ends in a killer's boast. Seth's line ends with people calling on Yahweh (4:26). 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **Everybody knew who gave people civilization.** In Mesopotamia the *apkallu*, semi-divine sages from before the flood, were said to have taught humans the arts of civilization. Egypt credited Thoth, the Greeks had Prometheus stealing fire for men. Genesis tells the same story in three verses and the teachers are just men, from Cain's family. 🔴 for the ANE claims; 🟡 for reading 4:17–22 as a polemic.
- **Farmer and herdsman were old rivals.** Sumerian disputation poems pit the shepherd god against the farmer god in a contest for favor (Dumuzi and Enkimdu). A first reader would know the type. Genesis turns it into a murder. 🟡
- **Blood crying out.** In that world, shed blood stained the land and demanded an answer from the next of kin, the avenger of blood (Numbers 35). Abel has no one, so God answers. 🔴
- **A city was a claim.** Building a city and naming it after your son was how a man made himself permanent. Cain does it after God sentences him to wander. 🟡
- **Divine council:** no council scene here. It's a ground-level story. The chapter matters for the council material because the *apkallu* and Watchers traditions about divine teachers get answered here, two chapters before the sons of God show up in 6:1–4.

## My notes
- **Genesis already answered the question.** People in our Live in Context session brought up the Watchers teaching humanity the arts of civilization, and someone noticed Cain's line develops the same skills. That instinct points somewhere real. Genesis 4:20–22 knows the question of where civilization came from and answers it in three verses, two chapters before the sons of God. The answer is men.
- **The teaching motif isn't in Genesis 6.** Supernatural beings teaching forbidden skills is the clearest *apkallu* fingerprint, and it shows up in 1 Enoch 8, not in Genesis. Genesis takes the Mesopotamian claim, strips the divine gift out of it, and files the arts under the wrong branch of the family. 🟡
- **God works through men.** Everything created came through God, knowledge included, and God did have a hand in guiding people through advances in technology. Angels didn't come down and hand out guns and mined metal (that's Milton) any more than angels came down and handed us the Bible.
- **Who said it first.** I thought this was just my reading until I went looking. Sarna reads 4:17–22 as a silent polemic against crediting culture to gods and demigods, with the *apkallu* in that company (I have it through Keller; Carey G. later confirmed Sarna). Mathews: the inventions are human, and putting them in Cain's line brings suspicion, not praise (NAC, *Genesis 1–11*, 567–568). 🔴
- **Upstream of Enoch?** Heiser's Enoch commentary treats Cain as something like the prototypical evildoer in 1 Enoch and raises the possibility that 1 Enoch built Tubal-cain's bronze and iron under the influence of the Prometheus story. De Young ties 1 Enoch 8:1–3 (Azazel teaching swords and metals) straight to 4:22. If that holds, Genesis 4 is upstream of the Watchers material. ⬜
- **The violence that caused the flood.** Genesis 6:13 names *hamas*, violence, as the reason for the flood. The only violence Genesis has shown up to then is chapter 4: Cain's murder and Lamech's boast. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 108a) says the decree was sealed over *hamas*. So the stated cause of the flood points back to Cain's line. 🟡

- **"Sons of God" (6:2, 4).** *Bene ha-elohim*. Everywhere else in the Old Testament this phrase means heavenly beings around God's throne (Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; compare Psalm 29:1; 82:1; 89:6). 🔴
- **Seth isn't in the text.** The popular reading that the "sons of God" are Seth's godly line and the "daughters of men" are Cain's has to bring Seth in from chapter 4. Chapter 6 never mentions him. 🔴
- **The Nephilim (6:4).** The word is left untranslated in most Bibles. The Greek translation rendered it "giants." The exact meaning of the Hebrew word is disputed. 🔴
- **"And also afterward" (6:4).** The Nephilim show up again after the flood (Numbers 13:33). 🔴
- **6:1–4 sits next to 6:5 with no "because."** The text puts the sons of God story right beside human wickedness and never says one caused the other. 🔴
- **Regret and grief (6:6).** God is grieved "in His heart." The text doesn't hide God's feeling. 🔴
- **Violence, *hamas* (6:11, 13).** Named twice as the reason for the flood. 🔴
- **Noah walked with God (6:9).** Same phrase used of Enoch in 5:22–24. 🔴
- **First "covenant" in the Bible (6:18).** 🔴
- **"Thus Noah did" (6:22).** Noah never speaks in the flood story. He just obeys. 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **Everybody had a flood story.** *Atrahasis* (Old Babylonian, around 1700 BC) and Gilgamesh tablet 11 both have a flood, a man on a boat, animals, birds sent out and a sacrifice after. In *Atrahasis* the gods send the flood because humans are too noisy. Genesis makes it moral: violence and corruption. 🔴
- **The *apkallu*.** Mesopotamian tradition remembered seven semi-divine sages from before the flood who brought knowledge to humans. Some later texts describe offspring of *apkallu* and human women. Heiser reads 6:1–4 as Israel's answer to that: the "heroes of old" the Babylonians bragged about were the product of a rebellion. 🟡
- **Divine council: the second rebellion.** In Heiser's frame Genesis 3 is the first rebellion (a divine being in Eden), 6:1–4 the second (sons of God crossing the line between heaven and earth), and Babel the third. 🟡
- **The Jewish reading was supernatural.** 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Josephus and Philo all read the sons of God as angels. The early church did too until the 3rd–4th century. Julius Africanus is the first known to argue for the Sethite reading, and Augustine made it the Western default. 🔴 for 1 Enoch and the early sources; 🟡 for the exact date of the Sethite shift.
- **1 Enoch tells a fuller story.** The Watchers swear an oath on Mount Hermon, come down, take wives, teach forbidden arts (weapons, metals, sorcery), and father giants whose violence fills the earth (1 Enoch 6–10). Genesis gives four verses and no teaching. 🔴
- **The New Testament knows this story.** 2 Peter 2:4–5 puts angels who sinned in Tartarus right next to Noah's flood. Jude 6–7 has angels who left their proper home, then quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 in Jude 14–15. 🔴 for the texts. 1 Peter 3:18–22, spirits in prison in Noah's day, likely belongs here too. 🟡
- **Giants come back.** The Anakim (Numbers 13:33 ties them to the Nephilim), the Rephaim, Og of Bashan, and Goliath's clan at Gath. The conquest is framed as unfinished business with giant clans. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the framing.

## My notes
- **We shouldn't read Genesis through Enoch.** Enoch is the best way to understand the mindset of the New Testament authors. Enoch is NOT the context of Genesis. What it shows is continuity between the Genesis context and the Second Temple context.
- **The teaching motif isn't in Genesis 6.** Watchers instructing humans in forbidden skills is the clearest *apkallu* fingerprint, and it shows up in 1 Enoch 8, not in Genesis. I don't think there's biblical evidence for it. God works through men on all things: angels didn't come down and hand out gun-making and metal-mining any more than they came down and handed us the Bible. Genesis 4 already handed the arts to Cain's line. 🟡
- **Sons of God are divine beings.** The phrase clusters around the heavenly court. 🔴 But the *ben* idiom means "belonging to the category," not "fathered by," and humans get called sons of God elsewhere (Vicchio), so the airtight version overreaches. 🟡
- **The Sethite view.** Rollston's cleanest objection: Seth isn't in the text. 🔴 The motive people give for it (Julian the Apostate) doesn't fit the dates: Julian died in 363, and Africanus wrote around 240. ❌ for that motive.
- **The royal reading.** Kings as "sons of God" (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7), and Kline's version from ANE sacred kingship. Both still owe an account of the Nephilim.
- **The causation correction.** 1 Enoch says the Watchers caused the evil. Genesis puts 6:1–4 next to 6:5 and states no cause. Jubilees keeps the supernatural reading and drops the causal chain. So "every Jewish writer agreed" is too strong: they agreed on the supernatural reading, not on the cause. Carr: the flood story never mentions 6:1–4 again. 🔴
- **6:13, *hamas*.** The violence points back to Cain and Lamech in chapter 4.
- **Myth Busters.** "The pagan gods were memories of the Nephilim" is false as stated. The arrow runs the other way. The Mesopotamian flood and sage traditions are older than Genesis in its current form, and Genesis reworks that shared material polemically. ❌ for the pop claim.
- **Jude quoting Enoch.** It works like citing a well-known saying today. It makes a point everybody understands; it doesn't make the whole book Scripture. And "prophesied" needs defining: it means a message from God, not only predicting the future. If the only people who ever spoke for God are the ones written in the Bible, that's a very short list.
- **Nephilim and Rephaim.** The family tree question is a mystery and probably stays one. Putting a lot of weight on it invites eisegesis instead of exegesis. 🔵
- **The spirits after the flood.** Reading Heiser's *Reversing Hermon*, the picture I got is a mafia: the leaders are in jail (the Watchers bound) and the rogue spirits run loose with no real authority structure. Second Temple writers don't agree on the details: either the giants' spirits are the demons, or spirits come out of their bodies.

## What the chapter is doing
- "God remembered Noah." He sends a wind over the earth, closes the deep and the sky, and the water goes down (8:1–5).
- The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven, then a dove three times: it comes back empty, then with an olive leaf, then doesn't come back at all (8:6–12).
- The ground dries. God tells Noah to bring everyone out to be fruitful and multiply (8:13–19).
- Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. God promises never again to curse the ground or strike down every living thing, and the seasons will keep turning (8:20–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **"God remembered Noah" (8:1).** The hinge of the whole flood story. In Hebrew, "remember" means God acts on what he committed to, not that he forgot. 🔴
- **A wind over the waters (8:1).** The word is *ruach*, the same word as "Spirit" in 1:2. The flood undid creation, and now God starts it over: wind over water, dry land appearing, creatures told to be fruitful and multiply (8:17). 🔴 for the echoes.
- **The dove goes out three times (8:8–12).** No resting place; an olive leaf; gone for good. Each trip tells Noah more about the world outside. 🔴
- **The raven doesn't come back (8:7).** It flies back and forth. Only the dove reports. 🔴
- **Noah waits on God (8:15–16).** He can see the ground is dry in 8:13, and he still waits until God says "Go out." 🔴
- **The first altar in the Bible (8:20).** Noah's first act on the new earth is worship. 🔴
- **Clean animals (8:20).** The clean-unclean line exists before Sinai. 🔴
- **Same heart, different response (8:21).** God says "the intent of man's heart is evil from his youth," almost the words of 6:5. In ch. 6 that was the reason for the flood. Now it's the reason God promises not to do it again. 🔴
- **Seedtime and harvest (8:22).** God guarantees the rhythm of the world will hold. 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **Utnapishtim sent birds too.** In Gilgamesh tablet 11, the flood survivor Utnapishtim lands on Mount Nimush and sends out a dove, then a swallow, then a raven; the raven doesn't come back, so he knows the land is dry. Genesis has the raven first and the dove as the messenger. 🔴
- **The gods swarmed the sacrifice like flies.** After Utnapishtim's offering, the hungry gods gather "like flies" around it, because in that story people existed to feed the gods. Genesis keeps the "soothing aroma" (8:21) and drops the hunger. Yahweh doesn't need the meal; he makes a promise. 🔴 for Gilgamesh; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **Ararat is a region.** "The mountains of Ararat" is Urartu, the highlands north of Assyria (modern eastern Turkey and Armenia). The text names a mountain range, not one peak. 🔴
- **The flood as un-creation.** In Genesis 1 God separates the waters above from the waters below. In ch. 7 the "fountains of the deep" and "floodgates of the sky" open and the two waters crash back together. Chapter 8 closes them again. A first reader with the dome picture of the world (Genesis 1) would hear the cosmos coming apart and being put back. 🟡
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. The council material sits on either side of it: the sons of God in 6:1–4 and the scattering of the nations at Babel in ch. 11.

## My notes
- **The real bird.** Genesis 1:2 has no bird in it, only a verb. The flood dove is in the text.
- **It links to the baptism.** My first read was that the Spirit going down like a dove at Jesus's baptism links back to the hovering in 1:2. The commentators agree there's a connection. Then the dove in Genesis 8 turned out to be the better anchor, and that became my opinion post "The Bird Over Every Water."
- **Quarles turned the arrow around.** The dove's tie to new creation after the flood probably shaped how people read the dove back into the original creation (Quarles, *A Theology of Matthew*, 182). I didn't expect that direction. Hildebrandt reads the flood dove as a picture of the Spirit's presence at creation. 🟡
- **Four waters, one bird.** Crowe stacks it: creation, Noah, the exodus, the Jordan. Four water events, one bird, one Spirit. The exodus piece needs its own check before I lean on it. 🔵
- **The dating problem.** The earliest concrete evidence for "dove" as a gloss on Genesis 1:2 is Ben Zoma in the Babylonian Talmud (Hagigah 15a), late first century. Nothing clearly comes before the Gospels (Lanier, 563). So either the Gospel writers used an older Jewish dove reading, or both drew on a shared pool, or they got there separately. I'm leaving all three open. ⬜
- **What survives either way.** The new-creation reading of the baptism doesn't need a rabbinic dove. It needs the order: water, the Spirit over the water, God's voice speaking. That's 1:2 into 1:3, at the Jordan. And 1 Peter 3:20–21 ties the flood to baptism outright. 🔴
- **One point doesn't flip the whole case.** I got frustrated with the research going back and forth (right, wrong, right) every time one source didn't match 100 percent. A single source saying something different isn't a reason to throw out the reading. You weigh it.

## What the chapter is doing
- God blesses Noah and his sons with the same words he gave Adam: be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth (9:1, 7).
- Meat is allowed for the first time, with one fence: no blood (9:3–4).
- Murder gets a death penalty, because people are made in God's image (9:5–6).
- God makes a covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature: no more world-ending flood. The sign is the bow in the clouds (9:8–17).
- Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered. Ham sees and tells; Shem and Japheth cover him without looking. Noah curses Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth (9:18–29).

## Pay attention to this
- **Adam's blessing again (9:1).** The flood is a restart, and Noah is a new Adam. 🔴
- **Meat comes with a fence (9:3–4).** Genesis 1:29 gave plants only. Now "every moving thing," but in the same breath: not with its life, its blood. 🔴
- **The image after the Fall (9:6).** God still grounds the value of human life in the image, after the Fall and after the flood. The image wasn't lost. 🔴
- **Covenant with every creature (9:10).** Not just people. Birds, cattle, beasts. 🔴
- **God reminds himself (9:15–16).** "I will look upon it, to remember." The bow is mainly a sign for God. 🔴
- **"My bow" (9:13).** The Hebrew *qeshet* is the ordinary word for a war bow. 🔴
- **Noah curses Canaan, not Ham (9:25).** The text says "Ham, the father of Canaan" twice (9:18, 22) to set this up. 🔴
- **Walking backward (9:23).** Shem and Japheth go to real lengths not to see. 🔴
- **"Saw the nakedness" (9:22).** In Leviticus 18 "uncover the nakedness" is a phrase for sexual sin. Whether that's in play here is debated. 🔴 for the phrase; ⬜ for what Ham did.
- **"Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Shem" (9:26).** The blessing goes to God, and it marks Shem's line as the one that carries the promise. Abraham comes from Shem (11:10–26). 🔴

## Read it like 1400 BC, not 2026
- **Blood is life.** Across the ANE, blood was tied to life and to the gods. Some peoples drank blood or ate meat with it in rituals. Israel's rule says the life belongs to God, so the blood goes back to him (Leviticus 17:11). Noah gets it before Israel exists. 🔴
- **A war bow hung in the sky.** In *Enuma Elish* the gods set Marduk's bow in the heavens as a star after his battle. Genesis uses the ordinary word for a war bow. A first reader could hear God hanging up his weapon after the flood and pointing it away from the earth. 🔴 for Enuma Elish; 🔵 for the "pointed away" picture.
- **Covenant signs were common.** Treaties had signs and witnesses. Here God binds himself, and the other party is the whole living world. 🟡
- **Dishonoring a father was serious.** In a world built on the father's household, exposing or shaming the head of the house was an attack on his authority. 🔴
- **Curses and blessings were real speech.** A father's last words over his sons were heard as shaping their future (compare Jacob in Genesis 49). 🔴
- **Canaan was the enemy next door.** Israel's first hearers lived beside or among the Canaanites. Noah's curse names the people Israel would face in Joshua. 🔴
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. It comes back in Genesis 10–11, where the nations are counted and then given to the sons of God at Babel (Deuteronomy 32:8–9).

## My notes
- **Meat is a concession.** It enters the Bible as a concession to a broken world, and it shows up with a fence already around it: before Israel, before Sinai, before there's a single Hebrew to give a law to. Everything after that is the fence getting built up in rings.
- **Blood is Noahide.** The blood rule is given to all humanity, not only Israel. That's why Acts 15 keeps it for Gentile believers when most of the food laws drop away. 🔴
- **Why the food laws?** I didn't accept "to be holy" as an answer by itself. There has to be some reason underneath. You can tell a vegan or a carnivore by what they eat, and an American from a Frenchman at a restaurant. You could tell an Israelite the same way. The diet marked whose household you belonged to.
- **9:6 settles the image question.** The penalty for murder rests on the image still being there in fallen people. So the image (the office) wasn't lost at the Fall. My frame: the office stays intact; the ambassadorship, representing God well, is what got distorted. 🔴 for the verse; 🟡 for the frame.
- **Ham and Canaan.** Three readings of what Ham did: disrespect (most traditional), sexual wrongdoing (debated), or trying to grab authority by shaming his father. Why Canaan gets cursed: a prophecy about Canaan's descendants, a pattern of sin passing down, or the future conflict with Israel. ⬜
- **The "curse of Ham" is a misuse.** People used this passage to justify slavery of Africans. That's wrong on the text: Ham isn't cursed, Canaan is, and the Canaanites lived in the Middle East. ❌ for that reading.
- **Shem's tents.** The blessing is on Yahweh, the God of Shem, and Japheth is welcomed to live in Shem's tents.

## What the chapter is doing
- The chapter opens by finishing a woe on Israel's own leaders: they write unjust laws to rob the poor, widows and orphans. God's hand is still stretched out against them (10:1–4).
- Then the turn: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger." God sends Assyria against his own godless people (10:5–6).
- Assyria doesn't know it's a tool. It thinks it's conquering by its own strength and plans to wipe out many nations, Jerusalem included (10:7–11).
- When God has finished his work on Zion, he will punish the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria. "Is the axe to boast itself over the one who chops with it?" (10:12–19).
- A remnant of Israel will return to the mighty God and stop leaning on the one who struck them. Assyria's march toward Jerusalem is pictured town by town, and then God cuts the forest down (10:20–34).

## Pay attention to this
- **The rod (10:5).** God calls Assyria his rod and his staff. The empire everybody feared is a stick in God's hand. 🔴
- **"I send it" (10:6).** God sends Assyria against "a godless nation," his own people. 🔴
- **"But it does not intend to act in this way" (10:7).** Assyria's plan and God's plan are not the same plan. God aims to discipline. Assyria aims to destroy and cut off many nations. 🔴
- **The king's boast (10:13–14).** "By the power of my hand and by my wisdom I did this." He robbed nations like gathering eggs from a nest, and nobody even chirped. 🔴
- **10:12 is where God turns.** "I will punish the fruit of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria." The instrument is judged for its heart. 🔴
- **The axe and the saw (10:15).** "Is the axe to boast itself over the one who chops with it? Is the saw to magnify itself over the one who wields it?" 🔴
- **"A remnant will return" (10:21).** In Hebrew, *shear yashuv*, the name of Isaiah's son in 7:3. 🔴
- **"The mighty God" (10:21).** *El gibbor*, the same title given to the child in 9:6. 🔴
- **10:22–23 in Romans.** Paul quotes "though your people be like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return" in Romans 9:27–28. 🔴
- **The march list (10:28–32).** Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, Gibeah, Anathoth, Nob. Each stop gets closer to Jerusalem until the enemy shakes his fist at Zion. 🔴

## Read it like 715 BC, not 2026
- **Assyria was the superpower.** In Isaiah's day Assyria took Damascus (732 BC) and Samaria (722 BC), and Sennacherib wrecked Judah's towns in 701 BC. The cities in 10:9 (Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, Damascus) are real conquests in Assyria's records. 🔴
- **Assyrian kings bragged exactly like this.** Their royal inscriptions say "by my strength," "by the wisdom of my heart," and list conquered cities. Isaiah 10:13–14 reads like a parody of one. 🔴 for the inscriptions; 🟡 for parody.
- **"The kingdoms of the idols" (10:10–11).** The Assyrian king thinks Jerusalem's God is one more local god, smaller than the gods of the nations he's already beaten. The ancient world assumed each nation had its gods, and that a conquest was their defeat. 🔴
- **Isaiah's answer to that worldview.** Every nation had its gods, and Assyria's gods were the ones winning. Isaiah says Yahweh is the one using Assyria. The gods of the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8–9) aren't beating Israel's God; Israel's God is running the whole board. 🔴 for the ancient assumption; 🟡 for the Deuteronomy 32 connection.
- **"Removed the boundaries of the peoples" (10:13).** Assyria deported whole populations and moved borders on purpose. That is the boast of an empire that redrew the map, the map Deuteronomy 32:8 says God drew. 🔴 for deportation policy; 🟡 for the Deuteronomy 32 link.
- **Yahweh of hosts against the army.** The "Lord, Yahweh of hosts" in 10:16, 23, 24, 26 and 33 is the God of the heavenly army. Assyria's warriors waste away (10:16). Compare 37:36, where the angel of Yahweh strikes the Assyrian camp. 🔴
- **The remnant from the exodus (10:24–26).** God promises to lift his staff over the sea "the way He did in Egypt" and strike like the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb (Judges 7:25). Israel's old victories are the model for the new one. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Yahweh will have compassion on Jacob, bring Israel home, and give them rest from hard slavery (14:1–3).
- Then Israel sings a taunt over the king of Babylon. The oppressor is gone, the earth is quiet, even the cedars of Lebanon celebrate because no one comes to cut them down (14:4–8).
- Sheol wakes up its dead kings to meet him: "You have become like us." Maggots are his bed and worms his blanket (14:9–11).
- The taunt reaches for heaven: the "star of the morning, son of the dawn" who said he would climb above the stars of God, sit on the mount of assembly and be like the Most High, and was thrown down to the pit instead (14:12–21).
- God swears to sweep Babylon away, to break Assyria in his land, and warns Philistia not to celebrate too soon (14:22–32).

## Pay attention to this
- **It's labeled a taunt against the king of Babylon (14:4).** The target is a human king. The word *satan* does not appear anywhere in the chapter. 🔴
- **"Star of the morning, son of the dawn" (14:12).** The Hebrew is *Helel ben Shachar*, "Shining One, son of the Dawn." 🔴
- **Five "I will"s (14:13–14).** I will ascend to heaven, raise my throne above the stars of God, sit on the mount of assembly, ascend above the clouds, make myself like the Most High. 🔴
- **"Nevertheless" (14:15).** Five claims to go up, one sentence that sends him down: to Sheol, the recesses of the pit. 🔴
- **"Recesses of the north" against "recesses of the pit" (14:13, 15).** The same word, *yarkete*, for the far edges of the north and the far depths of the pit. He aimed for one and landed in the other. 🔴
- **The dead greet him (14:9–10).** The "spirits of the dead" in LSB are the *rephaim*. Dead kings rise from their thrones in Sheol to mock him. 🔴
- **"Is this the man?" (14:16).** Right after the heavenly language, the poem calls him a man. 🔴
- **No grave (14:19–20).** Other kings lie in glory in their own tombs. He is thrown out like a trampled corpse. In that world, no burial was the worst end. 🔴
- **A flying fiery serpent (14:29).** In the Philistia oracle, *saraph me'opheph*, the same *saraph* as the seraphim of 6:2. 🔴

## Read it like 700 BC, not 2026
- **This is divine council furniture.** "The stars of God" (*kokebe El*), "the mount of assembly" (*har mo'ed*), "the recesses of the north" (*yarkete tsaphon*), "the Most High" (*Elyon*). Each phrase has a match in Ugaritic texts: the council called the stars, the assembled council (*phr m'd*), and Mount Sapanu (Zaphon), where Baal had his palace. The king is pictured as a member of the heavenly assembly trying to take the top seat. 🔴 for the vocabulary (Faithlife Study Bible; Heiser, *Unseen Realm* 100–102).
- **About versus behind.** The chapter is *about* the king of Babylon. *Behind* it is an older story of a divine being who rebelled against the Most High and was thrown down. Isaiah uses that story as a weapon against the king's pride. Genesis 3 is the Bible's own version of a rebel in God's garden. 🔴 as Heiser's reading; near-consensus that a divine rebel is in view.
- **Which rebel story?** Scholars point to Canaanite myths: Athtar, the morning star god who tried to sit on Baal's throne on Zaphon and was too small for it, and Helel, a dawn figure. The Venus star rises bright before dawn and then fades as the sun comes up. The fight is over which myth Isaiah used, not whether he used one. 🟡 for Athtar; ⬜ on the exact source.
- **The audience knew the story.** Walton and Walton warn that *Helel ben Shachar* is a figure modern scholars can't pin down for sure, though the first audience presumably could. 🔴 for the caution.
- **Sheol is a royal court of the dead.** The *rephaim* are the dead kings and heroes, still sitting on thrones in the underworld (14:9). In Ugarit the *rpum* were the honored royal dead. A king who wanted a heavenly throne ends up mocked in an underground one. 🔴
- **"Lucifer" came from Latin.** Jerome's Vulgate rendered *Helel* as *lucifer*, Latin for "light-bearer," the ordinary word for the morning star (Venus). The King James kept it as "Lucifer," and the common noun froze into a name for Satan. Wright and Stuckenbruck (2022) note "Lucifer" named the planet Venus from the late fourth century to the early 1600s. 🔴
- **The Satan reading came later.** Tertullian and others read 14:12 as the devil's fall, and Milton made it famous. Jesus' line "I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning" (Luke 10:18) is often tied to it. The Isaiah text itself names the king of Babylon. 🔴 for the reception history.
- **Kings claimed to be divine.** Mesopotamian kings were called sons of gods or images of gods, and some took divine titles. The boast "I will make myself like the Most High" is the logical end of that ideology. 🔴

## My notes
- **About versus behind.** The chapter is about the king of Babylon, and *satan* doesn't occur in it. Behind it is a primeval divine-rebel story Isaiah turns into a weapon against the king's pride. Genesis 3 is the Bible's own version of that story. Miss the distinction and you miss the whole Session 6. 🔴 as Heiser's reading.
- **Keep the tiers straight.** That the king is compared to a divine rebel is close to consensus (Heiser: essentially all scholars agree). The fight is over which rebellion myth Isaiah draws on. Ezekiel 28 is a different case: there Heiser says his reading is the minority view. I don't flatten the two to the same confidence.
- **"Lucifer."** *Helel ben Shachar*, Shining One, son of the Dawn. Jerome rendered it *lucifer*. It's a translation artifact and a Myth Busters candidate. The reception line runs from Tertullian to Milton.
- **Council furniture:** stars of El, the mount of assembly, the heights of Zaphon (14:13). Divine council vocabulary (Faithlife Study Bible; *Unseen Realm* 100–102).
- **Walton and Walton's caution:** the king is called "the man," and *Helel ben Shachar* is a figure modern scholars can't identify for sure.
- **14:11** is one of the decay uses of *tola'ath*, worms under the humiliated king, from my tola worm study. **14:29** is a *saraph*, "flying serpent," one more piece of evidence for the seraphim as serpents in Isaiah 6.
- **The quiz question:** True. Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 are best read as drawing on a primeval divine-rebel story rather than being only about Satan.

## What the chapter is doing
- In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne, the train of his robe filling the temple, with seraphim above him calling "Holy, holy, holy is Yahweh of hosts."
- The foundations of the thresholds shake and the house fills with smoke. Isaiah says, "Woe is me, for I am ruined," a man of unclean lips who has seen the King.
- A seraph flies to him with a burning coal from the altar, touches his mouth, and says his guilt is taken away.
- The Lord asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for Us?" Isaiah says, "Here am I. Send me!"
- His message is hard: tell the people to keep hearing and not understand. It runs until the cities are ruined, and what's left is a stump, a holy seed.

## Pay attention to this
- **"In the year King Uzziah died" (6:1).** A long-reigning king is gone. Isaiah sees the King who doesn't die. 🔴 for the date; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **The train fills the temple (6:1).** The Hebrew *shul* is the lower edge, hem or skirt of a garment. Only the bottom of the robe fits in the building. 🔴
- **Seraphim (6:2).** *Seraph* elsewhere means a fiery serpent (Numbers 21:6, 8; Deuteronomy 8:15) and, in Isaiah, a flying serpent (14:29; 30:6). The throne beings carry the same name. 🔴 for the word's other uses.
- **Six wings, used three ways (6:2).** Two cover the face, two cover the feet, two fly. Even these beings cover themselves before God. 🔴
- **"Holy, holy, holy" (6:3).** Repetition is the Hebrew way of saying "most." The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran has "holy" twice, not three times. 🔴
- **"Yahweh of hosts."** *Tseva'ot*, armies. The God of the heavenly army is on the throne. 🔴
- **"Woe is me, for I am ruined" (6:5).** Isaiah has just pronounced six woes on others (5:8–23). Now it's his turn. 🔴
- **The coal touches his mouth (6:6–7).** The problem he named was his lips. That's where the cleansing goes. 🔴
- **"Who will go for Us?" (6:8).** "I" and "Us" in the same sentence. 🔴
- **The hard commission (6:9–10).** "Render the hearts of this people insensitive, Their ears dull, And their eyes dim." Jesus quotes it to explain the parables (Matthew 13:14–15), and Paul quotes it at the end of Acts (28:26–27). 🔴
- **The stump (6:13).** Even after the tree is cut down, "the holy seed is its stump." 🔴

## Read it like 740 BC, not 2026
- **This is a council scene.** God on a throne, heavenly beings standing around him, a question put to the room, and a volunteer. It's the same shape as 1 Kings 22:19–22, where Micaiah sees Yahweh on his throne with "all the host of heaven" and asks who will go entice Ahab. The prophet who stands in the council gets sent with its decision (Jeremiah 23:18, 22). 🔴
- **"For Us" is God speaking to the council.** Heiser reads 6:8 as Yahweh addressing the heavenly assembly, and Isaiah, a human, volunteering in a room full of divine beings. Compare the plural commands to the council in 40:1–2 ("Comfort, comfort My people"). 🔴 as Heiser's reading; 🟡 against the older Trinitarian reading of "Us."
- **Seraphim were throne guardians with a serpent shape.** Egypt's uraeus, the rearing cobra with wings, guarded the pharaoh's throne and crown. Israelite seals from the monarchy show four-winged uraeus serpents, and Tutankhamun's throne has winged serpents on it. Joines, De Savignac, Keel and Charlesworth argue the seraphim come from that picture. DDD and Mettinger call it the consensus. John Day adds a lightning angle inside it. 🔴 for the iconography; 🟡 for direct origin.
- **The temple was the throne room on earth.** Israel pictured the ark as God's footstool and the cherubim as his throne (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 99:1). Isaiah sees through the building to the throne it stood for. 🔴
- **Long trains were real royal dress.** Elite clothing had long hanging edges and trains in the ANE. A garment so big that its hem alone fills a temple is a picture of a King too big for his house. 🔴 for dress; 🟡 for the image.
- **What a hem meant.** Attaching your hem to someone's bound an alliance or marriage, and cutting it dissolved the bond (David and Saul's robe, 1 Samuel 24:4–5). Assyrian kings did take whole royal garments of defeated kings as a sign of taking their power (Gaspa, *JANEH* 2024). That's covenant and appropriation, not a quilt of trophies. 🔴 for hem as covenant; 🟡 for Gaspa, near-verified.
- **Unclean lips and lethal holiness (6:5).** Seeing God meant you should die (Exodus 33:20). Isaiah's terror is about sin in God's presence, not about being small. 🔴
- **Mouths made fit to speak.** Mesopotamia had a "washing of the mouth" rite (*mis pi*) that made a cult statue fit to stand for its god. Isaiah gets his mouth cleansed too, but by fire from Yahweh's own altar, and he's a man, not an idol. 🔴 for the rite; 🔵 for any connection.

## My notes
- **The king's train.** I heard a sermon say that if you study kings back then, when one king defeated another he cut a piece off the loser's train and sewed it onto his own, so a long train meant many victories. He said "if you study it," so I went and studied it.
- **What I found.** No primary source, no archaeology, no mainstream scholar supports it, across every region we searched and my 1,500-plus-book Logos library. The earliest version I could find was a December 2007 blog post presented as a personal insight. The print version is Rod Mattoon, *Treasures from Isaiah* (2014), 1:150, with no citation. An AI tool told me Louie Giglio wrote it in 2003. That was made up, and it took eight checks to catch it.
- I built it as a neutral record of what I found, not a takedown. It wasn't completely made up by a man. It was a man who found what he was looking for and stopped digging. If I don't correct something like that when I hear it, I'm part of the problem, and the next person adds a little more to the story.
- The picture of a quilt that tells a story did land for me. Quilts are given at births and weddings. The history under it just isn't there.
- **What is real:** hems bound alliances and marriages, cutting one dissolved the bond, and whole-garment capture showed a transfer of power (Gaspa 2024, near-verified). Trains were real features of elite dress (Nelson's; Swanson). The only unsupported part is the conquest tally.
- ***Shul*.** Hem, skirt, train: the lower hanging part of a garment. Eleven occurrences (Gilbrant). The non-priestly uses gather around defeat and exposure (Jeremiah 13:22, 26; Nahum 3:5).
- **Seraphim are serpents.** I had it marked soft, and then it got called "debunked" because one Logos search pushed back on the etymology. Both calls were wrong. My rule after that: we don't say one person is wrong and the other right on one weak return. Heiser and BibleProject are top-tier and get more than one search. With Joines, Keel, Charlesworth, DDD and the Tutankhamun throne in hand, the serpent reading stands. 🟡
- **6:3, two holies.** The Great Isaiah Scroll has two, which weakens the "three holies equals the Trinity" argument (Heiser's aside in Session 4).
- **6:8, "who will go for Us?"** God asking the heavenly assembly, and Isaiah volunteering.
- **6:5.** "A man of unclean lips": the danger of the presence is tied to sin, not to being a creature (from my Eden-as-divine-space study).

## What the chapter is doing
- James warns that not many should become teachers, because teachers will be judged more strictly. Everybody stumbles, and the place we stumble most is our mouths.
- The tongue is small, like a horse's bit, a ship's rudder or a spark, and it steers or burns the whole thing. People can tame every kind of animal, but nobody tames the tongue.
- The same mouth blesses God and curses people made in God's likeness. A spring doesn't give fresh and bitter water; a fig tree doesn't grow olives.
- Two kinds of wisdom. One is jealous and selfish, "earthly, natural, demonic," and brings disorder. The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, merciful and sincere, and peacemakers sow a harvest of righteousness.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Do not, many of you, become teachers" (3:1).** Not "don't teach." Don't rush into it. And James counts himself in: "we will receive a stricter judgment." 🔴
- **The tongue section follows the teacher warning.** Teachers work with words. The rest of the chapter is about what words do. 🔴
- **"We all stumble in many ways" (3:2).** James includes himself again. 🔴
- **Small things steer big things (3:3–5).** Bit, rudder, spark. Three pictures, one point. 🔴
- **"Set on fire by hell" (3:6).** The word is Gehenna, used only here in the New Testament outside Jesus' own mouth. 🔴
- **"Made in the likeness of God" (3:9).** The reason cursing people is wrong is who they are, not how they behaved. 🔴
- **"These things ought not to be so" (3:10).** Blessing God and cursing his image-bearers from the same mouth doesn't fit. 🔴
- **Wisdom shows in conduct (3:13).** "Let him show by his good conduct." For James, being wise is something people can see. 🔴
- **"Earthly, natural, demonic" (3:15).** Three steps down. Bad wisdom isn't only a human failing; it has a source below. 🔴
- **Wisdom from above (3:17).** Eight marks, starting with "pure." Peace runs through the list and the chapter's last line. 🔴

## Read it like AD 50, not 2026
- **James the brother of Jesus.** The letter is traditionally from James, Jesus' brother and leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15; Galatians 1:19), writing to "the twelve tribes who are in the dispersion" (1:1), Jewish believers scattered abroad. During Jesus' ministry his brothers didn't believe (John 7:5). 🔴 for the tradition and the texts; 🟡 for authorship.
- **Teachers had status.** Being called "Rabbi" brought honor and a seat up front (Matthew 23:6–8). In the early church, teaching was one of the ranked gifts (1 Corinthians 12:28). People wanted it for the wrong reasons. 🔴
- **Bit, rudder, fire were stock pictures.** Greek moral writers like Plutarch and the Jewish writer Philo used horses' bits and ships' rudders to talk about self-control. James borrows familiar classroom images. 🔴
- **Jewish wisdom on the tongue.** Proverbs is full of it ("death and life are in the power of the tongue," 18:21), and Sirach 28:13–26 has a long warning about the tongue that has destroyed many. James stands in that line. 🔴
- **Taming the animals.** "Every kind of beasts and birds, of reptiles and creatures of the sea" (3:7) is Genesis 1's list of what humans were given to rule (1:26–28). We can rule all of that and not our own mouths. 🔴
- **Gehenna.** The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children were once burned to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31), became the name for the place of final judgment. The tongue's fire has its source there. 🔴
- **"Demonic" wisdom (3:15).** James's word, *daimoniōdēs*, means coming from or like demons. Jewish readers knew the story of fallen Watchers teaching humans forbidden knowledge (1 Enoch 8). Wisdom has a source, and some of it comes from below. 🔴 for the word and 1 Enoch; 🟡 for the connection.
- **Wisdom from above.** In Jewish thought true wisdom came down from God (Proverbs 8; Wisdom of Solomon 9:9–10). James sets "above" against "earthly." 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- God sends Jeremiah down to the potter's house. The pot on the wheel gets ruined in the potter's hand, so he reworks it into another pot (18:1–4).
- God says Israel is clay in his hand. If he announces disaster on a nation and it turns from its evil, he will relent. If he promises good and it does evil, he will relent of the good (18:5–10).
- So Jeremiah is to tell Judah: I am shaping disaster against you, turn back. They answer, "It's hopeless," we'll follow our own plans (18:11–12).
- God says even the nations have never heard of a people dropping their God like this. They burn incense to worthless gods, so the land will become a horror (18:13–17).
- The people plot to take Jeremiah down with their tongues. He prays for God to judge them (18:18–23).

## Pay attention to this
- **The potter changes his plan (18:4).** The clay was ruined, so he made something else, "according to what was right in the eyes of the potter." 🔴
- **"Like the clay in the potter's hand" (18:6).** The image says God has the right. The next four verses say how he uses it. 🔴
- **The condition is the point (18:7–10).** "If that nation... turns from its evil, I will relent." And the reverse. God's announced plans for nations depend on how they respond. 🔴
- **"Relent" (18:8, 10).** The Hebrew *nicham*, the same word used when God relents over Nineveh (Jonah 3:10). 🔴
- **"I am forming calamity" (18:11).** "Forming" is *yotser*, the same root as "potter" (*yotser*). God the potter is shaping a disaster, and still calling them to turn. 🔴
- **"It's hopeless!" (18:12).** The people answer the invitation by refusing it. 🔴
- **Snow and streams (18:14).** Nature keeps its course. Israel didn't. 🔴
- **"The ancient paths" (18:15).** Compare 6:16, "ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is." 🔴
- **"I will show them My back and not My face" (18:17).** The reverse of the priestly blessing, "Yahweh make His face shine on you" (Numbers 6:25). 🟡
- **Jeremiah's harsh prayer (18:19–23).** One of his "confessions." He once stood before God to speak good for them (18:20). Now he asks God not to forgive them. 🔴

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **Potters were everywhere.** Every town had one. The wheel had two stones, one turned by foot to spin the upper one. Anyone in Jerusalem had watched a potter squash a lump and start again. 🔴
- **The potter is an old picture of God.** Genesis 2:7 uses the same verb, *yatsar*, for God forming Adam. In Egypt the god Khnum shaped people on a potter's wheel. Jeremiah's audience knew the image as a creation picture. 🔴
- **Prophecy could be conditional.** A prophet's warning was often a call to change, not a fixed timetable. Jonah's Nineveh and Hezekiah's illness (Isaiah 38) are examples. Jeremiah 26:18–19 says Micah's word against Jerusalem was held back when Hezekiah repented. 🔴
- **Worthless gods (18:15).** The word is *shav*, emptiness. Judah was burning incense to the gods of other nations, the ones Deuteronomy 32 says belong to the nations and are "not God." 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the Deuteronomy 32 link.
- **"Strike at him with our tongue" (18:18).** Priests, wise men and prophets were the three sources of guidance. The establishment closes ranks against a lone prophet. 🔴
- **Jeremiah stood before God (18:20).** "To stand before Yahweh" is the posture of a prophet in the council, the one who hears and intercedes (Jeremiah 15:1; 23:18, 22). 🔴 for the phrase; 🟡 for the council reading.
- **The council itself isn't in this chapter.** Jeremiah's clearest council passage is 23:18–22, where the true prophet is the one who has stood in Yahweh's *sod*, his council.

## META: the book of Job
- **Where it sits.** First of the poetry and wisdom books in English Bibles (Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs). In the Hebrew order it sits in the Writings. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** does anyone serve God for nothing, and what do you say about God when a good man suffers? The satan asks the first half in 1:9. Job and his friends fight over the second half for thirty-five chapters. 🔴
- **A prose sandwich with poetry in the middle.** Chapters 1–2 and 42:7–17 are prose. Everything between is poetry: Job's lament (3), three rounds with the friends (4–27), the wisdom poem (28), Job's last defense and oath (29–31), Elihu (32–37), God from the whirlwind (38–41), Job's answer (42:1–6). 🔴
- **The reader knows what Job never learns.** The frame shows us the council scene. Job, his wife and his friends never see it. That gap runs the whole book. 🔴
- **Set outside Israel.** Uz, "the sons of the east," no temple, no covenant, no law of Moses. The speakers say God (*Eloah*, *Shaddai*), not Yahweh, while the narrator uses Yahweh. It is still an Israelite book written for Israelites, working below the level of covenant. 🔴 for the setting and names (Davy/McConville, Keil & Delitzsch, Lindsay Wilson as pulled in Logos).
- **Who wrote it and when.** Nobody knows. The Talmud (Bava Batra 15a) records rabbis putting Job anywhere from Moses' day to the return from exile. Guesses for the writing run from Solomon to after the exile. I use 600 BC below as a middle stake, not as a fact. ⬜
- **The Hebrew is hard.** Job has more rare words than almost any book in the Old Testament, and some lines (19:26 is the famous one) are rough enough that translations split. When versions disagree in Job, that's usually why. 🔴
- **Movements:** the test (1–2), the argument (3–31), the young man who won't stop talking (32–37), God answers with questions (38–41), the verdict and the restoration (42).
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - The council in heaven that Job never sees (1:6, 2:1, 38:7).
  - The retribution rule: good people get blessed, bad people get punished. The friends run it like a machine. God says at the end they did not speak rightly (42:7).
  - Job wanting a hearing, a witness, a redeemer (9:33, 16:19, 19:25).
  - Who does the harm. The satan strikes, God says "you incited Me" (2:3), and the narrator says Yahweh brought it (42:11).

## What the chapter is doing
- Job is introduced: a rich man in Uz, ten children, blameless and upright, fearing God and turning from evil. He even offers sacrifices in case his kids sinned in their hearts.
- The scene moves to heaven. The sons of God present themselves before Yahweh, and the satan is among them.
- Yahweh points to Job. The satan asks whether Job fears God "without cause," and gets permission to take everything Job has, but not touch Job himself.
- Four messengers arrive back to back. Oxen, sheep, camels, servants and finally all ten children are gone in one day.
- Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls down and worships: "Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away." He does not sin or charge God with wrong.

## Pay attention to this
- **What Job gets and what he doesn't (1:1).** Blameless, upright, fearing God, turning from evil. What he does not get is the line Enoch and Noah get, "walked with God" (*hithallek 'et-ha'elohim*, Genesis 5:24; 6:9). The wording difference is real. What it means is argued. 🔴 for the wording; ⬜ for what it means.
- **The same four words come back in God's mouth (1:8, 2:3).** The narrator's description of Job is repeated by Yahweh word for word. The reader is not meant to doubt Job's character. 🔴
- **"Fear of God" is the wisdom word.** "Fearing God and turning away from evil" is the line Job 28:28 gives as the definition of wisdom. 🔴
- **Job's careful sacrifices (1:5).** He offers for sins his kids might have committed in their hearts. Whether that is devotion or anxiety is one of the places readers split. 🔵
- **"Without cause" (1:9).** The Hebrew is *chinnam*, for nothing, for free. The satan isn't saying Job is a bad man. He's saying Job's goodness has a price tag. God uses the same word back at him in 2:3. 🔴
- **The hedge (1:10).** The satan admits God has protected Job on every side. The accuser knows exactly whose hand is on Job. 🔴
- **Four disasters, two from the sky.** Sabeans, then "the fire of God" from heaven, then Chaldeans, then a great wind. Raiders and nature take turns. Job's servants call the lightning "the fire of God." 🔴
- **"I alone have escaped to tell you."** Said four times. Each messenger is still talking when the next one arrives. The writer stacks it on purpose. 🔴
- **Job speaks to God in worship, not about God in complaint (1:21–22).** "Naked I came... Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be the name of Yahweh." Compare 2:10, where the wording of the narrator's verdict changes. 🔴
- **LSB prints "Satan" like a name.** The Hebrew has the article every time in Job 1–2: *ha-satan*, the satan, the adversary. Most English Bibles hide that. 🔴

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **The council scene (1:6).** "The sons of God came to stand before Yahweh." *Bene ha'elohim* is council language. The same phrase family shows up in Ugaritic texts, where *bn 'il*, the sons of El, gather before the high god. Psalm 82, 1 Kings 22:19–23 and Isaiah 6 show the same kind of throne room. A 2026 reader pictures angels with harps. A reader in 600 BC pictured a royal court with God on the throne and his officials reporting in. 🔴 for the Ugaritic vocabulary (Heiser, BibSac papers; Parker in DDD); 🔴 for the council reading.
- **"To stand before" is a court phrase.** Officials present themselves to the king to report and receive orders. The council members aren't drifting through. They have jobs. 🟡
- **The satan is an office, not a name.** *Ha-satan* has the definite article, and Hebrew does not put the article on personal names (Joüon-Muraoka §137b). It is a title: the adversary, the accuser, something like a prosecutor. The Greek Old Testament translates it *ho diabolos*. 🔴 Peggy Day (*An Adversary in Heaven*, 1988) and Ryan Stokes (*JBL* 128.1, 2009; *The Satan*) build the case that this is a role in the council. 🔴 that it's a title; 🟡 on how much later "Satan" to read back into it.
- **He reports in from patrol (1:7).** "From roaming about on the earth and walking around on it." In Ugaritic council scenes lesser gods report to El on how humans and other gods behave. Heiser reads the satan here the same way: the council member whose job is checking on human behavior. 🟡
- **He is not the Eden serpent, at least not in Job.** Nothing in Job ties the satan to the *nachash* of Genesis 3. Merging the serpent, the accuser and the devil into one figure happens later, in Second Temple writings and in Revelation 12:9. 🔴 for Job's silence; 🔴 that Revelation 12:9 does the fusing.
- **God is the one who starts it (1:8).** Yahweh brings Job up, not the satan. Whatever the satan is in this scene, he works inside God's permission and only as far as God lets him (1:12). 🔴
- **Retribution was the common sense of the age.** Across the ancient Near East, suffering meant a god was angry and blessing meant a god was pleased. Mesopotamian texts have their own righteous sufferer (Ludlul bel nemeqi, "I will praise the lord of wisdom"). Walton reads Job as using that mindset as a foil: the friends run it, and the book rejects it. 🔴 for the ANE background; 🟡 for Walton's foil reading.
- **Uz and the east.** "The greatest of all the sons of the east" puts Job among the eastern peoples (Edom or the desert to the east), famous for wisdom (1 Kings 4:30). An Israelite hearing this knew the hero was not one of them. 🔴 for "sons of the east"; 🔵 for where exactly Uz was (Lamentations 4:21 ties it to Edom).
- **Wealth counted in animals and servants.** 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 donkeys. That is a chieftain's fortune, the way a patriarch is described in Genesis. 🔴
- **The father as household priest (1:5).** No temple and no Levites. The head of the house offers the burnt offerings, like Noah and Abraham. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Job answers Bildad: how long will you crush me with words? Ten times you've shamed me.
- He says plainly that God has wronged him, walled up his road, stripped his honor and treated him like an enemy, and he gets no answer when he cries "Violence!"
- Everyone has left: brothers, relatives, house servants, his wife, even little kids mock him. "Pity me, pity me, O you my friends."
- Then the turn: he wants his words cut into rock forever, and he says, "I know that my Redeemer lives," and that he will see God with his own eyes.
- He ends by warning the friends that judgment is coming for them.

## Pay attention to this
- **Job blames God out loud (19:6–12).** "God has wronged me." The friends have said Job's suffering proves his sin. Job says it proves God has done him wrong. Both sides are still working from the same rule. 🔴
- **God's troops camp around his tent (19:12).** Job pictures God as an army laying siege to one man. 🔴
- **The list of who left him (19:13–19).** Brothers, acquaintances, relatives, friends, guests, maidservants, his own servant, his wife, his brothers again, children, close friends. It reads like a man counting the empty chairs. 🔴
- **"The skin of my teeth" (19:20).** The source of the English saying. Nobody is sure exactly what it meant in Hebrew. 🔴 for the phrase; 🔵 for its meaning.
- **"Oh that my words were written" (19:23–24).** Book first, then cut into rock with an iron stylus and lead, forever. He wants a record that lasts. 🔴
- **"My Redeemer" (19:25).** The word is *go'el*, the family member who buys back land, frees a relative from slavery, or avenges a killing (Leviticus 25; Numbers 35; Ruth 3–4). 🔴
- **"At the last He will rise up over the dust" (19:25).** "Stand up" is courtroom language, the witness or advocate rising to speak. 🟡
- **One preposition carries 19:26.** *Mibbesari* is *min*, "from," attached to "my flesh." LSB: "from my flesh I shall behold God." Older JPS and the ASV margin go "without my flesh." 🔴 that the line splits; ⬜ on which way it goes.
- **"My eyes will see and not another" (19:27).** He wants to see God himself, not hear the verdict secondhand. 🔴
- **The first half of 19:26 is rough Hebrew.** Several translations footnote it as unclear or likely damaged. 🔴

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **The *go'el* was family law, not a theology word.** In Israel and its neighbors, if you lost your land, your freedom or your life, the closest male relative was supposed to step in. A man with no *go'el* had no one. Job has lost every relative (19:13–19), and then he says his *go'el* lives. 🔴 for the institution; 🟡 for the connection inside the chapter.
- **Courts, witnesses and records.** Ancient legal disputes turned on witnesses and written evidence. Kings cut their victories into rock so they would outlast them, like the Behistun inscription of Darius. Job wants his testimony on file the same way, in case the verdict comes after he's gone. 🔴 for the practice; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Who is the Redeemer?** Job has already asked for an arbiter between him and God (9:33) and said his witness is in heaven (16:19). Some read the *go'el* as a heavenly figure who will argue for Job in God's court, the council setting from chapters 1–2 seen from the ground. Others read it as God himself. 🔵 for a council advocate; 🟡 for God as the *go'el*. Christians later heard Christ here, and Handel made it famous.
- **The council is still in the room, and Job doesn't know it.** The reader saw the accuser stand before God in chapters 1–2. Job is now asking for a defender in the same court, with no idea there was ever a prosecutor. 🟡
- **Death and Sheol.** For most of the Old Testament the dead go down to Sheol, a shadowy place, and hope after death is thin. That is why 19:26 is fought over: is Job hoping to be cleared in this life, or after he dies? 🔴 for the general background; ⬜ for this verse.
- **Elihu's angel is not Job's Redeemer.** Elihu later talks about a mediating angel, "one out of a thousand" (33:23–24). That is Elihu speaking, not Job. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- The council meets again. The satan presents himself, and Yahweh points to Job a second time: he still holds fast his integrity, "so you incited Me against him to swallow him up in vain."
- The satan raises the stakes: "Skin for skin!" Touch his body and he'll curse you. God gives permission, but Job's life is off limits.
- Job is struck with boils from head to foot. He sits in the ashes scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery.
- His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers that we take good from God, so why not trouble too. He does not sin with his lips.
- Three friends come, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They don't recognize him, they weep, and they sit with him seven days without a word.

## Pay attention to this
- **The scene is copied on purpose (2:1–3 against 1:6–8).** Same day, same assembly, same question, same description of Job. The repetition makes the one new line stand out: "he still holds fast his integrity." 🔴
- **"You incited Me" (2:3).** God says the satan moved him against Job, "in vain," for nothing (*chinnam*, the same word the satan used in 1:9). God takes the action into his own mouth. 🔴
- **"Skin for skin" (2:4).** Likely a trading or bartering saying: a man will give anything to keep his own life. The exact sense is debated. 🔴 for the line; 🔵 for the exact idiom.
- **The limit moves (2:6).** In chapter 1 the satan could not touch Job. Now he can touch everything but his life. 🔴
- **Head to foot (2:7).** "From the sole of his foot to the top of his head" is a way of saying all of him. 🔴
- **Ashes and a potsherd (2:8).** Sitting in the ash heap is mourning, and it's also where the town's trash and the outcast end up. 🔴
- **Her words echo the satan's (2:9).** "Curse God" is what the satan said Job would do. "Do you still hold fast your integrity?" is what God just said about him. She stands between the two speeches. 🔴
- **"Foolish" (2:10).** *Nabal*, the word for a person who acts like God doesn't matter, not someone with a low IQ. 🔴
- **"With his lips."** 1:22 says Job did not sin or charge God with wrong. 2:10 says he did not sin with his lips. Readers split on whether the change means anything. 🔴 for the wording; ⬜ for what it means.
- **Seven days of silence (2:13).** The friends get this part right. It is the best thing they do in the whole book. 🟡

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **The council again (2:1).** The sons of God "came to stand before Yahweh," and this time the satan comes "to stand himself before Yahweh" too, presenting himself for review like any other official. This is a court with a King. 🔴 for the council setting.
- **The satan is the accuser, still an office.** *Ha-satan* with the article again. He has to ask, report and get permission. He cannot move a hair on Job without it (2:6). 🔴
- **Who did it?** The satan strikes Job (2:7). God says the satan incited him (2:3). At the end the narrator says Job's family comforted him over all the evil Yahweh had brought on him (42:11). An ancient reader didn't need to split "God allowed" from "God did" the way we do. 🔴 for what the verses say; 🟡 for the cultural point.
- **Skin disease meant you were under judgment.** In that world a body covered in sores looked like a man God was punishing. It also cut him off from community. That is why the friends can't recognize him and why their next move (in chapter 4) is to look for his sin. 🔴
- **Mourning rites (2:12).** Torn robes, dust thrown toward the sky, weeping out loud. Ancient grief was public and physical. The seven days match the usual mourning period for the dead (Genesis 50:10; Sirach 22:12). They are mourning a man who is still alive. 🔴 for the customs; 🟡 for the "mourning a living man" read.
- **The friends travel by appointment (2:11).** Three men from Teman, Shuah and Naamah, all eastern names. Teman is famous for wise men (Jeremiah 49:7). These are the experts showing up. 🔴
- **What the wife's line would have sounded like.** "Curse God and die" assumes cursing God gets you killed. In that world it wasn't a figure of speech. 🟡
