## What the chapter is doing
- A poem about where wisdom can be found, sitting between the friends' last round and Job's final speech.
- Humans can dig anything out of the earth. Miners cut shafts, hang on ropes, find silver, gold, iron, sapphires, and dam up rivers to see what's underneath (28:1–11).
- Wisdom isn't down there. It isn't in the land of the living, the deep says "not in me," the sea says "not with me," and no amount of gold or jewels can buy it (28:12–19).
- Abaddon and Death have only heard a rumor of it. God alone understands the way to it, because he saw it when he set the wind, the waters, the rain and the thunder (28:20–27).
- To humankind he says: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn from evil is understanding (28:28).

## Pay attention to this
- **The same question asked twice (28:12, 28:20).** "But where can wisdom be found?" splits the poem into its parts. 🔴
- **Mining is the picture of human reach.** Ancient mining was the most impressive thing people could do: going where no bird or lion has gone (28:7–8), tunneling through rock, bringing hidden things into the light. The poem honors it before it shows the limit. 🔴
- **Wisdom can't be bought (28:15–19).** Gold, silver, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal, pearls, topaz. The longest list of precious things in the Bible, and none of it is enough. 🔴
- **The deep and the sea speak (28:14), and so do Abaddon and Death (28:22).** The places humans fear most are made to testify that they don't have it either. 🔴
- **God "saw it and declared it" at creation (28:25–27).** Wisdom is tied to how the world was made. Compare Proverbs 8:22–31. 🔴
- **28:28 matches Job 1:1.** "The fear of the Lord" and "turn from evil" are the words used to describe Job in 1:1, 1:8 and 2:3. Job already had what the poem says wisdom is. 🔴 for the matching words.
- **Who is speaking?** The poem sits inside Job's speech (27:1 to 31:40), but it is calm in a way Job isn't anywhere else. Many read it as the narrator's interlude. 🔴 that it sits in Job's speech; ⬜ on who speaks it.
- **"The Lord" in 28:28 is *Adonai*.** One of the very few places in the poetry where the speech uses a name close to Israel's own way of speaking about God. 🔴

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **Mining was real and known.** The Sinai turquoise and copper mines worked by Egyptians, the copper mines in the Arabah at Timna and Faynan, and Solomon's world of metal trade (1 Kings 10) were well known. The poem describes shafts and ropes from real practice. 🔴 for ancient mining in the region; 🟡 for how directly the poet knew it.
- **The deep, the sea, Abaddon, Death.** In the ancient picture of the world, the deep and the sea were chaos waters, and Abaddon (destruction) and Death sat at the bottom of everything. Other cultures made gods of some of these (Yam the Sea in Ugarit, Mot the god of death). Here they are only places, and even they don't have wisdom. 🔴 for the Ugaritic names; 🟡 for reading the poem as quietly demoting them.
- **International wisdom.** Egypt and Mesopotamia had their own wisdom teachers and books. Egyptian wisdom tied right living to *ma'at*, the order of the world. Job 28 says real wisdom is not something anyone can find or buy, only receive from God. 🔴 for the ANE wisdom background; 🟡 for the contrast.
- **The fear of the Lord is the Israelite core.** Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10 say it's the beginning of wisdom. Job 28:28 ends where Proverbs starts. 🔴
- **No council scene here.** The heavenly court of chapters 1–2 isn't in this poem. It comes back in 38:7, when God says the morning stars and the sons of God shouted at creation.

## My notes
- I worked this poem in Dale M.'s Job/Genesis echoes thread on drmsh.com.
- Structure as I laid it out: verses 1–11 human reach (miners, silver, sapphires, damming rivers); 12–22 wisdom isn't in the land of the living, the deep and sea deny having it, Abaddon and Death have heard a rumor; 23–27 God alone knows the way; 28 the human part.
- **The Genesis 3 link that didn't hold.** It was offered to me that 28:28 contrasts with the garden: Adam grabbed the knowledge of good and evil (*ra'*), Job 28 says wisdom can't be grabbed, and 28:28 tells humans to turn from *ra'*. It was tied to Job 1:1, 1:8 and 2:3. I said I didn't see the connection. On review it was thin: "turn from evil" (*sur me-ra'*) is stock wisdom wording (Psalm 34:14; Proverbs 3:7; 16:6, 17; Isaiah 1:16), *ra'* is one of the most common words in the Bible, and *la-adam* most plainly means "to humankind." It was first handed to me as solid. Honest tier is 🔵. My confusion was the right response. ❌ as a strong Genesis 3 echo.
- **The method point I carried out of it.** Nobody in the thread asked what makes an echo count. Adding a twenty-first echo to the pile is the same piling-up-instead-of-testing problem I named after the Live in Context call.
- Some scholars treat 28:28 as a later addition. I noted it and didn't chase it.
- **Divine council:** none in this chapter. The council shows up again in 38:7.

## What the chapter is doing
- Yahweh finally answers Job, out of the whirlwind. He doesn't explain the test from chapters 1–2. He asks questions.
- "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" God walks Job through creation: the earth's foundations, the sea held behind doors, the morning, the gates of death, light and darkness, snow and hail.
- Then the sky and the weather: rain on land where nobody lives, the constellations (Pleiades, Orion), the clouds and lightning.
- The chapter ends with animals: food for the lion and the raven's young. The animal tour keeps going into chapter 39.

## Pay attention to this
- **God shows up in a storm (38:1).** The whirlwind is the setting for God appearing in power (Ezekiel 1:4; Nahum 1:3). 🔴
- **"Who is this that darkens counsel?" (38:2).** The word *etsah*, counsel or plan. God says Job has been talking about God's plan without knowing it. 🔴
- **"Gird up your loins like a man" (38:3).** Tuck in your robe and get ready to fight or work. God has accepted Job's challenge to a hearing, just not on Job's terms. 🔴
- **Questions, not answers.** At the point where the reader expects God to explain, God asks. Count the questions. 🔴
- **Building language (38:4–6).** Foundation, measurements, a line stretched over it, bases sunk, a cornerstone laid. God talks about the earth like a builder laying out a temple. 🔴
- **38:7: "When the morning stars sang together And all the sons of God shouted for joy."** In Hebrew poetry the second line usually restates the first. So the morning stars and the sons of God are the same group. 🔴
- **They were there before the earth (38:7).** They sang when the cornerstone was laid. The sons of God are older than the world. 🔴
- **The sea in a crib (38:8–11).** God wraps the sea in clouds like a baby and sets a limit: "Thus far you shall come, but no farther." 🔴
- **The gates of death (38:17).** Job has been begging to die. God asks if he has seen the gates of death. 🔴
- **Rain where nobody lives (38:26).** God waters land with no people in it. The world doesn't run around Job. 🔴

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **The council was there at creation (38:7).** "Sons of God" is the same phrase as 1:6 and 2:1. Job 1–2 showed the council at the start of Job's trouble. 38:7 shows the council at the start of the world. Job never saw the first scene. Now God tells him about the second. 🔴 for the phrase; 🟡 for the connection to the prologue.
- **Stars as living beings.** Across the ancient Near East stars were tied to divine beings. Ugaritic texts put "stars" in parallel with gods the same way 38:7 does, and the council there is called "the congregation of stars" (*phr kkbm*). Parker (DDD, "Sons of (the) God(s)") notes the Ugaritic precedent. 🔴
- **The Bible keeps them created.** Heiser (*Bibliotheca Sacra* 158, 2001) groups Deuteronomy 4:19, Job 38:7 and Isaiah 14:13 as the "starry host" and argues that because these beings are created, the reading fits with one God. They sing to the Builder. They don't build. 🔴 for Heiser's argument; 🔴 that the text has them as witnesses, not makers.
- **The earliest Jewish reading agrees.** The Job Targum from Qumran (11QtgJob) renders 38:7 "all the angels of God shouted together." That is the oldest datable Jewish reading of the verse, and it already takes the stars as heavenly beings. 🔴
- **A subordinate court.** Elsewhere Job says God puts no trust in his holy ones and the heavens aren't pure in his sight (15:15), and that the stars aren't pure in his eyes (25:5). Lelli (DDD, "Stars") reads these with 38:7 as a heavenly entourage that is beneath Yahweh and can fail. 🟡
- **The sea needed fencing.** In Ugarit Baal fights Yam (Sea), and in Babylon Marduk splits Tiamat. In Job 38:8–11 there's no fight. God swaddles the sea like a newborn and tells it where to stop. 🔴 for the myths; 🟡 for reading 38:8–11 as a quiet answer to them.
- **The earth on foundations.** The ancient picture was a flat earth set on pillars over the waters, with the sky as a dome. God speaks inside that picture (38:4–6). The point isn't a science lesson. It's who did the building. 🔴
- **Storehouses of snow and hail (38:22).** Weather was kept in heavenly storerooms and released by God, often for battle (38:23; Joshua 10:11). 🔴

## My notes
- **What the speeches do.** The Logos pull from my Job guide: at the point an answer is expected, God asks questions instead of giving a reasoned answer, and the resolution comes through Job's changed perspective, not an explanation.
- **IP's reading of 38–41:** God answers "Who are you? Who am I?" to turn Job off his works. I laid it beside the Logos material without a verdict.
- **38:7 is one of the strong items.** In Dale M.'s echoes thread most of the list didn't hold up. This one did. It puts the council at creation. Poetry puts the equivalent in the second line, so the morning stars are a class of being, and they shout at the founding of the earth, so they come before it.
- I footnoted 38:7 into my Lesser Gods page with Parker (DDD) for the Ugaritic precedent and Heiser's *Bibliotheca Sacra* article for the "starry host."
- The Fact Book "morning stars" entry carries 11QtgJob and Lelli.
- I've always believed there were lesser gods and a divine council, even as a kid, before I could have told you why. But they're created. Nothing was made except by God.

## What the chapter is doing
- Job answers God: you can do all things, I spoke of things too wonderful for me. "I had heard of You by the hearing of the ear, But now my eye sees You." He retracts and repents in dust and ashes (42:1–6).
- God turns to Eliphaz: my anger burns against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7).
- The friends must bring seven bulls and seven rams, and Job will pray for them. God accepts Job's prayer (42:8–9).
- God restores Job's fortunes when he prays for his friends, and gives him twice what he had. His family comes to comfort him "for all the evil that Yahweh had brought on him" (42:10–11).
- Job has seven sons and three daughters again. The daughters are named, called the most beautiful in the land, and given an inheritance with their brothers. Job dies old and full of days (42:12–17).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Now my eye sees You" (42:5).** Job had asked to see God (19:27). He got it. 🔴
- **What Job repents of (42:3, 42:6).** He takes back speaking about things he didn't understand. The sources I pulled read it as intellectual overreach being corrected, not a confession of hidden sin and not an admission the friends were right. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for that reading.
- **"Dust and ashes" (42:6).** The Hebrew of 42:6 is hard. "Repent" (*nicham*) can mean to be sorry, to change one's mind, or to be comforted. Translations differ. 🔴 that it's hard; ⬜ on the exact sense.
- **The verdict (42:7).** God says twice that the friends did not speak what is right "as My servant Job has." This after all of Job's angry speeches. 🔴
- **Job prays for the men who accused him (42:8–10).** The restoration comes when he prays for them. 🔴
- **"All the evil that Yahweh had brought on him" (42:11).** The narrator, not a character, gives the book's last word on who did it. It names Yahweh, not the satan. The word is *ra'ah*, evil or disaster. 🔴
- **A piece of money and a gold ring (42:11).** Each visitor brings a *qesitah*, an old unit of value also mentioned in Genesis 33:19 and Joshua 24:32. 🔴
- **Double everything (42:12).** 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, 1,000 donkeys: exactly double 1:3. The children are not doubled: seven sons and three daughters again. 🔴
- **The daughters get names (42:14).** Jemimah (dove), Keziah (cassia, a spice), Keren-happuch (horn of eye paint). The sons stay unnamed. 🔴
- **Daughters inherit with brothers (42:15).** Under Israelite law daughters only inherited if there were no sons (Numbers 27). Job goes past that. 🔴

## Read it like 600 BC, not 2026
- **The satan is gone.** He doesn't appear in the epilogue at all. The heavenly court scene is never reported back to Job, and the accuser's question ("Does Job fear God for nothing?") is answered by what Job did, not by an announcement. 🔴 that he's absent; 🟡 for reading the ending as the answer to the council scene.
- **The friends were speaking the common sense of the ANE.** Walton (as pulled): suffering was read through retribution, gods punish the wicked and reward the righteous. Job "uses the mentality of the ancient Near East as a foil," keeping his integrity by refusing the appeasement the friends recommended. God's verdict in 42:7 lands on that mindset. 🔴 for the background; 🟡 for Walton's reading.
- **Burnt offerings for the friends (42:8).** Seven bulls and seven rams is a big offering, the size Balaam's king offered (Numbers 23:1). With no temple and no priesthood in the story, Job acts as the one who intercedes, like Abraham praying for Abimelech (Genesis 20:7). 🔴
- **The comforters come with gifts (42:11).** Family and old friends eating with Job and giving money and gold is how honor was restored in public. The shame of chapters 2 and 19 is undone in front of the same people. 🟡
- **Long life as blessing (42:16–17).** 140 years and four generations of children. "Old and full of days" is the patriarch's ending (Genesis 25:8; 35:29). 🔴
- **The Greek Job adds an ending.** The Septuagint adds lines after 42:17 saying Job will rise again with those the Lord raises and identifying him with Jobab king of Edom (Genesis 36:33). 🔴 that it's there; it is not in the Hebrew.

## What the chapter is doing
- Right after the man born blind is thrown out of the synagogue (ch. 9), Jesus tells a "figure of speech": the true shepherd comes in by the door, calls his sheep by name, and they follow his voice. Thieves and robbers climb in another way (10:1–6).
- He explains it twice more. "I am the door of the sheep." "I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep." The hired hand runs from the wolf (10:7–18).
- The crowd splits: demon-possessed and insane, or not? (10:19–21).
- In winter, at the Feast of the Dedication, they press him: "If You are the Christ, tell us openly." He says his sheep hear his voice, no one can snatch them from his hand, and "I and the Father are one." They pick up stones (10:22–31).
- He answers from Psalm 82, "I said, you are gods," and asks why it's blasphemy for the one the Father sent to say "I am the Son of God." He slips away beyond the Jordan (10:32–42).

## Pay attention to this
- **The chapter break is late.** Chapter numbers were added centuries later. The shepherd talk follows straight on the fight over the blind man in chapter 9: is Jesus from God? 🔴
- **"They did not understand" (10:6).** So he explains it three ways: the door, the good shepherd, and a later clarification. 🔴
- **"He calls his own sheep by name" (10:3).** The test of the real shepherd is whether the sheep know his voice. The blind man in chapter 9 just did. 🔴
- **"He goes ahead of them" (10:4).** A shepherd in that land leads from the front. He doesn't drive from behind. 🔴
- **"I am the door" (10:7, 10:9).** In some folds the shepherd slept across the opening. His own body was the gate. 🟡
- **"Thieves and robbers" (10:1, 10:8).** The word for robber is *lestes*, an armed gang member, the same word used of Barabbas (18:40). 🔴
- **"Lays down His life" (10:11, 15, 17, 18).** Four times. "No one takes it away from Me... I have authority to lay it down." He's directing the drama, not its victim. 🔴
- **"Other sheep, which are not from this fold" (10:16).** Gentiles. One flock, one shepherd. 🟡
- **Hanukkah (10:22).** The Feast of the Dedication is Hanukkah. 🔴
- **"I and the Father are one" (10:30).** Echoes the Shema, "the LORD is one." The crowd heard it as blasphemy: "You, being a man, make Yourself God" (10:33). 🔴 for their reaction; 🟡 for the Shema echo.
- **"I said, you are gods" (10:34).** Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6. One of the hardest verses in John. 🔴 that he quotes it; ⬜ on how it works.

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Shepherd means king.** God told David, "you shall shepherd My people Israel" (2 Samuel 5:2). Ezekiel 34 fires Israel's bad shepherds, then God says he will shepherd his flock himself and set "My servant David" over them. Micah 5 has a ruler from Bethlehem who shepherds the flock. "I am the good shepherd" is a claim to the throne, not a job title. 🔴
- **The thieves had names.** Wright: the revolutionary warlords who wanted war with Rome, and the house of Herod, happy to bow to Rome to keep its wealth. Several false shepherds in living memory. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Sheepfolds.** A village fold was a walled pen. In the wilderness, shepherds piled stones in a ring and lay down in the gap. Bailey: there "the shepherd literally becomes the door." 🟡
- **Hanukkah is a kingship festival.** It celebrates the Maccabees cleansing the Temple in 164 BC after Antiochus IV defiled it. Judas Maccabeus and his family became the closest thing Israel had to kings in centuries. Jesus is asked "are you the Christ?" at the feast of the last great liberators. 🔴 for the feast; 🟡 for the royal reading.
- **Solomon's Portico (10:23).** A covered walkway on the east side of the Temple courts. It's winter, so people walked under cover. 🔴
- **Stoning for blasphemy.** Leviticus 24:16. A man claiming God's place was a capital case. 🔴
- **Divine council: Psalm 82.** "God takes His stand in the congregation of God; He judges in the midst of gods" (82:1). Then: "I said, 'You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. Nevertheless you will die like men'" (82:6–7). Three main readings: (1) the "gods" are human judges; (2) they are Israel at Sinai, the people "to whom the word of God came" (a reading found in later rabbis); (3) they are divine beings, the council members God put over the nations who ruled them badly and are sentenced to die (Heiser). On the third reading, Jesus' argument runs: if Scripture can call created beings *elohim* and "sons of the Most High," how is it blasphemy for the one the Father "sanctified and sent into the world" to say "I am the Son of God"? 🔴 that all three readings exist; ⬜ on which is right.
- **Divine council: other folds.** In the Deuteronomy 32 picture the nations were handed to other gods, and Psalm 82 ends with "Arise, O God, judge the earth! For it is You who will inherit all the nations" (82:8). "Other sheep... I must bring them also" fits that hope of the nations coming back. 🟡 (Heiser's frame)

## What the chapter is doing
- Martha and Mary send word that their brother Lazarus, whom Jesus loves, is sick. Jesus waits two more days, then says "Let us go to Judea again," where they just tried to stone him (11:1–10).
- He says Lazarus has "fallen asleep." The disciples miss it, so he says it plainly: "Lazarus is dead." Thomas says, "Let us also go, so that we may die with Him" (11:11–16).
- Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Jesus: "I am the resurrection and the life... Do you believe this?" Mary falls at his feet weeping. Jesus is deeply moved, and he weeps (11:17–37).
- At the tomb he has the stone moved, prays, and calls "Lazarus, come forth." The dead man walks out wrapped in grave clothes (11:38–44).
- The Sanhedrin panics. Caiaphas says one man should die for the people, and from that day they plan to kill Jesus (11:45–57).

## Pay attention to this
- **"He whom You love" (11:3), then he waits (11:6).** John says Jesus loved them, and so he stayed two days. Love and delay in the same breath. 🔴
- **Back into danger (11:8).** "The Jews were just now seeking to stone You." Going to Bethany means going near Jerusalem. 🔴
- **Sleep and death (11:11–14).** Jesus calls death sleep. The disciples take him literally. 🔴
- **Thomas speaks (11:16).** His first line in John: "Let us also go, so that we may die with Him." He misreads the trip as a march to a funeral, theirs included, and goes anyway. 🔴
- **Four days (11:17, 11:39).** Not mostly dead. Dead long enough to smell. 🔴
- **"I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25).** Martha believes in a resurrection "on the last day." Jesus says the last day is standing in front of her. 🔴
- **Martha's confession (11:27).** "You are the Christ, the Son of God." A full confession from a woman, before the miracle. 🔴
- **"Jesus wept" (11:35).** The shortest verse in English Bibles. He knows he's about to raise Lazarus and he still weeps. 🔴
- **"Deeply moved" (11:33, 11:38).** The Greek word, *embrimaomai*, has anger in it, like a horse snorting. He's angry at death itself, or at the unbelief, or both. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for what he's angry at.
- **"Unbind him, and let him go" (11:44).** Lazarus comes out still wrapped. Compare Jesus' tomb in chapter 20, where the wrappings are left behind. 🔴
- **The sign that gets him killed (11:53).** Raising a dead man is what pushes the council to act. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Bethany.** About fifteen stadia, under two miles, from Jerusalem, on the far side of the Mount of Olives. Close enough to be dangerous. 🔴
- **Four days in the tomb.** A later rabbinic tradition said the soul hung near the body for three days, then left when the face changed. If people in Jesus' day thought the same, day four meant no hope at all. 🔴 for the tradition existing; 🟡 for dating it to Jesus' time.
- **Mourners.** Friends and neighbors came for days to sit with the family and wail. Even a poor family hired flute players and mourning women. That's the crowd in the house. 🔴
- **Martha's faith is Pharisee faith.** The Pharisees believed in a bodily resurrection on the last day (Daniel 12:2). The Sadducees didn't. Martha holds the hope of most Jews in her day. 🔴
- **Cave tombs.** Wealthier families buried in caves cut into rock, closed with a stone. Bodies were wrapped in strips with spices. 🔴
- **The Romans and "our place" (11:48).** The council's fear is political: a mass movement means Rome comes in and takes the Temple and the nation. They were right that Rome would come. It happened in AD 70. 🔴
- **The high priest prophesies (11:51).** Some Jews believed the high priest could speak for God by his office. John says Caiaphas said more than he knew. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the background belief.
- **Divine council: death as the enemy.** In the Second Temple world and in Paul, death is a power, "the last enemy" (1 Corinthians 15:26), tied to the devil who "had the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14). Jesus' anger at the tomb fits a man facing an enemy. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for reading 11:33 that way.
- **Divine council: the scattered children (11:52).** "Gather together into one the children of God who are scattered abroad." In the Deuteronomy 32 picture the nations were scattered at Babel and handed to other powers. Jesus' death gathers them back. 🟡 (Heiser's frame)

## What the chapter is doing
- The night before the cross, at the supper table. Jesus has just told Peter he'll deny him. Now: "Do not let your heart be troubled." There are many dwelling places in the Father's house, and he's going to prepare a place (14:1–4).
- Thomas says, "Lord, we do not know where You are going. How do we know the way?" Jesus answers, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life" (14:5–7).
- Philip asks to see the Father. "He who has seen Me has seen the Father" (14:8–14).
- Jesus promises "another Advocate," the Spirit of truth, who will be with them forever. "I will not leave you as orphans" (14:15–24).
- Peace, not the world's kind. "The ruler of the world is coming, and he has nothing in Me." Then, "Get up, let us go from here" (14:25–31).

## Pay attention to this
- **"You know the way" (14:4).** Jesus says they know. Thomas says they don't. Somebody has to say it. 🔴
- **"Lord, we do not know" (14:5).** Thomas says "we." He speaks for the room. 🔴
- **The answer is a person (14:6).** Thomas asks for directions. Jesus answers with "I am." 🔴
- **"No one comes to the Father but through Me" (14:6).** One of the sharpest claims in the Gospels, and it comes out of an honest question. 🔴
- **Philip next (14:8–9).** Two disciples in a row admit they don't get it. Jesus answers both. 🔴
- **"Another Advocate" (14:16).** The Greek is *parakletos*, someone called alongside: a helper, an advocate in court. "Another" means one like Jesus. 🔴
- **"I will come to you" (14:18).** Orphans have no father. He says that won't be them. 🔴
- **"The ruler of the world" (14:30).** Satan. "He has nothing in Me": no claim, no hold. 🔴
- **"Get up, let us go from here" (14:31).** But the talking goes on for three more chapters. A seam, or they talked as they walked. ⬜

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **"My Father's house."** In John 2:16 that phrase means the Temple. A house with many rooms is how a family grew: sons added rooms to the father's house. 🔴 for 2:16; 🟡 for the family-house picture.
- **Going to prepare a place.** In village life a groom went back to his father's house to build on a room before he came for his bride. Many read 14:2–3 that way. 🔵
- **"The way."** Psalm 119 and Proverbs talk about the way of the LORD, a path of life you walk. The first Christians were even called "the Way" (Acts 9:2). 🔴
- **A teacher and his students.** In Jewish learning, students asked questions out loud. The rabbis argued, questioned and pushed back. A question wasn't disrespect. 🔵 (not yet sourced in my notes)
- **Divine council: the ruler of this world.** John calls Satan "the ruler of this world" three times (12:31, 14:30, 16:11). In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview, the nations were under other powers, and Paul calls Satan "the god of this world" (2 Corinthians 4:4). Mark uses the same ruler word for Beelzebul, "the ruler of the demons" (Mark 3:22). Jesus says that ruler "has nothing in Me" and in 12:31 says he "will be cast out." 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the council read.
- **The Spirit of truth.** The Dead Sea Scrolls talk about a "spirit of truth" and a "spirit of deceit" battling in people (Community Rule, 1QS 3–4). John's language would have sounded familiar to some Jewish ears. 🔴 for the Scrolls text; 🔵 for any direct link.

## My notes
- This is scene 2 in my "Brave Thomas" study. My notes cover 14:5–6.
- **The brave question.** In church today everybody nods and says yes, and I'm sitting there going, OK, I have no clue what that means. You feel like if you ask, you're dumber than everybody else. But asking is a relief for everyone else sitting there, "cause I guarantee if I have the question in my head 90% of others do as well." The 90 percent is a figure of speech. It takes courage to ask what you don't know while everyone else nods.
- **So Thomas isn't doubting Thomas.** "He's brave Thomas. He's faithful Thomas." He's looking for what he assumes everyone else already has and is brave enough to admit he doesn't fully understand.
- **The church as monologue.** I think we're lost in a lot of ways, just agreeing with church jargon and afraid to ask questions. Too many churches are built so you can't really ask. It's a monologue. 🟡
- **Burns (*Bibliotheca Sacra*):** "way" doesn't mean directions. It means a commitment to follow Jesus in the Spirit. 🔴
- **Sylva holds a harder line.** He reads Thomas's words as unbelief and deficient understanding. I keep that as real tension, not something to smooth over. Thomas can be gently corrected and still be the one whose question pulls out the saying. 🟡
- **With and for.** Thomas was ready to die *with* Jesus (11:16). He doesn't yet see that the way means dying *for* others. Being with him means becoming like him. 🟡 (Sylva)

## What the chapter is doing
- Still the last night. "I am the true vine, and My Father is the vine-grower." Branches that bear nothing are taken away. Branches that bear fruit are cleaned so they bear more (15:1–3).
- "Abide in Me, and I in you." A branch can't bear fruit on its own. "Apart from Me you can do nothing." A branch that doesn't abide is thrown into the fire (15:4–8).
- The vine turns into love: abide in my love, keep my commands, love one another as I loved you. "Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his life for his friends." You're friends now, not slaves. "You did not choose Me but I chose you" (15:9–17).
- If the world hates you, it hated me first. The Advocate, the Spirit of truth, will bear witness, and so will you (15:18–27).

## Pay attention to this
- **"True" (15:1).** He doesn't say "a vine." He says the *true* one. True compared to what? 🔴
- **Takes away and cleans (15:2–3).** Two Greek verbs that sound alike: *airo*, take away, and *kathairo*, clean or prune. Then 15:3: "You are already clean," *katharos*. LSB translates it "cleans," so you can see the wordplay in English. 🔴
- **"Abide" (15:4–10).** The Greek is *meno*: stay, remain. It shows up again and again in these verses. Count it. 🔴
- **The prayer promise sits next to the warning (15:6–7).** Thrown into the fire, then "ask whatever you wish." Same people, same breath. 🔴
- **Fruit (15:8, 16).** Most likely results in other people and God's work spreading, not only character. "Go and bear fruit." 🟡
- **"Friends" (15:14–15).** In the Old Testament only Abraham is called God's friend outright (Isaiah 41:8, 2 Chronicles 20:7). Jesus gives that word to his disciples. 🔴
- **"I chose you" (15:16).** Rabbis' students picked their teacher. This teacher picked them. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the background.
- **From vine to hatred (15:18).** Belonging to the vine means the world treats you the way it treated him. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **The vine was Israel's name.** Psalm 80 is the vine God brought out of Egypt and planted, now trampled and needing rescue. Isaiah 5 is the vineyard that gave wild grapes. Jeremiah 2:21: "I planted you a choice vine." Ezekiel 15: a vine that bears nothing is good only for the fire. Every Jew in that room knew the vine meant Israel, usually Israel failing. 🔴
- **"True vine" means true Israel.** If the vine is Israel and Jesus is the true vine, he's saying God's people are being regathered around him. 🟡 (Wright)
- **The vine against the cedar.** Wright points to 2 Baruch, a Jewish writing from around AD 100, where the vine of Israel stands against the cedar of Rome. The vine was still a political picture. 🟡 (I haven't read 2 Baruch myself)
- **Gold vine on the Temple.** Josephus describes a huge golden vine over the Temple doorway, with grape clusters as tall as a man (*Antiquities* 15.395). If they walked from the upper room toward the Temple side of the city, that's the vine they'd know. 🔴 for Josephus; 🔵 for any link to this night.
- **Pruning.** A vine left alone grows wild and gives poor fruit. Vinedressers cut hard every year. 🔴
- **Covenant "in" language.** God promised to dwell "in the midst" of his people (Exodus 25:8, Leviticus 26:11–12, Ezekiel 37:27). "Abide in Me, and I in you" uses that kind of language. 🟡
- **Divine council: Yahweh of hosts and the vine.** Psalm 80, the vine psalm, keeps calling on "God of hosts," the God of the heavenly armies, to come back and tend his vine (80:7, 14, 19). The vine needed the commander of heaven's armies to save it. 🔴 for the psalm; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Divine council: the world and its ruler.** "If the world hates you" sits right between 14:30 and 16:11, where Jesus calls Satan "the ruler of this world." In John "the world" is often the realm under that ruler. 🟡

## My notes
- This is Parables draft 34, "The Vine and the Branches: Is It Even a Parable?"
- **Is it a parable?** Not on the strict definition. Snodgrass: "In the technical sense there are no parables in John." John's word is *paroimia*, a figure of speech. I included it anyway, as the last of the seven "I am" sayings, because it does what the parables do: it takes a picture the audience already owns and pushes them to a verdict about Jesus. 🔴
- **Vine equals Israel.** Psalm 80, Isaiah 5, Jeremiah 2:21, Ezekiel 15, 17 and 19, and 2 Baruch's vine against Rome's cedar. "True" means Jesus is the true Israel (Wright, and the ESV agrees). 🟡
- **My sentence.** The tenants parable said the vineyard would be given to others. The vine says who the others are. That line is mine; no source phrases it that way. 🟡
- **The knife.** Wright's rose bush: left alone it grows in on itself and gives second-rate flowers. You cut it to help it be what it is. "The vinedresser is never closer to the vine than when he has the knife in his hand." 🔴
- **The branch that's taken away.** The ESV lays out two views: "lifts up" a fallen branch (a real believer in a bad season), or a branch that was never really connected (like those who left in 6:66, or Judas). I take neither. Ezekiel 15 is behind both. ⬜
- **Abide.** Wright's two answers, kept together: stay in the community that worships Jesus, because there's no solitary Christian, and stay a person of private prayer. 🟡
- **Fruit** is results in others (Isaiah 27:6, Israel filling the world with fruit), not the Galatians 5 list, which is a different picture. 🟡
- **15:13 misused.** In World War I "greater love hath no man" was preached at young men to get them to the front. Wright doesn't doubt the men who died; he thinks God judges the people who used the verse as a lever. Love can be commanded here only because the one commanding it has already done everything love can do. Orwell's Big Brother is the parody: he orders love from people he's only terrified. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Early Sunday, still dark, Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to tell Peter and the disciple Jesus loved. They race to the tomb, find the linen wrappings lying there and the face-cloth folded by itself. The other disciple "saw and believed" (20:1–10).
- Mary stays, weeping. Two angels ask why. Then Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener, says her name, "Mary!" and she knows him. He sends her to tell his brothers. "I have seen the Lord" (20:11–18).
- That evening, doors locked, Jesus stands among the disciples: "Peace be with you." He shows his hands and side, sends them, breathes on them and says "Receive the Holy Spirit" (20:19–23).
- Thomas wasn't there and won't believe without seeing and touching. Eight days later Jesus comes again and invites him. Thomas says "My Lord and my God!" (20:24–29).
- John tells us why he wrote: "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" (20:30–31).

## Pay attention to this
- **A woman first (20:1, 20:18).** Mary Magdalene is the first to the tomb, the first to see him, and the first to announce "I have seen the Lord." 🔴
- **The face-cloth folded by itself (20:7).** Not the mess a grave robber leaves. 🔴
- **"Mary!" (20:16).** She doesn't know him by sight. She knows him when he says her name. Go back to 10:3: "he calls his own sheep by name." 🔴
- **"My brothers" (20:17).** After the resurrection, Jesus calls the disciples who ran away his brothers. 🔴
- **"Peace be with you" three times (20:19, 21, 26).** To men who abandoned him. 🔴
- **He breathed on them (20:22).** The same verb the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathed life into Adam (Genesis 2:7). 🔴
- **Thomas wasn't there (20:24).** John doesn't say why. And he wants what the other ten already got (20:20). 🔴
- **He stayed with the group (20:26).** For a week, still not believing, Thomas didn't leave. 🔴
- **The text never says Thomas touched him (20:27–28).** Jesus invites it. Thomas answers by confessing. 🔴
- **"My Lord and my God!" (20:28).** The highest confession in the Gospel. John opened with "the Word was God" (1:1). He closes with a disciple saying it to the risen Jesus. 🔴
- **"Blessed are those who did not see, and yet believed" (20:29).** That's the reader. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Women as witnesses.** In that world a woman's testimony counted for little in court. Josephus says women shouldn't be witnesses (*Antiquities* 4.219). Nobody inventing a story would make a woman the first witness. 🔴
- **Linen wrappings.** Jewish burial wrapped the body in strips with spices (19:39–40). A thief takes the body wrapped. These were left behind. 🔴
- **"Rabboni."** "My teacher," an Aramaic word of deep respect. 🔴
- **The first day of the week.** Sunday. Both appearances to the group happen on Sundays (20:19, 26). The church soon met on that day. 🔴
- **"Doors were shut... for fear of the Jews" (20:19).** Hiding from the Jerusalem leadership that had just had their teacher killed. 🔴
- **"My Lord and my God."** A Jew who said the Shema every day called a man standing in front of him "God." Later, the emperor Domitian liked to be called "our Lord and God" (Suetonius, *Domitian* 13). If John wrote in the 90s, his readers would have heard the clash. 🔴 for Suetonius; 🟡 for the clash in John's mind.
- **Divine council: a new garden.** The tomb was in a garden (19:41), and Mary thinks Jesus is the gardener. Then he breathes on his people the way God breathed into Adam. Creation starts over in a garden. 🔴 for the details; 🟡 for the new-creation reading.
- **Divine council: two angels.** One at the head and one at the feet of the place where his body lay (20:12). Some see the two cherubim at either end of the ark's cover, where God's presence sat. 🔵
- **Divine council: "My God and your God" (20:17).** The God of the risen Jesus is now theirs too. In the Deuteronomy 32 picture the nations had other gods. Here the Father becomes the God of a new family. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Heading north to Galilee, Jesus "had to pass through Samaria." Tired, at noon, he sits at Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink (4:1–9).
- He offers her "living water." She asks how, since he has nothing to draw with (4:10–15).
- He tells her to call her husband, and names her five husbands. She asks the big question between their peoples: this mountain or Jerusalem? He answers that true worshipers will worship "in spirit and truth," then tells her plainly, "I who speak to you am He" (4:16–26).
- She leaves her water jar and brings the town. Many Samaritans believe, first because of her word, then because of his, and call him "the Savior of the world" (4:27–42).
- Back in Cana, a royal official begs for his dying son. Jesus says "Go; your son lives," and the boy recovers at that hour. The second sign (4:43–54).

## Pay attention to this
- **"He had to pass through Samaria" (4:4).** Many Jews went around Samaria. "Had to" may mean geography, or it may mean God's plan. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for reading purpose into them.
- **"Wearied from His journey" (4:6).** John, the Gospel that calls Jesus God in its first line, shows him tired and thirsty. 🔴
- **The sixth hour (4:6).** Noon, the hottest part of the day. Women usually drew water early or late. 🔴 for the hour; 🟡 for what it says about her.
- **No bucket (4:11).** "You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep." He's the one in need. 🔴
- **Three walls in one sentence (4:9).** "You, being a Jew... me, being a Samaritan woman." Race, religion and gender. 🔴
- **Night and noon.** In chapter 3 Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, comes at night and leaves confused. Here a Samaritan woman at noon gets the clearest word Jesus has given anyone so far. 🔴
- **"I who speak to you am He" (4:26).** In Greek it's *ego eimi*, "I am." The first of John's "I am" sayings, and it's spoken to her. 🔴
- **She leaves her jar (4:28).** She came for water and goes back for people. 🔴
- **"No one said, 'Why are You speaking with her?'" (4:27).** They noticed, they wondered, and nobody asked. 🔴
- **"Savior of the world" (4:42).** Samaritans, outsiders, are the first in John to call him that. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Jews and Samaritans.** After Assyria took the northern kingdom (722 BC), foreign peoples were settled in Samaria and mixed with the Israelites left there (2 Kings 17). The Samaritans kept only the five books of Moses and built their own temple on Mount Gerizim. A Jewish leader, John Hyrcanus, destroyed it about 128 BC. The bad blood was centuries deep. 🔴
- **"Jews have no dealings with Samaritans" (4:9).** It can mean they didn't share vessels. Drinking from her jar would make him unclean in the eyes of strict Jews. 🔴 (Bailey)
- **Wells didn't come with buckets.** Travelers carried their own leather bucket and rope. The disciples had taken theirs into town. 🔴
- **Living water.** Running water from a spring, as opposed to standing water in a cistern. Jeremiah 2:13 calls the LORD "the fountain of living waters." 🔴
- **A Samaritan Messiah.** The Samaritans weren't waiting for a son of David. They expected a *Taheb*, a coming prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18), who would teach them the truth. That's why she says "He will declare all things to us." 🔴 (Bailey)
- **"Savior of the world."** The same title Rome gave Augustus and other emperors. 🔴
- **Divine council: the nations' gods in Samaria.** 2 Kings 17:29–33 says each nation settled in Samaria "made its own gods," and lists five peoples and their gods, while they also feared the LORD. ## What the chapter is doing
- At a feast in Jerusalem, Jesus goes to the pool of Bethesda, where crowds of sick people wait for the water to stir (5:1–4).
- He asks a man sick for thirty-eight years, "Do you wish to get well?" The man says he has no one to put him in. Jesus says "Get up, pick up your mat and walk," and he does. It's the Sabbath (5:5–9).
- The authorities go after the man for carrying his mat, then after Jesus. Jesus answers, "My Father is working until now, and I Myself am working," and now they want to kill him for "making Himself equal with God" (5:10–18).
- Jesus explains: the Son does what the Father does, gives life, and has been given all judgment. An hour is coming when the dead will hear his voice (5:19–29).
- Then the witnesses: John the Baptist, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures, including Moses, who "wrote about Me" (5:30–47).

## Pay attention to this
- **Verses 3b–4 are in brackets.** The angel stirring the water isn't in the oldest and best manuscripts. 🔴
- **John mentions the stirring, not the angel (5:7).** The man talks about the water being stirred. John lets that stand and doesn't explain it. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for reading it as deliberate.
- **Thirty-eight years (5:5).** Long enough that the waiting had become a way of life. 🔴
- **"Do you wish to get well?" (5:6).** A real question. Wright hears an edge in it. 🟡
- **"I have no man" (5:7).** Nobody to carry him, nobody in his corner. 🔴
- **"Get up" (5:8).** The same kind of word the New Testament uses for rising from the dead. Then in 5:25–29 the dead hear his voice and come out of the tombs. 🔴 for the link inside the chapter.
- **"Do not sin anymore" (5:14).** Read it next to 9:3, where a man's blindness is not because of anyone's sin. 🔴
- **"My Father is working until now, and I Myself am working" (5:17).** His whole defense. 🔴
- **"Making Himself equal with God" (5:18).** John tells you exactly how they heard it. 🔴
- **Four witnesses (5:31–40).** In Jewish law a claim needed witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus calls more than two. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Bethesda was a healing shrine.** Two big pools near the Sheep Gate, dug out in the couple of centuries before Christ, probably to wash sheep for the Temple. By Jesus' time a healing cult had grown up there, later tied to Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine. A pagan-style healing pool a stone's throw from the Temple. 🔴 for the pools; 🟡 for exactly when the cult started; 🔵 that the god there was Eshmun.
- **Popular religion.** Keener: the Temple leaders surely disapproved, but desperate sick people went where they thought healing might be. 🔴
- **How verse 4 got in.** Around two dozen later manuscripts that have it mark it with a scribe's asterisk, and most of its last words are words John never uses. Best guess: a scribe wrote a note in the margin to explain the stirring, and a later copyist moved it into the text. 🔴 (Heiser, Wright)
- **God works on the Sabbath.** Jewish thinkers said God can't really stop working, or creation would fall apart. Philo said God rests but works without getting tired. The rabbis pointed to births, deaths and rain on the Sabbath. That reasoning excused God. It never excused a man. 🔴
- **"The Jews" here means the Judeans.** Jesus, his disciples and the healed man are all Jews. John's word often points to the Jerusalem leadership, the people of Judea, not the Jewish people as a whole. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Divine council: the Son of Man judges.** "He gave Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man" (5:27). Daniel 7 again: the heavenly court sits, and one like a son of man is given dominion. 🔴 for the Daniel echo; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Divine council: "nor seen His form" (5:37).** Israel's story has people who did see God in some form: Abraham, Jacob, Moses, the Angel of the LORD. Heiser reads those as the visible Yahweh. Jesus tells his opponents they have never heard God's voice or seen his form. Standing in front of them is the one who has. 🔵 (Heiser's frame applied; John doesn't spell it out)
- **A pagan spirit or Yahweh's power.** The shrine said a spirit moved the water and the fastest got healed. Jesus heals with a word, for the one who can't race. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Near Passover, a huge crowd follows Jesus up a mountain by the Sea of Galilee. He tests Philip, takes a boy's five barley loaves and two fish, gives thanks, and feeds about five thousand men. Twelve baskets of leftovers (6:1–13).
- The crowd says "This is truly the Prophet" and gets ready to make him king by force. He slips away to the mountain alone (6:14–15).
- That night the disciples row into a storm. Jesus comes walking on the sea: "It is I; do not be afraid" (6:16–21).
- Next day in Capernaum the crowd wants more bread. Jesus says "I am the bread of life," the true bread from heaven, better than the manna, and then "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life" (6:22–59).
- Many disciples walk away. Jesus asks the Twelve, "Do you also want to go?" Peter: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have words of eternal life" (6:60–71).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Signs" (6:2, 6:14, 6:26).** John's word is *semeion*, a sign that points past itself. 🔴
- **"The Passover... was near" (6:4).** John drops the date on purpose. Passover means Egypt, the wilderness and manna, and that's exactly where the speech goes (6:31). 🔴
- **"To test him" (6:6).** Jesus already knew what he would do. The shortage is a setup. 🔴
- **Two hundred denarii (6:7).** About eight months' pay for a laborer, and still not enough for a bite each. 🔴
- **Barley loaves (6:9).** The bread of the poor. Only John says barley. 🔴
- **"Having given thanks" (6:11).** The Greek is *eucharisteo*, where "Eucharist" comes from. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for how much meal meaning to load on it.
- **"So that nothing will be lost" (6:12).** The verb is *apollymi*, lose or perish. It comes back in 6:39 ("of all that He has given Me I lose nothing"), in 17:12, and behind 3:16 ("shall not perish"). 🔴
- **He runs from the crown (6:15).** The crowd wants to make him king by force. He withdraws. 🔴
- **"It is I" (6:20).** In Greek it's *ego eimi*, "I am," said on the water. 🔴
- **"You seek Me... because you ate of the loaves" (6:26).** They came back for lunch, not for the sign. 🔴
- **The crowd shrinks (6:66).** "Many of His disciples went away." The high point of popularity turns into the low point in one chapter. 🔴
- **"One of you is a devil" (6:70).** He chose Judas knowing. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Manna.** In the wilderness God fed Israel with bread from heaven every morning. You couldn't keep it overnight; it bred worms (Exodus 16:19–20). Jesus' leftovers are gathered up and kept. 🔴
- **Elisha did a small version.** In 2 Kings 4:42–44 Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, and there are leftovers. Jesus feeds thousands with five. A prophet greater than Elisha is here. 🔴
- **"The Prophet who is to come" (6:14).** Deuteronomy 18:15–18 promised a prophet like Moses. Moses fed people bread in the wilderness, so a man who does it looks like the new Moses. 🔴
- **A king who feeds you.** People wanted a Messiah to drive out Rome. A man who could feed an army from a basket looked like the perfect war king. 🟡
- **Twelve baskets.** Twelve tribes. Prophets pictured God gathering scattered Israel back together. "One basket per disciple" is a later guess. 🟡
- **Divine council: the sea again.** In the Old Testament, God alone "treads upon the waves of the sea" (Job 9:8), and he makes a path through the waters (Psalm 77:19). Jesus walking on the stirred-up sea and saying "I am" does what only Yahweh does. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the council frame.
- **Grumbling (6:41, 6:43).** The same word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling about food in the wilderness. Same crowd, new desert. 🔴
- **"The Holy One of God" (6:69).** In Mark 1:24 that's what a demon calls Jesus. In John, Peter says it. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Early morning in the Temple. Scribes and Pharisees drag in a woman "caught in adultery, in the very act" and ask Jesus what Moses says to do. He writes on the ground, says "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her," and they leave one by one. "I do not condemn you, either. Go, and from now on sin no more" (7:53–8:11).
- "I am the Light of the world." The Pharisees say his witness about himself doesn't count. He says the Father is his second witness (8:12–20).
- "Unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins" (8:21–30).
- To Jews who had believed him: the truth will set you free. They say they're Abraham's children and never slaves. He says they're acting like children of the devil (8:31–47).
- They call him a demon-possessed Samaritan. It ends with "before Abraham was, I am," and they pick up stones (8:48–59).

## Pay attention to this
- **Where's the man? (8:3–4).** "Caught in the very act" takes two people. They brought one. 🔴
- **"Testing Him" (8:6).** John says it outright. The question is a trap, not a legal inquiry. 🔴
- **He writes on the ground, twice (8:6, 8:8).** Nobody knows what he wrote. John doesn't say. 🔴
- **"Beginning with the older ones" (8:9).** The oldest leave first. 🔴
- **"Woman, where are they?" (8:10).** The crowd that protected Jesus the day before is gone too. She's left alone with him. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the crowd reading (Bailey).
- **The brackets (7:53–8:11).** Your Bible marks this story because the oldest Greek manuscripts don't have it here. 🔴
- **"I am He" three times (8:24, 8:28, 8:58).** The Greek is *ego eimi* each time. It builds to 8:58. 🔴
- **The devil as a father (8:44).** "You are of your father the devil... He was a murderer from the beginning." 🔴
- **"You are a Samaritan and have a demon" (8:48).** The insult tries to push him outside Israel and outside God. 🔴
- **Was and am (8:58).** "Before Abraham was, I am." Abraham gets a verb that means came into being. Jesus gets a present tense with no beginning. 🔴
- **The stones (8:59).** They understood him, and their answer was to try to kill him. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **The law said both.** Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 put both the man and the woman to death. 🔴
- **The trap between Torah and Rome.** Under Rome, the Jewish leaders' power to carry out a death sentence was real but tied up in procedure. Josephus (*Antiquities* 20.9.1) tells how the high priest Ananus got in trouble for convening the Sanhedrin on his own, between governors, to stone James the brother of Jesus. The crime was calling the court without Roman consent. So the question corners Jesus: say "stone her" and he crosses Rome, say "don't" and he crosses Moses. 🔴
- **The witnesses throw first.** Deuteronomy 17:7: "the hand of the witnesses shall be first against him." Jesus turns the Torah's own rule inward. The one who purges evil has to be clean. 🔴 for the law; 🟡 for reading Jesus' line through it.
- **Rabbis made executions rare.** Later rabbinic law required two eyewitnesses, a formal warning the offender acknowledged, and a court of 23. The Mishnah (Makkot 1:10) says a court that executed once in seven years was called destructive. 🔴 for the Mishnah; 🔵 for how much of that applied in Jesus' day.
- **The Feast of Booths.** This is the day after the feast (7:37). Booths had water-pouring and huge lamps lit in the Temple courts. "I am the Light of the world" (8:12) is said in that setting. 🔴
- **Two witnesses (8:17).** The law needed two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus counts himself and the Father. 🔴
- **"Abraham is our father."** Being Abraham's seed was the heart of Jewish identity. Jesus says real children act like their father. 🔴
- **Divine council: the devil's family.** In the Second Temple world, the sons of God who fell, the serpent in Eden, and the powers behind the nations were all part of the story of evil. "A murderer from the beginning" points back to Eden and Cain (1 John 3:12). Jesus sorts people by which father's family they act like, God's or the devil's. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the Eden link.
- **Divine council: category and Name.** In the Old Testament, *elohim* is a category word. God, the council, angels, even the spirits of the dead can be called *elohim* (Psalm 82, 1 Samuel 28:13). When God says who he is, he uses his Name or a title that sets him apart: El Shaddai, El Elyon, El Olam, "I AM" (Exodus 3:14). Jesus skips the category and reaches for "I am." 🔴 for the Old Testament usage; 🟡 for reading 8:58 through it (Heiser).

- **It sounds like Luke.** To my ear it sounds more like a Luke story than a John story. Wright says the same: "more like Luke than like John." 🟡
- **8:58, category and Name.** *Elohim* is a category. When God identifies himself he uses his Name or a separator. Jesus skips the category and claims the Name. 🟡
- **The objection from Exodus 3:14.** In the Greek Old Testament God says *ego eimi ho on*, "I am the one who is," so some argue "I am" by itself isn't the divine name. Three answers. The crowd picked up stones (8:59), so they heard a claim to God's name. The grammar is the claim: Abraham came into being, Jesus simply is. And in my framework, created *elohim* have a beginning and Yahweh doesn't, so Jesus is on the un-originated side. That he existed before Abraham isn't in dispute. The divine-name claim is strong. 🟡

## META: the book of Joshua
- **Where it sits.** Right after Deuteronomy. The Torah ends with Moses dead and the promise of "a prophet like me" still open (Deuteronomy 34:10). Joshua opens "after the death of Moses." In the Hebrew Bible it's the first book of the Prophets, so the two books are stitched together on purpose. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** will God keep the promise of the land he swore to Abraham, and will Israel hold on to the covenant once it's in the land?
- **Who wrote it.** Nobody knows. Jewish tradition (Talmud, *Bava Batra* 15a) says Joshua wrote his own book, but it records his death (24:29) and keeps saying things are that way "to this day," so later hands finished it. ⬜
- **When.** The events are set at Israel's entry into Canaan, late in the Bronze Age or at the start of the Iron Age. The date of the exodus and conquest is debated (a 15th-century or a 13th-century setting), and the archaeology of sites like Jericho and Ai is argued over. ⬜
- **Canaan was a patchwork.** City-states with their own kings, many of them recently under Egypt's thumb. Joshua 12 lists thirty-one defeated kings. 🔴
- **Four parts:**
  - Chs. 1–5: crossing the Jordan and getting ready (Rahab, the twelve stones, circumcision, Passover, the commander of Yahweh's army).
  - Chs. 6–12: the conquest (Jericho, Achan and Ai, the Gibeonites, the sun standing still, the northern campaign).
  - Chs. 13–22: the land handed out by tribe. Mostly lists and borders; skim it.
  - Chs. 23–24: Joshua's farewell and the covenant at Shechem, "choose for yourselves today whom you will serve."
- **Things to track the whole way through:**
  - God keeps his promises, against every obstacle.
  - Outsiders end up inside (Rahab, the Gibeonites), which complicates any simple reading of holy war.
  - Israel's hold on the land is only as strong as its hold on the covenant.
  - Joshua as a Moses-like figure who still isn't the prophet like Moses.
  - The giant clans (11:21–22), the conquest as unfinished business.

## What the chapter is doing
- "Moses My servant is dead." Yahweh tells Joshua to cross the Jordan with all the people into the land he's giving them (1:1–2).
- He promises every place their feet tread, from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates, and that no one will stand against Joshua: "Just as I have been with Moses, I will be with you" (1:3–5).
- Three times he says "be strong and courageous," and ties it to keeping the law: "This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night" (1:6–9).
- Joshua orders the people to get ready to cross in three days, and reminds Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh of their promise to fight with the others. They answer that they'll obey Joshua as they obeyed Moses: "only be strong and courageous" (1:10–18).

## Pay attention to this
- **The book opens on Moses' death (1:1–2).** The last chapter of Deuteronomy and the first of Joshua are a seam. 🔴
- **"Just as I have been with Moses, I will be with you" (1:5).** Joshua is set up as a new Moses. 🔴
- **"Be strong and courageous" three times from God (1:6, 7, 9), and a fourth time from the people (1:18).** Courage here is tied to obeying the law, not to fighting skill. 🔴
- **"Meditate on it day and night" (1:8).** The verb is *hagah*, to mutter or read under your breath. Psalm 1:2 uses the same verb and the same "day and night" for the blessed man. 🔴
- **A written book of the law already exists (1:8).** Joshua is handed a text to keep, read and speak. 🔴
- **Prosperity comes from the book.** "Then you will make your way successful" (1:8). Success follows obeying, not strategy. 🔴
- **The east-side tribes (1:12–15).** They already had their land (Numbers 32), and they still have to cross and fight. Nobody rests until everybody rests. 🔴
- **The people echo God (1:18).** The chapter ends with the people telling Joshua the same thing God told him. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Land belonged to gods.** Around Israel each land had its gods, and war was fought in their names. God uses his name, Yahweh, in 1:9 against a land full of Canaanite gods. 🟡
- **Herem was shared ANE practice.** The "ban," devoting a defeated enemy wholly to a god, shows up outside Israel too, for example on the Moabite Mesha Stele. In Joshua it means the land is God's gift, and Israel isn't allowed to profit from the war. 🔴 for the parallel, 🟡 for the theology.
- **Big borders are royal language (1:4).** "As far as the great river, the river Euphrates" matches the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Ancient grants described land in sweeping terms. Israel held those borders only briefly, under David and Solomon. 🟡
- **Succession rites.** Kings and leaders passed authority with public commissioning. Moses laid his hands on Joshua (Deuteronomy 34:9), and God now confirms it in his own words. 🔴
- **Divine council: not in this chapter.** The council moments come in 5:13–15, where Joshua meets "the commander of the army of Yahweh," and in the giant clans and the land held by other gods. Walton and Walton's *The Lost World of the Israelite Conquest* takes on herem; Heiser's *Unseen Realm* chapters 23–25 take on the giants.

## My notes
- I came to Joshua 1 through the How We Got the Bible side note on Mackie's "Seam One." My source treats the chapter as the opening half of a seam, so my notes are thin.
- **The Prophets open by tying straight back to Moses' death.** Joshua is shaped as a Moses-like figure: he leads through water, brings the people to the land, and meditates on the Torah day and night, the same instruction as Psalm 1. 🟡
- **A preview, not the fulfillment.** Joshua gets fooled by the Gibeonites (ch. 9), he dies, and the next generation "did not know Yahweh" (Judges 2:10). Each candidate adds to the job description of Deuteronomy 18:15 and none fills it. 🟡
- **The name.** *Yehoshua*, then *Yeshua*, then Jesus: "Yahweh saves." The Torah ends waiting for the one like Moses, the Prophets open with a partial answer, and the New Testament names the final one. 🔴 for the name, 🟡 for the through-line.
- **Herem.** When the drmsh community asked what moral wisdom on warfare we get from the conquest, my point was that the Deuteronomy 32 worldview is a reading tool, not an ethical system. I own Walton and Walton on the conquest and haven't worked it yet.

## META: the book of Jude
- **Where it sits.** One chapter, 25 verses, near the end of the New Testament. It's a short alarm letter: Jude meant to write about salvation and had to write about intruders instead (v. 3).
- **The question the letter is asking:** what do you do when people inside the church turn grace into a license?
- **Who wrote it.** "Jude, a slave of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" (v. 1). That's most naturally Judas, one of Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55), the brother of James who led the Jerusalem church. He calls himself a slave of Jesus, not his brother. 🔴 for the family names; 🟡 for the identification.
- **Not Thaddaeus.** The apostle Judas is "Judas the son of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13). The letter's author is "brother of James." One phrase separates one of the Twelve from a member of Jesus' family who didn't believe during the ministry (John 7:5). 🔴
- **When.** Unknown. Anywhere from the 50s to the 80s. Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* 3.20, from Hegesippus) says Jude's grandsons were questioned by the emperor Domitian as relatives of Jesus, which fits a Jude who lived and had family in the first century. 🔴 for Eusebius; ⬜ for the date.
- **Disputed early.** Eusebius lists Jude among the books "spoken against" (3.25), partly because it quotes Enoch. It made it into the canon anyway. 🔴
- **Text issue.** In v. 5 some of the oldest manuscripts read "Jesus... saved a people out of the land of Egypt," and others read "the Lord." The LSB follows "Jesus." If that's right, Jude puts Jesus at the Exodus. 🔴
- **Structure:** greeting (vv. 1–2); why he's writing (3–4); three judgments from the past (5–7); the intruders described, with Michael, Cain, Balaam, Korah and Enoch (8–16); the apostles' warning (17–19); what the faithful should do (20–23); praise (24–25).
- **Threads to track:** the word "kept" (vv. 1, 6, 13, 21, 24), the repeated "these" pointing at the intruders (8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 19), and the heavy use of Jewish tradition outside the Old Testament.
- **Jude and 2 Peter.** 2 Peter 2 runs parallel to much of Jude. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Jude writes to "the called" and urges them to contend for the faith once for all handed down to the saints, because ungodly people have crept in who turn God's grace into sensuality and deny Jesus as Master and Lord.
- He reminds them of three judgments: the generation saved out of Egypt and then destroyed for unbelief, the angels who left their proper home and are kept in chains, and Sodom and Gomorrah.
- The intruders reject authority and slander "glorious ones," something even Michael the archangel wouldn't do when he disputed with the devil over Moses' body. They've gone the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah. Enoch prophesied their judgment.
- So build yourselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God's love, and show mercy to the wavering. The letter ends with one of the great blessings in the Bible: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Contend earnestly for the faith" (v. 3).** A wrestling word. The faith was "once for all handed down," finished, not open for revision. 🔴
- **"Crept in unnoticed" (v. 4).** The danger is inside, at the love feasts (v. 12). 🔴
- **Three examples (vv. 5–7).** Israel in the wilderness, the angels, Sodom. All three had something and lost it. 🔴
- **The angels' crime (v. 6).** They "did not keep their own domain, but abandoned their proper abode." The word for domain, *archē*, also means rule or rank. They left their post. 🔴
- **"Kept" twice (v. 6).** They didn't keep their place, so God keeps them in bonds. Jude's believers are "kept for Jesus Christ" (v. 1). 🔴
- **"Strange flesh" (v. 7).** Sodom went after flesh of a different kind, and "in the same way as these" ties Sodom's sin to the angels' in v. 6. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for the link.
- **Michael won't do it (v. 9).** Disputing with the devil, he didn't dare pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said "The Lord rebuke you!" 🔴
- **Cain, Balaam, Korah (v. 11).** Murder, greed for pay, rebellion against God's appointed leaders. 🔴
- **Five pictures from nature (vv. 12–13).** Hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. Each one looks like something and delivers nothing. 🔴
- **Enoch "prophesied" (vv. 14–15).** Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 by name. 🔴
- **"Have mercy" (vv. 22–23).** The letter that is hardest on the intruders tells the church to be merciful to the doubters and to snatch others from the fire. 🔴

## Read it like AD 65, not 2026
- **The angels who left their abode are the Watchers.** In 1 Enoch 6–16 the Watchers leave heaven, take human wives, father the giants, and God has them bound under the earth in darkness until the great day of judgment (1 Enoch 10:4–6, 12). Jude's v. 6 is the Watchers' story in Enoch's own vocabulary. 🔴
- **Their place was a post.** In the Old Testament, God's heavenly beings have assigned ranks and territories (Deuteronomy 32:8; Daniel 10:13, 20). "Did not keep their own domain" means they abandoned the station God gave them. 🟡
- **Michael and the body of Moses.** The story isn't in the Old Testament. Clement of Alexandria and others say it came from a book called the *Assumption of Moses* (or *Testament of Moses*). A Dead Sea Scroll (Visions of Amram, 4Q543–548) has two spirit beings quarreling over Moses' father. Jude's readers knew this kind of story. 🔴
- **Why Moses' body?** Deuteronomy 34:6 says nobody knows where Moses was buried, and he died outside the promised land, on the far side of the Jordan. Heiser reads it through cosmic geography: Michael is the prince over Israel (Daniel 12:1), God's own portion, and the devil, lord of the realm of the dead, claims the body of a man who died outside God's land. Michael contends to bring it home. 🔴 for Deuteronomy and Daniel; 🟡 for Heiser's reading.
- **Not Zechariah 3, per Heiser.** Most commentators connect "the Lord rebuke you" to Zechariah 3:2, where the satan accuses Joshua the high priest. Heiser points out Jude never says the devil accused Moses of anything. The words match; the scene doesn't. 🟡
- **"Glorious ones" are heavenly beings.** *Doxai*, the glorious ones, are members of the heavenly host. Michael wouldn't slander even a rebel one. Heiser: the devil is still an *elohim*, a spiritual being of that class, even in rebellion, and Michael appeals to God's authority instead of taking it on himself. 🟡
- **Wandering stars (v. 13).** In 1 Enoch 18:13–16 and 21:1–6, stars that didn't come out at their appointed times are bound as punishment. In that world, stars and heavenly beings were closely linked. 🔴
- **The quotation is 1 Enoch 1:9.** "Behold, the Lord came with many thousands of His holy ones, to execute judgment upon all." The holy ones are God's heavenly army, as in Deuteronomy 33:2 and Zechariah 14:5. Aramaic fragments of 1 Enoch were found at Qumran; the book was widely read in Jude's day. 🔴
- **Balaam and Korah.** Balaam, the prophet for hire (Numbers 22–24; 31:16). Korah, who rebelled against Moses and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16). 🔴

## My notes
- **v. 6:** angels who didn't keep their own domain but left their proper home, kept in eternal bonds. That's the Watchers' crime in Enochic vocabulary. With 2 Peter 2:4, it's Heiser's anchor that the New Testament picked the supernatural reading of Genesis 6. 🔴
- **vv. 14–15 is a direct quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9.** 🔴 My reading in the book club: Jude quoting Enoch works like citing an idiom. We quote other books today to make a point everyone understands, more than what the words themselves are saying. 1 Enoch is a lens for the New Testament authors, not for Genesis. Influence isn't inspiration.
- **Enoch is not the context of Genesis.** What Enoch shows is a continuity between the Genesis context and the Second Temple context. I never said Enoch was the context of Genesis.
- **"Enoch prophesied."** The word needs defining. Prophecy isn't only predicting the future; it's speech that comes from God. If the only people who ever spoke for God are the ones written in the Bible, that's a very short list. Caiaphas "prophesied" (John 11:51) and he was no saint. That takes the canonical weight off the verb. The attribution, "Enoch, in the seventh generation from Adam," is a separate question I haven't closed. ⬜
- **My Jude post (NT writers series):** Jude writes to people for whom that literature was usable. Citing a source as saying something true isn't ranking it; Paul quotes Greek poets. Eusebius (3.25) lists Jude among the disputed books, partly because of the Enoch quotation. The post's own inference: Jude's not claiming to be Jesus' brother may connect to his earlier unbelief. That's offered as a fit, not proof. 🔵
- **v. 9 and telling Satan off.** Michael wouldn't rebuke the devil himself; he said "the Lord rebuke you." So the popular practice of telling Satan he has no power over you fails on Jude's own ground. An archangel wouldn't do it, and it puts the believer in a two-party fight God isn't in. 🔴 for Jude; 🟡 for the application.
- **Divine council:** this letter is full of it. The Watchers, Michael and the devil, the glorious ones, the wandering stars, the holy ones.

## META: the book of Judges
- **Where it sits.** Between Joshua (the land taken, mostly) and Samuel (the kings). Joshua is dead, nobody replaces him, and the tribes are on their own in a land still full of Canaanites and their gods. Ruth is set in the same years and reads like the other side of the coin.
- **The question the whole book is asking:** what happens to God's people when nobody leads them and everybody does what looks right to him? The last line answers it: "In those days there was no king in Israel; each man did what was right in his own eyes" (21:25). 🔴
- **Who wrote it.** Nobody knows. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) says Samuel. The book itself gives two clues that pull in different directions. 1:21 says the Jebusites live in Jerusalem "to this day," which sounds like before David took the city (2 Samuel 5). 18:30 says Dan's priests served "until the day of the exile of the land," which sounds like after the Assyrians took the north in the 700s BC. Best read: older stories, put in their final form much later. ⬜
- **When it happens.** Roughly the 1300s or 1200s down to about 1050 BC, depending on how you date the Exodus. The judges overlap each other. They are local leaders, not a line of national rulers, so you can't add up the years end to end. 🟡
- **Text issues.** Two things are real. The old Greek translation of Judges survives in two noticeably different forms, so Greek readings in Judges come with a footnote. A Dead Sea Scroll fragment of Judges (4QJudg-a) skips 6:7–10, the unnamed prophet's speech. 🔴 for both facts. ⬜ for what the missing verses mean.
- **How it's built:**
  - 1:1–2:5 the land: who failed to take what.
  - 2:6–3:6 the pattern: sin, oppression, crying out, a judge, rest, and then worse.
  - 3:7–16:31 the judges themselves: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Deborah and Barak, Gideon (and his son Abimelech), Tola and Jair, Jephthah, three more minor judges, Samson.
  - 17–21 two closing stories with no judge at all: Micah's idol and Dan, then the Levite's concubine and the war on Benjamin.
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - The cycle sinks. Each turn ends lower than the last. Othniel is clean. Samson never leads an army.
  - Watch the women. Achsah asks her father for springs in chapter 1. The Levite's concubine is cut into twelve pieces in chapter 19. That distance is the book's moral thermometer.
  - Gideon is the hinge. He starts as the fearful man God calls and ends making a gold ephod Israel worships. After him the judges and their families get darker fast.
  - "Evil in the eyes of Yahweh" at the start of every cycle, "right in his own eyes" at the end of the book. Same eyes question, two answers.
  - The gods of the nations. Baal, Ashtaroth, Chemosh, Dagon. The book treats them as real powers Israel keeps choosing.

## What the chapter is doing
- Joshua is dead. Israel asks Yahweh who goes first, and Yahweh says Judah.
- Judah and Simeon win: Bezek, Jerusalem burned, Hebron, Debir, Hormah, three Philistine cities.
- Then it turns. Judah can't take the valley. Benjamin can't take Jerusalem. Joseph takes Bethel by a deal with a traitor.
- The last third is a list of tribes that didn't drive the Canaanites out. They put them to forced labor, or lived next to them, or (Dan) got pushed into the hills by them.

## Pay attention to this
- **The book opens and closes with the same question.** "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites?" (1:1). In 20:18 Israel asks again, "Who shall go up for us to begin the battle against the sons of Benjamin?" Both times the answer is Judah. At the start the enemy is Canaan. At the end it's a brother tribe. 🔴 for the matching question, 🟡 for reading it as a frame.
- **Adoni-bezek's confession (1:7).** A Canaanite king, thumbs and big toes gone, says "as I have done, so God has repaid me." The first theology spoken in the book comes out of a pagan's mouth. 🔴
- **Achsah asks well (1:14–15).** She asks her father for a "blessing," springs of water to go with dry land, and gets the upper and lower springs. Hold her against the women at the end of the book. 🔴 for the scene, 🟡 for the contrast.
- **Othniel shows up early (1:13).** Caleb's nephew takes Debir and marries Achsah. He'll be the first judge in 3:9, the clean one everyone after him gets measured against. 🔴
- **"Yahweh was with Judah... but" (1:19).** Look at the LSB. "Could" is in italics. Translators supplied it. The Hebrew just says they did not dispossess the valley people, because of iron chariots. Joshua had told Joseph's tribes they *would* drive out the chariot people (Joshua 17:16–18). So is this can't, or won't? The chapter leaves it hanging. 🔴 for the wording, ⬜ for the answer.
- **Jerusalem twice (1:8, 1:21).** Judah burns Jerusalem, then Benjamin can't dislodge the Jebusites from it. Burning a city and holding it are two different things. David finally takes it in 2 Samuel 5. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the explanation.
- **Watch the wording slide (1:27–34).** First "the Canaanites lived among them." Then "the Asherites lived among the Canaanites" (1:32). Then the Amorites push Dan into the hill country (1:34). Who is living among whom flips. 🔴 for the wording, 🟡 for reading it as a downhill slide.
- **Bethel falls by a deal (1:22–26).** The spies promise a man "lovingkindness" (*chesed*) if he shows them the way in. Sounds like Rahab in Joshua 2. But this man doesn't join Israel. He walks off and builds a new Luz in Hittite country. Canaan survives the conquest of its own city. 🟡

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Iron chariots meant the plains belonged to someone else.** Chariots were the tanks of the Late Bronze and early Iron Age. They ruled flat valleys like Jezreel and were useless in the hills. So the hill tribes held the hills and the Canaanite city-states held the plains. Chapter 1 is a map of exactly that. 🔴 for chariot warfare, 🟡 for "iron" meaning iron fittings rather than all-iron vehicles.
- **Cutting off thumbs and big toes.** A man without thumbs can't grip a sword or draw a bow. A man without big toes can't run or keep his balance in a fight. It ends a king as a warrior and shames him at the same time. Adoni-bezek had done it to seventy kings who ate scraps under his table. 🟡 for the purpose, 🔴 for what he says.
- **Hormah is a pun (1:17).** They "devoted it to destruction" (*charam*, the ban), so the place is called Hormah. Holy war, the ban, was not unique to Israel; Moab's Mesha Stele uses the same idea. In Israel the point was that the plunder belonged to God, not to the army. 🔴
- **Hebron's three giants.** Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai (1:10) are the same three sons of Anak the spies saw in Numbers 13:22, the ones that made Israel feel like grasshoppers. Caleb, one of the two spies who said "we can take them," is the one who finishes them (1:20). Heiser reads the Anakim as part of the giant-clan thread that runs back to Genesis 6 and the Nephilim, so clearing Hebron is more than real estate. 🔴 for the names, 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **A land came with its gods.** In the ANE every land had its gods, and its altars were their claim on it. Deuteronomy 32:8–9 says the Most High gave the nations to the sons of God and kept Israel for himself. Leaving the Canaanites in place meant leaving their altars in place, and 2:2–3 says that out loud. A 2026 reader sees an unfinished military campaign. An Israelite heard an unfinished religious one. 🟡
- **Canaan was a patchwork.** Before Israel, Canaan was a set of small city-states that answered to Egypt, as the Amarna letters show. By the time of Judges, Egypt's grip was gone, and every city was its own little kingdom with its own king. That's why there are so many "kings" in this chapter. 🔴
- **"Blessing" can mean a gift.** When Achsah says "give me a blessing" (1:15), she means a present, the same way Abigail calls her load of food a "blessing" in 1 Samuel 25:27. 🔴

## My notes

- It also files the "stayers," the Canaanites who were allowed to stay, as Wilcock's root of the downward spiral: leave the temptation in place and you've already lost the next round. That line is my summary of Wilcock and I haven't checked it against his book yet. 🔵
- The Heiser line in the same note: failing to take the land was failing to take holy ground back from the rebel *elohim*, and the iron chariots were a test of whether Israel would trust God over the other side's technology. Also unchecked. 🔵
