## What the chapter is doing
- Two quiet judges after the Abimelech mess: Tola for 23 years, Jair for 22. Jair has thirty sons on thirty donkeys with thirty towns.
- Then Israel serves every god in the neighborhood, seven groups of them. Yahweh hands them to the Philistines and the Ammonites for eighteen years.
- Israel cries out and confesses. For the first time Yahweh says no: go cry to the gods you chose.
- They confess again, throw out the foreign gods and serve Yahweh, and "He could bear the trouble of Israel no longer."
- Ammon musters in Gilead. Gilead's leaders ask who will fight, and promise him headship. That sets up Jephthah.

## Pay attention to this
- **Tola "arose to save Israel" (10:1).** Saved from what? No enemy is named. After Abimelech, maybe the danger was Israel itself. 🔴 for the text, 🔵 for the reading.
- **Jair's thirties (10:4).** Thirty sons riding thirty donkeys, holding thirty towns. Donkey riding was a mark of rank (5:10 has the rich "who ride on white donkeys"). Jair lives like a little king. And there's a pun: the Hebrew words for "donkeys" and "towns" here sound almost alike. 🔴
- **Seven groups of gods (10:6).** The Baals, the Ashtaroth, the gods of Aram, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines. Israel didn't drift into one idol. It took them all. 🔴 for the list, 🟡 for seven meaning "complete."
- **Seven rescues (10:11–12).** Yahweh's answer lists seven peoples he saved them from: Egyptians, Amorites, Ammon, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, Maonites. Seven gods chosen, seven rescues forgotten. 🔴 for the count, 🟡 for the match.
- **"I will no longer save you" (10:13).** The first time in the book God refuses the cry. 🔴
- **"Go and cry out to the gods which you have chosen" (10:14).** Sarcasm from God. If they're gods, let them help. 🔴
- **The second confession is better (10:15–16).** The first time they confessed and asked. The second time they say "do to us whatever seems good in Your eyes," and then they act: they throw out the gods. 🔴
- **"He could bear the trouble of Israel no longer" (10:16).** Literally "his soul grew short." Some read it as compassion, God unable to watch them suffer. Others read impatience, God fed up with Israel's routine. The words allow both. 🔴 for the words, ⬜ for the meaning.
- **No judge named at the end (10:17–18).** God hasn't raised anyone. The leaders go shopping for a "head" themselves, with a reward attached. Compare every earlier judge, raised by God. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Every nation had its gods, and Israel collected them.** Aram's storm god Hadad, Sidon's Baal and Ashtart, Moab's Chemosh, Ammon's Milcom, the Philistines' Dagon. In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview (32:8–9), the nations were handed to the sons of God, and Israel was Yahweh's own share. Heiser reads 10:6 as Israel surrendering to the very powers Yahweh had given up the nations to. 🔴 for the gods, 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **Choosing a god meant choosing a jurisdiction.** In the ANE you served the god of the land you lived in, and he was supposed to protect you. "Let them save you" (10:14) holds Israel to its own choice: you moved under their rule, now see what their rule is worth. 🟡
- **Donkeys were the status car.** Before horses were common in Israel, chiefs and their sons rode donkeys. Thirty sons riding means wealth and a lot of wives. 🔴
- **The two fronts.** The Philistines pressed from the west and Ammon from the east, across the Jordan. Chapters 10–12 deal with Ammon. Chapters 13–16 deal with the Philistines. 🔴
- **Gilead was frontier country.** East of the Jordan, the Gileadites lived on the edge, closest to Ammon and Moab, and furthest from the rest of Israel. That's why they have to find their own fighter. 🔴

## My notes
- Structure from my note: Tola and Jair (10:1–5), the sevenfold idolatry (10:6–9), Yahweh's rebuke (10:10–16), the hunt for a leader (10:17–18). Key verses 10:13 and 10:16.
- From the Jephthah paper: Block lines up 10:10–16 with 11:4–11. Ammon presses, Israel appeals to Yahweh / Gilead appeals to Jephthah, each answers with sarcasm, each gets asked again. Yahweh relents out of covenant grace. Jephthah relents out of calculation and grabs the headship.
- My pre-read note's Heiser lines: the seven groups of gods as Israel giving itself over to the sons of God allotted at Babel (Deuteronomy 32:8); by choosing other *elohim* Israel moved itself into their jurisdiction. My summary, not checked. 🔵
- Its Wilcock lines: the limits of patience; the quiet years of Tola and Jair as breathing room Israel wasted; God's sarcasm as tough love testing whether the repentance is real; God moved by their misery like a father with rebel children. Also my summary, not checked. 🔵
- My reading guide says skim chapter 10. It's worth more than a skim because of 10:13–16.
- **Divine council:** the gods of the nations, listed by name, and God's dare to let them save Israel.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jephthah is a mighty warrior and the son of a prostitute. His half-brothers throw him out of the inheritance. He ends up in Tob with a gang of "worthless men."
- When Ammon attacks, Gilead's elders come begging. Jephthah makes them promise he'll be head, not just general, and seals it before Yahweh at Mizpah.
- He sends Ammon's king a long argument: Israel never took your land, Yahweh gave it to us, Balak never fought over it, and you waited 300 years. "May Yahweh, the Judge, judge." The king doesn't listen.
- The Spirit of Yahweh comes on Jephthah. Then he vows: whatever comes out of my door to meet me when I come home, I'll offer as a burnt offering. Yahweh gives him the victory.
- His only child, his daughter, comes out dancing. She asks for two months to mourn with her friends, comes back, and "he did to her according to the vow." Israel's daughters remember her four days every year.

## Pay attention to this
- **More sinned against than sinning, at first (11:1–3).** A prostitute's son, thrown out by brothers who wanted his share. He didn't choose his start. 🔴
- **He bargains with the elders (11:4–11).** They offer "chief." He holds out for "head." It's the same scene as Israel and Yahweh in 10:10–16, played by different actors. 🔴 for both scenes, 🟡 for the parallel.
- **"May Yahweh, the Judge, judge" (11:27).** The only time in the book God is called "the Judge." The book is named for the human judges, but the real Judge is Yahweh. 🔴
- **Chemosh gets the credit (11:24).** "Do you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess?" Jephthah talks as if Chemosh is a real god who hands out land. 🔴
- **The Spirit comes before the vow (11:29–30).** Jephthah already has God's power when he starts bargaining for God's help. The vow adds nothing God hadn't already given. 🔴 for the order, 🟡 for the point.
- **The only time he speaks to God, he negotiates (11:30–31).** "If You will... then." And God doesn't answer him. 🔴
- **"Whatever comes out of the doors of my house" (11:31).** Animals could come out of a house. People always do. 🔴 for the wording, 🟡 that he expected a person.
- **Tambourines and dancing (11:34).** That's how women met returning winners in Israel (Miriam in Exodus 15:20, the women in 1 Samuel 18:6). He should have known who would come out. 🔴 for the custom, 🟡 for what he expected.
- **"One and only child" (11:34).** The word echoes Genesis 22:2, where God calls Isaac Abraham's "only son." 🔴
- **"You have brought me very low" (11:35).** His first words to her are about what she's done to him. 🔴
- **She has more faith than he does (11:36).** She points him to what Yahweh did and tells him to keep his word. 🔴
- **"He did to her according to the vow" (11:39).** A few short Hebrew words. The narrator won't describe it. 🔴
- **She's the one remembered (11:40).** Not Jephthah. The daughters of Israel went yearly to remember her. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Inheritance went to legitimate sons.** A prostitute's son had no claim. The brothers had law on their side, more or less, and greed driving it. 🔴
- **Chemosh and Milcom.** Chemosh was Moab's god. Ammon's was Milcom. Jephthah names the wrong one, either because Ammon held former Moabite land, or out of contempt, or as propaganda. 🔴 for the gods, ⬜ for why.
- **Gods owned land.** In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview, each nation's god got its territory and Yahweh got Israel. Jephthah's 11:24 is that worldview in a diplomatic letter: your god gave you yours, mine gave me mine. 🟡
- **300 years (11:26).** Jephthah claims Israel had held the land three centuries. People use this verse to argue for an earlier date of the Exodus. It's also a negotiator's round number. 🔴 for the verse, ⬜ for the chronology.
- **Child sacrifice was real in the neighborhood.** The king of Moab burned his own son on the wall to turn a battle (2 Kings 3:27). Ammon's god was tied to child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; 1 Kings 11:7). Israel's law banned it outright (Leviticus 18:21; 20:2–5; Deuteronomy 12:31). 🔴
- **Vows were binding, but there was a way out for persons.** Numbers 30:2 says keep your word. Leviticus 27:1–8 sets a price to redeem a person vowed to God. Jephthah never takes it. 🔴
- **Dying a virgin meant dying without a future.** No children meant no name carried on. She mourns her virginity because her line, and her father's, ends with her. 🔴
- **A yearly memorial by women.** The four-day remembrance (11:40) has no other mention in the Bible. A custom kept by women for a woman. 🔴

## My notes
- My first instinct when I came to this: I don't think God would ever require a human sacrifice. And he didn't. Jephthah came up with it himself.
- I read it as: she died and was sacrificed. That's just real heavy.
- Both of my commentators agree she died. Wilcock and Block give the same reasons: 11:31 allows a person, his grief makes no sense for a goat, and "he did to her according to the vow" is stark on purpose. Block sets it against Genesis 22 point by point: Abraham acts in faith at God's command, Jephthah acts on his own; God stops Abraham, God is silent here; Abraham's future is secured, Jephthah's line ends. 🔴 for what they say.
- Where they split: Block says the vow was pagan and deliberate, a man shaped by a Canaanized world trying to buy God's favor. Wilcock says rash, from spiritual immaturity. 🔴 for the split.
- On recruitment: Block says Jephthah's piety at Mizpah used God as a contract witness, like Abimelech did. Wilcock sees real divine oversight, Yahweh's name three times in three verses.
- Wilcock calls 11:27 ("may Yahweh, the Judge, judge") the thematic center of the whole book, and from the least likely mouth.
- Block catches the Chemosh slip. My reading plan flags the same verse the other way: Jephthah treats Chemosh as a real divine being over territory. That's the Deuteronomy 32 worldview in everyday speech.
- The daughter is the hero. Block: "You have made me miserable" is grief for himself. She stands for "all the courageous daughters of abusive fathers."
- Hebrews 11:32 still lists him. Wilcock: Scripture condemns what he did and commends what drove it, keeping his word. He heard one word from God (keep your vow) and missed another (don't kill). Block: Hebrews honors the deliverance, not the man.
- Block's closing line on God's silence: "But where is Yahweh in all this? He remains strangely silent." God had already spoken. Leviticus banned it and Leviticus 27 gave him a way out.
- The study turned into my research paper and then a jayms.com post.
- **Divine council:** 11:24, Chemosh as the god who gives land. No council scene.

## What the chapter is doing
- Ephraim crosses the Jordan, angry that Jephthah didn't call them against Ammon, and threatens to burn his house down on him.
- Jephthah says he did call and they didn't come. Then he fights them. Gilead holds the Jordan crossings and tests every man who tries to cross: say "Shibboleth." Ephraimites say "Sibboleth" and die. 42,000 fall.
- Jephthah judges six years and dies.
- Three minor judges follow: Ibzan of Bethlehem (thirty sons, thirty daughters, all married outside the clan), Elon of Zebulun, and Abdon (forty sons, thirty grandsons, seventy donkeys).

## Pay attention to this
- **Ephraim again (12:1).** Same complaint they made to Gideon in 8:1: why didn't you call us? Gideon calmed them with a compliment. Jephthah fights them. Same problem, much worse ending. 🔴 for both scenes, 🟡 for the contrast.
- **"We will burn your house down on you."** Ephraim threatens a fellow Israelite with what you'd expect from an enemy. The Philistines make the same threat in 14:15 and carry it out in 15:6. 🔴
- **Jephthah's version (12:2).** He says he cried to Ephraim for help and they didn't come. Chapter 11 never mentions it. Maybe true, maybe a negotiator's story. 🔴 for the gap, ⬜ for which.
- **"Fugitives of Ephraim" (12:4).** Ephraim insults Gilead as runaways from their own tribe. Words start the war. 🔴
- **The fords of the Jordan (12:5).** Ehud took "the fords of the Jordan" to trap Moab (3:28). Now Israelites take the same fords to trap other Israelites. 🔴
- **One sound decides life or death (12:6).** Ephraimites couldn't make the "sh" sound. 42,000 die over an accent. 🔴
- **No rest.** Jephthah judges "six years," then dies. No "the land was quiet" line for him. After Gideon (8:28) that line never shows up again in the book. 🔴
- **The minor judges live big (12:8–15).** Sixty marriages arranged by Ibzan, seventy donkeys for Abdon's family. Like Jair in 10:4, they look more like small kings than deliverers. No enemy, no battle, no God mentioned. 🔴 for the details, 🟡 for the reading.

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Dialects were real.** Hebrew had regional accents, and inscriptions from different areas show spelling and sound differences. East of the Jordan and west of it, people said things differently. A one-word test was a quick ID check at a river crossing. 🔴 for regional dialects, 🟡 for the exact sound difference.
- **What "Shibboleth" means.** Either an ear of grain or a flowing stream. At a river ford, "stream" fits. Any word with the sound would have done. 🔴
- **Fords were choke points.** You couldn't cross the Jordan just anywhere. Whoever held the shallow crossings controlled who got home. 🔴
- **Ephraim was the big tribe.** Ephraim was the leading tribe in the central hills, home of Shiloh and Joshua's tribe. Being left out of a victory meant losing honor and a share of the plunder. Hence the anger. 🔴 for Ephraim's weight, 🟡 for the motive.
- **Marriage as politics.** Ibzan marrying thirty sons and thirty daughters outside his clan was alliance-building. In that world, marriages tied families and towns together. 🟡
- **Which Bethlehem?** There was a Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) as well as the one in Judah. Ibzan's could be either. ⬜
- **"Buried in the cities of Gilead" (12:7).** The Hebrew is plural, "in the cities of Gilead." The LSB adds "one of" in italics to smooth it. A later Jewish tradition took the plural literally and said his body was buried in pieces in several towns. 🔴 for the Hebrew, 🔵 for the tradition.

## What the chapter is doing
- Israel does evil again and the Philistines rule them for forty years.
- The angel of Yahweh appears to the barren wife of Manoah, a Danite from Zorah. She'll have a son who will be a Nazirite from the womb: no razor on his head, and she's to drink no wine and eat nothing unclean. He'll "begin to save Israel."
- Manoah prays for the man to come back and tell them how to raise the boy. The angel comes again, to the wife again, and repeats himself.
- Manoah offers a meal. The angel says offer it to Yahweh instead, won't give his name ("it is wonderful"), and goes up in the flame of the altar. Manoah panics: we've seen God, we'll die. His wife talks sense.
- Samson is born, Yahweh blesses him, and the Spirit begins to stir him.

## Pay attention to this
- **Nobody cries out (13:1).** Every earlier cycle has Israel crying to Yahweh. This time there's no cry at all. God moves anyway. 🔴
- **The wife has no name, the husband does.** And she's the one the angel visits, both times. She's also the one who reasons clearly at the end. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the point.
- **"Begin to save" (13:5).** Not finish. Samson will start something somebody else has to complete. The Philistine problem is still there in Samuel and David. 🔴
- **The mother keeps the rules too (13:4, 14).** No wine, nothing from the vine, nothing unclean. Samson's Nazirite life starts in her body. 🔴
- **"To the day of his death" (13:7).** She adds the words when she tells Manoah. A lifelong vow, and a hint of how the story ends. 🔴
- **Manoah asks for instructions he already has (13:12–14).** The angel just repeats what he told the wife. 🔴
- **"Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?" (13:18).** Jacob got almost the same answer from the man he wrestled (Genesis 32:29). Then Yahweh "did a wondrous thing" (13:19), same root. The name is the miracle. 🔴
- **The angel goes up in the flame (13:20).** He rides the fire back to heaven. That's when Manoah knows who he was. 🔴
- **"We have seen God" (13:22).** Manoah calls the angel God. His wife answers: if Yahweh meant to kill us, he wouldn't have taken our offering or told us all this (13:23). 🔴
- **The Spirit "began to stir him" (13:25).** At Mahaneh-dan, "the camp of Dan." The word for stir is like a bell being struck. 🔴 for the place, 🟡 for the image.

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **The barren-wife announcement was a known pattern.** Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, then Hannah, then Elizabeth. When a barren woman gets a visit, a deliverer is coming. 🔴
- **The Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:1–21).** Three rules: nothing from the grapevine (not even raisins), no razor on the head, no touching a dead body. It was normally a vow a grown man or woman chose for a set time. Samson's is chosen for him before birth and is for life, like Samuel's later (1 Samuel 1:11). 🔴
- **The hair is the sign, not the power.** Uncut hair showed everyone the person was set apart. The strength came from Yahweh's Spirit, not from the hair. 🔴
- **The Philistines.** Sea Peoples who settled the southern coast around 1200 BC with five main cities. They had iron, organized armies and their own gods, Dagon above all. The tribe of Dan lived right on their border. 🔴
- **Angels don't eat Israel's food here.** Abraham's visitors ate (Genesis 18:8). This one refuses and points the offering to Yahweh (13:16). Gideon's visitor also burned the food instead of eating it (6:21). 🔴
- **Seeing God meant death.** "No man can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Manoah reacts the way Gideon did (6:22). 🔴
- **The angel of Yahweh, again.** Heiser reads this as the visible Yahweh: he speaks as God, accepts worship pointed to Yahweh, carries a "wonderful" name, and Manoah says "we have seen God." 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **"Samson" sounds like "sun."** His name likely comes from *shemesh*, sun. Zorah sits a few miles from Beth-shemesh, "house of the sun," an old Canaanite worship site. The Nazirite boy is named after something in his own backyard. 🔴 for the root and geography, 🔵 for any meaning beyond that.

## What the chapter is doing
- Samson sees a Philistine woman in Timnah and tells his parents to get her for him. They object. He insists: "she is right in my eyes."
- On the way, in the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion charges him. The Spirit rushes on him and he tears it apart bare-handed. He tells no one.
- Later he finds bees and honey in the lion's carcass, scoops some out, eats it and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from.
- At the seven-day wedding feast he bets thirty Philistine companions thirty sets of clothes on a riddle: "Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet."
- They can't solve it, so they threaten to burn his bride and her family. She cries on him for seven days until he tells her, and she tells them. He answers, "If you had not plowed with my heifer," kills thirty men in Ashkelon to pay the bet, and storms home. His bride is given to his best man.

## Pay attention to this
- **"She is right in my eyes" (14:3, 7).** The book ends with "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25). Samson says it about a woman, long before the narrator says it about Israel. 🔴
- **"It was of Yahweh" (14:4).** God is using Samson's wants to pick a fight with the Philistines who rule Israel. That isn't God approving of the marriage. It's God working through a man who isn't thinking about God at all. 🔴 for the verse, 🟡 for how to read it.
- **A Nazirite in the vineyards (14:5).** The one man forbidden anything from the grapevine is walking through vineyards. 🔴 for the setting, 🟡 for the point.
- **First broken rule: the dead body (14:8–9).** He reaches into a carcass for honey. Then he feeds his parents unclean food without telling them. 🔴
- **Second broken rule, likely: the feast (14:10).** The Hebrew word for this "feast" means a drinking party. Seven days of it. 🔴 for the word, 🟡 that Samson drank.
- **He tells no one (14:6, 9, 16).** Not about the lion, not about the honey. The secret is his riddle. 🔴
- **Thirty companions (14:11).** The Philistines assign thirty men to him "when they saw him." Honor guard, or guards? 🔴 for the number, 🔵 for the motive.
- **The threat is fire (14:15).** "We will burn you and your father's house with fire." Hold that. They do it in 15:6. 🔴
- **"Plowed with my heifer" (14:18).** You used my wife to get into what was mine. It's an insult and an accusation. 🔴
- **The Spirit and the payback (14:19).** The Spirit comes on him mightily, and he uses it to kill thirty men in Ashkelon and strip their clothes to pay a bet. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Parents arranged marriages.** "Take her for me" is Samson ordering his father to make the deal. His parents' objection, "the uncircumcised Philistines," is the covenant objection: Israel was not to marry out (Deuteronomy 7:3). 🔴
- **"Uncircumcised" marked the Philistines.** They came from the Aegean world and didn't practice circumcision, unlike most of Israel's Semitic neighbors. The word was an insult. 🔴
- **Riddles were contests, not puzzles.** The Hebrew word is *chidah*. An ANE riddle tested who had hidden knowledge, and winning or losing was about honor and shame. The Queen of Sheba tests Solomon with *chidot* (1 Kings 10:1). God tells Ezekiel to "propound a riddle" (Ezekiel 17:2). Psalm 78:2 promises "dark sayings," and Matthew quotes it about Jesus's parables (Matthew 13:34–35). 🔴
- **A rigged riddle on purpose.** No one could reason out "lion with honey in it." That was the point. The person posing it shows he has knowledge the others can't reach. 🟡
- **The wager was expensive.** Thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes was a fortune. The guests stood to lose real wealth, and face. 🔴
- **Plowing with someone's heifer.** Working another man's animal in your field without permission. Calling his bride his heifer also hints the men got closer to her than they should have. 🟡
- **Wedding feasts ran seven days.** Jacob's did too (Genesis 29:27). 🔴
- **Spirit power for a task.** "Came upon him mightily" (*tsalach*, rushed) is the Spirit giving power for a job, the same word used of Saul and David later (1 Samuel 10:6; 16:13). It isn't a comment on Samson's character. 🔴

## My notes
- This riddle bothered me, or at least it didn't make sense to me. I get what it is, the honey from the lion's carcass. But in today's culture, if I told that riddle to somebody, they'd call BS on it. That's not a riddle. That's just something you made up.
- The answer is that ANE riddles were a different category. Not a fair puzzle you can reason out, but a wisdom contest: the one who asks is showing he has knowledge you can't get to, and losing is public shame. The *chidah* runs through Sheba and Solomon, Ezekiel's eagles, Psalm 78:2 and Jesus's parables.
- So riddles are like trivia, with one difference: the question writer already knows you can't possibly know the answer. The Philistines didn't beat him at trivia. They broke into the answer key.
- When the explanation called Samson's riddle a trap, I asked: does Block say that, or is that from you? It came from Claude, not Block. I could see where it came from, but it's a good rule: when something is synthesized and not in the commentary in front of you, flag it. 🔵 on the "trap" reading.
- The Nazirite violations start here. The dead lion is the first. The drinking feast is the second, likely. The hair comes in 16:19. Block reads the three as planned by the narrator.
- 14:4 is the uncomfortable verse. God routes his purpose through Samson's appetites. Not an endorsement.
- My pre-read note adds *tsalach* (the Spirit rushing) and Wilcock's "gifted but undisciplined." The Wilcock line is my summary, unchecked. 🔵
- **Divine council:** none. The supernatural element is the Spirit giving strength.

## What the chapter is doing
- At wheat harvest Samson comes back for his wife with a young goat. Her father says he gave her to the best man and offers the younger sister.
- Samson ties 300 foxes tail to tail with torches and burns the Philistines' grain, vineyards and olive groves.
- The Philistines burn his wife and her father to death. Samson slaughters them in revenge and hides in a cave at the rock of Etam.
- The Philistines move into Judah. 3,000 men of Judah come to tie Samson up and hand him over. He lets them.
- At Lehi the Spirit rushes on him, the ropes melt like burned flax, and he kills 1,000 men with a fresh donkey jawbone. Then he nearly dies of thirst, calls on Yahweh, and God splits the ground for water.

## Pay attention to this
- **"I shall be innocent" (15:3).** Samson decides this round is justified before he starts. Every step is a private score. 🔴
- **The fire comes back on her (15:6).** The Philistines threatened to burn her and her family in 14:15 if she didn't get the answer. She did, and they burned her anyway. 🔴
- **"As they did to me, so I have done to them" (15:11).** The book's first chapter had a Canaanite king say "as I have done, so God has repaid me" (1:7). Now an Israelite judge talks the same way, only about himself, not God. 🔴 for both lines, 🟡 for the echo.
- **Judah hands over its own deliverer (15:11–13).** "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?" The tribe that went up first in chapter 1 now sends 3,000 men to tie up the one man fighting the enemy. 🔴
- **Samson doesn't fight Judah (15:12).** He only asks them to swear they won't kill him themselves. 🔴
- **The ropes "as flax that is burned with fire" (15:14).** Fire again. It runs all through these two chapters: torches, a burned wife, burned ropes. 🔴 for the images, 🟡 for the pattern.
- **A fresh jawbone (15:15).** Fresh means from a recently dead animal. One more brush with a dead body for a Nazirite. 🔴 for "fresh," 🟡 for the vow issue.
- **"Heaps upon heaps" (15:16).** A Hebrew pun. The word for donkey and the word for heap sound the same. "With a donkey's jaw, a donkey-heap, two donkey-heaps." Samson writes himself a victory song. 🔴
- **His first prayer (15:18).** After a thousand dead, Samson finally calls on Yahweh. It's about his thirst, but he does call himself God's servant and calls the win God's "great salvation." 🔴
- **"Judged Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines" (15:20).** Not "the land had rest." The Philistines are still in charge. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **The wife stayed at her father's.** Some ANE marriages left the bride in her father's house with the husband visiting. That fits Samson showing up with a goat as a gift. 🔵
- **Burning a harvest was economic war.** Grain, vines and olives were the whole economy: bread, wine, oil. One fire at harvest could ruin a region for a year. 🔴
- **Foxes or jackals.** The word can mean either. Jackals ran in packs and were easier to catch in numbers. 🔴 for the word.
- **Dagon and the grain.** The Philistines' chief god Dagon was linked to grain in older Semitic tradition (*dagan* is a word for grain). Burning Philistine fields hits the god's own claim to give the harvest. That's a reading from my pre-read note. 🔴 for the word, 🔵 for the polemic.
- **Occupation meant collaboration.** Under a stronger power, local leaders often kept the peace by handing over troublemakers. Judah's men do exactly that. 🟡
- **A donkey's jawbone was a real weapon.** A fresh jaw is heavy and hard, with teeth still set. Ancient sickles were sometimes made on the same shape. 🟡
- **Water from a split rock.** God splitting "the hollow place" for a thirsty man calls up Moses striking the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6). 🟡
- **Spirit power is for the task.** "Came upon him mightily" is the Spirit giving strength for a job. It says nothing about Samson's character, and the narrator never says Samson asked for it. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Samson spends the night with a prostitute in Gaza. The men of Gaza wait to kill him at dawn. At midnight he rips the city gate out, posts and all, and carries it up a hill toward Hebron.
- He falls for Delilah in the Sorek valley. Each Philistine lord offers her 1,100 pieces of silver to find the secret of his strength.
- Three times he lies to her and three times he breaks free. She keeps at him until "his soul was annoyed to death," and he tells her: no razor has touched my head.
- She has him shaved while he sleeps on her knees. "He did not know that Yahweh had left him." The Philistines gouge out his eyes and set him grinding grain in a Gaza prison. His hair starts to grow.
- At a festival to Dagon, they bring him out to entertain them. He asks the boy leading him to put his hands on the pillars, prays for strength one last time, and brings the temple down on the lords and 3,000 people.

## Pay attention to this
- **Samson's eyes.** He "saw" the woman at Timnah (14:1), she was "right in my eyes" (14:3), he "saw" the prostitute at Gaza (16:1). The Philistines take his eyes (16:21). He goes down the way he went wrong. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for the pattern.
- **Gaza's gate on his shoulders (16:3).** He carries it uphill toward Hebron, in Judah. Mocking the city, and maybe Judah too, which had handed him over. 🔴 for the text, 🔵 for any message to Judah.
- **Delilah isn't called a Philistine.** The text never says what she is. She's the only woman in Samson's story with a name, and the only one he's said to love (16:4). 🔴
- **1,100 pieces of silver from each lord (16:5).** Five lords, so a fortune. Hold the number: Micah steals exactly 1,100 shekels in 17:2. 🔴
- **Every lie comes closer to the hair (16:7, 11, 13).** Fresh cords, new ropes, then his locks woven into a loom. He's flirting with the truth. 🔴 for the sequence, 🟡 for reading it as flirting.
- **The third broken rule (16:17–19).** "A razor has never come on my head." The hair was the last sign of the vow still standing. 🔴
- **"He did not know that Yahweh had left him" (16:20).** The saddest line in the Samson story. He thinks it'll go like always. 🔴
- **Grinding grain (16:21).** Work for slaves and women, done blind, in bronze chains. The strongest man in Israel is a mill animal. 🔴
- **"However, the hair... began to grow" (16:22).** One verse, set right after his worst moment. 🔴
- **"Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hands" (16:23–24).** The Philistines give Dagon the credit. The fight is now between gods. 🔴
- **His last prayer (16:28).** "Please remember me and please strengthen me just this time... that I may at once be avenged... for my two eyes." Real faith, and still about himself. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for the reading.
- **More in his death than in his life (16:30).** The narrator counts the dead. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **City gates were the city's strength.** The gate was where trials were held, deals were made and the town defended itself. Carrying it off was the worst insult you could give a city. 🔴
- **Five lords.** The Philistines had five chief cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath), each with a ruler the Bible calls *seren*, "lord." 1,100 from each is 5,500 pieces of silver. 🔴
- **Looms and pins (16:13–14).** A woman's loom worked by weaving thread on a frame and beating it tight with a pin. In the LSB part of these verses is in brackets. That text is missing from the Hebrew and comes from the Greek translation, which fills in the lines that dropped out. 🔴
- **Blinding prisoners.** Gouging out a captured enemy's eyes was standard ANE treatment, Assyrian and Babylonian too. King Zedekiah gets the same (2 Kings 25:7). 🔴
- **Dagon was a major god.** Older Semitic texts know Dagan as a great god, and at Ugarit he is called the father of Baal. The Philistines took him over as their chief god. The popular idea that he was half fish comes from medieval wordplay on Hebrew *dag*, "fish," not from the ancient sources. 🔴 for Dagan at Ugarit, 🔴 for the fish idea being late.
- **Temples with two central pillars.** Excavated Philistine temples, like the one at Tell Qasile, have two pillars on stone bases holding up the roof beams. A man standing between them really could bring the roof down. 🔴 for the layout, 🟡 for the exact match.
- **A god's festival was a victory party.** Captives were paraded before the god who "won." Samson is the trophy. 🔴
- **Yahweh against Dagon.** This is the first round. The second is in 1 Samuel 5, where Dagon falls face down before the ark and breaks. 🔴

- 16:20 is the verse I flagged: he didn't know the LORD had left him.
- The Philistines credit Dagon with the win (16:23). My pre-read note has Heiser reading Samson's last act as shaming Dagon in his own temple. My summary, not checked. 🔵 Dagon comes back in 1 Samuel 5.

- **Divine council:** Yahweh against Dagon, the god of the Philistines, in Dagon's own house.

## What the chapter is doing
- The last section of Judges starts here. No more judges, no more enemies from outside. Just Israel.
- Micah of Ephraim confesses he stole 1,100 pieces of silver from his mother, after hearing her curse the thief. She blesses him and dedicates the silver "to Yahweh" to make an idol.
- She gives 200 pieces to a silversmith. Micah sets up a shrine with the idol, an ephod and household gods, and makes one of his sons priest.
- A young Levite from Bethlehem, drifting and looking for a place, shows up. Micah hires him for ten pieces of silver a year, clothes and food.
- Micah: "Now I know that Yahweh will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."

## Pay attention to this
- **"No king in Israel" (17:6).** The first time the refrain shows up: "every man did what was right in his own eyes." It comes back in 18:1, 19:1 and 21:25. 🔴
- **The name drops God.** In 17:1 and 17:4 he's *Mikayehu*, "Who is like Yahweh?" After that he's just *Mikah*. The name loses God at the same time the idolatry starts. 🔴 for the spellings, 🟡 that it's deliberate.
- **The curse turns the thief (17:2).** He returns the silver because he's scared of his mother's curse, not because he's sorry. Then she blesses him to cancel it. 🔴
- **"Holy to Yahweh" for an idol (17:3).** She dedicates the silver to Yahweh and in the same breath orders a carved image and a cast image. It breaks the second commandment while using God's name. 🔴
- **Only 200 of 1,100 (17:4).** She "wholly" dedicates it, then the silversmith gets 200. Where did the other 900 go? 🔴 for the numbers, ⬜ for the rest.
- **1,100 again.** The same sum each Philistine lord paid Delilah (16:5). 🔴
- **A shrine at home (17:5).** The Hebrew is *beth elohim*, which can mean "house of God" or "house of gods." Shiloh, the real house of God, is a short walk away (18:31). 🔴
- **He "ordained" his son (17:5, 12).** Literally "filled the hand." Priesthood belonged to Aaron's line. Micah hands it out himself. 🔴
- **The Levite has no name (17:7).** Young, from Bethlehem, drifting, looking for "a place." The narrator tells you all that and holds his name back until 18:30. 🔴
- **"Be a father and a priest to me" (17:10–11).** Then the narrator says the Levite became like one of Micah's sons. The titles flip right away. 🔴
- **Micah's theology (17:13).** Having the right professional on staff means God has to bless me. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Curses were real force.** People believed a spoken curse went out and did damage. Micah's mother couldn't take it back, so she pronounced a blessing over the same person to cover it. 🔴
- **Household gods.** The *teraphim* were small figures kept in the house for protection, luck or guidance. Rachel stole her father's (Genesis 31:19). Michal hid one in David's bed (1 Samuel 19:13). Ordinary in the ANE, and banned in Israel. 🔴
- **Private shrines were common, Israel's law wasn't.** Families in the ANE kept their own gods and altars. Deuteronomy 12 told Israel to worship at the one place Yahweh would choose. Micah does what everyone around him did. 🔴
- **Levites had no land.** They were spread among the tribes and lived on the offerings (Numbers 18:21–24; Deuteronomy 18:6–8). When Israel stopped giving, Levites ended up wandering. Bethlehem wasn't one of the Levite towns, which adds to the question of what he was doing there. 🔴 for the law, 🟡 for the picture.
- **A Levite as a status symbol.** Owning a shrine was one thing. Having a real Levite running it gave it a stamp of legitimacy. Ten silver pieces a year was decent pay. 🟡
- **The ephod again.** Like Gideon's, an ephod in a home shrine was most likely used to get answers from God. Micah built his own oracle. 🟡

## My notes
- I came into this right after finishing Samson, just working through the Old Testament for my own study, no group prep.
- My first questions: is this the same Micah as the prophet? No. That Micah is centuries later. And what does "pious" mean?
- My take: he thinks he's doing the right thing, but he's obviously wrong, and that fits the culture of Israel in that period. They were all getting it wrong.
- I noticed the running line through these last chapters, that there was no king. And the Levite showing up to be Micah's personal priest looked like idolatry in itself. Micah is putting his faith in the priest, not in God. He's trying to get a special connection, his own direct line to God, favors.
- The Levite isn't doing this against his will. He's selling himself. In this situation he's the prostitute, a spiritual mercenary going to whoever pays more. That personal sin grows into a tribe's apostasy in chapter 18.
- Block's frame, from the study: chapters 17–18 show Israel turning Canaanite at three levels, the household (Micah), the priesthood (the Levite) and the tribe (Dan). No judge, and nobody calls on Yahweh.
- Block on the refrain: it isn't pro-king. Israel doesn't need a king to sin. The refrain points to Israel rejecting Yahweh as its king.
- Block's list: four things that look good and eight that are wrong. Fear of the curse, stolen silver, silver dedicated to Micah's house and not to Shiloh, only 200 of 1,100 reaching the smith, the Exodus 20:4–5 ban, the Deuteronomy 12 ban, a fake ephod and household gods in place of the Urim and Thummim, his son as priest.
- Block on the tone: a farce and a tragedy at once. "The actors do not realize the incongruity of their actions." Like Jephthah, deadly sincere and thoroughly pagan.
- **Silver and gold.** I asked how the ANE saw silver against gold. Gold was the metal of the sacred, priests and kings. Silver was common money, the metal of trade. So you're trading your spiritual standing for the common man's currency. If gold is heaven, silver is earth. And gold doesn't tarnish or rust, which ties to laying up treasure in heaven where rust can't touch it. That reminded me of the Christian symbolism class on heaven and earth. 🟡 as a reading I built, not a claim the text makes.
- I also saw silver in Judas's thirty pieces. Micah's blessed stolen silver and Judas's payment are both insiders trading the sacred for money.
- The study became a jayms.com post.
- **Divine council:** no council scene. The hook is the *beth elohim*, a house for "gods," and household gods standing in for Yahweh.

## What the chapter is doing
- The tribe of Dan still has no land of its own. They send five scouts north.
- The scouts stop at Micah's house, recognize the Levite's voice, and ask him to check with God. He tells them, "Go in peace; your way... is before Yahweh."
- They find Laish, a quiet, unguarded town far from anyone who could help it, and come back with a glowing report.
- Six hundred armed Danites march north, stop at Micah's, and take his idol, ephod, household gods and priest. The Levite is delighted to move up to a whole tribe.
- Micah chases them and cries, "You have taken away my gods which I made." They threaten him and he goes home.
- Dan slaughters Laish, burns it, rebuilds it as Dan, sets up Micah's idol, and the priest turns out to be Jonathan, grandson of Moses. The shrine lasts until the exile, the whole time the real house of God stood at Shiloh.

## Pay attention to this
- **A spy story turned upside down.** Scouts, a report that the land is "very good," a call not to be "silent" or "delay," and a conquest (18:7–10). It sounds like Numbers 13 and Joshua 2. But nobody sent them, God promised them nothing, and the people they kill did nothing to anyone. 🔴 for the echoes, 🟡 for the parody.
- **They recognize his voice (18:3).** Maybe an accent from the south, maybe they'd met. Either way they want to know who hired him. 🔴 for the text, 🔵 for the accent.
- **A vague oracle (18:6).** "Your way... is before Yahweh." It can mean God approves, or God is watching. It's quick, it doesn't name a method, and it tells them what they want to hear. 🔴 for the wording, 🟡 for the read.
- **Laish was "quiet and secure" (18:7, 27).** Said twice. No army, no allies, no dealings with anyone. That's why they picked it. 🔴
- **"Is it better for you to be a priest to the house of one man or... to a tribe?" (18:19).** A promotion. "The priest's heart was merry" (18:20). 🔴
- **The thief gets robbed (18:24).** Micah stole silver from his mother. Now Dan steals his idols from him. 🔴
- **"My gods which I made."** Micah says it himself. Gods you made can be carried off by the next stronger man. 🔴
- **Women and children in front (18:21).** The Danites put the little ones and livestock ahead of them, so the soldiers guard the rear against Micah. This is a whole clan moving. 🔴
- **Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses (18:30).** The priest finally gets a name, and it's Moses's grandson. 🔴
- **"All the time that the house of God was at Shiloh" (18:31).** The true sanctuary was open the whole time. Dan didn't have to do any of this. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **The scribes tried to hide Moses's name.** In the Hebrew text of 18:30, a small letter *nun* is written raised above the line, which turns Moses (*Mosheh*) into Manasseh (*Menasheh*). The scribes were sparing Moses's family the shame. Many translations, the LSB included, read Moses. 🔴
- **Dan sat at the foot of Mount Hermon.** Laish/Dan was near the springs of the Jordan below Hermon. Heiser makes a lot of that region: the mountain later Jewish tradition tied to the rebel Watchers, and the area of Caesarea Philippi where Jesus asks "who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:13–18). My pre-read note flags Dan's move toward Hermon. 🔴 for the geography, 🔵 for reading anything spiritual into Dan's move.
- **Dan became an official worship site.** Jeroboam later put one of his two golden calves at Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30). Excavations at Tel Dan uncovered a large Iron Age cult platform. The shrine started by Micah's idol became a state shrine. 🔴
- **"Until the day of the exile of the land."** That points to the Assyrian deportations from the north in the 700s BC (2 Kings 15:29). The book's final form is later than its stories. 🔴 for the date, 🟡 for which deportation.
- **Spy stories were a known pattern.** Israel told its conquest in a pattern: scouts, report, attack (Numbers 13; Joshua 2; Judges 1:23–25). Dan's story uses the pattern to show a conquest God never sent. 🟡
- **Dan's long record.** Jacob's blessing calls Dan "a serpent in the way" (Genesis 49:17). Dan never took its first allotment (Joshua 19:40–48; Judges 1:34). Samson was a Danite. Dan is missing from the tribe list in Revelation 7. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for reading them as one pattern.

## My notes
- Block's frame from my study: chapter 18 is a parody of the spy stories (Numbers 13–14; Deuteronomy 1). The land is reported good, but the response is faithless aggression. It's human from start to finish. They grab what nobody promised them. And they succeed, which shows success isn't a sign God approves.
- "The house of Micah" sounds like "the house of a prostitute" in Joshua 2:1, and the harlot language for idolatry runs through the book (2:17; 8:27; 8:33).
- The Levite's oracle (18:6): quick, vague, swaps Yahweh in for the "God" they asked about, and tells them what they want.
- Micah the thief becomes the one robbed. "You took my gods that I made" is the whole case against idols in one line.
- Block's verdict: "There is not an admirable character in these chapters."
- I asked whether this is where Dan gets disinherited, and went back to Jacob's blessing: Dan as a serpent by the way. Then: is Dan just left out later, or a troublemaker all the way through? The idol shrine lasts until the Assyrian exile, Jeroboam makes it official, and Dan is gone from Revelation 7.
- **Divine council.** I asked whether Dan, in a divine council frame, started interbreeding with the Canaanites, got mixed up with the giants, and fell under another lesser god. The answer was honest: there's no text that ties Dan to the Nephilim or giant bloodlines. I appreciated being told it can't see something instead of guessing. 
- **Judas and Dan.** I asked whether there's a similarity. Dan is one of the twelve and falls into idolatry. Judas is one of the twelve and falls. Both insiders who break faith from inside. Then silver: Judas sells Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, and Micah's blessed silver becomes the idol Dan carries off. 🟡 as my own reading.
- My pre-read note has Heiser on Dan moving toward the Hermon region. Unchecked. 🔵

## What the chapter is doing
- "No king in Israel" again. A Levite from the back country of Ephraim has a concubine from Bethlehem. She leaves him and goes home to her father.
- After four months he goes to win her back. Her father keeps him eating and drinking for four days and most of a fifth.
- Leaving late, he refuses to stop at Jebus, a non-Israelite city, and pushes on to Gibeah in Benjamin. Nobody takes them in until an old man, an outsider himself, gives them a bed.
- The men of the town surround the house and demand the Levite. The old man offers his daughter and the concubine. The Levite shoves his concubine out the door. They abuse her all night. At dawn she falls at the door with her hands on the threshold.
- In the morning he tells her "get up," gets no answer, puts her on the donkey, goes home, cuts her into twelve pieces and sends them through Israel. Everyone says nothing like this has happened since Egypt.

## Pay attention to this
- **Another Levite from Ephraim and Bethlehem.** Chapter 17's Levite came from Bethlehem to Ephraim. This one goes from Ephraim to Bethlehem. The two closing stories mirror each other. 🔴
- **"Played the harlot against him" (19:2).** The Hebrew says that, but the old Greek translation says she "became angry with him." Either way, she leaves, and he waits four months to go after her. 🔴 for the variant, ⬜ for which is right.
- **"To speak to her heart" (19:3).** Tender words. Shechem uses them of Dinah (Genesis 34:3) and God uses them of Israel (Hosea 2:14). Compare what he does at Gibeah. 🔴
- **The father's hospitality goes on and on (19:4–9).** Eat, drink, stay one more night, "let your heart be merry." It's almost comic. The point: the only safe hospitality in the chapter comes before the trip. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the point.
- **"Not into the city of foreigners" (19:12).** He skips Jebus, a Canaanite city, because Israelites will be safer. The Israelite town turns out worse than anything he feared from the Canaanites. 🔴
- **No one takes them in (19:15, 18).** A town of Israelites leaves travelers in the square at night. The one man who helps is an outsider from Ephraim. 🔴
- **Sodom, almost word for word (19:22–25).** Men surround the house, demand the guest "that we may know him," the host goes out, calls them "my brothers," begs them not to do this evil, and offers the women. Read Genesis 19:4–8 next to it. Israel has become Sodom. 🔴 for the echoes.
- **"Whatever is good in your eyes" (19:24).** The eye language of the whole book shows up in the worst possible place. 🔴
- **In Sodom the angels pulled Lot in. Here nobody saves her.** The Levite "took hold of his concubine and brought her out" (19:25). 🔴
- **"Get up and let us go" (19:28).** Her hands are on the threshold. His first words to her since the trip are an order. 🔴
- **Was she already dead?** "There was no answer." The text never says when she died. 🔴 for the silence, ⬜ for the fact.
- **God is never named except once (19:18).** The Levite says he's going to "the house of Yahweh." No one prays, no one asks God, no one hears from God. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Hospitality was a sacred duty.** In the ANE you took in a traveler for the night and protected him with your life. A town leaving strangers in the square was already a judgment on the town. 🔴
- **A concubine was a lower-rank wife.** Legally bound to him, but with fewer rights and her children with less standing. The text still calls him her "husband" (19:3) and her father his "father-in-law." 🔴
- **Gibeah was Saul's hometown.** Israel's first king comes from this town (1 Samuel 10:26). And when Saul summons Israel to war, he cuts oxen into pieces and sends them out (1 Samuel 11:7). The book is quietly setting up its view of Saul's roots. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the setup.
- **Dismemberment as a summons.** Sending pieces of a body or an animal was a call to arms: come, or this happens to you. An old letter from Mari describes cutting off a prisoner's head and parading it through towns to make the troops turn out. 🟡
- **Twelve pieces, twelve tribes.** He uses her body as a message to all Israel. 🔴
- **Jebus was still Canaanite.** Jerusalem stayed a Jebusite city until David took it (2 Samuel 5:6–9), which fits 1:21. 🔴
- **"Vile fellows."** The Hebrew is "sons of Belial," sons of worthlessness. By Paul's day Belial is a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). 🔴

## My notes
- My reading plan: the last two stories in Judges are the darkest passages in the book, and that's on purpose. Judges 19 echoes Genesis 19 almost word for word. The writer wants you to feel how far Israel has fallen. Israel has become Sodom.
- My reading guide called this the most disturbing passage in the Old Testament.
- From the chat that framed my read of the book: the women are the moral thermometer. Compare how women are treated at the start (Achsah) with the end (this concubine).
- My pre-read note's structure: the trip to Bethlehem (19:1–9), choosing Gibeah over Jebus (19:10–21), the outrage (19:22–26), the cut-up summons (19:27–30). Its Heiser line: deliberate Genesis 19 language, Gibeah as a new Sodom. Its Wilcock line: the low point of the book, and God doesn't speak in the chapter. Both my summaries, not checked. 🔵

- **Divine council:** no council scene. What stands out is God's silence.

## What the chapter is doing
- The angel of Yahweh comes up from Gilgal to Bochim and charges Israel: you made deals with the people of the land and left their altars standing, so I won't drive them out. The people weep and sacrifice.
- The story backs up to Joshua's death. His generation serves Yahweh. The next one doesn't know him.
- Then the narrator lays out the pattern that runs the rest of the book: Israel serves the Baals, Yahweh hands them to raiders, they groan, he raises a judge, the judge dies, and they go back worse than before.
- The nations stay, on purpose, as a test.

## Pay attention to this
- **The angel talks like God (2:1).** "I brought you up out of Egypt... I said, 'I will never break My covenant with you.'" A messenger would say "Yahweh says." This one says "I." 🔴
- **From Gilgal to Bochim.** Gilgal was the conquest base camp, where Israel was circumcised and kept the first Passover in the land (Joshua 5). The angel leaves the place of beginnings and shows up at a place that gets named "weepers." 🔴 for the places, 🟡 for the contrast.
- **They weep, then nothing changes (2:4–5).** Tears and a sacrifice, but no torn-down altars. The next verses go straight to Baal. 🟡
- **"Thorns" is supplied (2:3).** In the LSB "as thorns" is in italics. The Hebrew just says the nations will be "in your sides." Translators fill it in from Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13, where the full phrase is "thorns in your sides." 🔴
- **A flashback (2:6–10).** Joshua sends the people home and dies at 110. That already happened in Joshua 24. The book has two openings: chapter 1 is the land, chapter 2 is the heart. 🔴
- **"Did not know Yahweh" (2:10).** Not that they'd never heard of him. They had no lived history with him. The generation that "saw all the great work of Yahweh" (2:7) didn't pass it on. 🟡
- **The pattern (2:11–19).** Evil in the eyes of Yahweh, anger, sold to enemies, groaning, a judge, rest, the judge dies, back to the gods. Read it once slowly and you'll see it in every story to chapter 16. 🔴
- **Worse each time (2:19).** "They would turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers." The narrator tells you up front that it's a slide, not a merry-go-round. 🔴
- **No repentance in the loop (2:18).** Yahweh acts because he "was moved to pity by their groaning." The text never says they turned back to him. He moves first. 🔴 for the wording, 🟡 for the weight on it.
- **"Played the harlot" (2:17).** First use of the harlot language for idolatry in the book. It comes back with Gideon's ephod (8:27) and the Baals after his death (8:33). 🔴
- **The test (2:22).** The nations left in the land are there "to test Israel by them." 3:1–4 picks it up. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **The angel of Yahweh is Yahweh, seen.** Heiser reads this figure as the visible Yahweh, the second person of what later Jews called "two powers in heaven." Here the angel claims the Exodus, the oath to the fathers and the covenant as his own. Other texts give the Exodus to God and to the angel both (Exodus 23:20–23; Micah 6:4). 🔴 for what the angel says, 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **Baal was the rain god, and Canaan ran on rain.** Egypt had the Nile. Canaan had whatever fell from the sky (Deuteronomy 11:10–12). In the Ugarit texts Baal is the storm god who brings the rain and the crops. A shepherd people learning to farm in a rain-fed land would feel the pull to keep the local rain god happy. 🔴 for Baal's role, 🟡 for the pull.
- **"The Baals" and "the Ashtaroth" are plural.** Baal and Ashtart (Astarte) were worshiped in local forms, Baal of this town and that town, so the text uses the plural. Ashtart was a goddess of fertility and war. 🔴
- **The gods of the peoples around them (2:12).** Deuteronomy 32:8–9 and 4:19 picture the nations handed over to lesser gods while Israel belonged to Yahweh alone. Serving the gods around you was switching sides in the unseen world, not just picking a new religion. That's Heiser's Deuteronomy 32 worldview. 🟡
- **"Sold" is treaty language.** Israel's covenant has the shape of an ANE treaty between a great king and a lesser one. Break it and the curses kick in (Deuteronomy 28). "He sold them into the hands of their enemies" (2:14) is the great king handing a rebel vassal over. 🔴 for the treaty shape, 🟡 for the reading of "sold."
- **"Judges" doesn't mean courtroom.** The *shophetim* here are deliverers and leaders. The same root names rulers and governors in texts from Mari and Ugarit. Deborah is the only one shown hearing cases (4:5). 🔴
- **"Gathered to their fathers" (2:10).** Families were laid in shared tombs, the bones moved aside for the next burial. You literally joined your fathers. 🔴

## My notes
- My reading-plan notes flag 2:1–5 as the angel of Yahweh at Bochim and say plainly: this is not a created messenger. Heiser: the *mal'ak YHWH* is a distinct divine person, the presence of Yahweh before the incarnation.
- I marked this chapter as the template for the whole book. The cycle is apostasy, oppression, crying out, deliverer, rest, repeat, and it runs six times.
- My pre-read note gives Wilcock's frame: each cycle doesn't come back to the starting line but sinks lower. A spiral, not a circle. The nations left behind are a test for a generation that never fought. That's my summary of Wilcock and still needs checking against his book. 🔵
- **Thorns.** In the Paul's thorn conversation I said my own opinion had always been a physical adversary, since Paul talks about people causing him trouble. When I traced the phrase later, the Old Testament uses it of a hostile people who won't leave (Numbers 33:55; Joshua 23:13; Ezekiel 28:24), and Judges 2:3 is in the same family. That strengthens the adversary reading for Paul. 🟡 One catch from the LSB: in 2:3 the word "thorns" is supplied, so the weight sits on Numbers and Joshua, not here.
- **Divine council:** two hooks. The angel of Yahweh at Bochim, and "the gods of the peoples who were around them." No council scene.

## What the chapter is doing
- All Israel gathers at Mizpah "as one man," 400,000 strong, and hears the Levite's story.
- They demand Benjamin hand over the men of Gibeah. Benjamin refuses and musters 26,000, including 700 left-handed slingers who never miss.
- Israel asks God who goes first. Judah. Benjamin kills 22,000 Israelites the first day. Israel weeps and asks again. Benjamin kills 18,000 the second day.
- The third time Israel weeps, fasts, offers sacrifices before the ark at Bethel, with Phinehas the priest, and asks. Yahweh promises victory.
- An ambush, like the one at Ai, takes Gibeah. Benjamin loses 25,100 men. Israel burns Benjamin's towns. Only 600 Benjamites escape to the rock of Rimmon.

## Pay attention to this
- **"As one man" (20:1, 8, 11).** The only time in Judges all Israel unites, it's to fight one of its own tribes. 🔴
- **The Levite trims his story (20:4–7).** He says the men meant to kill him and that they raped his concubine and she died. He leaves out that he pushed her out the door himself. 🔴
- **Benjamin protects the guilty (20:13).** "Give up the men... that we may... purge this evil from Israel." Benjamin picks tribe over justice. 🔴
- **700 left-handed slingers (20:16).** "Each one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss." Benjamin, "son of the right hand," known for left-handed fighters again, the way Ehud was. 🔴
- **The book's first question, asked again (20:18).** "Who shall go up for us to begin the battle?" Yahweh says "Judah," the same answer as 1:2. In chapter 1 the enemy was Canaan. Now it's Benjamin. 🔴
- **God says "go" and Israel loses (20:21–25).** Twice. 40,000 dead. The text doesn't explain why. 🔴 for the losses, ⬜ for the reason.
- **Each time they ask, they go lower (20:18, 23, 26–28).** First they just ask. Then they weep and ask. Then they weep, fast, sacrifice and ask through the priest before the ark. Only the third time does God promise victory: "tomorrow I will give them into your hand." 🔴 for the steps, 🟡 for reading them as the point.
- **"My brother Benjamin" (20:23, 28).** Israel calls them brothers while asking whether to keep killing them. 🔴
- **"Benjamin did not know that calamity was about to reach them" (20:34).** The same not-knowing as Samson in 16:20. 🔴 for the line, 🟡 for the echo.
- **"Yahweh defeated Benjamin" (20:35).** God fights against one of his own tribes. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **This story happens early.** Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, is the priest (20:28), and the ark is at Bethel. That puts the events near the start of the judges period, even though the book tells them last. The book is arranged by theme, not by date. 🔴 for Phinehas, 🟡 for the date.
- **Tribes were bound by covenant.** The twelve tribes were a league held together by their covenant with Yahweh. A crime in one tribe was the whole league's problem, and refusing to deal with it was rebellion against the league. 🟡
- **"Purge the evil from Israel" (20:13).** That's Deuteronomy's phrase for capital crimes (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7; 22:21–24). Israel is acting as a court. 🔴
- **The Ai playbook (20:29–48).** Fake a retreat, draw the defenders out, and spring an ambush that burns the city. That's how Joshua took Ai (Joshua 8). Israel uses its conquest tactic on Benjamin. 🔴
- **Slingers were deadly.** A trained slinger could throw a stone fast enough to kill at distance. Slingers show up in Assyrian reliefs of sieges. "At a hair and not miss" is praise for real skill. 🔴
- **The ban turned inward (20:48).** Israel burns Benjamin's towns and kills people and animals, the way it was told to treat Canaanite cities. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the comparison.
- **Numbers.** 400,000 and the death counts may be literal, or "thousand" (*eleph*) may mean a military unit. Scholars split on it. 🔴 for the word's range, ⬜ for which.

## My notes
- From my Ehud study: 20:16's 700 left-handed Benjamite slingers are the evidence that left-handedness was a trained tribal trait in Benjamin, which helps explain Ehud.
- My pre-read note's structure: the assembly at Mizpah (20:1–11), Benjamin's defiance (20:12–17), two defeats and seeking the LORD (20:18–28), the ambush (20:29–48).
- Its Heiser line: Phinehas and the ark at Bethel place this early in the period, and the ban gets turned on an Israelite tribe. My summary, not checked. 🔵
- My reading guide: chapters 19–21 are civil war, and the book ends in ruins.
- My notes on this chapter are thin. I haven't worked it beyond the pre-read note.
- **Divine council:** none. Yahweh answers through the priest at the ark and fights against Benjamin.

## What the chapter is doing
- Israel had sworn at Mizpah never to give a daughter to Benjamin. Now Benjamin is down to 600 men and Israel weeps at Bethel: why is one tribe missing?
- They find that Jabesh-gilead sent nobody to Mizpah. They send 12,000 men to wipe the town out, men, women and children, except 400 young virgins, who are handed to Benjamin.
- That's not enough. So the elders tell the rest of the Benjamites to hide in the vineyards at Shiloh's yearly feast and each grab a girl when the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance. Their oath technically stays unbroken.
- Everyone goes home. Last line: "In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes."

## Pay attention to this
- **They made the oath, then they cry about it (21:1–3).** "Why, O Yahweh... has this come about?" They ask God why, when they did it themselves. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the irony.
- **"Yahweh had made a breach" (21:15).** The narrator reports what the people felt: God did this. No word from God answers them. 🔴
- **God goes quiet.** In chapter 20 God answered three times. In chapter 21 Israel weeps and builds an altar and gets no reply. Every plan in this chapter is theirs. 🔴
- **A second oath, a second massacre (21:5, 10–11).** They had also sworn death on anyone who skipped Mizpah. So Jabesh-gilead dies. To fix the results of one civil war they start another one. 🔴
- **"Devote to destruction" (21:11).** The ban, meant for Canaanite cities, used on an Israelite town. 🔴
- **"Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan" (21:12).** Shiloh is Israel's sanctuary. The narrator files it under Canaan. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for the jab.
- **Directions to Shiloh (21:19).** North of Bethel, east of the Shechem road, south of Lebonah. The elders give directions to the house of God as if nobody goes there. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the point.
- **A loophole for an oath (21:22).** "You did not give your daughters to them," so you're not guilty. They keep the letter of the oath and break the daughters' families. 🔴
- **Daughters again.** Achsah asked her father and got springs (1:15). Jephthah's daughter died for her father's words (11). The concubine was thrown out a door (19). Now the daughters of Shiloh are grabbed at a worship festival. The book's women end here. 🔴 for the stories, 🟡 for the arc.
- **The last line (21:25).** The refrain closes the book: no king, everyone doing what is right in his own eyes. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Losing a tribe was a disaster.** Twelve tribes meant one people under Yahweh. A missing tribe meant a broken Israel and a lost inheritance in the land. That's why they're desperate. 🔴
- **Oaths couldn't be undone.** An oath sworn "by Yahweh" bound you, and breaking it brought the curse on you. So instead of repenting of a rash oath, they work around it. Jephthah thought the same way in chapter 11. 🔴 for oath culture, 🟡 for the comparison.
- **Jabesh-gilead and Saul.** This town comes back. Saul, a Benjamite from Gibeah, rescues Jabesh-gilead in his first act as king (1 Samuel 11), and its men risk their lives to bury his body (1 Samuel 31:11–13). If Benjamin's wives came from Jabesh, those were family ties. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the family link.
- **Harvest festivals had dancing.** Young women dancing in the vineyards at a yearly feast fits a grape harvest celebration. Which feast it was isn't named. 🔴 for dancing at feasts, 🔵 for which feast.
- **Marriage by capture.** Taking women by force happened in ANE warfare and raids. Here Israel organizes it against its own daughters, at its own sanctuary. 🟡
- **Shiloh was the sanctuary in this period.** The tabernacle and the ark were there (Joshua 18:1; 1 Samuel 1:3). By the opening of 1 Samuel it's run by Eli's corrupt sons. 🔴

## My notes
- Block's reading of the refrain, from my Micah study and the jayms.com Judges timeline post: the missing king is Yahweh. "Evil in the eyes of the LORD" and "right in their own eyes" describe the same condition. The refrain shows up at 17:6, 18:1, 19:1 and 21:25.
- From the Micah study: the refrain isn't a campaign for monarchy. Israel doesn't need a king to sin. It's rejecting Yahweh as king.
- My reading guide: the last line is the thesis of the book. It's meant to leave you desperate for a king, which sets up Samuel. Chapters 19–21 are civil war, and the book ends in ruins.
- This chapter links to my "What Is a King" series. That series comes at the same problem from my own day: the self that recognizes no King and calls it freedom.
- My pre-read note's Heiser line: the twelve tribes as an earthly picture of order, so losing one is a breach. Its Wilcock line: no happy ending, only a desperate compromise, and 21:25 points ahead to the search for a king. My summaries, not checked. 🔵
- **Divine council:** none. God is silent, and the last word goes to the narrator's refrain.

## What the chapter is doing
- The nations left in the land are listed, the ones meant to test Israel. Israel marries into them and serves their gods.
- Othniel, the first judge, beats a king from Mesopotamia. Forty years of quiet.
- Moab's king Eglon takes Jericho and squeezes Israel for eighteen years. Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, carries in the tribute, gets the king alone, and kills him with a hidden sword. Israel takes the Jordan fords and Moab is beaten. Eighty years of quiet.
- One verse for Shamgar: 600 Philistines with an oxgoad.

## Pay attention to this
- **Othniel is the model (3:9–11).** Israel cries out, Yahweh raises a savior, the Spirit of Yahweh comes on him, he judges, he goes to war, Yahweh gives the enemy into his hand, the land rests. No flaws, no details, no story. Every judge after him gets measured against this clean outline. 🔴
- **"Cushan-rishathaim" sounds like a joke.** It means something like "Cushan of double wickedness." Probably a mocking nickname, not what his mother called him. 🟡
- **Left-handed, literally "bound in his right hand" (3:15).** The LSB says "a left-handed man." The Hebrew says his right hand was restricted. Either a trained lefty or a man who couldn't use his right. 🔴 for the phrase, ⬜ for which.
- **Benjamin means "son of the right hand."** And the tribe of the right hand keeps turning out left-handed fighters: 700 elite slingers in 20:16, men who could sling and shoot with either hand in 1 Chronicles 12:2. 🔴
- **The sword on the right thigh (3:16).** A right-handed man draws across his body, so his sword hangs on the left. Guards check the left hip. Ehud's is on the right. 🟡
- **He turns back at the idols (3:19, 3:26).** The "graven images" at Gilgal are where he turns around to go back in, and where he passes on his way out. Gilgal was Israel's first camp in the land. Now there are idols there. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the irony.
- **"A message from God for you" (3:20).** The Hebrew word *davar* means both "word" and "thing." Ehud has a *davar* from God, and it's a foot and a half long. 🟡
- **The hilt goes in after the blade (3:21–22).** The fat closes over it and Ehud leaves it there. That detail tells you how deep it went and why he couldn't pull it out. 🔴
- **The servants wait outside (3:24–25).** They think he's "relieving himself." They wait "until they were ashamed," then get the key. Ehud is gone by then. The narrator wants you to laugh. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the tone.
- **Ehud leads from the front (3:27–28).** "Yahweh has given your enemies the Moabites into your hands." He gives God the credit before the battle. 🔴
- **Shamgar "son of Anath" (3:31).** Anath was a Canaanite war goddess. An Israelite deliverer with a Canaanite goddess in his name. Maybe a hometown (Beth-anath), maybe a warrior title. 🔴 for who Anath was, 🔵 for what the name means here.

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Right was strong, left was weak.** Across the ANE the right hand meant strength, honor and blessing, and the left meant weakness and bad luck. Mesopotamian omen readers sorted signs into right (good) and left (bad). Priests got the right thigh, and blood went on the right ear, thumb and toe (Leviticus 8). The Hebrew word for left carries a bad feel. So a left-handed man coming to pay tribute looks harmless. 🔴 for the right/left pattern, 🟡 for how it plays in the story.
- **Tribute day was a ceremony.** Vassals came in person with porters and gifts and bowed before the overlord. Ehud has a reason to be in the room. 🔴
- **"Very fat" means rich.** In a world where most people were thin, a fat king was a well-fed king, fattened on eighteen years of Israel's tribute. The same word (*bari*) is used of fattened animals. 🔴 for the word, 🟡 for the picture.
- **Eglon, the calf.** His name likely comes from *egel*, "calf." A fat calf in a private room, and a man arrives with a blade. Sacrifice humor. 🔵
- **The cool roof chamber.** Wealthy houses had an upper room built to catch the breeze. It was private, which is why everyone leaves when the king says "Keep silence." 🔴
- **"Covering his feet."** The servants' phrase is a polite idiom for going to the bathroom. In a private chamber, waiting outside was simple manners. 🔴
- **The sword.** A "cubit" here is a short measure, a one-off word. Think 18 inches or so, two-edged, small enough to hide on a thigh under a cloak. 🟡
- **Moab's god.** Moab belonged to Chemosh (Numbers 21:29). In the Deuteronomy 32 picture, Moab's oppression is Chemosh's people pressing on Yahweh's. The text never names Chemosh here. 🟡
- **"Baal-hermon" (3:3).** Mount Hermon, at the north edge of the land, carries Baal's name. Heiser's *Reversing Hermon* tracks Hermon as the place later Jewish tradition tied to the rebel Watchers. The narrator only gives it as a border marker. 🔴 for the name, 🔵 for leaning on it here.

## My notes
- My Ehud study started with a plain question: why does it matter that he did it with his left hand? The answer is the plot. The sword on the right thigh gets past a search built for right-handed men.
- I pushed further into right and left in the ANE: right as power, honor, blessing; left as weakness and uncleanness. Psalm 110's "sit at My right hand" is the same royal picture.
- Then I asked how fat the king was, and what a hilt even is. Once you know the parts of a sword (grip, guard, pommel, tang), "the handle also went in after the blade" is a lot more graphic than it reads in English.
- The tribal irony stuck with me: Benjamin is the "son of the right hand," and it's famous for left-handers.
- The big picture: God working through the unlikely, the despised hand, the man nobody would search properly.
- My pre-read note gives Wilcock's contrast: Othniel the ideal judge, Ehud the gritty one with deceptive methods, the first step down. And Shamgar as proof God can win with a farm tool. Both are my summaries of Wilcock, not checked against the book. 🔵
- **Divine council:** no council scene. The hooks are the gods Israel serves (3:7), Moab's god in the background, and Hermon carrying Baal's name.

## What the chapter is doing
- Ehud is dead and Israel does evil again. Jabin of Hazor and his general Sisera, with 900 iron chariots, crush Israel for twenty years.
- Deborah, a prophetess who judges Israel under a palm tree, calls Barak and gives him Yahweh's order: take 10,000 men to Mount Tabor.
- Barak won't go without her. She goes, and tells him the honor will go to a woman.

## Pay attention to this
- **Deborah is already judging before the war (4:4–5).** People come to her for decisions. She's the only judge in the book shown settling cases, and she's a prophetess too. 🔴
- **"Has not Yahweh... commanded?" (4:6).** She doesn't ask Barak. She reminds him of an order. 🔴
- **"If you will go with me" (4:8).** Barak sets terms on God's command. Is that weak faith or wanting the prophet at his side? Deborah's answer makes it cost him: "the honor shall not be yours" (4:9). 🔴 for the text, ⬜ for Barak's motive.
- **Which woman?** When Deborah says Yahweh will sell Sisera "into the hand of a woman," you assume she means herself. Then the story walks over to a tent you've never heard of. 🟡
- **Heber had moved (4:11).** The narrator stops the battle story to tell you Heber the Kenite left his clan and camped near Kedesh. That one verse sets up the ending. 🔴
- **Heber had peace with Jabin (4:17).** That's why Sisera runs there. He expects a safe house. 🔴
- **Yahweh fights, Barak mops up (4:15).** "Yahweh threw Sisera and all his chariots... into confusion." The general gets off his chariot and runs. The 900 chariots that held Israel down for twenty years end up useless. 🔴
- **Jael mothers him, then kills him (4:18–21).** "Do not be afraid." A rug, milk instead of water, covering him again. Then the peg. 🔴
- **"Is there a man here?" (4:20).** Sisera tells her to answer "No." She's about to make that true. 🟡
- **"God subdued... Jabin" (4:23).** The narrator credits God, not Deborah, Barak or Jael. 🔴

## Read it like 1150 BC, not 2026
- **Hazor was the big city of the north.** It was the largest Canaanite city in the land, and Joshua had already burned it (Joshua 11:10–13). So a "Jabin king of Hazor" again raises a question. Some read Jabin as a dynasty name, some see the city rebuilt, some see two accounts of one war. 🔴 for Hazor's size and Joshua 11, ⬜ for the fit.
- **Chariots need dry flat ground.** The Jezreel Valley around the Kishon was chariot country. Chapter 5 says the Kishon swept the enemy away, so rain and mud turned the Canaanites' best weapon into a trap. 🔴 for chapter 5, 🟡 for the mud.
- **A woman's tent was off limits.** Among tent dwellers the women's tent was private. A man hiding there was hiding where no searcher should look. That's why Sisera picks it. 🟡
- **Hospitality was sacred, and Jael breaks it.** Taking in a guest meant protecting him. A modern reader may cheer her. An ancient reader would also feel the shock of a host killing her guest. The song in chapter 5 blesses her anyway. 🔴 for the hospitality code, 🟡 for the reader's reaction.
- **Women pitched the tents.** In nomad camps the women set up and struck the tents, so a peg and a mallet were Jael's own tools. She didn't need a sword. 🟡
- **Women leading was rare, not unheard of.** Deborah holding both prophetic and judicial authority is unusual in the ANE. Other cultures had prophetesses (Mari has women prophets), but a woman leading Israel to war is striking. 🔴 for Mari, 🟡 for the rest.
- **Names with meaning.** Barak means "lightning." Lappidoth means "torches," so "wife of Lappidoth" could also be read "woman of torches." Lightning and torches go with a storm battle. 🔴 for the words, 🔵 for reading Deborah's title that way.
- **Divine Warrior.** "Has not Yahweh gone out before you?" (4:14) is the picture of God marching ahead of his army, the same picture the song in chapter 5 paints with the stars fighting from heaven. 🔴
