## What the chapter is doing
- Deborah and Barak sing the battle of chapter 4 as worship. It's a poem, not a second report.
- Yahweh marches out from Seir and Edom, the earth shakes and the clouds pour.
- The song calls the roll of the tribes: who came (Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar, Naphtali) and who stayed home (Reuben, Gilead, Dan, Asher). A town called Meroz gets cursed.
- The stars fight from heaven, the Kishon sweeps the enemy away, Jael is "most blessed of women," and Sisera's mother waits at her window for a son who isn't coming.

## Pay attention to this
- **Read chapter 4 first, then this.** The prose tells you what happened. The song tells you what it meant, and adds things the prose leaves out: the rain, the flooded river, the stars. 🔴
- **The volunteers (5:2, 5:9).** "When the people volunteered, bless Yahweh!" The song is as much about who showed up as about who won. 🔴
- **"A mother in Israel" (5:7).** Deborah doesn't call herself a judge or a general. She calls herself a mother who got up when nobody else would. 🔴
- **Roads empty, villages empty (5:6–7).** Before the battle, travelers took back roads and farm life had stopped. That's what twenty years of chariot raids did. 🔴
- **The roll call has teeth (5:15–17).** Reuben had "great probings of the heart" and stayed with the sheep. Dan stayed with the ships. Asher sat at the seashore. Lots of thinking, no showing up. 🔴
- **Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives (5:18).** "A people who despised their lives even to death." 🔴
- **Meroz is cursed by the angel of Yahweh (5:23).** Not for fighting on the wrong side. For not coming "to the help of Yahweh." Staying neutral was a choice. 🔴
- **The song slows Jael's blow down (5:26–27).** "He bowed, he fell, he lay," three times over. The poem puts Sisera at her feet like a man bowing to a queen. 🔴 for the repetition, 🟡 for the bowing picture.
- **Sisera's mother (5:28–30).** She assumes he's late because he's dividing the plunder: "a maiden, two maidens for every mighty man." The Hebrew is cruder than the LSB, literally "a womb, two wombs." She's counting the Israelite girls her son will bring home. He's lying in a tent at a woman's feet. 🔴
- **Forty years of quiet (5:31).** Same as after Othniel. 🔴

## Read it like 1150 BC, not 2026
- **One of the oldest poems in the Bible.** Many scholars date the Song of Deborah close to the battle itself, around the 1100s BC, because its Hebrew is so old. That's why some lines are hard to translate. 🟡
- **Yahweh comes from the south.** "When You went out from Seir, when You marched from the field of Edom" (5:4). Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3 also have God coming from the southern wilderness, Sinai country. "This Sinai" in 5:5 likely means "the One of Sinai," a title. Israel's God travels from his mountain to fight. 🔴 for the parallels, 🟡 for the title.
- **The storm belongs to Yahweh, not Baal.** Baal was the Canaanite storm god, the rider of the clouds. Here the earth quakes, the heavens drip and the clouds pour at Yahweh's coming, and the rain floods the Kishon on the Canaanites. Heiser reads it as a shot at Baal on his own turf. 🔴 for Baal's role, 🟡 for the polemic.
- **"The stars fought from heaven" (5:20).** In the ANE the stars were tied to divine beings, and the Bible does the same: the morning stars sing with the sons of God (Job 38:7), and "the host of heaven" can mean stars or God's heavenly army. Heiser reads 5:20 as the heavenly host, the council, fighting for Israel in the unseen realm while Israel fights on the ground. 🔴 for the star/host language, 🟡 for Heiser's read.
- **Victory songs were normal.** Egypt and Assyria had them, and Israel had the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15). The women sang them. Miriam led one, Deborah leads this one. 🔴
- **Mothers waiting at windows.** "Woman at the window" was a common image in ANE art and poetry. Here it's turned into the enemy's grief. 🟡
- **Captive women as plunder.** Taking women was standard in ancient war. Sisera's mother counting "wombs" shows how the Canaanite side saw Israel's daughters. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Midian and its allies swarm in every harvest like locusts, with camels past counting, and strip the land for seven years. Israel hides in caves.
- Israel cries out and Yahweh first sends a prophet with a rebuke: I brought you out of Egypt and you still feared the gods of the Amorites.
- The angel of Yahweh finds Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress, calls him "mighty man of valor," and sends him. Gideon asks for a sign, fire comes out of the rock, and he's terrified he'll die.
- That night Gideon tears down his father's Baal altar and Asherah pole. The town wants him dead. His father says let Baal fight his own battles, and Gideon gets the name Jerubbaal.
- Midian camps in Jezreel, the Spirit clothes Gideon, he calls the tribes, and then he asks for the fleece, twice.

## Pay attention to this
- **A prophet before a judge (6:7–10).** This time Israel's cry gets a sermon first, not a rescue. The charge: "you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites... But you have not listened to My voice." 🔴
- **Threshing in a winepress (6:11).** You thresh wheat on an open hilltop so the wind carries the chaff. Gideon is down in a pit hiding it from Midian. That's the man God calls "mighty man of valor" (6:12). 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the humor.
- **The angel turns into Yahweh (6:12–14).** "The angel of Yahweh appeared to him," and two verses later "Yahweh turned to him and said." The narrator switches names in the middle of one conversation. 🔴
- **Gideon's honest question (6:13).** "If Yahweh is with us, why then has all this happened to us?" He's heard the Exodus stories and doesn't see that God now. God doesn't argue. He sends him. 🔴
- **"I have seen the angel of Yahweh face to face" (6:22).** He's afraid he'll die, because seeing God meant death (Exodus 33:20). Yahweh answers, "Peace to you... you shall not die," and Gideon names the altar "Yahweh is Peace." 🔴
- **The idolatry is in his own family (6:25).** "The altar of Baal which belongs to your father." Before Gideon fights Midian, he has to fight his father's religion. 🔴
- **He obeys by night (6:27).** Too afraid to do it by day. He still does it. 🔴
- **"Let Baal contend" (6:31–32).** Joash, the altar's owner, turns it around: if Baal is a god, let him defend himself. The name Jerubbaal is a dare that Baal never answers. 🔴
- **The Spirit "clothed" Gideon (6:34).** The Spirit puts Gideon on like a garment. 🔴
- **The fleece comes after the Spirit and after God already spoke (6:36–40).** "As You have spoken," Gideon says twice. He's not looking for God's will. He knows it. He wants proof. Then he asks God not to be angry and tests again. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the read that the fleece isn't a model for decisions.

## Read it like 1150 BC, not 2026
- **Midian raided at harvest.** Desert peoples hit farmers right when the crop was in, took the food and the animals, and left. Coming "like locusts" with tents and herds means a whole population moving through, not an army. 🔴
- **Camels changed raiding.** Domesticated camels let desert raiders cover long distances fast and strike deep. Judges 6 is one of the early pictures of camel raiders in the Bible. 🟡
- **Seeing God meant death.** "No man can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Jacob (Genesis 32:30) and Manoah (Judges 13:22) react the same way. So Gideon's panic tells you he knew who he'd been talking to. 🔴
- **The angel of Yahweh is Yahweh.** Heiser counts this as one of the key texts: the narrator calls the visitor the angel and Yahweh in the same scene, and Gideon reacts as if he's seen God. Yet the angel goes away and Yahweh keeps speaking (6:21–23). Two personages, one Yahweh, in Heiser's words. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **Baal and Asherah side by side.** A Baal altar with an Asherah pole next to it was standard Canaanite worship: the storm god and the mother goddess, her symbol a wooden pole or tree. Gideon burns the pole as firewood for Yahweh's offering. 🔴
- **A family altar was a clan matter.** Joash owned the altar, and the whole town worshiped at it. Tearing it down was an attack on the town's protection. That's why they want Gideon dead. 🔴 for the reaction, 🟡 for the reason.
- **"The gods of the Amorites in whose land you live" (6:10).** The prophet frames the land as having its own gods. In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview, Israel was living in their territory and fearing them instead of Yahweh. 🟡
- **A seven-year-old bull for seven years of Midian.** The number may be the point. 🔵
- **Text note.** A Dead Sea Scroll fragment of Judges (4QJudg-a) goes straight from 6:6 to 6:11 and lacks the prophet's speech in 6:7–10. Scholars argue whether the scroll dropped it or the speech was added later. 🔴 for the omission, ⬜ for why.

## What the chapter is doing
- Yahweh tells Gideon his army is too big. Anyone afraid goes home, and 22,000 leave. A drinking test at the water cuts the rest to 300.
- Yahweh sends Gideon, scared, to sneak down to the Midianite camp. He hears a soldier tell a dream about a barley loaf flattening a tent, and the friend says it means Gideon's sword.
- Gideon splits the 300 into three groups with trumpets, jars and torches. At the change of the night watch they smash the jars, blow, and shout. Midian panics and turns its swords on itself.
- The other tribes join the chase. Ephraim catches the princes Oreb and Zeeb and brings their heads to Gideon.

## Pay attention to this
- **Too many, not too few (7:2).** "Lest Israel honor themselves, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'" God cuts the army so nobody can take the credit. 🔴
- **The spring of Harod and the trembling (7:1–3).** Harod sounds like the Hebrew for "trembling," and the order is "whoever is afraid and trembling, let him return." They camp at Tremble Spring and the tremblers go home. 🔴
- **Two-thirds walk away (7:3).** 22,000 out of 32,000. Gideon gets to watch his army leave. 🔴
- **The water test is hard to picture (7:5–6).** Some lap "as a dog laps," some kneel, and the 300 lapped "putting their hand to their mouth." Which group was which, and why it mattered, isn't spelled out. The point is that God picks, not Gideon. 🔴 for God choosing, ⬜ for the mechanics.
- **"If you are afraid" (7:10).** God already knows Gideon is scared and makes room for it. He sends him with his servant to overhear the enemy. 🔴
- **The enemy preaches to Gideon (7:13–14).** A Midianite soldier interprets the dream: "God has given Midian and all the camp into his hand." Gideon's final sign comes from the other side's mouth. 🔴
- **He worships first (7:15).** Before he wakes the 300, he bows. 🔴
- **"For Yahweh and for Gideon" (7:18, 20).** God said cut the army so nobody could boast. Gideon puts his own name in the battle cry. Small thing. Watch where it goes in chapter 8. 🔴 for the cry, 🟡 for the warning sign.
- **Yahweh does the fighting (7:22).** "Yahweh set the sword of one against another even throughout the whole camp." The 300 just stand in their places (7:21). 🔴
- **Oreb and Zeeb (7:25).** Raven and Wolf. Killed at places later named after them. 🔴

## Read it like 1150 BC, not 2026
- **The fear clause was in the law.** Before battle the officers were to say, "Who is the man who is afraid and fainthearted? Let him go and return to his house" (Deuteronomy 20:8). Gideon follows the rulebook, and God uses it to shrink the army. 🔴
- **Dreams were taken as messages from the gods.** Egypt and Mesopotamia kept dream books for interpreting them. A soldier telling a dream and his friend reading it would sound normal in any ANE camp. God speaks into the enemy's own religious habits. 🔴 for the dream culture, 🟡 for reading the point.
- **Barley bread vs. a tent.** Barley was the cheap grain of poor farmers. A tent was the home of the desert raiders. So a farmer's loaf rolls in and flattens the raiders' tent. 🟡
- **The middle watch (7:19).** The night was split into watches. The middle one had "just set up." The new guards haven't got their bearings, the old ones are half asleep. Best moment for a panic. 🔴 for the watch, 🟡 for the tactics.
- **Torches and trumpets mean a big army.** Normally only a few men in a company carried a horn or a torch. Three hundred horns and three hundred lights in the dark sounds like thousands of men. 🟡
- **Panic as God's weapon.** The divine warrior throwing an enemy into confusion so it turns on itself shows up again with Jonathan (1 Samuel 14:20) and Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:23). Israel saw it as Yahweh fighting. 🔴
- **Heads as proof.** Bringing back an enemy leader's head was standard proof of a kill in ANE war. 🔴
- **The day of Midian became a proverb.** Isaiah 9:4 and 10:26 and Psalm 83:11 look back to this night as the model of God breaking an oppressor. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Ephraim is angry it wasn't called first. Gideon talks them down with flattery.
- Gideon's 300 cross the Jordan, exhausted, chasing the kings of Midian. Succoth and Penuel refuse to feed them. Gideon promises payback.
- He catches the kings Zebah and Zalmunna, then comes back and punishes Succoth with thorns and destroys Penuel's tower and men. He kills the two kings himself to avenge his brothers.
- Israel offers him a dynasty. He says "Yahweh shall rule over you," then asks for gold earrings and makes an ephod that all Israel worships.
- Forty years of quiet, seventy sons, many wives, a son by a concubine named Abimelech. The minute Gideon dies, Israel goes back to Baal.

## Pay attention to this
- **Gideon the diplomat (8:1–3).** He soothes Ephraim with a farm proverb: your leftovers beat my whole harvest. It works. Compare Jephthah with Ephraim in 12:1–6, where it ends in a massacre. 🔴 for both scenes, 🟡 for the contrast.
- **"Weary yet pursuing" (8:4).** The 300 are spent and still chasing. 🔴
- **Fellow Israelites refuse bread (8:6).** Succoth and Penuel won't bet on Gideon until the kings are caught. They're hedging against Midian coming back. 🔴 for the refusal, 🟡 for the reason.
- **The fight changes shape (8:18–19).** "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother." This is the first time you hear Gideon's brothers died at Tabor. The war against Midian ends as Gideon's family revenge. 🔴
- **His son won't do it (8:20).** Gideon tells his firstborn Jether to kill the kings. The boy is afraid, the way Gideon used to be. 🔴
- **"Yahweh shall rule over you" (8:23).** The right words. Then the very next verse: "Yet Gideon said... give me an earring." 🔴
- **The crown he turned down shows up anyway.** Many wives, seventy sons, gold, purple robes, and a son he names Abimelech, which means "my father is king" (8:30–31). 🔴 for the name's meaning, 🟡 for what Gideon was thinking.
- **The ephod becomes a snare (8:27).** "All Israel played the harlot with it there, so that it became a snare to Gideon and his household." The man who tore down his father's altar sets up a new one. 🔴
- **"As soon as Gideon was dead" (8:33).** Israel serves Baal-berith, "Baal of the covenant." Chapter 9 happens at his temple. 🔴
- **They forget God and Gideon both (8:34–35).** No memory of Yahweh, no kindness to Gideon's family. That sets up the massacre in chapter 9. 🔴

## Read it like 1150 BC, not 2026
- **Thorns as punishment (8:7, 16).** Gideon "will thrash your bodies with the thorns of the wilderness." Dragging or beating captives with thorny branches, maybe under threshing sledges, was a known ANE cruelty. "Taught... a lesson" in 8:16 is literally "made known." Some old manuscripts read "threshed" instead, which fits the threat. 🔴 for the threat, ⬜ for the exact punishment.
- **A youth who could write (8:14).** A young man from Succoth writes down the names of seventy-seven officials. Writing was more widespread than people assume. 🔴
- **Blood vengeance.** Killing the men who killed your brothers was the family's duty in that world, the "avenger of blood" (Numbers 35:19). Gideon's oath "as Yahweh lives" makes it a sacred obligation. 🔴
- **Gold earrings and crescents (8:21, 24–26).** The Ishmaelite raiders wore gold earrings, and their camels wore crescent ornaments. Crescents were moon symbols, and the moon god was big among desert peoples. Gideon collects it all. 🔴 for the ornaments, 🟡 for the moon-god link.
- **Earrings make idols.** In Exodus 32 Aaron collects gold earrings and makes the calf. Same move here: plunder gathered from the people, melted into a sacred object, and Israel worships it. 🔴 for both texts, 🟡 for the echo being deliberate.
- **What an ephod is.** In Exodus 28 the ephod is the high priest's vest, tied to the Urim and Thummim used to get yes-or-no answers from God. A gold ephod in Gideon's town likely worked as his own oracle, a way to ask God without Shiloh. Heiser and others read it as a divination object. 🔴 for Exodus 28, 🟡 for the oracle use.
- **"Rule" vs. "king."** Israel says "rule over us, you and your son and your son's son." They don't use the word king, but they're asking for a dynasty. 🔴
- **Baal of the covenant (8:33).** Shechem had a temple to Baal-berith, "lord of the covenant." Israel's covenant God gets swapped for a Baal with the covenant in his name. 🔴

## My notes
- I came at this chapter while driving, in the middle of a conversation about Paul's thorn. I asked what it meant that Gideon punished people with thorns. We talked through it as ANE captive torture.
- Then I asked about the earrings. Each man gave one gold earring. What's the symbol? The answer went to Exodus 32, where earrings became the golden calf. Foreign wealth turned into an object of worship.
- I asked what an ephod is, and then pushed: if an idol is supposed to have a mouth, how did a garment get counted as an idol? The answer: it doesn't need a face. People put their worship on it anyway, and it became the focal point.
- Where I landed: symbols that point to Christ are fine. Objects treated as having power of their own are idolatry. If I wear a cross necklace as something I can remember Christ by, that's all right. If I wear it thinking the cross itself will protect me, that's crossing the line. Then I asked about a printed Bible. People treat the paper like it's sacred; rip a page out and they call it sacrilege. Is that idolatry? Same line: the power is in what it says, not in the paper and ink.
- My pre-read note's Heiser line: the ephod as a divination object, and the crown offer as a preview of Israel demanding a king in 1 Samuel 8. Unchecked against the books. 🔵
- My reading plan's line on chapters 8–9: Gideon wins the battle and slowly becomes what he defeated, an idol-builder with a harem and a ruthless son.
- **Divine council:** no council scene. The hook is Baal-berith and the ephod as a channel to the unseen world that God didn't authorize.

## What the chapter is doing
- Abimelech, Gideon's son by a concubine from Shechem, pitches himself to his mother's family: one king from your own blood beats seventy of Gideon's sons. They fund him with seventy pieces of silver from Baal-berith's temple.
- He hires thugs and kills his seventy brothers on one stone. Only Jotham, the youngest, hides and lives. Shechem crowns Abimelech king.
- Jotham shouts a fable from Mount Gerizim: the good trees turned down the crown and the bramble took it. If you did this in good faith, enjoy him. If not, may fire come out of each of you and burn the other.
- Three years in, God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem. Gaal leads a revolt, Abimelech crushes it, salts the city and burns a thousand people alive in the temple tower.
- At Thebez he tries the same trick. A woman drops a millstone on his head. He has his armor bearer finish him so nobody can say a woman killed him. God paid them all back, and Jotham's curse came true.

## Pay attention to this
- **Abimelech's name.** "My father is king." The son Gideon named that way grows up to make it true (8:31). 🔴
- **"Bone and flesh" (9:2).** He runs on family, not on God's call. No one cries out to Yahweh, no Spirit comes on him, no enemy is named. He's the first leader in the book who isn't raised up by God at all. 🔴
- **Seventy for seventy (9:4–5).** Seventy pieces of silver from Baal's temple pay for the murder of seventy brothers. One coin per brother. 🔴 for the numbers, 🟡 for the price tag.
- **"On one stone" (9:5, 18).** Said twice. It reads like an execution, or an altar. 🔴 for the phrase, 🟡 for the altar picture.
- **Jotham stands on Gerizim (9:7).** The mountain of blessing (Deuteronomy 27:12) becomes the place a curse is spoken. 🔴
- **The fable (9:8–15).** The olive, the fig and the vine all have real work to do and turn down the throne. The bramble, which gives no fruit and no shade, says yes and offers its "shade." Then it threatens fire that will burn the cedars of Lebanon. 🔴
- **"In truth and integrity" (9:16, 19).** Jotham says it twice. Did you act in good faith toward Gideon's house? If yes, be happy. If no, burn. The rest of the chapter answers him. 🔴
- **God sends the evil spirit (9:23).** Nobody prays. God acts anyway, and the text says why: "so that the violence done to the seventy... might come" back on them (9:24). 🔴
- **The fire comes both ways.** Abimelech burns Shechem's tower with a thousand inside (9:49). Then he walks up to the next tower with fire and gets killed. Just what Jotham said: fire from Abimelech, fire against Abimelech. 🔴
- **"Lest they say... a woman killed him" (9:54).** He dies worrying about his reputation. It didn't work. Joab still remembers it was a woman with a millstone (2 Samuel 11:21). 🔴
- **The narrator's last word (9:56–57).** "Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech." God is barely mentioned in the chapter, but he gets the final say. 🔴

## Read it like 1150 BC, not 2026
- **Shechem was covenant ground.** Joshua renewed the covenant there and set up a stone under the oak by Yahweh's sanctuary (Joshua 24:25–26). Now Abimelech is crowned "by the oak of the pillar" in Shechem (9:6). Same town, same tree maybe, a very different covenant. 🔴 for both texts, 🟡 for the same spot.
- **Baal-berith and El-berith.** Shechem's god is "Baal of the covenant" (9:4) and "El of the covenant" (9:46). Excavations at Shechem found a large fortified temple, often linked to the "tower of Shechem" in this chapter. 🔴 for the names, 🟡 for the match with the ruin.
- **Plant fables were a known genre.** Mesopotamian scribes wrote debates between trees, like the Tamarisk and the Palm. Jotham uses a form his audience would recognize. Its message is pointed: the useful people don't want power and the worthless ones grab it. 🔴 for the genre.
- **"Shade" from a bramble.** In that climate, shade was protection, and the king's "shade" was a royal promise of safety. A bramble's shade is a joke, and thorn bushes in dry country catch fire fast. 🔴
- **A concubine's son.** A concubine was a wife of lower rank, and her children stood lower in the family. Abimelech's mother's family in Shechem gives him the base his father's house never would. 🔴
- **An evil spirit from God.** In the ANE, misfortune was often blamed on hostile spirits. In Mesopotamia the "evil wind" and the seven evil spirits did that work. Israel's version puts even the hostile spirit under Yahweh's control: God sends it, for justice. The same pattern shows up with Saul (1 Samuel 16:14) and Micaiah's lying spirit (1 Kings 22:19–23). 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the comparison.
- **Sowing salt (9:45).** Scattering salt on a destroyed city shows up in Hittite and Assyrian records as a ritual curse, marking a place as dead. 🟡
- **Millstones were women's tools.** Grinding grain was daily women's work. The upper millstone was a hand stone, heavy enough to kill when dropped from a tower. A warrior killed by a woman with a kitchen tool was the worst shame he could imagine. 🔴

## My notes
- My Judges 9 note leans on Wilcock more than any other chapter. His key is two Hebrew words Jotham uses twice, *'emeth* and *tamim*, "truth and integrity" (9:16, 9:19). They're the lens for the whole story.
- Wilcock reads Judges as a downward spiral, not a circle, and chapter 9 is where it bottoms out.
- How the chapter moves, the way I summarized Wilcock: rejected (Abimelech takes the throne by murder, funded by Baal's temple, and every honorable name and place in the scene gets corrupted); recalled (Jotham's fable); abandoned (God sends the spirit and the alliance unravels exactly as Jotham said); maintained by God (the millstone; God barely mentioned, still running everything, letting evil destroy itself).
- Wilcock's point on the fable that I wrote down: it's not that monarchy is bad. It's that *this* king is a disaster.
- And his line I keep: it only takes one tear in the fabric of good faith for everything to unravel. When everyone abandons truth and integrity, God's own truth and integrity get vindicated. The Judge of all the earth does right.
- That Wilcock section reads like it came straight from the commentary, but it's still my summary, not his words. 🟡
- My reading plan: Jotham's parable is the sharpest political satire in the Old Testament, read it twice. And 9:23 is hostile spiritual agency working under God's permission, a pattern that runs through Samuel and Kings.
- From my Jephthah paper: Block reads chapter 11 against this one. Abimelech and Jephthah both sacrifice their own family on the altar of their ambition.
- The gospel thread in my note: Abimelech's head is crushed by a stone, an echo of Genesis 3:15. Jesus wore a crown of thorns, Jotham's bramble, and took the curse instead of bringing it. 🔵
- My pre-read note's Heiser lines: the evil spirit shows Yahweh's authority over spirits (compare 1 Kings 22), Baal-berith is a parody of Israel's covenant, and the bramble king can be read against the divine council. The last one is a stretch I haven't checked. 🔵
- **Divine council:** the hook is 9:23, a spirit sent by God. It's the first time the book shows God using a hostile spirit.

## What the chapter is doing
- God sorts the animal world into clean and unclean: land animals, water creatures, birds, flying insects, and things that swarm on the ground.
- Land animals need both a split hoof and a chewed cud. Water creatures need fins and scales. Birds get a list with no rule. Insects that hop on jointed legs are allowed.
- Touching the carcass of an unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening, and the chapter spells out what to wash and what to break.
- It closes with the reason: "be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45). Israel is to *badal*, to tell the difference, between unclean and clean (11:47).

## Pay attention to this
- **The animals it names on the "no" side are near-misses.** Camel, rock badger and hare chew the cud but have the wrong foot. The pig has the right foot and doesn't chew the cud. The text teaches the rule by showing where it bites. 🔴 for the list, 🟡 for reading it as teaching by borderline cases.
- **Birds get no rule at all (11:13–19).** Just names, and most of them are raptors and carrion-eaters. The unstated pattern is birds that eat blood or dead things. 🔴 for the list, 🟡 for the pattern.
- **The insects break the health theory (11:20–23).** Locusts and grasshoppers are clean. Shrimp are out. 🔴
- **Two different words for "no."** *Tame'* is unclean. *Sheqets* is "detestable," a stronger word used for the water creatures and the swarming things. 🔴
- **"Be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45).** Peter quotes it in 1 Peter 1:16. The chapter's own reason is holiness, not hygiene. 🔴
- **The verb at the end is *badal*, "distinguish" (11:47).** It's the same verb Leviticus 20:25–26 uses for God separating Israel from the peoples. The animal line and the people line are drawn with one word. 🔴
- **Read it with Deuteronomy 14.** Same rules, plus a named list of clean animals and a line (14:21) that tells you what the food laws are really about. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Everybody else ate pork.** Philistine sites at Ekron, Gath and Ashdod have pig bones up to about a quarter of the animal remains. Israelite Beth-shemesh, a few miles away, has almost none. If pork were making people sick in a way anyone could see, the whole coast would have noticed. 🔴
- **The health reading came late.** Trichinosis wasn't identified until 1835, and scholarship has dropped the pig-and-trichinosis explanation. 🔴
- **Josephus had the hygiene argument sitting there and didn't use it.** Writing to Greek-educated readers who would have liked it, he talks about holiness and discipline instead (*Against Apion* 2). In *Antiquities* 3.11.2 he promises to explain the causes of the food laws and never does. 🔴 for what he wrote, 🟡 for reading the silence.
- **Purity is about access to God, not cleanliness.** Every culture around Israel kept lines between sacred and common. "Unclean" in Leviticus means not fit to come near God's presence, which is why it can wash off by evening. 🔴
- **Food marked who you were.** Meat was rare and mostly eaten at sacrifices. Rules about what you eat showed up at every meal, so they worked as a daily badge of belonging. That's why food is the flashpoint later in Acts 10 and Galatians 2. 🔴
- **No council material here.** The chapter is about Israel's table, not the unseen realm. See My notes.

## My notes
- My question going in: "Just saying 'to separate themselves for being holy' isn't good enough. There has to be some underlying reason of why this makes them holy." I wanted to know why an animal is clean or unclean, and why Gentiles aren't under it.
- I came in thinking the health reasons were obvious (pig and trichinosis, blood spoils) and that "you have to assume the ANE people knew this as well." I dropped that. ❌ The reading doesn't fail because it's modern. It fails because it doesn't fit the list: your theory doesn't predict the rabbit, and it can't explain locust in and shrimp out. 🔴
- **My answer to the hooves.** The named unclean animals are near-misses, so the criterion is the point. It trains discernment. Leviticus 10:8–11 backs it: the priest stays sober so he can *badal* and teach. 🟡
- **Douglas, through summaries.** Holiness as wholeness. Creatures that straddle categories are out of order, and the animal list rehearses a people who stay in their category. It doesn't explain the split hoof well. Nobody has fully solved that. ⬜
- **Milgrom, through summaries.** Three rings that restrain appetite against life: which animals, how it dies, what you don't get to keep (blood and *chelev*). The line I keep: he doesn't care about hooves; he cares about what a man becomes when he has to think, every time he eats, about the fact that something died. 🟡 until I read Milgrom himself.
- **Why Gentiles aren't under it.** Sort the food laws by type and they come apart. The clean and unclean list is a boundary marker, and it lifts (Acts 10, Mark 7:19, Ephesians 2:14). Blood stays (Acts 15), because it was given to Noah, to everybody, before Sinai. 🔴
- **The word "diet."** I thought "diet" came from a word for lifestyle. It does: Greek *diaita*, "way of life." That became the post "How You Know Someone's Jewish." The deeper root sense of separating or selecting is a speculative stretch, so I don't build on it. 🔵

## What the chapter is doing
- It opens "after the death of the two sons of Aaron" (16:1). Nadab and Abihu died coming near God the wrong way, so this chapter is the right way.
- Once a year the high priest goes behind the veil into the holy place, in plain linen, with incense and blood: a bull for himself and his house, a goat for the people.
- Two goats are chosen by lot. One is killed as a sin offering. The other is kept alive, Aaron lays both hands on its head, confesses all Israel's sins over it, and a man leads it into the wilderness.
- The blood cleanses the holy place, the tent and the altar from Israel's uncleanness, and the day becomes a permanent sabbath of rest, the tenth day of the seventh month, when the people humble their souls (16:29–31).

## Pay attention to this
- **Two lots, two names (16:8).** One lot is "for Yahweh," the other is "for Azazel." LSB prints "for the scapegoat" and the Hebrew name is *Azazel*. It shows up four times, all in this chapter (16:8, 10 twice, 26). 🔴
- **The parallel argues for a name.** "For Yahweh" is a person. Read the other lot the same way and Azazel is a name too, not a place or an action. 🟡
- **Two hands and a confession (16:21).** Everywhere else in Leviticus the offerer lays one hand on his animal. Here Aaron lays both hands on the live goat and says the sins out loud over it. This is the one place in the Torah where sin is clearly put onto an animal. 🔴
- **The goat that carries the sin is never sacrificed.** It isn't killed, its blood isn't used, it never touches the altar. It's sent away. The goat that dies and the goat that carries are two different goats. 🔴
- **The blood cleans the building, not the person.** It goes on the mercy seat, the tent and the altar (16:14–19). Israel's uncleanness has soaked into God's house, and the day wipes it clean so he can keep living there. 🔴
- **The man who leads the goat out has to wash before he comes back (16:26).** He has been near the thing that carries the sin. 🔴
- **Hebrews 9 is built on this chapter.** The high priest who goes in once a year with blood is the picture Hebrews uses for Jesus. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Sending evil away was a known kind of ritual.** Hittite and North Syrian rites loaded trouble onto an animal and drove it out of the community. The scapegoat belongs to that family, and it's a different thing from altar sacrifice. DDD judges this Anatolian background the most likely one for Azazel. 🔴 for the parallels, 🟡 for DDD's call.
- **"Atone" here means purge.** The Hebrew *kipper* matches the Akkadian *kuppuru*, "wipe clean." In the Babylonian New Year festival a shrine was wiped with a ram's carcass, and then the carcass and the men who handled it were put out of the city. Leviticus 16 has the same shape: the holy place is cleaned and the handlers wash outside. 🔴
- **The wilderness wasn't empty.** In that world the desert was the place outside God's ordered land, where chaos and unclean things lived. Sending the goat "to Azazel" sends the sin into territory under Azazel's rule, outside the land held holy for Yahweh. The goat is not an offering to Azazel. 🟡
- **Divine council: Azazel.** Read as a name, Azazel is a being, and later Jewish writers took it that way. In 1 Enoch (8:1; 10:4–8) Azazel is a leader of the fallen Watchers, bound in the desert, and in the Apocalypse of Abraham he's the unclean bird and the serpent. Heiser (*Demons*, 90–91) reads Azazel as a being and the goat as sent off to his ground, not offered to him. 🔴 for what the later texts say, ⬜ for what Azazel meant in Leviticus.
- **"Scapegoat" is an English invention.** William Tyndale coined it in 1530, reading the word as "the goat that goes away." The Greek, Aquila, Symmachus, the Vulgate and Luther all read it as what the goat does, not who it goes to. 🔴

## My notes
- **Azazel, from the Fact Book work.** Four uses in three verses, all in this ritual. The paired lots make the place reading hard to hold, so I read it as a personal name. DDD lays out three models: a desert demon, an Egyptian root, and Anatolian elimination rites. DDD picks the third. 🟡 for the name reading.
- **I had the hands backwards once.** In the Leviticus 24 study I first read the blasphemer as a scapegoat, because the witnesses put their hands on his head. The sources showed the opposite. Here the guilt moves off the people onto the goat and away. In Leviticus 24 the hands are testimony and the guilt lands back on the offender. Same gesture, opposite direction. ❌ for my first read.
- **Barabbas as an inverted scapegoat.** Barabbas means "son of the father." He is released and Jesus dies. In the ritual the released goat goes away from the people. Barabbas is released to the crowd, so he comes back toward them. That's Lunn's argued literary reading. 🔴 for the ritual, 🟡 for the claim that the Gospels meant the allusion.
- I've only worked the two goats. The rest of the chapter I haven't studied.

## What the chapter is doing
- The first nine verses are tent business: clear olive oil for the lamp that burns all night, and twelve loaves set out before Yahweh every sabbath.
- Then a story. A man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father fights another man in the camp and "blasphemed the Name and cursed" (24:11).
- Nobody knows what to do with him, so they hold him until Yahweh rules. The ruling: everyone who heard him lays hands on his head, and the whole congregation stones him outside the camp.
- Right after the ruling come the laws on taking a life and on injury, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth," with one standard for the sojourner and the native (24:17–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **Two verbs, two penalties (24:15–16).** Whoever *qalal*s (curses, makes light of) his God "will bear his sin." Whoever *naqav*s the name of Yahweh is put to death. Cursing God is not the death-penalty crime here. *Naqav* is something more. 🔴
- **What *naqav* means.** The base sense is to bore or drill a hole. It then comes to mean designate or name (Numbers 1:17; Isaiah 62:2), then designate as bad, then blaspheme. Arabic, Aramaic and Akkadian cousins back up the drilling sense. 🔴
- **"The Name."** The text says the man blasphemed "the Name," with no other word. The holy name has become a thing in itself. 🔴
- **His mother is named (24:11).** Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, of Dan. His father is only "an Egyptian." 🔴
- **They wait for God (24:12).** Nobody had faced this case before: does a half-Egyptian man fall under the covenant's law? 🔴
- **The answer is one law for everyone in the camp (24:16, 22).** "The sojourner as well as the native." Accountability goes by where you stand, not by your blood. 🔴
- **The name sits next to murder.** The blasphemy ruling runs straight into "if a man strikes down the life of any human being, he shall surely be put to death" (24:17). Both carry the same penalty. 🔴 for the placement, 🟡 for reading it as deliberate.
- **"Eye for eye" limits revenge.** The punishment can't go past the injury. 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **The priests guard the tent. Israel guards the Name.** The ordinary Israelite never goes inside the tabernacle. What he carries is God's name. Dishonoring it is for the people what Nadab and Abihu's strange fire was for the priests (Leviticus 10). 🟡
- **The book is built in a ring.** Mary Douglas read Leviticus as a ring that folds back on itself, and Milgrom agreed. In that ring the blasphemer story faces the Nadab and Abihu story across the book: one warning for priests, one for the whole people. 🔴 for the ring proposal, 🟡 for the pairing.
- **Hands on the head is testimony here.** The witnesses lay hands on him to say "I heard it, it was this man." Jewish tradition kept the words: "your blood is on your own head." The responsibility lands on him, not on the community. 🟡
- **Capital crimes in Israel were about the covenant.** Israel had no death penalty for property crimes, unlike its neighbors. The death penalties cluster around what threatens the covenant: idolatry, blasphemy, the Sabbath. Blasphemy is treason against the King. 🔴
- **Lex talionis was common ANE law.** Hammurabi and Eshnunna have versions. In Israel it is grounded in God's covenant and applies to everyone the same, sojourner and native. 🔴
- **Why nobody says the Name.** The Greek translation renders *naqav* as "named," and the Mishnah says a blasphemer isn't guilty until he pronounces the Name as it is spelled. This verse is the root of the Jewish practice of not saying God's name out loud. 🔴
- **No divine council scene.** The holy thing in this chapter is the Name. See My notes.

## My notes
- This came out of my study for the post on blasphemy of the Holy Spirit. I wanted to know what blasphemy actually was before I touched Mark 3.
- **Three readings of *naqav*, and I'm not picking one.** (1) He said the Name out loud. That's the Greek translation and the Mishnah. (2) He dragged the Name down, made the heavy thing light, which matches *qalal*. (3) Kamionkowski: his words broke through into God's own sphere, holiness moved from the tent to the Name. The third one surprised me most. 🟡 on her, one scholar in a serious commentary. My call in the chat: "we should not resolve this, but go in all the directions that it goes. That's the best we can do."
- **Why it won't resolve.** Gilbrant notes the Israelites were so afraid of blasphemy they wouldn't write down what he said. The record has a hole exactly where the crime was. That isn't a gap in the evidence. It is the evidence.
- **The part where I had to correct myself.** I first read the hands on his head as a scapegoat move, sin going onto him and out of the camp like Leviticus 16. That's backwards. ❌ On the Day of Atonement the guilt goes off the people onto the goat. Here the hands are testimony and the guilt lands back on him. Same gesture, opposite direction. The backwards version was more poetic, and that's not a reason.
- **Placement next to murder (Kruschwitz).** The penalties run on proportion, and boring the Name lands where murder lands because both wreck something that can't be replaced. 🟡
- **Half-Egyptian.** This is a story about who is inside the covenant and who is accountable. That's where it connects to Mark 3, where Jesus stands in the middle of another argument about who is inside. Mackie's life-source reading of "unforgivable" in Mark 3 is 🟡.

## META: the book of Luke
- **Where it sits.** The third gospel and the first half of a two-part work. Acts is volume two, written to the same man (Acts 1:1). Luke and Acts together are the longest single work in the New Testament, more words than all of Paul's letters. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** who is this man, and can you trust what you were taught about him? Luke says it out loud in 1:4: "so that you may know the certainty about the things you have been taught." 🔴
- **Who wrote it.** Luke, the doctor who traveled with Paul. The book never names him, but the early church does, and with one voice: Irenaeus, the Muratorian Canon, the anti-Marcionite prologue. The "we" passages in Acts (16, 20–21, 27–28) put the writer on the road with Paul. 🔴 for the tradition; 🟡 for reading the "we" passages as Luke himself.
- **Probably not Jewish.** In Colossians 4:10–14 Paul lists the coworkers who are "of the circumcision" and then names Luke separately. Add the polished Greek of 1:1–4 and the way he explains Jewish customs like an outsider. That makes Luke likely the only Gentile writer in the New Testament. 🟡
- **Who it's for.** Theophilus, "God-friend." Luke calls him "most excellent" (*kratistos*), the same title Acts uses for the Roman governors Felix (23:26, 24:3) and Festus (26:25). Best read: a real Roman of standing who has already been taught the faith and needs solid ground under it. 🟡 The name also lets every "friend of God" who reads the scroll hear it as addressed to them. 🔵
- **When.** Two camps. Early, around AD 60–64: Acts ends with Paul alive under house arrest in Rome, no trial, no execution, no fall of Jerusalem. Later, around AD 80–85: often argued from Luke 21 knowing about AD 70, which tends to assume Jesus couldn't predict the temple's fall. I lean early. ⬜
- **The world it was written in.** Jesus ministers under Tiberius; Luke likely writes under Nero. Rome keeps the peace with legions and taxes. Herod the Great is dead (4 BC), his sons split the country, Antipas runs Galilee, Pilate governs Judea (AD 26–36). Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots, Samaritans and God-fearing Gentiles all show up in the story. 🔴
- **Text issues.** A few, and they're known. Luke 22:43–44 (the angel and the sweat like blood) is missing from some early copies, so many Bibles bracket it. A handful of Old Latin copies give the Magnificat (1:46) to Elizabeth instead of Mary. The "Western" text of Luke-Acts (Codex Bezae) runs longer and freer than the main line, mostly in Acts. None of it touches a core claim. 🔴
- **Three movements:**
  - Galilee and Judea, chs. 1–9.
  - The long walk to Jerusalem, 9:51–19:27. More than a third of the book. "He set his face to go to Jerusalem" (9:51) is the hinge.
  - Jerusalem and the temple, 19:28–24:53.
- **The shape: temple to nations.** Luke opens with one priest alone in the temple, unable to give the blessing (1:5–23). It closes with the disciples in the temple praising God after Jesus blesses them (24:50–53). Acts opens in the temple and ends in Rome. 🔴
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - Outsiders brought in: women, Samaritans, the poor, tax collectors, Gentiles.
  - Prayer at every threshold: baptism (3:21), before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), the Transfiguration (9:28–29), Gethsemane, the cross.
  - The Holy Spirit, more than Matthew and Mark combined, setting up Acts.
  - Joy, from "great joy for all the people" (2:10) to "great joy" in the temple (24:52).
  - A doctor's eye on bodies: high fever (4:38), full of leprosy (5:12), the bent woman (13:11), dropsy (14:2), sweat like blood (22:44).
  - The "wrong" Messiah: right title, wrong dictionary, from Nazareth to Emmaus.
  - The powers: the wilderness offer of the kingdoms (4:5–6), Legion and the abyss (8:31), "I was watching Satan fall" (10:18), "this hour and the power of darkness" (22:53).

## What the chapter is doing
- Luke opens like a Greek historian (1:1–4): others have written, he checked with eyewitnesses, he's putting it in order so Theophilus can stand on it.
- Then he switches voice to sound like the Old Testament and tells two birth announcements side by side. An old priest in the Holy Place hears he'll have a son, doubts, and goes mute. A young girl in Nazareth hears she'll bear the King, asks how, and says yes.
- Mary goes to Elizabeth. John leaps in the womb, Elizabeth prophesies, and Mary sings the Magnificat: God brings down rulers and lifts the humble.
- John is born and named. Zechariah writes "His name is John," gets his voice back, and prophesies the Benedictus: God has visited his people.
- Wright reads the chapter as an overture. Israel's long barrenness and silence are ending, and the Davidic King is announced. 🔴 for Wright's reading.

## Pay attention to this
- **Two registers of Greek.** Verses 1–4 are the most polished Greek in the New Testament, a historian's preface. From verse 5 on it sounds like the Greek Old Testament. Luke is earning trust with a Roman reader, then planting him inside Israel's story. 🔴
- **"Eyewitnesses" (1:2).** *Autoptai*, "self-seers," same root as autopsy. Luke is making a sourcing claim, not telling a pretty story. 🔴
- **"Certainty" (1:4).** *Asphaleia* means firm footing, ground that won't slip. Wright translates it "reliability." Theophilus doesn't need to feel sure. He needs the ground to hold. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for Wright's slant.
- **"Taught" (1:4).** *Katecheo*, where we get catechism. Theophilus is already instructed. This is a book for someone inside the faith, not a tract for an outsider. 🟡
- **Dated to the king (1:5).** "In the days of Herod." Luke keeps doing this (2:1–2, 3:1–2) so a reader can check him. 🔴
- **Righteous and barren (1:6–7).** Both things are true at once. Barren here isn't punishment. It's the setup Scripture always uses before God sends someone: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Manoah's wife, Hannah. 🔴
- **Chosen by lot (1:9).** Thousands of priests in 24 divisions. Burning incense in the Holy Place came by lot, and later rabbinic tradition says a man could do it only once. This is the high point of Zechariah's life. 🔴 for the lot; 🟡 for the once-in-a-lifetime rule, which comes from later rabbinic sources.
- **"To the right of the altar" (1:11).** The right side is the side of honor and power (Exodus 15:6; Psalm 110:1; Genesis 48). The staging tells you this is a formal announcement from the throne. 🟡
- **"Do not be afraid" (1:13, 1:30, then 2:10).** Three visits, three times the first word is "fear not." Real angels are terrifying. 🔴
- **"Your prayer has been heard" (1:13).** His private prayer for a son, the people's prayer outside, and the prayer for Israel's redemption he is offering with the incense all get one answer. 🟡
- **Three names in a row.** Zechariah ("Yahweh remembers"), Elizabeth ("my God is an oath"), John ("Yahweh is gracious"). Read together: Yahweh remembers his oath, and Yahweh is gracious. 🔴 for the meanings; 🟡 for reading them as a sentence.
- **Malachi picks back up (1:17).** The Old Testament ends with the promise of Elijah turning "the hearts of the fathers back to the children" (Malachi 4:5–6). Gabriel's words to Zechariah quote that line. God picks up the sentence where he stopped. 🔴
- **Same question, different answer.** Zechariah asks "How will I know this?" (1:18) and goes mute. Mary asks "How will this be?" (1:34) and gets an answer. The difference is posture: he wants proof against the word, she wants to understand inside trust. 🟡
- **Temple, then Nazareth.** The first announcement is to a priest in the holiest room in Jerusalem. The second is to a village girl in a town the Old Testament never names. God's action is moving. 🔴
- **"Favored one" (1:28).** *Kecharitomene*, graced by God's choosing. The Latin "full of grace" grew into a lot of Marian teaching the Greek doesn't carry. 🟡
- **Five promises in two verses (1:32–33).** "Great," "Son of the Most High," "the throne of His father David" (2 Samuel 7), reigning over the house of Jacob (Isaiah 9), "no end of His kingdom" (Daniel 7). 🔴
- **"Overshadow" (1:35).** *Episkiazo* is the Greek Old Testament's word for the glory cloud settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). It comes back at the Transfiguration (9:34). Mary is being treated like the tabernacle. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for the tabernacle read.
- **"May it be done to me according to your word" (1:38).** She says yes before she sees how it ends. Wright calls her the first real disciple in the gospel. 🟡
- **"The mother of my Lord" (1:43).** *Kyrios*, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Yahweh. Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, calls an unborn child Lord. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for how much weight it carries here.
- **The Magnificat sounds like Hannah (1:46–55; 1 Samuel 2:1–10).** Proud scattered, rulers off thrones, hungry filled, rich sent away. Past tense for things that haven't happened yet: what God has promised is as good as done. 🔴
- **The Spirit fills four people.** John in the womb (1:15), Mary is overshadowed (1:35), Elizabeth (1:41), Zechariah (1:67). Luke is setting up Acts. 🔴
- **"His name is John" (1:63).** His mouth opens the moment he obeys. His first words after nine months of silence are praise. 🔴

## Read it like AD 60, not 2026
- **Gabriel isn't a greeting-card angel.** He's named in only one other book, Daniel (8:16, 9:21), both times explaining the timetable of Israel's future and the coming anointed one. Here he says he "stands before God" (1:19), which is throne-room language. Heiser counts him a named member of the loyal divine council. A Jewish reader hears Daniel's clock running out. 🔴 for Daniel; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Angels are a job, the host is an army.** *Mal'ak* and *angelos* both mean messenger, a function, not a species. The wider population is the heavenly host, the sons of God, the council, and "Yahweh of hosts" means Yahweh of armies. When Zechariah is "troubled" and "fear fell upon him" (1:12), that's the right response, not a misunderstanding. 🔴
- **"Most High" (1:32, 1:35, 1:76).** *Hypsistos* is the Greek Old Testament's word for *Elyon*, the title of the God who "divided the nations" and kept Israel as his portion (Deuteronomy 32:8–9, read with the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek). It names God as high over every other spiritual power. Gentile God-fearers used the title too, so it works for both of Luke's audiences. 🟡
- **The "mighty" off their thrones (1:52).** Mary is talking about Herod and Caesar. Wright and Heiser both hear more: the arrival of the King unseats the powers above them too, not only the men in palaces. 🟡
- **No glory in the second temple.** Solomon's temple was filled with the cloud (1 Kings 8). Ezekiel watched the glory leave (Ezekiel 10–11) and saw it come back only in a vision (Ezekiel 43). The second temple had priests, sacrifice and Herod's gold, and no recorded return of the cloud. Wright: Israel was a barren temple in a barren land. Then an angel shows up in the smoke. 🟡
- **Barren meant shamed.** In a village culture a childless wife was publicly disgraced, and people read it as God's disfavor. Elizabeth's "my disgrace among men" (1:25) uses *oneidos*, a hard shame word. Bailey reads her five months of seclusion against that background. 🔴 for the culture; 🟡 for Bailey's read of the seclusion.
- **A mute priest is a public scene.** The crowd outside was waiting for the priest to come out and give the blessing of Numbers 6. Zechariah comes out and can only make signs (1:22). Bailey: in an honor culture that is a public humiliation, and it lasts nine months. 🟡
- **The people praying outside (1:10).** The incense hour went with the daily *tamid* sacrifice. The smoke rising was the picture of Israel's prayers going up before God (Psalm 141:2). 🔴
- **Nobody had heard of Nazareth.** It isn't named in the Old Testament, Josephus or the Talmud. "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46) is how it sounded. 🔴
- **Betrothed is married.** Mary is probably in her early teens. Betrothal was a legal marriage before the couple lived together; ending it took a divorce. That's why a pregnancy here is dangerous for her. 🔴 for the law; 🟡 for her age.
- **"Good news" was Caesar's word.** *Euangelizomai* (1:19) was imperial language for a ruler's birthday, victory or accession. Gabriel uses it about a priest's son and a peasant's son. 🔴
- **Theophilus paid for this.** A copy of Luke on papyrus ran to hundreds of denarii, and Luke plus Acts was near a year of a laborer's wages. No ordinary believer owned one. The church owned it and read it out loud, and a rich patron made that possible. 🟡 for the cost estimate.
- **Four hundred years of quiet.** No prophet since Malachi. People were waiting on Daniel's seventy weeks, Isaiah's return from exile, Malachi's Elijah. The air was thick with it (1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Qumran scrolls). 🔴

## My notes
- I first assumed Luke was Jewish, because he explains Jewish customs so much and he ran with Paul. I had that backwards. ❌ He explains the customs because he's an outsider writing for outsiders. That's also why I'd start a new believer in Luke, not John. Luke gives you the historical ground first; John goes deeper once you have it.
- I put the date around AD 50 at first. I still think early is right, because Paul's death would have been the natural ending for Acts and Luke doesn't write it. The working date we landed on is around AD 60. 🟡
- **The prologue.** Luke is saying he's not the first to write this. There were accounts, rumors and other writings going around, and Mark is the one I'd bet he means. He's done his work: gone to the eyewitnesses, not just collected rumors.
- **Theophilus isn't so different from a believer now.** A believer in AD 60 could die for it. In 2026 America you lose standing, get dismissed, get taken less seriously. Death is worse, but a test that grinds every day is still a test. The form of the test changed; the test didn't get easier.
- **Right hand and Psalm 110.** The right side is the side of honor. Christ seated at God's right hand "until I make your enemies a footstool": those enemies aren't Herod or Pharaoh or Hitler. They are the rebel divine beings, the lesser gods who pulled the nations away and kept the worship for themselves (Psalm 82; Deuteronomy 32:8–9; 1 Corinthians 15:25–26; Ephesians 1:20–21). 🔴
- **Fear.** When these beings show up there's a tangible essence of God dripping off them. That's why the first thing out of every angel's mouth is "do not be afraid."
- **"Your prayer has been heard."** It should almost read "prayers." Zechariah prayed for a son, and the priest in the temple was praying for Israel's redemption. God isn't sending Gabriel just to grant an old man a son. One answer covers both.
- **John's name.** I didn't know why God named him John. If it means "Yahweh is gracious," then God is saying grace is coming to the nation. That was my guess, and the name lists back it up.
- **Divine council in this chapter:** Gabriel, "Most High," the mighty off their thrones, and Psalm 110 behind the right-hand staging. The big council scenes come later: the wilderness (4:1–13), Legion (8:26–39), the Transfiguration (9:28–36), Satan falling (10:18), and "the power of darkness" (22:53).

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus sends out seventy (some manuscripts say seventy-two) in pairs ahead of him, with nothing in their hands, to say "The kingdom of God has come near to you" (10:1–16).
- They come back thrilled that "even the demons are subject to us." Jesus says, "I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning," and tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven (10:17–24).
- A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, then asks "who is my neighbor?" Jesus answers with the Good Samaritan and turns the question around: which one "proved to be a neighbor"? (10:25–37).
- Martha works the kitchen while Mary sits at Jesus's feet listening, and Jesus says Mary chose the good part (10:38–42).

## Pay attention to this
- **Seventy, not twelve (10:1).** Twelve matched the tribes of Israel. Seventy is a different number, and it points past Israel. 🔴 for the numbers; 🟡 for what they mean (see below).
- **Same instructions as the Twelve (10:4–7).** No money belt, no bag, eat what they give you. They go in need, as guests. 🔴
- **"Even the demons" (10:17).** The seventy didn't expect it. Jesus's answer is bigger than their report: Satan falling. 🔴
- **"Do not rejoice in this" (10:20).** Power over spirits isn't the thing to celebrate. Having your name written in heaven is. 🔴
- **"All things have been handed over to Me" (10:22).** In the wilderness the devil said the kingdoms "have been handed over to me" (4:6). Same verb. Now Jesus says the Father handed all things to him. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for reading it as the answer to 4:6.
- **The lawyer's question is backwards (10:25).** "What shall I do to inherit?" Nobody earns an inheritance. It comes to you because of whose family you're in. 🟡 (Bailey)
- **"Wishing to justify himself" (10:29).** He wants a boundary: tell me who counts so I know who doesn't. 🔴
- **The question changes (10:29, 10:36).** He asks "who is my neighbor?" Jesus asks "which of these three proved to be a neighbor?" Neighbor is something you become, not a list you sort people into. The lawyer's own question never gets answered. 🔴
- **Down from Jerusalem (10:30–31).** The priest is going down, away from the temple. His duty is done. 🔴 for the direction; 🟡 that it weakens his excuse.
- **The lawyer won't say "Samaritan" (10:37).** He answers "the one who showed mercy." 🔴
- **An inn, not a guest room (10:34).** Luke uses *pandocheion* here, a commercial inn. In 2:7 he used *katalyma*, a guest room. Same writer, both words, on purpose. 🔴
- **Mary sits at his feet (10:39).** That is where a student sits with a rabbi (Acts 22:3, Paul "at the feet of Gamaliel"). A woman taking a disciple's seat. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Seventy is the number of the nations.** Genesis 10, the table of nations right before Babel, lists seventy nations in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. The manuscripts of Luke 10:1 split the same way, seventy and seventy-two. Either way the number belongs to the nations of the world. 🔴 for Genesis 10 and the manuscript split; 🟡 that Luke means it.
- **The Deuteronomy 32 map.** After Babel, the Most High "separated the sons of man" and divided the nations by number (Deut 32:8). The Dead Sea Scroll reads "according to the number of the sons of God," and the Greek reads "angels of God." The nations went to lesser gods; Israel stayed Yahweh's portion (32:9). Those gods went bad (Psalm 82), and the psalm ends asking God to inherit all the nations (82:8). Sending seventy is Jesus starting to take that map back. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the read on 10:1.
- **Satan falls (10:18).** Heiser reads this as a legal turning point, not a picture of Satan's original fall before creation. The satan was the accuser in God's court (Job 1–2; Zech 3:1–2). When the kingdom arrives and the demons give way to Jesus's name, the accuser loses his claim. Revelation 12:9–10 tells the same story: the accuser "has been thrown down." 🔴 for the accuser texts; 🟡 for Heiser's legal reading.
- **Lightning and the fallen shining one.** Isaiah 14:12 mocks a king of Babylon who wanted to climb above the stars of God and was "fallen from heaven." The rebel-against-the-council picture behind that taunt is the same one Jesus uses. Luke does not use the name Lucifer, and Isaiah's word is a description, not a name. 🔴
- **Serpents and scorpions (10:19).** Psalm 91:13 promises the faithful will tread on the lion and the serpent, and Genesis 3:15 promises the serpent's head will be crushed. Snakes and scorpions stood for the powers of evil. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the link.
- **Names written in heaven (10:20).** The book God keeps: Exodus 32:32–33, Daniel 12:1. 🔴
- **Capernaum "brought down to Hades" (10:15).** Jesus borrows Isaiah 14's taunt against the proud king (14:13–15) and points it at his own home base. 🔴
- **Tyre and Sidon (10:13–14).** Gentile cities the prophets condemned (Isa 23; Ezek 28). Ezekiel 28's king of Tyre is pictured as a guardian cherub thrown off God's mountain. Jesus says those cities would have repented faster than Galilee. 🔴
- **The Jericho road.** It drops about 3,300 feet in roughly seventeen miles of rough desert, and robbers worked it. 🔴
- **The priest's dilemma.** Touching a corpse made a man unclean for seven days (Num 19:11). A stripped, unconscious man has no clothes and no accent, so nobody can tell if he's a fellow Jew or alive at all. Bailey thinks the priest's fear was real. Others (Levine, Snodgrass, Blomberg) doubt purity was the issue going down from Jerusalem. 🔴 for the law; ⬜ for what the priest was thinking.
- **Samaritans.** Descendants of the northern tribes mixed with Assyrian settlers. They had their own Pentateuch, their own mountain (Gerizim), and a temple a Jewish king (John Hyrcanus) had destroyed about 128 BC. Jews and Samaritans hated each other. A good Samaritan was a contradiction to the first audience. 🔴
- **Oil and wine.** Ordinary first aid, and also the language of temple offerings. Bailey hears Hosea 6:6, "I delight in mercy and not sacrifice," under the story, with the Samaritan doing what the priest and Levite were supposed to stand for. 🔴 for the first aid; 🟡 for Hosea.
- **2 Chronicles 28:8–15.** Men of Samaria free captives from Judah, clothe them, give them food and drink, anoint them, put the weak on donkeys, and bring them to Jericho. The story may already be in the Bible. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 that Jesus is drawing on it.
- **Two denarii (10:35).** About two days' wages. An inn could hold a man who couldn't pay his bill, so without the money and the promise the rescue fails. 🟡 (Bailey)
- **Lev 19 reads both ways.** "Love your neighbor" (Lev 19:18) is about "the sons of your people." Sixteen verses later the same chapter says love the stranger as yourself (19:34). The lawyer wants to stop at verse 18. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 (Bailey) for the point.

## My notes
- **The post frame (post 9):** the lawyer's question is never answered. Bailey and Wright both see it.
- How I want it told: more along the lines of the story itself. A man is walking, he gets beaten, and he's unconscious. Start there, not with the theology.
- What I taught my mentee from Bailey: the man is stripped and unconscious, so his ethnicity is erased and he's just a human being. The priest is going away from temple duty, probably riding, with the means to help. The Samaritan takes a real risk bringing a wounded Jew into a Jericho inn. 🟡
- Bailey's seven scenes: the Samaritan undoes the robbers, the priest and the Levite in reverse order. The robbers took, he pays. The priest didn't carry him, he carries him. The Levite didn't bind the wounds, he binds them. 🟡
- **Two readings of "justify himself."** Bailey: earn acceptance. Wright: draw the boundary of the covenant people. I keep both.
- **Corrections from the third pass.** I dropped a "synagogue curse" line because it rested on late sources used wrong. ❌ I present the priest's purity problem as Bailey's reading against Levine, Snodgrass and Blomberg, not as settled. I added 2 Chronicles 28 next to Hosea 6 as a source text.

What I have comes from working Heiser on Revelation 12: Luke 10:18 is the accuser being disbarred, and if you belong to Christ's kingdom, Satan has no claim on you. He can bring accusations, but he has no ownership. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray. He gives Luke's short form of the Lord's Prayer, then the parable of the friend at midnight and the ask, seek, knock poem: if you give good things to your children, how much more will the Father give the Holy Spirit (11:1–13).
- Jesus casts out a mute demon, and some say he does it by Beelzebul. He answers that a kingdom divided can't stand, that he does it "by the finger of God," and that a stronger man has come to plunder the strong man's house (11:14–23).
- He warns about an unclean spirit that leaves, finds the house swept and empty, and comes back with seven worse (11:24–26). Then "this generation" gets only the sign of Jonah (11:29–32).
- At a Pharisee's dinner Jesus skips the hand-washing and pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers. They start plotting to trap him (11:37–54).

## Pay attention to this
- **He was praying first (11:1).** The disciples ask for the prayer after watching him pray. Luke keeps showing Jesus praying at the big moments. 🔴
- **"Father" (11:2).** Luke's version opens with the single word. No "our," no "in heaven." 🔴
- **"Which of you" (11:5).** The opening expects the answer "no one." Nobody in that village could picture a neighbor refusing bread for a guest. 🟡 (Bailey, Snodgrass)
- **He calls, he doesn't knock.** The man asks once. There is no knocking and no repeating in the parable itself. The knocking is in the poem that follows (11:9–10). 🔴
- **The LSB says "persistence" (11:8).** The Greek word is *anaideia*, which means shamelessness. Whose shame and what kind is the whole fight over this parable (see below). 🔴 for the word; ⬜ for whose it is.
- **The Holy Spirit (11:13).** Matthew has "good things." Luke has "the Holy Spirit." The best gift is the Spirit. 🔴
- **Satan has a kingdom (11:18).** Jesus doesn't deny it. He argues that it can't be fighting itself. 🔴
- **"The finger of God" (11:20).** Pharaoh's magicians said it when they couldn't copy the third plague: "This is the finger of God" (Exod 8:19). Matthew has "Spirit of God." 🔴
- **The stronger one (11:21–22).** The strong man guards his house until someone stronger takes his armor and splits the plunder. Jesus is the stronger one, and the exorcisms are the plunder being carried out. 🔴 for the saying; 🟡 for the identification.
- **The swept, empty house (11:24–26).** A cleaned-out house with nobody living in it is worse off than before. 🔴
- **"Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it" (11:28).** Same move as 8:21. Hearing and doing beats family ties, even his mother's. 🔴
- **Gentiles as witnesses (11:31–32).** The Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh, both foreigners, will stand up at the judgment against "this generation." 🔴
- **Abel to Zechariah (11:51).** The first murder in Genesis to the last one in the Hebrew Bible's order, which ends with Chronicles (2 Chr 24:20–22). A to Z of the prophets' blood. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **The guest belongs to the village.** In Bailey's Middle East, a traveler is told "you have honored our village," not "you have honored me." The sleeping neighbor is being asked to do his own duty, not a favor. 🟡 (Bailey)
- **Bread is the fork and spoon.** You tear bread and dip it in the common dish. A host who asks for bread is also gathering the rest of the meal, which is why the story ends with "as much as he needs." 🟡 (Bailey)
- **One room, one bed (11:7).** A peasant family slept together on a mat in one room, often with the animals brought in at night. Getting up meant waking everyone. 🔴 for the house; 🟡 for the detail.
- **Shameless.** *Anaideia* is negative in every ancient Greek use anyone has found (Snodgrass counts 258 to the end of the fourth century). Bailey reads it as the sleeper avoiding shame: he gets up so the village won't call him stingy. Snodgrass reads it as the borrower's rude nerve. Wright and most English Bibles keep "persistence." Bailey and Snodgrass agree there is no persistence in the story. 🔴 for the word's meaning; ⬜ for whose shamelessness.
- **Look-alike gifts (11:11–12).** A snake for a fish, a scorpion for an egg: each bad gift looks like the good one. Bailey thinks the "snake" is the Galilee catfish called the barbut, which crawls on land and was unclean. 🔵
- **Beelzebul.** "Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron" was the Philistine god a king of Israel consulted instead of Yahweh (2 Kgs 1:2–3). "Beelzebul" probably means "Baal the prince." By Jesus's day it was a name for the ruler of demons. Calling Jesus his agent is calling him a servant of the enemy god. 🔴 for 2 Kings; 🟡 for the meaning of the name.
- **Other exorcists (11:19).** "By whom do your sons cast them out?" Jewish exorcists were real. Tobit drives a demon off with fish smoke, and Josephus describes an Eleazar who drew a demon out with a ring and Solomon's incantations. Jesus uses a word. 🔴
- **The finger of God.** Egypt's magicians knew their limit when they saw it (Exod 8:19). Wright hears a new Exodus: the same God is now fighting the real Pharaoh behind the scenes. 🔴 for Exodus; 🟡 for the reading.
- **The strong man.** Isaiah 49:24–25: "Can the prey be taken from the mighty man?" and God answers that the captives of the mighty will be taken. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 that Jesus is drawing on it.
- **Divine council frame.** Jesus treats Satan as the head of a real kingdom with a household and armor. The exorcisms are not stunts. They are territory changing hands. Wright: the battle was not with Rome but with the accuser, the satan. 🔴 for the sayings; 🟡 for the frame.
- **Waterless places (11:24).** Deserts were where evil spirits lived (Isa 13:21; 34:14; the goat sent "to Azazel" in the wilderness, Lev 16:8–10). 🔴
- **The empty house is Israel.** Wright reads the house as Israel and its temple, swept by reform movements and left empty. The best candidate is the Maccabees, who literally cleansed the temple, carried out the defiled stones and relit the lamps (1 Macc 4:36–50). Without God living there again, the house is open to worse. Compare "your house is left to you desolate" (13:35). 🔴 for 1 Maccabees; 🟡 for Wright's reading.
- **Seven (11:26).** The number of completeness. Seven worse spirits means full possession. 🔴
- **Washing before meals (11:38).** Not hygiene. It was a purity ritual the Pharisees kept. Jesus skipping it was a statement. 🔴
- **Hidden tombs (11:44).** Walking over a grave made you unclean (Num 19:16), so tombs were whitewashed to warn people. Jesus says the Pharisees are unmarked graves: people get defiled by them without knowing. 🔴

## My notes
- **Friend at Midnight (draft 27).** Where I sit: on the word, Snodgrass has the evidence and Bailey has the structure, and 258 occurrences outweigh a stanza diagram. On the story, Bailey and Snodgrass together persuaded me persistence isn't in it. The man calls once, there's no refusal, and the parable teaches that God hears and answers.
- Bailey's two six-line stanzas still matter: the outside lines are about giving and the centers are about honor.
- **The poem (11:9–13) is its own unit.** It's where the knocking lives. Augustine read the three loaves as the Trinity, and his line on delay is the best thing in his sermon: God wants to give, so knock on.
- **Pairing with 18:1–8.** The same Greek phrase shows up in both reluctant men: "do not bother me" (11:7) and "this widow bothers me" (18:5). The widow keeps coming; the text says so. The host comes once. Persistence belongs to Luke 18 and got loaned to Luke 11 for most of church history.
- **Unclean spirit (draft 36).** I adopted Wright's reading: the house is Israel and its temple. Read on its own the story says exorcisms don't last, which is a strange thing for an exorcist to say. The observation that Luke supplies "this generation" two verses late (11:29) is mine. 🟡
- Chrysostom applied it first to Israel and then to the baptized. The individual application isn't a modern flattening, but the national one comes first.
- **Three types of spirits?** I asked once whether there are three types: unclean, familiar and seducing. Scripture uses all three phrases, but never as a list of three kinds. The grouping comes from later deliverance teaching. "Unclean spirit" is the normal gospel term.

## What the chapter is doing
- With thousands crowding in, Jesus warns his disciples about the Pharisees' hypocrisy and tells them who to fear: not the one who can kill the body, but God. Confess him before people and the Son of Man will confess you before the angels of God. When you are dragged before synagogues and rulers, the Holy Spirit will teach you what to say (12:1–12).
- A man wants Jesus to make his brother split the inheritance. Jesus refuses and tells the parable of the rich fool, who plans bigger barns and dies that night (12:13–21).
- Don't worry about food and clothes. Look at the ravens and the lilies. Seek the kingdom, sell your possessions, keep your treasure in heaven (12:22–34).
- Be dressed and ready like servants waiting up for their master. When he comes, he will serve them. A faithful steward feeds the household; a wicked one beats the servants and gets drunk (12:35–48).
- Jesus came to bring fire and division, and the crowds can read the weather but not the time they're living in (12:49–59).

## Pay attention to this
- **"My friends" (12:4).** The only place in the Synoptic Gospels where Jesus calls the disciples friends. It comes right before he tells them they might be killed. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for "only place."
- **Fear the right one (12:4–7).** Fear God, and then "Do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows." Both in four verses. 🔴
- **Two courtrooms, one paragraph (12:8–12).** Verses 8–9 are the heavenly court, the Son of Man speaking for you "before the angels of God." Verses 11–12 are the earthly court, the synagogue and the rulers. Same paragraph, two rooms. 🔴 for the text; 🔴 for reading them together (field note sources).
- **"Do not worry" is the verb (12:11).** It forbids anxiety. It does not forbid study or preparation. 🔴
- **"Man" (12:14).** Jesus doesn't use the petitioner's name or call him friend. Bailey hears real displeasure. 🟡
- **The rich fool talks only to himself (12:17–19).** "I will... my barns... my grain... my goods... my soul." There is nobody else in his speech. 🔴
- **"Your soul is required of you" (12:20).** Bailey reads it as loan language: the life was on loan and the lender is calling it in. 🟡
- **Ravens, not just birds (12:24).** Matthew says "birds of the air." Luke says ravens, which were unclean (Lev 11:15). God feeds even those. 🔴
- **"Little flock" (12:32).** Don't fear, because the Father is pleased to give you the kingdom. 🔴
- **The master serves (12:37).** "He will gird himself to serve, and have them recline at the table, and will come up and wait on them." The world's order turned over. 🔴
- **Peter's question (12:41).** "Are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else?" Jesus answers with another parable about a steward, and doesn't say "just you." 🔴
