## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Leaven (12:1).** Leaven worked through a whole batch of dough, and Israel cleared it out of the house at Passover. It was the picture of something that spreads quietly. 🔴
- **The heavenly court.** "Before the angels of God" (12:8–9) is a courtroom. The Old Testament shows God's council sitting in judgment, with the satan as accuser (Job 1:6–12; Zech 3:1–5), and Daniel 7 sets the Son of Man before the Ancient of Days while the court sits and the books are opened. Luke 12:8–9 shares that scene. In the Old Testament scenes, God himself defends the accused; nobody stands as advocate. Here the Son of Man does. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for Daniel 7 behind Luke 12.
- **Stephen saw it.** In Acts 7:56 Stephen sees the Son of Man *standing* at God's right hand, when he is usually seated. F. F. Bruce connects it to 12:8: Jesus standing up as advocate for the man confessing him before the Sanhedrin. Stephen lost his case and died that afternoon. 🔴 for Acts; 🟡 for Bruce's link.
- **Synagogue courts were real.** Local courts of seven, larger towns twenty-three. The synagogue officers who taught you Torah on the Sabbath also judged you. The standard sentence was thirty-nine lashes, one-third on the chest and two-thirds on the back, and you had to submit to it to stay in the community. Paul did five times (2 Cor 11:24). 🔴
- **Roman courts.** No public prosecutors; private accusers brought the charges. A governor sat on his platform with his advisers and could skip normal procedure. Noncitizens had little protection. Paul used his citizenship when it counted (Acts 22:25–29; 25:11). 🔴
- **Luke 12 versus Luke 21.** Luke 12:11 says "when they bring you," any time it happens, and forbids worry. Luke 21:14 points at a specific coming season and forbids rehearsing a defense speech ahead of time. 🔴 for the wording; 🔴 (Walton) for the difference.
- **Rabbis settled inheritance fights.** Asking a teacher to rule on a family dispute was normal. Jesus refuses the role, the way Moses was asked "Who made you a judge over us?" (Exod 2:14). 🔴 for the custom; 🟡 for the echo.
- **The fool misquotes his Bible.** "Eat, drink and be merry" comes from Ecclesiastes 8:15, which adds "the days of his life which God has given him." He drops the God part. Sirach 11:18–19 has a man who says "I have found rest, now I will eat my goods" and doesn't know when his time will come. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 that Jesus is reworking Sirach.
- **The man has no friends.** In a village, big decisions took hours of talk with family and neighbors. A man deciding alone has pulled out of the human family. Bailey puts Isaiah 5:8 under it: woe to those who add field to field until they live alone. 🟡
- **The Land.** Wright reads the parable against Israel's hold on its inheritance. Possessing the Land was a sacred symbol, and Israel was in danger of becoming the man with barns. 🟡
- **Passover clothes.** "Gird up your loins, and keep your lamps lit" (12:35) is how Israel ate the first Passover: belt on, ready to go (Exod 12:11). 🔴 for the phrase; 🟡 (Wright) for the link.
- **Night watches (12:38).** Jews divided the night into three watches, Romans into four. The second and third watches are the middle of the night. 🔴
- **A wedding can run all night.** Bailey reads the master as slipping out of a wedding banquet still going on, carrying food on a tray for his servants. The household had seven ranks and these are the bottom. 🟡 (Bailey)
- **Fire and division (12:49–53).** The family lines come from Micah 7:6. In a world where family was everything, following Jesus could cost you your household. 🔴
- **Weather (12:54–55).** A cloud from the west came off the Mediterranean and meant rain. A south wind came off the desert and meant heat. Everybody could read that. 🔴

- **"Let it alone" (13:8).** The Greek verb is the ordinary New Testament word for forgive. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for reading forgiveness into it.
- **Eighteen and eighteen (13:4, 13:11).** Eighteen killed by the tower, a woman bound eighteen years. Luke puts the number twice in one chapter. 🔴
- **"A sickness caused by a spirit" (13:11) and "whom Satan has bound" (13:16).** The doctor describes a bent spine and names a spiritual cause, and Jesus says Satan tied her up. 🔴
- **"Daughter of Abraham" (13:16).** That phrase appears nowhere else in the New Testament. She is a full member of the covenant family, and Satan has been holding her. Pair it with "son of Abraham" for Zacchaeus (19:9). 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Pilate's record.** Josephus records several of Pilate's outrages against Jews (the army standards in Jerusalem, temple money for an aqueduct and the riot that followed) but not this one. It fits the man. 🔴 for Josephus; 🔴 that this incident is known only from Luke.
- **Blood mixed with sacrifices.** Galilean pilgrims killing their own animals at the temple, likely at a feast, cut down at the altar. To a Jew this was a massacre and a desecration at once. 🟡
- **Suffering means sin, people assumed.** The disciples ask it about the blind man (John 9:2), and Job's friends argued it for chapters. Jesus says no twice. 🔴
- **"Perish likewise."** Wright reads it as literal and near: Roman swords for those who go the way of revolt, falling Jerusalem stones when the city is besieged. In AD 70 both happened. The ESV notes read it as final judgment. Snodgrass says in light of 13:34–35 it's probably Jerusalem, and the two aren't always kept apart. 🔴 for AD 70; ⬜ for which Jesus meant.
- **The fig tree is Israel.** The fig is a symbol for Israel in Jeremiah 24, Hosea 9:10 and Micah 7:1, and Isaiah 5 is the vineyard named as the house of Israel. Bailey narrows the tree to Israel's leaders. Snodgrass and Wright say the nation. 🔴 for the Old Testament symbols; ⬜ for leaders or nation.
- **Jesus changed Isaiah's picture.** In Isaiah 5 the owner tears down the whole vineyard himself. Here the owner wants the vineyard healthy and argues about one tree. 🟡
- **You dig a tree out.** In Palestine you don't just cut a tree, you dig it out, roots and all, which is why John's axe is laid "at the root" (3:9). And the gardener's manure was a little funny to farmers. 🟡 (Bailey)
- **Three years.** If Leviticus 19:23–25 is in view (no fruit eaten for the first years), the owner has waited a long time. Snodgrass says the tree's age isn't stated and the three years only mean complete failure. 🔵
- **Spirits and sickness.** Second Temple Jews believed evil spirits could cause disease, and Luke doesn't treat every illness that way, only some (compare 4:39 and 13:11). Here the binding is Satan's, and the healing is a release from his hold, a small picture of the strong man's house being plundered (11:21–22). 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the link to 11:21–22.
- **Sabbath means release.** Deuteronomy ties the Sabbath to remembering slavery in Egypt (Deut 5:15). Freeing a captive on the day that remembers freedom is the most Sabbath thing Jesus could do. 🔴 for Deuteronomy; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Birds in the branches (13:19).** The tree with birds nesting in its branches is the picture of a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezek 17:23; 31:6; Dan 4:12). In Daniel 4 that tree is Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom, cut down by the decree of the heavenly "watchers" and "holy ones" (Dan 4:13–17). Jesus gives the image to a mustard seed. Levine and Snodgrass doubt Jesus meant the Ezekiel and Daniel echoes. 🔴 for the texts; ⬜ for the allusion.
- **Three measures of flour (13:21).** Around forty to sixty pounds of flour, bread for a crowd. Sarah made cakes from three measures for Abraham's divine visitors (Gen 18:6). 🔴 for the amount and Genesis; 🔵 for the echo.
- **Leaven.** Leaven usually stood for corruption, and Israel purged it at Passover. Using it for the kingdom is a jolt. The claim that yeast is "always" evil in Scripture overreaches. 🔴 for the usual symbol; 🟡 against "always."
- **The feast of the nations (13:29).** Isaiah 25:6 promises a feast on God's mountain "for all peoples." Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are at the table, and the guests come from every direction. 🔴
- **The fox and the lion.** A fox was a small, sly predator, not a lion. Calling a king a fox cuts him down to size. 🟡
- **Prophets die in Jerusalem (13:33).** The city had a long record of killing prophets (Jer 26:20–23; 2 Chr 24:20–22). 🔴
- **Wings (13:34).** God's people take refuge under his wings (Ruth 2:12; Ps 91:4). Jesus says he wanted to do that for Jerusalem. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the echo.
- **"Your house is left to you desolate" (13:35).** The words of Jeremiah against the temple and the royal house (Jer 12:7; 22:5). The line at the end is Psalm 118:26, which the crowds will shout at the entry in 19:38. 🔴

- **Barren fig tree (draft 28).** Bailey reads the Pilate report as an atrocity story, from his own months in the Lebanese war: one massacre spawns rumors of ten, and anyone who asks "have you checked your sources" gets called a traitor.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, and everyone is watching him. He heals a man with dropsy, then comments on the guests grabbing the best seats and on who the host invited.
- A guest says "Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!" (14:15). Jesus answers with a story about a big dinner where every invited guest sends an excuse, so the master fills the house with the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame.
- Then he turns to the crowds walking behind him and makes following him sound expensive: hate your family, carry your cross, give up everything.
- Between those demands he tells two short stories about doing the math first: a man building a tower and a king facing a bigger army. The chapter ends on salt that has gone bad.

## Pay attention to this
- **The same list twice.** "The poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind" (14:13) is the guest list Jesus tells the host to use. Eight verses later the master in the story sends for "the poor and crippled and blind and lame" (14:21). The parable acts out the advice. 🔴
- **The second call (14:17).** The guests were already invited. The slave goes out "at the dinner hour" to say "Come, for everything is ready now." Saying no at that point is saying no to a meal you already agreed to. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for how sharp an insult it was (Bailey).
- **The excuses are thin on purpose.** Nobody buys land without seeing it first, and nobody buys five yoke of oxen without trying them out. The third man doesn't even ask to be excused (14:20). 🟡 Bailey reads all three as a planned snub; other readers think they are just lame excuses.
- **"Compel them to come in" (14:23).** Augustine used this verse to justify forcing the Donatist churches back into line, and later persecutors leaned on it too. In the story it means talking a nobody into believing the invitation is real. 🔴 for the history; 🟡 for the reading.
- **"My dinner" (14:24).** The "you" in "I tell you" is plural in Greek. Up to here the master talks to one slave. The last line sounds like Jesus talking to the men at the table about his own banquet. 🔴 for the plural; 🟡 for the reading (Bailey).
- **"Cannot be My disciple" three times (14:26, 27, 33).** The section is built around that refrain, and the word under it is "able": the builder is "not able to finish" (14:29–30) and the king asks if he is "strong enough" (14:31). 🔴
- **"Hate" (14:26).** Not hatred as we feel it. In Hebrew idiom it means "love less by comparison." Matthew's version says "whoever loves father or mother more than Me" (Matt 10:37). 🔴
- **"Terms of peace" (14:32).** Remember that phrase. Weeping over Jerusalem, Jesus says "If you knew in this day, even you, the things which make for peace!" (19:42). 🔴 for the echo; 🟡 for how much weight it carries.
- **Luke the doctor.** Only Luke tells this healing, and he names the condition: "dropsy," swelling from fluid. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Meals were seating charts.** Where you reclined told everyone your rank. Proverbs 25:6–7 already gives Jesus's advice: better to be told "come up here" than to be sent lower. A 2026 reader hears table manners. A first-century guest heard his honor on the line in front of the whole room. 🔴
- **The banquet everyone was waiting for.** Isaiah 25:6–9 pictures God throwing a feast on his mountain for all peoples, with death swallowed up. By Jesus's day that hope had been narrowed. The Targum of Isaiah turns the feast into a shame for the nations, 1 Enoch puts the angel of death at the table, and the Qumran Rule of the Congregation (1QSa) bars the lame, the blind and anyone with a visible blemish from the end-time assembly. 🔴 for what those texts say.
- **Jesus reads the banned list as a guest list.** The people Qumran shut out are exactly the people the master sends for in 14:21. 🟡 Bailey's reading, and the other scholars James weighed grant it.
- **Invitations came twice.** You were invited ahead of time, then a servant came to say the food was ready. Esther 6:14 shows the same second summons. 🔴
- **"Hate your father and mother" in a world built on family.** Family and land were how a Jew knew he was a Jew. Your inheritance was your tribe's piece of the promise. Telling a crowd to put both second was telling them to put the nation's identity second. 🟡 Wright, *Jesus and the Victory of God*.
- **Carrying a cross (14:27)** meant one thing in Roman Judea: a condemned man walking to his own execution. Nobody heard it as a metaphor for a bad week. 🔴
- **Towers and wars were not abstract.** Herod's temple was still being built, and plenty of people wanted a war with Rome. Wright hears both stories as a quiet warning to Israel; Snodgrass thinks that reads Israel into a discipleship saying. 🔵
- **Salt that goes bad (14:34–35).** Most salt came from the Dead Sea and carried other minerals. Badly processed salt tasted wrong and couldn't even be dumped on a field or a manure pile. 🟡
- **Divine council:** none in this chapter. The banquet hope belongs to the end of the age, but no spiritual powers show up here. See "My notes."

## My notes
- I picked 14:26 as the lead demo in my plan for the first mentee session. I wanted something very clear: read it as it's written and it means one thing, explain it and it means something else. "Hate" as Semitic "love less by comparison," with Matthew 10:37 next to it, does that. 🔴
- **Great Banquet (post 7).** I built it on Bailey: two-stage invitation, the excuses as insults, the master taking his anger and turning it into grace, "compel" as pleading with people who can't believe they're wanted. 🟡
- My third pass changed how I present it. The coordinated-insult reading is Bailey's. Snodgrass, Blomberg and Boice read the excuses as lame, not hostile. What holds for everyone: the Qumran exclusion list turned into a guest list, and the plural "you" in 14:24. 🔴

- **Tower Builder and King (draft 33).** The disciple counts the cost, not God. Snodgrass and Blomberg both reject Derrett's view that God is the builder. 🔴 Wright hears Herod's temple and the war with Rome; Snodgrass calls that co-opting. I think the fight is smaller than it looks. Snodgrass is asking what Jesus meant when he first told it. ## What the chapter is doing
- Tax collectors and sinners crowd in to hear Jesus. The Pharisees and scribes grumble: "This man receives sinners and eats with them" (15:2).
- Jesus answers with three stories about something lost and found: one sheep out of a hundred, one coin out of ten, one son out of two.
- Each find ends in a party. Heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents.
- The third story doesn't end with a party. It ends with the older brother standing outside, angry, his father pleading with him, and no answer given.

## Pay attention to this
- **One answer to one complaint.** All three stories answer 15:2. Eating with someone meant accepting them, and the grumblers are the audience. 🔴
- **The numbers shrink.** One in a hundred, one in ten, one in two. The loss gets more personal each time. 🔴
- **"A man had two sons" (15:11).** That's how Jesus opens it. "The Prodigal Son" is a heading added later, and it points your eyes at the younger son when the story ends on the older one. 🔴
- **"Prodigal" means wasteful,** not "runaway" or "returning." It comes from Latin *prodigus*, lavish. The LSB says he "squandered his estate living recklessly" (15:13). 🔴
- **The speech he rehearsed vs. the speech he gave.** In the pigpen he plans to say "make me as one of your hired men" (15:19). When he actually speaks, after the father's embrace, that line is gone (15:21). 🔴 for the text; 🟡 that the embrace is what cut it (Bailey).
- **The father moves first.** He sees the son "while he was still a long way off," feels compassion, runs, embraces and kisses him before the boy says a word (15:20). 🔴
- **The father goes out twice.** Once to the younger son on the road, once to the older son in the yard (15:28). 🔴
- **Listen to the pronouns.** The servant says "your brother" (15:27). The older son says "this son of yours" (15:30). The father hands it back: "this brother of yours" (15:32). 🔴
- **"Dead and alive" twice (15:24, 32).** Hold onto it. In the next chapter Abraham says the rich man's brothers won't listen "even if someone rises from the dead" (16:31). 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for linking them (Wright).
- **"Child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours" (15:31).** If the older brother stands for the Pharisees, that is a kind thing to say about them. Snodgrass presses this point. 🔴 for the text.

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Eating together meant belonging.** Sharing a table said "you are one of mine." That's why the complaint in 15:2 is about meals, not sermons. 🔴
- **Shepherds and God.** Ezekiel 34 has God himself searching for the lost sheep that Israel's shepherds ignored (34:11–16). A Pharisee hearing "what man among you" with a lost sheep had that chapter in his head. 🔴 for Ezekiel 34 behind the story; 🟡 for Bailey's Psalm 23 layer, which Snodgrass doubts.
- **"Which woman" could not be said.** Jesus asks "what man among you" (15:4) but "what woman" (15:8). Calling a mixed crowd women would have been an insult, so he changes the frame and still puts a woman in God's place. 🟡 Bailey.
- **The coin.** Wright suggests it may have been her savings or dowry. Bailey narrows it: Bedouin women wore dowry coins on a veil, village women more often on a necklace. 🔵
- **Asking for the inheritance early.** In that world it meant "I wish you were dead." The father was expected to refuse, get angry, maybe beat him. He does none of it. 🟡 Bailey, and the core of his reading.
- **Two requests, not one.** Under Mishnah Bava Batra 8:7 a son could be given ownership while the father kept the use of it. Selling it off was a second step the law didn't provide for, and that is what the son does when he "gathered everything together" (15:13). 🟡 Bailey.
- **Pigs.** A Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile in a foreign country has hit bottom. Pigs were unclean, and the far country was the place covenant people didn't go. 🔴
- **The pods.** Carob pods were animal feed. Bailey thinks the pigs were rooting a wild, bitter carob a man could eat all day and still starve on. 🔵
- **Elders don't run.** A man of the father's age and standing would have to hitch up his robe to run, which was shameful. Bailey reads the run as the father drawing the village's contempt onto himself so he reaches the boy first, "the cross in miniature." 🟡
- **The cutting-off ceremony.** Bailey says a son who lost family land among Gentiles faced the *kezazah*: a pot broken in front of him and a declaration that he was cut off from his people. Snodgrass and Levine see no evidence it stands behind the parable. 🔵
- **Robe, ring, sandals, calf.** The best robe is honor, the ring is authority, sandals mark a son (slaves went barefoot), and a fattened calf feeds a whole village. A public homecoming the village can't overturn. 🟡
- **Coming home from exile.** Many Jews in Jesus's day believed the exile hadn't really ended: they were back in the land, but pagans still ruled. Since Ezekiel 37, "dead and alive again" had been picture language for coming home. Wright hears the parable that way. 🟡
- **"Never have I neglected a command of yours" (15:29).** Wright hears the same boast Paul makes about his old life in Philippians 3:6, "as to the righteousness which is in the Law, found blameless." 🔵
- **Divine council:** "joy in the presence of the angels of God" (15:10). Heaven is pictured as a court, with God's attendants around him reacting to what happens on earth. A small hook, not a council scene. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- A rich man's steward is caught wasting his master's goods and fired. Before he hands in the books he calls in his master's debtors and cuts their bills, so someone will take him in. The master praises him for being shrewd.
- Jesus adds sayings about money: be faithful with little, you can't serve God and wealth (16:9–13).
- The Pharisees, "lovers of money," scoff. Jesus answers them, then says a word about the Law and divorce (16:14–18).
- Then a rich man who feasts every day and a poor man named Lazarus lying at his gate. Both die. Lazarus is carried to Abraham, the rich man wakes up in torment, and Abraham refuses to send anyone back to warn his brothers.

## Pay attention to this
- **Same verb as the prodigal.** The steward is "squandering" his master's possessions (16:1), the same Greek word as the younger son who "squandered his estate" (15:13). Luke 15 and 16 are one block of teaching. 🔴
- **The steward doesn't argue.** Told to hand over the books, he says nothing to his master. He talks only to himself (16:3–4). 🔴 for the text; 🟡 that the silence admits guilt (Bailey).
- **The debtors write the new numbers themselves (16:6–7).** That puts the changes in their own handwriting. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for why (Bailey, following the eleventh-century Arabic commentator Ibn al-Tayyib).
- **Praised for shrewdness, not honesty (16:8).** The master calls him "the unrighteous steward" in the same breath. T. W. Manson's line: there's a difference between "I praise the dishonest steward because he was clever" and "I praise the clever steward because he was dishonest." 🔴
- **"Sons of light" (16:8)** was a name the Qumran community used for themselves. 🔴
- **Lazarus is the only named person in any of Jesus's parables.** The rich man never gets a name. 🔴
- **The rich man is still giving orders.** From torment he asks Abraham to "send Lazarus" with water, then "send him to my father's house" (16:24, 27). He still sees Lazarus as an errand boy. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the reading (Bailey).
- **Abraham calls him "Child" (16:25).** He's still a son of Abraham by blood. It didn't save him. 🔴
- **"Even if someone rises from the dead" (16:31).** One chapter after "this brother of yours was dead and is alive" (15:32). 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for linking them (Wright).
- **The dogs (16:21).** Most English versions make the dogs one more misery. Bailey argues the Greek "but" sets them against the rich man: the guard dogs treat Lazarus as a friend. 🔵 Scholars split on it.

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **A steward was an estate manager,** running land for an owner and collecting rent in kind, oil and wheat. Not a banker. 🟡
- **Two readings of the bill-cutting.** Bailey: the steward was already fired, so the cuts were his gamble that a generous master would let them stand rather than shame himself before the village. Wright: lending at interest to a fellow Jew was banned (Exod 22:25; Lev 25:36–37; Deut 23:19), so lenders hid interest in oil and wheat, and the steward struck the interest off, leaving the master unable to complain without exposing himself. The two can't both be right. 🔵
- **"Wealth of unrighteousness" (16:9).** The word behind "wealth" is *mammon*, money treated as something you trust. Bailey points to an Aramaic wordplay in 16:9–13 on the root *amn* (to trust, to be faithful): if you aren't faithful with *mammon*, who will trust you with the true riches? 🟡
- **Two masters (16:13).** A slave belonged to one house. Jesus sets wealth up as a rival lord who wants worship. 🔴 for the picture; 🟡 for reading *mammon* as more than money.
- **Purple and fine linen, every day.** Purple dye was the most expensive cloth color there was. "Joyously living in splendor every day" also means no Sabbath for his servants; Bailey reads that as the commandments broken on a schedule. 🔴 for the luxury; 🔵 for the Sabbath point.
- **Lazarus means "God helps"** (Hebrew *El'azar*). A man covered in sores at a rich man's gate, and his name is "God helps." 🔴
- **Dogs were unclean scavengers** in Jewish eyes. Bailey adds that the ancient world knew licked wounds heal, and a dig at Ashkelon found more than 1,300 dog burials. 🔴 for the general view of dogs; 🔵 for what it means here.
- **A borrowed story with the ending changed.** Tales of rich and poor trading places after death were common. In the usual version the man in torment is allowed to send a warning back. Here Abraham refuses. Wright reads the refusal as the point, and the afterlife as the stage set, not the subject. 🟡
- **Abraham's side, Hades, a great chasm.** Jews of the time pictured the dead waiting in separate places. 1 Enoch 22 has the spirits of the dead held in separate hollows, the righteous apart from sinners, with a spring of water for the righteous. A first-century hearer recognized the scenery. 🔴 for 1 Enoch; 🟡 that Jesus is using the stock picture.
- **Divine council:** "carried away by the angels" (16:22). Angels as escorts for the righteous dead was common Jewish belief. God's attendants are working in the story, though no council meets. 🟡
- **"They have Moses and the Prophets" (16:29).** Scripture is enough. The rich man's brothers already have everything they need to treat the poor right (Deut 15:7–11). 🔴

## My notes
- **Unjust Steward (post 5).** Bailey: the account is a dismissal on the spot, the silence, the bill cuts as a gamble on the master's generosity, fired but not jailed. 🟡
- **Wright (added live).** The interest-in-kind reading, master as God and steward as Israel. My post says straight out that Bailey and Wright can't both be right, and that's on purpose. A reader who wants to teach this passage should know the choice is live. 🔵
- From my research: Ibn al-Tayyib on why the debtors are accomplices, Bailey's answer to Derrett, five parallels between the prodigal and the steward, and 16:9–13 as a separate "poem on mammon." Snodgrass rejects both readings and calls it a plain crisis parable with a comic rogue. 🔵
- Bailey's trilogy holds the chapters together: a son wastes his father's goods, a steward wastes his master's, a rich man wastes his own. 🟡
- **Lazarus and the Rich Man (post 8).** Bailey: Lazarus is "the one whom God helps"; the story is about how each man responds, not what happened to him; the rich man is still giving orders from the fire. 🟡
- **Wright (added live).** The folk tale with the request refused, the afterlife not the subject, 15:32 linked to 16:31, and the rich man as the older brother: both want a ragged relative kept out of sight, and both end the story outside. 🟡
- My research also turned up Bailey's dogs reading (the "but" makes them helpers), and it's now a three-to-two split among the voices I checked. The church fathers built their teaching on the state of the dead between death and resurrection on this parable. Levine undercuts the idea that Jesus's hearers took wealth as proof of God's blessing. 🔵
- **Divine council:** no council scene. The angels in 16:22 are the hook. The council material in Luke comes at 4:1–13, 8:26–39, 10:17–20, 11:14–26 and 22:53.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus warns his disciples about causing "little ones" to stumble and tells them to forgive a brother who repents, even seven times a day. They ask for more faith; he answers with a mustard seed and a mulberry tree.
- Then a short story: a slave comes in from the field and serves his master supper before he eats. When you've done everything you were told, you've only done your duty (17:7–10).
- Still on the road to Jerusalem, Jesus heals ten men with leprosy. One comes back to thank him, and he's a Samaritan.
- The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming. Jesus says it's "in your midst," then tells the disciples the Son of Man's day will come suddenly, like the flood in Noah's day and the fire in Lot's.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Which of you" (17:7)** is a question that expects the answer "nobody." No master seats his slave first. 🔴
- **"Is he grateful to the slave?" (17:9).** The Greek is *echei charin*, "does he have grace for him." Bailey and Blomberg both read it as "is the master now in his debt?" not "does he say thank you." 🟡
- **"Unworthy slaves" (17:10).** The word is *achreios*. "Useless" can't be right, since the slave did everything asked. Bailey reads it from the root as "without need," meaning nothing is owed us. 🟡
- **The serving master run backwards.** In 12:37 the master girds himself, seats his slaves and serves them. Here the slave girds himself, serves, and the master reclines. Same three pictures, opposite direction. 🔴
- **The story follows a request for more faith (17:5).** The disciples want more; Jesus answers that faith is not something you bank credit with. 🔴 for the order; 🟡 for the link.
- **The leprous men "stood at a distance" (17:12)** and were healed "as they were going" to the priests (17:14), before they saw anything. 🔴
- **"Except this foreigner" (17:18).** The only one who turns back is a Samaritan, and Luke saves that for the end of 17:16. Only Luke tells this. 🔴
- **"In your midst" (17:21)** can be read "within you" or "among you." With Jesus standing in front of them, "among you" fits the scene. 🔵
- **Noah's day was ordinary.** "They were eating, they were drinking, they were marrying" (17:27). Jesus doesn't list their sins. The danger is going on as usual with no idea what's coming. 🔴
- **"Remember Lot's wife" (17:32).** She looked back. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **A slave in a great house had a place.** He was fed, housed and protected, and he owed loyalty and work, not an invoice. Bailey says that kind of security was what the relationship meant in that world. 🟡
- **Supper wasn't late.** Bailey says the meal in view was in the afternoon, so the slave isn't being worked into the night. The question is whether a day's chores earn him special standing. 🟡
- **A world built on favors returned.** In Greco-Roman life, patrons and clients kept score; a favor done put the other side in your debt. Saying "nothing is owed us" cut against that. 🟡
- **The rabbis said it too.** Antigonus of Soko, a disciple of Simeon the Just, taught: be like slaves who serve the master without thought of a reward (Mishnah Avot 1:3). 🔴
- **"Without need" in village speech.** Bailey heard it in Arabic villages: a workman finishes a small job, the homeowner asks *fi haja?*, "is there any need?", meaning "do I owe you?", and the workman says *ma fi haja*, "there is no need." The seventh-century Harclean Syriac renders *achreios* the same way. 🟡
- **Leprosy laws.** A person with a skin disease had to live apart and cry "Unclean!" (Lev 13:45–46). Only a priest could declare him clean again (Lev 14). That's why Jesus sends them to the priests. 🔴
- **Samaritans** were the half-cousins Jews avoided, with their own temple site at Gerizim and their own copy of the Torah. 🔴
- **Divine council: the days of Noah.** In Second Temple writing, Noah's generation meant the Watchers, the sons of God who came down in Genesis 6 and corrupted the earth (1 Enoch 6–11; Jubilees 5). A first-century hearer may have heard "the days of Noah" with that story attached. 🔴 for what those texts say; 🔵 that Jesus's hearers made the link here.
- **"Son of Man" (17:22–30)** comes from Daniel 7, a throne-room scene where the Ancient of Days sits with the court and one like a son of man receives the kingdom. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Two stories about prayer. A widow keeps coming to a judge who fears neither God nor people until he gives her justice. Then a Pharisee and a tax collector go up to the temple to pray, and only one goes home justified.
- Jesus welcomes babies the disciples were shooing away. A rich ruler asks how to inherit eternal life, is told to sell everything and follow, and leaves sad.
- "Easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle." The disciples ask who can be saved; Jesus says what's impossible with people is possible with God.
- He tells the Twelve, for the third time, that he'll be killed and rise. They don't understand. Outside Jericho a blind beggar shouts "Son of David!" over the crowd and gets his sight.
- Luke 18 states the problem: the rich can't save themselves. Luke 19 shows a rich man saved.

## Pay attention to this
- **Luke tells you the point first.** "To show that at all times they ought to pray and not to lose heart" (18:1), and "to some people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous" (18:9). 🔴
- **The judge is not God.** It's an argument from the worse case: if a crooked judge gives in, how much more will God? 🔴
- **"Bothering me" (18:5)** is the same Greek phrase the sleeping neighbor uses in the friend at midnight, "Do not bother me" (11:7). The two prayer stories are paired. 🔴
- **"Will He delay long over them?" (18:7).** Most translations make it a question. Bailey reads it as a statement: God puts his anger far away from them, he is patient with them. 🔵
- **The Pharisee prays about himself.** "I am not like other people... I fast twice a week; I pay tithes of all that I get" (18:11–12). 🔴
- **"God, be merciful to me, the sinner!" (18:13).** The verb is the atonement word. Bailey renders it "God, make an atonement for me." 🟡
- **Beating the chest.** The only other place anyone does this in the Bible is the crowd at the cross (23:48). 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for Bailey's point that men in that culture didn't do it.
- **Up and down.** Both men "went up into the temple" (18:10); the tax collector "went down to his house justified" (18:14). 🔴
- **The ruler gets the second half of the commandments only (18:20):** adultery, murder, stealing, false witness, honoring parents. Jesus leaves out "no other gods." Then "sell all that you possess" shows where his god actually is. 🔴 for the list; 🟡 for the reading.
- **"Then who can be saved?" (18:26).** The disciples panic, which shows they heard "impossible," not "hard." 🔴
- **"Hidden from them" (18:34).** The third death prediction, and Luke says plainly they couldn't grasp it. 🔴
- **The crowd is the wall.** "Those who went ahead were rebuking him" (18:39). Jesus stops and orders the same crowd to bring him over. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for Bailey's pairing with Zacchaeus in 19:3.
- **"What do you want Me to do for you?" (18:41).** The obvious answer still has to come from the man's own mouth. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Widows had no one.** No husband to speak for her in court. The Law repeatedly orders protection for the widow and orphan (Exod 22:22; Deut 10:18). 🔴
- **Sirach 35 behind the widow.** Ben Sira 35:14–18 also pairs a widow's cry with God's justice, but ends with God taking vengeance on the nations. Bailey thinks Jesus is answering that text, and Jesus ends instead with a question about whether the Son of Man will find faith. 🟡
- **Two ways to appeal.** In that world you asked "for God's sake" or "for my sake." A judge who fears no God and respects no one is deaf to both, so the widow has no lever but showing up. 🟡 Bailey.
- **Fasting twice a week** went far past the Law, which commands one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement. Many Jews fasted Monday and Thursday; the Didache (8:1) knows that custom. 🔴
- **Tithing everything.** The Mishnah spends pages on what is exempt. The Pharisee claims no exemptions at all. 🟡
- **Prayer was said out loud.** The Pharisee "standing by himself" is preaching to the people he's keeping away from. 🟡 Bailey.
- **The hour of prayer** in the temple was tied to the daily burnt offering, the sacrifice for the people. A man asking God to "make atonement for me" while it burns is asking for that sacrifice to cover him. 🟡 Bailey.
- **Tax collectors** bought the right to collect for Rome and took a cut. They were seen as collaborators and thieves. 🔴
- **Isaiah 66:1–6 underneath.** Bailey lists nine points of contact between that passage and this parable: the temple, a humble man who trembles at God's word, proud men shutting others out. 🟡
- **"Justified" is courtroom language,** the judge ruling in your favor. Wright reads both stories as about God's verdict. 🟡
- **The camel and the needle.** The rabbis used an elephant going through the eye of a needle as a stock picture of the impossible (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b and Bava Metzia 38b). The camel was the biggest animal in Judea. 🔴
- **There was no Needle Gate.** No first-century source mentions a small gate in Jerusalem's wall called the Eye of the Needle. The idea shows up centuries later and spread in nineteenth-century preaching. The "rope" reading (*kamilos* for *kamelos*) only appears in late manuscripts. 🔴
- **Alms were the welfare system.** Giving to beggars was a duty, not a nice extra. The Hebrew word for almsgiving, *tzedakah*, is the word for righteousness. Healing the blind beggar ended his income. 🟡
- **"Son of David"** was a royal title for the Messiah. The blind man says it out loud on the road to Jerusalem. 🔴
- **Divine council:** the Son of Man coming (18:8) points to Daniel 7, the heavenly court where one like a son of man receives the kingdom. And "hidden from them" (18:34): Paul says none of "the rulers of this age" understood God's plan, "for if they had understood it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:8). Heiser reads those rulers as spiritual powers kept in the dark along with everyone else. 🔴 for Daniel 7; 🟡 for Heiser's reading.

That defeats the point, because then it's possible, just hard, and a man only needs to work at it. What Jesus was saying is a real camel and the eye of a real needle, something truly impossible and only possible with God. I asked for it to go on jayms.com as its own story. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- In Jericho, a rich chief tax collector named Zacchaeus climbs a sycamore tree to see Jesus. Jesus calls him down and invites himself to his house. The crowd grumbles. Zacchaeus pledges half his goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone he cheated, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house.
- Near Jerusalem, Jesus tells a parable about a nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom, leaves money with his slaves, and comes back to settle accounts with them and with the citizens who didn't want him as king.
- He rides into Jerusalem on a colt while his disciples shout "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord."
- He weeps over the city and predicts its destruction, then drives the sellers out of the temple and teaches there every day while the leaders look for a way to kill him.

## Pay attention to this
- **Zacchaeus is the last named person Jesus meets before Jerusalem.** Ten verses, and the placement is why. 🔴
- **He's the answer to the rich ruler.** In 18:23 a rich man walks away sad. In 19:6 a rich man "received Him gladly" and gives his money away without being asked. 🔴 for the contrast in the text; 🟡 that Luke set it up on purpose.
- **"Today" and "must" (19:5, 9).** "Today I must stay at your house." "Today salvation has come to this house." 🔴
- **The same grumbling as 15:2.** "He has gone to be the guest of a man who is a sinner" (19:7). Luke uses the same verb for the Pharisees' complaint in 15:2. 🔴
- **"He, too, is a son of Abraham" (19:9).** John warned in 3:8 that being Abraham's child by blood counts for nothing. Here a man the town wrote off is called a real son. 🔴
- **19:10 is Luke's mission statement:** "the Son of Man has come to seek and to save the lost." It echoes God in Ezekiel 34:16, "I will seek the lost." 🔴
- **Why the parable (19:11).** "Because He was near Jerusalem, and they thought that the kingdom of God was going to appear immediately." Luke tells you what it's answering. 🔴
- **"Your mina has made ten minas" (19:16).** The faithful slaves credit the master's money, not their own work. 🔴
- **"Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!" (19:38).** Compare the angels at Jesus's birth: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace" (2:14). 🔴
- **Only Luke has the tears (19:41–44).** At the height of the parade Jesus weeps over the city. 🔴
- **"The things which make for peace" (19:42)** is the phrase from the king asking for terms in 14:32. 🔴 for the wording.
- **"The time of your visitation" (19:44).** The same word family as Zechariah's "He has visited us" (1:68). God came to visit, and the city missed it. 🔴
- **Luke cuts Isaiah short (19:46).** Isaiah 56:7 says "a house of prayer for all the peoples." Luke quotes only "a house of prayer," then adds Jeremiah 7:11, "robbers' den." 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Jericho** sat on the trade road into Judea from the east, a natural place for a tax post. A chief tax collector there was rich, and seen as a traitor working for Rome. 🔴
- **Grown men didn't run or climb trees.** It meant hiking up your robe in public. Bailey reads the sycamore as a hiding place too: big leaves, low branches, a hated man who didn't dare push through the crowd. 🟡
- **The village picks the host.** When an important visitor came, the community decided which house would host him, to honor the town. Jesus skips all that and picks the one house everyone would have vetoed, and takes the crowd's anger himself. 🟡 Bailey.
- **Two repayment laws.** A man who confessed on his own repaid what he took plus a fifth (Lev 6:5; Num 5:7). Fourfold was the penalty for a convicted sheep thief (Exod 22:1). Zacchaeus qualifies for the lighter rate and volunteers for the heavier one. 🔴 for the laws.
- **The pledge is over the top on purpose.** Half to the poor plus fourfold back can't all be paid. Bailey says in that culture the exaggeration is what makes the promise believable, and nobody expected the math to work. 🟡
- **A nobleman who went to get a kingdom.** When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus went to Rome to be confirmed as king, and a Jewish delegation followed him to argue against it (Josephus, *Antiquities* 17). Jesus's hearers in Jericho, where Archelaus had built, knew that story. 🔴
- **A mina** was about a hundred days' wages. 🔴
- **The slaughter order (19:27) is never carried out** in the story. Bailey argues the master has been generous three times and the order is a pause, not the last word. Wright takes it straight, as judgment on Jerusalem. 🔵
- **Return of the King.** Wright reads the parable as Israel's God coming back to Zion, promised in Malachi 3:1 ("the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to His temple") and Zechariah 14. Jesus isn't describing that return; he's doing it as he rides in. Most of church history read it as the second coming. 🔵
- **A donkey, not a warhorse.** Zechariah 9:9 has the king coming "humble, and mounted on a donkey," and 9:10 says he will cut off the war horse and speak peace to the nations. A king rode a horse to war and a donkey in peace. 🔴
- **Cloaks on the road** is how Israel crowned Jehu (2 Kgs 9:13). "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD" is Psalm 118:26, a pilgrim psalm sung going up to the temple. 🔴
- **The Mount of Olives** is where Zechariah 14:4 puts the LORD's feet on the day he comes. Jesus starts down it toward the city. 🔴 for Zechariah; 🟡 for the link.
- **"Barricade against you" (19:43).** In AD 70 the Roman general Titus built a wall around Jerusalem to starve it out, then leveled the temple. Josephus describes it. 🔴
- **The temple courts** covered about thirty-five acres. The selling happened in the outer court, the one place Gentiles could come to pray. Bailey says the action stopped the afternoon sacrifice that day; that detail rests on him alone. 🔴 for the size and the court; 🔵 for the stopped sacrifice.
- **Divine council:** if Wright is right, the King coming up the road is Yahweh himself returning to his house, and the crowd's "peace in heaven" sounds like the angels of 2:14. There's no council scene, but the question in the air is who the real king is. 🔵

## My notes
- I always thought Zacchaeus would have a much bigger role, with as much as we sang about him in Sunday school, and then it turns out that's it. Ten verses. 🔴
- What changed it for me is where he sits. He's the last person Jesus meets before Jerusalem, and he's the answer to the rich ruler: "The ruler walked away. The tax collector ran up a tree." Luke 18 says the rich can't save themselves; Luke 19 shows a rich man being saved. 🟡
- 19:9, "son of Abraham," is John's warning in 3:8 turned positive. 19:10 is Luke's thesis sentence, saved for the moment that proves it. 🟡
- From Bailey, for my mentee: the village decides who hosts a visitor, and Jesus going to Zacchaeus's house was a slight to the crowd. Zacchaeus promising half to the poor and fourfold back would have been impossible to pay; he's being hyperbolic. 🟡
- The teaching line I use for the Jericho pair (18:35–19:10): the crowd between you and Jesus is never the final word, and sometimes the church is the crowd. 🟡
- **Pounds (post 15).** Archelaus going to Rome; Bailey on doing business openly as the servant of a hated king. **Wright (added live):** not the second coming but the return of Yahweh to Zion (Mal 3:1–2). Snodgrass gives a third position: the kingdom will not come immediately, but the king has. 🔵

Bailey adds the size and the stopped sacrifice, and reads it as an acted-out parable of the temple's end. I flagged the stopped sacrifice as single-source. 🔵

## What the chapter is doing
- Caesar Augustus orders a census, and that sends Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, David's town. Mary gives birth and lays the baby in a manger.
- An angel and then a whole army of heaven announce the birth to shepherds working the night shift. They go, find the baby, and tell everyone.
- Forty days later the family brings Jesus to the temple. Two old people waiting on God, Simeon and Anna, recognize him. Nobody else does.
- At twelve Jesus stays behind in the temple. His first words in Luke are about "My Father's house" (2:49). Then he goes home and grows up (2:52).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Guest room," not "inn" (2:7).** The LSB already reads "there was no place for them in the guest room." The Greek word is *kataluma*. Luke knows the word for a commercial inn, *pandocheion*, and uses it in the Good Samaritan (10:34). The only other time he uses *kataluma* is the upper room of the Last Supper (22:11), a guest room in a private house. 🔴
- **No grumpy innkeeper.** There's no innkeeper anywhere in the text. That character comes from later retellings, not from Luke. 🔴
- **The manger is the sign (2:12).** The angel doesn't tell the shepherds to look for a palace or a crowd. He tells them to look for a baby lying where the animals eat. Wright: the one who will feed the world is lying in a feeding trough. 🔴 for the sign; 🟡 for Wright's reading of it.
- **Three titles in one sentence (2:11).** "A Savior, who is Christ the Lord." Savior was a title Rome used for emperors. Christ is Israel's anointed king. Lord (*kyrios*) is how the Greek Old Testament says the name of God. All three get hung on a newborn. 🔴
- **"Do not be afraid" again (2:10).** Zechariah (1:13), Mary (1:30), now the shepherds. Three for three. When heaven shows up, people come undone, and the messenger has to steady them first. 🔴
- **Shepherds hear it first.** Not priests, not kings. People on the bottom rung, outside at night. Same pattern as Mary's song in 1:52: God lifts up the humble. 🔴
- **Two birds, not a lamb (2:24).** Leviticus 12:8 lets a family that can't afford a lamb bring two turtledoves or pigeons. The Messiah's family is poor. 🔴
- **The Spirit three times (2:25–27).** The Spirit is upon Simeon, the Spirit told him, the Spirit brings him into the temple. Luke is the gospel of the Spirit, and this is how it keeps showing it. 🔴
- **"A Light for revelation to the Gentiles" (2:32).** Simeon quotes Isaiah 49:6, and it reaches past Israel to the nations. Paul quotes the same verse in Acts 13:47. The Gentile thread starts in a baby's dedication. 🔴
- **A sword for Mary (2:35).** The good news has a shadow on it already. Simeon says the child will make many fall and rise, and his mother's own soul will be pierced. Most read this as pointing to the cross. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for the cross reading.
- **A man and a woman.** Simeon and Anna. Luke pairs men and women over and over (the lost sheep and the lost coin in ch. 15 is the famous one). 🔴
- **First words (2:49).** "Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?" Before any miracle or sermon, Jesus knows whose he is. His parents don't get it (2:50). 🔴
- **He grew (2:52).** "Advancing in wisdom and stature." Wright takes this straight: Jesus really grew up. He didn't arrive knowing everything. 🔴

## Read it like 5 BC, not 2026
- **Augustus thought he was running the world.** Augustus called himself son of a god (*divi filius*) and the bringer of peace. His census decree is what puts the true Son of God in David's town. Wright: the Empire thought it was running history. It was running an errand. 🔴 for Augustus's titles; 🟡 for reading Luke as deliberate counter-story.
- **The census date is a real puzzle.** Herod the Great died in 4 BC, and Matthew has Jesus born under Herod. The well-known census under Quirinius as governor of Syria is AD 6. Several solutions are on the table (an earlier enrollment, a different reading of "first"). 🔴 that the question is real; ⬜ for the answer.
- **The house had the animals in it.** A Palestinian peasant house was mostly one room. The family lived on a raised floor, and the animals came in at night to a lower level by the door, for warmth and so nobody stole them. Mangers were cut into the floor at the edge of the family's part. So a manger means a house, not a barn. Some houses had a guest room built on the end or on the roof. (Bailey, *Jesus through Middle Eastern Eyes*, ch. 1.) 🔴
- **Nobody turns away a son of David in David's town.** Joseph was coming home to his family's village. In an honor and shame culture, sending a pregnant relative out to the animals would have shamed the whole family and village. The guest room was full, so they were taken into the family room. "Full of census relatives" is a guess, and a reasonable one. 🔴 for the culture; 🟡 for who filled the room.
- **Shepherds had a low name.** They worked nights outside town and were often treated as unreliable. Wright notes they couldn't be trusted as witnesses in court. 🟡
- **"The heavenly host" is an army (2:13).** "Host" means army. This is the same God of armies Israel prayed to, and the army of heaven, the council around his throne, shows up singing over a feeding trough. Real angels are frightening. The greeting-card babies with wings came much later. 🔴 for "host" as army; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Peace means more than calm (2:14).** In Israel's Bible, *shalom* is everything set right. Wright reads the angels' "peace on earth" as that, not a private feeling. Rome also sold peace, the *Pax Romana*, kept by legions. 🔴
- **Forty days and eight days.** Circumcision on the eighth day (Lev 12:3), the mother's purification after forty days (Lev 12:4–8), and the firstborn given to God (Exod 13:2). Luke shows the family doing all of it. Jesus comes into the world inside the covenant, not around it. 🔴
- **Twelve is the edge of manhood.** In Jewish practice a boy was close to taking on the commandments for himself. Families traveled to Passover in big village caravans, which is how a twelve-year-old could be missing a whole day without anyone panicking. 🔴 for the caravan in the text (2:44); 🟡 for the age custom in the first century.

## My notes

Matthew puts them at a house (Matt 2:11), not a manger, and Herod kills boys "two years old and under" (2:16). Every manger scene with shepherds and wise men together is two books mashed into one. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus is teaching in the temple the week he dies. The chief priests, scribes and elders come at him: "by what authority are You doing these things?" (20:2). He answers with a question about John's baptism and they won't touch it.
- He tells the people a parable: a vineyard, tenants who beat the owner's slaves, and a beloved son they throw out and kill. The leaders know it's about them (20:19).
- Then the traps. Spies ask about taxes to Caesar. Sadducees ask about a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus walks out of both.
- He finishes on offense: how can the Messiah be David's son when David calls him "Lord" (Psalm 110)? Then a warning about scribes who love long robes and "devour widows' houses" (20:47).

## Pay attention to this
- **The question behind the whole chapter is authority.** 20:2 asks it, the parable answers it (the son is the heir), and Psalm 110 closes it (David's Lord sits at God's right hand). 🟡
- **Isaiah 5 is the backdrop, and Jesus changes it.** In Isaiah 5:1–7 the vineyard is Israel and the vineyard gets destroyed. In Jesus' story the vineyard isn't criticized at all. The *renters* get replaced. Bailey: Jesus' judgment is milder than his source. 🔴 for the Isaiah parallel; 🟡 for the "change of management" read.
- **"Perhaps they will respect him" (20:13).** Arabic versions for a thousand years read it "they will feel shame before him." Bailey's point: the owner isn't hoping for good manners. He's gambling that total vulnerability will wake up a dead sense of honor in violent men. 🟡
- **They throw him out of the vineyard first, then kill him (20:15).** Outside the walls. Hold it next to the cross. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the echo.
- **"May it never be!" (20:16).** The crowd hears the ending and recoils. Jesus "looked at them" before he answers with the psalm. 🔴
- **The stone and the son.** Hebrew *ben* is son, *'eben* is stone. The stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22) is the son of the parable. Bailey offers it as a possible wordplay, not a settled one. 🔵
- **Psalm 118 is the entry psalm.** "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord" (19:38) and "the stone which the builders rejected" (20:17) come from the same stretch of Psalm 118. The day before, Jesus said the stones would cry out (19:40). 🔴
- **20:18 pulls in two more stones:** Isaiah 8:14–15 (the stone people trip on) and Daniel 2:34–45 (the stone that crushes the statue and becomes a kingdom). 🔴
- **"Render to Caesar" (20:25).** The coin carries Caesar's image. The listener knew who carries God's image. 🔴 for the coin; 🟡 for the image read.
- **"Sons of God, being sons of the resurrection" (20:36).** Jesus says the raised are "like angels" in that they can't die and don't marry. Not that people become angels. 🔴
- **The widows at the end (20:47).** The scribes who want the best seats are eating widows out of house and home. Chapter 21 opens with a widow giving everything. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Absentee landlords were normal.** In the Herodian period wealthy owners often lived far from their estates and leased them to tenants for a share of the crop. The setting was ordinary to Jesus' audience. 🔴
- **What the tenants were counting on.** The post first said the tenants were banking on squatters' rights. That needed fixing. The Mishnah does give title after three years of occupation, but *Bava Batra* 3.1–6 shuts tenants out of that claim. So the tenants aren't working a legal loophole. They're grabbing, the way Ahab grabbed Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21). 🔴 for the Mishnah ruling; 🟡 for the Naboth parallel.
- **Why the son comes alone.** Bailey sets the parable next to a later rabbinic story (Rabbi Nissim, died 1040) where God goes in person to avenge a mere verbal slight to Moses, and the going is the tenth plague. That's what a first-century audience expects after three slaves are beaten: force. Instead the owner sends his son, unarmed. Bailey calls it anger turned into grace. 🔴 that the source exists; 🟡 for using a much later text as a window on the expectation.
- **The heir alone looks like weakness.** An heir with no armed men behind him could look like a son whose father is dead or has no force left. Kill him and nobody is left to claim the land. "That is not stupidity. It is a calculation, and it is wrong." 🟡
- **The vineyard was not a riddle.** Isaiah 5 made Israel God's vineyard and every listener knew it. The slaves are the prophets (2 Chr 24:21; 36:16; Neh 9:26; Jer 26:20–24). Luke says the leaders got it in real time and wanted to arrest him "that very hour." 🔴
- **The tax question was a trap with two jaws.** Say yes and the crowd, who hated Roman tax, turns. Say no and you're a rebel handed to the governor, which is exactly what 20:20 says they wanted. The denarius under Tiberius carried the emperor's face and a title calling him son of the divine Augustus. 🔴
- **Sadducees ran the temple and read only Moses.** No resurrection, no angels (Acts 23:8). So Jesus answers them from the burning bush in Exodus 3, their own Torah: God is still "the God of Abraham" long after Abraham died. 🔴 The seven-brothers case was likely a stock argument against the Pharisees; Tobit has a woman with seven dead husbands. 🟡
- **Divine council in 20:36 and 20:42–43.** "Sons of God" is council language in the Old Testament (Job 1:6; Psalm 82; Deut 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek). Jesus puts raised humans in that family: "sons of God, being sons of the resurrection." 🟡 for reading it as council language; 🔴 that the phrase is there. Then Psalm 110: "Sit at My right hand, until I put Your enemies as a footstool." In Heiser's frame those enemies are the rebel powers, not only human kings (1 Cor 15:25–26; Eph 1:20–21). 🔴 for the New Testament's use of the psalm; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Long robes and best seats.** Honor in that world was public and it was seated. Where you sat at a banquet told everyone your rank (14:7–11). 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- A poor widow drops two tiny coins in the temple treasury, and Jesus says she gave more than all the rich (21:1–4).
- People admire the temple's stones. Jesus says not one will be left on another (21:5–6). They ask when.
- He answers on two tracks: what comes first (fakes, wars, persecution, Jerusalem surrounded by armies) and what comes at the end (signs in the sky, the Son of Man on a cloud).
- In the middle sits a promise for the courtroom: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your opponents will be able to resist or refute" (21:15).
- It closes with the fig tree, a call to stay awake, and a picture of Jesus teaching in the temple by day and sleeping on the Mount of Olives by night.

## Pay attention to this
- **The widow comes right after 20:47.** Jesus just said the scribes "devour widows' houses." Then a widow puts in "all that she had for living." The chapter break hides the link. 🔴
- **"Not one stone upon another" (21:6).** Herod's temple was one of the great buildings of the world. Jesus says it comes down. 🔴
- **"The end does not follow immediately" (21:9).** Wars and earthquakes are not the clock. Jesus slows his hearers down. 🔴
- **"Before all these things" (21:12).** Persecution comes first, before the cosmic signs. The disciples' own trial is the front of the line. 🔴
- **Don't rehearse, not don't study (21:14).** The verb is *promeletao*, used only here in the New Testament. It's the classical word for rehearsing a speech ahead of time. Robertson: what's forbidden is preparing the defense speech, "not preparation of a sermon." 🔴
- **"I will give you" (21:15).** In Luke 12:12 the Holy Spirit teaches you. Here Jesus says "I myself." Luke doesn't treat that as a conflict. In Acts 16:6–7 "the Holy Spirit" and "the Spirit of Jesus" sit in back-to-back verses doing the same job. 🔴
- **Then Acts 6:10.** Stephen's opponents "were unable to oppose the wisdom and the Spirit by whom he was speaking." Same Greek verb, *antistenai*, as "resist" in 21:15. Luke writes the promise, then shows it coming true. 🔴
- **"Not a hair of your head will perish" (21:18), one verse after "they will put some of you to death" (21:16).** So the promise isn't that nobody dies. It's full protection of the person, an Old Testament idiom (1 Sam 14:45; 2 Sam 14:11). 🔴
- **"Jerusalem surrounded by armies" (21:20).** Where Mark and Matthew say "the abomination of desolation," Luke says it plainly for Gentile readers: armies around the city. 🔴
- **"The times of the Gentiles" (21:24).** Jerusalem trampled by the nations for a set time, and then that time ends. 🔴 for the phrase; ⬜ for what ends it.

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **The courtroom was real and close to home.** Second Temple Jews ran local courts of seven elders, and courts of twenty-three in bigger towns. The men who taught Torah on the Sabbath also sat as judges. The standard sentence was thirty-nine lashes (Deut 25:1–3 says forty; they stopped one short). Mark 13:9, "you will be beaten in synagogues," is not a figure of speech. 🔴
- **You could only be flogged if you submitted to it.** The lashes were for Jews who wanted to keep their place in the community. So when Paul says "five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one" (2 Cor 11:24), he kept walking back in. 🔴 for the practice; 🟡 for the read of Paul.
- **The Roman side.** No public prosecutors. Private accusers brought the charges, the governor sat on his tribunal with a council of advisers, and he could skip normal procedure if he chose. Non-citizens had no claim to Roman protections. Citizens could appeal, and Paul did (Acts 22:25–29; 25:11). 🔴
- **"Kings and governors" (21:12) is Acts in outline.** Paul stands before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa. 🔴
- **Isaiah 50:4 is behind "a mouth and wisdom."** The Servant has "the tongue of those who are taught." The Hebrew *limmud* means a pupil, a disciple. Keil and Delitzsch: his ear is woken every morning and he's taught "what and how" to speak. So the Old Testament picture behind this promise is a man in daily lessons, not a man who never prepares. 🔴
- **God putting words in a messenger's mouth is an old pattern.** Moses (Exod 4:12), Jeremiah (Jer 1:9), the prophet like Moses (Deut 18:18). Jesus puts his disciples inside it. 🔴
- **The temple fell in AD 70.** Rome surrounded Jerusalem, the city fell, the temple burned. Eusebius says the Judean Christians fled to Pella before the end. 🔴 for the war; 🟡 for the Pella report (it comes from Eusebius, writing much later).
- **"The powers of the heavens will be shaken" (21:26).** The prophets used sun, moon and stars going dark for God judging nations and the powers behind them (Isa 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10). In Deut 32 and Psalm 82 the nations sit under heavenly rulers, and "the host of heaven" in Isaiah 34:4 sits right next to judgment on the nations. 🔴 for the prophetic language; 🟡 for reading "powers" here as more than stars.
- **"The Son of Man coming in a cloud" (21:27)** is Daniel 7:13. In Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days in a heavenly court and receives the kingdom. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Passover is close. The leaders want Jesus dead but fear the crowd. Then "Satan entered into Judas" (22:3), and Judas sells them a way to take him quietly.
- Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve and gives it a new meaning: "This is My body which is given for you," and the cup after supper is "the new covenant in My blood" (22:19–20).
- At the same table they argue about who's greatest. Jesus tells Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, that Peter will deny him three times, and that it's time for money bags and swords. "It is enough" (22:38).
- On the Mount of Olives he prays "not My will, but Yours be done." An angel strengthens him. His sweat is "like drops of blood."
- Judas arrives with a kiss and a crowd. A disciple cuts off a slave's ear and Jesus heals it. Peter follows to the high priest's courtyard and denies him three times. The rooster crows, "the Lord turned and looked at Peter," and Peter goes out and cries.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Satan entered into Judas" (22:3).** Luke names who is behind the betrayal before Judas says a word. The devil left Jesus in 4:13 "until an opportune time." This is that time. 🔴
- **Judas still chose (22:4–6).** He goes, he negotiates, he takes the money, he looks for his chance. The text holds both, Satan in him and Judas choosing, and never explains how. 🔴
- **"Iscariot" doesn't mean "liar."** That idea started with a misread entry in Jastrow's Aramaic dictionary and spread into reference books. There's no such Aramaic word. 🔴
- **The guest room again (22:11).** "Where is the guest room?" is *kataluma*, the same word as "no room in the inn" at 2:7. Luke uses it twice: Jesus has no guest room at his birth and borrows one before his death. 🔴
- **Two cups (22:17, 22:20).** Luke is the only Gospel with a cup before the bread and a cup "after they had eaten." The one he makes the new covenant is the one after supper. 🔴
- **"Benefactors" (22:25).** Greek kings and Roman officials took that word as an official title. Jesus says "not so with you" and calls himself "the one who serves." 🔴
- **"Satan has demanded to sift all of you" (22:31).** The "you" is plural. Satan asks for all of them, and Jesus prays for Peter, so Peter can strengthen the rest once he's turned back. 🔴
- **"Numbered with transgressors" (22:37).** Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 the night he's arrested. Two swords are enough to make him look like a criminal. They aren't enough to fight. 🟡
- **"It is enough" (22:38).** Most likely "enough of this!" Hours later Jesus stops the sword and heals the wound. 🟡
- **The cup in the garden (22:42).** Hours after handing them the cup of the covenant, he asks the Father to take a cup away from him, and then drinks it. 🔴
- **The last healing is for an enemy (22:50–51).** Only Luke tells it. Jesus touches the ear of a man who came to arrest him. 🔴
- **"This hour and the authority of darkness are yours" (22:53).** Jesus names who's running the night. 🔴
- **"The Lord turned and looked at Peter" (22:61).** Only Luke has the look. No words. It breaks him. 🔴
- **"At the right hand of the power of God" (22:69).** At his trial Jesus puts Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 together about himself. The trial is about to turn on that sentence. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Passover was the Exodus told around a table.** Every food on the table already retold the rescue from Egypt. Jesus doesn't invent a new ritual. He takes the one they had and says it's about him. 🔴 The later seder has four cups. Calling Luke's cup "after supper" the third cup, the cup of redemption, reads the later order back in. 🟡
- **"In remembrance of Me."** Hebrew remembering (*zakar*) meant more than recall. At Passover a father told his son it was because of what Yahweh did for *me* when I came out of Egypt (Exod 13:8). Remembering meant taking part. 🔴
- **Satan in the council frame.** "The satan" in Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 is the accuser who comes before God and asks permission to test someone. "Satan has demanded" (22:31) uses that same move: he asks, and Jesus goes over his head in prayer. 🔴 for the Old Testament scenes; 🟡 for reading 22:31 through them.
- **Darkness as a power, not a time of day.** "The authority of darkness" (22:53) is the same language Paul uses for the domain believers are rescued out of (Col 1:13). The meta notes for Luke rank 22:53 as one of the clearest places the gospel names the cosmic powers. 🔴
- **The powers walked into their own trap.** Paul says none of "the rulers of this age" understood God's plan, because "if they had understood it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:8). Heiser reads those rulers as spiritual powers, not only Pilate and Caiaphas, and reads the Old Testament picture of the Messiah as a scattered mosaic, clear only after the fact. So the satan pushes the crucifixion forward through Judas and ends up serving the plan that strips him (Col 2:15). 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **An angel strengthens him (22:43).** The council isn't only enemies tonight. Heaven sends help to the man in the garden. ⬜ on the verse itself (see the manuscript note below).
- **Gethsemane means oil press.** *Gat shemanim*: a stone installation where olives were crushed under weighted beams. Luke just says "the Mount of Olives," but the place the other Gospels name is the crushing place. 🔴 for the name; 🟡 as a teaching picture.
- **The cup was God's wrath.** In the prophets the cup is what the guilty are made to drink: Psalm 75:8, Jeremiah 25:15–28, Isaiah 51:17. And Isaiah 51:22 has God promising to take that cup out of his people's hand. 🔴 for the Old Testament picture; 🟡 that this is the cup in 22:42.
- **The sweat "like" blood (22:44).** Two honest notes. Verses 43–44 are missing from some early manuscripts, so many Bibles bracket them. And "like drops of blood" is a comparison. There is a rare stress condition (hematidrosis) where blood mixes into sweat, and Luke the doctor chose "like." 🔴 for the manuscript note; 🔵 for hematidrosis as what Luke saw.
- **Night trial, morning council.** Luke has the beating and mocking at night and the council meeting "as the day came" (22:66). They needed a daytime verdict to take to Pilate, who held the power of death. 🔴
- **Peter's denial was public.** In an honor culture, saying "I do not know Him" in front of a courtyard crowd was cutting himself off from Jesus before witnesses. John 21 answers it with three questions, one for each denial. 🔴 for John 21; 🟡 for the honor read.

## What the chapter is doing
- The council hands Jesus to Pilate with political charges: misleading the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, claiming to be a king (23:2).
- Pilate finds no guilt. He sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who wants a miracle, gets silence, mocks him and sends him back. Herod and Pilate become friends that day.
- Pilate says three times that Jesus has done nothing worthy of death. The crowd asks for Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, and Pilate gives them what they want.
- On the way out Simon of Cyrene carries the cross and Jesus warns the women of Jerusalem. At The Skull he prays "Father, forgive them," promises a dying criminal "today you shall be with Me in Paradise," and gives up his spirit after three hours of darkness and a torn veil.
- A Roman centurion praises God and says "Certainly this man was righteous." Joseph of Arimathea buries him, and the women watch where he's laid.

## Pay attention to this
- **The charges are political, and two of them are false.** 20:25 already showed he didn't forbid taxes to Caesar. 🔴
- **Three times "no guilt" (23:4, 14, 22).** Herod finds nothing too (23:15). Luke stacks up the Roman verdicts on purpose. 🔴
- **Herod's silent prisoner (23:9).** Herod "had wanted to see Him for a long time" and hoped for a sign. Jesus gives him nothing. 🔴
- **Two enemies become friends over him (23:12).** 🔴 Acts 4:27 picks it up: Herod and Pilate gathered together against Jesus. 🔴
- **Barabbas means "son of the father."** The guilty son of the father goes free and the innocent Son of the Father dies. 🔴 for the name; 🟡 for the pairing (Just).
- **"Release" runs all through the scene.** Pilate keeps wanting to release Jesus (23:16, 20, 22) and ends up releasing the murderer (23:25). 🔴
- **Simon carries the cross "behind Jesus" (23:26).** That's discipleship language from 9:23 and 14:27, acted out by a stranger. 🟡
- **"Father, forgive them" (23:34)** and **"today you shall be with Me in Paradise" (23:43)** are in Luke only. Jesus is still saving people while he dies. 🔴
- **"He saved others; let Him save Himself" (23:35).** The rulers, the soldiers and one criminal all say "save yourself." That's the one thing he won't do. 🔴
- **The second criminal gets it right (23:41–42).** "This man has done nothing wrong" and "remember me when You come in Your kingdom." A dying thief sees the king nobody else sees. 🔴
- **"Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit" (23:46)** is Psalm 31:5, an evening prayer of trust. 🔴
- **Breast-beating (23:48).** Bailey: the only other place in the Bible anyone beats his chest is the tax collector in 18:13. Men in that culture didn't, so it marks real anguish. The man asking for atonement and the crowd that just watched it made. 🟡
- **The women saw where he was laid (23:55).** They're the witnesses who make Easter morning possible. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Rome held the power of death.** The council could condemn but needed the governor to execute. Rome had no public prosecutor, so private accusers brought the case, which is what the chief priests do. 🔴
- **Pilate and Caiaphas are real people.** The Pilate Stone at Caesarea names "Pontius Pilatus, Prefect of Judea." The Caiaphas ossuary carries the high priest's family name. 🔴
- **Crucifixion was the penalty for rebels and slaves.** The Yehohanan heel bone (Givat HaMivtar, 1968), with an iron nail still through it, is the only physical remains of a crucifixion victim ever found. It proves the method. The details of how he was nailed were revised in 1985, so it doesn't show exactly how Jesus was hung. 🔴
- **"Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."** Deut 21:23 made a crucified Messiah a contradiction to a Jewish listener. That's why the rulers can scoff, and why Paul calls the cross a stumbling block (1 Cor 1:23). 🔴
- **The inverted scapegoat.** On the Day of Atonement one goat died and the other was sent away carrying the people's sin (Lev 16). Lunn argues the Barabbas scene runs that backward: the innocent one dies, and the guilty one is released *to* the crowd, so the sin comes back on them instead of going away. 🔴 for Leviticus 16; 🟡 for the allusion.
- **Paradise.** In Second Temple Judaism *paradeisos* (a Persian word for a walled garden) was the name for the garden where the righteous dead are kept with God (2 Cor 12:4; Rev 2:7). "Today" puts the thief there the same day. 🔴
- **Darkness at noon (23:44–45).** It can't be a solar eclipse: Passover falls at full moon. In the prophets darkness at midday is judgment (Amos 8:9; Joel 2:10). 🔴 for the eclipse point and the prophets; 🟡 for reading it as judgment falling on Jesus.
- **Divine council in the darkness.** The meta notes on Luke list 23:44–45 with the council passages: the sky goes dark the way the prophets describe when God judges nations and the powers over them. Put it beside 22:53, "this hour and the authority of darkness are yours." The powers have their hour, and it ends at the ninth hour. 🟡
- **The veil.** The curtain between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place (Exod 26:31–33), where only the high priest went, once a year (Lev 16). Luke says it was "torn in two." 🔴 Mark and Matthew add "from top to bottom," God tearing it from his side. 🔴
- **No archaeology for the veil or the darkness, and there couldn't be.** A torn curtain leaves no artifact, and the temple burned in AD 70. Those details rest on the Gospel witnesses. The later pagan mentions of the darkness (Thallus, Phlegon) are secondhand and disputed. 🟡
- **Jewish sources record the temple failing, not the curtain tearing.** The Talmud (Yoma 39b) says that in the forty years before the temple fell, around AD 30 on, the doors of the sanctuary opened by themselves, and Yohanan ben Zakkai read it with Zechariah 11:1 as a sign of the end. Josephus and Tacitus report doors opening too, but tied to the war in AD 66–70, not the crucifixion. Doors are not the curtain, so don't claim it's the same event. 🔴 that the texts say it; 🟡 for linking it.
- **"Righteous" (23:47).** The centurion's word, *dikaios*, also means innocent. A Gentile soldier who ran the execution gives the last Roman verdict. 🔴
