## What the chapter is doing
- Women come at dawn with spices to finish a burial. The stone is rolled away, the body is gone, and two men in dazzling clothes ask, "Why do you seek the living One among the dead?" (24:5).
- The apostles think the women's report is nonsense. Peter runs to look and finds only the linen wrappings.
- Two disciples walk to Emmaus and a stranger joins them. They tell him "we were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel." He walks them through Moses and the prophets, and they know him when he breaks the bread.
- Jesus stands among the eleven, shows his hands and feet, eats broiled fish, opens their minds to the Scriptures, and sends them to all the nations as witnesses.
- At Bethany he lifts his hands, blesses them and is carried up into heaven. They go back to Jerusalem with great joy and are "continually in the temple blessing God."

## Pay attention to this
- **They came to bury a body (24:1).** Nobody at the tomb is expecting a resurrection. 🔴
- **"Two men... in dazzling clothing" (24:4).** Luke calls Moses and Elijah "two men" at the Transfiguration (9:30), and the angels at the ascension are "two men" in white (Acts 1:10). In 24:23 these two are called angels. 🔴
- **"Remember how He spoke to you" (24:6–8).** Jesus said this three times (9:22, 9:44, 18:31–33). They had heard it and it didn't register. 🔴
- **The men didn't believe the women (24:11).** "Nonsense." Stein: the people least ready to invent a resurrection are the ones who wouldn't believe it. 🔴
- **"We were hoping" (24:21).** Past tense. A dead Messiah meant a failed Messiah. That's the whole problem of 9:22 said out loud. 🔴
- **"Was it not necessary" (24:26).** The Messiah *had* to suffer and then enter his glory. Stein calls the Emmaus walk the most important passage in Luke on why Jesus died. 🔴
- **"Their eyes were prevented" (24:16) and "their eyes were opened" (24:31).** Both are things done to them. God hid him and God showed him. It wasn't the nail marks or a special way of breaking bread (Stein). 🔴
- **Word, then table.** Their hearts burned while he opened the Scriptures (24:32), and they knew him in the breaking of the bread (24:35). 🔴
- **"Touch Me and see" (24:39).** Luke never mentions nail marks. The hands and feet prove he has a body, not a ghost. Then he eats fish in front of them. 🔴
- **"Not believing because of their joy" (24:41).** Too good to be true. 🔴
- **"He opened their minds" (24:45).** First their eyes at Emmaus, then their minds. They didn't figure it out; he gave it to them. 🔴
- **"To all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem" (24:47).** Forgiveness for the nations is itself "what is written." That's Acts 1:8 in one line. 🔴
- **"You are witnesses" (24:48).** Back to 1:2, "eyewitnesses and servants of the word." 🔴
- **Temple at the start, temple at the end.** Luke opened with Zechariah in the temple, unable to speak the blessing (1:22). It closes with Jesus blessing them, and the disciples in the temple blessing God. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Women's word counted for little in court.** Josephus says women's testimony wasn't accepted (Antiquities 4.219). Nobody inventing a story in that world makes women the first witnesses. Luke does it anyway, and names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James (24:10). 🔴
- **Resurrection was for the end of the world, for everyone at once.** Martha says it: "he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" (John 11:24). One man rising in the middle of history wasn't a category anyone had. 🔴
- **A suffering Messiah wasn't on the menu.** Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Zechariah 12:10 were there, but nobody had put them together as "the Messiah dies and rises." Whether any pre-Christian Jews saw a suffering Messiah is debated (Stein). 🔴 that it's debated.
- **"Moses... all the prophets... the Psalms" (24:27, 44).** That's the three-part Hebrew Bible: Law, Prophets and Writings, with Psalms leading the Writings. "All the Scriptures" means the whole thing. 🟡 for the three-part canon this early.
- **Ghosts were real to them.** "They were thinking that they were seeing a spirit" (24:37). Same fear as the night on the lake: "It's a ghost!" (Mark 6:49). A bodiless spirit was the obvious explanation. Eating fish rules it out. 🔴
- **Hospitality flips at Emmaus.** They're the hosts ("Stay with us"), but he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it, the host's job. 🟡
- **Lifted hands and a blessing (24:50).** That's how the high priest blessed the people (Lev 9:22; Sirach 50:20–21 shows the high priest raising his hands over the assembly). Zechariah the priest couldn't give the blessing in chapter 1. Jesus gives it at the end. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the priestly reading.
- **Divine council: the ascension is an enthronement.** In Daniel 7:13 the Son of Man goes up "with the clouds of heaven" to the Ancient of Days and is given the kingdom. Jesus told the council he'd be "seated at the right hand of the power of God" (22:69). The New Testament says that seat puts him over "all rule and authority and power and dominion" (Eph 1:20–21) and that angels, authorities and powers are subject to him (1 Pet 3:22). In Heiser's frame those are the powers of the nations from Deut 32:8–9. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the council read.
- **The nations are the point.** The meta notes for Luke read the book through Deut 32:8–9: the nations were handed to lesser powers, and Israel was kept as God's portion. Starting from Jerusalem and going to all the nations is the reclaiming of what was handed off. 🟡
- **"Clothed with power from on high" (24:49).** The Spirit at Pentecost, Acts 2. The verb is clothing language, like putting on a robe. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's work against every ruler in the region, Roman and Jewish, and then says the word of God came to a man in the wilderness.
- John calls the crowds to repent and be baptized, and tells them their family tree won't save them (3:8). He gives plain, practical answers to crowds, tax collectors and soldiers.
- John points past himself to one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Herod locks John up.
- Jesus is baptized. While he prays, heaven opens, the Spirit comes down, and the Father speaks: "You are My beloved Son" (3:22).
- Luke then runs Jesus' family line backward, past David and Abraham, all the way to "Adam, the son of God" (3:38).

## Pay attention to this
- **Seven names to set the date (3:1–2).** Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, Philip, Lysanias, Annas, Caiaphas. Luke is the careful historian, pinning the story to a year the other gospel writers don't give. Then the word of God skips all of them and lands on John in the desert. 🔴
- **"All flesh will see the salvation of God" (3:6).** Luke quotes Isaiah 40 one line further than Mark and Matthew do, and that extra line is the one about all flesh. 🔴
- **Abraham is not a ticket (3:8).** "Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham for our father.'" Ancestry is not covenant standing. Luke pays this off at 19:9, when Jesus calls Zacchaeus "a son of Abraham" because of what he does, not his blood. 🔴
- **Repentance is concrete (3:10–14).** Share your second tunic. Don't overcharge. Don't shake people down. John doesn't ask tax collectors or soldiers to quit, he tells them to stop cheating. 🔴
- **"For the forgiveness of sins" (3:3).** A sharp reader will ask about this line. John's baptism comes before Christian baptism exists. Repentance is the thing; the water is the sign of it. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for how it fits with later Christian baptism.
- **Jesus is praying (3:21).** Only Luke says Jesus was praying when heaven opened. Luke shows Jesus praying at every big turn: here, before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), at the Transfiguration (9:28–29), in the garden (22:41). 🔴
- **The whole Trinity in one scene (3:22).** The Son in the water, the Spirit coming down "in bodily form like a dove," the Father's voice. 🔴
- **The voice quotes Scripture.** "You are My beloved Son" echoes Psalm 2:7, the coronation psalm for David's king, and "in You I am well-pleased" echoes Isaiah 42:1, the Servant God delights in. King and Servant in one sentence. 🔴 for the echoes; 🟡 for reading them as deliberately joined.
- **"As was supposed" (3:23).** Luke has just told the virgin birth in ch. 1, so he flags that people thought Jesus was Joseph's son. 🔴
- **The line goes backward.** Matthew starts at Abraham and walks forward to Jesus. Luke starts at Jesus and walks back to Adam and then to God. Matthew goes back to the Jews. Luke goes back to Adam. 🔴
- **Through Nathan, not Solomon (3:31).** Matthew's line runs through King Solomon. Luke's runs through David's son Nathan. That is one of the main reasons the two lists differ. 🔴
- **An extra Cainan (3:36).** Luke lists a Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah who isn't in the Hebrew of Genesis 11. He's in the Greek Old Testament, the Bible Luke's readers used. 🔴

## Read it like AD 28, not 2026
- **The fifteenth year of Tiberius** works out to about AD 28–29. Pilate governed Judea AD 26–36. Herod here is Antipas, Herod the Great's son, ruling Galilee. Annas had been high priest and still held the power; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office. That's why Luke names both. 🔴
- **The high priest was a Roman appointment.** Rome put high priests in and took them out. The temple was the center of Jewish life, and the men running it sat inside Rome's system. Luke lists them right next to the Romans. 🔴
- **Washing rites were everywhere.** Jews washed for purity all the time, and the community at Qumran in the same wilderness made ritual washing central. What made John different was a one-time washing tied to turning your life around, done in the open for anyone. 🔴 for the washings; 🟡 for how unusual John's was.
- **The wilderness and the Jordan mean exodus.** Israel crossed the Jordan to enter the land. A prophet calling the whole nation back out to the Jordan to start over is a loaded picture. 🟡
- **"Brood of vipers" was an insult with teeth.** John is calling the crowd snakes' children, the opposite of Abraham's children. 🔴
- **Genealogies were not family trees.** Ancient lists telescoped. They skipped generations on purpose, and "son of" (Hebrew *ben*) can mean grandson or descendant. Matthew drops three kings to make his three sets of fourteen. Lists were built to make a point, not to list every uncle. 🔴
- **"Adam, the son of God" (3:38).** In the Bible, "son of God" is a title for beings God made directly and set in his family: Adam, the heavenly sons of God in Job 1 and Psalm 82, Israel as God's firstborn (Exod 4:22), David's king (Ps 2:7). Luke ends the line on that title two verses after the voice calls Jesus "My beloved Son," and then ch. 4 opens with the devil saying "If You are the Son of God." The first son of God failed his test in a garden; this one gets tested in a desert. 🔴 for the uses of the title; 🟡 for reading Luke's placement as on purpose (Heiser's sonship frame).
- **Prophets had been quiet.** Many in that day felt prophecy had faded since Malachi. "The word of God came to John" (3:2) is the same way the Old Testament prophets' books open (Jer 1:2, Hos 1:1). 🔴 for the formula; 🟡 for the "silence" feeling.

## My notes
- I first said the genealogy is "slightly different from Matthew's, but that's not the point." It's bigger than that. The direction is the point: Matthew writes for Jews and starts at Abraham; Luke writes for Gentiles and goes back to Adam, so Jesus belongs to everyone. 🔴
- On the "contradiction" between Matthew and Luke: these aren't detailed family trees. It's a list of people who are part of his line, and they're not including Uncle Bob, who nobody ever heard of. 🔴 The specific fixes (Matthew follows Joseph and Luke follows Mary, or a levirate marriage somewhere in the line) are theories. I'd say scholars have several answers and not pick one. ⬜
- I had the four women in the wrong gospel. I said Luke includes four Gentile women with scandal in their stories. That's Matthew (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba). Luke has no women in his list. ❌ Both still preach Gentile inclusion, by opposite methods: Matthew writes the outsiders into the line, Luke runs the line to Adam. 🟡
- Water baptism doesn't forgive sin. It's a sign of leaving your own way and being made new, like the world made out of chaos and water in Genesis 1. It's not a requirement for heaven; the thief on the cross was never baptized, and Jesus told him he'd be in paradise that day (23:43).
- John preached repentance, not forgiveness by water. Two different things. You can repent and not be forgiven, but you can't be forgiven if you don't repent.
- 3:8 gets answered at 19:9. John warns that Abraham's blood won't save you; Zacchaeus is called a son of Abraham for what he does.

## What the chapter is doing
- Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led into the wilderness for forty days and tested by the devil three times. He answers each one with Deuteronomy. The devil leaves "until an opportune time" (4:13).
- Back in Galilee, he reads Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and says, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing" (4:21).
- He reminds his hometown that Elijah and Elisha were sent to outsiders. The synagogue tries to throw him off a cliff, and he walks through them.
- In Capernaum he throws a demon out in the synagogue, heals Simon's mother-in-law, and heals the sick at sundown. Then he moves on to other towns, because "I was sent for this purpose" (4:43).

## Pay attention to this
- **"If You are the Son of God" (4:3, 4:9).** The chapter before ends with "Adam, the son of God." The devil goes straight at that title. 🔴
- **Three answers, all from Deuteronomy.** 8:3, 6:13, 6:16. These are the lessons Israel was supposed to learn in its own forty years in the wilderness. Jesus passes where Israel failed. 🔴 for the quotes; 🟡 for the Israel reading.
- **"It has been handed over to me" (4:6).** The devil claims the kingdoms of the world are his to give. Jesus doesn't argue the claim. He refuses the deal. 🔴
- **Luke's order is different.** Matthew ends with the mountain and the kingdoms. Luke ends at the temple in Jerusalem, the place his whole gospel is heading. 🔴
- **"Until an opportune time" (4:13).** The devil comes back. Luke names him again at 22:3, when Satan enters Judas. 🔴
- **Where Jesus stops reading (4:19).** Isaiah 61:2 goes on: "and the day of vengeance of our God." Jesus rolls up the scroll before that line. Mid-sentence. (Bailey, *Jesus through Middle Eastern Eyes*, p. 162.) 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for how deliberate it was.
- **He stitches in a line.** "To set free those who are oppressed" (4:18) isn't in Isaiah 61. It's from Isaiah 58:6. The reading has been edited. 🔴
- **"Speaking well of Him" may not be friendly (4:22).** Bailey, following Joachim Jeremias, says the Greek can be read as the crowd bearing witness *against* him. That would mean the hostility starts right away, not after a sudden mood swing. 🔵
- **The two examples are enemies (4:25–27).** The widow lived in Sidon, Jezebel's home ground. Naaman was a commander of the Syrian army that was raiding Israel. 🔴
- **The crowd snaps at the examples, not the claim.** "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled" gets wonder. Elijah and Elisha going to outsiders gets rage (4:28). 🔴
- **Demons know who he is (4:34, 4:41).** "I know who You are, the Holy One of God!" The unseen world recognizes him before the town does, and he shuts them up. 🔴
- **He "rebuked" a fever (4:39).** Same verb he uses on the demon in 4:35 and on the storm in 8:24. Luke also calls it a "high fever," the doctor noticing the details. 🔴

## Read it like AD 28, not 2026
- **The devil's claim fits the Deuteronomy 32 world.** In Deuteronomy 32:8–9 (with the Dead Sea Scroll and Greek reading), God divided the nations among the sons of God and kept Israel for himself. The nations ended up under other powers. So when the devil says the kingdoms have been "handed over" to him, a first-century Jew with that Bible would not hear an empty boast. Heiser reads Jesus' mission as taking those nations back. My meta notes rank this the most divine-council-loaded saying in the gospels. 🔴 for the Deut 32 text; 🟡 for how much of the devil's claim is true.
- **The kingdoms offer is the warrior shortcut.** Everything Israel wanted from a Messiah, the nations under his feet, with no cross. Jesus turns it down. The same offer comes back from Peter in 9:22 and from the crowd with palms in 19. 🟡
- **Forty days in the wilderness means Israel.** Forty years for Israel, forty days for Moses on the mountain (Exod 34:28), forty days for Elijah's walk to Horeb (1 Kgs 19:8). 🔴
- **How a synagogue Sabbath worked.** The Scripture was read aloud from a scroll, a visiting man could be invited to read, and the teacher sat down to teach (4:20). Every eye on him when he sits is a room waiting for the sermon. 🔴
- **They knew how Isaiah 61 ended.** Favor for us, vengeance on them, meaning Rome and the Gentiles, was the package. The messianic age was "a golden age for us and a day of God's vengeance upon them" (Bailey). Stopping before the vengeance line was like a song stopping right before the chorus. 🟡
- **Jubilee language.** "The favorable year of the Lord" points to the Jubilee in Leviticus 25, when debts were cleared and land went back to its families. Wright calls it the Jubilee of Jubilees, a manifesto meant for the real world. 🔴 for the Jubilee background; 🟡 for Wright's read.
- **Nazareth was nowhere.** A small village, not named in the Old Testament, Josephus or the Talmud. "Is this not Joseph's son?" means "we know his family; who does he think he is?" 🔴
- **Demons and synagogues.** People believed unclean spirits were everywhere, and Jewish exorcists used long rituals and names of power. Jesus uses one command, "Be quiet and come out" (4:35), and the crowd notices that difference: "with authority and power" (4:36). 🔴

## My notes
- What threw me in Nazareth: it had nothing to do with him saying who he was. It was the whole idea of "what do you mean you're coming for those scum Gentiles? You're supposed to give us everything back from the Gentiles." 🔴 Bailey backs this.
- My line for teaching it: they didn't try to kill him for saying "I'm the one." They tried to kill him for saying who else God loves.
- This is the first public look at the "wrong" Messiah. No crushing Rome, no settling scores. The same collision runs through John's question from prison (7:19), Palm Sunday, and Emmaus ("we were hoping," 24:21). 🔴
- **Why the placement matters.** Luke moves the Nazareth scene to the front of the ministry. Stein: Nazareth had no exclusive claim on Jesus, and neither did Israel. Tuckett calls it "a programmatic summary" of Luke's whole story. 🔴
- The best dissent I found is Pao and Schnabel: the link between Jewish rejection and Gentile inclusion isn't a strict cause and effect. It's a prophetic warning calling Israel to repent, and the Jewish mission keeps going all through Luke and Acts. I keep that in, in their words. 🔴
- Wright: the people had domesticated the prophets and turned the promises toward their own agenda. God's plan was always bigger than they wanted. 🟡
- I haven't studied 4:1–13 in depth yet. What's above on the temptation is from my book notes and the session I taught, not a full session on it.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus borrows Simon's boat to teach from, then tells him to put out into the deep and drop the nets after a night of catching nothing. The nets start to tear and two boats nearly sink. Peter falls at his knees. Jesus tells him he'll be catching men, and they leave everything.
- He touches a man covered with leprosy and makes him clean.
- Friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof. Jesus forgives his sins first, then heals him to prove he has the right to forgive.
- He calls Levi the tax collector, eats with tax collectors and sinners, and answers the complaints with a doctor, a wedding, a patched coat and new wine.

## Pay attention to this
- **Jesus asks before he gives (5:3).** The first thing he does with Peter is ask to use his boat. Bailey: Jesus "needed to be served," and coming in need "affirms the dignity of the helper." Need first, gift second. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for Bailey's reading.
- **Master, then Lord (5:5, 5:8).** Peter starts with *epistates*, "Master," a boss or teacher. After the catch he's on his knees saying *kyrios*, "Lord." One scene moves Jesus from teacher to Lord in Peter's mouth. 🔴
- **"Go away from me Lord, for I am a sinful man!" (5:8).** The catch doesn't make Peter excited. It makes him afraid. Same pattern as Zechariah, Mary and the shepherds: God shows up, a person comes undone, "Do not fear," then a job (5:10). 🔴
- **"Nets," plural (5:2, 4, 5, 6).** In the Gospels the plural marks the trammel net, a wall of linen that only worked at night because fish could see it by day (Laney). Peter's "we labored all night" fits the gear in his boat. 🔴 for the plural; 🟡 for what it identifies.
- **"Catching men" is a capture word (5:10).** Mark and Matthew say "fishers of men." Luke uses a verb, *zogreo*, "take alive." It comes from war: the alternative to being taken alive was being killed. It doesn't mean "rescue," and it doesn't mean "make alive." 🔴
- **Bailey's ring.** Bailey reads 5:1–11 as seven scenes in a ring. The boat goes out and comes back (1 and 7), a command to fish and a call to catch men (2 and 6), "at Your word" and "I am a sinful man" (3 and 5), and the catch in the center (4). 🟡
- **"Covered with leprosy" (5:12).** Mark and Matthew say "a leper." Luke the doctor says how bad it was. 🔴
- **He touched him (5:13).** Touching a leper made you unclean. Jesus touches him and the uncleanness runs the other way. Then he sends the man to the priest so he can be declared clean and go home (Lev 14). Wright: Jesus gives him back his place among his people along with his skin. 🔴
- **Jesus slips away to pray (5:16).** Luke keeps showing it. 🔴
- **Forgiveness first (5:20).** The friends want legs. Jesus starts with sins. The scribes get it exactly right: "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?" (5:21). That's the point. 🔴
- **"The Son of Man has authority on earth" (5:24).** First time in Luke Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, Daniel 7's figure who receives authority from the Ancient of Days. 🔴
- **He calls a tax collector (5:27).** Levi works for the system everybody hates, and Jesus says "Follow Me." Levi throws a party (5:29). 🔴
- **"The old is good enough" (5:39).** Only Luke has this last line. People who like the old wine don't want the new. A dry joke about why the religious leaders resist him. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the reading.

## Read it like AD 28, not 2026
- **The lake killed people, and the boats were small.** The first-century boat found in the mud near Ginosar in 1986 is about 26.5 feet long, 7.5 wide and 4.5 deep. A big open canoe with a mast and four rowers. Two of these "began to sink" (5:7) under the catch. 🔴
- **Daytime fishing wasn't hopeless in general.** The old line that daytime deep-water fishing was "doubly hopeless" traces to A. B. Bruce in 1897 with no evidence. Mendel Nun, who spent his life on that lake, describes daytime seine crews hauling hundreds of kilos. What holds is narrower: Peter's trammel nets were night gear. Bailey, who watched Galilean fishermen, still calls the order "ridiculous," and quotes Joel Green that "the nets used are for night fishing only." Wright: fish are "more likely" caught after dark. 🔴 for Nun and the trammel net; 🟡 for how absurd the order sounded.
- **The deep isn't far out.** Bailey notes the Sea of Galilee drops off close to shore. "Deep water" (*bathos*) is a plain sailing word. Luke had *abyssos*, the abyss, available and used it at 8:31 for where the demons beg not to go. He didn't use it here. 🔴
- **The sea stood for chaos and the nations.** Psalm 65:7 puts the roaring seas next to the roar of the peoples. Isaiah 17:12–13 does the same. In Daniel 7 the four beasts, Gentile empires, come up out of the churned sea. 4 Ezra 11–12 has Rome rising from the sea, and the Qumran Habakkuk commentary reads the "fish of the sea" as the Kittim, the Gentile power. A first-century reader had that picture available. 🔴 for the texts; 🔵 for Luke using it here.
- **The prophets fished for judgment.** Jeremiah 16:16, Amos 4:2, Ezekiel 29:4–5 and Habakkuk 1:14–17 all picture people caught like fish for judgment. Scot McKnight holds both: the call recalls deliverance and judgment, and Luke's verb is "decidedly more positive." 🔴
- **Leprosy was social death.** Leviticus 13–14: a person with a skin disease lived outside the camp, called out "unclean," and couldn't go to worship. Healing meant getting your family back. 🔴
- **Roofs were flat.** Houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair. Luke says "tiles" (5:19), the kind of roof his Greek readers would picture. 🔴 for flat roofs and the word; 🟡 for why Luke chose it.
- **Tax collectors were collaborators.** They bought the right to collect for Rome or Herod, took a cut, and were treated as traitors and unclean. Eating with someone meant accepting him. 🔴
- **"Son of Man" came with a throne room.** In Daniel 7 the Ancient of Days sits in a heavenly court with thrones set up, and one like a son of man is given dominion over the nations. When Jesus claims that title while forgiving sins, he's claiming a seat in that court. 🔴 for Daniel 7; 🟡 for how much the crowd caught.

## My notes
- How Jesus called Peter matters. He didn't say "Peter, come, I can do a lot for you." He came to Peter in need: "I need your boat." Afterwards he returns the favor. Same thing when he sends out the Twelve with nothing in ch. 9: they have to depend on the kindness of strangers. If you come to someone as the one who can do everything for them and they can do nothing for you, you're not really coming to them free. 🔴 Bailey backs the first half (pp. 136–138); the hospitality point comes from Harper's Bible Dictionary.
- My reading of the deep water: Jesus tells Peter to fish where people haven't fished before, then tells him he'll be a fisher of men. I think it's a little foreshadowing of fishing in the Gentile lane. I never said that's confirmed; it's how I read it. 🔵
- That reading isn't new. Holtzmann proposed it in the nineteenth century, Bruce recorded it and declined it ("tempts to symbolic interpretation"), Constable still holds it, and Blaiklock calls that kind of reading strained. So I'm reviving a reading, not inventing one. 🔴 for the history.
- The word won't carry it. No lexicon makes *bathos* a symbol for the nations. What the background gives me is that a first-century reader had the sea-as-nations picture available, not that Luke used it. That step is mine. 🔵
- Holtzmann put Acts 10 inside the reading: Peter's objection ("we labored all night") is a picture of his later resistance to the Gentile mission. Acts 10 survives as Peter's usual threefold failure rewritten, three refusals to match three denials. 🟡
- Cyril of Alexandria reads the catch as "the shoals of the heathen" and uses Jeremiah 16:16, the judgment text, as his warrant. Someone saw the tension in the fifth century and went the same way I'm going. 🔴 for Cyril.
- The "make alive" sermon on *zogreo* mixes up two words that look the same. The honest version: a prisoner-of-war word, where the other option was being killed. The salvation sense comes from the story, not the verb. 🔴
- I keep the counter-pull in, working against me: the rescue sense comes "from context and metaphor, not from the verb's inherent meaning."
- Bailey and Wright never go near the Gentile mission in Luke 5. I'll say so when I write it up.
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. The hook is the sea as chaos and the nations, and the Son of Man title (Dan 7). The council material comes in ch. 4 (the kingdoms) and ch. 8 (the storm and Legion).

## What the chapter is doing
- Two Sabbath fights. The disciples pick grain, and Jesus heals a man's withered hand in a synagogue. The leaders are "filled with rage" (6:11).
- Jesus prays all night on a mountain, then picks twelve and names them apostles.
- He comes down to a level place and teaches a huge crowd: blessings on the poor and hungry, woes on the rich and full, love your enemies, don't judge.
- He ends with two builders. Both hear his words. One digs down to rock, one doesn't. The flood hits both houses.

## Pay attention to this
- **"The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (6:5).** Jesus claims authority over the day God himself made holy. 🔴
- **"To save a life or to destroy it?" (6:9).** He turns the Sabbath question back on the people watching him. They're the ones planning harm that day (6:11). 🔴
- **A whole night of prayer before picking the Twelve (6:12).** Only Luke says it. Luke shows Jesus praying at every turn. 🔴
- **Twelve, on purpose (6:13).** Twelve tribes, twelve apostles. Jesus is rebuilding Israel around himself. 🔴 for the number; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Simon the Zealot and Matthew the tax collector on the same list (6:15).** A man tied to the anti-Roman cause and a man who worked for the Roman tax system. 🔴 for the names; 🟡 for "Zealot" meaning the political party this early.
- **"Blessed are the poor" (6:20).** Matthew has "poor in spirit." Luke has plain poor, and he pairs every blessing with a woe (6:24–26). Luke's gospel keeps putting money on the table. 🔴
- **"Sons of the Most High" (6:35).** Love your enemies and you'll be sons of the Most High, because he's kind to the ungrateful and evil. 🔴 for the text. See below for the council echo.
- **"Lord, Lord" (6:46).** Calling him Lord and not doing what he says is the problem the last parable answers. 🔴
- **Luke's builder "dug and went deep" (6:48).** Matthew just says he built on the rock. Luke adds the digging, the work you can't see once the house is up. 🔴
- **Both men hear (6:47, 6:49).** Hearing is the common ground. The split is doing. So the parable divides one audience, not believers from outsiders. 🔴
- **The flood hits both houses.** The wise builder isn't spared the weather. 🔴

## Read it like AD 29, not 2026
- **Sabbath rules were a badge.** Keeping the Sabbath marked a Jew off from the nations. Rules about what counted as work (reaping, threshing) grew up around it. Picking and rubbing grain could be read as both. 🔴
- **David and the holy bread (6:3–4).** 1 Samuel 21: David ate the bread from God's table that only priests could eat. Jesus puts himself in David's place, the anointed king with his men. 🔴
- **"Sons of the Most High" is council language.** Psalm 82:6 calls the members of God's heavenly council "sons of the Most High," and then judges them for ruling the nations unjustly. Jesus gives the title to people who love their enemies and show mercy like the Father. The gods of Psalm 82 failed at justice; his people get the family name by doing it. 🔴 for the shared phrase; 🟡 for reading Luke 6:35 against Psalm 82.
- **Building happened in summer.** Village houses went up in the dry season, when the clay was "like bronze" (Lev 26:19 for the picture). Walls were field stones set in mud mortar. Digging through baked clay to bedrock by hand, in the heat, was miserable. (Bailey.) 🔴
- **Winter rains turned clay to mud.** Heavy rain soaks the ground, runoff streams form, the clay turns soft, a stone pops out, a wall bulges and goes. Bailey asked village builders how deep you dig. The answer was always the same: down to rock, whether that's an inch or ten feet. 🔴 for Bailey's report.
- **Isaiah 28 sits behind it.** Isaiah 28:14–18: Judah's leaders made "a covenant with death" (a pact with Egypt) and built a shelter of lies; a storm is coming; God will lay in Zion a tested stone, a sure foundation. Ezekiel 33:30–33 supplies the hear-but-don't-do line: the people listen to the prophet like a love song and do nothing. Jesus takes the frame from Ezekiel and the picture from Isaiah. (Bailey.) 🟡
- **Two groups already claimed Isaiah's stone.** Qumran's *Rule of the Community* said its council was the tested wall and precious cornerstone, and 1QH 14 has the storm, the rock and the tested stones in one passage. The temple claimed it too: the Mishnah names a stone in the holy of holies the *shetiyah*, the foundation. Bailey reads Jesus as a third claim: build on me and my words. 🔴 for the Qumran and Mishnah texts; 🟡 for Bailey's reading of Jesus.
- **The prophets said "hear the word of the Lord."** Jesus says "hears My words and does them" (6:47). He puts a life's security on his own words. 🔴

## My notes
- My post's line: the storm hits both houses. The wise builder isn't spared the weather, and any reading that treats faith as protection from trouble has to explain why the flood shows up at both addresses. The promise isn't immunity. The house on the foundation survives the storm that comes anyway. 🔴 for the text.
- A person taught that faith prevents the flood has been handed something that will break the first time weather arrives. That's why I lead with this.
- Both builders hear. The parable is about two people in the same audience, both of whom listened, and one of whom went and dug.
- On a dry day nobody could tell the two houses apart. The cheap one goes up faster, costs less and looks the same when it's finished.
- Bailey reads the foundation as Jesus himself over against the temple, the stone Isaiah promised. Wright and Boice go a similar way. Snodgrass rejects the temple allusion and the *shetiyah* link (different Greek word for rock, *petra* not *lithos*, and a late legend). I present it as Bailey and Wright against Snodgrass and leave it open. 🟡
- Snodgrass and Blomberg read the storm as final judgment. That means "faith is not immunity" is my application, not the parable's main point, and I say so. 🟡
- Wright reads the four short sayings in 6:39–49 as deliberately funny, verbal cartoons (a blind guide, a log in the eye). The Bible has humor if you know how to see it. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his slave from a distance. Jesus says he hasn't found faith like that in Israel.
- At the gate of Nain, Jesus stops a funeral, raises a widow's only son and gives him back to his mother.
- John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask, "Are You the One who is to come?" Jesus answers with what he's doing, then praises John.
- Jesus compares his generation to children who won't play either the wedding game or the funeral game. They rejected John for fasting and Jesus for feasting.
- At a Pharisee's dinner, a sinful woman does every courtesy the host left out. Jesus tells a short parable about two debtors and forgives her.

## Pay attention to this
- **A Gentile soldier's faith (7:9).** "Not even in Israel have I found such great faith." The man who runs a Roman unit understands authority better than anyone in the crowd. 🔴
- **He doesn't feel worthy (7:6–7).** The Jewish elders say he's "worthy" (7:4). He says he isn't. 🔴
- **"Gave him back to his mother" (7:15).** Word for word from the story of Elijah raising the widow's son at Zarephath (1 Kgs 17:23 in the Greek Old Testament). The crowd catches it: "A great prophet has arisen among us!" (7:16). Luke 4 just mentioned that same widow. 🔴
- **"God has visited His people!" (7:16).** Same verb Zechariah used in 1:68. 🔴
- **John's doubt (7:19).** The man who baptized Jesus asks if he got it right. The axe-and-fire judgment John preached (3:9, 3:17) isn't showing up. 🔴 for the question; 🟡 for the reason.
- **Jesus answers with Isaiah (7:22).** The blind see, the lame walk, the poor hear good news: Isaiah 35 and 61. He leaves out the vengeance again, like at Nazareth. Then: "Blessed is he who does not take offense at Me" (7:23). 🔴
- **Two ways to hear John (7:29–30).** Tax collectors "acknowledged God's justice." The Pharisees and lawyers "rejected God's purpose for themselves." 🔴
- **The children in the square (7:32).** One game is a wedding (flute and dancing), the other a funeral (a dirge). John came like the funeral, Jesus like the wedding, and the same people refused both. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for which side is which (see below).
- **"A gluttonous man and a drunkard" (7:34).** That's an insult with a legal history (see below). 🔴
- **She was there when he arrived (7:45).** "Since the time I came in, she has not ceased to kiss My feet." She saw how the host treated him. 🔴
- **Three missing courtesies (7:44–46).** No water for his feet, no kiss, no oil for his head. She answers each one: tears, kisses on his feet, perfume. 🔴
- **"Simon, I have something to say to you" (7:40).** An idiom for "you won't like this." 🟡
- **Which comes first, love or forgiveness? (7:47).** "Her sins... have been forgiven, for she loved much" can be read either way. The parable he just told settles it: the debts are cancelled first and the love follows. 🔴
- **"Who is this man who even forgives sins?" (7:49).** The chapter ends on Luke's big question. 🔴

## Read it like AD 29, not 2026
- **Centurions built synagogues.** A centurion commanded about a hundred men. A Gentile who backed the local synagogue was the kind of God-fearer Luke's readers knew well (Cornelius in Acts 10 is another). This is the first Gentile Jesus helps in Luke. 🔴
- **"Under authority" is a chain of command (7:8).** The centurion sees that Jesus speaks with authority over sickness the way he speaks to soldiers. In Luke, diseases and "evil spirits" (7:21) both answer to that authority. Behind it is a world where unseen powers were real and ranked, and Jesus outranks them. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the powers reading.
- **A widow with no son had nothing.** No husband and no son meant no income and no protection. When Jesus gives the son back, he gives her life back. 🔴
- **Touching the bier made you unclean (7:14).** Contact with the dead defiled a person (Num 19). Jesus touches it and death runs the other way. 🔴
- **"Glutton and drunkard" is Deuteronomy's rebellious son.** Deuteronomy 21:18–21: parents bring a stubborn son to the elders and say "he is a glutton and a drunkard," and the town stones him. Wright hears the critics reaching for that charge, a rebellious son leading Israel astray. Wright himself flags that the Greek Old Testament words aren't the same ones. 🟡
- **Banquets had open doors.** At a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbow, feet pointing away from the table, so a person standing behind could reach the feet. Doors stayed open, and beggars and the curious wandered in to watch (Wright). The woman isn't breaking into a sealed room. 🔴
- **The host owed three courtesies.** Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting, oil for the head. Leaving out one could be an oversight. Leaving out all three, in front of guests, says something. Bailey reads it as a deliberate insult; Snodgrass, Blomberg and Boice read Simon as cool, not hostile. 🔴 for the customs; 🟡 for the insult.
- **Loose hair was a serious act.** The Mishnah lists a woman going out with unbound hair among the grounds for divorce. A bride let her hair down for her husband on the wedding night. Nobody in that room missed what it meant. (Bailey.) 🔴 for the Mishnah; 🟡 for how the room read it.
- **She couldn't pay back.** In the rabbinic system as G. F. Moore summarizes it, repentance for wrongs against people required paying them back. For a woman like her that was impossible. That is why "your sins have been forgiven" set her free. (Bailey.) 🟡
- **Five hundred and fifty denarii.** A denarius was a day's wage. Five hundred is well over a year and a half of work. Fifty is under two months. Both men are broke. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus travels the towns with the Twelve and a group of women who pay for the mission out of their own money (8:1–3).
- He tells the parable of the sower and then explains it. The seed is the word of God, and the soils are four ways of hearing it (8:4–15). His real family is "these who hear the word of God and do it" (8:21).
- On the lake a storm nearly sinks the boat. Jesus rebukes the wind and the waves, and the disciples ask, "Who then is this?" (8:22–25).
- They land on the Gentile side and meet a man with a legion of demons. The demons beg not to go to the abyss, go into the pigs, and the pigs drown. The town begs Jesus to leave (8:26–39).
- Back home, a woman bleeding for twelve years touches his garment, and Jairus's twelve-year-old daughter is raised (8:40–56).

## Pay attention to this
- **Women pay for the mission (8:2–3).** Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna "and many others" were "ministering to them from their possessions." Joanna's husband ran Herod's household. Herod's money ends up feeding the kingdom Herod is afraid of. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the irony.
- **Jesus explains this parable himself (8:11–15).** Most parables he leaves open. This one shows you how a parable works: the story is short, and the hearer is the one being tested. "So beware how you listen" (8:18). 🔴
- **The devil is in the sower (8:12).** The seed on the road is taken by "the devil." Even the farming parable has an enemy in it. 🔴
- **"Rebuked" (8:24).** Same verb Luke uses when Jesus rebukes demons (4:35, 4:41, 9:42). He talks to the storm the way he talks to an unclean spirit. 🔴
- **More afraid after the calm (8:25).** They were in danger in the storm. After it stops "they were fearful and marveled." The storm could kill them. The calm means something is in the boat that rules the sea. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Storm, then demons, back to back.** Chaos on the water, then chaos in a man, and one voice silences both. Luke puts them side by side on purpose. 🟡
- **"Son of the Most High God" (8:28).** The demon gets Jesus's identity right instantly. The humans in the story keep asking who he is; the spirits never have to ask. 🔴
- **"Legion" (8:30).** A Roman legion was roughly 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. The name means thousands, not "several." Mark adds that the herd was about 2,000 pigs (Mark 5:13). 🔴
- **The abyss (8:31).** The demons know there is a prison and that Jesus holds the key. They are bargaining for time. 🔴
- **The town is afraid of the healed man (8:35–37).** They find him "sitting down at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind. And they were afraid." The fear attaches to the healing, not only the dead pigs. 🔴
- **The first Gentile preacher (8:39).** The man wants to come along. Jesus sends him home to tell what God did, and he tells what Jesus did. The region that asked Jesus to leave keeps a witness. 🔴
- **Twelve and twelve (8:42–43).** A girl twelve years old and a woman sick twelve years. One has lived as long as the other has suffered. Luke braids the two stories together. 🔴
- **Luke goes easy on the doctors (8:43).** Mark says the woman "suffered much at the hands of many physicians" and got worse (Mark 5:26). Luke only says she "could not be healed by anyone." The doctor softens the line about doctors. 🟡

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Women traveling with a rabbi.** Leaving home and family to follow a teacher on the road, and paying for it, would have shocked a first-century village. Wright compares it to the woman letting her hair down in 7:38. 🟡
- **The sower is Isaiah's seed.** Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 in 8:10. Isaiah 6 ends with Israel cut down to a stump, and "the holy seed is its stump" (Isa 6:13). Wright reads the sower as Yahweh sowing his returning remnant, with the parable telling Israel why not every hearer is that seed. 🟡
- **The farming is normal.** Old commentaries argued about whether Galilean farmers sowed before or after plowing. The field has settled that both were done, so the sower is not careless. A hundredfold crop is a very good harvest, not a miracle crop. 🟡
- **The boat was small.** A first-century Galilee fishing boat was found in the mud near Ginosar in 1986: about 26.5 feet long, 7.5 wide, 4.5 deep. Put thirteen men in it. 🔴
- **The lake kills people.** It sits about 700 feet below sea level in a bowl of hills. Cold air drops off the heights and storms come up with almost no warning, with waves over six feet. Luke's wording is that the storm "descended on the lake." 🔴
- **The sea was the realm of chaos.** In Israel's Scriptures the sea is the enemy God conquers (Ps 74:13–14; Ps 89:9; Isa 51:9–10), and only Yahweh stills it (Ps 107:28–29). Galileans also believed spirits haunted the lake at night; the disciples later scream "It's a ghost!" on the same water (Mark 6:49). 🔴 for the Psalms; 🟡 for the folk belief.
- **The other side is Gentile land.** "Opposite Galilee" (8:26) is the Decapolis. Pigs, tombs, a man with no clothes: everything here is unclean to a Jew. Jesus crosses the lake through a storm to get to it. 🔴
- **"Most High" is the nations title.** *Elyon*, Most High, is the name in Deuteronomy 32:8 for the God who divided the nations and gave them over to lesser gods, keeping Israel for himself. A demon on Gentile ground calls Jesus by the name that claims every nation, including this one. Heiser's frame: the kingdom is now pushing into territory the powers thought was theirs. 🔴 for Deut 32; 🟡 for reading the scene through it.
- **The abyss was a known prison.** Second Temple Jews had a place where rebel spirits were held until judgment. 1 Enoch puts the fallen Watchers in it, and the New Testament knows it too (2 Pet 2:4; Jude 6; Rev 9:1–2; 20:1–3). Matthew has the demons ask, "Have You come here to torment us before the time?" (Matt 8:29). The surprise is the schedule. They expected the judge at the end of the age. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for "the surprise is the clock."
- **"Legion" in an occupied country.** Everyone in that region knew what a legion did to a territory: it held it. The Tenth Legion, later stationed in the area, had a boar among its emblems. 🔴 for the emblem; 🔵 that the story is winking at it.
- **Water judges the powers.** Flood, Red Sea, and now the lake. Each time the water takes down what opposed God and his people come through alive. The demons beg to stay out of the abyss and end up in the deep anyway. 🟡
- **Touching unclean things.** A bleeding woman made whatever she touched unclean (Lev 15:25–27). A corpse did the same. Jesus is touched by one and takes the hand of the other, and the uncleanness runs the wrong way: he makes them clean. 🔴 for Leviticus; 🟡 for the reading.
- **The fringe (8:44).** The edge of a Jewish man's garment carried the tassels commanded in Numbers 15:38–39. She grabbed the part of his clothes that stood for the commandments. 🟡

## My notes
- **Legion's number.** I asked what the number of a legion was, just out of curiosity, and whether Legion was surprised that Jesus was there or surprised that God was there in a human body. Where it landed: the demons were never fooled by the body. What threw them was the timing, the judge showing up mid-history (Matt 8:29). 🟡
- **Why the pigs.** My question: why let the demons kill 2,000 pigs, probably the town's biggest income, instead of sending them straight to the abyss? The text never answers. Luke just says "He gave them permission." ⬜
- **"The town flunked it."** My first take was that one man restored against 2,000 dead pigs, from the town's side, looked like more suffering, and they flunked the test. I was speaking from the town's point of view, not Jesus's.
- What I landed on: the town was afraid. The angels say "do not be afraid" three times in chapters 1–2, Jesus tells Peter not to be afraid, and now this town is afraid and the demons are afraid. God is a terrifying being. Not evil in any way, just that power is terrifying.
- That turned into a question for my mentee: count who is afraid in these stories, then tell me what each one does next. Mary, Peter, the shepherds, the demons and the town are all afraid. They go five different directions.
- **Water and demons.** I wanted to chase this: the flood, the drowning of the pigs, the Red Sea and baptism, as the times God took demons down with water. I had to fix the front of it. Water doesn't kill spirits. It judges the powers, and God's people pass through it alive. Paul calls the Red Sea a baptism (1 Cor 10:1–2), and Peter ties the flood to baptism (1 Pet 3:20–21). 🔴 for those texts; 🟡 for the pattern.
- **I spliced two boat trips. ❌** I had Jesus walking on water, Peter getting out, then Jesus falling asleep and the storm picking back up. Those are two crossings. Luke 8 is the one where he is asleep in the boat. The walking on water is Mark 6, Matthew 14 and John 6, and Luke skips it. Peter walking is Matthew only.
- **8:1–3** is the passage to know if you only remember one about women and Jesus. I built the Jesus and Women intro on it.
- **The sower (post 23).** Wright's Isaiah 6:13 reading holds up, and Snodgrass backs it. His line on Isaiah 6: parables hide in order to reveal.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus sends the Twelve out with authority over demons and with nothing in their hands. Herod hears about it and wonders who Jesus is. Then Jesus feeds five thousand in a deserted place (9:1–17).
- The hinge of the gospel: Peter says "The Christ of God." Jesus orders silence and in the same breath says the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and be raised (9:18–27).
- On a mountain Jesus is changed, Moses and Elijah talk with him about his "departure" at Jerusalem, and a voice from the cloud says, "This is My Son, My Chosen One; listen to Him!" (9:28–36).
- Down the mountain the disciples fail, argue about who is greatest, and want fire on a Samaritan village (9:37–56).
- At 9:51 "He set His face to go to Jerusalem." From here to 19:27 everything happens on the road. Three would-be followers find out what it costs (9:57–62).

## Pay attention to this
- **Sent with nothing (9:3).** No staff, bag, bread or money. It isn't about being poor for its own sake. They have to arrive as guests who need something, not as patrons handing out favors. 🟡
- **Who is this? (9:9, 9:18–20).** Herod asks it, the crowds guess, and Peter answers. The whole first half of Luke has been building to this question since the boat in 8:25. 🔴
- **Two questions.** "Who do the crowds say that I am?" gets safe answers: John, Elijah, a prophet. "But who do you say that I am?" is the one nobody answers by committee. 🔴
- **Silence because it's true (9:21–22).** He doesn't silence them because Peter is wrong. He silences them because the word "Messiah" in public meant war with Rome, and he is about to give it a new meaning: suffer, be rejected, be killed, be raised. 🔴 (Stein)
- **"Daily" (9:23).** Only Luke has "take up his cross daily." 🔴
- **"Departure" (9:31).** The Greek word is *exodos*. Moses and Elijah talk about the exodus Jesus is about to fulfill at Jerusalem. Luke alone tells you what they talked about. 🔴
- **"Listen to Him!" (9:35).** At the baptism the Father spoke to Jesus. Here he speaks to the disciples, and the words echo Deuteronomy 18:15, the prophet like Moses: "you shall listen to him." Then "Jesus was found alone" (9:36). The Law and the Prophets stepped back. 🔴
- **The cloud overshadowed them (9:34).** Same verb Gabriel used for Mary in 1:35, *episkiazō*, the Greek Old Testament verb for the glory cloud covering the tabernacle (Exod 40:35). 🔴
- **Peter's shelters (9:33).** Three booths, equal billing, and Luke adds "not realizing what he was saying." The voice interrupts him mid-sentence. 🔴
- **It was hidden from them (9:45).** "It was concealed from them so that they would not perceive it." The disciples can't hear the death prediction, and Luke says the hiding was done to them. 🔴
- **He set his face (9:51).** The turning point of the book. From here Jesus is walking toward Jerusalem on purpose, and the travel section runs to 19:27, more than a third of the gospel. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **A stranger had no standing.** In a village a traveler had no place until a host took him in, and a guest ate what he was given. Sending the Twelve empty-handed made them depend on the people they came to. (Harper's Bible Dictionary on hospitality.) 🔴 for the custom; 🟡 for reading it as strategy.
- **Messiah meant winner.** The popular hope was a Davidic king who would throw off Rome and restore Israel (Psalms of Solomon 17 is the clearest example). When the crowd tried to make Jesus king by force after the feeding, that is what they meant (John 6:15). 🔴
- **A crucified Messiah was a contradiction.** "He who is hanged is accursed of God" (Deut 21:23). In Peter's Bible a cross didn't prove you were Messiah. It proved you weren't. Paul still calls it a stumbling block (1 Cor 1:23). 🔴
- **Nobody expected one man to rise early.** Resurrection was an end-of-the-age event for everyone at once (John 11:24). Mark says they came down the mountain arguing about "what rising from the dead meant" (Mark 9:10). 🔴
- **The Son of Man of Daniel 7.** "When He comes in His glory... and of the holy angels" (9:26) is Daniel 7's figure who comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom. 🔴
- **The powers were reading the same wrong dictionary.** Paul says none of "the rulers of this age" understood God's hidden wisdom, "for if they had understood it they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:8). Heiser reads those rulers as spiritual powers and calls Old Testament messianic prophecy a "mosaic profile," pieces kept apart so the plan couldn't be assembled ahead of time. 9:45 fits it: even the disciples have it hidden from them. 🔴 for Paul's words; 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **Mountains are where God meets people.** Moses met God on Sinai, Elijah on Horeb (the same mountain). Now both stand on a mountain with Jesus. 🔴
- **Booths.** Peter's "booths" are the same word as the Feast of Booths, the shelters Israel lived in to remember the wilderness. He wants to settle in. Lane reads it as wanting the glory now, before the suffering Jesus just announced. 🟡
- **Which mountain?** Luke says only "the mountain" (9:28). Tabor is the later tradition. Heiser argues for Hermon: near Caesarea Philippi, high enough, and no travel south in the eight days. In 1 Enoch, Hermon is where the rebel Watchers came down and swore their oath (1 Enoch 6). If it's Hermon, Jesus shows his glory on the rebels' own mountain. 🔴 that the text doesn't name it; 🔵 for Hermon.
- **Samaritans and Jerusalem (9:52–53).** Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim and rejected Jerusalem's temple. A rabbi with his face set toward Jerusalem wasn't welcome. 🔴
- **Fire from heaven (9:54).** James and John want to do what Elijah did to the king's soldiers (2 Kgs 1:10–12). Elijah was just on the mountain. They got the wrong lesson from him. 🔴 for the echo.
- **The bracket at 9:55–56.** The line "You do not know what kind of spirit you are of" is missing from the oldest manuscripts, which is why the LSB puts it in brackets. 🔴
- **Hand on the plow (9:61–62).** Elijah called Elisha while he was plowing, and Elisha asked to kiss his parents goodbye first and was allowed to (1 Kgs 19:19–21). Jesus asks for more than Elijah did. 🔴 for the parallel.

## My notes
- **Request first, gift second.** Jesus started with Peter by asking for his boat (5:3), and he does the same thing when he sends the Twelve. Take nothing, so you have to rely on the kindness of strangers. If you come to someone in a position where you can do everything for him and he can't do anything for you, you're not really coming in free will. They go out in need. The line I landed on: the gospel comes to the door as a guest, not a landlord. 🟡
- **The wrong Messiah.** The Messiah they expected was not the Messiah Jesus turned out to be. They wanted a deliverer from Rome, and that is why Jesus told people not to tell anybody. He didn't want them building him up as a conqueror. Stein on 9:21 backs this: the silence is because the confession was true and public talk was dangerous. 🔴
- **Why Peter fought the cross.** He didn't know the ending; we read the Old Testament with the lights on. A cross meant cursed. Messiah meant winner. And nobody had a category for one man rising in the middle of history. My compressed answer for the mentee: you know the ending, Peter didn't.
- **Three tabernacles.** Even after Peter gets called the rock (Matthew's version), he still doesn't fully understand. He wants to build three equal-size shelters, one each for Moses, Elijah and Jesus. The voice corrects him: not three, one Son, and listen to him.
- **The exodus word.** My mentee had just learned the Red Sea, so this is where he catches Luke picking *exodos* on purpose.
- **Hermon.** I like Heiser's case and keep it tiered as speculative. 🔵
- **Matthew 16 sidebar** (not in Luke): Caesarea Philippi at the foot of Hermon, by the cave of Pan the locals tied to the underworld. Gates are defensive, so Hades is the city under siege. In Aramaic Jesus said *kepha* both times, so the *petros*/*petra* argument is weaker than people think. The fathers' tally I found (Whelton) has most of them reading the rock as Peter's confession or as Christ, and I flag that it is a rough count from a 17th-century survey.

## What the chapter is doing
- The day is coming, burning like a furnace. The arrogant and the wicked will be chaff, left with neither root nor branch (4:1).
- For those who fear God's name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they'll jump like calves let out of the stall (4:2–3).
- "Remember the law of Moses My servant," given at Horeb (4:4).
- "I am going to send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome day of Yahweh." He will turn the hearts of fathers and children to each other, or God will come and strike the land (4:5–6).
- These are the last words of the Prophets in the Hebrew order, and the last words of the Old Testament in English Bibles.

## Pay attention to this
- **Two outcomes from one day (4:1–2).** The same day burns the arrogant like a furnace and rises like the sun on those who fear God. 🔴
- **"Neither root nor branch" (4:1).** Nothing left to grow back. 🔴
- **"The sun of righteousness... with healing in its wings" (4:2).** A rising sun pictured with wings. Charles Wesley put it in "Hark! the Herald Angels Sing." 🔴
- **Calves from the stall (4:2).** Joy you can see: young animals let out to run. 🔴
- **Moses and Elijah (4:4–5).** One looks back to the law, one looks forward to a coming prophet. Both met God at Horeb (Exodus 3; 1 Kings 19:8). 🔴
- **Horeb, not Sinai (4:4).** Deuteronomy's name for the mountain. 🔴
- **Elijah never died.** He was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). That's part of why he's the one who can come back. 🔴
- **Fathers and children (4:6).** The coming prophet restores families, and with them the covenant passed from parents to children. 🔴
- **The last word is "destruction."** *Cherem*, "devoting it to destruction," the word for things put under the ban (Joshua 6:17). The Old Testament in English ends on a warning. 🔴

## Read it like 450 BC, not 2026
- **Malachi has three chapters in Hebrew.** English 4:1–6 is Hebrew 3:19–24. If a Hebrew Bible or a Jewish source cites "Malachi 3:23," that's our 4:5. 🔴
- **Ending on a curse was avoided.** In synagogue reading, 4:5 is read again after 4:6 so the book doesn't end on "destruction." The Greek Old Testament moves 4:4 to the very end for the same kind of reason. 🔴
- **After the return.** Malachi preaches after the second temple was built (about 450 BC), to priests who offer blemished animals (1:8), men who divorce their wives (2:14–16) and people who rob God in tithes (3:8). The fire of 4:1 lands on a religious community, not on pagans. 🔴
- **The winged sun was a well-known image.** Egypt's winged sun disk sat over temple doors. Persian royal art showed a winged disk too. Judah's own royal seal stamps from Hezekiah's time (the *lmlk* jar handles) include a two-winged sun disk. Malachi takes an image of royal and divine protection and gives it to Yahweh's righteousness. 🔴 for the iconography; 🟡 for the borrowing.
- **The book of remembrance (3:16).** Just before this chapter, those who fear God talk together and "a book of remembrance was written before Him." That's the heavenly record kept in God's court, like the books opened in Daniel 7:10 (Heiser, Unseen Realm 101 Session 4). The council is in the background of Malachi's ending. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the council reading.
- **"Yahweh of hosts" runs all through Malachi.** About two dozen times in four short chapters, including 4:1 and 4:3. The God of the heavenly army is the one coming to judge. 🔴
- **Second Temple Jews were waiting for Elijah.** Sirach 48:10 says Elijah is ready to calm God's wrath before it breaks out, to turn the hearts of parents to their children, and to restore the tribes of Jacob. At Passover a cup and a seat are still set for Elijah. 🔴
- **The Gospels pick it up.** Gabriel says John the Baptist will go "in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children" (Luke 1:17). Jesus says John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:10–13). Moses and Elijah show up together at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). 🔴

## My notes
- My work on this chapter is thin. It comes from my How We Got the Bible side note on the seams that hold the Hebrew Bible together.
- **Seam Two.** The Prophets close by pointing back to Moses (Torah) and forward to Elijah (a coming prophet). The Writings then open with Psalm 1 (the righteous person meditating on Torah day and night, as Joshua was told) and Psalm 2 (the Messianic king, "My Son"). Put together: Scripture plus Messiah equals blessing.
- **The question it leaves open.** The Writings open by answering what Malachi left hanging: what does faithfulness look like while you wait, and who is the coming king?
- **The expectation it carries.** Elijah is one of the Moses-like figures who isn't the final prophet (Deuteronomy 18:15). The outline of the prophet like Moses keeps getting drawn and never filled in until the Gospels.
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. The hook is the book of remembrance "written before Him" in 3:16.

## What the chapter is doing
- On the way south, Pharisees test Jesus on divorce. He goes past Moses' permission back to creation: "What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate" (10:1–12).
- The disciples shoo children away. Jesus is indignant, takes them in his arms and blesses them (10:13–16).
- A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life. Jesus loves him, tells him to sell everything and follow, and he walks away sad. Then the camel and the needle, and "Who can be saved?" (10:17–31).
- The third death prediction, the most detailed one (10:32–34).
- James and John ask for the seats on his right and left. Jesus says the Son of Man came "to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many" (10:35–45).
- At Jericho, blind Bartimaeus shouts "Son of David," gets his sight, and follows him on the road (10:46–52).

## Pay attention to this
- **The road.** "On the road going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking on ahead of them" (10:32). The whole chapter is on the move. Bartimaeus ends it "following Him on the road." 🔴
- **"Jesus loved him" (10:21).** Only Mark says it. The hard command comes out of love. 🔴
- **"Who can be saved?" (10:26).** The disciples assumed rich men were the ones God had blessed. If they can't get in, who can? 🔴
- **The hinge is 10:27.** "With people it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God." The whole saying points here. 🔴
- **"One hundred times as much... along with persecutions" (10:30).** Mark slips persecution into the reward list. 🔴
- **Three predictions, three misses.** After 8:31 Peter rebukes him. After 9:31 they argue about greatness. After 10:33–34 James and John ask for thrones. 🔴
- **The same question twice.** "What do you want Me to do for you?" to James and John (10:36) and to Bartimaeus (10:51). The disciples ask for power. The blind man asks to see. 🔴
- **The cup and the baptism (10:38).** Both mean his death. "The cup" comes back in Gethsemane (14:36). 🔴
- **"A ransom for many" (10:45).** The price paid to free a slave or a prisoner. "Many" echoes Isaiah 53:11–12. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for the Isaiah link.
- **"Son of David" (10:47).** The first time anyone in Mark calls Jesus that, right before he rides into Jerusalem. 🔴
- **He throws off his cloak (10:50).** For a beggar, that cloak was his bed and the place he caught coins. He leaves it. 🟡

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Divorce debates.** In Jesus' day the rabbis argued over Deuteronomy 24:1. Shammai's school said divorce only for something shameful. Hillel's school allowed it for almost anything. And Herod Antipas had just divorced his wife to marry his brother's, which got John the Baptist killed (6:17–29). The question was a trap with a body count. 🔴
- **Wealth meant blessing.** Most people read Deuteronomy as saying God rewards the faithful with land and plenty. A rich, law-keeping man looked like God's favorite. That's why the disciples are shocked. 🔴
- **The elephant and the needle.** The Babylonian Talmud uses an elephant going through the eye of a needle for something impossible (Berakhot 55b). Jesus uses the biggest animal in Palestine, the camel. Same kind of saying: impossible, not hard. 🔴
- **There was no Needle Gate.** No archaeology, no manuscript and no rabbinic text mentions a small Jerusalem gate called "the eye of the needle." The story shows up a thousand years later in medieval commentary and spread through Victorian preaching. 🔴 that there's no evidence; 🟡 on exactly who started it.
- **Children didn't count.** Children had no standing, no rights and no honor of their own. Saying the kingdom "belongs to such as these" turned the ladder upside down. 🔴
- **Rulers of the Gentiles (10:42).** Everyone knew how kings ran things: Rome, Herod, the high priests. "It is not this way among you." 🔴
- **Divine council: thrones and the Son of Man.** James and John want the seats beside his throne "in Your glory." That's royal court talk, and behind it is Daniel 7, where thrones are set up and the Son of Man is given a kingdom that all nations will "serve." Jesus turns it around: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. 🔴 for the Daniel wording; 🟡 for the council read.

## My notes
- I built a Needle Gate demo for a mentoring session, and it's on the myth-busters list for my NT study plan.
- **The myth.** A small gate in Jerusalem where a camel could squeeze through if you unloaded it, so the rich can get in if they just drop their stuff. There's no archaeological, manuscript or rabbinic evidence for any such gate. 🔴
- **Correction to my own outline.** My session outline says Theophylact of Ohrid "around the 9th century." Theophylact lived in the 11th century, and who first floated the gate is debated. The point stands: it's a late invention. ⬜ on the origin.
- **What it actually means.** Standard Jewish exaggeration for impossible. The Talmud uses an elephant. Jesus uses a camel.
- **Same text, opposite gospel.** The gate reading turns grace into works: unload enough and you'll fit. The real reading drives you to grace: you can't fit, and God can do it anyway. 🔴
- **Teaching note.** I almost left this one out of the session because it isn't obvious to someone who has never heard the gate story. With someone who has, it's a "what you were told is wrong" moment. Without it, it falls flat. Know your listener first.

- **"Threw him out of the vineyard" (12:8).** The son dies outside. Hebrews 13:12 says Jesus suffered outside the gate. 🟡
- **The stone (12:10–11).** Psalm 118:22–23. The crowds sang Psalm 118 when he rode in (11:9). Now he quotes the next part: the stone the builders threw away. 🔴
- **"Whose likeness and inscription is this?" (12:16).** The coin bears Caesar's image. People bear God's image (Genesis 1:27). Give each what has its image on it. 🔴 for the question; 🟡 for the image-of-God read.
- **"You do not understand the Scriptures nor the power of God" (12:24).** Two mistakes, not one. 🔴
- **"Like angels" (12:25).** Not "become angels." Like them in that they don't marry. 🔴
- **"I am the God of Abraham" (12:26).** God says *am*, not *was*, long after Abraham died. He's still their God, so they're still alive to him. 🔴
- **The Shema (12:29).** Jesus starts with "Hear, O Israel! The Lord our God is one Lord," the prayer every Jew said twice a day, then adds Leviticus 19:18. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Absentee landlords.** In Herod's time the wealthy often lived far from their estates and leased them to tenants. Jesus' listeners knew exactly this setup. 🔴 (Bailey)
- **The tax and the coin.** The head tax went to Rome and was paid in silver denarii. Tiberius's denarius called him "son of the divine Augustus." A coin that called Caesar the son of a god, in the Temple courts. Say "pay it" and you lose the crowd. Say "don't" and you're a rebel. 🔴
- **Pharisees with Herodians (12:13).** Rivals working together again, as in 3:6. 🔴
- **Sadducees.** The priestly party. They took only the five books of Moses as binding and denied resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). That's why Jesus answers from Exodus and talks about angels. 🔴
- **Levirate marriage.** If a man died with no son, his brother married the widow to "raise up a seed" for him (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). The Sadducees use it to make resurrection look silly. 🔴
- **Divine council: Psalm 110.** "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at My right hand." Two figures called Lord, one seated beside the other. Heiser reads this with Daniel 7 as part of the "two powers in heaven" idea that later rabbis fought. Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most. 🔴 for how often it's quoted; 🟡 for the two-powers frame.
- **Angels don't marry.** "Like angels in heaven." In 1 Enoch 15 the Watchers are rebuked for doing the very thing heaven's angels don't do: they left heaven and took wives (Genesis 6). 🔴 for the Enoch text; 🔵 that Jesus has it in mind.
- **The treasury.** The Temple had trumpet-shaped offering boxes in the Court of the Women. Two lepta were the smallest coins there were. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Leaving the Temple, a disciple admires the huge stones. Jesus says not one will be left on another (13:1–2).
- On the Mount of Olives, facing the Temple, four disciples ask privately: when, and what sign? (13:3–4).
- Jesus warns: deceivers, wars, earthquakes and famines are "the beginning of birth pains." His people will be dragged into courts and synagogues, and the Holy Spirit will give them their words (13:5–13).
- When "the abomination of desolation" stands where it shouldn't, Judea must run for the hills. Then cosmic signs and the Son of Man coming in clouds, gathering his elect (13:14–27).
- The fig tree, "this generation," nobody knows the day or hour, and a doorkeeper told three times to stay awake (13:28–37).
- This is the longest speech Jesus gives in Mark, and it sits right before the cross.

## Pay attention to this
- **Two questions asked as one (13:4).** The disciples ask about "these things," the Temple. Matthew's version adds "your coming and the end of the age" (Matt 24:3). They probably thought it was all one event. 🔴
- **"See to it that no one deceives you" (13:5).** The first command in the speech isn't "figure out the date." It's "don't get fooled." 🔴
- **"Not yet the end" (13:7).** Wars and earthquakes are labor pains, not the birth. 🔴
- **"Do not worry beforehand" (13:11).** Mark's verb is *promerimnate*, be anxious ahead of time. It forbids the panic, not the preparation. 🔴
- **"Let the reader understand" (13:14).** Mark breaks into Jesus' speech to talk to his own readers. He expects them to catch something. 🔴
- **Local details (13:14–18).** Judea, rooftops, the field, nursing mothers, "pray that it may not happen in the winter." This is the ground in Judea, about real people running. 🔴
- **Then the language goes cosmic (13:24–27).** Sun, moon, stars, the Son of Man in clouds, the four winds. 🔴
- **"This generation will not pass away" (13:30).** One of the hardest verses in the Gospels. 🔴 that it's hard; ⬜ on what it means.
- **"Not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son" (13:32).** Jesus says he doesn't know the hour. 🔴
- **Four watches (13:35).** Evening, midnight, rooster crow, morning. The four Roman watches of the night. 🔴
- **"I say to all, 'Stay awake!'" (13:37).** It doesn't stop with the four disciples. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Herod's Temple.** Herod the Great rebuilt it on a massive scale. Some of the stones were enormous, and it was one of the wonders of the Roman world. Saying it would fall was like saying the sun would go out. 🔴
- **It did fall.** Rome burned the Temple in AD 70, about forty years later. Early Christians were said to have fled Jerusalem before the siege (Eusebius reports they went to Pella). 🔴 for AD 70; 🟡 for the flight.
- **The abomination of desolation.** Daniel's phrase (9:27, 11:31, 12:11). Its first fulfillment was in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the Temple (1 Maccabees 1:54). Every Jew knew the story from Hanukkah. Jesus says it will happen again. 🔴
- **Birth pains.** The prophets used labor pains for the suffering before God's new age (Isaiah 26:17–19, Micah 4:9–10). Later Jewish writers called it "the birth pangs of the Messiah." 🔴
- **Divine council: the powers in the heavens.** "The stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers that are in the heavens will be shaken" (13:25) quotes Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4. In the Old Testament, the sun, moon and stars are tied to "the host of heaven," the heavenly beings the nations worshiped (Deuteronomy 4:19, Isaiah 24:21). When God judges, the powers behind the nations get shaken too. 🔴 for the Isaiah sources; 🟡 for reading "powers" as spiritual beings, not only lights in the sky.
- **Coming in clouds.** Riding the clouds was a title for a god. Baal was "the rider of the clouds" at Ugarit. The Old Testament gives the title to Yahweh (Psalm 68:4, 104:3, Isaiah 19:1). Daniel 7:13 gives it to "one like a son of man." 🔴
- **Angels gather (13:27).** The Son of Man sends "the angels" to gather his elect. The heavenly host works for him. 🔴
- **Four watches.** Romans split the night into four three-hour watches, six in the evening to six in the morning. Jews used three. Mark uses the Roman four. 🔴

## My notes
- This is my most heavily noted chapter in Mark: a chapter note, six passage notes, a field note on 13:11, and Parables draft 38, The Doorkeeper.
- **Two questions.** The Temple's fall and the end of the age, likely taken as one event. Some verses fit AD 70 (13:2, 14, 18). Others are cosmic (13:24–26). Prophecy compresses events like mountain peaks seen from far away: two peaks look side by side until you get there and find the valley between them. 🟡
- **Birth pains.** Contractions start slow and get closer and harder. "The end won't follow immediately." False messiahs have shown up all through history (bar Kokhba, Sabbatai Zevi, Jim Jones, Koresh). We detect more earthquakes now; that doesn't mean there are more. The pattern lines up with the first seals of Revelation 6. 🟡
- **13:11, the Spirit will give you the words.** Mark's verb forbids anxiety, not study. Steve Walton: Mark 13 and Luke 12 open with a general "whenever," which is why they get the anxiety word, and Luke 21 gets the rehearsal word. 🔴
- **"This generation" (13:30).** I laid out four readings: the first-century generation and AD 70; the generation that sees the signs start; *genea* as a people or race; double fulfillment. Verse 31 stresses that it's certain, whatever the timing. ⬜
- **A humble reminder** I kept writing into these notes: the first coming fulfilled prophecy perfectly and still surprised nearly everyone. Preparation over prediction (13:33).
- **The Doorkeeper.** *Gregoreo* means be ready, not never sleep (Blomberg). Wright reads the first level as the Temple's fall, the subject of the whole chapter, as a preview of judgment on the world. Snodgrass and Blomberg read it as the end. 🟡
