## What the chapter is doing
- Two days before Passover, the chief priests plot to seize Jesus quietly (14:1–2).
- In Bethany a woman breaks a jar of costly nard over his head. Some call it waste. Jesus says she anointed his body for burial (14:3–9).
- Judas goes to the chief priests, and they promise him money (14:10–11).
- At the Passover meal Jesus says one of them will betray him, then gives bread ("this is My body") and the cup ("My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many") (14:12–25).
- On the way to the Mount of Olives he says they'll all fall away. Peter swears he won't (14:26–31).
- In Gethsemane he prays "Abba! Father!... not what I will, but what You will," and three times finds his friends asleep (14:32–42).
- Judas kisses him, a sword comes out, everyone runs, and a young man flees naked (14:43–52).
- Before the high priest, false witnesses fail. Asked if he's the Christ, Jesus says "I am," and they condemn him for blasphemy. Below in the courtyard, Peter denies him three times, and the rooster crows (14:53–72).

## Pay attention to this
- **A sandwich again.** Mark wraps the woman's costly gift (14:3–9) between the plot (14:1–2) and Judas selling him (14:10–11). One gives everything; one takes money. 🔴
- **"Anointed My body beforehand for the burial" (14:8).** The only anointing Jesus gets. The women who come on Sunday with spices are too late (16:1). 🔴
- **"Blood of the covenant" (14:24).** Moses' words at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). "For many" echoes Isaiah 53. 🔴
- **"Abba! Father!" (14:36).** Mark keeps the Aramaic word Jesus prayed. 🔴
- **The cup (14:36).** The same cup he told James and John they'd drink (10:38). 🔴
- **"Could you not keep watch for one hour?" (14:37).** The same "stay awake" verb from the end of chapter 13. Three times he finds them sleeping. 🔴
- **"As you would against a robber?" (14:48).** The word is *lestes*, an armed bandit or rebel. They came at him like he was leading a revolt. 🔴
- **"They all left Him and fled" (14:50).** Every one of them. 🔴
- **The naked young man (14:51–52).** Only Mark has him. He's never named and never comes back. 🔴
- **The Temple charge (14:58).** "I will destroy this sanctuary made with hands." The witnesses can't even agree on that. 🔴
- **"I am" (14:62).** For the first time in Mark, Jesus says it straight out, at the one moment saying it gets him killed. 🔴
- **Peter is "below" (14:66).** Mark cuts between Jesus upstairs telling the truth and Peter downstairs lying. Same night, same building. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Passover.** The feast remembered the exodus. The lamb was killed, its blood had marked the doors, and the meal retold how God freed a nation of slaves. Jesus takes the bread and the cup that pointed back to Egypt and points them at himself. 🔴
- **Nard.** Imported from India. Three hundred denarii was about a year's pay for a laborer (14:5). She poured out a fortune in one go. 🔴
- **Gethsemane means "oil press."** *Gat shemanim*: the press where olives were crushed for oil. Jesus kneels in a place named for crushing. 🔴 for the meaning of the name.
- **The cup of wrath.** In the prophets, God hands a cup of his anger to the nations and to his rebellious people (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15, Psalm 75:8). 🔴
- **A kiss.** Students greeted a respected teacher with a kiss. Judas uses an honor sign as the signal to arrest him. 🔴
- **"Son of the Blessed One" (14:61).** The high priest uses a respectful way around saying God's name. 🔴
- **Divine council: two thrones.** Jesus answers with two Old Testament texts at once: Psalm 110:1 ("sit at My right hand") and Daniel 7:13 ("coming with the clouds of heaven"). In Daniel 7, thrones are set up in the heavenly court, and the one who rides the clouds is given everlasting rule. Riding the clouds is something only God does in the Old Testament. Claiming that seat, in front of the high priest, is why they call it blasphemy. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the council read (Heiser).
- **Tearing his clothes (14:63).** A high priest tearing his garments was the formal sign that he had heard blasphemy. 🔴
- **"Prophesy!" (14:65).** They blindfold him and mock him as a prophet, while downstairs his prophecy about Peter is coming true. 🟡
- **Rooster crow.** The third Roman watch of the night was called "cockcrow," roughly midnight to three. 🔴

## My notes
- I worked this chapter in my vault chapter note and three passage notes (Gethsemane, the arrest, the trial), plus a few side studies.
- **Themes I tagged.** Getting ready for the cross (the anointing "for burial ahead of time"), betrayal (Psalm 41:9), the new covenant (14:22–24), human weakness (the sleeping disciples, 14:38), and who Jesus is (14:62). The Old Testament meets here: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the Suffering Servant (Isaiah 53) and the Son of Man (Daniel 7).
- **Two gardens.** Adam chose his own will in a garden. Jesus says "not what I will" in a garden (1 Corinthians 15:22). 🟡
- **The press.** I checked the *gat shemanim* oil-press link from a video against a real source for my Two Gates study and kept it. Jesus goes into the ultimate crushing in a place literally named "the press." 🔴
- **The arrest.** The kiss is honor turned into betrayal. Peter's sword hits Malchus (John names him), and Luke says Jesus healed the ear (Luke 22:51), the last healing before the cross. Jesus won't fight, and 14:49 says why: "that the Scriptures would be fulfilled." 🔴
- **The naked young man.** Readings: Mark himself (many early fathers), someone woken up following in his linen, or a picture of total abandonment. He may pair with the young man in a white robe at the tomb (16:5): naked flight, then clothed resurrection. In my NT writers post I called the Mark-himself idea "a very old guess with nothing behind it." Attractive, nothing more. 🔵
- **The trial.** Silence (Isaiah 53:7). "I am" (Exodus 3:14). Psalm 110:1 plus Daniel 7:13. The mocking (Isaiah 50:6). I link this to my Unseen Realm notes on Daniel 7 and the Son of Man as a divine figure. 🟡
- **The charge comes home.** The blasphemy charge from the paralytic's house (2:7) comes back here, answered with the same Son of Man phrase. 🔴
- **The rooster.** I'd heard it was a horn or bugle signal, not a bird. I weighed it and set it aside. The Greek *alektor* is a rooster, and the details of the text fit a real bird. ❌ on the horn theory.

## What the chapter is doing
- At dawn the Sanhedrin ties Jesus up and hands him to Pilate. "Are You the King of the Jews?" "You yourself say it." Then silence (15:1–5).
- Pilate offers the crowd a prisoner. The chief priests stir them up, they choose Barabbas, and they shout "Crucify Him!" Pilate has Jesus scourged and handed over (15:6–15).
- Soldiers dress him in purple, crown him with thorns, hail him as king and spit on him (15:16–20).
- Simon of Cyrene carries the cross to Golgotha. They crucify Jesus at the third hour between two robbers, under the sign "THE KING OF THE JEWS," while everyone mocks (15:21–32).
- Darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth. Jesus cries "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" and dies. The Temple veil tears top to bottom, and a Roman centurion says "Truly this man was God's Son!" (15:33–39).
- Women watch from a distance. Joseph of Arimathea asks for the body, wraps it in linen and lays it in a rock tomb (15:40–47).

## Pay attention to this
- **"King of the Jews" five times, and "King of Israel" once.** Pilate, the soldiers, the sign over the cross and the chief priests all say it (15:2, 9, 12, 18, 26, 32). Mark lets the mockers announce the truth. 🔴
- **Barabbas (15:7).** In prison with the insurrectionists who had committed murder. The crowd picks the violent rebel and condemns the one who refused to be that kind of king. The guilty man walks free while the innocent one dies in his place. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the substitution picture.
- **Silence (15:5).** Pilate is amazed. Isaiah 53:7: "like a sheep that is silent before its shearers." 🔴
- **Alexander and Rufus (15:21).** Mark names Simon's sons as if his readers knew them. A Rufus shows up in Romans 16:13. 🔴 for the names; 🔵 that it's the same Rufus.
- **One on His right and one on His left (15:27).** James and John asked for those seats "in Your glory" (10:37). This is what the seats looked like. 🔴
- **"He saved others; He cannot save Himself" (15:31).** True, but not the way they meant it. He won't save himself so he can save them. 🟡
- **The hours.** Third hour (9 am) crucified, sixth hour (noon) darkness, ninth hour (3 pm) the cry. 🔴
- **"Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?" (15:34).** Aramaic, quoting Psalm 22:1. The only words Jesus speaks from the cross in Mark. 🔴
- **Torn top to bottom (15:38).** The verb is the same one Mark used when the heavens were "torn open" at Jesus' baptism (1:10). Torn from the top means God did the tearing. 🔴 for the verb; 🟡 for the meaning.
- **"God's Son" from a Roman (15:39).** Mark's first line calls Jesus "the Son of God" (1:1). The first human in Mark to say it straight out is a Gentile soldier, watching him die. 🔴
- **The women stayed (15:40–41, 47).** The men ran in 14:50. The women watch the death and see where he's buried. 🔴
- **Linen (15:46).** Joseph wraps him in a *sindon*, the same word for the linen sheet the young man left behind in 14:51–52. 🔴 for the word; 🔵 for any link.

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Why Pilate.** Under Rome, the Jewish council couldn't carry out a crucifixion. Only the governor could. And the charge they brought him, "King of the Jews," was treason against Caesar. 🔴
- **The Passover pardon.** Outside the Gospels we have no record of the custom of releasing one prisoner at the feast. It may have been a local practice of Pilate's. 🔴 that no outside source mentions it; ⬜ on the custom itself.
- **Scourging.** The Roman flog had leather straps with bone or metal in them. Men sometimes died from the flogging alone. 🔴
- **Purple and a crown.** Purple was the color of emperors and kings. The soldiers stage a fake coronation. "Hail, King of the Jews!" mocks the way crowds greeted Caesar, "Hail, Caesar!" 🔴
- **Crucifixion.** Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels. It was designed to be public, slow and shameful. A man carried his own crossbeam. Jesus is too weak, so they grab a passerby. 🔴
- **Wine mixed with myrrh (15:23).** A drug to dull the pain. He refuses it. 🔴
- **The ninth hour.** Three in the afternoon was the hour of the evening sacrifice and of prayer in the Temple (Acts 3:1). 🔴
- **Quoting a first line.** Jews often named a psalm by its first line. Psalm 22 moves from "why have You forsaken Me" through mockery, pierced hands and feet and divided clothes, and ends with all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD. 🔴 for the psalm; 🟡 that he meant the whole psalm.
- **Darkness at noon.** Amos 8:9: "I will make the sun go down at noon and make the earth dark in broad daylight," a picture of God's judgment day. 🔴
- **The veil.** A huge curtain hung in front of the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest went, once a year. 🔴
- **Divine council: the nations come back.** Psalm 22 ends with all the families of the nations bowing before the LORD, because the kingdom is his and he rules over the nations (22:27–28). In the Deuteronomy 32 picture the nations were handed to other powers. A Roman soldier confessing God's Son at the foot of the cross is the first of those nations turning back. Paul says the cross disarmed "the rulers and authorities" (Colossians 2:15). 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for reading the centurion that way (Heiser).

I hold three readings together: he bears the weight of sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), he feels real human suffering, and he's declaring the psalm fulfilled. The bystanders hear "Eloi" and think he's calling Elijah (15:35). 🟡

The popular story of a mother worm that dies on a tree, stains it red and turns white after three days has no ancient source at all. I dropped it. ❌ The real thing is better: the Hebrew *tola'ath* is both the lowly maggot and the source of prized crimson dye. One word, the lowest thing and the royal color. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- After the Sabbath, three women bring spices to anoint the body, worrying about who will roll the stone away. It's already rolled back (16:1–4).
- Inside, a young man in a white robe tells them: "He has risen; He is not here." Go tell "His disciples and Peter" that he's going ahead of them to Galilee (16:5–7).
- They run from the tomb shaking, and "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." The oldest manuscripts end here, at 16:8.
- Bracketed in your Bible: a longer ending (16:9–20) with appearances to Mary Magdalene, to two disciples and to the Eleven, a commission, signs, and the ascension. Some manuscripts have a short two-sentence ending instead, and LSB prints that too.

## Pay attention to this
- **They came to anoint a body (16:1).** Nobody expected a resurrection, not even the ones who loved him most. 🔴
- **"Who will roll away the stone?" (16:3).** They're worried about the wrong problem. 🔴
- **A young man in white (16:5).** Mark doesn't say angel, though the others do. Same word, *neaniskos*, as the young man who ran away naked in 14:51. 🔴 for the word; 🔵 for any link.
- **"And Peter" (16:7).** The one who denied him three times gets named. 🔴
- **"Just as He told you" (16:7).** Jesus said so in 14:28. His word holds. 🔴
- **"For they were afraid" (16:8).** The oldest copies stop on that line, in Greek ending on a small word, *gar*, "for." An odd way to end a book. 🔴
- **The brackets (16:9–20).** Your Bible marks these verses because the oldest and best manuscripts don't have them. 🔴
- **16:9 restarts the story.** It introduces Mary Magdalene as if we hadn't just met her in 16:1. That's a seam. 🔴
- **"Seven demons" (16:9).** That detail comes from Luke 8:2. The longer ending borrows from the other Gospels. 🔴
- **Snakes and poison (16:18).** Not found anywhere else in Mark. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Burial spices.** The body was wrapped fast on Friday because of the Sabbath. Sunday was the first chance to finish the job properly. 🔴
- **Rolling stones.** Some wealthy tombs were closed with a big disc-shaped stone set in a groove. Most were closed with a square block. Either way, three women couldn't move it. 🔴
- **The first day of the week.** Sunday. Christians soon began meeting on it instead of only the Sabbath, "the Lord's day." 🔴
- **Women as witnesses.** In that world a woman's testimony counted for little in court. Josephus says women shouldn't be witnesses at all (*Antiquities* 4.219). If you were making up a resurrection story, you wouldn't pick women as the first witnesses. 🔴
- **How manuscripts work.** Scribes copied by hand. When a book seemed to end too sharply, a scribe might add what he thought was missing. That's why modern Bibles mark these verses instead of hiding them, and the footnote isn't new. Church writers talked about it centuries ago. 🔴
- **Divine council: the right hand.** The longer ending closes with Jesus "taken up into heaven" and seated "at the right hand of God" (16:19). That's Psalm 110 again, the same throne claim Jesus made at his trial (14:62). Even where the ending is late, it says what the whole New Testament says. 🔴
- **Demons and the name.** "In My name they will cast out demons" (16:17). The strong man is tied up (3:27). The Twelve did this in his name before (6:13). 🔴

- **In the church course.** I taught the longer ending as one of three passages (with John 7:53–8:11 and 1 John 5:7) that modern Bibles footnote, not hide. No doctrine stands or falls on any of them. Don't get defensive about it. 🔴

It reads like someone fixing the sharp stop at 16:8 by stitching together appearances from the other Gospels, with words Mark doesn't use and snake-and-poison material that sits oddly with the rest. Mark's ending looks composed. John's story looks relocated. 🟡

- **The young man.** The one in white at the tomb (16:5) may pair with the naked young man of 14:51–52: naked flight, then clothed resurrection. 🔵

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus is back in Capernaum. Four men dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man, and Jesus tells him his sins are forgiven. The scribes call it blasphemy, so Jesus heals him to prove the point.
- Jesus calls Levi out of a tax booth and then eats with a house full of tax collectors and sinners. The complaint is about who he eats with.
- People ask why his disciples don't fast. He answers with a bridegroom, a patch and new wine.
- His disciples pick grain on the Sabbath. He answers with David and ends on "the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath."
- Four scenes, four fights. This is the first run of the conflicts that end at the cross.

## Pay attention to this
- **"He was at home" (2:1).** Jesus had moved to Capernaum, so the roof the four men dug through was probably his own. 🟡
- **Forgiveness comes before the healing (2:5).** The man came to walk. Jesus starts with his sins, and that is what makes the room tense. 🔴
- **"Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (2:7).** The scribes get the theology right. Jesus doesn't argue with it. He proves he has the authority. 🔴
- **Which is easier to say (2:9).** Anyone can say "your sins are forgiven" because nobody can check it. "Get up and walk" gets checked in seconds. The healing is the receipt for the claim nobody can see. 🔴
- **First "Son of Man" in Mark (2:10).** Jesus uses it for authority on earth to forgive. The same phrase comes back at his trial (14:62), against the same charge of blasphemy. 🔴
- **"Follow Me!" (2:14).** Two words, and Levi stands up and leaves the booth. 🔴
- **The problem is the meal (2:16).** They don't ask why he teaches sinners. They ask why he eats with them. 🔴
- **The bridegroom (2:19–20).** In the prophets the bridegroom is Israel's God (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2). Jesus puts himself in that role and says he'll be "taken away." The first hint of his death in Mark. 🟡
- **Abiathar (2:26).** First Samuel 21 names Ahimelech, Abiathar's father, as the priest when David ate the bread. Mark says "around the time of Abiathar." The phrase can mean "in the section of Scripture about Abiathar" or just "in his days," since Abiathar was there and became the better-known priest. Real problem, no settled answer. ⬜
- **"The Sabbath was made for man" (2:27).** This doesn't abolish the Sabbath. It says what the Sabbath is for. Then 2:28 makes the bigger claim: he is Lord of it. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Roofs.** A Galilean house had a flat roof of beams, branches and packed mud, reached by an outside stair. Mark says they "dug an opening." Messy, but doable. 🔴
- **Who could pronounce forgiveness.** That went through the Temple, the priests and the sacrifices in Jerusalem. A man in a house in Capernaum saying it on his own was claiming the Temple's job. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Levi's booth.** When Herod the Great died in 4 BC his kingdom was split. Antipas got Galilee, Philip got the land to the north and east, and the line between them ran down the Jordan into the lake. Capernaum was the last Galilee town on that road. Levi likely collected Herod Antipas's toll on a border people could remember being drawn, not Rome's tax directly. 🔴 for the geography; 🟡 for whose toll it was.
- **Table fellowship.** Eating with someone said you belonged together. A rabbi at table with toll collectors was making a public statement about them, and about himself. 🔴
- **The Pharisees weren't police.** They were an unofficial party, a pressure group with influence and no power to arrest anyone. They're in the grainfield because Jesus is in public view. 🔴
- **The Sabbath was a flag.** Under occupation, Sabbath, circumcision and food laws were how Israel stayed Israel. Defending it wasn't petty. That is why claiming authority over it was worse than ignoring it. 🔴
- **God works on the Sabbath.** Jewish thinkers knew God keeps creation running on the seventh day: the sun rises, babies are born, rain falls. In a Jewish ear "Lord of the Sabbath" sounds like "I'm the one who makes the sun come up." 🔴 that the idea existed (Philo, rabbis); 🟡 for the sun-rise line, which is Huff's and was flagged for checking.
- **Fasts looked back.** The regular fasts mourned national disasters like the fall of the first Temple (Zechariah 7–8). Jesus says this is a wedding, not a funeral. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Divine council: the Son of Man.** The phrase comes from Daniel 7, a throne room scene: "thrones were set up," the Ancient of Days sits, the court is seated, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds and gets dominion. In Heiser's frame that's the heavenly council. In Daniel the son of man is given authority to judge. Here he uses it to forgive. 🔴 for the Daniel source; 🟡 for the council read.

## My notes
- I wrote three posts out of this chapter in the Conflict With the Pharisees series (posts 1, 3 and 4), mostly working from Wright's *Mark for Everyone*.
- **The paralytic.** The roof was probably Jesus' own. Wright hears the first line with a rueful smile: a man looks up at a new hole in his ceiling and says "all right, I forgive you," and something in it isn't about the roof. 🟡
- **Daniel 7 flipped.** In Daniel the son of man gets authority to hand out God's judgment. Here he hands out God's forgiveness. Same office, opposite output. 🟡

Wright's comparison is a parking attendant: all day taking money from people who resent it, for a government they want gone. "Follow me" may have been the first time in years anyone treated him like a person. 🟡
- **A doctor throwing a party.** That's Wright's picture of Jesus at Levi's table. The doctor has to be where the sickness is.

- **David is a king.** The precedent Jesus picks is the anointed king, not yet on his throne, hungry, with his men. Anyone who caught that knew what was being claimed. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Another Sabbath fight. Jesus heals a man's withered hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees go out and plot with the Herodians to kill him (3:1–6).
- Crowds pour in from everywhere. Unclean spirits fall down and shout "You are the Son of God," and he orders them quiet (3:7–12).
- On a mountain he appoints twelve "to be with Him" and so he could send them out with authority over demons (3:13–19).
- His family comes to "take custody of Him" because they say "He has lost His senses." Scribes from Jerusalem say "He is possessed by Beelzebul." Jesus answers with a divided kingdom, a strong man tied up, and the one sin that never gets forgiven (3:20–30).
- His mother and brothers stand outside. He looks at the people sitting around him and says these are his family (3:31–35).

## Pay attention to this
- **The sandwich.** Mark starts the family story (3:21), cuts to the scribes (3:22–30), then finishes the family story (3:31–35). He wants the two read through each other. Family says "crazy," scribes say "demonic." Same mistake, two volumes. 🔴
- **Scribes, not Pharisees.** Mark says scribes "who came down from Jerusalem" (3:22). Matthew has Pharisees. Keep Mark's word in Mark. 🔴
- **They never deny the exorcisms.** The argument is about where the power comes from. Nobody says it isn't happening. 🔴
- **"They were saying" (3:22, 3:30).** Imperfect tense in Greek: ongoing, repeated. A campaign, not a slip of the tongue. 🔴
- **"Because they were saying" (3:30).** Mark nails the whole saying about the unforgivable sin to this scene. The sin is calling the Spirit's work a demon's work, and doing it with your mind made up. 🔴
- **The strong man (3:27).** You can't rob a strong man's house unless you tie him up first. The strong man is Satan. The exorcisms aren't the fight. They're the robbery after the fight. 🔴
- **The demons know (3:11).** The first ones in Mark to call him the Son of God out loud are the unclean spirits. 🔴
- **Twelve on a mountain (3:13–14).** Twelve tribes, a mountain, a new people. And the first job is "to be with Him," then to be sent. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the new-Israel read.
- **Grief and anger together (3:5).** Mark says Jesus looked at them "with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart." 🔴
- **The plot starts early (3:6).** Pharisees and Herodians hated each other. They agree on this. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Beelzebul is an old god's title.** In the Ugarit texts, a thousand years before Jesus, Baal carries the title *zbl*, "prince" or "exalted." Baal-zbl, Prince Baal. By the first century the old title names the head of the dark powers. 🔴 (Marcus, Heiser)
- **"Ruler of the demons" was already a slot.** Jubilees calls its chief dark power, Mastema, "chief of the spirits" and "ruler of the demons." Same formula the scribes use. 🔴
- **Divine council: the nations' powers.** In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview the nations were handed over to lesser *elohim* who went bad. Baal is the face of that rebel order in Israel's own land. Calling Jesus' power Beelzebul files him under the enemy's chain of command. 🟡 (Heiser)
- **Unclean spirits.** Some Second Temple writers (1 Enoch 15) said the spirits of the dead Nephilim became the evil spirits that roam the earth. That's one reason they're "unclean": they don't belong to either world. 🔴 that the tradition existed; 🔵 that Mark assumes it.
- **An investigation, not a heckle.** Lane reads the scribes from Jerusalem as possibly sent by the central authority, checking whether a town had been led astray (the "seduced city" of Deuteronomy 13). The later Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a) remembers Jesus as charged with sorcery. 🟡 (Lane)
- **Honor, challenge and answer.** In that world, a public accusation was a challenge. Silence meant you lost, and the crowd went home thinking the scribes were right. Jesus has to answer. 🔴 (deSilva)
- **Family was everything.** Your honor and your safety came from your kin. Saying "these are my mother and brothers" about strangers on the floor would have shocked the room. 🔴
- **Herodians and Pharisees.** One group backed Herod's family and Rome. The other kept themselves apart from both. Seeing them plot together tells you how big a threat Jesus looked. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus teaches from a boat, and Mark gives us his parable chapter. The sower first, with four kinds of ground (4:1–9).
- Alone with the Twelve, he says the parables reveal to insiders and hide from outsiders, quoting Isaiah 6. Then he explains the sower (4:10–20).
- A lamp, a measure, a seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, and a mustard seed that ends up big enough for birds (4:21–34).
- That night a storm nearly sinks the boat. Jesus is asleep, wakes, tells the sea to be quiet, and it is. The disciples are more scared after than before: "Who then is this?" (4:35–41).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Listen to this!" (4:3) and "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (4:9).** The chapter is about hearing. Count how many times "hear" shows up. 🔴
- **The Isaiah 6 quote (4:12).** "While seeing, they may see and not perceive." Hard words. In Isaiah, God's people have gone deaf and the prophet is sent anyway. Parables work the same way: they open up for people who lean in and close up for people who don't. 🔴 for the quote; 🟡 for how it works.
- **Satan in the explanation (4:15).** The birds that eat the seed on the road are Satan. The chapter has a dark power working against the word from the start. 🔴
- **Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold (4:8).** Big yields, not miraculous ones. A good harvest, which is the point: the kingdom grows in normal ground, not magic ground. 🟡
- **The seed that grows "by itself" (4:28).** The Greek is *automatē*, the word we get "automatic" from. The farmer sleeps and gets up and doesn't know how. Only Mark has this parable. 🔴
- **"He immediately puts in the sickle" (4:29).** Lifted from Joel 3:13, a judgment on the nations. The harvest is judgment day. 🔴
- **Mustard seed (4:31–32).** It becomes the largest garden plant. A shrub, not a cedar. Birds nest in its shade, which echoes the great trees of Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 17 and 31. 🔴 for the echo; 🟡 for reading the birds as Gentiles.
- **Insiders, outsiders, and still confused.** He explains "everything privately to His own disciples" (4:34), and then they panic in the boat. Being inside doesn't mean getting it. 🔴
- **"Silence! Be still" (4:39).** Mark uses the word Jesus used to shut up a demon in 1:25. He rebukes the storm the way he rebukes a spirit. 🔴
- **Sleeping in the stern (4:38).** The same "sleeps and rises" picture from the growing-seed parable shows up a few verses later with Jesus himself. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Sowing came before plowing, sometimes.** Farmers in Galilee scattered seed by hand, and seed landed on paths, thin soil over limestone and thorn patches. The debate over whether they plowed first or after doesn't change the story. The field is Israel, and the prophets already used this picture (Jeremiah 4:3). 🟡 (Wright)
- **The seed is a remnant.** Isaiah 6 ends with "the holy seed is its stump" (6:13). Wright reads the sower as Israel's God sowing the returning remnant, which is why Jesus reaches for Isaiah 6 to explain it. 🟡 (Wright, *Jesus and the Victory of God*)
- **The day starts at sundown.** "Sleeps and rises, night and day" is in Jewish order. Night comes first. It marks time passing, not a lazy farmer. 🔴
- **Joel's harvest.** Many in Jesus' day hoped for Joel's Day of the Lord: Israel restored and the nations judged. Jesus borrows Joel's sickle and says the harvest is coming, but not the way they pictured it. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Kingdom trees.** Big trees with birds in their branches were pictures of great empires (Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4, the cedar in Ezekiel 17 and 31). Jesus picks a garden shrub. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the deflation.
- **Divine council: the sea.** In the ancient world the sea was chaos, the home of monsters, the thing gods fought (Leviathan, Rahab). In the Old Testament only Yahweh rules it: "You rule the swelling of the sea; when its waves rise, You still them" (Psalm 89:9), and Psalm 107:29 has him calming a storm for sailors. So when the disciples ask "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" the Old Testament answer is: Yahweh. 🔴
- **Rebuking a storm like a spirit.** Treating the wind and sea as something to rebuke fits a world where chaos and the dark powers were tied together. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem see his disciples eating with unwashed hands and ask why they don't keep "the tradition of the elders" (7:1–5).
- Jesus quotes Isaiah ("This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far away from Me") and uses Corban to show tradition cancelling a commandment (7:6–13).
- He tells the crowd a riddle: nothing going into a man defiles him, only what comes out. Indoors, the disciples still don't get it, so he explains, and Mark adds, "Thus He declared all foods clean" (7:14–23).
- He goes into Gentile land near Tyre. A Greek woman begs for her daughter, takes his hard line about the children's bread and the dogs, and wins (7:24–30).
- In the Decapolis he heals a deaf man with fingers, spit and one Aramaic word: "Ephphatha," "Be opened!" (7:31–37).

## Pay attention to this
- **Mark explains the washing (7:3–4).** He stops the story to tell readers what the Pharisees do with hands, cups and pots. He's writing for people who didn't know Jewish practice. 🔴
- **"The tradition of the elders" vs. "the commandment of God."** Count how often the two are set against each other in 7:8–13. That's the argument. 🔴
- **Corban (7:11).** Declare your property "given to God" and you no longer have to support your parents. A commandment cancelled by a religious-sounding device. 🔴
- **The list (7:21–22).** Evil thoughts, sexual immoralities, thefts, murders, adulteries, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. None of it is about ritual. All of it is about the heart. 🔴
- **"Thus He declared all foods clean" (7:19).** That's Mark talking, not Jesus. It's an aside to the reader, written after the church had already fought over food. 🔴
- **The house again (7:17).** Public riddle, private confusion, explanation indoors. Same pattern as the parables in chapter 4. 🔴
- **Verse 16 is in brackets.** "If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear" isn't in some of the oldest manuscripts. 🔴
- **"Yes, Lord" (7:28).** She calls him Lord. She accepts his picture (children first, dogs under the table) and finds room inside it. 🔴
- **"Because of this answer" (7:29).** Her daughter is healed from a distance because of what she said. 🔴
- **"Spoke with difficulty" (7:32).** Mark uses a rare Greek word, *mogilalos*. The only other place it shows up in the Greek Bible is Isaiah 35:6, about the day God comes and "the tongue of the mute will shout for joy." The crowd's line in 7:37 echoes the same passage. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Handwashing was purity, not hygiene.** Nobody knew about germs. Washing hands before eating came from the tradition built around the law, priestly purity rules stretched to ordinary tables. 🔴
- **Food laws were a flag.** Under Greek and Roman rule, what you ate is how people could tell you were a Jew. Some of Israel's national heroes, the Maccabean martyrs, were tortured to death for refusing pork (2 Maccabees 7). Food was not a small question. 🔴
- **Why Jesus is cryptic.** Saying plainly "all foods are clean" would tell a nation its martyrs "died in the wrong ditch." So he answers in public, in a riddle, without handing his enemies a headline. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Tyre and Sidon.** Old Phoenician land, Gentile, the home of Baal worship and Jezebel's family. Jesus walks into the region of the widow of Zarephath, the Gentile he praised in his Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:26). 🔴
- **Divine council: an unclean spirit in Gentile land.** In the Deuteronomy 32 picture the nations belonged to other powers, and Israel's land was Yahweh's. Here a Gentile girl in Baal's old territory is held by an unclean spirit, and a word from Jesus frees her from miles away. The Gentile territory isn't out of his reach. 🔴 for the healing; 🟡 for the council frame.
- **The Decapolis.** Ten Greek cities east of the lake. Gentile again. The healing happens on their side of the line. 🔴
- **Dogs.** Jews sometimes used "dogs" for Gentiles. Jesus uses the word for little house dogs, the ones under the table. That softens it a little. Not much. 🟡
- **Honor and a woman alone.** A foreign woman approaching a Jewish teacher in public, without a man to speak for her, crosses two lines at once. 🔴 (Bailey)

## My notes
- I wrote this up in the Conflict With the Pharisees series (post 2, "Clean and Unclean: Why Jesus Was Cryptic") and the Jesus and Women series, plus my dietary-laws study.
- **Wright's comparison.** You might as well try telling the leaders of the old South Africa that all races are equal before God. It's not something they want to hear, so it has to come carefully. 🟡
- **The disciples are confused too.** The obvious reading of "what goes in, what comes out" points at the toilet joke, which isn't what a kingdom announcement is for. They ask indoors, and only then does he explain.
- **The wall.** The food laws were never about food. They were a wall built out of habit, kept three times a day by every person without a priest in the room, so Israel couldn't be absorbed by the empires that kept rolling over her. The pressure wasn't persecution. It was dinner. 🟡
- **And then the wall comes down.** Once the Messiah came through that people and the mission turned out to the nations, a wall that kept the nations out was working against the reason Israel existed. The wall was scaffolding, not the building. Peter's vision (Acts 10:28) moves from animals to people. Ephesians 2:14: he "broke down the dividing wall." 🟡
- **The teaching came early.** The principle that settled the church's first big fight in Acts was given years earlier, in a riddle, to men who didn't understand it yet.
- **The Syrophoenician woman.** Bailey reads it as an examination. A good coach honors a good runner by putting her in the toughest race. That isn't a full answer and I don't present it as one. The words are hard and the text doesn't soften them. What the reading has going for it is the ending: he praises her. 🟡
- **The disciples are the audience.** Bailey: evil can't be fixed until it's exposed. Jesus says out loud what the disciples were thinking, and a Gentile woman takes it apart in one sentence in front of them. The same men later took the message to the Gentiles. 🟡
- **Two things she believed.** That he had God's power to heal, and that he cared about people outside Israel. The second is the one being tested. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus feeds four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish. Seven baskets left over (8:1–10).
- The Pharisees demand a sign from heaven. He sighs and refuses (8:11–13).
- In the boat he warns about "the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." The disciples think he's upset about bread. "Do you not yet understand?" (8:14–21).
- At Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two steps. First he sees people "like trees, walking around," then clearly (8:22–26).
- Near Caesarea Philippi Peter says "You are the Christ." Jesus starts teaching that the Son of Man must suffer, die and rise. Peter rebukes him and gets "Get behind Me, Satan!" Then the cost: deny yourself, take up your cross (8:27–38).
- This is the hinge of Mark. Before it, Galilee. After it, the road to Jerusalem.

## Pay attention to this
- **A second feeding (8:1–9).** This one happens after Jesus has been in Gentile country (7:24–37). Twelve baskets the first time, seven this time. Jesus makes them count both (8:19–20). 🔴 for the numbers; 🟡 for reading twelve as Israel and seven as the nations.
- **A sign right after a feeding (8:11).** He just fed thousands. What sign are they asking for? 🔴
- **"Sighing deeply in His spirit" (8:12).** Mark lets us see Jesus' frustration. 🔴
- **One loaf in the boat (8:14).** They're worried about bread with the bread-maker sitting next to them. 🟡
- **"Having eyes, do you not see?" (8:18).** The Isaiah 6 and Jeremiah 5 language from chapter 4 is now aimed at the Twelve. 🔴
- **The two-stage healing (8:22–26).** The only healing in the Gospels that takes two tries. It sits right between "do you not yet understand" and Peter's half-right confession. The disciples see, but blurry. 🔴 for the placement; 🟡 for the read.
- **"You are the Christ" (8:29).** Mark gives the bare confession. The rock and the keys are Matthew's (Matt 16:17–19). 🔴
- **"Tell no one" (8:30).** The title came with a job description: drive out Rome. Jesus won't take that job. 🟡
- **"Must suffer" (8:31).** The first of three times he predicts his death on the road (8:31, 9:31, 10:33–34). Each time, the disciples miss it. 🔴
- **"Get behind Me, Satan!" (8:33).** The same offer as the wilderness: the crown without the cross. Peter is voicing the adversary's line. 🔴
- **"Ashamed of Me" (8:38).** In an honor-shame world, being ashamed of someone was a public verdict. The Son of Man will return the verdict when he comes "with the holy angels." 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Leaven.** Every Passover Jews cleared every bit of leaven out of the house to remember leaving Egypt in a hurry. Leaven was the thing you got rid of at the festival of freedom. Jesus uses it for something small that works through the whole batch unseen. 🔴
- **Two wrong kingdoms.** The Pharisees wanted God's kingdom for the strictly observant. Herod wanted it to be his family's throne. Opposite parties, both wanting God to act and both wanting to end up in charge. 🟡 (Wright)
- **"Messiah" meant a war.** The Psalms of Solomon, from the century before, ask God to raise up a son of David to smash the nations like pottery. Say "Christ" in public and people heard "revolt against Rome." 🔴
- **Why Caesarea Philippi.** It's in the far north, outside Herod Antipas's land, about two days' walk from the lake. A safe place to ask the dangerous question. 🟡 (Wright)
- **Divine council: Hermon and the gods.** Caesarea Philippi sat at the foot of Mount Hermon, in the old land of Bashan, which the Old Testament ties to Og and the giant clans (Deut 3:11). The town was called Panias after the cave of Pan, and Herod built a temple to Augustus there. More than twenty temples have been surveyed on and around Hermon. In 1 Enoch 6, Hermon is where the Watchers came down to rebel. Jesus asks "who do you say that I am?" in the most crowded patch of rival gods' territory in the country. 🔴 for the geography and the cult sites; 🟡 for reading the setting as deliberate (Heiser).
- **The nations' gods.** In the Deuteronomy 32 worldview the nations were handed to other powers at Babel. Hermon's open-air shrines to the "celestial gods" are that host of heaven. 🟡 (Heiser)
- **Crosses were real.** "Take up his cross" wasn't a metaphor yet. Galileans had seen Rome crucify rebels by the road. A man carrying a crossbeam was a man walking to his death. 🔴
- **Holy angels (8:38).** The Son of Man coming in glory with angels goes back to Daniel 7, where the heavenly court surrounds the throne. 🔴 for the source; 🟡 for the council read.

## What the chapter is doing
- Six days after Caesarea Philippi, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain and is transfigured. Moses and Elijah talk with him. A voice from the cloud: "This is My beloved Son, listen to Him!" (9:1–8).
- Coming down, he tells them to keep quiet until he rises, and says Elijah has already come (9:9–13).
- At the bottom, the other disciples have failed to free a boy from a spirit. His father says "if You can," and then "I do believe; help my unbelief." Jesus frees the boy (9:14–29).
- He predicts his death a second time. The disciples don't understand, and on the road they argue about who is greatest. He puts a child in front of them (9:30–37).
- Then hard sayings: don't stop the outsider who casts out demons in his name, don't trip up the little ones, cut off what makes you stumble, be salted with fire (9:38–50).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Six days later" (9:2).** Mark ties the mountain straight to the confession and the first death prediction. 🔴
- **Three booths (9:5).** One each. Peter puts Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah. Very high praise, wrong category. The voice answers by singling out one: "listen to Him!" And then they see "Jesus alone" (9:8). 🔴
- **"He did not know what to answer; for they became terrified" (9:6).** Mark is hard on Peter, and the tradition is that Peter was Mark's source. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the Peter link.
- **"Listen to Him!" (9:7).** It repeats the baptism voice with one addition, right after Peter argued with Jesus about the cross. 🔴
- **Elijah already came (9:11–13).** John the Baptist, and "they did to him whatever they wished." 🔴
- **"If You can?" (9:23).** Jesus throws the father's words back at him. 🔴
- **"I do believe; help my unbelief" (9:24).** He doesn't sort out his doubt before he asks. He says it as part of the asking, and it's answered. 🔴
- **"Like a corpse... Jesus took him by the hand and raised him" (9:26–27).** Death and resurrection words in a healing story. 🔴
- **The disciples couldn't do it (9:18, 9:28).** They had done exorcisms before (6:13). This time they failed. "This kind cannot come out by anything but prayer." Some manuscripts add "and fasting." 🔴
- **Who is the greatest (9:34).** Right after he tells them he'll be killed. 🔴
- **Verses 44 and 46 are in brackets.** They repeat 9:48 and aren't in the oldest manuscripts. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Mountains are where God shows up.** Moses on Sinai, Elijah at Horeb, the same mountain. Both had strange endings: Moses buried by God where nobody knows, Elijah taken up alive. Now both stand with Jesus on a mountain. 🔴
- **The cloud.** The cloud that "overshadowed" is the glory cloud of the wilderness and the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Booths fit too: the Feast of Booths remembered the wilderness. 🔴 for the echoes; 🟡 for Peter thinking of the feast.
- **Exodus talk.** Luke's version says they discussed his "departure," and the Greek word is *exodos* (Luke 9:31). The second exodus the prophets had promised would happen at Jerusalem. 🔴
- **Elijah first.** Malachi 4:5 said Elijah would come before the great day of the LORD. The scribes taught it. Jesus says it already happened, in John. 🔴
- **Divine council: which mountain.** Mark only says "a high mountain." Tradition picked Tabor, but that tradition shows up in the fourth century, and Tabor is under 2,000 feet. Hermon is over 9,000 and right next to Caesarea Philippi. In 1 Enoch 6, Hermon is where the Watchers came down to start their rebellion. If it's Hermon, Jesus shows his glory on the rebels' own mountain. 🔴 for the heights and the Enoch tradition; 🟡 for Hermon as the site (Heiser).
- **Spirits that harm.** The father says the spirit throws the boy into fire and water "to destroy him." First-century Jews saw some sickness as the work of hostile spirits. Mark has Jesus address it as a spirit: "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you." 🔴
- **Hell is a valley.** "Hell" here is *Gehenna*, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where kings once burned children to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31). "Their worm does not die" is the last verse of Isaiah (66:24). 🔴
- **Salt and fire.** Every offering was salted (Leviticus 2:13). "Salted with fire" sounds like sacrifice language. 🟡

## META: the book of Matthew
- **Where it sits.** First book of the New Testament, and the hinge back to the Old. It opens with "the book of the genealogy," the same wording the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. Matthew starts the story of Jesus the way Genesis starts the story of the world. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for the Genesis echo being on purpose.
- **The question the whole book is asking:** is Jesus the king Israel was promised, and if he is, why does his kingdom look nothing like what Israel expected?
- **Who wrote it.** The book never names its author. Papias (early 2nd century, quoted by Eusebius, *Church History* 3.39.16) says Matthew put together the sayings "in the Hebrew language." Every early title says "according to Matthew." Mark and Luke call the tax collector at the booth Levi; only this gospel calls him Matthew (9:9, 10:3). 🔴 for what Papias said; ⬜ for the authorship itself.
- **When.** Contested. The case for after AD 70 leans on 22:7 (the king burns the city) read as written after the fact, and on Matthew's running fight with the Pharisees looking like the synagogue after the Temple fell. Every one of those is an inference. If Luke is before 70, Matthew moves early with it. ⬜
- **Text issues are small.** The doxology at the end of the Lord's Prayer (6:13, "For Yours is the kingdom...") is missing from the oldest manuscripts, which is why the LSB puts it in brackets. A few verses (17:21, 18:11) drop out of the earliest copies too. 🔴
- **Five big speeches.** The Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the sending of the Twelve (10), the parables (13), life in the community (18), and the end of the age (24–25). Each one closes with "when Jesus had finished" (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1). 🔴 Some read the five as a new set of five books of Moses. 🔵
- **Two turns.** "From that time Jesus began to preach" (4:17) and "From that time Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem" (16:21). The first opens his public work, the second points it at the cross. 🟡
- **Things to track the whole way through:**
  - "To fulfill what was spoken through the prophet." Matthew says it about ten times. 🔴
  - God with us. "Immanuel" in 1:23, "I am with you always" in 28:20. The book is bookended by the promise. 🔴
  - The nations. Gentile women in the family tree (ch. 1), Gentile magi at the cradle (ch. 2), "make disciples of all the nations" at the end (28:19). 🔴
  - The kingdom of heaven. Matthew's own phrase for the kingdom of God, out of Jewish respect for the name. 🔴
  - The powers. A tempter in ch. 4, demons in ch. 8, Beelzebul in ch. 12, the gates of Hades in ch. 16, "the devil and his angels" in ch. 25. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for reading them as one thread.

## What the chapter is doing
- A family tree from Abraham to Jesus, cut into three sets of fourteen generations: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Messiah.
- Four women show up in a list of fathers: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and "the wife of Uriah."
- Mary is pregnant before she and Joseph live together. Joseph, a righteous man, plans to end the betrothal quietly.
- An angel tells him in a dream the child is from the Holy Spirit and to name him Jesus, "for He will save His people from their sins." Matthew ties it to Isaiah 7:14, Immanuel.
- Joseph wakes up and does exactly what he was told.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Son of David, son of Abraham" (1:1).** The two promises the whole Old Testament hangs on: a king from David (2 Samuel 7) and blessing for every nation through Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Matthew names both in the first line. 🔴
- **The list is built, not copied.** Three sets of fourteen. To get there Matthew skips kings that 1–2 Kings and Chronicles name (Joram to Uzziah in 1:8 leaves out three). "Father of" can mean ancestor. 🔴
- **Four women, and Mary makes five.** Tamar (Genesis 38), Rahab the Canaanite, Ruth the Moabite, and Bathsheba, who Matthew won't name. He calls her "the wife of Uriah" (1:6), which keeps David's sin in the family record. 🔴 Why these four is debated: outsiders, irregular stories, or both. 🟡
- **The exile is a whole section (1:11–12).** Matthew counts Israel's history by the exile. The third set of fourteen runs from Babylon to the Messiah, so the story he's telling is that the exile isn't really over until Jesus. 🟡
- **"Joseph her husband" before the wedding (1:19).** Betrothal was a legal marriage. Breaking it took a divorce. 🔴
- **Joseph the righteous man (1:19).** He's righteous and he doesn't want to shame her. Matthew puts those side by side on purpose. 🔴
- **Matthew tells you Joseph's feelings.** "When he had considered this" (1:20) is a word for turning something over, upset. Joseph had a hard night. 🟡 (Bailey; see below.)
- **The name is the mission (1:21).** "Jesus" is *Yeshua*, short for *Yehoshua*, "Yahweh saves." The angel explains the name with the verb inside it: he will save. 🔴
- **His people, from their sins.** Not from Rome. 🔴
- **Joseph never says a word.** In the whole birth story he only obeys (1:24; 2:14; 2:21). 🔴

## Read it like 5 BC, not 2026
- **A family tree was a legal claim.** In a world with no birth certificates, your genealogy was your standing: your land, your tribe, your right to a throne or the priesthood. After the exile, priests who couldn't prove their line were shut out (Ezra 2:62). Opening with a royal family tree is a claim to the throne before the baby is born. 🔴
- **Fourteen may be David's number.** Hebrew letters count as numbers, and David (D-W-D) adds to 4+6+4 = 14. Matthew may be stamping David's name on the whole list. 🔵
- **A modern reader sees a list of names. A Jew in 5 BC saw a story with holes in it.** Tamar posed as a prostitute to get justice out of Judah. Rahab ran a house in Jericho. Ruth came from Moab, a people barred from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3). Bathsheba was taken by the king. Matthew puts the scandals in the Messiah's own line. 🔴 for the stories; 🟡 for reading them as a message about grace and the nations.
- **Betrothal was binding.** A Jewish betrothal lasted about a year, the girl often in her early teens, and the couple was legally married without living together. Unfaithfulness in that year was treated as adultery, and the Law named stoning (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). By the first century that sentence was rarely carried out, but public shame was certain. 🔴 for the law; 🟡 for how it worked in Jesus' day.
- **Joseph's two roads.** He could take Mary to a public hearing and clear his own name, or hand her a quiet divorce in front of a couple of witnesses. He picked quiet. 🟡
- **Bailey on "just."** Kenneth Bailey reads Joseph's justice through the Servant of Isaiah 42, the one who won't break a bruised reed. Justice there isn't payback and it isn't equal law for everyone; it's mercy for the weak. That's the kind of just man Joseph is. 🟡
- **Joseph was angry, and that's normal.** Bailey points out the oldest Arabic translation (8th century or earlier) renders 1:20 "while he was disturbed over this matter." Centuries of "Saint Joseph" made him calm. Matthew didn't. 🟡
- **Saved from what?** An occupied people wanted saving from Rome. Bailey notes the angel's answer, "from their sins," redefines the rescue Israel was praying for. Bailey also says the name and the verb make a wordplay in Hebrew or Aramaic that Greek and English lose. 🔴 for the occupation; 🟡 for Bailey's read.
- **Dreams were God's mail.** In the Bible and the world around it, dreams were a normal way the gods spoke to kings and priests. Joseph, son of Jacob in Matthew 1:16, gets dreams and ends up in Egypt in ch. 2, just like Joseph son of Jacob in Genesis. 🔴 for the parallel names; 🟡 for the echo being intended.
- **Isaiah 7:14.** The Hebrew word is *'almah*, a young woman of marriageable age. The Greek Old Testament that Matthew quotes has *parthenos*, virgin. Matthew is reading Isaiah the way the Greek-speaking synagogue already read it. 🔴
- **"An angel of the Lord" (1:20).** In the Old Testament "the angel of Yahweh" is often Yahweh himself in visible form. Heiser reads the New Testament "angel of the Lord" as a messenger, because the Son is now the one in the womb. 🟡

## My notes
- Joseph the just is Bailey's best surprise in the chapter for me. Justice that protects the weak person instead of settling the score.
- **The genealogy isn't a contradiction.** People say Matthew and Luke disagree. This isn't a detailed family tree. It's a list of people who are part of his line, and they're not including Uncle Bob, who nobody ever heard of. Matthew runs forward from Abraham to the King of the Jews. Luke runs backward to "Adam, the son of God." Two purposes, two designs. 🔴 Which reconciliation is right (Mary's line vs. Joseph's line, levirate marriage) I leave open. ⬜
- **The four women.** I first put them in Luke's genealogy. Wrong gospel. ❌ They're Matthew's. Luke has no women in his list at all. I was reaching for Luke because Luke is the gospel with the most women in it, and the cross-check caught it. That's why we double-check.
- **Dating.** I pushed back on treating Matthew as written after AD 70. That's one estimate. There's good evidence Luke wrote before 70 and before Paul died (Acts ends with Paul alive), and if Matthew and Luke are working at the same time, Matthew moves up with it. The post-70 arguments are all inferences. 🟡
- **Where Matthew sits in my plan.** I read Matthew late, as a comparison gospel after Luke. It got bumped up in priority because the Sermon on the Mount is the most distorted text in the New Testament ("judge not" as never judge, "turn the other cheek" as just take it).
- **Divine council:** no council scene in ch. 1. It's a family tree and a dream. The council thread starts with the star in ch. 2, the tempter in ch. 4, and the Gadarene demons in ch. 8, and it peaks at Caesarea Philippi in ch. 16.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and sickness, and Matthew lists their names.
- He sends them only to "the lost sheep of the house of Israel," with no money, no bag, no spare clothes. Preach the kingdom, heal, cast out demons, stay with whoever takes you in.
- Then mostly warnings: sheep among wolves, courts, floggings, governors and kings, families split.
- Don't worry what to say when you're arrested; the Spirit of your Father will speak in you.
- Don't fear people who can only kill the body. Confess me before people and I'll confess you before my Father. Take up your cross. Even a cup of cold water given to a disciple will be rewarded.

## Pay attention to this
- **Twelve on purpose.** Israel had twelve tribes. In 19:28 Jesus says the Twelve will sit on twelve thrones judging the tribes. Picking twelve is a claim to rebuild Israel. 🔴
- **"The first, Simon" (10:2).** Matthew alone says "first." 🔴
- **"Matthew the tax collector" (10:3).** Only this gospel tags Matthew with his old job. 🔴
- **"Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed Him" (10:4).** The list ends with the betrayal already named. 🔴
- **Israel first (10:5–6).** Not to Gentiles or Samaritans, yet. At the end of the book it's "all the nations" (28:19). 🔴
- **The job description is Jesus' own (10:7–8).** Preach the kingdom, heal, raise, cleanse, cast out. Exactly what chs. 4–9 showed him doing. 🔴
- **More warning than instruction.** About half the speech is what will go wrong. 🔴
- **"Do not worry" (10:19).** The verb is about anxiety, *me merimnesete*. The supplier is "the Spirit of your Father." 🔴
- **The setting is a courtroom.** Courts, synagogues, governors, kings (10:17–18). The promise is for testimony under arrest. 🔴
- **"Beelzebul" (10:25).** They already call Jesus the head of a demon household. Chapter 12 is where it blows up. 🔴
- **Two courts (10:32–33).** What you say about Jesus "before men" decides what he says about you "before My Father." 🔴
- **"Not peace, but a sword" (10:34).** The sword is the split in the family, quoted from Micah 7:6 (10:35–36). Not a call to fight. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **"Apostle" means one sent.** Jewish law had the idea of an agent: "a man's agent is like himself" (m. Berakhot 5:5). That's 10:40: "He who receives you receives Me." 🔴
- **Travel light, look different.** Wandering Greek philosophers of the day carried a bag and a staff and begged. Jesus' men carry neither. They live on the hospitality of the towns they serve. 🟡
- **Hospitality was sacred.** Taking in a stranger was a duty, and turning away a messenger was an insult to the sender. Sodom and Gomorrah (10:15) are the Bible's worst hosts (Genesis 19). 🔴
- **Shaking off the dust.** Jews coming back from Gentile land were said to shake off its dust. Doing it to a Jewish town treats it like pagan ground. 🟡
- **Flogged in synagogues.** Local synagogue courts could give thirty-nine lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3). Paul got it five times (2 Corinthians 11:24). 🔴
- **Wolves were rulers.** "Her princes within her are like wolves" (Ezekiel 22:27). 🔴
- **Beelzebul was a god's name.** Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2). "Zebul" means prince or lofty house, so Beelzebul is "Baal the prince," and "head of the house" in 10:25 is a pun on it. A Canaanite god's title had become a name for the prince of demons. 🔴 for the names; 🟡 for the pun.
- **A cross was not a metaphor yet.** In 4 BC the Roman general Varus crucified two thousand Jews after a revolt (Josephus). Galileans had seen men carry crossbeams. "Take his cross" meant walk to your execution. 🔴
- **Two sparrows for an *assarion*.** A small copper coin. The cheapest meat in the market, and God still tracks each one. 🔴
- **The heavenly court is real.** The Old Testament shows God judging among a council, with an accuser (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3). In 10:32–33 Jesus places himself in that court, standing up for the ones who stood up for him. 1 John 2:1 calls him our "Advocate with the Father." Stephen sees him standing in Acts 7:56. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for reading 10:32 as a council scene.
- **Authority over spirits (10:1).** Jesus doesn't pass on a technique. He hands out authority, which is a king's word. The kingdom is going after the territory of the unclean spirits. 🟡

## My notes
- **10:19–20 is one of four places** the promise appears (with Mark 13:11, Luke 12:11–12, Luke 21:14–15). Lange/Schaff: given on two different occasions, the sending of the Twelve and the end-times speech. 🔴
- **It doesn't mean don't study.** The folk use turns this into permission not to prepare. That itself does not mean you shouldn't study. It just means you don't have to write your argument. The promise covers the words under interrogation, not the knowledge you bring into the room. 🔴
- **The Servant was a disciple.** Jesus' wording draws on Isaiah 50:4, the Servant as a *limmud*, a learner, taught every morning what to say. Stephen's Spirit-filled defense in Acts 7 is a structured legal argument. So the field note became a case for study.
- **Not just for the Twelve.** We will never say a saying was only for the Twelve. If that were the case, why record it?
- **The Twelve Apostles post.** Twelve because Israel had twelve tribes. Read chapter 10 and then Acts, and Acts reads like the fulfillment: flogged, dragged before councils, governors and kings.
- **10:37 and Luke 14:26.** Same teaching, two styles. Luke says "hate your father." Matthew says "loves father or mother more than Me." I used the pair in a mentee session to show Semitic hyperbole. "Hate" means love less by comparison. 🔴
- **Divine council:** 10:32–33 is a heavenly courtroom with Jesus as advocate. 🟡 That's its own file.

## What the chapter is doing
- John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask: "Are You the One who is to come, or shall we look for someone else?" Jesus answers with what's happening: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor hear good news.
- Jesus tells the crowd who John is: more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi, the Elijah who was to come.
- "This generation" is like kids in the market who won't play wedding or funeral. John fasted and they called him demon-possessed; Jesus eats and they call him a glutton and a drunkard.
- Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, the towns that saw the most miracles and didn't repent.
- Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and showing them to children, and says, "Come to Me, all who are weary."

## Pay attention to this
- **John doubts from a cell.** The greatest man "born of women" (11:11) asks if he got it wrong. Jesus doesn't scold him. 🔴
- **Jesus answers with evidence, not a title.** He lists what John's men "hear and see" (11:4–5), all lines from Isaiah (35:5–6; 61:1). 🔴
- **"Blessed is he who does not take offense at Me" (11:6).** The word is "stumble." Jesus isn't the Messiah John expected either. 🔴
- **The least is greater than John (11:11).** Not more holy. Living on the other side of the line where the kingdom has come. 🟡
- **"If you are willing to accept it" (11:14).** John is Elijah, but only for those with ears for it. 🔴
- **The rhyme.** Flute and dance, dirge and mourning (11:17). Two games kids played: wedding and funeral. 🔴
- **Nothing pleases them.** John fasted: "He has a demon." Jesus feasts: "a gluttonous man and a drunkard." 🔴
- **The pagan cities come off better.** Tyre, Sidon and even Sodom would have repented (11:21–23). Miracles add to the judgment of the towns that saw them. 🔴
- **"Infants" (11:25).** The ones who get it are the ones with nothing to protect. 🔴
- **The invitation is to a yoke (11:29).** Not to no yoke. A different one, and he's "gentle and humble in heart." 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **John's prison.** Josephus says Herod Antipas held John at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea, and killed him there (*Antiquities* 18.116–119). 🔴
- **The Messiah's to-do list was known.** A Dead Sea Scroll (4Q521) says when God's Messiah comes, the Lord will heal the wounded, raise the dead and bring good news to the poor. Jesus' answer to John uses the same list. 🔴
- **A reed and soft clothing.** Reeds grew all along the Jordan. Herod Antipas put a reed on his early coins, and he's the man in "kings' palaces" who has John locked up. John is no bending reed and no courtier. 🔴 for the coins; 🔵 for Jesus meaning Antipas.
- **Elijah had to come first.** Malachi 4:5: "I am going to send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day." The scribes taught it too (17:10). 🔴
- **Hired mourners.** Families paid flute players and wailing women for a funeral (see 9:23). Kids copied it in the street, the way kids play house. 🔴
- **"Glutton and drunkard" is a death-sentence phrase.** Deuteronomy 21:20 calls the stubborn son "a glutton and a drunkard," and the sentence was stoning. Wright hears it as a charge, not a joke. 🔴 for Deuteronomy; 🟡 for the echo (the Greek words differ).
- **"He has a demon."** Calling a prophet demon-possessed was how you dismissed him. Jesus gets the same charge in 12:24 and John 8:48. 🔴
- **Three towns close together.** Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum sit within a few miles of each other on the north shore of the lake. Most of Jesus' miracles happened in that small triangle. 🔴
- **Capernaum and the fallen star (11:23).** "Exalted to heaven... descend to Hades" borrows Isaiah 14:13–15, the taunt over the king of Babylon who said "I will ascend to heaven" and was brought down to Sheol. That chapter is read as the fall of a rebel heavenly being as much as a king. A Jewish town gets the language of the rebel. 🔴 for the quote; 🟡 for the council read.
- **The yoke of Torah.** Rabbis spoke of taking on "the yoke of Torah" (m. Avot 3:5). Sirach 51 has Wisdom say, "Put your neck under her yoke." Jesus talks like Wisdom herself, and that fits 11:19, "wisdom is vindicated." 🔴
- **Rest for your souls.** Word for word from Jeremiah 6:16, "Ask for the ancient paths... and you will find rest for your souls." 🔴
- **"All things have been handed over to Me" (11:27).** Like Daniel 7:14, where dominion is given to the son of man. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- Two Sabbath fights. The disciples pick grain, and Jesus heals a man's withered hand in a synagogue. The Pharisees start planning to kill him.
- Matthew quotes Isaiah 42: God's gentle Servant, who won't break a bruised reed.
- Jesus frees a blind and mute man from a demon. The Pharisees say he does it by Beelzebul. Jesus answers: a divided kingdom falls, he is tying up the strong man, and blasphemy against the Spirit won't be forgiven.
- They ask for a sign. He gives them Jonah, and warns about an evil spirit coming back to a swept, empty house.
- His mother and brothers come looking for him. He points at his disciples: "whoever does the will of My Father" is family.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Something greater than the temple is here" (12:6).** Then "greater than Jonah" (12:41) and "greater than Solomon" (12:42). Priest, prophet, king. Jesus is more than all three. 🔴
- **"I desire compassion, not sacrifice" (12:7).** Hosea 6:6, the second time Jesus has thrown it at the Pharisees (also 9:13). 🔴
- **Healing on the Sabbath is a reason to kill him (12:14).** The first plot against his life in Matthew comes over a healed hand. 🔴
- **The Servant (12:18–21).** The longest Old Testament quote in Matthew sits right between a death plot and a demon accusation. Jesus is gentle, and he will bring justice to the Gentiles. 🔴
- **"Can this man really be the Son of David?" (12:23).** The crowd is asking the right question. The leaders answer it with Beelzebul. 🔴
- **The charge admits the miracle.** Nobody denies the demon left. They only argue about whose power did it. 🔴
- **Satan has a kingdom (12:26).** Jesus talks about it as a real realm with a ruler. 🔴
- **The strong man (12:29).** You can't rob a strong man's house without tying him up first. Jesus is the robber. 🔴
- **"The kingdom of God has come upon you" (12:28).** One of the few places Matthew says "kingdom of God" instead of "kingdom of heaven." 🔴
- **Words show the tree (12:33–37).** Good tree, good fruit; you'll answer for every careless word. The Beelzebul charge is bad fruit. 🔴
- **The empty house (12:43–45).** Ends with "That is the way it will also be with this evil generation." It's about a nation, not only a person. 🔴
- **Family is redefined (12:50).** Doing the Father's will, not blood. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Picking grain counted as harvest.** Deuteronomy 23:25 lets you pick grain by hand from a neighbor's field. The Pharisees' problem is the day: the Mishnah lists reaping among the 39 kinds of work banned on the Sabbath (m. Shabbat 7:2). 🔴
- **Healing on the Sabbath was allowed only if a life was at risk** (m. Yoma 8:6). A withered hand could wait a day. That's why it's a test. 🔴
- **The sheep in the pit.** Jesus assumes they'd pull a sheep out. Some wouldn't: the Damascus Document from the Dead Sea community says not to lift an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (CD 11:13–14). Jews argued about this. 🔴
- **Other Jews cast out demons.** Josephus tells of a Jewish exorcist named Eleazar pulling a demon out through a man's nose with a ring and a root, using spells said to come from Solomon (*Antiquities* 8.45–49). Jesus asks: "by whom do your sons cast them out?" (12:27). 🔴
- **The Spirit and the finger.** Matthew has "by the Spirit of God" (12:28). Luke has "by the finger of God" (Luke 11:20), the phrase Pharaoh's magicians used when they couldn't copy the plague (Exodus 8:19). 🔴
- **The strong man was in Isaiah.** "Can the prey be taken from the mighty man?... the prey of the tyrant will be rescued" (Isaiah 49:24–25). 🔴
- **Binding the rebel.** In 1 Enoch, God tells Raphael to "bind Azazel hand and foot" and throw him into darkness (1 Enoch 10:4). A Jew who knew that story heard "first binds the strong man" as the Watchers' punishment coming due. Heiser reads Jesus' ministry as the reversal of the rebellion at Hermon. 🔴 for 1 Enoch; 🟡 for the link.
- **Beelzebul, "ruler of the demons."** An old Canaanite god's title (see 10:25), now the name for the chief of the evil spirits. In the council picture the gods of the nations and the demons are tied together (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20). 🔴
- **Spirits live in the desert.** "Waterless places" (12:43). The goat for Azazel went into the wilderness (Leviticus 16), and in Tobit 8:3 the demon flees to the far parts of Egypt. 🔴
- **Three days and three nights.** Jews counted part of a day as the whole day. A rabbinic saying: "a day and a night make an *onah*, and part of an *onah* counts as the whole." Friday afternoon to Sunday morning fits. 🔴
- **Nineveh and the Queen of the South.** Pagans who listened: Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and the queen of Sheba crossed the desert to hear Solomon (1 Kings 10). They will judge Israel's generation. 🔴
- **The swept house is Israel.** Wright: the house is Israel and its Temple, cleaned up by reform movements (the Maccabees cleansing the Temple in 1 Maccabees 4:36–50, the Pharisees, Herod's rebuilding) and left empty. "Nothing short of a new inhabitation of the house would do." 🟡

## My notes
- **The charge is evidence.** Wright: as plain history, the church would never make up the claim that their Lord worked for the devil. So Jesus was doing something nobody could deny. A man building a house doesn't hire a crew to tear it down. 🔴
- **The Son of Man saying (12:32).** Speaking against the Son of Man can be forgiven, against the Spirit can't. Heiser and France tie it to what the Pharisees just did. Another line says forgivable before Easter, unforgivable after. My call: map the fight, don't resolve it. We should not resolve this, but go in all the directions it goes. That's the best we can do. ⬜
- **The empty house (draft 36).** Read alone it says exorcisms don't last, which no exorcist would say. Wright's Israel reading fixes that. Chrysostom read it as Israel first (idols driven out by the prophets, worse suffering under Vespasian and Titus) and then turned it on the baptized.
- **Three texts that aren't contradictions.** John 10:28 ("no one will snatch them out of My hand"), Hebrews 6, and Matthew 12. No one can come and steal you from Christ. That's a theft word. But it doesn't change your own free will. If somebody leaves Christ's hand, and the unforgivable sin, both come down to one thing: rejecting the Holy Spirit when he came calling to reveal God to your heart. Hebrews 10:29, "insulted the Spirit of grace," ties falling away to the same Spirit. 🟡
- **The lifeguard.** "Lost it" or "never had it" is a word game. A man jumps off a boat, the lifeguard grabs him, he fights, gets pulled toward shore again and drowns. Was he saved twice, or never? If I never made it to the shore, was I ever saved? Salvation has three tenses. I honestly think it's simpler than we make it. God wants you saved. We can't accept that we don't have to do anything.
- **Don't pick a fight with the satan yourself.** I hear church people say "tell Satan he has no power over you." That gets dangerous. We stop looking at God and try to stand up to the satan on our own. In 12:29 Jesus is the one who ties up the strong man. 🟡
- **12:50** is the family definition the Sheep and Goats post leans on.
- **Divine council:** this is the big one. The ruler of the demons, Satan's kingdom, the strong man bound, spirits in the wilderness.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus teaches from a boat to a crowd on the shore, all in parables. The sower and four kinds of ground.
- The disciples ask why parables. He quotes Isaiah 6 (seeing, not perceiving) and then explains the sower.
- More parables: wheat and weeds, the mustard seed, the yeast. Then, in the house, he explains the weeds.
- Three more to the disciples: treasure in a field, a merchant and one pearl, a net that catches every kind.
- A scribe trained for the kingdom brings out new and old. Then his hometown, Nazareth, takes offense at him.

## Pay attention to this
- **This is the third big speech.** Matthew's parable chapter, closed with "when Jesus had finished these parables" (13:53). 🔴
- **The sower is the one Jesus explains.** So it shows how parables work. 🔴
- **Parables hide as well as show (13:10–17).** The hiding is on purpose. To those who have, more is given. 🔴
- **The weeds get an enemy.** "An enemy has done this" (13:28). In the explanation the enemy is the devil (13:39). 🔴
- **"Allow both to grow together until the harvest" (13:30).** The servants want to pull weeds now. The owner says wait. The sorting is the angels' job at the end. 🔴
- **Small things that win.** A mustard seed and a pinch of yeast. The kingdom starts tiny and ends up everywhere. 🔴
- **The woman "hid" the yeast (13:33).** The Greek is "hid," not "mixed." Hidden is a theme here (13:35, 44). 🔴
- **Two finds, two kinds of finders.** The treasure man stumbles on it. The merchant was searching. Both sell everything, with joy. 🔴
- **The net.** Same ending as the weeds: the angels separate, the furnace, weeping and gnashing (13:42, 50). 🔴
- **"New and old" (13:52).** New first. The kingdom is new, and rooted in the old. 🔴
- **His hometown takes offense (13:57).** They know his family. "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown." He did few miracles there "because of their unbelief." 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **A parable is a *mashal*.** The Hebrew word covers proverbs, riddles, taunts and stories. A parable isn't a sermon illustration; it's a riddle you have to step into. 🔴
- **The boat as a stage.** The shore near Capernaum has coves that carry a voice up a slope, a natural amphitheater. 🟡
- **Farming wasn't sloppy.** Paths ran through unfenced fields, limestone sat under thin soil, thorns grew at the edges. A Galilean farmer lost seed to all three every year. 🔴 Whether he plowed before or after sowing is argued and doesn't change the point. 🟡
- **The yields.** Ordinary harvests ran around five- to fifteenfold. Thirty, sixty, a hundred is huge but not magic. Isaac reaped a hundredfold in a famine year when God blessed him (Genesis 26:12). 🔴
- **Isaiah 6 ends with seed.** Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 on hearing and not understanding. The same chapter ends, "the holy seed is its stump" (6:13). Wright reads the sower as Yahweh sowing his people again after exile. 🔴 for Isaiah; 🟡 for Wright.
- **Darnel.** The weed is *zizanion*, darnel, which looks just like wheat until it heads out, and is mildly poisonous. Roman law records a case of someone sowing weeds in an enemy's field out of spite. 🔴
- **A mustard "tree" with birds.** A mustard plant is a big shrub, maybe head-high. The birds nesting in the branches are lifted from Daniel 4:12 and Ezekiel 17:23 and 31:6, where great trees shelter the nations. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 that the birds are Gentiles.
- **Three measures of flour.** About forty pounds, enough bread for a hundred people. Sarah used three measures for the angels (Genesis 18:6). 🔴 Yeast was usually a bad image in Jewish teaching (see 16:6). Jesus uses it for the kingdom. 🔴
- **Burying money was normal.** No banks for ordinary people. In war or before a trip you buried your valuables, and sometimes you died before digging them up. 🔴
- **A pearl was the top luxury.** Roman writers treat pearls as the most valuable things money could buy. 🔴
- **The net and unclean fish.** A dragnet pulled between boats takes everything. Fish without fins and scales were unclean (Leviticus 11:9–12). The "bad" fish (*sapra*) are unclean ones, not rotten ones. 🔴
- **The enemy is the devil (13:39).** Wright: Jesus moves the enemy from Rome to the satan. The real war isn't with the Romans. And the reapers are angels (13:39, 41), the heavenly host doing the final sorting. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for Wright's point.
- **"The evil one snatches away" (13:19).** The birds on the path are the evil one. The spirit world is in the parable of the sower. 🔴
- **"The righteous will shine forth as the sun" (13:43).** From Daniel 12:3. 🔴

## My notes
- **How I read parables.** Bailey never says "this is 100% what it means." He shows how it reads through Middle Eastern eyes, which gives you a new way to look. Don't find that one bullet and try to fire it. Get inside the house and see what's going on there, and live in it. A parable isn't a shell casing you throw away once the point's fired. 🟡
- **No author gets the last word.** We're not tearing anything down because one author disagrees with another. You'll always find another author who says the opposite. The only thing I treat as absolute truth is Scripture.
- **The Sower (post 23).** Wright reads the seed as the returning remnant and the sower as Yahweh. Chrysostom says the blindness is self-chosen.
- **The Weeds (post 26).** "Why doesn't God do something?" Judgment is about timing. Chrysostom: "it is not right to put a heretic to death." Augustine against the Donatists: "Is Donatus the reaper?" That's the charter for a mixed church.
- **Mustard and yeast (post 24).** The misfit is the point: a shrub, not Ezekiel's cedar. I called the mustard bush a deliberate put-down of Ezekiel's cedar. That's my claim and it isn't sourced yet. 🔵 Levine denies mustard-seed smallness was a proverb before Jesus.
- **Treasure and pearl (post 25).** Irenaeus makes Christ the treasure hidden in Scripture, not the buyer, which corrected a secondhand summary in my post. Bailey: the kingdom is compared to the merchant who searches, not to the pearl.
- **The Net (draft 31).** The net isn't the church and isn't evangelism. Same ending as the weeds but no enemy, the bad caught from the start, and the sorting is right away. A net was already a judgment picture (Habakkuk 1:14–17; Ezekiel 32:3).
- **The scribe.** Wright: the new rooted in the old, maybe Matthew describing his own book. 🔵
- **Structure.** Chrysostom: power, then value, then "an awful parable" so nobody thinks faith alone is enough. Snodgrass: the weeds bracket mustard and yeast; the weeds explanation and the net bracket treasure and pearl.
- **Divine council:** the devil sows, the evil one snatches, angels reap. The enemy is the satan, not Rome.
