## What the chapter is doing
- Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem ask why his disciples don't wash their hands before eating. Jesus asks why they break God's command to honor parents for the sake of their tradition.
- He tells the crowd that what defiles a person comes out of the mouth from the heart, not what goes in.
- In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs him to free her daughter from a demon. He's silent, then talks of children's bread and dogs. She answers, and he praises her great faith and heals the girl.
- Back by the Sea of Galilee he heals crowds of the lame, blind and mute, and feeds four thousand men with seven loaves and a few fish.

## Pay attention to this
- **Jerusalem sends inspectors (15:1).** The hand-washing question comes from the capital, not the village. 🔴
- **Tradition against command.** Jesus doesn't argue hand-washing. He hits back with a case where their tradition cancels the fifth commandment (15:3–6). 🔴
- **The heart list (15:19).** Evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, slanders. Mostly the second half of the Ten Commandments. 🔴
- **"Canaanite" (15:22).** Mark calls her a Syrophoenician. Matthew picks the old word for Israel's enemies from the conquest. 🔴
- **She says it right.** "Lord, Son of David" (15:22). A pagan woman uses the Messiah's title that Jerusalem's scholars won't. 🔴
- **He says nothing (15:23).** Silence first. Then the disciples want her gone. 🔴
- **"Only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (15:24).** The same line he gave the Twelve in 10:6. 🔴
- **She takes his own picture and works it (15:27).** "Even the dogs feed on the crumbs." She doesn't argue with the word. She finds room inside it. 🔴
- **"O woman, your faith is great" (15:28).** Peter got "you of little faith" in 14:31. A Canaanite woman gets "great." 🔴
- **The crowd "glorified the God of Israel" (15:31).** That phrase suggests a crowd that wasn't Israel. 🟡
- **Seven baskets (15:37).** Twelve baskets in the first feeding (14:20), seven here. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Hand-washing was about purity, not germs.** Priests washed before eating holy food. Pharisees pushed that purity out to ordinary meals at home. Mark 7:3–4 explains it for his Gentile readers. 🔴
- **Corban.** A man could declare his property "given to God" (*qorban*) and then legally refuse to use it to support his parents (Mark 7:11). Jesus calls that breaking the commandment by tradition. 🔴
- **"This people honors Me with their lips"** is Isaiah 29:13. 🔴
- **Tyre and Sidon were old enemy ground.** Jezebel was a princess of Sidon (1 Kings 16:31), and Baal worship came into Israel from there. Elijah also stayed with a widow of Zarephath in Sidon (1 Kings 17). 🔴
- **"Have mercy on me" was a beggar's cry.** Bailey: she starts with the traditional plea of someone on the street. 🔴
- **Two lines crossed.** A Jewish teacher talking with a strange woman in public (compare the disciples' surprise in John 4:27), and a Jew helping a Gentile. 🔴
- **"Dogs."** Jews sometimes called Gentiles dogs. The word Jesus uses is the small form, *kunaria*, house dogs or puppies. Some say that softens it. 🔴 for the word; ⬜ for how much it softens.
- **Son of David and healing.** Solomon, the son of David, was remembered as a master over spirits; Josephus says Solomon composed charms against demons (*Antiquities* 8.45). A woman asking the "Son of David" to drive out a demon fits that memory. 🔴 for Josephus; 🟡 for the link.
- **Into the nations' land.** Heiser's frame: the nations were given over to other gods (Deuteronomy 32:8–9), and Jesus' trips into Tyre, Sidon and the Decapolis are raids into that territory. A demon in a Canaanite house is exactly what you'd expect to find there. 🟡

## My notes
- **Bailey reads it as an exam.** Like a coach running alongside a runner. The dialogue drags the disciples' prejudice into the open so it can be fixed. His question: was this a hinge on their way to the mission to the nations? 🟡
- **Nazareth again.** In Luke 4:24–30 Jesus held up the widow of Sidon and Naaman, and his hometown almost threw him off a cliff. Here he does it for real, in the very region of the widow he named.
- **Two barriers.** Talking with a woman in public and healing a Gentile. His movement argued about the second one for decades in Acts.
- **What her faith is in.** That he has God's power to heal, and that his mercy reaches outside Israel. The exchange tests the second. She's right, and he tells her so.
- **The little-dog word doesn't settle it.** People wave the diminutive like it makes the hard words disappear. It doesn't.
- **Divine council:** a demon in a Canaanite home, in the territory of Baal and Jezebel. It's one of the incursions into the nations Heiser lists.

## What the chapter is doing
- Pharisees and Sadducees ask for a sign from heaven. Jesus says they can read the sky but not the times, and offers only the sign of Jonah.
- He warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. They think he means bread. He means their teaching.
- At Caesarea Philippi he asks who people say he is, then who they say he is. Peter: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
- Jesus answers with the rock, the church, the gates of Hades, and the keys, then orders them to tell no one.
- From then on he tells them he must suffer, die and rise. Peter rebukes him and gets "Get behind Me, Satan!" Then: deny yourself, take up your cross.

## Pay attention to this
- **Two questions.** "Who do people say?" and "But who do you say?" (16:13, 15). The second "you" is plural. Peter answers for the group. 🔴
- **"Son of the living God" (16:16).** "Living" stands out at a place full of shrines to gods made of stone. 🟡
- **Flesh and blood didn't tell him (16:17).** The Father revealed it. Peter didn't reason his way there. 🔴
- **A name and a rock (16:18).** "You are Peter (*Petros*), and upon this rock (*petra*) I will build My church." 🔴 What the rock is has split the church for centuries. ⬜
- **"My church."** Only Matthew among the Gospels uses the word *ekklesia* (16:18; 18:17). 🔴
- **The gates won't hold (16:18).** "The gates of Hades will not overpower it." Gates don't attack. 🔴
- **Keys, binding and loosing (16:19).** The LSB keeps the Greek tense: "shall have been bound in heaven." Heaven decides first; earth follows. 🔴 for the tense; 🟡 for how hard to press it.
- **The silence and the suffering come together (16:20–21).** Right after the confession he says tell no one, and "from that time" he starts teaching the cross. 🔴
- **Hero to "Satan" in six verses (16:17, 23).** "Blessed are you" becomes "Get behind Me, Satan!" Peter is offering a kingdom without a cross, the same offer the devil made in 4:8–10. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for the echo.
- **The cross is for followers too (16:24).** Not just for him. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Caesarea Philippi was a pagan holy site.** It sat at the foot of Mount Hermon, beside a huge cave with a spring, the grotto of Pan. The town was called Panias. Herod the Great built a white marble temple to Augustus there, and his son Philip renamed the town for Caesar and himself. Shrines to Pan and others were cut into the cliff. 🔴
- **The cave was an underworld door.** Locals tied the cave and its deep spring to the underworld. 🔴 Whether the phrase "gates of Hades" was a name for this exact spot is less certain. 🟡
- **Old idolatry was close by.** Dan, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:29), is a few miles away. 🔴
- **Hermon is the rebels' mountain.** In 1 Enoch 6:6, the Watchers, the sons of God of Genesis 6, come down on Mount Hermon and swear an oath there. Hermon is also the north edge of Bashan, the land of Og, last of the Rephaim giants (Deuteronomy 3:11). Psalm 68:15–16 has the mountain of Bashan looking with envy at Zion. 🔴 for the texts.
- **A war speech at the enemy's front door.** Heiser: Jesus walks his men two days north into openly pagan ground and announces the siege where the rebellion began. 🔴 for the site; 🟡 for reading it as staged on purpose.
- **Gates are defense.** A city's gates are where it holds out against an attack. "The gates of Hades will not overpower it" puts Hades under siege and the church on the attack. 🟡
- **Rock in Aramaic.** Jesus likely spoke Aramaic, where the word is *kepha* both times ("You are Kepha, and on this kepha"). Paul calls Peter "Cephas." So the Greek *petros*/*petra* difference may not carry much. 🔴 for *Kepha*; 🟡 for the conclusion.
- **Keys of the house of David.** Isaiah 22:22: "I will set the key of the house of David on his shoulder; when he opens no one will shut." The steward of the king's house held the keys. 🔴
- **"Bind and loose" were rabbis' words.** To forbid and to permit. Teachers "bound" and "loosed" practices for their students. 🔴
- ***Ekklesia* is Israel's assembly.** The Greek Old Testament uses it for the *qahal*, the congregation of Israel gathered before God. Jesus is building a people, not a building. 🔴
- **A Messiah meant a revolution.** For most Jews "Messiah" meant a king who would throw Rome out. After the feeding of the five thousand, crowds tried to make Jesus king by force (John 6:15). 🔴

## My notes
- **The location is the sermon.** Most people miss where this was said. Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Hermon, beside the grotto of Pan, a center of pagan worship tied to the underworld.
- **Gates don't attack. Gates defend.** The gates of hell will not stand against the attack he's bringing on them. The church isn't huddled behind doors holding off the devil's battering ram. Hades is the city under siege. The church is on offense.
- **The rock.** This is where the big divide comes from. I don't read it as "on Peter, the Pope, I'll build my church." I read it as built on the statement that was revealed to him, not by flesh and blood but by "My Father who is in heaven." Peter didn't come to it on his own. Nobody does. It's revealed. 🟡 Chrysostom read the rock as the confession too.
- **Heiser.** A declaration of war spoken at the headquarters of the rebellion. Jesus' later trips into Tyre, Sidon and the Decapolis read as raids into disinherited territory. 🟡
- **The silence order.** I asked for a fact check when the reason for "tell no one" was stated as the political Messiah problem. The order and the suffering prediction come welded together. The political motive is an inference, supported by John 6:15. 🟡
- **Matthew and Luke.** In a mentee session on Luke 9, the rock, the gates and the keys aren't there. Luke gives the confession bare. All of that is Matthew's.
- **Divine council:** this is the center of it in Matthew. Hermon, Bashan, the Watchers, the gates of the underworld, and "Get behind Me, Satan."

## What the chapter is doing
- Six days after Caesarea Philippi, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. His face shines like the sun, Moses and Elijah talk with him, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says, "This is My beloved Son... listen to Him!"
- Coming down, the disciples ask about Elijah. Jesus says Elijah already came, meaning John the Baptist.
- At the bottom, a father's boy is thrown into fire and water by a demon, and the disciples couldn't free him. Jesus does, and talks about faith the size of a mustard seed.
- He tells them a second time he'll be handed over, killed and raised.
- In Capernaum the temple-tax collectors ask Peter if his teacher pays. Jesus says the sons are exempt, then sends Peter fishing for a coin to pay for both of them.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Six days later" (17:1).** Ties the mountain to the confession at Caesarea Philippi and the "some standing here" promise of 16:28. 🔴
- **The face first (17:2).** His face shone like the sun, his clothes white as light. 🔴
- **Moses and Elijah.** The Law and the Prophets standing with him and talking. 🔴
- **Peter talks when he should listen (17:4–5).** He offers to build three tents. The Father cuts him off "while he was still speaking." 🔴
- **"Listen to Him!" (17:5).** Same words as the baptism in 3:17, plus a command. 🔴
- **Jesus touches them (17:7).** They're face down in terror. He touches them and says, "Get up, and do not be afraid." 🔴
- **"Jesus Himself alone" (17:8).** Moses and Elijah are gone. Only he is left. 🔴
- **The disciples failed (17:16).** Down off the mountain, the nine left behind couldn't help the boy. 🔴
- **Second prediction (17:22–23).** "They were deeply grieved." This time they heard it. 🔴
- **The collectors' question expects "yes" (17:24).** "Does your teacher not pay?" is a nudge. Peter says yes by reflex. 🔴
- **Jesus speaks first (17:25).** Before Peter can bring it up. 🔴
- **"For Me and you" (17:27).** One coin, two people. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Which mountain?** Tradition says Tabor, but in Jesus' day Tabor had a fortified settlement on top (Josephus later fortified it again). Hermon is near Caesarea Philippi and very high. Heiser argues for Hermon: Jesus shows his glory on the rebels' own mountain. ⬜ for which mountain; 🟡 for Heiser's reason.
- **Both men met God on a mountain.** Moses on Sinai, Elijah on Horeb, the same mountain (1 Kings 19). Both had strange exits: Moses buried by God where no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:6), Elijah taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). 🔴
- **A shining face was Moses' sign.** Moses' face shone after he spoke with God (Exodus 34:29). Jesus' face shines from the inside, like the sun. 🔴
- **The cloud is the glory.** The cloud that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34) and the Temple. God shows up the way he did in the wilderness. 🔴
- **"Listen to Him" is Deuteronomy 18:15.** "Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet like me... you shall listen to him." 🔴
- **Tents.** Peter's word is the one used for the booths at the Feast of Booths, when Israel camped to remember the wilderness. 🟡
- **Heavenly-being glory.** Daniel 10:6 describes a heavenly figure whose face was like lightning. Daniel 12:3 has the wise shining. This is how Jews pictured beings from the divine council. On the mountain the disciples see Jesus the way the council sees him. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the read.
- **"Moonstruck."** The father says his son is *seleniazetai*, literally "moonstruck." People blamed the moon for seizures. Matthew says a demon was behind it (17:18). 🔴
- **The missing verse.** "But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting" (17:21) isn't in the oldest manuscripts. It was likely copied in from Mark 9:29. 🔴
- **The temple tax.** The half-shekel of Exodus 30:11–16, by Jesus' day a yearly tax every Jewish man paid for the Temple, about two drachmas. The Mishnah tractate *Shekalim* describes the collecting each spring. It's a Jewish religious tax, not Roman tribute. 🔴
- **The stater.** A four-drachma coin, exactly enough for two men's tax. 🔴
- **Kings tax outsiders.** In that world a king taxed his subjects, not his own family. The Temple is his Father's house. 🔴
- **After 70.** When the Temple fell, Rome kept the same tax and sent it to the temple of Jupiter in Rome (Josephus, *Jewish War* 7.218). Some readers think that's why Matthew kept this story. The story doesn't need it. 🔴 for Josephus; ⬜ for whether it bears on Matthew.

## My notes

## What the chapter is doing
- The disciples ask who is greatest. Jesus stands a child in front of them: become like this or you won't get in.
- Woe to anyone who trips up one of these little ones. Their angels see the Father's face. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find the one.
- If a brother sins against you: go to him alone, then with one or two others, then to the church.
- Whatever they bind and loose on earth has been bound and loosed in heaven. Where two or three gather in his name, he is there.
- Peter asks if seven times is enough to forgive. Jesus says "seventy times seven" and tells of a servant forgiven a debt he could never pay, who then chokes a fellow servant over a small one.

## Pay attention to this
- **This is the fourth big speech.** Life together in the community, ending "when Jesus had finished these words" (19:1). 🔴
- **"Unless you are converted" (18:3).** The disciples asked who's on top. Jesus says you won't get in at all unless you turn around. 🔴
- **"Little ones" isn't only kids.** By 18:6 it's "these little ones who believe in Me." Small, easily hurt believers. 🔴
- **The hand, foot and eye again (18:8–9).** Same hyperbole as 5:29–30, now aimed at what trips up others. 🔴
- **Their angels (18:10).** "Their angels in heaven continually see the face of My Father." 🔴
- **The lost sheep in Matthew is about believers (18:12–14).** In Luke 15 it's about sinners coming home. Here it's about one straying member of the flock and the Father not wanting him lost. 🔴
- **The steps start private (18:15).** "Between you and him alone." The goal is "you have won your brother." 🔴
- **"Seventy times seven" (18:22).** The LSB reads 490. The Greek can also mean seventy-seven. Either way it means stop counting. 🔴
- **The debt is impossible.** Ten thousand talents against one hundred denarii. 🔴
- **The same plea, word for word.** "Have patience with me and I will repay" (18:26, 29). The first servant hears his own words come back and doesn't recognize them. 🔴
- **The other servants are the witnesses (18:31).** They're "deeply grieved" and report it. The community sees what he did. 🔴
- **"From your hearts" (18:35).** Not a show of forgiving. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Children had no status.** A child had no rights and no voice in public. Picking a child as the picture of greatness turns the ladder upside down. 🔴
- **A heavy millstone.** The Greek is "a donkey's millstone," the big upper stone turned by an animal, not the small hand mill. Drowning with a weight was a Roman punishment too. 🔴
- **Angels who see the face.** At a king's court, "those who saw the king's face" were his inner circle (2 Kings 25:19; Esther 1:14). Daniel 10 has angel princes over nations, and in Tobit the angel Raphael is one of seven who enter before the glory of the Lord (Tobit 12:15). Jesus puts the weakest believers' angels in God's own council. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the council read.
- **Two or three witnesses** is Deuteronomy 19:15. 🔴
- **"As the Gentile and the tax collector" (18:17).** Treat him as an outsider. Then remember who Jesus ate with (9:10–11) and who wrote this book (10:3). 🟡
- **"Where two or three have gathered."** A saying in the Mishnah: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, God's presence rests between them (m. Avot 3:2). Jesus says *he* is there. 🔴
- **Rabbis set a limit.** A later rabbinic rule says forgive a repeat offense up to three times (b. Yoma 86b). Peter's seven already looks generous. 🔴
- **Lamech in reverse.** Lamech boasted of vengeance "seventy-sevenfold" (Genesis 4:24). The Greek Old Testament uses the same number phrase Matthew uses here. Jesus turns unlimited revenge into unlimited forgiveness. 🔴 for the wording; 🟡 for the reversal.
- **Ten thousand talents.** "Ten thousand" was the biggest number Greek had a word for, and the talent the biggest money unit. A talent was about six thousand denarii; a denarius was a day's wage (20:2). Herod's whole kingdom brought in under a thousand talents a year. 🔴
- **A hundred denarii** is a few months' work. Real money, but payable. 🔴
- **Selling the family was real law.** Debt slavery of a man's wife and children shows up in 2 Kings 4:1 and across the ancient world. 🔴
- **"Debts" and "sins" are one word in Aramaic** (*hoba*). Bailey: in Jesus' mouth a debt parable is a sin parable. 🔴
- **The debt records burned.** When the revolt against Rome broke out in AD 66, rebels burned the public archives to destroy the debt records (Josephus, *Jewish War* 2.427). Debt was a live wound. 🔴

## My notes
- **The arithmetic is the spine of my post.** 10,000 talents is more than a whole province's tax take, against 100 denarii, with a chart. The sale of wife and children was a real legal remedy. The fellow servants' grief is the outside view.
- **Seven against seventy-seven: stop counting.**
- **The ending.** It's the withdrawal of a mercy that visibly failed to take. 🟡
- **Not earned.** Forgiveness isn't earned by forgiving. The cancellation comes first. The king forgave before the servant did anything. 🔴
- **Wright's lungs.** Forgiveness as the ability to breathe, not as currency. Breathe in and refuse to breathe out and you suffocate. And "never give up making forgiveness and reconciliation one's goal." 🟡
- **Bailey's three patterns.** Matthew 6, Luke 11 and Matthew 18 each order forgiveness differently. This one is God first.
- **The fathers.** Chrysostom (Homily 61): it wasn't the king who revoked it, but the man who received it. Tertullian ties seventy-seven back to Lamech.
- **Do we have to ask?** I asked whether the Bible actually says we have to ask for forgiveness. The servant in this story asks for time, not forgiveness, and gets the whole debt cancelled. Grace isn't grace if asking is the price. ⬜
- **Divine council:** 18:10, the little ones' angels standing in the Father's presence.

## What the chapter is doing
- Magi from the east show up in Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews is. They saw his star.
- Herod is troubled, and "all Jerusalem with him." The scribes point to Bethlehem (Micah 5:2). Herod sends the magi to find the child and report back.
- The star leads them to the house. They worship and give gold, frankincense and myrrh, then go home another way after a dream.
- Joseph takes the family to Egypt. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem two years old and under.
- After Herod dies they come back, but not to Judea. They settle in Nazareth.

## Pay attention to this
- **Two kings in one chapter.** "Herod the king" (2:1, 2:3) and "He who has been born King of the Jews" (2:2). Rome had given Herod that title. The magi ask for a different one. 🔴
- **The outsiders worship, the insiders don't move.** The scribes know the verse and the town, six miles away. Nobody from Jerusalem goes. The Gentiles walk hundreds of miles. 🔴
- **Matthew never says three.** No number of magi. Three gifts, so people counted three men. 🔴
- **They aren't called kings.** That comes later, from reading Psalm 72:10–11 and Isaiah 60:3 back onto them. 🔴
- **A house, not a stable (2:11).** By the time the magi arrive the family is in a house and Jesus is a "Child," not a newborn. Herod's "two years old and under" (2:16) points the same way. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for how much time passed.
- **Dreams steer everything.** Five dreams in chs. 1–2 (1:20, 2:12, 2:13, 2:19, 2:22). Nobody in this story is guided by what they can see except the magi, and they follow a star. 🔴
- **Moses all over again.** A king kills Hebrew baby boys, one boy escapes. In 2:20 the angel says, "those who sought the Child's life are dead," which is almost word for word what God tells Moses in Exodus 4:19. 🔴
- **Israel all over again.** "Out of Egypt I called My Son" is Hosea 11:1, and Hosea is talking about the nation of Israel and the Exodus. Matthew applies it to Jesus. Jesus is living Israel's story over. 🔴 for the quote; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Rachel weeping (2:18).** Jeremiah 31:15. Rachel was buried near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19), and Ramah was where the exiles were gathered for the march to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1). The mothers of Bethlehem cry with the mothers of the exile. 🔴
- **"He shall be called a Nazarene" (2:23).** No Old Testament verse says that. Note Matthew says "the prophets," plural. The best guess is a wordplay on *netser*, the "branch" of Jesse in Isaiah 11:1. ⬜

## Read it like 5 BC, not 2026
- **Who the magi were.** In Greek writers the *magoi* were a priestly class from Persia and Babylon: dream readers, star watchers, advisers to kings. A 2026 reader pictures three wise kings. A reader in 5 BC pictured foreign court astrologers. 🔴
- **Which "east"?** A Christian in Rome heard "the east" as Persia. Bailey says a Christian in the Holy Land heard it as across the Jordan, the Arabian desert. Justin Martyr in the 2nd century says the magi came "from Arabia" (*Dialogue with Trypho* 77–78). Gold and frankincense were Arabian trade goods, and Isaiah 60:6 has them coming from Sheba. ⬜ for which east; 🔴 for Justin.
- **Isaiah 60 behind the scene.** "Nations will come to your light... they will bring gold and frankincense." Bailey reads the whole visit as that chapter coming true in a small way. 🟡
- **Herod belonged everywhere and nowhere.** His father was Idumean, his mother a Nabataean Arab. The Idumeans had been forced into Judaism by John Hyrcanus about 125 BC. He was culturally Greek and politically Rome's man. Religiously Jewish, politically Roman (Bailey). 🔴
- **Herod killed his own family.** Josephus records him executing his wife Mariamne and three of his sons. Macrobius has Augustus joking it was better to be Herod's pig than his son. A few boys in a village fits the man. 🔴 for Josephus; 🟡 for the joke being Augustus's real words.
- **Nobody else records Bethlehem.** Josephus doesn't mention it. Bethlehem was a village; the number of boys under two may have been around twenty. A small massacre by Herod's standards is the kind of thing Josephus skips. 🟡
- **Archelaus (2:22).** Herod's son, so brutal that Rome removed him in AD 6. Josephus says he killed about three thousand people at a Passover early in his reign. Joseph had good reason to be afraid. 🔴
- **Stars were more than lights.** In the Old Testament stars and heavenly beings overlap: "the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy" (Job 38:7); "the stars fought from heaven" (Judges 5:20). Balaam, a seer "from the mountains of the east" (Numbers 23:7), saw that "a star shall come forth from Jacob" (Numbers 24:17). Eastern star-readers following a king's star is that story come back around. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the Balaam link.
- **The nations come home.** Heiser's frame: in Deuteronomy 32:8–9 God gave the nations over to lesser gods and kept Israel for himself. The New Testament is God taking the nations back. The first people to worship Jesus in Matthew are pagans from those nations. 🟡
- **The heavenly side of this chapter.** Revelation 12 shows a dragon waiting to devour a child the moment he's born, and the child is caught up to safety. Herod is the earthly face of that. 🟡

## My notes
- **Myth-buster: the three wise men.** Matthew never gives a number. Three came from the gifts, not the givers. The names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar show up in a sixth-century manuscript, not the Bible. They're never called kings; that comes from reading Psalm 72 and Isaiah 60 back onto them. 🔴
- Bailey on "the east": a Roman Christian thought Persia, a Christian in the Holy Land thought across the Jordan. I like that he makes you ask who is reading.
- **Herod in four worlds.** Arab by blood, Jewish by forced conversion under Hyrcanus, Greek by culture, Roman by politics. He belonged to all four and none. That insecurity sits behind the killings. 🟡
- **Why the violence is in the Christmas story.** The usual reason is Matthew presenting Jesus as the new Moses. Bailey adds his own life: decades in the Middle East through war, and the question of how people keep their faith when soldiers come. The birth story was never soft colors and music. 🟡
- **Divine council:** the hook is the star and the nations. Stars and heavenly beings overlap in the Old Testament, and pagans from the disinherited nations are the first to worship. No council scene; the first one in Matthew is the testing in ch. 4.

## What the chapter is doing
- A landowner hires workers at dawn for a denarius, then hires more at nine, noon, three, and five o'clock. At sundown everyone gets a denarius, the last hired paid first. The all-day crew complains. "Is your eye envious because I am generous?" The last will be first.
- On the road to Jerusalem Jesus tells the Twelve, a third time, that he'll be handed over, mocked, flogged and crucified, and raised on the third day.
- The mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at his right and left in his kingdom. He asks if they can drink his cup. The other ten are angry. Jesus: the great among you must serve, "just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many."
- Leaving Jericho, two blind men shout "Son of David!" The crowd tells them to be quiet. Jesus stops, has compassion, touches their eyes, and they follow him.

## Pay attention to this
- **It answers Peter.** Peter just asked, "we have left everything... what then will there be for us?" (19:27). The parable comes right after, and it starts with "For." 🔴
- **The same line brackets it.** "Many who are first will be last; and the last, first" (19:30 and 20:16). 🔴
- **Only the first crew gets a contract.** "A denarius for the day" (20:2). The rest get "whatever is right" (20:4), and the last group gets no wage named at all (20:7). 🔴
- **"No one hired us" (20:7).** They're not lazy. They stood there all day. 🔴
- **The order of pay is staged.** Last paid first, so the first crew watches the one-hour men get a full day's pay. 🔴
- **"You have made them equal to us" (20:12).** That's the real complaint. Not underpaid; outranked. 🔴
- **"Friend" (20:13).** The owner calls the complainer friend. Matthew uses the word again for the man without a wedding garment (22:12) and for Judas (26:50). 🔴
- **Right after "serve," they ask for thrones (20:20–21).** The third and most detailed death prediction, and the next thing is two brothers asking for the best seats. 🔴
- **"You do not know what you are asking" (20:22).** In 27:38 the men on his right and his left are two crucified robbers. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the irony being intended.
- **The ransom saying (20:28).** The plainest line in Matthew on why he's dying. 🔴
- **Blind men see what the disciples don't.** They call him Son of David, won't be shushed, get healed, and follow (20:34). 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **The market was the hiring hall.** Day laborers stood in the village square waiting for work. Bailey: they're standing, not sitting, ready. 🔴
- **A denarius was a day.** A day's wage for a laborer, enough to feed a family for that day. 🔴
- **Pay before sundown was the law.** "You shall give him his wages on his day before the sun sets" (Deuteronomy 24:15; Leviticus 19:13). 🔴
- **Going home empty meant a hungry house.** Bailey: a man going home in the dark with nothing meant kids without bread. The owner pays every man a living. 🟡
- **The owner went himself, five times.** A landowner had a foreman (20:8). Going to the market himself in the heat, again and again, is odd. Bailey sees Jesus describing his own ministry. 🟡
- **The vineyard is Israel.** Isaiah 5:1–7. A Jewish crowd heard "vineyard" and thought of themselves. 🔴
- **The envious eye.** "Is your eye envious" (20:15) is the "bad eye," Hebrew idiom for stinginess. Same picture as 6:22–23. 🔴
- **The cup.** In the prophets the cup is God's wrath that the nations and Israel must drink (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus' cup is that one. 🔴
- **Right and left of a king.** The seats of top power at a royal court. The mother is asking for her boys to be his chief ministers. 🔴
- **Gentile rulers "lord it over" them (20:25).** Everyone knew what Roman power looked like. 🔴
- **Ransom.** A *lytron* was the price to free a slave or a prisoner of war. "For many" echoes Isaiah 53:11–12, the Servant who "bore the sin of many." 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for the Isaiah link.
- **Jericho at Passover.** The last stop before the climb to Jerusalem. The road was full of pilgrims going up for the feast. 🔴

## My notes
- **My post (13) is built on Bailey's "Compassionate Employer."** A denarius as a living wage. Men standing, ready to work. Going home in the dark to a hungry family. The owner going himself five times through the heat though he has a manager. A job, not a handout. The last crew trusting him with no wage named. "Not the underpaid but the overpaid." Justice that includes dignity and survival. The complainers trying to control the master's grace.
- **Bailey's line:** he comes to us where we live, and the parable builds a house the listener is invited to move into.
- **Wright:** the audience is the disciples after Peter's question. Covenant, not contract. 🟡
- **The fathers.** Augustine reads the hours as the ages of a life; Chrysostom hears a hint at the Jews and Gentiles.
- **Bailey against Snodgrass.** Snodgrass denies any picture of Jesus in the owner ("a symbol for God, not Jesus") and any grace reading ("more charitable than generous"). So Bailey's reading has to be presented as Bailey's, with Snodgrass on the other side. We don't tear down Bailey because another author disagrees. You'll always find one who does.
- **Refusing the bookkeeping.** Boice and Bailey's Luke 17 chapter both cite 20:1–16 as the other place Jesus refuses to keep score.
- **Divine council:** no council scene in this chapter. The heavenly court comes back in ch. 22 (like the angels, Psalm 110) and in force in chs. 24–25.

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey. Crowds spread cloaks and branches and shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" The whole city is stirred: "Who is this?"
- He drives the buyers and sellers out of the Temple, heals the blind and lame there, and children shout Hosanna. The priests are furious.
- Next morning he curses a fig tree with leaves and no fruit, and it withers.
- The chief priests and elders ask by what authority he does these things. He answers with a question about John's baptism, and they won't answer.
- Two parables aimed at them: two sons (one says no and goes, one says yes and doesn't), and tenants who kill the owner's servants and then his son. The leaders realize he's talking about them.

## Pay attention to this
- **He plans the entry (21:1–3).** He sends for the donkey. This is a staged act, and Matthew ties it to Zechariah 9:9. 🔴
- **"Who is this?" (21:10).** The crowd answers "the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth in Galilee." True, and not enough. 🔴
- **Children say what adults won't (21:15–16).** Jesus answers with Psalm 8:2: out of the mouths of infants. 🔴
- **The blind and lame come to him in the Temple (21:14).** The healing happens right where the tables were. 🔴
- **The fig tree sits between Temple scenes.** Cursed on the way in, withered by the next day. A tree all leaves and no fruit, next to a Temple all activity and no fruit. 🟡
- **Their answer about John (21:25–27).** They don't ask "what is true?" They ask "what happens to us if we say it?" 🔴
- **The leaders judge themselves.** "Which of the two did the will of his father?" "The first" (21:31). "What will he do to those vine-growers?" "Bring those wretches to a wretched end" (21:41). They pass sentence before they see it's them. 🔴
- **"Before you" (21:31).** Tax collectors and prostitutes "will get into the kingdom of God before you." The word means going ahead of, not instead of. 🔴
- **The son is thrown out, then killed (21:39).** Mark has killed, then thrown out. Matthew's order matches a crucifixion outside the city wall. 🔴 for the order; 🟡 for the reason.
- **The stone (21:42, 44).** Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, and then a stone that crushes. 🔴
- **"Given to a nation, producing the fruit of it" (21:43).** Fruit is the test in the fig tree, the two sons and the tenants. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **A king on a donkey.** Zechariah 9:9: "your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey." Solomon rode David's mule to be crowned (1 Kings 1:33). A donkey said king, and king of peace, not a war horse. 🔴
- **Cloaks on the road.** When Jehu was proclaimed king, men threw their cloaks under him (2 Kings 9:13). 🔴
- **Branches meant victory.** When Simon Maccabee took Jerusalem's citadel, and when the Maccabees rededicated the Temple, the people waved palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7). The crowd was greeting a liberator. 🔴
- **"Hosanna" means "save now."** From Psalm 118:25–26, part of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover. 🔴
- **What the Temple market was for.** Pilgrims needed animals without blemish and the right coins for the Temple tax. Doves were the poor family's offering (Leviticus 12:8). The trade was set up in the Temple's outer court, the court of the Gentiles. 🔴
- **"A robbers' den" comes from Jeremiah 7:11.** In that sermon Jeremiah warned the Temple would end up like Shiloh, destroyed. A robbers' den is where thieves hide between crimes. 🔴
- **Bailey on the scale.** Taking over the courts of the Temple, about thirty-five acres, meant stopping the business of the place for a time. Then Jesus and his men withdrew on their own. 🟡
- **The blind and the lame.** David's men said "the blind and the lame shall not come into the house" (2 Samuel 5:8). The Son of David lets them in and heals them. 🔴
- **Israel as a fig tree.** "There will be no figs on the fig tree" (Jeremiah 8:13); "I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness... like the first fruit on the fig tree" (Hosea 9:10). A fig tree with nothing on it was a prophet's picture of Israel. 🔴
- **"This mountain" (21:21).** Said on the road beside the Temple Mount. Throwing "this mountain" into the sea may point at the Temple. 🔵
- **Isaiah's vineyard.** The tenants parable opens with Isaiah 5:1–2 almost word for word: wall, winepress, tower. Isaiah's vineyard was Israel, and the song ends in judgment. 🔴
- **Absentee owners and angry tenants.** Wealthy landowners rented Galilean land to tenants and sent agents to collect. Tenants sometimes fought back. 🔴
- **Son and stone.** In Hebrew "son" is *ben* and "stone" is *'eben*. The son they kill becomes the stone they rejected. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for the pun being intended.
- **The crushing stone.** Daniel 2: a stone cut without hands smashes the statue of the world's empires and becomes a mountain that fills the earth. Wright hears that stone in 21:44. 🔴 for Daniel; 🟡 for the link.

## My notes
- **The Two Sons (draft 30).** A juridical parable, like Nathan's ewe-lamb story to David. The priests pass sentence on themselves.
- **One exchange.** Wright: the John question and the parable belong together. If John was a prophet, he was the last, and after him comes the king. The first son is the tax collectors and prostitutes, the second is the Temple leadership. 🟡
- **"Going ahead of you."** Blomberg: none of the other New Testament uses of *proagousin* means "instead of." The leaders are behind, not shut out. Some priests did believe later (Acts 6:7). Chrysostom: Jesus said it "as having a hope, if they were willing." 🟡
- **My observation:** the priests answered correctly and are condemned for not acting on their own judgment.
- **The text.** Snodgrass sorts out three manuscript versions of the Two Sons and defends 21:32 as original. 🔴
- **The Tenants (post 14).** Built on Bailey's "Noble Vineyard Owner": having the vineyard turns into owning it; the son is sent alone; killing him is "not stupidity, a calculation"; the owner runs out of everything except vulnerability. The judgment falls on the managers, not the vineyard.
- **Correction.** My post used "squatters' rights" to explain the tenants' plan. Snodgrass shows the Mishnah (m. Baba Batra 3) says tenants could never gain title that way. ❌ That support came out.

- **Divine council:** no council scene. The stone of Daniel 2 is the closest, the kingdom that breaks the world's kingdoms. The council comes back in ch. 22 and in force in chs. 24–25.

## What the chapter is doing
- A king throws a wedding feast for his son. The invited guests won't come, some kill his servants, and the king burns their city. The servants fill the hall from the highways, "both evil and good." One guest has no wedding clothes and is thrown out. "Many are called, but few are chosen."
- Pharisees and Herodians try to trap him: is it lawful to pay tax to Caesar? "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God the things that are God's."
- Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, bring a riddle about a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus: you don't know the Scriptures or the power of God.
- A scholar of the Law asks for the great commandment. Love God with everything; love your neighbor as yourself.
- Jesus asks them: if the Messiah is David's son, why does David call him "Lord" in Psalm 110? Nobody dares ask him anything after that.

## Pay attention to this
- **The third parable in a row against the leaders.** Two sons, tenants, now the feast. The judgment gets heavier each time. 🔴
- **Two invitations (22:3–4).** "Those who had been called" are called again when dinner is ready. They'd already said yes. 🔴
- **Excuses, then murder (22:5–6).** One goes to his farm, one to his business, the rest kill the messengers. 🔴
- **"Set their city on fire" (22:7).** A king who burns a city over a dinner snub. The line jumps out of the story. 🔴
- **"Both evil and good" (22:10).** The hall is filled with everyone. The sorting comes after. 🔴
- **"Friend" and "speechless" (22:12).** He has no excuse to give. 🔴
- **The traps come in a row.** Pharisees with Herodians (politics), Sadducees (resurrection), a lawyer (the Law). Then Jesus asks one question and ends it (22:46). 🔴
- **"Whose likeness and inscription is this?" (22:20).** The coin has Caesar's image. People carry God's. 🟡
- **Two commandments, one hook (22:40).** "On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets." 🔴
- **David calls his son "Lord" (22:43–45).** The Messiah is more than David's heir. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **The double invitation was the custom.** Bailey: a host sent an invitation, counted acceptances, slaughtered for that number, then sent a servant at the hour: "come, it's ready." Esther does the same (Esther 5:8; 6:14). Refusing at the second call after saying yes was a public insult to the king. 🔴
- **The messianic banquet.** Isaiah 25:6 promises a feast on the mountain for all peoples. 1 Enoch 62 has the righteous eating with the Son of Man and wearing "garments of glory." A Dead Sea text (1QSa) describes the Messiah's meal and who is barred from it. 🔴
- **Wedding clothes.** Hosts could provide garments for guests (Genesis 45:22; 2 Kings 10:22). Refusing what the king gives you is the insult. 🟡
- **The burned city.** Readers after AD 70 couldn't miss Jerusalem. That's the main argument for dating Matthew after 70. It's also an ordinary picture of a king's revenge, and the prophets threatened Jerusalem with fire long before (Jeremiah 21:10). 🔴 for both facts; ⬜ for what it proves.
- **Pharisees and Herodians together.** The Pharisees resented Roman rule; the Herodians backed Herod's family, Rome's clients. Enemies on the same side for one afternoon. 🔴
- **The poll tax.** Since AD 6 Judea paid a head tax straight to Rome, and Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, saying God alone was Israel's master (Josephus). Say "pay it" and lose the crowd; say "don't" and get arrested. 🔴
- **The coin was an idol in your pocket.** The denarius of Tiberius showed his head and read "Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus." A coin calling Caesar the son of a god. Jesus makes them produce one in the Temple courts. 🔴
- **Image and owner.** Caesar's face is on the coin, so give it to him. Humans were made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), so give yourself to God. 🟡
- **Sadducees.** The priestly party. They denied the resurrection and, Luke says, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). 🔴
- **Levirate marriage.** A brother married a dead brother's widow to raise up a son in his name (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). The Sadducees use it to make resurrection look silly. 🔴
- **"Like angels in heaven" (22:30).** Not that people become angels. The faithful angels don't marry. In 1 Enoch 15 the Watchers sinned by leaving heaven to take wives. Jesus tells men who deny angels exist that the raised will be like them. 🔴 for 1 Enoch; 🟡 for the link.
- **Exodus 3 for people who trusted Moses.** Jesus answers the resurrection question from the burning bush: "I am the God of Abraham." Present tense. 🔴
- **613 commandments.** The rabbis later counted 613 commands in the Law (b. Makkot 23b), and asking which was greatest was a known question. Jesus joins Deuteronomy 6:5 (the Shema) and Leviticus 19:18. 🔴
- **Psalm 110 and the throne room.** "The LORD said to my Lord, sit at My right hand." Two Lords, one seated beside God. The New Testament quotes this psalm more than any other. Heiser hears an Old Testament "second Yahweh" figure in passages like this, the one Jews later called "two powers in heaven." 🔴 for the quote count; 🟡 for Heiser.

## My notes
- **Post 4 follows Wright.** King and wedding as kingdom and Messiah. The refusals climb to murdering servants, the prophets. The replacement guests are "the people who thought they'd been forgotten." His love reached them where they were but refused to let them stay. "Many are called" is a warning, not a statistic.
- **Bailey's double invitation.** The guests had already accepted, so the excuses are a public shaming of the king.
- **What the garment is.** Four directions: the prodigal's robe and Isaiah 61:10, "the robe of righteousness" (Jeremias, Bailey); Wright (love, justice, truth, mercy, holiness; a new heart); Irenaeus (works of righteousness, the Spirit); Augustine (love, faith working by love). - **Dating.** 22:7 came up when I pushed back on the post-70 date. The burned city read as prophecy after the fact is one of the main post-70 arguments for Matthew, and every one of those arguments is an inference. 🟡
- **Divine council:** "like angels in heaven," and Psalm 110's second Lord seated at God's right hand.

## What the chapter is doing
- Leaving the Temple, the disciples point out its buildings. Jesus says not one stone will be left on another.
- On the Mount of Olives they ask two things: when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of your coming and the end of the age?
- Jesus warns: false messiahs, wars, famines, persecution, love growing cold. When the abomination of desolation stands in the holy place, Judea must run for the hills.
- Then sun and moon go dark, the stars fall, the powers of the heavens shake, and the Son of Man comes on the clouds, sending his angels to gather his people.
- Nobody knows the day or hour, not the angels, not the Son. It'll be like Noah's day. Stay awake like a homeowner who knew a thief was coming, and be the servant found doing his job when the master shows up.

## Pay attention to this
- **This is the fifth big speech.** It runs through ch. 25 and ends "when Jesus had finished all these words" (26:1). 🔴
- **Two questions (24:3).** "When will these things happen" (the Temple) and "what will be the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age." Mark 13:4 blurs them; Matthew makes both visible. 🔴
- **The first words are "no one deceives you" (24:4).** The main worry isn't the timeline. It's being fooled. 🔴
- **Birth pains (24:8).** Wars and earthquakes aren't the end. They're the start of labor. 🔴
- **"Let the reader understand" (24:15).** A note to the reader in the middle of a speech. 🔴
- **Very local instructions.** Judea, housetops, fields, winter, the Sabbath (24:16–20). This part is for people living there. 🔴
- **The coming won't be secret (24:26–27).** Not in the desert, not in a back room. Like lightning across the whole sky. 🔴
- **"This generation" (24:34).** "This generation will not pass away until all these things take place." The hardest verse in the chapter. ⬜
- **The Son doesn't know the day (24:36).** Jesus says it plainly. 🔴
- **Noah's people weren't wicked in this verse (24:38).** Eating, drinking, marrying. Normal life, with no attention to what was coming. 🔴
- **The servant's problem is a calendar in his head.** "My master is not coming for a long time" (24:48). He beats the other servants and parties. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Herod's Temple was a wonder.** Herod rebuilt it on a huge platform with stones that weighed many tons each; some still sit in the Western Wall. The rabbis said whoever hadn't seen Herod's building had never seen a beautiful building (b. Bava Batra 4a). 🔴
- **It burned in AD 70.** Josephus describes the Temple burning under Titus and Rome tearing down the city. About forty years after Jesus said it. 🔴
- **The abomination of desolation.** Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11. In 167 BC Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the Temple and sacrificed on it (1 Maccabees 1:54). Every Jew knew that story. Jesus says it will happen again. 🔴
- **The church fled.** Eusebius says Jerusalem's Christians were warned to leave before the war and went to Pella across the Jordan (*Church History* 3.5.3). 🔴 for Eusebius.
- **Flat roofs.** Houses had flat roofs with outside stairs. You could run from roof to street without going inside. 🔴
- **Winter and Sabbath.** Winter rains flooded the wadis and made roads hard. Travel on the Sabbath was limited. 🟡
- **False messiahs were real.** Josephus names men who led crowds into the desert promising signs: Theudas at the Jordan, and "the Egyptian" at the Mount of Olives (see Acts 5:36 and 21:38). 🔴
- **Falling stars and the gods of the nations.** Jesus quotes Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4. In Isaiah those lines are about God judging Babylon and Edom, and 34:4 adds "all the host of heaven will wear away." In the Old Testament the "host of heaven" can mean the heavenly beings behind the nations (Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 24:21). Heiser reads shaken "powers of the heavens" as those powers losing their place. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the read.
- **Coming on the clouds is Daniel 7.** In Daniel 7:9–14 thrones are set, the court sits, and "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and gets dominion over every nation. It's a heavenly courtroom, and the beasts lose. 🔴
- **"Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather" (24:28).** A proverb: where there's a carcass, birds show up. Some hear the Roman eagle standards too. 🔴 for the proverb; 🔵 for the eagles.
- **The days of Noah.** Genesis 6 opens with the sons of God taking human wives, and 1 Enoch builds the Watchers story on it. Jesus' point is the ordinary life, but his first hearers knew what else was in "the days of Noah." 🔴 for the texts; 🔵 for Jesus meaning it.
- **Two women at the mill (24:41).** Grinding grain with a hand mill took two women facing each other. Side by side, two outcomes. 🔴
- **A steward with the keys.** A trusted slave ran the household and fed the staff. Joseph in Potiphar's house is the classic case. 🔴

## My notes
- **Two questions, two events.** The disciples probably thought the Temple's fall and the end were one event. Jesus answers both, which is why the chapter moves between AD 70 and the end of the world. Think of mountain peaks seen from far away. Two peaks look side by side until you get there and find a valley between them. 🟡
- **The faithful and wicked servant (draft 37).** One servant, two possible paths. Snodgrass calls it a double antithetical similitude. Matthew and Luke share 85 of Matthew's 111 words here, including "cut in pieces." 🔴
- **"My master is delayed" isn't the church's worry written back in.** The verb isn't a technical term, and the problem in the story is that the master came back too soon (Snodgrass, Blomberg). Chrysostom: the thought arises "because the servant is evil." 🟡
- **"Cut in pieces."** Snodgrass hears Psalm 37 underneath (the wicked cut off, gnashing their teeth). The divided man is divided. Blomberg adds Jeremiah 34:18–20, the men who walked between the cut calf. 🟡
- **Leaders or everyone?** Irenaeus applied it to elders who serve their own lusts; Chrysostom to teachers and then the rich; Snodgrass and Blomberg to everyone who claims to follow.
- **AD 70 or the second coming.** Wright reads it as events within a generation; Snodgrass and Blomberg as the return of Christ. My reading: Wright has the first readers, Snodgrass the reason the parable outlived them. 🟡
- **The order.** This parable heads the sequence that follows: bridesmaids, talents, sheep and goats.
- **The thief (24:42–44).** I used it as a parallel in the Doorkeeper draft. Chrysostom: people sit up for a thief but not for their souls.
- **Divine council:** heavy. Daniel 7's court, the powers of the heavens shaken, angels gathering the elect, and "not even the angels" know the day.

## What the chapter is doing
- Ten virgins wait with lamps for a bridegroom who's late. Five brought extra oil and five didn't. At midnight the shout comes, the foolish five go to buy oil, and the door shuts. "I do not know you."
- A master going on a journey hands his slaves five, two and one talents. Two trade and double it. The third buries his. "Well done, good and faithful slave" for the first two; the outer darkness for the third.
- The Son of Man sits on his glorious throne with all the angels, and all the nations are gathered and split like sheep and goats.
- The sheep fed, gave drink, welcomed, clothed, visited the sick and the prisoners, and never knew they were doing it to him. The goats didn't, and also never knew.
- The end of Jesus' last speech in Matthew. Eternal punishment, eternal life.

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Village weddings.** The groom went to fetch the bride and brought her back to his father's house in a procession through the village, with friends and lamps. It could run late. Bailey: weddings came in the dry summer months, and the parade winding through the alleys always took longer than anyone planned. 🔴 for the custom; 🟡 for Bailey's detail.
- **Why young women carry lamps.** For a girl to be out at night without a light was a danger to her safety and her name. The lamp was part of being respectable. 🟡
- **Lamps or torches.** The word can mean clay oil lamps or torches with oil-soaked rags. Torches burned through oil quickly, which fits the panic. ⬜
- **Ten.** Ibn al-Tayyib, an 11th-century Syrian scholar Bailey quotes, notes it took ten men to form a Passover company or witness a wedding. Jesus uses ten women. 🟡
- **A talent was a fortune.** About six thousand denarii, roughly twenty years of a laborer's wages. The one-talent man still got more money than most people saw in a lifetime. 🔴
- **Burying it was the safe move.** Rabbinic law said a man who buried money given him for safekeeping wasn't liable if it was stolen. But this money was handed over to be put to work, not to be kept. 🔴 for the rule; 🟡 for the distinction.
- **Banks and interest (25:27).** Money changers paid interest on deposits. The least effort would have earned something. 🔴
- **Sheep and goats grazed together.** Palestinian shepherds ran mixed flocks by day and separated them at night; the usual explanation is that goats need more warmth. 🔴 for mixed flocks; 🟡 for the reason.
- **Ezekiel 34.** God judges "between sheep and sheep, between the rams and the male goats" (Ezekiel 34:17). The flock can't sort itself. 🔴
- **The Son of Man on the throne of glory.** In 1 Enoch 62 the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory and the kings and the mighty are judged before him. Daniel 7 is behind both. 🔴
- **"With all the angels" (25:31).** Zechariah 14:5: "Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him." The holy ones are the heavenly host. 🔴
- **The devil and his angels.** The satan has angels, and a judgment is waiting for them. In Jewish tradition the rebel Watchers were held for judgment (1 Enoch 10; Jude 6). The goats share the rebels' sentence. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the link.
- **"All the nations" (25:32).** The phrase that ends the book: "make disciples of all the nations" (28:19). 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- At dawn the chief priests hand Jesus to Pilate. Judas sees him condemned, brings back the thirty pieces of silver, says "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood," throws the money into the sanctuary and hangs himself. The priests buy the Potter's Field with it.
- Pilate asks if he is King of the Jews. Jesus barely answers. Pilate offers the crowd Barabbas or Jesus, and they choose Barabbas. Pilate's wife warns him from a dream. Pilate washes his hands; the people say "His blood be on us and on our children."
- Soldiers flog him, mock him with a robe, a crown of thorns and a reed. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross to Golgotha. He's crucified between two robbers under the sign "THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS," and everyone mocks.
- Darkness from noon to three. He cries "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" and gives up his spirit. The veil tears, the earth shakes, tombs open, and the centurion says, "Truly this was God's Son!"
- Joseph of Arimathea buries him in his own new tomb. The priests get a guard and seal the stone.

## Pay attention to this
- **Judas sees it too late (27:3).** "When Judas... saw that He had been condemned, he felt remorse." 🔴
- **"Remorse," not "repented."** Matthew's verb (*metamelomai*) means regret. It's the word for the son who "regretted it and went" in 21:29. It isn't the usual word for turning to God (*metanoeo*). 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for how much weight that can carry.
- **"What is that to us?" (27:4).** The priests have no pastoral word for a man confessing sin in the Temple. 🔴
- **They won't put blood money in the treasury (27:6).** Careful about the coins, careless about the blood. 🔴
- **The Jeremiah problem (27:9).** Matthew says "Jeremiah," but the thirty pieces and the potter are from Zechariah 11:12–13. 🔴
- **Innocent, innocent, innocent.** Judas says "innocent blood" (27:4). Pilate's wife calls him "that righteous Man" (27:19). Pilate washes his hands (27:24). The centurion confesses him (27:54). 🔴
- **"King of the Jews."** Pilate asks it (27:11), the soldiers mock it (27:29), the sign announces it (27:37). The magi asked for the King of the Jews in 2:2. 🔴
- **Psalm 22 runs through the cross.** The garments divided (27:35), the mocking and head-shaking (27:39), "He trusts in God; let God rescue Him" (27:43), and the cry itself (27:46) are all Psalm 22. 🔴
- **Matthew alone has the raised saints (27:52–53).** Tombs open at his death; they come out "after His resurrection." 🔴
- **The Gentile soldier says it (27:54).** "Truly this was God's Son!" The first to say it after he dies is a Roman. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Pilate was real.** A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names "Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea." He governed AD 26–36. Josephus and Philo describe him as stubborn and harsh. 🔴
- **Thirty pieces of silver.** The price the Law set for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32). In Zechariah 11:12–13 it's the insulting wage paid to God's shepherd, which he throws "to the potter in the house of Yahweh." 🔴
- **Why Jeremiah?** Jeremiah buys a field (Jeremiah 32), visits a potter (18), and smashes a potter's jar in the Valley of Hinnom, renamed the "valley of slaughter" (19). A field of blood near Hinnom bought with a potter's price pulls both prophets in. Many think Matthew names the bigger prophet for a combined quote. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the combined reading.
- **Akeldama has been dug.** Archaeologists found more than seventy first-century family tombs in the area traditionally called Akeldama, where the Hinnom and Kidron valleys meet. A burial ground for "strangers" fits a place of tombs. 🔴 for the excavations; 🟡 for the identification.
- **Judas and Ahithophel.** David's adviser Ahithophel betrayed the king, then "set his house in order and strangled himself" (2 Samuel 17:23). The only other man in the Bible who hangs himself is the one who betrayed David's son. 🔴
- **Washing hands was a Law ritual.** When a murder couldn't be solved, the town elders washed their hands over a heifer and said, "Our hands did not shed this blood" (Deuteronomy 21:6–7). A Roman borrows a Jewish rite. 🔴
- **Flogging before crucifixion.** Roman scourging used whips weighted with bone or metal. Men sometimes died from it. 🔴
- **Crucifixion was a billboard.** Romans crucified by busy roads, outside the city, naked, to warn everyone. Cicero called it the cruelest and most disgusting penalty. The charge was posted above the head. 🔴
- **The ninth hour.** Three in the afternoon, the time of the evening sacrifice and prayer at the Temple (Acts 3:1). 🔴
- **Darkness at noon.** Amos 8:9: "I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight." 🔴
- **"Eli, Eli."** Psalm 22:1 in Hebrew-Aramaic. Quoting a psalm's first line called up the whole psalm, and Psalm 22 ends in rescue and the nations worshiping (22:27–28). 🔴 for the psalm; 🟡 for the first-line custom.
- **Bulls of Bashan around the cross.** Psalm 22:12 says "strong bulls of Bashan have encircled me." Bashan was the region of the Rephaim and of Hermon (see ch. 16). Heiser reads it as the dark powers surrounding the dying king, and Colossians 2:15 has Christ disarming the rulers and authorities at the cross. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for Heiser.
- **The veil had cherubim on it.** The curtain before the holy of holies was woven with cherubim (Exodus 26:31). Josephus says the outer Temple curtain showed the heavens. Torn "from top to bottom," it's torn from God's side. 🔴
- **Saints raised.** Ezekiel 37 has God opening Israel's graves; Daniel 12:2 has many who sleep in the dust waking. Matthew shows a first taste of that at the cross. 🔴 for the texts; ⬜ for what exactly happened.
- **A sealed stone and a guard (27:62–66).** Rolling-stone tombs belonged to the wealthy. A seal on the stone meant tampering would be obvious. 🔴

## Pay attention to this
- **He sits down (5:1).** Teachers in Jesus' world taught sitting. Standing was for reading Scripture. Sitting means class is in session. 🔴
- **The Beatitudes describe, they don't command.** "Blessed are" says who is already blessed. None of them says "try to be." 🔴
- **Bookends.** The first and eighth Beatitudes both end "for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (5:3, 5:10). Everything in between sits inside that promise. 🔴
- **The ninth one turns to "you" (5:11).** It switches from "those who" to "you" and to "because of Me." Jesus puts himself where God's name would go. 🔴
- **"You are," not "try to be" (5:13–14).** Salt and light are statements. Who they are comes first, then what they do. 🔴
- **"Fulfill" (5:17).** A promise reaching where it was going. Not cancel, not just keep. 🟡
- **"But I say to you."** Prophets said "thus says the LORD." Jesus says "I say." The crowd notices at the end of the Sermon: he taught "as one having authority, and not as their scribes" (7:29). 🔴
- **He goes deeper, not looser.** Murder goes to anger. Adultery goes to the look. Every "but I say" is harder than the rule it starts from. 🔴
- **The right cheek (5:39).** A right-handed slap to someone's right cheek has to be the back of the hand. 🔴
- **"Sons of your Father" (5:45).** Loving enemies is what makes you look like your Father, who sends rain on both. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **A mountain means Moses.** Matthew's readers knew who went up a mountain and came down with God's law. Jesus goes up and gives the law's true meaning. 🟡
- **"Blessed."** Bailey: the Hebrew *'ashre* and Greek *makarios* don't wish a blessing on you. They point out a quality that's already there. Psalm 1 opens the same way: "How blessed is the man." 🟡 for Bailey's sharp line; 🔴 for the Psalm 1 form.
- **The poor and the lowly were a known group.** Isaiah 66:2: "to this one I will look, to him who is humble and contrite of spirit." "The lowly shall inherit the land" is Psalm 37:11. Bailey says "land" in Jesus' mouth meant the land of promise, and Jesus is widening it. 🔴 for the quotes; 🟡 for Bailey.
- **Salt that goes flat.** Salt in Palestine often came from the Dead Sea mixed with other minerals. The real salt could wash out and leave the useless rest. 🟡
- **Light to the nations was Israel's old job.** "I will appoint You as a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6, 49:6). Wright: Jesus isn't handing out a new metaphor. He's giving Israel's vocation to this little group. 🔴 for Isaiah; 🟡 for Wright.
- **The smallest letter (5:18).** The *yod*, the smallest Hebrew letter, and the little stroke that tells one letter from another. 🔴
- **"Raca" (5:22).** Aramaic, roughly "empty head." 🔴
- **Hell is Gehenna.** The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where kings of Judah burned children to Molech (Jeremiah 7:31). The story that it was a burning trash dump comes from a rabbi around AD 1200, not from Jesus' day. 🔴
- **Oaths had loopholes.** People swore by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or their head to avoid using God's name, then argued about which oaths counted. The Mishnah has a whole tractate on it (*Shevuot*), and Jesus mocks the same game in 23:16–22. 🔴
- **The backhand.** The Mishnah fines a slap and doubles the fine for a backhand (m. Bava Kamma 8:6). A backhand was an insult from a superior. Turning the other cheek makes him hit you as an equal or stop. 🔴 for the Mishnah; 🟡 for Wright's read of it.
- **The cloak was protected by law.** A poor man's cloak was his blanket. If you took it as a pledge you had to give it back by sundown (Exodus 22:26–27). Jesus says hand it over anyway. 🔴
- **The mile.** A Roman soldier could force a civilian to carry his gear a mile. Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross (27:32) is the same word. 🔴
- **"Hate your enemy" isn't in the Old Testament.** Leviticus 19:18 says love your neighbor. The Dead Sea community did write a rule to "hate all the sons of darkness" (1QS 1:10). Jesus is answering how people heard the law, not the law. 🔴
- **Tax collectors and Gentiles (5:46–47).** The two groups his hearers least wanted to be compared to. 🔴
- **"Sons of God" (5:9, 5:45).** In the Old Testament the "sons of God" are members of God's heavenly council (Job 1:6, 38:7; Psalm 82:6). Heiser's frame: God's plan is to make humans his sons, a family that takes back what the rebel sons lost. Peacemakers get that title. 🔴 for the Old Testament usage; 🟡 for the council read here.
- **Heaven a throne, earth a footstool (5:34–35).** Isaiah 66:1. The throne-room picture behind every oath. 🔴
- **"The evil one" (5:37).** Matthew's name for the satan, again in 6:13 and 13:19, 38. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Three religious practices, one warning: giving, praying and fasting done to be seen by people get the people's applause and nothing else.
- In the middle of the prayer section Jesus gives the Lord's Prayer, then underlines the line about forgiving.
- Treasure: store it in heaven, because your heart follows your treasure. You can't serve God and wealth.
- Worry: look at the birds and the lilies. Seek first his kingdom. Tomorrow will worry about itself.

## Pay attention to this
- **The same three lines, three times.** Don't do it like the hypocrites. "They have their reward in full." Your Father who sees in secret will reward you (6:2–4, 5–6, 16–18). 🔴
- **"Reward in full" is a receipt.** The Greek verb was used on business receipts for "paid in full." The show worked. The account is closed. 🔴
- **The prayer sits between two warnings.** Right after "don't pray to be seen" and "don't use meaningless repetition." It's short on purpose. 🔴
- **"Our," not "my."** Every "us" and "our" in the prayer is plural. 🔴
- **God's name, kingdom and will come first.** Three requests about God, then three about us: bread, debts, testing. 🔴
- **Forgiveness gets a second word (6:14–15).** Of all the lines, the only one Jesus stops to explain is forgiving others. 🔴
- **The doxology is in brackets.** "For Yours is the kingdom..." isn't in the oldest manuscripts. It sounds like David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11 and was added for church use. 🔴
- **"Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (6:21).** The order. Treasure first, heart follows. 🔴
- **The eye (6:22–23).** Sits between treasure and two masters, so it's about money. 🟡 (See below.)
- **"Seek first" (6:33).** It ties the worry problem and the money problem together. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **"Hypocrite" was a theater word.** A *hypokrites* was an actor on a stage, wearing a mask. Jesus is calling them performers. 🔴
- **The trumpet.** Could be a figure of speech for making noise about your gift. The Temple did have thirteen collection chests shaped like trumpets (m. Shekalim 6:5). 🔵 for the link.
- **Jews already prayed on a schedule.** The Shema morning and evening, and set prayers three times a day (Daniel 6:10; Psalm 55:17). Jesus isn't against set prayer. He's against prayer as a stage. 🔴
- **Pagan prayer piled up words.** Gentile prayers stacked up names and titles of a god to make sure they hit the right one and wore him down. Think of Baal's prophets shouting from morning to noon (1 Kings 18:26). Jesus says your Father already knows. 🔴
- **"Hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come."** A Jewish prayer called the Kaddish runs close: "Magnified and sanctified be His great name... may He establish His kingdom." 🔴 for the parallel; ⬜ for how old the Kaddish wording is.
- **"On earth as it is in heaven."** In the Bible's picture, heaven is where God's will is already done by his hosts, "who perform His word" (Psalm 103:20–21). The prayer asks for earth to run like the throne room. 🟡
- **Daily bread.** The Greek word *epiousios* is almost unknown outside this prayer. "For today," "for tomorrow," or "what we need to live" are all possible. ⬜
- **Debts and sins.** In Aramaic one word, *hoba*, means both. Matthew keeps "debts." Luke's version (11:4) says "sins" in one line and "indebted" in the next. 🔴
- **"Deliver us from the evil one."** Matthew means a person, the satan, the same as "the evil one" in 5:37 and 13:19. 🔴
- **Fasting days.** Pious Jews fasted Mondays and Thursdays. The Didache (8:1) tells Christians to fast Wednesdays and Fridays instead so they won't look like "the hypocrites." 🔴
- **Anoint your head (6:17).** Oil on the hair was normal grooming. Look ordinary. 🔴
- **Treasure that eats itself.** Wealth was clothing (moths), stored goods (the word for "rust" means eating), and coins in a house with mud-brick walls thieves could dig through. 🔴
- **The good eye and the bad eye.** In Hebrew idiom a "bad eye" is stinginess and a "good eye" is generosity (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 22:9). Matthew 20:15 uses the same idiom: "is your eye envious because I am generous?" 🔴 for the idiom; 🟡 that it's the meaning here.
- **Grass in the furnace (6:30).** Dried grass and weeds were oven fuel. Today's flowers, tomorrow's kindling. 🔴

## My notes
- **The receipt.** Public piety isn't called useless. It worked at exactly what it aimed at. They got paid. (Wright.) 🟡
- **The budget tells on you.** Caring follows funding. A budget is a more honest statement of what you believe than a creed. 🟡
- **How I used to pray it.** I prayed the Lord's Prayer every time, in my own words. Instead of "Our Father who art in heaven" I'd say "Father God, who lives outside of space and time, creator of everything," and on down the lines. I fell out of it and want it back. That turns out to be Luther's method in *A Simple Way to Pray* (1535). I drafted "How I Pray the Lord's Prayer, Line by Line" with Bailey's petition-by-petition reading next to it.
- **Structure without power.** The Didache (8:3) says pray it three times a day. My line: you have to have the structure without thinking the structure has any power.
- **Like lifting.** There's no power in lifting at 8 AM over 5 PM. There's power in staying consistent. One day is better than zero. Miss a day and you don't lose your gains, and you can't make it up by doing double the next day. Rest is part of it too.
- **The church is so afraid of legalism** it forgets the New Testament was written to Jews who already kept a strict daily rhythm. If there's no start, you don't go from zero to a hundred. You don't start.
- **Do we have to ask?** I asked whether the Bible actually says we have to ask for forgiveness. The Lord's Prayer doesn't say "ask." It says forgive us as we forgive. Grace saves us, not works, and if asking were the price it wouldn't be a free gift. ⬜
- 6:7–9 is in my personal theology list under praying plainly, like to a father.
- **Divine council:** "on earth as it is in heaven" and "the evil one." No scene. The first council scene in Matthew is the testing in ch. 4.

## What the chapter is doing
- Don't judge the way you'd hate to be judged. Get the log out of your own eye first. Don't throw holy things to dogs.
- Ask, seek, knock. If you give your kids good things, how much more will your Father.
- The Golden Rule: treat people the way you want to be treated. "This is the Law and the Prophets."
- Four closing warnings, each one a pair: two gates, two trees, two kinds of "Lord, Lord," two builders.
- The crowds are stunned. He taught with authority, not like their scribes.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Do not judge" is followed by judging.** Five verses later Jesus calls people dogs and swine (7:6), and in 7:15–20 he tells you to inspect fruit. The ban is on the log-in-your-eye kind of judging, not on telling right from wrong. 🔴
- **"You hypocrite" (7:5).** Same actor word as ch. 6. The judge is performing. 🔴
- **Ask, seek, knock, and "find."** The word "find" in 7:7–8 comes back in 7:14: "few who find it." Seeking and the narrow gate belong together. 🔴
- **The Golden Rule closes a bracket.** "The Law and the Prophets" in 7:12 matches 5:17. The body of the Sermon sits between them. 🔴
- **Four warnings, one point.** Gates, trees, confessions, builders. Every one is about the gap between saying and doing, and every one puts a confident-looking group on the wrong side. 🔴
- **"Constricted" (7:14).** The Greek is *tethlimmene*, from *thlibo*, to press or crush. The noun from the same root, *thlipsis*, is "tribulation." The road to life is a squeeze. 🔴
- **"Few who find it."** Many enter the wide gate. The narrow one has to be found. 🔴
- **They did real things (7:22).** Prophecy, exorcisms, miracles, all "in Your name." Jesus doesn't say they faked it. He says "I never knew you." 🔴
- **"Depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness" (7:23).** Quoting Psalm 6:8. 🔴
- **Both houses get the storm.** Same rain, same rivers, same wind (7:25, 27). Faith isn't storm insurance. 🔴
- **Both builders hear.** The split isn't between people who heard Jesus and people who didn't. It runs through the crowd that heard. 🔴

## Read it like AD 30, not 2026
- **Measure for measure was a known rule.** The Mishnah: "With the measure a man measures, they measure to him" (m. Sotah 1:7). 🔴
- **The speck and the beam.** A carpenter's joke. A rabbinic version turns up too: someone says "take the splinter from your eye" and gets "take the beam from yours" (b. Arakhin 16b). 🔴
- **Dogs weren't pets.** Street dogs were scavengers and pigs were unclean. Both are the opposite of holy. 🔴
- **Bread and stones.** Flat loaves and the round limestone stones on a Galilee hillside look alike. The devil used the same pair in 4:3. 🟡
- **The Golden Rule had a negative version.** Hillel, a generation before Jesus: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah" (b. Shabbat 31a). Tobit 4:15 says the same. Jesus turns it positive. Not doing harm becomes doing good. 🔴
- **The Two Ways was an old teaching form.** "I have set before you life and death" (Deuteronomy 30:15–20), Psalm 1, Jeremiah 21:8. The Dead Sea community wrote it as two spirits of light and darkness. The Didache (chs. 1–6) opens with "There are two ways, one of life and one of death." Matthew's life-or-death wording follows Deuteronomy. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the Deuteronomy line.
- **Wolves in sheep's clothing.** Prophets were known by their clothes, a hairy mantle (2 Kings 1:8; Zechariah 13:4). A fake prophet puts on the uniform. 🔵
- **Thorns and thistles.** The curse words from Genesis 3:18. Bad trees grow on cursed ground. 🟡
- **Exorcism by name was common.** Jewish exorcists invoked powerful names to drive out spirits. In Acts 19:13–16 the sons of Sceva use "Jesus whom Paul preaches" as a formula, and the demon beats them. Using the name like a password doesn't mean the owner of the name knows you. 🔴 for Acts; 🟡 for the link.
- **Building in Galilee.** Dry riverbeds that flood in a winter storm. Bailey: building on rock meant digging through hard clay to bedrock; Luke says the man "dug deep" (Luke 6:48). The foolish man saves himself a week of digging. 🔴
- **Hearing and not doing.** Ezekiel 33:31–32: they hear your words and do not do them; to them you're like a love song sung well. 🔴
- **"Not as their scribes" (7:29).** Scribes taught by citing earlier teachers. Jesus quotes nobody but Scripture and himself. 🔴

## My notes
- **Who the gates are for.** I don't read this as a sinner deciding whether to accept Jesus. He's talking to people who already believe. The wide gate is the man sitting in the pew every Sunday going through the motions, living his life the way he wants. The narrow gate is the people digging in and doing the work, showing fruit, yielding to his will. God is your manager. You do what he wants. 🟡
- **"Enter the narrow gate" isn't "make a decision."** It means enter the life the last three chapters described. Carson: poverty of spirit, prayer and righteousness are impossible without grace because they are alien to us. 🟡
- **The two employees.** Before the Greek, open with a parable: two employees. One gives lip service. One does the work the manager needs, not perfectly, not always on time, but trying. Layoffs come. Who goes?
- **The Chevette and the Corvette.** The first man parks a Chevette in a garage and calls it a Corvette. The garage didn't change the car. He says he "got into church" the way other people say they got into CrossFit. My favorite line in the draft.
- **The wrestling is the road.** The second man isn't polished, cusses at the car seat, has a beer with his pizza. But somebody keeps moving him and he keeps wrestling. That's not failure. I don't call drinking a beer or cussing "sin" in the piece. The point isn't a cleanup list.
- **Gethsemane.** A video tied the crushing in *tethlimmene* to Gethsemane, the "oil press." I checked it and kept that link. Other claims from the same video were overstated and got cut.
- **The builders.** Bailey reads Jesus as the foundation over against the Temple. A later pass found that reading contested (the word for rock here isn't the Temple's foundation-stone word), so I qualified it. ❌ for presenting it as settled.
- **Judging.** Wright: looking down on people is playing God, which is acting.
- **7:23 on hell.** I filed "depart from Me" under hell as chosen separation, with a note to myself to check how hard I want to lean on it. ⬜
- **Where this went.** The Two Gates study became the seed of a book, *Walking With God*. People who had a real relationship with God are described as walking with him (Enoch, Noah, Abraham). Gates, paths and walking are one picture.
- **Divine council:** the hook is 7:22, people casting out demons in his name whom he never knew. The big spirit-world chapters are 8 and 12.
