## What the chapter is doing
- Yahweh tells Moses to send twelve men, one leader from each tribe, to spy out Canaan. Moses renames Hoshea son of Nun "Joshua" (13:16).
- They go forty days, see Hebron and the sons of Anak, and cut a cluster of grapes at the valley of Eshcol so big it takes two men on a pole.
- They come back and say the land really does flow with milk and honey, but the people are strong and the cities walled.
- Caleb says go up now, we can take it. The others give a bad report: a land that eats its people, men of great size, the Nephilim, and "we became like grasshoppers in our own sight" (13:33).

## Pay attention to this
- **Joshua gets his name here (13:16).** Hoshea means "salvation." Moses makes it *Yehoshua*, "Yahweh saves." The same name becomes *Yeshua*, Jesus. 🔴
- **The facts and the fear are two different things.** Everyone agrees the land is good. They split on whether God can give it to them. 🔴
- **The Nephilim line comes from the spies who gave the bad report (13:32–33).** The text itself calls it a "bad report." Whether the giants were really that big or the fear made them bigger, the narrator puts the words in frightened mouths. 🔴 for who says it, 🟡 for reading exaggeration into it.
- **"The sons of Anak are part of the Nephilim" (13:33).** This is the one verse after Genesis 6:4 that names the Nephilim. It ties the giant clan at Hebron back to the days before the flood. 🔴
- **Grasshoppers "in our own sight, and so we were in their sight."** They decided how small they were before anyone else did. 🔴
- **Hebron and Anak's sons by name (13:22).** Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai. Caleb drives them out later (Joshua 15:14). 🔴
- **The next chapter is the cost.** Because of this report the generation that left Egypt dies in the wilderness, all but Caleb and Joshua (14:30). 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **"Nephilim" meant giants to the first readers.** Heiser's argument: in Numbers 13:33 the middle vowel of *nephilim* is written out in full, and that spelling gives "giants." "The fallen ones" would need a different form (*nophelim* or *nephulim*) (*Unseen Realm*, 132–133). 🔴 for the spelling, 🟡 for the meaning.
- **The field isn't settled.** The Faithlife Study Bible calls the etymology uncertain and notes the "fallen" derivation. Gilbrant proposes a root meaning "separated" or "distinct." The Greek has *gigantes* here, but it translates *gibborim* and *rephaim* loosely elsewhere, so that settles less than it looks. ⬜
- **The chain runs through the Anakim.** Numbers 13:33 links the Anakim to the Nephilim. Deuteronomy 2:10–11 links the Anakim to the Rephaim. The Old Testament never links Nephilim and Rephaim directly (Routledge, *Tyndale Bulletin* 66:1). 🔴
- **Divine council: the giant clans.** In Heiser's frame the giants are the offspring of the sons of God from Genesis 6, and the conquest is aimed at the land they hold. Israel is being sent against the leftovers of a rebellion in the unseen realm, which is why the spies' fear is fear of something more than tall men. 🟡 for the frame. The fuller case sits in *Unseen Realm* chapters 23–25.
- **Where the Ugaritic texts have divine Rephaim, the Old Testament shrinks them.** The shades of the dead lose strength and status in Israel's telling. Same demotion pattern that shows up all over. 🟡

## My notes
- I came to this verse through the Live in Context Session 5 prep on Genesis 6. For me it's the hinge between Genesis 6 and the giant clans of the conquest.
- **My position in the session, in my own words:** "On Nephilim and Rephaim, I'd separate two things. The genealogy question is a mystery and probably stays one, and you're right that stacking weight on it invites reading in. But the narrative function isn't a theory." Numbers 13:33, Deuteronomy 2–3, Joshua 11:21–22 and the Gath detail behind Goliath all use giant-clan language on purpose. "The conquest is being framed as unfinished business. That part's exegesis."
- So: the family tree, ⬜. The way the story uses giants, 🔴.
- **Why the Nephilim show up after the flood** is one of the questions Heiser takes up in *Reversing Hermon* chapter 1. I haven't settled it.
- I'd only worked 13:33. The rest of the chapter (the renaming, Caleb, the grapes) I haven't studied.

## What the chapter is doing
- Israel camps in the plains of Moab, and Balak king of Moab is terrified. He sends elders of Moab and Midian, with the fees for divination in their hands, to hire Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel.
- God tells Balaam not to go and not to curse them, "for they are blessed" (22:12). Balak sends bigger men with a bigger offer. Balaam says a house full of silver and gold won't move him past the word of Yahweh, but asks them to stay the night anyway.
- God says, "If the men have come to call you, rise up and go with them" (22:20). Balaam goes, and God is angry because he goes. The angel of Yahweh stands in the road against him.
- The donkey sees the angel three times and turns aside, Balaam beats her three times, and Yahweh opens her mouth. Then Balaam's eyes are opened, he is sent on with the same instruction, and Balak takes him up to the high places to look down at Israel.

## Pay attention to this
- **The same God under two names.** Balaam says "Yahweh" (22:8, 13, 18). The narrator says "God," *Elohim* (22:9, 20, 22), and then "the angel of Yahweh." The names swap back and forth inside one scene. LSB prints "Yahweh," so you can see it on the page. 🔴 for the swapping, 🟡 that both mean the one God (the commentators agree).
- **Permission, then anger (22:20–22).** God says go, Balaam goes, God is angry. That's the knot of the chapter. ⬜
- **The permission had an "if."** "If the men have come to call you." Verse 21 has Balaam getting up and saddling his donkey with no mention of anyone calling him. 🔴 for the "if," 🟡 for reading verse 21 as breaking it.
- **The fees came first (22:7).** The elders arrive "with the fees for divination in their hand." Balaam keeps talking about silver and gold even while refusing them (22:18). 🔴
- **The angel stands in the road "as an adversary" (22:22).** The Hebrew is *satan*, the ordinary word for an opponent. Here the satan is Yahweh's own messenger. 🔴
- **The donkey sees what the seer can't.** Balaam's whole trade is seeing into the divine world, and his animal does it better. 🔴 for the scene, 🟡 for the irony as the point.
- **Sent on with the same order (22:35).** "Go with the men, but you shall speak only the word which I tell you." The anger doesn't cancel the trip. Whatever it's about, it isn't the trip. 🔴
- **The New Testament reads Balaam as greedy.** 2 Peter 2:15–16, Jude 11, Revelation 2:14 (with Numbers 31:16). 🔴

## Read it like 1200 BC, not 2026
- **Balaam is a hired professional.** Diviners worked for pay, reading signs, offering sacrifices, cursing enemies for kings. Balak isn't asking a prophet for God's will. He's buying a curse. 🔴
- **Balaam outside the Bible.** At Deir Alla in Jordan, archaeologists found ink on a plaster wall, rebuilt from 119 fragments, dated mid-8th to 7th century BC. It opens "the book of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods." Same name, same father. 🔴 for the find, 🟡 that it's the same figure.
- **That Balaam serves many gods.** At Deir Alla he works with Shgr, the Shadday gods, El and Ashtar, and he reports a night vision of coming darkness and disaster. The Bible's Balaam gets overridden by one God. 🔴
- **Divine council: same furniture, different government.** At Deir Alla the gods meet in council, the *Shaddayin*, and argue among themselves to stop a disaster. Nobody presides. In 1 Kings 22:19 and Psalm 82:1, Yahweh presides and the others carry out his will. The council idea is shared across the West Semitic world; who's in charge is not. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the contrast as Israel's point.
- **The Shaddayin and El Shaddai.** The word *Shaddayin* shows up only at Deir Alla. It may be related to "El Shaddai," the name for God in Genesis. ⬜
- **"The satan" isn't a name yet.** In 22:22 and 22:32 it's a job, an opponent in the road, and Yahweh's own angel holds it. The same use shows up in the opening of Job. 🔴
- **Diviner turning into prophet.** Walton notes Balaam's first oracles come after sacrifices on the high places, and the later ones come with no ritual at all. 🟡

## META: the book of Proverbs
- **Where it sits.** Between Psalms and Ecclesiastes in English Bibles, in the Writings in the Hebrew order. It's the plainest of the wisdom books: how to live in God's world day to day. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** what does a life lived in line with God's order look like, in money, words, work, sex, friends and family? Its answer starts with the fear of Yahweh (1:7; 9:10). 🔴
- **Who wrote it.** The heading names Solomon (1:1), but the book itself names other hands: "the words of the wise" (22:17; 24:23), proverbs of Solomon copied by the men of Hezekiah (25:1), Agur (30:1) and King Lemuel's mother (31:1). It's a collection put together over centuries, from Solomon's court (around 950 BC) to Hezekiah's (around 700 BC) and maybe later. 🔴 for the named sources; 🟡 for the dates.
- **Borrowing is in the open.** Proverbs 22:17–24:22 lines up closely with the Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope*, mostly in 22:22–23:11. Israel's wise men read their neighbors and put Yahweh at the center. 🔴
- **Text note.** The Greek Old Testament orders chapters 24–31 differently from the Hebrew and adds some lines. When a verse in a study Bible looks different, that's often why. 🔴
- **Structure:**
  - 1–9: a father teaching his son, long poems, Lady Wisdom and the strange woman. Read it as one argument.
  - 10:1–22:16: the classic one-verse proverbs of Solomon.
  - 22:17–24:34: the words of the wise.
  - 25–29: more Solomon, copied under Hezekiah.
  - 30: Agur. 31: Lemuel, and the woman of strength (31:10–31).
- **Pattern, not promise.** A proverb says how life usually goes, not a contract God signs. "Train up a child" (22:6) is a proverb. 🔴
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - The fear of Yahweh: 1:7, 9:10 and 31:30 bracket the book.
  - Two ways and two women: wisdom and folly, life and death.
  - Wisdom as a person beside God at creation (8:22–31).

## What the chapter is doing
- A title and a purpose statement: these are Solomon's proverbs, given so the naive get prudence and the young get knowledge, and so the wise grow wiser (1:1–6).
- The motto of the book: "The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and discipline" (1:7).
- A father tells his son to keep his parents' teaching like a wreath on his head and a chain on his neck (1:8–9).
- He warns him about a gang that wants him to help ambush the innocent and split the loot. Their trap catches themselves: greed takes away the life of its owners (1:10–19).
- Wisdom herself stands in the street and shouts. Those who refuse her now will call later and she won't answer. Whoever listens will live secure (1:20–33).

## Pay attention to this
- **A pile-up of words for wisdom (1:2–6).** Wisdom, instruction, understanding, insight, righteousness, justice, equity, prudence, knowledge, discretion. *Chokmah* is skill, the way a craftsman has skill. 🔴
- **"The beginning" (1:7).** *Reshit*, first and foundational, the same word as Genesis 1:1. You don't graduate past it. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for the Genesis echo.
- **"Fools despise" (1:7).** The fool in Proverbs (*evil*, *kesil*) isn't stupid. He refuses correction. 🔴
- **"My son" (1:8, 10, 15).** The book is set as a parent teaching a child. Mother's teaching counts too (1:8). 🔴
- **The gang's pitch is all "we" (1:11–14).** Come with us, we'll find wealth, one purse for all of us. Belonging is the bait. 🔴
- **Their own trap (1:17–19).** A bird sees the net and flies in anyway. The ambushers end up ambushing their own lives. 🔴
- **Wisdom shouts in public (1:20–21).** In the street, the squares, the busiest corners, the city gate. She isn't hidden. 🔴
- **Wisdom laughs last (1:26).** "I will laugh at your calamity." Hard words, put in Wisdom's mouth, not God's. 🔴
- **"Complacency" kills (1:32).** The naive are killed by their turning away and fools by their ease. 🔴

## Read it like 950 BC, not 2026
- **Kings collected wisdom.** In Egypt and Mesopotamia, wisdom books were court documents, written by scribes and royal fathers to train officials. Solomon is pictured as that kind of king (1 Kings 4:29–34). 🔴
- **Father to son is the standard form.** Egyptian instructions (Ptahhotep, Amenemope) are written as a father teaching his son. Proverbs 1–9 uses the same frame. 🔴
- **The fear of Yahweh is the difference.** Egypt grounded right living in *ma'at*, the order built into the world. Proverbs grounds it in the fear of Yahweh, Israel's covenant God, by name. 🔴
- **Fear means awe before the one above you.** Heiser (as recorded in my notes) reads the fear of Yahweh as recognizing the gap between Creator and creature, which puts a human in the right place relative to God and his council. 🔵 as Heiser's reading; I don't have a page reference for it.
- **The city gate was the courthouse.** Wisdom calls out at the gate (1:21) where elders judged and business was done. She's speaking where decisions get made. 🔴
- **Bandits on the roads.** Highway robbery and ambush were common in the ancient world, and kings bragged about making roads safe. The gang in 1:10–19 was a real danger, not a metaphor. 🔴
- **No council scene here.** Proverbs 1 has no heavenly court. The closest the book gets is Wisdom beside God at creation in Proverbs 8.

## What the chapter is doing
- Wisdom stands at the crossroads and the city gates and calls to everyone, even the naive and the fools (8:1–5).
- She says her words are true and straight, worth more than silver, gold and jewels. Kings reign by her and rulers make just laws by her (8:6–21).
- Then she goes back before the world: Yahweh possessed her at the beginning of his way, before the depths, the springs, the mountains and the fields (8:22–26).
- She was there when he set the heavens, drew a circle on the deep and marked out the earth's foundations, beside him, delighting and playing before him and in his world (8:27–31).
- She closes with an invitation: listen, watch at my doors. Whoever finds me finds life. Whoever misses me hurts himself, and all who hate me love death (8:32–36).

## Pay attention to this
- **Wisdom is a person here.** She speaks in the first person for the whole chapter. Personification is a poem's way of talking, and readers have argued for two thousand years about how far to take it. 🔴 that she speaks; ⬜ on what she is.
- **"Yahweh possessed me" (8:22).** The verb is *qanah*, which can mean possess, acquire, get, or create. That one word is why this verse became a battlefield. 🔴
- **"Brought forth" (8:24–25).** The language of birth. She came before the depths and the mountains. 🔴
- **She was beside him at creation (8:30).** The word for what she was there is *'amon*. Two main readings: "master craftsman" or "little child, nursling." Translations split hard. 🔴 that it's a crux; ⬜ on which.
- **Playing (8:30–31).** The verb is used twice: *mesacheqet*, playing, sporting, laughing. Delighting daily, playing before him always, playing in his inhabited world, delighting in the sons of men. 🔴 on the verb.
- **Kings rule by her (8:15–16).** Good government depends on wisdom, not just power. 🔴
- **"All who hate me love death" (8:36).** The chapter ends on the two-ways choice that runs all through Proverbs 1–9. 🔴
- **The same creation picture as Job 28 and Job 38.** The circle on the deep, the sea given its limit (8:29), the foundations of the earth. 🔴

## Read it like 950 BC, not 2026
- **Wisdom beside the throne.** In the ancient Near East a king's wise counselors sat beside him. Proverbs 8 puts Wisdom beside Yahweh before anything else existed. She is not one of the council voting on creation. She is there before the mountains, and God does the making. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the court picture.
- **Egypt's Ma'at.** In Egyptian art Ma'at, the goddess of order and truth, is shown as the daughter of the sun god, sometimes delighting before him. Some scholars (Keel) read Proverbs 8:30–31 against that picture. Israel's poet keeps Wisdom subordinate to Yahweh and never makes her a goddess. 🔴 for Ma'at; 🔵 for direct borrowing.
- **The circle on the deep (8:27).** The ancient picture was a disc of earth surrounded by waters, with a boundary drawn at the horizon. God marks the line the sea can't cross (8:29). 🔴
- **Second Temple readers made her bigger.** Sirach 24 has Wisdom come out of the mouth of the Most High and settle in Israel as the Torah. Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26 calls her a breath of God's power and a reflection of eternal light. That's the language John 1 and Hebrews 1:3 pick up. 🔴
- **Two Powers.** Heiser reads Wisdom here as a distinct persona who is also one with Yahweh, part of the Jewish "two powers in heaven" background to John's prologue and later Trinitarian thought. 🟡 as Heiser's frame; my notes don't have page numbers for it.
- **The verse the church fought over.** The Greek translates *qanah* in 8:22 as *ektisen*, "created." In the fourth century Arius used it to argue the Son was created. Athanasius and the Nicene side answered that the verse speaks of the Son's role in creation, or of his human nature, not of him being made. 🔴 for the history; ⬜ for how to read 8:22 itself.

- **8:30–31, playing at creation.** I came to this verse from my own kitchen. I made a gourmet peanut butter and jelly sandwich and treated each piece like it was going to be the whole meal, and something clicked about what cooks mean when they say a thing was made with love. Then I tried it on a pain-in-the-butt job, relighting the pilot on the hot water tank, and decided to enjoy doing it instead of getting mad. The verb is *mesacheqet*, playing. Whether *'amon* means master craftsman or little child, creation is craft done with delight, or it's play. Joy is native to how making happens, and attention is the word that holds it up.

## What the chapter is doing
- Lady Wisdom builds her house on seven pillars, slaughters meat, mixes wine and sets her table. She sends her maids to call from the high places of the city: whoever is naive, come in, eat and live (9:1–6).
- A middle section on taking correction: rebuke a scoffer and he'll hate you, rebuke a wise man and he'll love you. The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom (9:7–12).
- Lady Folly sits at her door, loud and knowing nothing, and calls to the same people with the same words: whoever is naive, turn in here. "Stolen water is sweet" (9:13–17).
- The last line: he doesn't know the dead are there, and her guests are in the depths of Sheol (9:18).

## Pay attention to this
- **Two hostesses, one invitation.** Wisdom (9:4) and Folly (9:16) say the exact same words: "Whoever is naive, let him turn in here." The difference is what's on the table and where the house leads. 🔴
- **Wisdom works, Folly sits.** Wisdom builds, hews, slaughters, mixes, sets, sends (9:1–3). Folly sits at her doorway on a seat (9:14). 🔴
- **Seven pillars (9:1).** A big, complete house. Seven is the number of fullness. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the meaning of seven.
- **Bread and wine (9:5).** Wisdom's meal is real food. Folly's is stolen water and bread eaten in secret (9:17). 🔴
- **The middle section breaks in (9:7–12).** Between the two invitations, a short lesson on who can be taught. Some read it as a later insertion. 🔴 that it breaks the flow; 🔵 on insertion.
- **9:10 repeats 1:7.** "The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom." Proverbs 1–9 opens and closes on it. 🔴
- **"Stolen water is sweet" (9:17).** Folly sells the thrill of the forbidden. Compare the water imagery for sex in marriage in 5:15–18. 🔴 for the line; 🟡 for the connection to chapter 5.
- **The dead are there (9:18).** The word is *rephaim*. 🔴

## Read it like 950 BC, not 2026
- **A house on pillars was a temple or a palace.** Ordinary houses didn't need seven pillars. Heiser (as recorded in my notes) reads Wisdom's house as reflecting ancient temple building, a sacred space or a small picture of the cosmos. 🔴 that pillared halls were palace and temple architecture; 🔵 for the temple reading here.
- **A meal was an alliance.** In the ancient world eating at someone's table bound you to them. Accepting Wisdom's invitation, or Folly's, means joining her household. 🔴 for meal customs; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Cult prostitution and the "strange woman."** Folly's seat on "the high places of the city" (9:14) uses the same phrase as Wisdom's call in 9:3. Some see Canaanite religion and its sexual rites behind Folly. 🔵
- **Rephaim and the underworld (9:18).** *Rephaim* in the Bible means both the dead in Sheol (Isaiah 14:9; 26:14) and a race of giants in Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:11; 3:11). In Ugaritic texts the *rpum* are the honored dead, tied to the old kings. 🔴 for both uses and the Ugaritic parallel.
- **Heiser's read of 9:18.** As I recorded it: the "dead" of 9:18 are the *rephaim*, the spirits of the giant clans, so Folly's guests join the rebellious assembly under the earth. 🔵 as recorded; my note has no citation for it, and the plain sense is "the shades of the dead."
- **Sheol is the grave, not a fiery hell.** Down, dark and silent. The Greek translates it *hades*. Folly's house is a front door to the grave. 🔴
- **Divine council here is thin.** The only unseen-world hook is *rephaim*. The heavenly court itself does not appear.

## META: the book of Revelation
- **Where it sits.** Last book of the Bible, and the one that gathers up the rest. It opens with Genesis threads still loose (tree of life, the serpent, the nations scattered at Babel) and closes with them tied off (Rev 21–22).
- **The question the whole book is asking:** who is really on the throne, and whose name do you carry while it looks like Rome is winning?
- **What kind of book.** It calls itself three things at once: an apocalypse ("revelation," 1:1), a prophecy (1:3), and a letter to seven real churches (1:4). 🔴
- **Who wrote it.** A man named John, exiled on Patmos "because of the word of God" (1:1, 4, 9). Early church writers (Justin, Irenaeus) say John the apostle. Some ancient readers doubted it because the Greek is so different from the Gospel of John. Heiser works as if it is the same author but doesn't argue it. ⬜
- **When.** Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 5.30.3) puts the vision near the end of Domitian's reign, about AD 95. Some date it before AD 70. Heiser won't settle it: "no one knows for sure," first century at the very least, and the Babylon = Rome argument (ch 14) is "not a slam dunk either way." 🔴 for what Irenaeus says; ⬜ for the date.
- **The Greek is rough on purpose.** Revelation has more grammar "errors" than any other ancient Greek text. R. H. Charles said John "writes in Greek but thinks in Hebrew." Beale and Heiser treat many of them as planted flags pointing back to a specific Old Testament text. 🔴 for the oddities; 🟡 for reading them as deliberate.
- **The Old Testament is everywhere and never quoted.** More OT allusions than any NT book, zero formal quotations. John never says "as it is written." He weaves words and pictures in and expects you to hear the source. Isaiah is used most (122 allusions by Moyise's count), then Psalms (97), Ezekiel (83), the Torah (82) and Daniel (74). 🔴
- **How I'm reading it.** My spine is Heiser's 26-episode series *The Old Testament in the Book of Revelation*. It is not a prophecy series. No end-times system. The question every chapter is: what is John doing with the Old Testament? 🔴
- **Movements:**
  - chs 1–3: the risen Christ and seven letters to the churches
  - chs 4–5: the throne room, the courtroom, the Lamb and the sealed scroll
  - chs 6–16: seals, trumpets, bowls, with interludes (7, 10–11, 12–14)
  - chs 17–20: Babylon falls, the rider on the white horse, the dragon bound and judged
  - chs 21–22: new heavens, new earth, Eden restored
- **Seals, trumpets and bowls may repeat more than they march.** Heiser came to find Kline's recapitulation reading convincing: chs 16, 19 and 20 cycle the same final battle. 🟡
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - The Deuteronomy 32 worldview: the nations handed to lesser gods at Babel, those gods judged, the nations brought home.
  - The divine council, and believers joining it.
  - Name theology: the seal of God's name against the mark of the beast's.
  - Two Powers: Jesus described with language that belongs to Yahweh.
  - Chaos (sea, dragon, Babylon) against Eden.

## What the chapter is doing
- John greets seven churches in Asia "from the One who is and who was and who is to come," from the seven Spirits, and from Jesus Christ (1:4–5).
- He's on Patmos, worshiping on the Lord's day, and hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write (1:9–11).
- He turns and sees one like a son of man standing among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, with a sword coming out of his mouth (1:12–16).
- John falls like a dead man. Jesus puts his hand on him: I am the first and the last, I was dead, I'm alive forever, and I have the keys of death and Hades (1:17–18).
- Jesus explains the picture: the stars are the angels of the churches, the lampstands are the churches (1:20).

## Pay attention to this
- **"The One who is and who was and who is to come" (1:4, 8; 4:8).** This three-part name shows up nowhere else in early Christian writing. Normal Christian greetings say "God our Father." John drops "Father" here and uses this instead. 🔴
- **The grammar breaks on purpose (1:4).** "From" (*apo*) needs the next word in a different case. John leaves "the One who is" (*ho on*) in the exact form it has in Greek Exodus 3:14, "I am the One who is." Scribes later "fixed" it. Beale: John left it wrong so readers would stop and find the burning bush. 🔴 for the grammar and the scribal fixes; 🟡 for the intent.
- **"A kingdom, priests" (1:6).** That's Exodus 19:6, Israel's calling at Sinai, now said of the church. Heiser: the church is *a* new Israel, not *the* new Israel, and he doesn't hold replacement theology. 🔴 for the allusion.
- **"Coming with the clouds" (1:7).** In the Hebrew Bible, riding the clouds is something God does: Deut 33:26, Ps 68:33, Ps 104:3, Isa 19:1. The fifth time, Daniel 7:13, it's the son of man who comes on the clouds. 1:7 also pulls in Zechariah 12:10, "those who pierced Him." 🔴
- **Jesus gets God's white hair (1:14).** In Daniel 7:9 the white hair like wool belongs to the Ancient of Days, not the son of man. John gives it to Jesus. 🔴 for the move; 🟡 that he means to blur the two.
- **The robe and golden sash (1:13) come from Daniel 10:5,** the man in linen. Heiser argues that figure is the Angel of the LORD, higher than Gabriel or Michael. 🟡
- **The sword from his mouth (1:16).** Isaiah 11:4 says "the rod of his mouth," but the Greek Old Testament reads "word of his mouth." John's sword follows the Greek. 🔴 It returns in 2:16 and 19:15, 21. 🔴
- **Seven stars, seven lampstands, seven Spirits, seven angels.** Read 1:4, 1:16, 1:20 and 3:1 together and they lock into one picture. The lampstands are menorah branches from Zechariah 4. 🔴
- **"First and last" moves from God to Jesus.** God says "Alpha and Omega" in 1:8. Jesus says "the first and the last" in 1:17. Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 are where that title comes from, and there it is God's. Same title, two persons, ten verses apart. 🔴
- **"I was dead... and I have the keys" (1:18).** Died, alive, has the keys. In that order. Someone else held them before. This gets worked out in ch 3. 🔴 for the order; 🟡 for what it implies.
- **The Lord's day (1:10) is a Sunday,** not the "day of the LORD." The Greek phrases differ (*kyriake hemera* vs. *hemera tou kyriou*), and John can't be standing in a day he's prophesying as future. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Two Powers in Heaven.** Before Jesus, some Jewish readers saw two figures in Daniel 7 who were both Yahweh: the one on the throne and the one riding the clouds. After the Christians claimed it, the rabbis banned it. So John isn't inventing a high view of Jesus. He's using a Jewish category that already existed, around AD 95, centuries before Nicaea. 🔴
- **The swipe at Zeus.** Exodus 3:14 only gives "who is." Why add "was" and "is to come"? McDonough found a Greek oracle at Dodona praising Zeus: "Zeus was, Zeus is, Zeus shall be." Zeus was also called *hupsistos*, "Most High," the same word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's God Elyon. A Greek ear in Asia would hear John saying it about Yahweh. 🔴 for the oracle and the title; 🟡 that John is aiming at Zeus.
- **The name wasn't always unspeakable.** In the Old Testament people said "Yahweh" out loud. God tells Moses to use it (Exod 3:13–15), and the priests speak it over Israel (Num 6:22–27). Holding back the name is a Second Temple habit. The Dead Sea Scrolls sometimes write four dots instead. Philo used *ho on* as a name for God at least eight times. John uses the same accepted Greek form. 🔴
- **Divine council: the seven Spirits are the eyes of the LORD.** Zechariah 4:10 says the seven lamps are "the eyes of the LORD which range through the whole earth." Oppenheim (*JAOS* 1968) showed "eyes" in that world are agents who patrol and report back: Zech 1:8–11, Zech 6:5–7, Job 1:7, 2 Chr 16:9. So the stars and Spirits around Jesus are heavenly beings, and "the whole earth" is why the seven letters speak to every church. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for how far the council reading reaches.
- **Stars are angels.** 1 Enoch already says it (1 Enoch 21:3; 86:1–3; 90:20–25). A first-century Jewish reader knew that before John explained it in 1:20. 🔴
- **The church as temple.** Where God lives, his council lives. Heiser ties the menorah, Zechariah's stone with seven eyes (Zech 3:9) and Daniel 7 into one picture: the church is the new temple, the line that runs from John 2 to Rev 21:22. 🟡
- **Patmos was not a desert island.** It was a populated island with a garrison. John was held there, but visitors could reach him and bring scrolls. That's how he could weave in this much Old Testament. 🔴
- **The Lord returns as a warrior.** Beale ties the sun-like face (1:16) to Judges 5:31 and the stars fighting from heaven in Judges 5:20. Heiser calls that link "a little loose." 🔵 What he does land on: the returning Christ comes to judge, and judgment starts with God's own household, which is why the letters come next. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- The trumpets stop after number six, the same way the seals stopped after number six in ch. 7. This pause runs from 10:1 to 11:14.
- A strong angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow on his head, a face like the sun and feet like pillars of fire. He plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a little open scroll.
- He roars, seven thunders speak, and John is told to seal up what they said and not write it.
- The angel swears there will be no more delay. John eats the little scroll: sweet in his mouth, bitter in his stomach. Then he is told he must prophesy again.

## Pay attention to this
- **Who is this angel? (10:1).** Cloud (Dan 7:13; Rev 1:7), rainbow (the throne in 4:3; Ezek 1:28), face like the sun (Christ in 1:16), feet like fire (1:15). It all points at God. But in 10:6 he swears "by Him who lives forever and ever," which sounds like a created being calling on someone higher. Heiser leaves it open and leans toward a very high angel carrying God's presence and authority. 🟡
- **One foot on the sea, one on the land (10:2).** Sea plus land means all of it. God plants his claim on both before the beasts come up out of the sea and the earth in ch. 13. 🔴
- **He roars like a lion (10:3).** Amos 3:8: "A lion has roared! Who will not fear? Lord Yahweh has spoken! Who can but prophesy?" The roar is what sends a prophet out, and by 10:11 John is being sent. 🔴
- **The seven thunders are God's voice.** Ps 29 says "the voice of Yahweh" seven times, and "The God of glory thunders" (29:3). Thunder is how God's voice sounded at Sinai (Exod 19) and in John 12:28–29. 🔴
- **Sealed, not written (10:4).** Daniel was told "seal up the book until the time of the end" (Dan 12:4). John is told the opposite for the whole book: "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book" (22:10). This is the one place he's told to seal. 🔴
- **There's nothing to decode.** John didn't write the thunders down, so nobody can recover them. Heiser: God has not told us everything, and this is him saying so. 🔴
- **"Delay no longer" (10:6).** Not "time will stop." Daniel's angel over the river swore "it would be for a time, times, and half a time" (Dan 12:7). John's angel swears the waiting is over. 🔴
- **This answers "How long?"** In 6:10–11 the martyrs asked how long, and they were told to rest "a little while longer." This is that wait ending. 🔴
- **"The mystery of God is finished" (10:7).** *Musterion* in the Bible isn't a puzzle. It's a plan God kept hidden and has now brought out (Dan 2:28–29; Rom 16:25–26; Eph 3:3–6). Here it's the whole hope the prophets announced, finished at the seventh trumpet. 🔴
- **A little scroll, not the big one (10:2, 9).** Ch. 5 uses *biblion*, a sealed scroll. Here it's *biblaridion*, a little scroll, already open. Heiser reads them as two different scrolls: one is the title deed whose opening releases judgment, the other is a prophet's commissioning scroll. 🟡
- **Ezekiel ate one first.** Ezek 3:3: "Then I ate it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth." John adds the bitter stomach. 🔴
- **Kings get added (10:11).** "Peoples and nations and tongues and kings." The usual formula (5:9; 7:9) has "tribes" where this one has "kings." The rulers are on notice. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **A scroll you eat.** To a Jewish reader this was a prophet's commissioning, straight out of Ezekiel 2:8–3:3. You don't just carry God's word, you take it in, and it becomes part of you. 🔴
- **Sweet and bitter.** God's word is "sweeter than honey to my mouth" (Ps 119:103; also Ps 19:10). The bitter part is the judgment inside it, and what it costs to preach woe to people who won't repent (ch. 9). Heiser: the prophet doesn't get only the sweet part. 🔴
- **An angel who carries God's name.** Israel already had a figure who was called an angel and spoke as God: the Angel of Yahweh. Gen 48:15–16 puts "the God" and "the angel who has redeemed me" in the same blessing. Heiser calls this the "two powers" pattern. He holds that Revelation blurs the line on purpose, because a representative carrying God's own presence is how the council and name theology work. 🟡
- **Angel or Christ, from the Q&A.** A listener asked if the angel on sea and land is Christ shown as an angel. Heiser: the rainbow link to creation is weak (the rainbow doesn't show up until Gen 9), but standing on the sea could echo Jesus walking on water, a victory over chaos. Whether John meant that depends on which was written first, Matthew or Revelation. 🟡
- **Divine council:** this is a heavenly messenger sent from the throne with an oath and a commission, the way prophets were sent from God's council in the Old Testament (Isa 6; Jer 23:18, 22). The thunders are God himself speaking. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- John is handed a measuring rod and told to measure the sanctuary of God, the altar and the worshipers, but to leave out the outer court. The nations will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
- God's two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days in sackcloth. Fire comes from their mouths, they shut the sky, they turn water to blood.
- When they finish, the beast from the abyss kills them. Their bodies lie in the street of the great city for three and a half days while the world celebrates. Then God breathes life into them and calls them up to heaven in a cloud.

## Pay attention to this
- **Three names for one stretch of time.** Forty-two months (11:2), 1,260 days (11:3), and in ch. 12 "a time and times and half a time" (12:14). All three are three and a half years, and all come from Daniel: "they will be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time" (Dan 7:25; also 12:7). 🔴
- **Read ch. 11 and ch. 12 together.** Same numbers, same reality. Heiser: you can't crack one without the other. 🔴
- **The measuring rod comes from Ezekiel 40.** A man with a measuring reed walks Ezekiel through the vision temple (Ezek 40:3). Measuring can mean marking for destruction (2 Kgs 21:13; Amos 7:7–9) or marking for protection (Zech 2:1–5). Heiser follows Aune: protection here, like the measuring of the New Jerusalem in 21:15. 🔴 for the two meanings, 🟡 for protection here.
- **Nobody actually measures anything.** The speaker isn't named, and the measuring never happens on the page. 🔴
- **Fire from their mouths (11:5).** Nearly everyone reads that line as a figure of speech. Heiser's question: if that line is figurative, why read the rest as two literal men? 🔴 for the question; the answer is his reading, below.
- **Elijah and Moses are in the job description (11:6).** Shutting the sky is Elijah (1 Kgs 17:1). Water to blood and plagues is Moses (Exod 7). 🔴
- **"The two olive trees and the two lampstands" (11:4).** John names his source. It's Zech 4, where the two olive trees are "the two anointed ones who are standing by the Lord of all the earth" (Zech 4:14). The Hebrew there is "sons of oil." 🔴
- **"Spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified" (11:8).** John tells you himself the city's name is not literal. 🔴
- **"Come up here" (11:12).** The same words John heard in 4:1. They die, lie dead three and a half days, rise and go up in a cloud. Their story runs on their Lord's. 🔴
- **The seventh trumpet is the end.** "He will reign forever and ever" (11:15), "the time came for the dead to be judged" (11:18). Ps 2 is underneath: "Why do the nations rage" becomes "the nations were enraged, and Your rage came." Heiser: this did not happen in AD 70, so the chapter is pointed at the last day. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The wall in the temple.** Herod's temple had a low stone barrier (the *soreg*) around the inner courts, with signs warning that a Gentile who went past it would die. Outside it was the court of the Gentiles, the "court which is outside" that is "given to the Gentiles" (11:2). Paul calls that wall "the dividing wall" that Christ tore down (Eph 2:14). 🔴
- **Which temple? The dating fight.** If 11:1 is the stone temple in Jerusalem, Revelation was written before AD 70, when the temple still stood. If it's the heavenly or spiritual temple, a date after 70 works fine. Aune argues the earthly temple: "sanctuary of God" shows up again only at 11:19, where it's marked "in heaven," so 11:1 must be the other one. The other side says 11:19 defines 11:1. Heiser doesn't pick. 🔴 that both readings exist, ⬜ which is right.
- **Heiser's irony on the dating.** The people who read Revelation most literally everywhere else go spiritual here, and the people who read it symbolically everywhere else go literal here. Both flip their own method because their system needs it. 🔴
- **The calendar fight was real.** In the Second Temple period Jews argued hard about the calendar. The people behind Jubilees, 1 Enoch and the Qumran scrolls held to a solar calendar of 364 days, where every feast falls on the same weekday every year, and they called the moon-based calendar (the one Judaism uses today) a human corruption. It helped split the Qumran group off. 🔴 Heiser works this through Gabriele Boccaccini's study of the calendars in Daniel and Enoch.
- **Daniel's numbers sort into two piles.** Boccaccini, through Heiser: the 2,300 evenings and mornings (Dan 8:14) point back to Antiochus defiling the temple and its rededication, which is Hanukkah. The 1,260, 1,290 and 1,335 days (Dan 12) point forward to the resurrection and the Day of Yahweh. 🔴 for the two horizons; 🔵 for the calendar math behind them.
- **"Change the seasons and the law" (Dan 7:25).** Some read this as Antiochus forcing a Greek lunar calendar on Israel. 🔵
- **A side point Heiser is honest about.** If the numbers only add up on a calendar known from the Second Temple period, at least part of Daniel was written late. He calls it a side issue but doesn't hide it. 🟡
- **Zechariah 4 is a council vision.** The seven lamps are "the eyes of Yahweh which roam to and fro throughout the earth" (Zech 4:10), the same seven-spirits picture as Rev 1 and 5. The vision's center is "Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit" (Zech 4:6). Heiser: the two "sons of oil" stand in God's council as the Spirit-filled people of God. The two witnesses are the church bearing witness, not two men. 🟡 He calls it a reading, not a proof.
- **Beale lands close.** Beale calls the witnesses figures like Elijah and Moses who stand for the church. 🔴 for what Beale says.
- **Divine council:** the two olive trees "stand before the Lord of the earth" (11:4), which is council language. The twenty-four elders on their thrones fall down (11:16). Heaven's sanctuary and the ark (11:19), with lightning, thunder, earthquake and hail, is Sinai again. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The dragon was an old enemy.** Every people around Israel had a story about a storm god killing a sea dragon to bring order out of chaos. The Old Testament takes that picture and gives the win to Yahweh: "You broke the heads of the sea monsters in the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan" (Ps 74:13–14); "Yahweh will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent… and He will kill the dragon who lives in the sea" (Isa 27:1). The dragon is also Egypt (Ezek 29:3; Ps 87:4, where Rahab is Egypt) and Babylon (Jer 51:34). 🔴
- **Zion in labor.** The prophets pictured Jerusalem as a woman in childbirth, her pain the exile and the birth the rescue: "Writhe and labor to give birth, Daughter of Zion, like a woman in childbirth… There Yahweh will redeem you" (Mic 4:10; also Isa 26:17–18; 66:7–9). A Jewish reader saw Zion, not one woman. 🔴
- **A Qumran parallel.** One of the Thanksgiving Hymns from the Dead Sea Scrolls (1QH 11:7–12) pictures a woman in agony giving birth to a "wonderful counselor." Someone at Qumran was reading the same promise the same way. 🔵
- **The wilderness was where God fed you.** Manna, Elijah fed in the wilderness (1 Kgs 17; 19), Moses in Midian. Josephus reports first-century would-be messiahs leading crowds into the desert expecting a new Exodus (*Jewish War* 2.259–262). Running to the wilderness meant rescue was coming. 🔴
- **A flood out of the dragon's mouth.** In the Psalms floods are what enemies do to God's people: "The cords of death encompassed me, and the torrents of vileness terrified me" (Ps 18:4). The Hebrew there is *beliyya'al*, Belial, which later became a name for Satan. 🔴
- **Michael (12:7).** Daniel calls Michael "the great prince who stands guard over the sons of your people" (Dan 12:1), Israel's angel prince. In Deut 32 the nations were handed to lesser *elohim*, and Israel was kept for Yahweh. Michael fighting the dragon for the woman fits that map. 🔴 for Daniel, 🟡 for the Deut 32 link.
- **Michael is not Jesus.** A listener asked about the Jehovah's Witness and Adventist claim. Heiser: God has authority over Michael, Michael is "one of the chief princes" (Dan 10:13), and the chief princes sit under "the prince of the host." ## What the chapter is doing
- Right after the beast and his mark, the Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who have his name and his Father's name written on their foreheads. They sing a new song only they can learn.
- Three angels fly through midheaven. The first carries "an eternal gospel" to every nation: fear God, the hour of his judgment has come. The second: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great." The third: anyone who worships the beast and takes his mark will drink the wine of God's wrath.
- A voice from heaven: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on!"
- One like a son of man sits on a white cloud with a sickle and reaps the earth. Then an angel gathers the grapes of the earth into the great wine press of God's wrath, and blood flows up to the horses' bridles for 1,600 stadia.

## Pay attention to this
- **Name against name (14:1).** Ch. 13 ends with a mark that is "the name of the beast." Ch. 14 opens with the Lamb's name and the Father's name on the foreheads of his people. Every person in these two chapters bears somebody's name. 🔴
- **The Lamb is on Zion (14:1), and the beast was on the seashore (13:1).** Zion is God's mountain, where his king is set (Ps 2:6). 🔴
- **"Gospel" means good news, even here (14:6–7).** The eternal gospel is "Fear God, and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come." Judgment is good news for the people who've been crushed. Heiser: it's Ps 82 being carried out, the powers judged and the nations called back to worship their Creator. 🔴 for the text, 🟡 for the Ps 82 reading.
- **"Fallen, fallen is Babylon" (14:8).** Isa 21:9: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the graven images of her gods are shattered on the ground." "Babylon the great" is Nebuchadnezzar's boast in Dan 4:30. The fall of Babylon is announced here and told in full in chs. 17–18. 🔴
- **The cup of wrath (14:10).** "The cup of His rage" is Old Testament language: Ps 75:8; Isa 51:17; Jer 25:15. 🔴
- **"Here is the perseverance of the saints" (14:12).** The warning about the mark is written to the church, to make them hold on. 🔴
- **The son of man on the cloud (14:14).** Christ, not an angel. Seated plus cloud joins Ps 110:1 to Dan 7:13, the same pair Jesus put together at his trial: "you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62). 🔴
- **The angel doesn't give Jesus orders (14:15).** The angel comes out of the sanctuary with word that the hour has come. That's God's timing being announced, not an angel bossing the Son. 🔴
- **Sickle and wine press come from Joel (14:15–19).** "Send in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full; the vats overflow, for their evil is great" (Joel 3:13). Both harvests are in one verse, and in Joel it's judgment on the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat. 🔴
- **Isaiah 63's wine press (14:19–20).** "I have trodden the wine trough alone, and from the peoples there was no man with Me… their lifeblood is sprinkled on My garments" (Isa 63:3). In Isaiah the one treading is Yahweh. John hands it to Christ, and does it again at 19:15. 🔴
- **Blood to the bridles (14:20).** About 184 miles of it. It's a stock way of saying "a slaughter beyond counting," not a measurement. 1 Enoch 100:3 has a horse walking up to its chest in the blood of sinners. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Flying doesn't mean wings (14:6).** The Greek verb for "flying" was used for any fast motion: horses, javelins, a soul. Aune notes this is the earliest Jewish or Christian text with an ordinary angel flying, and he isn't given wings. In the Bible only cherubim and seraphim have wings. Winged angels show up in church writers later (Tertullian). 🔴
- **"Midheaven."** The Greek word (*mesouranema*) means the top of the sky, the spot where someone could be heard by the whole earth. It assumes the ancient picture of a flat earth with the sky over it. The message comes through the old picture of the world, and that's fine. 🔴
- **Babylon meant Rome.** Babylon burned the first temple and exiled Judah. Rome burned the second temple in AD 70. Jewish writers after 70 called Rome "Babylon" (2 Baruch, the Sibylline Oracles, 4 Ezra), and so does 1 Pet 5:13. 🔴
- **Does that date the book?** Aune points out that every Jewish "Babylon means Rome" text comes after 70, which would push Revelation after 70. Then he answers himself: a Qumran commentary on Isaiah already uses "Babylon" as a code name (for Assyria) before 70. Heiser: not a slam dunk either way. 🟡
- **Fire in front of the righteous.** Punishment by fire in the sight of the holy ones is common in Jewish apocalypses (1 Enoch 48:9), and it goes back to Isa 66:24. 🔴
- **Hell or annihilation?** Heiser: 14:10–11 is apocalyptic language with Old Testament and Second Temple roots, and it can be read either way. "Both views are on the table." This verse alone doesn't settle it. 🔴 In the Q&A he says he leans toward annihilation and won't rule out the traditional view. 🟡
- **An angel over fire (14:18).** Jewish tradition gave angels charge of parts of creation: the winds (7:1), the waters (16:5). The Testament of Abraham names an archangel, Purouel ("fire"), who tests people's works by fire. 🔵
- **One Divine Warrior.** In the Old Testament there is only one Divine Warrior: Yahweh, or the Angel of Yahweh who is Yahweh. The commander of Yahweh's army stands before Joshua with "his sword drawn in his hand" (Josh 5:13). The drawn sword shows up only twice more, Balaam's road (Num 22:23) and David's census (1 Chr 21:16), both the Angel of Yahweh. John puts Jesus in that seat. Heiser, via Tremper Longman: that's as high as Christology gets. 🔴
- **The Lamb's people as priests in a holy war (14:4).** "Not defiled with women… virgins." Heiser in the Q&A: the Bible thinks well of marriage, so a soldiers'-abstinence rule (temporary) is a weak fit. He leaves open that the language sets the 144,000 against the Watchers, the sons of God who did defile themselves with women in Gen 6. Spiritual faithfulness, no idolatry, is part of it. 🟡
- **Divine council:** the Lamb's people stand on Zion, the mountain of God's assembly. The angels "in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb" (14:10) are God's court watching the verdict. Heiser reads the eternal gospel as the Ps 82 judgment of the gods and the nations brought home. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- The shortest chapter in the book, and it's a setup. Seven angels hold seven last plagues, "because in them the wrath of God is finished" (15:1).
- The people who beat the beast stand on a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb (15:2–4).
- The sanctuary in heaven opens. Seven angels come out dressed like priests, and one of the four living creatures hands them seven golden bowls (15:5–7).
- Smoke from God's glory fills the sanctuary, and nobody can go in until the plagues are done (15:8). Chapter 16 pours the bowls.

## Pay attention to this
- **We're still in the throne room of chapters 4–5.** Living creatures, sanctuary, throne. Every judgment in the book comes out of that room. 🔴
- **"Seven plagues, which are the last" (15:1).** The trumpets hit a third. The bowls finish the job. Hold that partial/total contrast when you read ch. 16. 🔴
- **The sea of glass is back (15:2; first seen in 4:6).** This time there's fire in it, and the winners are standing on it. 🔴
- **Two songs, one song (15:3).** "The song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb." Moses sang after the Red Sea (Exodus 15). John fuses that victory with the Lamb's. 🔴
- **The song is about the nations, not about the singers.** "King of the nations," "all the nations will come and worship before You" (15:3–4). The people saved out of Babylon sing about everyone else coming in. 🔴
- **"Tabernacle of testimony" (15:5).** That's wilderness language for the tent that held the tablets. Exodus vocabulary all the way down: song of Moses, plagues, tent. 🔴
- **Priests, not soldiers (15:6).** Clean bright linen and golden sashes. The judgment is handled like temple service. 🔴
- **Nobody can enter (15:8).** Same as when the glory filled the tabernacle and Moses couldn't go in (Exodus 40:34–35). The decision is made and can't be bargained with. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The sea meant chaos.** To an Israelite the sea was where Leviathan lived and where death came from (Psalm 74:12–15; Isaiah 51:9–11). The beast in 13:1 comes up out of it. A sea you can stand on is chaos beaten flat. In 21:1 it's gone entirely. 🔴
- **Heiser (with Beale and McDonough): the sea of glass does three jobs at once.** It's the heavenly Red Sea of a new Exodus (song of Moses, plagues, tent all point there) 🔴, the crystal floor under God's throne from Ezekiel 1:22 🔴, and maybe Solomon's bronze "sea" in the temple court 🟡.
- **Ezekiel 1 was a shot at Babylon's gods.** Heiser's carry-over from ch. 4: the throne vision told exiles that Yahweh, not Marduk, ran the sky and the calendar, even in Babylon. The floor under the throne here says the same thing right before the final judgments. 🟡
- **A new Exodus.** First century Jews already told the coming rescue as a second Exodus (Isaiah 43; 51). John's readers, under Rome, would hear: God is about to do to the beast what he did to Pharaoh. 🔴
- **"All the nations will come and worship" is the Deuteronomy 32 reversal.** At Babel God handed the nations over to lesser gods (Deut 32:8–9) and kept Israel. Psalm 82 says he'll take them back. This song is that happening. 🔴
- **The divine council is all over this.** Living creatures, the heavenly sanctuary, angels in priest clothes. This is the council's courtroom handing down a sentence. 🔴
- **The bowls are temple equipment.** Heiser follows Aune: *phiale* means a libation bowl, the kind used in offerings. In the Old Testament, bowls like these carried ash and fat out of the holy place. 🔴 Heiser's read: pouring them on the earth means the earth is being cleaned out and made holy again, ready for the Messiah to move in. 🟡
- **Linen and golden sashes = priests.** The man in linen in Ezekiel 9–10 marks the faithful and then carries fire out for judgment. Daniel 10:5 has the same clothing. The closest match for this whole scene is Ezekiel 10:2–4: linen-clad angel, cherubim, glory cloud, then judgment. 🔴
- **Heiser floats a link to the 144,000.** If they're a priestly class kept pure (14:4), they're the opposite of the Watchers, who defiled themselves and spread chaos. These priestly angels fit that picture. 🔵

## What the chapter is doing
- A voice from the sanctuary sends the seven angels out: "pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God" (16:1).
- Bowls 1–5 hit the people with the mark of the beast: sores, sea and rivers turned to blood, a scorching sun, darkness on the beast's throne. They curse God and don't repent.
- Bowl 6 dries up the Euphrates for "the kings from the east," and three frog-like demon spirits gather the kings of the world to Har-Magedon (16:12–16).
- Bowl 7 goes into the air. A voice says "It is done." Earthquake, the great city split in three, Babylon remembered, hundred-pound hail (16:17–21).

## Pay attention to this
- **The target is named in the first bowl.** "The people who have the mark of the beast and who worship his image" (16:2). Read every bowl after that with this group in mind. 🔴
- **The bowls are total.** The trumpets hit a third of the sea and rivers (8:8–11). Here "every living thing in the sea died" (16:3). Same pictures, no limit. 🔴
- **You took the mark, now you get one.** The first bowl is a sore on the people who took the beast's mark. 🔴
- **"They deserve it" (16:6).** They poured out blood, so they get blood to drink. The punishment matches the crime. 🔴
- **The altar talks (16:7).** The altar where the martyrs cried "how long?" (6:9–10) now says God's judgments are true and righteous. 🔴
- **They curse the name (16:9, 11, 21).** Three times they blaspheme and twice "they did not repent." The people who took the beast's name now curse God's. 🔴
- **The throne of the beast (16:10).** His kingdom goes dark. "Throne" means his rule, wherever it reaches, not a building. 🔴
- **A sudden aside from Jesus (16:15).** "Behold, I am coming like a thief." Right before the armies gather, the reader gets a warning to stay awake and dressed. 🔴
- **"It is done" (16:17).** Same words as 21:6 at the new creation. The two bookend each other. 🔴
- **Babylon was remembered (16:19).** That points back to 14:8, 10 and forward to chs. 17–18, which narrate her fall in full. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **These are the Exodus plagues again.** Sores = the boils (Exodus 9:8–11). Water to blood = the Nile (Exodus 7:14–21). Darkness = the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–29). Hail = the seventh (Exodus 9). A Jewish reader hears Egypt. 🔴
- **Four elements = everything.** The bowls are poured "on the earth," yet they hit the sea, rivers, sun and air. Heiser follows Aune: the Greek world thought all matter was earth, water, fire and air. Hit all four and you've hit everything. 🔴
- **Heiser's key point: the bowls can't be literal.** Believers live under the same sun and breathe the same air. A literal burning sun or poisoned air would hit them too. The four-element picture says every mark-bearer, everywhere, gets judged and God misses no one. Supernova, virus and climate readings break the context. 🔴
- **The waters are people.** Heiser follows Beale: in Revelation the sea and waters stand for the mass of godless nations (17:1, 15; 13:1), and "blood" always means the suffering of the wicked or of Christ and his people. Bowls 2–3 judge people, not plumbing. 🔴
- **The angel of the waters quotes Psalm 79.** That psalm was written after Babylon sacked Jerusalem: "they have poured out their blood like water... let the avenging of your servants' blood be known" (Ps 79:3, 10). What Babylon did to God's people now comes back on Babylon's people. 🔴
- **Heiser adds Deuteronomy 32:43, which Beale leaves out.** In the Dead Sea Scroll and Greek text it reads: rejoice, heavens; bow down, all gods; he avenges the blood of his children. That one verse is the whole bowl sequence in miniature: the loyal host rejoices, the gods of the nations bow, the blood is avenged. Divine council, plain as day. 🔴
- **"An angel of the waters" (16:5).** Jews in John's day assigned angels over parts of creation. 1 Enoch 66:2 has angels "over the powers of the waters." John just mentions one in passing. 🔴 for the Enoch parallel; 🟡 for reading this angel that way.
- **The kings from the east are Babylon, not China.** For someone in Asia Minor in AD 95, "beyond the Euphrates" meant Mesopotamia: Babylon, the Medes and Persians, and the Parthians Rome feared in his own day. Bowl 6 matches trumpet 6 (9:14). 🔴 for Babylon; 🟡 for the Parthian echo.
- **Frogs were Egypt's second plague (Exodus 8).** John calls these spirits "unclean" outright. Three of them, from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet: evil spirits running the gathering. 🔴
- **Har-Magedon is the mount of assembly.** Heiser (*Unseen Realm*, ch. 41): read it as *har mo'ed*, the mountain of the divine council (Isaiah 14:13), which is Zion. Megiddo is a plain with no mountain. The question the whole book asks: who sits on the throne of Zion? 🔴 that Heiser holds it firmly; 🟡 as a reading, since the spelling is argued.
- **Babylon beat Jerusalem once.** Heiser's grand reversal: after Babel, Egypt was the first face of chaos, then Babylon, and Babylon succeeded where Egypt failed. It took Jerusalem, burned the temple and exiled the people. This time the nations march on Zion and Babylon loses. 🔴
- **A talent was about 75–100 pounds.** Hailstones that size are past anything a farmer had seen. The scale tells you this is the last plague. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- One of the bowl angels takes John into a wilderness to show him "the great harlot who sits on many waters" (17:1–3).
- She rides a scarlet beast covered in blasphemous names, with seven heads and ten horns. She's dressed in purple and gold, holding a cup of abominations, drunk on the blood of the saints. Her forehead says "BABYLON THE GREAT" (17:3–6).
- The angel explains: seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings; ten horns are ten kings who rule "for one hour" with the beast and make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb wins (17:7–14).

## Pay attention to this
- **The text names her.** "BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS" (17:5). John isn't hiding who she is. 🔴
- **Wilderness and many waters at the same time (17:1, 3).** Looks like a contradiction. It's two pictures from one Old Testament chapter (see below). 🔴
- **The angel decodes the waters for you (17:15).** "Peoples and crowds and nations and tongues." That's Babel's list. 🔴
- **"Here is the mind which has wisdom" (17:9).** Same phrase as 13:18. John is telling you to do the math on this one. 🔴
- **Seven heads = seven mountains = seven kings (17:9–10).** Two meanings for one picture, right in the text. 🔴
- **"Was, and is not, and is about to come" (17:8).** A twisted copy of God's name in 1:4, "who is and who was and who is to come." The beast imitates God. 🔴
- **"One hour" (17:12).** The ten kings get a short lease. "One hour" comes back three times for Babylon's fall (18:10, 17, 19). 🔴
- **The Lamb wins in one sentence (17:14).** "Lord of lords and King of kings." And the people with him are "called and elect and faithful." 🔴
- **Evil eats evil (17:16).** The beast turns on the woman riding it. And God put it in their hearts to do it (17:17). Even the rebellion runs on his schedule. 🔴
- **A city, not a mood (17:18).** "The great city, which has a kingdom over the kings of the earth." 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Prostitution means idolatry.** In the prophets, sexual unfaithfulness is the picture for worshiping other gods. The "blasphemous names" on the beast (17:3) are the names of the gods of the nations. Heiser: this is the Deuteronomy 32 worldview, the nations under rival gods, now coming to judgment. 🔴
- **Babylon was a dead city by AD 95.** No Babylonian empire, just ruins. So "Babylon" was a code name, and Jewish writers after AD 70 used it for Rome (2 Baruch 11; 4 Ezra 3; also 1 Peter 5:13). 🔴 for the usage; Heiser treats the 2 Baruch and 4 Ezra links lightly. 🔵
- **Rome was the city on seven hills.** Romans called it that, and it shows up on Roman coins. Neither Jerusalem nor old Babylon has seven hills. 🔴
- **Heiser: Babylon is Rome, and bigger than Rome.** In John's day Rome was the face of it. Behind Rome is the whole Deuteronomy 32 rebellion: the fallen sons of God who were given the nations, and the nations they enslave. The judgment on her is the Psalm 82 judgment on the gods. 🔴
- **The powers are already stripped.** Heiser ties this to Colossians 2:15: the cross and resurrection disarmed the principalities and powers. Chapters 17–18 narrate the end of an authority that's already broken. 🔴
- **John stitched two lines from Isaiah 21.** Isaiah 21:1 is "the wilderness of the sea"; Isaiah 21:9 is "Fallen, fallen is Babylon." Same chapter. Using both tells a Jewish reader this is Babylon. (Heiser via Beale and McDonough.) 🔴
- **"Sits on many waters" is a quote.** Jeremiah 51:13 says it of old Babylon, on the Euphrates and its canals. 🔴
- **Desert and sea are both anti-Eden.** Heiser's "recipe for chaos": the desert is where you die of thirst, the sea is where you drown. Eden is the opposite of both. The odd pictures in this chapter all point at one thing: the system set against God. 🔴
- **Daniel 7 is the source.** Heads and horns come from Daniel's four beasts (Dan 7:4–8). Horns are kings (Dan 7:24). The fourth beast that persecutes the saints is Rome. 🔴
- **"One hour" echoes Daniel 4.** Heiser points to Daniel 4:17 in the Greek, where God makes Nebuchadnezzar like a beast for a fixed time. The kings get their hour because God allows it. 🔴
- **Divine council.** The blasphemous names are rival gods, the beast comes up out of the abyss (17:8), and the judgment is on the gods of the nations. This chapter is Psalm 82 told as a vision. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- A bright angel shouts "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!" She's now a home for demons and unclean spirits (18:1–3).
- A voice from heaven calls God's people out of her before the plagues hit, and tells heaven to pay her back double (18:4–8).
- Three groups mourn from a distance: the kings who slept with her, the merchants who got rich off her, and the sailors who shipped her goods. Each says "in one hour" it's over (18:9–19).
- Heaven is told to rejoice. An angel throws a millstone into the sea: Babylon goes down like that and is never found again (18:20–24).

## Pay attention to this
- **"Come out of her, my people" (18:4).** The call isn't "fight her." It's "leave." Don't share her sins and you won't share her plagues. 🔴
- **The queen's boast (18:7).** "I sit as a queen and I am not a widow, and will never see mourning." Then mourning comes "in one day" (18:8). 🔴
- **Read the cargo list slowly (18:12–13).** Gold, silver, pearls, silk, ivory, cinnamon, wheat, horses, carriages, and at the very end "human beings and human lives." People are the last item on a shopping list. 🔴
- **Everyone stands "at a distance" (18:10, 15, 17).** The kings, merchants and sailors loved her and won't come near her when she burns. 🔴
- **They mourn the money, not the woman.** "No one buys their cargo anymore" (18:11). "Such great wealth has been laid waste" (18:17). 🔴
- **"In one hour," three times (18:10, 17, 19).** An empire that took centuries to build is gone in an hour. 🔴
- **Heaven gets a different instruction (18:20).** The earth mourns; heaven rejoices, "because God has pronounced judgment for you against her." 🔴
- **The silence list (18:22–23).** No music, no craftsmen, no millstone, no lamp, no bride and groom. Ordinary life switched off. 🔴
- **The last line names the charge (18:24).** "In her was found the blood of prophets and of saints and of all who have been slain on the earth." 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **This is a funeral song for a city, and it's borrowed.** "Fallen, fallen is Babylon" is Isaiah 21:9 (used already at 14:8). The queen's boast is Isaiah 47:7–8, said to old Babylon. "Come out of her, my people" is Jeremiah 51:45. The millstone thrown into the water is Jeremiah 51:63–64, where a scroll against Babylon is tied to a stone and sunk in the Euphrates. The merchants' and sailors' lament copies Ezekiel 27, the dirge over Tyre. 🔴
- **Rome ran on imports.** The cargo list in 18:12–13 reads like the luxury trade that flowed into Rome from the whole empire. Rome also had a huge slave market. For a reader in Asia Minor, whose cities lived off that trade, this was close to home. 🔴
- **The Psalm 82 backstory.** Heiser lays it out: after Babel, God gave the nations to the sons of God (Deut 4:19–20; 32:8–9) and took Israel for himself, then called Abraham to start a new family that would bring the nations back. Psalm 82 says those gods were judged because they ruled unjustly: they didn't defend the weak, the fatherless, the poor. 🔴
- **Babylon is how that injustice works on the ground.** Heiser: the gods seduce God's people into idolatry and enslave the nations through fear, power and abuse. Revelation 18 shows it as an economy. Merchants get rich, people get sold. 🔴
- **"Buy or sell" (13:17) is the same machine.** Heiser's political-economy read: when a system owns what you eat, own and buy, it has you and won't let you walk away. Behind the human power brokers is "a more sinister intelligence" that wants to be worshiped. God is against coercive power, whether people or gods use it. 🔴
- **Divine council and demons.** The fallen city becomes "a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit" (18:2). Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14 say the same about ruined Babylon and Edom: wild creatures and spirit beings haunt the rubble. The gods behind the city end up living in its ruins. 🔴 for the Isaiah parallel; 🟡 for linking it to the gods of Ps 82.
- **"Sorcery" (18:23).** The nations were "deceived by your sorcery." Nahum 3:4 says the same of Nineveh, "the mistress of sorceries" who sold nations. Same harlot-empire picture as ch. 17. 🔴
- **Tyre and wealth as seduction.** Heiser points to Ezekiel 28, the Eden chapter, which also lists Tyre's stones and wealth. Trade as a way to get nations under your thumb feeds this chapter. 🟡
- **Why it all has to fall.** Heiser's endgame: the earth is being wiped clean of chaos so it can be holy ground again. When the King returns he moves into a global Eden with his family and his rebuilt council, and that includes us. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Heaven answers Babylon's fall with four "Hallelujahs": God has judged the harlot and avenged his slaves (19:1–5).
- The marriage of the Lamb has come, the bride is dressed in fine linen, and "blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb" (19:6–10).
- Heaven opens. A rider on a white horse called Faithful and True, the Word of God, comes with the armies of heaven, a sword from his mouth, and "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS" on his thigh (19:11–16).
- An angel calls the birds to "the great supper of God." The beast and the kings gather, the beast and false prophet are thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest fall by the sword (19:17–21).

## Pay attention to this
- **Two suppers.** "The marriage supper of the Lamb" (19:9) is a celebration for the invited. "The great supper of God" (19:17) is birds eating the enemy dead. Same day, two sides of it. Don't merge them. 🔴
- **The bride's dress is given to her (19:8).** "It was given to her to clothe herself." The linen is "the righteous acts of the saints," and she didn't weave it alone. 🔴
- **John tries to worship the angel (19:10).** "Do not do that! I am a fellow slave... Worship God!" He'll do it again in 22:8–9. Even John gets it wrong. 🔴
- **The rider has three names.** Faithful and True (19:11), a name no one knows (19:12), the Word of God (19:13), plus King of kings on his thigh (19:16). 🔴
- **The blood is on his robe before the battle (19:13).** He comes already "clothed with a garment dipped in blood." 🔴
- **No battle is described.** The armies gather (19:19), and the next verse is the beast captured. The sword is from his mouth. He wins by speaking. 🔴
- **The armies wear the bride's clothes (19:14).** Fine linen, white and clean. Same as 19:8. That's a hint about who's riding with him. 🔴
- **"Rule them with a rod of iron" (19:15).** Psalm 2:9. Jesus already promised the same thing to the overcomer in 2:26–27. 🔴
- **The beast and false prophet go "alive" into the lake of fire (19:20).** The dragon joins them in 20:10. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Meals with God run through the whole Bible.** Heiser's tour: the tree of life in Eden; Abraham feeding Yahweh in human form (Genesis 18); the elders on Sinai who "beheld God, and ate and drank" (Exodus 24:9–11); Jesus eating with sinners and disciples; the Lord's Supper, which in 1 Corinthians 11 was a real meal. The marriage supper is the end of that line. 🔴 Manna as "the food of angels" (Ps 78:25) may belong on the list. 🔵
- **The feast on the mountain is Isaiah 25.** Heiser via Brant Pitre and Dennis Smith: Isaiah 24–27 is the Old Testament's fullest end-time banquet. Yahweh of hosts prepares "a lavish banquet for all peoples on this mountain," and "He will swallow up death for all time" (Isa 25:6–8). It happens on Zion, with "His glory... before His elders," the divine council (Isa 24:23). 🔴
- **The host of heaven and the kings of the earth get judged together.** Right before the feast, Isaiah 24:21 says Yahweh will punish "the host of heights on high, and the kings of the earth on earth." Heaven and earth at once. That's the Psalm 82 judgment of the gods next to the defeat of the kings here. 🔴
- **Leviathan on the menu.** Second Temple Jews said the righteous would eat Leviathan and Behemoth at the end (2 Baruch 29). The root is Psalm 74:13–14: God "crushed the heads of Leviathan" at the Red Sea and gave him "as food for the creatures of the desert." Chaos gets eaten. That's what the birds are doing in 19:17–21. 🔴 Heiser wonders if it started with Egyptian bodies washing up on the shore. 🔵
- **Why a wedding.** Marriage is the prophets' picture of God and Israel (Hosea 2; Isaiah 54:5). Isaiah 54:5–55:5 puts a divine marriage, a free feast, the vindication of God's people and the nations coming to Zion all in one stretch. Jesus' wedding-feast parables come out of that (Matthew 22:1–10). 🔴
- **Ethnicity doesn't get you a seat.** Matthew 8:11–12: many come from east and west to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob while "the sons of the kingdom" are thrown out. The table is set for whoever comes to Israel's Messiah. 🔴
- **The Divine Warrior from Isaiah 63.** Edom's winepress, the robe stained red, Yahweh treading alone. Revelation 14 introduced it; here it's cashed out. The sword from the mouth is Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2. 🔴
- **The birds come from Ezekiel 39.** Ezekiel 39:4, 17–20 is the only Old Testament passage where birds are called to eat the dead at God's mountain after Gog's defeat. John lifts it straight into 19:17–18. 🔴
- **The divine council rides.** "The armies which are in heaven" are the holy ones of Zechariah 14:5, "Yahweh, my God, will come, and all the holy ones with Him!" Heiser: they include glorified believers. The rod of iron is promised to overcomers (2:26–27), and they share his throne (3:21). We're the council riding back to judge. 🔴
- **Har-Magedon is the mount of assembly.** Kline and Heiser: *har mo'ed*, the council mountain of Isaiah 14:13, which is Zion. Psalm 48:1–2 calls Zion "the far north," Baal's mountain title, even though Jerusalem is in the south. That's cosmic geography, taken from the enemy and given to Zion. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Jesus sends four letters, to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum and Thyatira. Each one opens with a piece of the ch 1 vision and closes with "he who has an ear" and a promise to the one who overcomes.
- Ephesus works hard, tests false apostles and hates the Nicolaitans, but has left its first love. Repent or lose the lampstand.
- Smyrna is poor, slandered and about to suffer. No rebuke at all. Be faithful until death.
- Pergamum lives where Satan's throne is and held fast when Antipas was killed, but some hold the teaching of Balaam.
- Thyatira is growing in love and service, but tolerates "Jezebel" and her teaching. The overcomer gets authority over the nations and the morning star.

## Pay attention to this
- **Who is speaking.** The letter comes from Jesus, the one holding the stars (2:1), and closes with "what the Spirit says to the churches" (2:7). Heiser's answer to "which one is it?": yes. This is where Trinitarian thinking comes from. 🔴
- **"To the angel of the church."** *Angelos* shows up 77 times in Revelation. 69 are plainly heavenly beings. The only debated 8 are these church angels. Heiser, with Aune: they're heavenly beings too, not pastors. "Write to" can mean "write concerning." The singular "you" speaks to the whole church, the way Greek often does for a group. 🔴 for the count; 🟡 for the reading.
- **"You have left your first love" (2:4).** Verses 2–3 praise them for toil, endurance and suffering for his name, so it isn't cold hearts toward Jesus. Beale reads it through Matthew 24:12–14: love grows cold under persecution while the gospel is supposed to go to every nation. Ephesus stopped loving the lost. "Do the deeds you did at first" (2:5) fits. 🔴 that vv. 2–3 rule out the soft reading; 🟡 for the missionary reading.
- **"I will remove your lampstand" (2:5).** The lampstand and the angel go together. Heiser: the threat is that the Lord pulls the church's guardian and its witness. Like Judges 2, where the Angel of the LORD tells Israel he won't drive out their enemies anymore. 🟡
- **The Nicolaitans aren't a sect.** Church fathers tied them to Nicolaus the deacon (Acts 6:5). Aune calls that legend. *Nikolaos* means about "conquers the people." The rabbis read Balaam's name the same way, "swallows the people" or "lord over the people." The name is a label: these are Balaam people. 🔴 that no such sect is known from John's day; 🟡 for the wordplay.
- **Balaam (2:14).** He couldn't curse Israel, so he taught Balak to get Israel into idol feasts and sex with Moabite women at Peor (Num 25; 31:16). By the NT he's the standard false teacher (2 Pet 2:15; Jude 11). 🔴
- **"Things sacrificed to idols" (2:14, 20).** Every NT use of *eidolothuton* means meat eaten at the idol's table, in the temple (Witherington, via Beale). Paul lets believers eat meat from the market (1 Cor 10:25) and forbids the idol's table (1 Cor 10:21). John and Paul agree. 🔴
- **"Synagogue of Satan" (2:9).** John is a Jew. The target is specific people slandering believers and handing them to Rome, not Jews as a people. The cure he gives is endurance, not revenge. 🔴
- **Hidden manna, white stone, new name (2:17).** Manna is "bread of angels" (Ps 78:25). The stone is a *psephos*, a voting pebble, and white was the vote to acquit. Heiser and Beale: the new name is God's name, because 3:12 answers it: "I will write on him the name of My God... and My new name." 🔴 for the vote background and 3:12; 🟡 that the name is God's, not the believer's own.
- **Rod of iron and the morning star (2:26–28).** Psalm 2 is about the Messiah. Here Jesus shares it: "as I also have received authority from My Father." 🔴
- **The second death (2:11).** Named here, defined in 20:14. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The Deuteronomy 32 worldview.** At Babel God handed the nations to lesser gods, "according to the number of the sons of God" (Deut 32:8, Dead Sea Scroll and Greek reading), and kept Israel for himself. Those gods went bad (Ps 82). In Daniel, nations have heavenly princes (Dan 10:13, 20). Heiser: angels over churches are a NT version of the same idea. Israel had one guardian; the scattered church has one over each congregation. 🔴 for Deut 32 and Ps 82; 🟡 for the church-angel application.
- **Who rules the nations now, and who rules them later.** The nations sit under fallen powers, the ones Paul calls demons (1 Cor 10:20). At the end those powers are judged ("like men you shall die," Ps 82:7) and believers inherit their rule. That's why 2:26 promises "authority over the nations" and why Paul says "we will judge angels" (1 Cor 6:3). 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for how Heiser connects them.
- **Ephesus.** Home of the great temple of Artemis. The riot in Acts 19 shows what open Christianity cost there. Before beating Ephesus up for its first love, see what holding on already cost them. 🔴
- **Smyrna.** Won the right to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius in AD 26 (Tacitus, *Annals* 4.55–56). Loyalty to Rome was civic pride, and Christians who wouldn't join in looked like traitors. 🔴 "Ten days" (2:10) reads as a short, set time. 🟡
- **Pergamum and "Satan's throne."** The Greek has "the throne," one the readers would know. Aune lists eight candidates: the temple of Augustus, the Great Altar of Zeus Soter, the proconsul's judgment seat, the temple of Asclepius with its serpent, and more. Heiser's favorite is the altar of Zeus, carved with the war of gods and giants, and Zeus was "Most High." His bottom line: "who knows." 🔵 What is clear: the dragon's throne is later handed to the beast (13:2), the empire. 🔴
- **Thyatira had more trade guilds than any other city in Asia.** Wool, linen, bronze, dyers, potters. Guild meetings were held in temples with a meal of meat offered to the gods. Skip it and you could lose your living. That's why Jezebel's teaching sold: work, feed your family, don't look strange to your neighbors. 🔴 for the guilds; 🟡 for the link to Jezebel.
- **Christianity was not legal.** It stayed outside the law for over two hundred years after Revelation. These churches are small, suspected and watched. 🔴
