## What the chapter is doing
- An angel with the key of the abyss chains the dragon, "the serpent of old, who is the devil and Satan," and seals him in the abyss for a thousand years "so that he would not deceive the nations any longer" (20:1–3).
- John sees thrones, judges seated on them, and the souls of the martyrs who refused the mark. They come to life and reign with Christ a thousand years. "This is the first resurrection" (20:4–6).
- Satan is let out, gathers Gog and Magog from the four corners of the earth, and surrounds "the camp of the saints and the beloved city." Fire falls, and the devil goes into the lake of fire with the beast and false prophet (20:7–10).
- A great white throne. Books are opened, the dead are judged by their deeds, death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, "the second death," along with anyone not written in the book of life (20:11–15).

## Pay attention to this
- **All four of his names (20:2).** Dragon, serpent of old, devil, Satan. John ties Genesis 3's serpent to the dragon of ch. 12 in one line. 🔴
- **Bound for one stated reason (20:3).** "So that he would not deceive the nations any longer." Not "so he can't do anything." Watch what he does when he's let out. 🔴
- **"They sat on them" (20:4).** Thrones, plural, and John never says who "they" are. 🔴
- **The martyrs are the ones who said no to the mark (20:4).** That ties the reign straight back to ch. 13. 🔴
- **"First resurrection" is in the text. "Second resurrection" isn't.** John names a first resurrection and a second death. Read 20:5–6 and 20:14 again and look for a second resurrection. It isn't there. 🔴
- **Gog and Magog by name (20:8).** Ezekiel 38–39 shows up openly here, after being used without names in chs. 16 and 19. 🔴
- **"The beloved city" (20:9).** The target is Zion, same as Har-Magedon in 16:16. 🔴
- **The sea gives up its dead (20:13).** The chaos sea has to hand people back. In 21:1 it's gone. 🔴
- **Death and Hades are thrown in (20:14).** The places of the dead get destroyed themselves. 🔴
- **Judged "according to their deeds" (20:12–13), and saved by the book of life (20:15).** Both are in the text, side by side. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **"Thousand" is a number Jews used for God's time, not a stopwatch.** "A thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday" (Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8). Heiser via Aune: both the church age and the kingdom to come are far longer than a literal thousand years anyway. 🔴
- **The abyss is where rebel spirits get locked up.** 1 Enoch has the Watchers bound and shut in the dark until judgment (1 Enoch 10). Revelation 9 already opened the abyss. Here the dragon himself goes in. 🔴 for the Enoch parallel.
- **Thrones in the council room.** The only other places Revelation has plural thrones are the twenty-four elders (4:4; 11:16). Daniel 7:9–10 has "thrones were set up" and "the court sat," and in Daniel 7 the kingdom goes to the Son of Man and "the saints of the Highest One" together (7:13–14, 18). Heiser follows Aune: the unnamed "they sat" points straight back to Daniel's court. 🔴 for the Daniel link; 🟡 for reading the missing subject as a deliberate clue.
- **Heiser on who sits: the divine council, believers included.** Beale lists five options and lands on exalted believers with angels; Heiser agrees. Jesus promised the overcomer a seat on his throne (3:21). If you die before he returns, you join the council now (Zechariah 14:5; Hebrews 12). What you wait for is ruling in a body on a renewed earth. 🔴
- **Two outcomes from one resurrection was a known Jewish idea.** Daniel 12:2: some to everlasting life, some to disgrace. Heiser via Aune cites 2 Baruch 50, 4 Ezra 7:32 and 1 Enoch 51:1–2, and John 5:28–29, one resurrection with two sides. The later rabbis don't use the first/second scheme, and Heiser's point is that they wrote after John and don't get to decide what he meant. 🔴
- **Gehenna was a real valley.** *Ge hinnom*, the Valley of Hinnom on Jerusalem's south side, where children were burned to Molech, until Josiah desecrated it (2 Kings 23:10). By Jesus' day it was the name for the place of fiery judgment. 🔴
- **Hell has Old Testament roots.** Heiser (via Justin Bass): anyone who says the Hebrew Bible has no fiery judgment hasn't read Isaiah 33:14 ("Who among us can sojourn with continual burning?") or Isaiah 66:24 ("their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched"), which is the line Jesus uses for gehenna. Deuteronomy 32:22 may be another root. 🔴 for Isaiah; 🔵 for Deut 32:22.
- **The lake of fire may come from Daniel 7.** "A river of fire was flowing" from before God's throne where the beast is judged (Dan 7:10–11). Bass suggests that's the source. 🔵 Gehenna and the lake of fire are treated as the same place (Matthew 25:41, "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels"). 🔴
- **Death and Hades as powers.** Heiser via Bass: they're personified, like rulers of the dead. Jesus holds their keys (1:18), so he says who stays. Throwing them into the fire ends the realm of the dead itself, because "there will no longer be any death" (21:4). 🔴

- **The binding of Satan.** This is Heiser's best move in the series, and I flagged it as a flagship jayms.com post: "How is Satan 'bound' when he's obviously running loose?" 🔴
  - If the thousand years is the church age, Satan is bound now. But the New Testament has him busy now: he enters Judas (Luke 22:3), fills Ananias' heart (Acts 5:3), hinders Paul (1 Thess 2:18), prowls like a lion (1 Pet 5:8), and more.

## What the chapter is doing
- A new heaven and a new earth, "and there is no longer any sea." The holy city, new Jerusalem, comes down out of heaven like a bride (21:1–2).
- A voice from the throne: God's tabernacle is with people, he'll wipe away every tear, no more death or mourning or pain. "Behold, I am making all things new... They are done." (21:3–8).
- One of the bowl angels shows John the bride from a great high mountain: a city shining like jasper, twelve gates named for the tribes, twelve foundations named for the apostles, a perfect cube, walls of jasper, foundations of gems, gates of pearl, streets of gold (21:9–21).

## Pay attention to this
- **"No longer any sea" (21:1).** Of everything that could have been listed as gone, John starts with the sea. 🔴
- **Comes down, not goes up (21:2, 10).** The city comes out of heaven to earth. Nobody floats away. 🔴
- **"The tabernacle of God is among men" (21:3).** Tent language, like the wilderness tabernacle. 🔴
- **"They are done" (21:6).** Echoes "It is done" at the last bowl (16:17). Judgment finished there; creation finished here. 🔴

- **Israel and the apostles on one wall (21:12–14).** Twelve tribes on the gates, twelve apostles on the foundations. One city, one people. 🔴
- **A cube (21:16).** Length, width and height equal. Only one room in Israel's temple was a cube. 🔴

- **"I saw no sanctuary in it" (21:22).** Read slowly. John doesn't say there's no temple at all; he says God and the Lamb are it. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026

Heiser calls 21:1 his favorite verse, and the saltwater reading "ridiculous." It means no more enemy, sin or death. 🔴

- **Renewed, not replaced.** Beale and McDonough: Jews in John's time read new creation as renovation, like a resurrection body is still your body (Jubilees 1, 4; 1 Enoch 45; 2 Baruch 32). 🔴
- **The temple was already turning into a city and a person in the prophets.** Heiser's Part 1: 🔴
  - Ezekiel: God's glory leaves the temple in stages (Ezek 9–11), and the restoration is described as Eden come back (Ezek 34:25–31).
  - Jeremiah 3:16–17: the ark "will not be made again," and "they will call Jerusalem 'The Throne of Yahweh.'" The throne moves from a box to a city.
  - Isaiah 28:16's cornerstone lands on Jesus (Matthew 21:42; Acts 4:11). Heiser: "You didn't get a building, you got the Messiah."
  - Zechariah 6:12–13: "a man whose name is Branch... will build the temple of Yahweh... He will be a priest on His throne." A priest-king builds it.
  - Jesus: "Destroy this temple" meant his body (John 2:19–21). Paul and Peter make believers the temple (1 Cor 3:16; 1 Pet 2:5).

John uses that promise for the city and the whole new creation, and opens it to every believer, Jew and Gentile (with Leviticus 26:11–12; Ezekiel 37:26–28). 🔴
- **"Tabernacle" is the John 1:14 verb.** *Skenoo*. "The Word became flesh and tabernacled among us" uses the same word. Heiser: "It's inescapable." 🔴
- **The great high mountain is Eden (21:10).** Zion isn't actually tall. In Ezekiel 28:13–14 Eden is "the garden of God" and "the holy mountain of God." That's the first cosmic mountain, and the council met there. Beale and McDonough: 21:10 combines Ezekiel 43:5 and 40:2, the very high mountain where Ezekiel's temple vision starts. 🔴
- **The gems are Eden's stones, not the high priest's.** Heiser, reading from *Unseen Realm*: every stone in the Greek of Ezekiel 28:13 but one shows up in the city of Revelation 21, and the one that seems missing is a kind of onyx, which matches the sardonyx in 21:20. - **The cube is the holy of holies (1 Kings 6:20).** Heiser reads a commentator (the guide credits Beale and McDonough): the glory "formerly limited to the back room of the temple has burst forth and filled the entire cosmos." The word for sanctuary in 21:22 is *naos*. 🔴
- **The size is meant to be impossible.** 12,000 stadia is around 1,400 miles each way, up as well as across. The wall is 144 cubits, about 72 yards. Josephus and Philo describe the temple as a picture of the whole universe, to say God fills everything. Heiser: "He's not picking his spots anymore; he fills everything." 🔴 for the sizes and the Josephus/Philo device; 🟡 that the tiny wall is a deliberate joke on defense.
- **The nations walking in its light (21:24–26).** Isaiah 60: nations come to your light, kings to your brightness, your gates open continually. Heiser didn't get to it in the recorded episode. 🔴 for the Isaiah 60 source.
- **Divine council.** Twelve angels at the gates (21:12), an angel measuring with a gold rod, "human measurements, which are also angelic" (21:17), and the throne at the center. The council's home and God's family's home are now one place. 🔴

- **"No longer be any curse" (22:3).** The Genesis 3 curse, cancelled in one line. 🔴
- **"They will see His face" (22:4).** In the Old Testament seeing God's face meant death (Exodus 33:20). Here it's the reward. 🔴

- **John does it again (22:8–9).** He bows to the angel a second time (first at 19:10) and gets the same answer: "Worship God!" 🔴
- **"Do not seal up" (22:10).** Daniel was told to seal his book (Daniel 12:4). John is told the opposite, because "the time is near." 🔴

- **The invitation is open (22:17).** "Let the one who is thirsty come. Let the one who wishes receive the water of life without cost." 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The river is Ezekiel 47 and Eden.** Ezekiel saw water flowing from the temple, getting deeper, with fruit trees on both banks whose fruit comes monthly and whose leaves are for healing (Ezek 47:1–12). Genesis 2:10 has a river flowing out of Eden. Zechariah 14:8 has living waters flowing out of Jerusalem. John fuses all three. 🔴
- **"Clear as crystal" closes the sea story.** Heiser's 15–16 guide: the chaos sea becomes a glass floor (4:6; 15:2), then disappears (21:1), and the only water left is a clean river from the throne (22:1). 🔴
- **The healing of the nations is Babel undone.** Heiser's Q&A answer to the question "why medicine in the new earth?": it's a metaphor, there's nothing sick to cure. - **Divine council: the Lamb finally sits.** Heiser's Rev 5 point: chapter 5 is the Lamb receiving authority, not taking his seat, and he never sits through the whole book until 22:1. - **His servants reign (22:5).** The shared rule promised in 2:26–27, 3:21 and 20:4–6 goes on "forever and ever." The council God lost at the fall is rebuilt with his people in it. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the council framing.
- **No sun and no night (22:5).** Isaiah 60:19: "No longer will you have the sun for light by day... But you will have Yahweh for an everlasting light." Heiser used this against his own speculation about the feasts lining up on a calendar: no sun means no calendar. 🔴
- **The bright morning star (22:16).** Numbers 24:17, Balaam's oracle: "a star shall come forth from Jacob." Jews read it as a Messiah text. Jesus also promised "the morning star" to the overcomer in Thyatira (2:28). 🔴
- **Root and descendant of David (22:16).** Isaiah 11:1, 10: a shoot from Jesse's stump, the root of Jesse that the nations seek. Jesus is both where David came from and where David's line goes. 🔴
- **"Dogs" outside (22:15).** A common Jewish insult for outsiders (Tyndale study notes point to Matthew 7:6 and Philippians 3:2). 🔴
- **Don't add, don't take away (22:18–19).** Moses said the same about the law (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). Covenant documents ended with warnings like this. 🔴
- **Alpha and Omega (22:13).** God says it at 1:8, and "the first and the last" is Jesus' title at 1:17. Heiser's ch. 1 guide calls it the bookend: the same words at the front and back of the book, now in Jesus' mouth. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Death has a name.** The Hebrew *mavet*, "death," is the same word as Mot, the Canaanite god of death who swallowed Baal. The Old Testament talks about Death and Sheol like persons: Sheol opens its mouth (Isa 5:14), "O Death, where are your thorns?" (Hos 13:14). In the Greek world, Hades was both a god and a place. So "keys of death and Hades" can mean keys to the places or keys taken from the jailers. Heiser favors the jailers and keeps both on the table. 🔴 for the background; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Nobody came back.** Bass: the Old Testament never records a living human going down to the underworld and coming back. Enoch and Elijah skipped Sheol. Everyone else went down. Jesus is the first to go down and come back up. 🔴
- **Hecate held the keys.** In the Greek magical papyri, Hecate is keyholder of Hades and gets hymned as "beginning and end." In Revelation those titles belong only to God and Christ. 🔴 for the papyri; 🟡 that John is answering Hecate.
- **An angel who refuses worship.** The Apocalypse of Zephaniah has a great angel with a face like the sun, a golden belt and bronze feet, set over the abyss and Hades. When the seer bows, the angel says not to worship him. Jesus in Rev 1 doesn't stop John. 🔴 for the parallel; 🟡 for the date relationship.
- **"He descended into hell."** The early church agreed Christ went to the realm of the dead and won there. Heiser and Bass trace that agreement up to the late 1400s. 1 Peter 3:19 has him announcing doom to the imprisoned spirits. 🔴 for the early belief; 🟡 for the date the belief faded.
- **Divine council: the book of life.** Behind it sit the Mesopotamian Tablets of Destiny, where the gods fixed and recorded fates. In the Bible the books come out at the judgment: "the court sat, and the books were opened" (Dan 7:10). 3:5 sets that inside the council: "I will confess his name before My Father and before His angels." 🔴
- **Sardis was taken by surprise twice.** Cyrus' men got up the cliffs to its citadel in the 540s BC, and Antiochus III did it again about 214 BC, both times because nobody was watching. "If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief" (3:3) lands on a city that knew that story. 🔴 for the history; 🟡 that John means the history.
- **Laodicea was rich and proud of it.** After the earthquake of AD 60 it rebuilt without help from Rome (Tacitus, *Annals* 14.27). It was known for banking, glossy black wool, and an eye salve from its medical school. So: "I am rich," "buy from Me gold," "white garments," "eye salve." 🔴 for the city; 🟡 for each link.
- **Lukewarm water.** Hierapolis, six miles off, had hot springs. Colossae had cold water. Laodicea piped its water in and it came lukewarm and full of minerals. Hot heals, cold refreshes, lukewarm makes you spit. So the problem is being useless, not being unspiritual. 🟡 Heiser doesn't work Laodicea in this series, so this one comes from the background commentaries, not from him.
- **Eating together (3:20).** In that world a shared meal meant acceptance and covenant, not a snack. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- A door opens in heaven and the same trumpet-like voice from 1:10 calls John up (4:1).
- He sees a throne and One sitting on it, shining like jasper and sardius, with an emerald-like rainbow around it (4:2–3).
- Around the throne: twenty-four elders on thrones in white with gold crowns, seven lamps of fire, a sea of glass, and four living creatures full of eyes (4:4–8).
- The creatures never stop saying "Holy, holy, holy." The elders fall down, throw their crowns before the throne, and praise God as Creator (4:8–11).
- This is the room chs 2–3 were pointing at. Ch 5 happens in it.

## Pay attention to this
- **It's a courtroom.** Heiser: there's solid agreement that chs 4–5 are a divine council scene built on the Old Testament covenant lawsuit, the *riv*. God brings a case against his people for breaking covenant, with Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 as the charges. Micah 6:1–8 is the classic form: "Arise, plead your case before the mountains." 🔴
- **It follows Daniel 7 step by step.** Beale and McDonough count 14 parallels between Rev 4–5 and Daniel 7:9–28 in the same order: thrones set, God seated, his appearance, fire before the throne, servants around him, a kingdom for all peoples. 🔴
- **A voice like a trumpet (4:1).** The verse says a voice like the sound of a trumpet. It's the same voice as 1:10, the risen Christ, and nobody reads a rapture into 1:10. Heiser: no link to rapture texts. 🔴
- **"The church disappears after 4:1."** The word *ekklesia* doesn't show up again until 22:16, but "saints" (*hagioi*), the NT's normal word for believers, shows up 13 times from ch 5 on. 🔴
- **The stones (4:3).** Jasper, sardius and emerald are dwelling-of-God stones: the tabernacle, Eden (Gen 2:12), and the new Jerusalem (21:11, 19–20). Heiser uses the same point on Ezekiel 28: those stones match God's dwelling, not the high priest's breastplate. 🔴
- **The rainbow (4:3).** Ezekiel 1:28 has a bow-like brightness around God's throne. Genesis 9 adds the covenant bow after the flood. Heiser: judgment is coming, and the bow says God will keep a remnant by covenant. 🟡
- **Lightning and thunder (4:5).** Sinai (Exod 19:16). The same storm list comes back at 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18, louder each time. 🔴
- **Seven lamps are the seven Spirits (4:5).** Ties back to the seven Spirits of 1:4 and the eyes of Zechariah 4. 🔴
- **Four living creatures (4:6–8).** Faces like Ezekiel's cherubim (Ezek 1:10). Six wings like Isaiah's seraphim (Isa 6:2). The song is Isaiah's "Holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6:3). In Ezekiel it's the wheels that are full of eyes; John moves the eyes onto the creatures. 🔴
- **"Who was and who is and who is to come" (4:8).** The Exodus 3:14 name from 1:4 again. 🔴
- **They throw their crowns (4:10).** The elders wear crowns and lay them down. Whatever authority they have is on loan. 🔴 for the act; 🟡 for the reading.

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The lawsuit runs in Deuteronomy 32 order.** First God judges his own people, then the nations who hurt them (Deut 32:43). Bandy: the seven letters were already lawsuit speeches, Jesus examining his churches. Now the case turns toward the nations. 🔴
- **Council members take part.** In 1 Kings 22:19–23 God asks the host how Ahab should fall, and a spirit volunteers. Mullen's study of the council: Yahweh is prosecutor and judge, and the host sits with him. Daniel 7:9 has thrones, plural. 🔴
- **The trumpet was God's voice.** At Sinai the trumpet came with God speaking (Exod 19:16, 19). Greek writers compared Athena's voice to a trumpet and called thunder "the trumpet of Zeus" (Aune). The voice to listen to here is Israel's God speaking through the risen Christ. 🔴 for the sources; 🟡 for the polemic.
- **Eyes and stars.** Daniel Block: the Hebrew word for "eye" in Ezekiel 1:18, *ayin*, is the same word translated "gleam" earlier in the chapter, the way ancients described stars. He also links the four faces to four points of the Babylonian zodiac. Ezekiel saw this in Babylon, so the message to the exiles was that Yahweh runs time and history, not Marduk. John says the same to churches under Rome. 🔴 for Block; 🟡 for the read-through to John.
- **Seraphim may be serpents.** *Saraph* means "burn" and also names a serpent (Num 21:6). Egyptian thrones were guarded by cobras. Heiser: burning and serpentine both. 🟡
- **The 24 elders: Heiser says "all three."** Isaiah 24:23 has God reigning "before His elders," which Willis reads as heavenly officials. Exodus 24:9–11 has seventy human elders seeing God. Beale leans human. Heiser keeps three things in play: council members, glorified believers, and star imagery. 🔴 that both OT lines exist; 🟡 for "all three."
- **Why humans can belong in the council.** Second Temple readers took "your seed will be like the stars" (Gen 15:5) as a promise about what believers would become, as well as how many. Daniel 12:3 says the wise "shine like the stars." Hebrews 12:22–23 puts believers with "myriads of angels." Qumran saw itself serving with angels. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the synthesis.
- **24 courses.** David set the priests in 24 divisions (1 Chr 24). 🔴 One possible source for the number. 🔵
- **The star reading.** Malina connects the 24 to star groups. Diodorus Siculus (2.31.4) says the Babylonians placed 24 stars outside the zodiac and called them "judges of the universe." Heiser: Malina never ties it to the Old Testament, which is a weakness, but the data is real. 🔵
- **Divine council:** this is the council chapter of the book. The throne, the host, the elders on thrones, the Spirits, the creatures. Everything the letters promised the overcomers is on display here.

## What the chapter is doing
- God holds a scroll written on both sides and sealed seven times. An angel asks who is worthy to open it, and nobody in heaven, on earth or under the earth can (5:1–3).
- John weeps. An elder tells him to stop: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome (5:4–5).
- John turns and sees a Lamb standing, as if slain, with seven horns and seven eyes. He takes the scroll (5:6–7).
- The creatures and elders sing a new song: you were slain and bought people from every tribe and nation and made them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth (5:8–10).
- Myriads of angels, then every creature everywhere, join in praise to the One on the throne and to the Lamb (5:11–14).

## Pay attention to this
- **John hears "Lion" and sees a Lamb (5:5–6).** Heard one thing, saw another. Same person. The conqueror won by being slain. 🔴
- **"Has overcome" (5:5).** The verb is *nikao*, the same root as "death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Cor 15:54) and "I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). His death is the win. 🔴
- **Standing, as if slain (5:6).** Dead and alive in one picture. Heiser: every model of the atonement adds something, but using the others to get rid of Christ dying in our place is a mistake. The slain Lamb keeps the death in the middle. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for how hard Heiser presses it.
- **Seven horns, seven eyes (5:6).** Horns mean power. The eyes are "the seven Spirits of God, sent out into all the earth," Zechariah 4:10 again. 🔴
- **Lamb is *arnion*, not *amnos*.** Revelation uses *arnion* 29 times, every time for Jesus except 13:11, where the second beast has horns "like a lamb." John 1:29, "the Lamb of God," uses *amnos*. 🔴
- **The scroll, front and back (5:1).** Ezekiel 2:9–10 has a scroll written on front and back, full of "lamentations, mourning and woe." 🔴
- **Sealed seven times.** Picture it. Break one seal and you still can't read it. Six more hold it shut. So the seals breaking in ch 6 aren't the scroll's contents. The book never tells you what's written inside. 🔴
- **The Lamb takes the scroll. He doesn't sit down.** Heiser, with Aune: this is an investiture, a public showing of authority Jesus has held since the resurrection, not a coronation. In Daniel 7 the son of man gets the kingdom and is never shown sitting. 🟡 But see 3:21, where Jesus says he already sat down with his Father. ⬜
- **"Kingdom and priests" (5:10).** Exodus 19:6 again, as in 1:6, now for people "from every tribe and tongue and people and nation." 🔴 And "they will reign upon the earth." On the earth, not in the clouds. 🔴
- **Bowls of incense are the prayers of the saints (5:8).** Psalm 141:2: "May my prayer be counted as incense before You." 🔴 Those prayers come back as fire on the earth in 8:3–5. 🔴
- **"Myriads of myriads" (5:11).** Daniel 7:10: "thousands upon thousands were attending Him, and myriads upon myriads were standing before Him." 🔴
- **Both get the same worship (5:13).** "To Him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb." 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Sealed until the end.** In the Old Testament, books sealed until the last days show up only in Daniel 12:4, 9: "seal up the book until the end of time." Beale and McDonough: Revelation presents itself as that book getting opened. 🔴 for Daniel 12; 🟡 for the claim.
- **Why seal it?** Isaiah 29:11: a vision like a sealed book nobody can read, because the people are blind. Daniel 12: sealed so it stays hidden until the right time. Heiser: maybe both. The wicked get caught off guard and the righteous get told ahead. 🟡 1 Enoch 89:71–77 has a sealed book whose opening means punishment. 🔵
- **Ezekiel's scroll hit everybody.** Ezekiel's woes fall on Judah (chs 4–24) and then the nations (chs 25–32). Heiser: a scroll modeled on Ezekiel's doesn't fit the idea that Revelation is only about Jerusalem in AD 70. 🔴 for Ezekiel; 🟡 for the inference.
- **Heaven, earth, under the earth (5:3).** The three-level world of the ancient Near East. Nobody, anywhere, among the living, the dead or the spirits. 🔴 Aune points to the Testament of Solomon, where Beelzebul rules spirits in all three. If John meant that, the dark powers can't open the scroll either. 🔵
- **A right hand means power.** "Your right hand, O Yahweh, shatters the enemy" (Exod 15:6). What's in God's right hand won't change. 🔴
- **Lambs could be rulers.** In the wider ancient world rams and sheep stood for gods and kings. The Lamb here makes war (17:14) and people dread his anger (6:16). Sacrifice and king at once. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the ANE background.
- **Passover was rescue.** The Passover lamb's blood turned the destroyer away. It wasn't a sin offering. So "Lamb" in Revelation doesn't have to mean Passover only. 🔴 Aramaic *talya* means lamb and also servant or child, which may tie the Lamb to Isaiah 53's servant "like a lamb led to the slaughter." 🔵
- **Divine council: the holy ones and their people.** Daniel 7 gives the kingdom to "the holy ones of the Most High" (7:18) and to "the people of the holy ones" (7:27). Most commentators read both as human believers. Heiser breaks with them: the holy ones are the loyal heavenly council, their people are human believers, and both get the kingdom together. 🟡 That's his reconstituted council: God gets the human family he always wanted, sharing rule on the earth. 🔴 as Heiser's thesis.

## What the chapter is doing
- The Lamb opens six of the seven seals. The seventh waits until 8:1.
- Seals one to four: each living creature says "Come," and a rider goes out. White horse with a bow and a crown, red horse with a great sword, black horse with scales, pale horse ridden by Death with Hades behind (6:1–8).
- Seal five: the souls of those killed for God's word, under the altar, cry "How long?" They get white robes and are told to rest a little longer (6:9–11).
- Seal six: earthquake, black sun, blood moon, stars falling, the sky rolled up like a scroll. Kings and slaves alike hide in caves from the One on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb (6:12–17).
- It ends on a question: "Who is able to stand?" Ch 7 answers it.

## Pay attention to this
- **The Lamb starts it.** Every rider goes out because the Lamb opens a seal and a creature by the throne says "Come." Beale: the chapter shows Christ ruling over a world that looks out of control. Nothing here happens by chance. 🔴
- **Zechariah's horses.** Red, black, white and dappled horses pulling four chariots go out "after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth" (Zech 6:1–8, with Zech 1:8–11 behind it). Almost every scholar sees the link. Heiser won't spend an episode lining up the colors. 🔴 for the link.
- **Chariots mean war.** If you're only scouting, you send a rider. In Zechariah the chariots go out against the nations that crushed God's people. So judgment is already there in John's source. 🟡
- **The pale horse names the four judgments (6:8).** Sword, famine, pestilence, wild beasts. That's Ezekiel 14:21, "My four severe judgments," which in turn sums up the covenant curses of Leviticus 26. Beale: Ezekiel uses the list to punish the faithless majority and purify the faithful few. 🔴
- **Death and Hades are on a leash.** "Authority was given to them," and only over a fourth of the earth. In 1:18 Jesus took their keys. 🔴
- **Together, not in a line.** Beale: the four riders are probably happening at the same time. The fourth sums up the first three, Ezekiel and Zechariah picture them together, and the Gospels list the same troubles in different orders. Heiser adds the seal logic from ch 5: nothing is read until all seven are broken. 🟡
- **"Come" isn't a call to John.** Each creature calls a rider out. 🔴
- **The altar (6:9).** Aune: the temple had two altars, the bronze one outside and the gold incense altar by the curtain. Beale and Heiser lean to the incense altar, closest to God's throne, and it's clearly that altar in 8:3–5. Under it means these dead are kept safe in God's presence even though they lost their lives. 🟡
- **White robes (6:11).** Same as 3:4–5: belonging, not a prize. 🔴
- **"Until the number... would be completed" (6:11).** Justice is scheduled, not forgotten. 🔴
- **The wrath of the Lamb (6:16).** The One on the throne and the Lamb are named side by side, and verse 17 says "their wrath." A lamb with wrath is a deliberate jolt. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Jesus as the Destroyer.** On the first Passover, the LORD would not let "the destroyer" (*mashchit*) into the houses marked with blood (Exod 12:23), and yet the Psalms say Yahweh struck the firstborn himself (Ps 105:36; 135:8; 136:10). The same word names the angel with the drawn sword over Jerusalem (1 Chr 21:15). Heiser reads that figure as the Angel of the LORD, the same commander with drawn sword in Joshua 5:13. In Revelation 6 that role goes to the Lamb. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for Heiser's identification. Tremper Longman traced the Divine Warrior picture of Jesus across the NT ("The Divine Warrior," *Westminster Theological Journal*, 1982). 🔴
- **Falling stars are fallen powers.** The best match for 6:13–14 is Isaiah 34:4, where God is furious with the nations "and all their host," and "all the host of heaven will wear away, and the sky will be rolled up like a scroll." Heiser: the Hebrew form *tseva'am*, "their host," always means heavenly bodies in the Old Testament, never earthly armies. The Greek Old Testament there uses *dunameis*, "powers," Paul's word for spiritual rulers. 🔴 for Isaiah 34; 🟡 for the word study.
- **1 Enoch uses falling stars for the Watchers.** 1 Enoch 86:1–3; 88:1; 90:21. Jude 13 calls false teachers "wandering stars." So a first-century Jewish reader would hear judgment on the dark powers behind the empires, along with the human rulers hiding in the caves. That's the Deuteronomy 32 and Daniel 10 picture. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the reading.
- **Not an asteroid.** The Old Testament uses darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of real kingdoms: Babylon in Isaiah 13:10, Edom in Isaiah 34. Heiser prefers "metaphorical" over "figurative," because a metaphor points at something more real than the picture, not less. 🔴 for the OT usage.
- **A whole quarry of Old Testament.** Beale lists the sources piled into 6:12–17: Isaiah 13, 24 and 34, Ezekiel 32, Joel 2–3, Habakkuk 3. The Gospels mine the same texts (Matt 24:29). Hiding in the rocks comes from Isaiah 2:19, and "fall on us" from Hosea 10:8, which Jesus also quoted (Luke 23:30). LSB marks those words as OT quotes. 🔴
- **"How long?"** The cry of the lament psalms (Ps 13:1; 79:5) and of the Angel of the LORD himself in Zechariah 1:12. "Avenge our blood" echoes Deuteronomy 32:43, God avenging the blood of his servants, and Abel's blood crying from the ground (Gen 4:10). 🔴 for the texts. Heiser doesn't work these in this episode; the links are standard in the commentaries. 🟡
- **A day's pay for a day's bread (6:6).** A denarius was a day's wage (Matt 20:2). A *choinix* was about a quart of grain, roughly one person's daily ration. Wheat at that price is famine pricing, and barley is the poor man's grain. Oil and wine are spared. 🔴 for the prices; 🔵 for links some draw to Domitian's edict on vineyards (Suetonius, *Domitian* 7).
- **The bow (6:2).** Rome's feared enemy to the east was the Parthian mounted archer. Some read the first rider that way. 🔵 Heiser in the Q&A: *toxon* in the Greek Old Testament can cover the bow and the quiver, so no arrows need mentioning. 🔴
- **An astral reading of the altar.** Boll and Malina note a constellation called the Altar sat over the Milky Way, and read the white-robed souls as stars beneath it. Aune calls it forced. Heiser: Aune's own heavenly-temple point cuts against him, and Daniel 12:3 already links the righteous with stars. It can sit as one more layer, never the only one. 🔵
- **Divine council:** the riders go out from the throne room of chs 4–5, and the stars falling are the heavenly powers being judged with their human puppets.

## What the chapter is doing
- A pause between the sixth and seventh seals. Four angels hold back the four winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads (7:1–3).
- John hears the number sealed: 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel, and the tribes are listed (7:4–8).
- Then he looks and sees a multitude nobody could count, from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, in white robes with palm branches, standing before the throne and the Lamb (7:9–12).
- An elder asks who they are and answers himself: these come out of the great tribulation, robes washed white in the Lamb's blood (7:13–14).
- They serve God in his sanctuary. No more hunger, thirst or scorching sun. The Lamb shepherds them to springs of the water of life, and God wipes every tear (7:15–17).
- It answers 6:17's question, "Who is able to stand?"

## Pay attention to this
- **The seal is Ezekiel 9.** In Ezekiel 9:4–6 a man in linen marks the foreheads of those who groan over Jerusalem's abominations, and the executioners are told, "do not touch any man on whom is the mark." Moyise: the sealing is almost certainly modeled on that. 🔴
- **The seal carries a name.** 14:1 says it's the Lamb's name and the Father's name on their foreheads, and 22:4 says "His name will be on their foreheads." The beast's mark goes on forehead or hand in 13:16. Two marks, two owners. 🔴
- **It's a census.** Counting by tribe is what Numbers does (Num 1; 26). Aune: censuses were mostly for war, and 14:4 has the 144,000 keeping the purity of holy warriors. Then Aune backs off, since 7:4–8 has no war language, and leans to the restoration of all twelve tribes (Ezek 37:15–23). Heiser keeps a little of the military flavor as spiritual war. 🔴 for the census form; 🟡 for the military reading.
- **The list is strange.** Bauckham: its order matches no other tribe list. Judah is first, which puts the Lion's tribe at the head. Joseph and Manasseh are both listed and Ephraim isn't. Levi, left out of Moses' military counts, is in. Dan is missing. 🔴
- **Heard, then saw.** John *hears* 144,000 from Israel's tribes, then *sees* a multitude no one could count from every nation. Compare 5:5–6: heard Lion, saw Lamb. 🔴 What that means is the fight (see below).
- **"Out of the great tribulation" (7:14).** They come out of it, not around it. Washed white in blood: purity from the Lamb's death. 🔴
- **Palm branches (7:9).** Palms belong to the Feast of Booths (Lev 23:40) and to victory (1 Macc 13:51; John 12:13). 🔴
- **The last three verses quote Isaiah.** "They will hunger no longer, nor thirst... nor will the sun beat down on them" is Isaiah 49:10, and "wipe every tear from their eyes" is Isaiah 25:8. LSB marks both. A Lamb as shepherd turns Psalm 23 around. 🔴
- **"He who sits on the throne will dwell over them" (7:15).** The verb is "tabernacle" (*skenoo*), the same one in 21:3, "the tabernacle of God is among men." 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Marked to live.** In old Hebrew script the letter *taw*, the mark in Ezekiel 9, looked like an X or a cross. Jewish tradition linked it to *tam*, "blameless," and to *tichyeh*, "you shall live." 🔴 for the letter shape; 🟡 for the traditions.
- **Passover sits behind Ezekiel 9.** Beale: blood on the doorposts kept the destroyer out (Exod 12:23), the mark in Ezekiel 9 kept the faithful alive, and the trumpet and bowl plagues that follow are modeled on the Exodus plagues. Beale then settles on spiritual protection only. Heiser pushes back: Beale's own Passover data leaves room for some real physical protection, and he won't cancel it out. Protection from losing faith is also in view. 🔴 for Beale's parallels; 🟡 for Heiser's "leave it open."
- **Who are the 144,000? Heiser's view.** Ethnic Jews who follow the Lamb, so Jewish Christians. Everything in 7:1–8 is Israelite: the census, the tribes, Ezekiel 9. The multitude of 7:9–17 is a different group from every nation. Aune lists the differences: one is counted, the other can't be; one is from Israel's tribes, the other from every nation; one is on earth facing danger, the other in heaven having come through. Both are on the Lamb's side. They're two ways of describing who makes up the people of God. 🟡 He says the 144,000 of 14:1 are the same group. 🟡
- **The other views.** Beale: the 144,000 is the whole church, Jew and Gentile, and the two visions are the same people. Dispensational readers: Jews who come to faith during a future seven-year tribulation. Heiser calls splitting "Jew" and "Christian" into either/or a confusion; a Jewish follower of Jesus is both. ⬜
- **The twelve tribes still mattered.** Some say nobody knew their tribe by the first century. Aune answers that Josephus, writing at the end of that century, still reckons with twelve tribes, and the hope of regathering them was alive. 🔴
- **Dan's missing.** Bauckham calls it arbitrary: with Joseph's sons counted, one tribe has to drop to keep twelve. Heiser won't dismiss it. Dan left its land, set up idols (Judg 18), got "a serpent in the way" for a blessing (Gen 49:17), and became a center of false worship. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 5.30.2) is the first to say the antichrist comes from Dan, partly because Dan is missing here. Bauckham thinks that idea is Christian, not Jewish. 🔴 for the texts and Irenaeus; 🔵 for any link to John's reason.
- **Heiser's Dan wild card.** Some scholars connect Dan with a Sea People group called the Denyen. If Gentile blood got into the tribe, an end-times enemy "from Dan" could still be a Gentile. Heiser floats it, uses it in his novels, and calls the history probably unanswerable. 🔵
- **Ephraim's missing too.** Ephraim led the northern kingdom that broke off and worshiped the calves. Two names gone, both tied to northern idolatry. 🔵 Bauckham's other guess: Ezekiel 37:16–19 uses "Joseph" for Ephraim's line, so a reader would hear Ephraim in "Joseph." 🔵 In the Q&A Heiser says the order of the tribes means nothing special, since the Old Testament lists them half a dozen ways. 🔴
- **Divine council: the 144,000 and the Watchers.** 14:4 says they "have not been defiled with women." Olson (*Catholic Biblical Quarterly*, 1997) and a second article read that against 1 Enoch's Watchers, heavenly beings who did defile themselves with women and left their place. The 144,000 are the pure priests on the other side of that coin, taking the role the fallen ones abandoned. Heiser makes the same point in *Reversing Hermon* and wants more research done. 🔵 Heiser in the Q&A: pre-battle abstinence is a weak fit, because it was temporary and the Bible thinks well of marriage. 🟡
- **"The great tribulation" has a home.** Daniel 12:1: "a time of distress such as never occurred... and at that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book." Jeremiah 30:7 ("the time of Jacob's distress") and Matthew 24:21 use the same language. 🔴 Nothing in Daniel 9:24–27 says "seven years of tribulation," and the tribulation words never sit next to the "week" words anywhere in Scripture. So the great tribulation may be the 70th week, but there's no verse to hang that on. 🔴
- **Already and not yet.** 1 Maccabees 9:27 says a great tribulation had already come on Israel in the 160s BC. Beale reads it as something believers were already in when John wrote, with a final peak still ahead. If 3:10's "hour of testing" also points to Daniel 12:1, the letters and ch 7 describe the same thing. 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- The Lamb opens the seventh seal, and nothing happens. Heaven goes silent for about half an hour.
- An angel at the golden altar adds incense to "the prayers of all the saints." The smoke goes up before God. Then the same censer is filled with altar fire and thrown down to the earth.
- Seven angels blow trumpets. The first four hit the land, the sea, the fresh water and the sky, a third of each.
- An eagle cries "Woe, woe, woe" over the people of the earth. Three trumpets are still to come, and they are worse.

## Pay attention to this
- **The seventh seal is a silence (8:1).** You wait six seals for the last one and get quiet. The prophets told the earth to hush when God gets up to judge: "let all the earth be silent before Him" (Hab 2:20), "Be silent before Lord Yahweh! For the day of Yahweh is near" (Zeph 1:7), and Zech 2:13. 🔴
- **The scroll is open and you still never read it.** All seven seals are broken now, but John never quotes what the ch. 5 scroll says. The trumpets are released by the opening, not read off the page. 🔴
- **The prayers are the trigger (8:3–5).** The incense rises "with the prayers of the saints," then the angel fills that same censer with fire from that same altar and throws it at the earth. Thunder, lightning, earthquake. Go back to 6:9–10: the souls under the altar cried "How long?" This is the answer starting. 🔴
- **Half an hour is short.** It is a pause, not a number to calculate with. 🔴
- **It's the Exodus again.** Hail and fire (8:7) is the seventh plague (Exod 9:23–25). The sea turning to blood (8:8–9) is the first plague, the Nile (Exod 7:20–21). Darkness over a third of the sky (8:12) is the ninth plague (Exod 10:21–23). The seals ran on covenant curses; the trumpets run on Egypt. Heiser: God is judging a new Egypt. 🔴
- **Count the thirds.** The seals hit "a fourth" (6:8). The trumpets hit "a third." The bowls in ch. 16 will hit everything. Judgment is climbing, and it is held back on purpose so there's still room to turn. 9:20–21 says people didn't. 🔴
- **Wormwood (8:10–11).** A real, bitter plant. In the Old Testament it's the stock picture of bitter judgment and the poison fruit of turning from God (Deut 29:18; Jer 9:15; 23:15; Lam 3:15; Amos 5:7). Heiser sets aside the Chernobyl reading (the Ukrainian word for a related plant sounds similar) as a coincidence, not a fulfillment. 🔴
- **The first four trumpets undo Genesis 1.** Land, sea, fresh water, then sun, moon and stars, which God made on the fourth day (Gen 1:14–19). Heiser calls it de-creation: God taking apart the rebel world order. 🔴 for the order of the targets, 🟡 for the Genesis reading.
- **"Those who dwell on the earth" (8:13).** Revelation's fixed label for the world that won't belong to God (3:10; 6:10; 11:10; 13:8). The woes are aimed at them, not at the sealed. 🔴
- **The star that falls (8:10).** Is it an object or a being? Ch. 8 doesn't say. In ch. 9 the fallen star is clearly a "him" who is handed a key. 🟡

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **Incense is prayer.** The golden incense altar stood right in front of the veil (Exod 30:1–10). Every Jewish reader knew Ps 141:2, "May my prayer be established as incense before You." John's readers already pictured heaven as the real temple, with the earthly one as its copy. 🔴
- **A trumpet meant God showing up, or war.** The *shofar* blew at Sinai when God came down (Exod 19:16–19), it sounded the alarm for the day of Yahweh (Joel 2:1), and it signaled holy war at Jericho (Josh 6) and with Gideon (Judg 7). 🔴 Jericho fell to seven priests with seven trumpets (Josh 6:4), and a reader who knew that would hear it here. 🟡
- **Egypt was the template for judgment.** Jews had been reading the plagues as the pattern for how God deals with an oppressor for a long time. The Wisdom of Solomon (chs. 11–19) works through the plagues as a lesson in justice. Revelation's readers lived under a new Pharaoh. 🔴 for Wisdom 11–19, 🔵 for how directly John leans on that tradition.
- **Silence in heaven, in Jewish tradition.** Later Jewish writings picture the angels pausing their praise so the prayers of Israel can be heard. Heiser reads that as a second layer under the Day of Yahweh hush. 🟡
- **The angels "who stand before God" (8:2).** These are throne-room servants, members of God's court. The trumpets are blown by the council, not by nature. In Heiser's frame this is the divine council carrying out a verdict already passed in chs. 4–5. 🟡
- **A burning mountain in the sea (8:8).** Jer 51:25 calls Babylon a "destroying mountain" that God will make "a burnt-out mountain." 🟡 The Tyndale notes add that Vesuvius blew in AD 79, sixteen years before John wrote, and destroyed ships and sea life (Pliny the Younger, *Letters* 6.16). His readers may have pictured it. 🔵
- **The eagle (8:13).** Hos 8:1: "Put the trumpet to your mouth! Like an eagle the enemy comes against the house of Yahweh." The word can mean eagle or vulture, the bird that circles over the dead (Deut 28:49; Rev 19:17–18). 🟡

## What the chapter is doing
- The fifth trumpet: a star that has fallen to earth is handed the key to the abyss. Smoke pours out, and out of the smoke come locusts that sting like scorpions. They can't touch plants or anyone with God's seal. They torment everyone else for five months.
- The locusts have a king, the angel of the abyss: Abaddon in Hebrew, Apollyon in Greek.
- The sixth trumpet: a voice from the golden altar orders four bound angels at the Euphrates set loose. A cavalry of two hundred million kills a third of mankind.
- The rest of mankind sees all of it and does not repent. They keep worshiping demons and idols.

## Pay attention to this
- **The star is a "him" (9:1).** "The key of the pit of the abyss was given to him." A star that gets handed a key is a being, not a rock. That settles the question ch. 8 left open. Revelation calls angels stars (1:20) and the dragon's tail sweeps a third of the stars (12:4). 🔴 Who he is, John doesn't say. 🟡
- **Everything is "given."** The key is given (9:1), power is given to the locusts (9:3), they are told what they may not touch (9:4). The worst things in the chapter work on a leash. 🔴
- **Joel's locusts, turned around.** Joel 1–2 has a locust army that looks like horses, sounds like chariots, and darkens the sun. John's locusts have all of that (9:7–9). But Joel's locusts eat the crops, and John's are ordered not to touch "the grass of the earth, nor any green thing" (9:4). They go after people instead. 🔴
- **Five months (9:5, 10).** About the length of a locust season, spring to late summer. Bounded and limited. 🟡
- **"Men will seek death and will never find it" (9:6).** The martyrs of ch. 6 died and were vindicated. These people can't even die. 🔴
- **Don't decode the hardware.** Crowns, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, iron breastplates, scorpion tails (9:7–10). Heiser flatly rejects the helicopter readings. It's a picture of terror built out of Joel, not a parts list. 🔴
- **Abaddon (9:11).** Hebrew *'abaddon*, "destruction." In the Old Testament it's a name for the grave, paired with Sheol: "Naked is Sheol before Him, and Abaddon has no covering" (Job 26:6; also Prov 15:11; Ps 88:11). John turns the place into a person. 🔴
- **The voice comes from the golden altar (9:13).** The same altar where the prayers went up in 8:3–5. The censer thread is still running. 🔴
- **Four angels bound, then released (9:14–15).** In ch. 7 four angels held the winds back. Here four angels who have been held are let go, on a schedule down to "the hour and day and month and year." 🔴
- **Two hundred million (9:16).** Literally "two myriads of myriads." The same idiom counts God's angels around the throne (Dan 7:10; Rev 5:11). It means more than you can count, and it's a spirit army. Heiser: not China's army. 🔴
- **"They did not repent" (9:20–21).** This is where the chapter lands. The thirds left room to turn, and nobody turned. Same as Pharaoh: plague, hard heart, next plague. 🔴
- **Idols are demons (9:20).** John puts "demons" and "idols of gold and of silver" in one breath. That's Deut 32:17, "They sacrificed to demons who were not God," and Paul in 1 Cor 10:20. The idol list ("which can neither see nor hear nor walk") comes from Ps 115:4–7 and 135:15–17. 🔴
- **"Sorceries" (9:21).** Greek *pharmakeia*: magic, potions, spell-work. 🔴

## Read it like AD 95, not 2026
- **The abyss was a known prison.** A Jewish reader in John's day had read or heard 1 Enoch: the Watchers, the sons of God who sinned in Genesis 6, were bound in the depths until the judgment. The New Testament runs on the same map: 2 Pet 2:4 (cast into Tartarus), Jude 6 (kept in eternal bonds), and the demons in Luke 8:31 begging Jesus not to send them into the abyss. Heiser: Rev 9 is Genesis 6 played out at the end. 🔴 for the Second Temple prison idea, 🟡 for reading these locusts as the Watchers released.
- **Who comes out of the pit.** In the Q&A a listener asked about Mesopotamian scorpion-men and the *apkallu* (the semi-divine sages of Babylonian myth). Heiser: Rev 9 is quoting Joel 2 for certain. The Gilgamesh and Watcher background is a real second layer, since the Book of the Watchers and the Book of Giants were read at Qumran. 🔴 for Joel, 🟡 for the Babylonian layer.
- **When are the Watchers let out?** Heiser in the Q&A: before Christ returns, and God lets cosmic evil loose to bait it into its own insane attack on Zion, where it is destroyed. He also says the imprisoned Watchers are not the Nephilim, and Matt 24 is not a "return of the Nephilim." 🟡
- **Apollyon and Apollo.** Apollo was linked with locusts and plague, and emperors (Domitian among them) claimed him as their patron. A reader in Asia Minor would hear the pun: the god the empire honors is the destroyer from the pit. Heiser reads it as a deliberate swipe at the imperial cult. 🟡
- **The Euphrates was where the enemy came from.** Assyria and Babylon came over "the River" when God judged Israel (Isa 7:20; 8:7). Jer 46:10 puts a day of the Lord's vengeance at the river Euphrates. It was also the eastern edge of the Roman world, and Rome feared the Parthians on the far side. 🔴 for the Old Testament; 🟡 for how much Parthia was in John's readers' heads.
- **Fire, smoke and brimstone (9:17–18).** Sodom's judgment (Gen 19:24) and the underworld. The lake of fire is coming in ch. 20. 🔴
- **Divine council:** the angel of the abyss rules as a king (9:11), the four angels are bound and released on orders, and the whole thing answers prayers made at the altar before God. This is the unseen realm under God's control, the rebel side being used against the people who worship it. 🟡

- The other side of it is 9:4. The only people the abyss can't touch are the ones with God's seal on their foreheads, which sets up the mark in ch. 13.

## META: the book of Romans
- **Where it sits.** Paul's longest letter, written to a church he had never visited. He's planning to come through Rome on his way to Spain (15:24, 28) and wants them to know the gospel he preaches before he gets there. 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** has God kept his promises to Israel, and how do Jews and Gentiles end up as one people in Christ?
- **Who wrote it and when.** Paul, with Tertius writing it down (16:22). Most likely from Corinth around AD 56–57, at the end of his third journey, with the collection for Jerusalem in hand (15:25–26). Phoebe from Cenchreae, Corinth's port, probably carried it (16:1–2). 🔴 for Paul; 🟡 for place and year.
- **The church in Rome.** Mixed Jews and Gentiles, meeting in several house churches (16:5, 14–15). The emperor Claudius threw Jews out of Rome around AD 49 (Acts 18:2), and they came back after he died in 54. Gentile believers ran the churches in the meantime. That history sits under chapters 9–11 and 14–15. 🔴 for the expulsion; 🟡 for how much it shaped the letter.
- **Text issues.** The closing praise (16:25–27) shows up in different places in different manuscripts: after 14:23, after 15:33, after 16:24, or in more than one spot. A few manuscripts also leave "in Rome" out of 1:7 and 1:15. 🔴
- **Four movements:** chs. 1–4 everyone is under sin and God's righteousness comes by faith; chs. 5–8 new life in Christ and the Spirit; chs. 9–11 Israel and God's faithfulness; chs. 12–16 how to live it, together.
- **Threads to track the whole way through:**
  - "To the Jew first and also to the Greek" (1:16, 2:9–10) and "no distinction" (3:22, 10:12).
  - The righteousness of God: God being faithful to what he promised.
  - Sin as a power that reigns, more than a list of acts (5:21, 6:14, 7:11).
  - Adam and Christ, and creation waiting to be set free (5, 8).

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul introduces himself as a slave of Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel promised in the Scriptures, and sums up that gospel: Jesus, David's seed, declared Son of God in power by the resurrection.
- He thanks God for the Roman believers, tells them he's been trying to come for a long time, and says he owes the gospel to everyone.
- He states the theme: he isn't ashamed of the gospel, the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
- Then the bad news. God's wrath is revealed against people who suppress what they know. They traded God's glory for idols, so God "gave them over," three times, to what they wanted.

## Pay attention to this
- **"A slave of Christ Jesus" (1:1).** *Doulos*. Paul opens with the lowest title a man could take, then "called as an apostle." In the Old Testament "servant of the LORD" was also an honor (Moses, David). 🔴
- **The gospel in two lines (1:3–4).** "Born of the seed of David according to the flesh" and "designated as the Son of God in power... by the resurrection." King of Israel and enthroned Son. 🔴
- **"The obedience of faith among all the Gentiles" (1:5).** Faith that obeys, among all the nations. Paul brings the phrase back at the very end of the letter (16:26). 🔴
- **"I am not ashamed" (1:16).** Rome measured people by honor. A crucified Jew as Lord was shameful by every Roman standard. 🔴
- **"To the Jew first and also to the Greek" (1:16).** First in order, not first in rank. Paul uses the same order for judgment and reward in 2:9–10 and then says "there is no distinction" in 10:12. 🔴
- **"The righteous will live by faith" (1:17).** From Habakkuk 2:4. The whole letter works this line out. 🔴
- **Everyone already knows (1:19–20).** "That which is known about God is evident within them." Creation shows his "eternal power and divine nature," so "they are without excuse." 🔴
- **The exchange (1:23, 25, 26).** Glory traded for an image, truth traded for a lie, natural traded for unnatural. Three exchanges. 🔴
- **"God gave them over" three times (1:24, 26, 28).** God's wrath here is God letting people have what they chose, all the way down. 🔴
- **The list ends at home (1:29–32).** Murder sits next to gossip and "disobedient to parents." Nobody gets to read this list as being about somebody else, which is exactly where chapter 2 goes. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **"Gospel" was an empire word.** *Euangelion* was the word for news of a victory or a new emperor. A Greek inscription from Priene (9 BC) calls Augustus's birthday the beginning of "good news" for the world. Paul's "gospel of God" announces a different king. 🔴
- **"Son of God" was on the coins.** Augustus called himself *divi filius*, son of the deified Julius. Romans heard "Son of God" and thought of the emperor. Paul gives the title to a Jewish man raised from the dead. 🔴 for the title; 🟡 that Paul means the contrast.
- **Psalm 2 behind 1:4.** "You are My Son, today I have begotten You" is a coronation psalm about God's king and the nations raging. The resurrection is the coronation. 🟡
- **Greeks and barbarians (1:14).** Greek speakers called everyone else "barbarians," people who said "bar-bar." Paul owes the gospel to both, and to the educated and the foolish. 🔴
- **1:18–32 sounds like a synagogue sermon.** Jewish writers had a standard attack on Gentile idolatry and sex. Wisdom of Solomon 13–14 says the nations should have known the Maker from what he made, worshiped images instead, and that idolatry is the start of every evil. A Jewish reader would be nodding along. Chapter 2 springs the trap. 🔴 for the parallels; 🟡 for the trap.
- **"Exchanged the glory" echoes Israel's own sin.** Psalm 106:20 says Israel "exchanged their glory for the image of an ox" at the golden calf, and Jeremiah 2:11 says the same. Paul uses Israel's words for the nations' idolatry, so Israel isn't standing outside the story. 🔴
- **Idols weren't empty to them.** In Deuteronomy 32:17 Israel sacrificed to *shedim*, demons, "not God." Worship given to images went to real beings God never approved of. Paul says the same in 1 Corinthians 10:20. 🔴 for the texts.
- **"Gave them over" and the nations.** Deuteronomy 4:19 says God "allotted" the sun, moon and stars, the host of heaven, to the nations. After Babel the nations were handed off to other gods (Deuteronomy 32:8–9), and Romans 1 shows humanity choosing those gods. In Acts 7:42 Stephen uses the same idea for Israel: God "delivered them up to serve the host of heaven." 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the divine council reading of Romans 1.
- **Rome's daily religion.** Every street had shrines, every guild had a patron god, every meal could involve an offering. Paul's readers didn't meet idolatry as an idea; they walked past it every day. 🔴

## My notes
- **Jew first.** The priority was in time, not in rank. The same order shows up for judgment and reward (2:9–10), and 10:12, "no distinction," shows the "first" was temporal. Acts shows it in story: Peter says God sent his servant "to you first" (Acts 3:26), and at Antioch Paul says the word had to go to the Jews first, "Behold, we are turning to the Gentiles!" (13:46). The priority obligated Jewish hearers. It never locked Gentiles out. 🔴
- **Greek I hold onto.** *Euangelion*, good news as an announcement of victory. *Dikaiosynē*, righteousness, justice, right standing.
- **Creation still shows God (1:19–20).** I put it in an arc: Genesis 1, the office given (we're God's imagers); Genesis 3, the ambassadorship broken; Romans 1, creation still reflects God and humanity suppresses it; Romans 8, creation groaning to be set free. 🟡
- **Evil as misdirected worship (1:21–25).** They knew God, didn't honor him, and traded his glory for idols and the truth for a lie. I read evil as a good thing bent. Worship is good; aimed at the wrong thing it's idolatry. Evil isn't a new creation; it's a perversion of what God made. Augustine called it *privatio boni*, the privation of good. Desire is good until it's disordered (James 1:14–15). Love is good until it's misaimed (1 Timothy 6:10). Even the tree in Genesis 3:6 was "good for food." 🟡
- **Divine council:** the hook is idolatry and "gave them over." The idols stand for real powers that took worship that belonged to God.

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul prays for Israel's salvation. They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge: they tried to set up their own righteousness instead of submitting to God's.
- "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes" (10:4).
- The righteousness of faith doesn't climb to heaven or dig into the abyss. The word is near: confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord, believe in your heart God raised him, and you will be saved. No distinction between Jew and Greek.
- But how will people call on someone they haven't heard of, without a preacher sent? Israel did hear. Moses and Isaiah both said the nations would find God and Israel would hold out against him.

## Pay attention to this
- **Zeal without knowledge (10:2).** Paul knows this from the inside. He persecuted the church out of zeal (Philippians 3:6). 🔴
- **"The end of the law" (10:4).** *Telos* can mean end, goal or finish line. Christ is what the Law was aimed at. 🔴 for the word; ⬜ on how much "end" and how much "goal."
- **Paul rereads Deuteronomy 30 (10:6–8).** Moses said the commandment isn't up in heaven or across the sea; it's near, in your mouth and heart. Paul says that nearness is Christ. 🔴
- **Mouth and heart (10:9–10).** Confess "Jesus as Lord" out loud; believe God raised him. Both. 🔴
- **"No distinction" (10:12).** The same Lord is Lord of all. This is the line that shows the "Jew first" of 1:16 was about order, not rank. 🔴
- **10:13 quotes Joel 2:32.** "Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." In Joel the Lord is Yahweh. In 10:9–13 the Lord is Jesus. 🔴
- **The chain backward (10:14–15).** Call, believe, hear, preacher, sent. Somebody has to go. 🔴
- **Beautiful feet (10:15).** Isaiah 52:7, the messenger running over the mountains to announce that God reigns. 🔴
- **"Faith comes from hearing" (10:17).** And hearing by the word of Christ. 🔴
- **God's hands stretched out (10:21).** The chapter ends on God still reaching for a stubborn Israel, which opens chapter 11. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **"Jesus is Lord" was a political sentence.** *Kyrios*, Lord, was a title Romans used for Caesar. Later Christians were killed for refusing to say "Caesar is Lord." Confessing Jesus as Lord meant he had the top title, not the emperor. 🔴
- **"Lord" was also God's name.** The Greek Old Testament used *Kyrios* for Yahweh. Calling Jesus *Kyrios* and then quoting Joel's "name of the Lord" about him put Jesus in Yahweh's place. 🔴
- **Up to heaven, down to the abyss (10:6–7).** Jewish writers already used Deuteronomy 30 this way. Baruch 3:29–30 asks who went up to heaven and brought down wisdom. Paul swaps in Christ: nobody has to bring him down (he came) or up from the dead (God raised him). The abyss was the deep under the earth, the place of the dead and of imprisoned spirits. 🔴 for Baruch; 🟡 for the abyss imagery.
- **The heralds of the King (10:15).** In Isaiah 52:7 the good news is "Your God reigns!" That's royal announcement language, and it's where Paul's "gospel" comes from. 🔴
- **The heavens preach first (10:18).** Paul quotes Psalm 19:4, which is about the sky declaring God's glory. Heiser's angle: the heavenly host had already broadcast the King. Paul uses it for the gospel going out to the whole world. 🔴 for Psalm 19; 🟡 for the host reading.
- **The Song of Moses again (10:19).** "I will make you jealous by that which is not a nation" is Deuteronomy 32:21. In the same verse Israel had made God jealous with "what is not God," their no-gods. God answers by taking in the no-people. Deuteronomy 32 keeps showing up behind Romans 9–11. 🔴
- **Isaiah's two sides (10:20–21).** Isaiah 65:1–2: found by people who weren't looking, and holding out his hands all day to his own people. 🔴

## My notes
- **Structure I worked from:** the goal of the Law (10:1–4); faith near and the confession (10:5–13); the need for preaching (10:14–17); Israel's accountability (10:18–21).
- **Key verses I hold:** 10:4, 10:10, 10:12 ("no distinction between Jew and Greek"), 10:13.
- **Greek:** *telos*, end, goal, fulfillment. *Kyrios*, Lord (vv. 9, 13).
- **10:12 is the hinge of my "Jew first" essay.** The priority in 1:16 and 2:9–10 was about time. "No distinction" shows equality overrides it. The "first" obligated Jewish hearers; it never kept Gentiles out. 🔴
- **Heiser references in my vault note:** calling on the name (10:13) ties to Name of Yahweh theology, Jesus as the visible Yahweh. 10:18 quoting Psalm 19:4 as the heavenly host having already broadcast the King's arrival. *Telos* as the target the Mosaic system was aiming at, not only a stopping point. 🟡
- **Divine council:** the Name of Yahweh, the heavens' witness in Psalm 19, and Deuteronomy 32:21 with its "no-gods."

## What the chapter is doing
- Has God rejected his people? No. Paul himself is an Israelite. Like the seven thousand in Elijah's day, there's a remnant chosen by grace. The rest were hardened.
- Did they stumble so as to fall for good? No. Their stumbling brought salvation to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous, and their full return will be "life from the dead."
- The olive tree: some natural branches broken off, wild branches grafted in, natural branches able to be grafted back. Gentile believers, don't boast. The root holds you up.
- A partial hardening is on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, "and so all Israel will be saved." God's gifts and calling don't get taken back. Paul ends in praise: "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!"

## Pay attention to this
- **"May it never be!" twice (11:1, 11).** God hasn't rejected his people, and their stumble isn't a final fall. 🔴
- **The remnant (11:2–5).** Elijah thought he was alone; God had seven thousand. There's always more of God's people than the gloomy prophet can see. 🔴
- **Grace is grace (11:6).** "If it is by grace, it is no longer of works, otherwise grace is no longer grace." 🔴
- **Jealousy as a strategy (11:11, 14).** Paul hopes Gentiles being blessed will make Jews want back in. 🔴
- **One tree (11:17–24).** One root, one trunk. Branches come off, branches go on, branches go back on. It's the same tree the whole time. 🔴
- **"Do not boast against the branches" (11:18).** The warning goes to Gentile believers. "It is not you who supports the root, but the root supports you." 🔴
- **Kindness and severity (11:22).** Both are true of God, and both apply to Gentiles too: "otherwise you also will be cut off." 🔴
- **"Contrary to nature" (11:24).** Paul knows grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is backwards. That's his point: what God did for Gentiles was harder than bringing Israel back. 🔴
- **"And so all Israel will be saved" (11:26).** "And so" means "in this way": by being grafted back into the one tree. 🔴 for the words; ⬜ for who "all Israel" is.
- **"The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" (11:29).** God doesn't take his word back. 🔴
- **Everyone shut up so everyone can get mercy (11:32).** Disobedience is the great equalizer, and mercy is the point. 🔴
- **The chapter ends in worship (11:33–36).** After three chapters of argument, Paul runs out of argument and praises. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **Israel was already an olive tree.** Jeremiah 11:16 says God named Israel a green olive tree, beautiful in fruit, and Hosea 14:6 says Israel's beauty will be like the olive tree. Paul's picture isn't new to a Jewish reader. 🔴
- **Olive growers grafted.** Farmers grafted cultivated shoots onto wild stock, not the other way around. The Roman farm writer Columella does mention putting a wild olive shoot into a tired old tree to revive it. Either way Paul says plainly that what he describes is "contrary to nature." 🔴 for Paul's words and Columella; 🟡 for how much Paul knew about farming.
- **Gentile believers in Rome were in charge.** After Claudius expelled the Jews (around AD 49), Gentile believers led the Roman churches. When Jewish believers came back, Gentiles may have looked down on them. 11:18 speaks right into that. 🔴 for the expulsion; 🟡 for the attitude.
- **Firstfruits dough (11:16).** Numbers 15:20–21: the first piece of dough was offered to God, and that made the whole batch holy. The patriarchs are the first piece and the root. 🔴
- **"Mystery" (11:25).** Not a puzzle. In Jewish apocalyptic writing (Daniel 2) a mystery is God's plan, hidden until he reveals it. 🔴
- **The fullness of the nations.** In Deuteronomy 32 God handed the nations to other gods and kept Israel. Here the plan is "the fullness of the Gentiles" coming in and then all Israel. God gets both back. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for the council frame.
- **"Who became His counselor?" (11:34).** Paul quotes Isaiah 40:13. God has a heavenly council (1 Kings 22:19–22; Psalm 89:7), but he doesn't need anyone to tell him what to do. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for reading 11:34 against the council.
- **Elijah and Baal (11:4).** The seven thousand who "have not bowed the knee to Baal" were holding out against a real rival god whose prophets ran the royal court (1 Kings 18–19). 🔴

## My notes
- **I've held one tree all my life,** well before Heiser or Wright. Paul chose one olive tree, one root. Branches off, grafted in, grafted back, same tree throughout (11:17–24). If Paul meant two peoples with two destinies, a single tree is the worst picture he could have picked. 🔴
- **How I handled 11:25–29 with a dispensationalist:** I gave the verse honestly and then fenced it. The whole chapter is about grace; God will have grace for Israel. It means what they say. It doesn't prove two completely separate paths. One verse doesn't overturn fifty that say we're one people now.
- **"All Israel will be saved" (11:26)** happens by re-grafting into the one tree, not by a separate track.
- **The chapter's real subject is no branch boasting over another (11:18).** It's against superiority, not for parallel programs.
- **Where I land:** the chapter establishes God's ongoing covenant faithfulness toward ethnic Israel. Grant that fully. Its one-tree shape argues against the two-track system it usually gets quoted for. 🔴
- **Logos backing:** Kaiser has the church grafted into Israel's root, "one new man," not two programs. 🔴 that Kaiser says it.
- **My theology framework:** "Israel chosen, Gentiles grafted in (not replaced)," with 11:17–24 and Ephesians 2:11–13. And "God's ways past our understanding," with 11:33.
- **Divine council:** in the background. The nations coming in, God's counsel that needs no counselor, and Baal as the rival god in 11:4.

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul turns on the person who has been nodding along to chapter 1. If you judge others for those things and do the same, you condemn yourself.
- God's judgment is by truth and by works, and he shows no partiality: trouble for evil and glory for good, "to the Jew first and also to the Greek."
- Having the Law doesn't save anyone; doing it is the measure. Gentiles without the Law still show its work written on their hearts, and their conscience accuses or defends them.
- Then Paul names the Jew who boasts in the Law and breaks it. Real circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, and that person's praise comes from God.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Therefore you are without excuse, O man" (2:1).** The same "without excuse" Paul used for the idolaters in 1:20. The judge gets the idolater's verdict. 🔴
- **God's kindness has a purpose (2:4).** "The kindness of God leads you to repentance." Patience is not approval. 🔴
- **"According to his works" (2:6).** Paul quotes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12. Judgment by works is in the letter that teaches justification by faith. 🔴
- **Jew first, for bad news too (2:9–10).** The same order as 1:16, now for trouble and for glory. First means first in line, both ways. 🔴
- **"There is no partiality with God" (2:11).** That's the hinge of the chapter. 🔴
- **Hearers and doers (2:13).** "Not the hearers of the Law who are just before God, but the doers." Paul isn't setting up a works road to heaven; he's raising the bar no one clears (3:9–20). 🟡
- **The Gentile conscience (2:14–15).** The work of the Law written on their hearts, "their thoughts alternately accusing or else defending them." That makes Gentiles accountable. 🔴
- **The resume (2:17–20).** Bear the name "Jew," rely on the Law, boast in God, guide to the blind, light to those in darkness. Every line is something good Israel was called to be. 🔴
- **The questions (2:21–23).** Teach others, steal, commit adultery, rob temples. Paul uses short questions like punches. 🔴
- **"The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you" (2:24).** From Isaiah 52:5. Israel was supposed to make God's name known to the nations. 🔴
- **A Jew inwardly (2:28–29).** Circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit, not the letter. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **The imaginary opponent.** Teachers in the Greek world argued with a made-up listener ("O man," "do you suppose...?"). It's called diatribe, and Epictetus and other Stoic teachers used it. Paul isn't attacking someone in the room; he's teaching by sparring. 🔴
- **Jewish readers agreed with chapter 1.** The standard Jewish line was that Gentiles were idolaters and Israel had the Law. Wisdom of Solomon 15:1–2 even says Israel will not sin because it knows God counts it as his own. Paul goes right at that confidence. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 that Paul has this kind of reader in mind.
- **Conscience was a Greek idea.** *Syneidēsis* came from the moral thinking of the Greek world. Stoics taught a law of nature everyone could know. Paul borrows the word and ties it to Jeremiah 31:33, the law written on the heart. 🔴
- **Circumcision was life and death.** Under Antiochus IV, Jewish mothers were killed for circumcising their sons (1 Maccabees 1:60–61). It was the line that said who belonged to Israel. 🔴
- **Heart circumcision is an Old Testament idea.** "Circumcise your heart" (Deuteronomy 10:16), "Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart" (Deuteronomy 30:6), and Jeremiah 4:4. Paul isn't inventing something new. 🔴
- **A play on "Jew."** "Jew" comes from Judah, and Leah named Judah from "praise" (Genesis 29:35). "His praise is not from men, but from God" (2:29) is wordplay. 🔴 for the name; 🟡 that Paul meant it.
- **"Do you rob temples?" (2:22).** Jews were supposed to have nothing to do with idols. Deuteronomy 7:25 forbids taking the silver and gold off them. Josephus tells of Jews in Rome swindling a noblewoman out of temple gifts around AD 19, which led to Jews being thrown out of the city. 🔴 for Josephus; 🔵 that Paul has it in mind.
- **The day of wrath (2:5).** The prophets' "day of the LORD." Jewish readers expected one final court with God on the bench. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul answers the objection chapter 2 raised: then what good is being a Jew? A lot. They were trusted with the oracles of God, and their unfaithfulness doesn't cancel God's faithfulness.
- He strings Old Testament verses together to close the case: Jews and Greeks are all under sin. "There is none righteous, not even one."
- "But now" the righteousness of God has shown up apart from the Law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe, because there is no distinction.
- God put Jesus forward as a propitiation so he would be "just and the justifier." Boasting is shut out, God is God of Gentiles too, and faith doesn't abolish the Law; it establishes it.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Entrusted with the oracles of God" (3:2).** Israel's advantage was a job: to hold God's word for the world. 🔴
- **"May it never be!" (3:4, 6, 31).** Paul's strongest no. He uses it every time someone draws the wrong conclusion from grace. 🔴
- **"Let us do evil that good may come" (3:8).** People were already twisting Paul's gospel into this, and he says so. 🔴
- **"Under sin" (3:9).** Paul says they're under sin, like people under a ruler. Sin is a power in Romans before it's a list of acts. 🔴 for the phrase; 🟡 for the power reading here.
- **The chain of verses (3:10–18).** Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10 and 36 and Isaiah 59. The body parts move in order: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes. The whole person is bent. 🔴
- **"Every mouth may be shut" (3:19).** A courtroom picture. The accused has nothing left to say. 🔴
- **"But now" (3:21).** The turn of the whole letter so far. Everything before it is the bad news. 🔴
- **"No distinction" twice.** No distinction in sin (3:22–23) and none in how God saves (3:29–30; 10:12). 🔴
- **Three pictures in three verses (3:24–25).** Justified (a courtroom), redemption (buying back a slave), propitiation (the temple). 🔴
- **"Just and the justifier" (3:26).** God doesn't wink at sin to forgive it. He deals with it so he can stay just while declaring sinners righteous. 🔴
- **"God... is one" (3:30).** Paul reaches for the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4). If God is one, he's God of the nations too. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **The mercy seat.** *Hilastērion* (3:25) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the gold lid on the ark of the covenant, the "mercy seat," where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for reading 3:25 as "mercy seat."
- **Hidden, then public.** The mercy seat sat in the Holy of Holies, seen once a year by one man. Paul says God "displayed publicly" Jesus as the *hilastērion*. Out in the open, on a Roman cross. 🟡
- **The throne between the cherubim.** The ark was God's footstool and the cherubim his throne guards (1 Samuel 4:4 calls him Yahweh of hosts enthroned above the cherubim). The place of atonement was a throne room. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 for connecting it to 3:25.
- **Redemption was a market word.** *Apolytrōsis* meant buying a slave's or captive's freedom. Every Jew also heard the Exodus in it: God "redeemed" Israel out of Egypt. 🔴
- **"Passed over the sins previously committed" (3:25).** The sacrifices covered sin for a time. God's patience before Christ raised a fair question about his justice, and the cross answers it. 🔴 for the line; 🟡 for the reading.
- **"Works of the Law."** Jews in Paul's day did not, as a rule, think they earned God's favor. They believed they were God's people by covenant and kept the Law as the response. The Dead Sea Scrolls use "works of the Law" (4QMMT) for specific rulings that marked the community off. Whether Paul means all good deeds or the Law as Israel's badge is a real argument. 🔴 for 4QMMT; ⬜ for Paul's meaning.
- **A courtroom with God as judge.** "Justify" (*dikaioō*) is a verdict word: declared in the right. The Old Testament judge was to justify the righteous and condemn the wicked (Deuteronomy 25:1). God justifies the ungodly (4:5), which by that rule is scandalous until 3:26 explains it. 🔴
