## What the chapter is doing
- Paul takes his test case to the top: Abraham. If anyone could boast, it would be him. But Scripture says "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6).
- David says the same: blessed is the man whose sin the Lord won't count against him (Psalm 32).
- Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so he's the father of believing Gentiles and believing Jews alike.
- The promise that he'd be "heir of the world" came by faith, not Law. Abraham believed the God who gives life to the dead, even with his body and Sarah's womb as good as dead. That same faith is counted to us when we believe in the God who raised Jesus.

## Pay attention to this
- **"Counted" runs through the whole chapter.** *Logizomai*, an accounting word: credit to someone's account. Count how many times it shows up. 🔴
- **Wages vs. gift (4:4–5).** A wage is what you're owed. Righteousness is credited to "the one who does not work, but believes upon Him who justifies the ungodly." 🔴
- **"Justifies the ungodly" (4:5).** The Law told judges never to do that (Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 17:15). God does it, which is the scandal Romans 3:26 explained. 🔴
- **Timing is the argument (4:10).** Was he counted righteous circumcised or uncircumcised? Uncircumcised. Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17. 🔴
- **Circumcision as a seal (4:11).** It confirmed something Abraham already had. It didn't make it. 🔴
- **Father of two groups (4:11–12).** Of uncircumcised believers, and of circumcised ones who "follow in the steps of the faith" he had. 🔴
- **"Heir of the world" (4:13).** Genesis promised Abraham land. Paul says *kosmos*, the world. 🔴
- **"Who gives life to the dead and calls into being that which does not exist" (4:17).** Resurrection and creation in one line. Abraham's faith was faith in that kind of God. 🔴
- **"Hope against hope" (4:18).** He looked straight at the facts (a hundred-year-old body, a dead womb) and believed anyway. Faith here isn't ignoring reality; it's trusting God over it. 🔴
- **"Not for his sake only" (4:23–24).** Paul says Genesis was written for us too. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **The peace of Rome.** The *Pax Romana* was peace by conquest, announced on coins and monuments. Paul's "peace with God" comes from the enemy being reconciled, not crushed. 🔴 for the *Pax*; 🟡 for the contrast being in Paul's mind.
- **Access to a king.** *Prosagōgē* was the word for being brought before a ruler by someone with the right to bring you. You didn't walk in on your own. 🔴
- **Dying for someone (5:7).** Greek and Roman writers praised dying for a friend or a good man. Nobody praised dying for an enemy. That's the point of 5:8. 🔴
- **Adam was already a Jewish question.** Wisdom of Solomon 2:23–24 says God made humans for incorruption, in his own image, but "through the devil's envy death entered the world." Paul is joining a live argument. 🔴 (4 Ezra and 2 Baruch were written after Paul, around AD 100.)
- **The serpent was more than a snake.** Wisdom 2:24 already reads Genesis 3 as the devil's work. Heiser reads the serpent (*nachash*) as a divine being from God's council who rebelled and led humanity into death. 🔴 for Wisdom; 🟡 for Heiser's reading.

- **Sin and Death as powers.** Jewish apocalyptic writing described the present age as ruled by hostile forces. Paul uses the singular "sin" almost always as a ruling power, and personifies Death as a king. 🔴 for Paul's usage; 🟡 for how literally to take it.

- **"Instruments" (6:13).** The Greek *hopla* usually means weapons. Your body parts are weapons in somebody's army. 🔴
- **No neutral ground (6:16).** You're a slave of whatever you obey. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **Baptism was immersion.** *Baptizō* means to dip or immerse. Going under the water and coming up looked like burial and rising. Jews also used immersion for purity, and converts to Judaism were immersed. 🔴 for the word and Jewish washings; 🔵 for how early proselyte baptism was standard.
- **Rome ran on slaves.** A large share of the people in Rome were slaves or freed slaves. Some of Paul's readers were slaves; their names in chapter 16 (Ampliatus, Persis, Tryphaena) were common slave names. When Paul says "slave," they knew exactly what owning and being owned meant. 🔴 for slavery's scale; 🟡 for specific names.
- **A slave could change owners.** Slaves were sold or set free. A freed slave owed his former master loyalty. Paul's picture is a transfer of ownership: sin's slave becomes God's. 🔴
- **Wages were soldiers' pay.** *Opsōnia* was the ration money paid to a soldier. Put it next to "weapons" in 6:13 and the picture is military: sin pays its troops in death. 🔴 for the word; 🟡 for the military picture across the chapter.
- **"Gift" (6:23).** *Charisma*, a free gift. In Rome, emperors gave gifts to troops and people on special days; this gift has nothing to do with service rendered. 🔴 for the word; 🔵 for the imperial echo.
- **Sin as a ruling power.** Jewish writers of the time pictured the present age under hostile powers. Paul uses Sin and Death as rulers with subjects. Chapter 8 and Colossians 2:15 put Christ's victory over the powers on the cross. 🟡

- A marriage picture: law binds a wife to her husband only while he lives. Believers died to the Law through Christ's body, so they're free to belong to another, the risen Christ, and serve in the newness of the Spirit.

- Then the struggle in the first person: I don't do the good I want, I do the evil I hate. Sin dwells in me, and a different law in my members wars against the law of my mind.

## Pay attention to this

- **Coveting is the test case (7:7–8).** The one commandment about the inside of a person. You can keep the others in public; you can't keep this one by effort. 🔴
- **Sin is the actor (7:8, 11).** Sin takes opportunity, works out coveting, revives, deceives, kills. The "I" mostly gets acted on. 🔴
- **"Sin revived and I died" (7:9).** Something that was dormant woke up when the commandment arrived. 🔴
- **"Deceived me" (7:11).** Paul's word (*exapataō*) belongs to the family the Greek Old Testament uses for the serpent deceiving Eve (Genesis 3:13). Paul uses the same word for that event in 2 Corinthians 11:3. 🔴
- **"Sold into bondage under sin" (7:14).** A slave-market picture. 🔴
- **The tense changes at 7:14.** Verses 7–13 are past tense; 7:14–25 are present tense. Who is the "I" now? 🔴 for the change; ⬜ for what it means.
- **"Not I, but sin which dwells in me" (7:17, 20).** Said twice. Paul isn't dodging blame; he's showing sin as an occupier. 🔴 for the words; 🟡 for the reading.

- **"Those who know the law" (7:1).** Both Jewish believers who knew Moses and Romans who knew Roman law. Every reader understood that a contract ended at death. 🔴
- **Desire was the root sin.** Jewish writers of the time put desire (*epithymia*) at the head of all sin. The Apocalypse of Moses has the serpent planting "desire" as the head of every sin, and 4 Maccabees uses "You shall not covet" as the commandment against desire itself. Paul picks the tenth commandment for that reason. 🔴 for the texts; 🟡 that Paul has this tradition in view.
- **The evil inclination.** Later rabbis taught that every person has a *yetzer hara*, an evil inclination, and a good one; the Torah was the cure. The idea is older (Sirach 15:14). Paul's twist: the Law alone doesn't cure it; sin uses the Law. 🔴 for the tradition; 🟡 for Paul pushing against it.

- **The Eden echo.** The commandment came, desire was stirred, the "I" was deceived and died. Read 7:7–11 next to Genesis 3: one command, a deceiver, desire, death. Many read the "I" here as Adam, or as humanity in Adam. 🔴 for the parallel; ⬜ for whether the "I" is Adam.

## What the chapter is doing
- After the cry of chapter 7: "There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." The Spirit of life has set us free from the law of sin and death. God did what the Law couldn't.
- The Spirit lives in believers, gives life to mortal bodies, and makes us sons of God. We cry "Abba! Father!" and we're heirs with Christ, if we suffer with him.
- Creation itself groans like a woman in labor, waiting for the sons of God to be revealed. We groan too, and the Spirit groans for us when we don't know how to pray.
- God works all things for good for those he called. Nobody can bring a charge, nobody can condemn, and nothing (death, life, angels, rulers, powers, height or depth) can separate us from God's love in Christ.

## Pay attention to this
- **"No condemnation" (8:1).** A courtroom word, right after "wretched man that I am." The verdict is in. 🔴
- **"He condemned sin in the flesh" (8:3).** Sin, the power, got the sentence, carried out in Jesus' flesh. 🔴
- **The Spirit is everywhere.** Count *pneuma* in this chapter: about twenty times, more than anywhere else in Romans. 🔴
- **"Sons of God" (8:14, 19).** Paul uses the Old Testament title for God's heavenly family for believers. 🔴
- **"Abba! Father!" (8:15).** Aramaic and Greek side by side. Jesus prayed "Abba" in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). 🔴
- **Heirs, if we suffer with him (8:17).** The road to glory runs through suffering, same as his. 🔴
- **Creation groans (8:19–22).** Paul gives creation feelings: "anxious longing," "subjected to futility," "slavery to corruption," "groans." It's waiting on us. 🔴
- **Three groans.** Creation groans (8:22), we groan (8:23), the Spirit groans for us (8:26). 🔴
- **8:28 has a context.** "All things work together for good" sits inside a chapter about suffering and groaning, and the good is defined in 8:29: being conformed to the image of the Son. 🔴
- **The chain (8:29–30).** Foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified. "Glorified" is past tense, as if it's already done. 🔴
- **The courtroom again (8:33–34).** Who brings a charge? Who condemns? Christ is at God's right hand and "intercedes for us." 🔴
- **The list of what can't separate us (8:38–39).** It includes angels, rulers and powers. Paul names the unseen world and says it's not strong enough. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **"Sons of God" was a heavenly title.** In the Old Testament the *bene elohim*, sons of God, are the members of God's heavenly council (Job 1:6, 38:7; Psalm 89:6–7; Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scroll reading). Paul now calls believers sons of God. Heiser reads this as God rebuilding his family: humans adopted into the council, set to rule with Christ where the rebel sons of God failed. 🔴 for the Old Testament usage; 🟡 for Heiser's reading.
- **Adoption was Roman law.** *Huiothesia* was a legal act. An adopted son got a new father, a new name, full rights of inheritance, and his old debts were cancelled. Emperors adopted their heirs (Augustus was adopted by Julius Caesar). Witnesses confirmed it, the way "the Spirit testifies with our spirit" (8:16). 🔴
- **"The revealing of the sons of God" (8:19).** Creation and the powers are waiting to see who God's true sons are. In Heiser's reading, when they're revealed the rebel powers' rule over the nations is over. 🟡
- **Creation under a curse.** "Subjected to futility... because of Him who subjected it" goes back to Genesis 3:17–19, "cursed is the ground because of you." Jewish writers expected the whole world to be renewed (Isaiah 65:17; 1 Enoch 45:4–5). 🔴
- **Labor pains.** Jewish writers called the hard times before the messianic age the "birth pains" (Jesus too, Mark 13:8). Birth pains hurt, but they end in a birth. 🔴
- **Rulers, powers, height and depth (8:38–39).** "Rulers" (*archai*) and "powers" (*dynameis*) are Paul's words for spiritual authorities (Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 1:16, 2:15). "Height" and "depth" were also words used in ancient astrology for the zones where the stars rose and set, the stars people believed ruled their fate. Paul names the whole unseen system and says none of it can cut you off. 🔴 for the power words; 🟡 for the astrology terms.
- **Sheep for the slaughter (8:36).** Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, a psalm of faithful Israel suffering and asking why God seems asleep. Suffering doesn't mean God has left. 🔴

## What the chapter is doing
- Paul grieves for his own people. He'd be cut off from Christ himself if it would save them. They have the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the Law, the temple service, the promises, the fathers, and the Messiah.
- So has God's word failed? No: "they are not all Israel who are descended from Israel" (9:6). God's promise has always run through his call, not by descent alone: Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau.
- Is God unjust? No. He has mercy on whom he has mercy, he raised up Pharaoh to show his power, and the potter has authority over the clay.
- God has called a people from Jews and Gentiles, as Hosea and Isaiah said. The twist at the end: Gentiles who weren't looking found righteousness by faith, and Israel, pursuing it by works, tripped over the stone God laid in Zion.

## Pay attention to this
- **The chapter opens in grief, not in doctrine (9:1–3).** Whatever Paul says about election, he says it weeping over Israel. 🔴
- **Israel's list of gifts (9:4–5).** Adoption, glory, covenants, Law, temple service, promises, fathers, Christ. Paul isn't writing Israel off. 🔴
- **"Who is God over all, blessed forever" (9:5).** One of the plainest places Paul calls Christ God, depending on where you put the comma. 🔴 for the debate; 🟡 for reading it of Christ (LSB does).
- **9:6 is the question of the whole chapter.** "It is not as though the word of God has failed." Everything after answers that, about Israel. 🔴
- **Two pairs of sons (9:7–13).** Isaac over Ishmael, then twins from one father, chosen before they'd done anything good or bad. 🔴
- **"Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" (9:13).** From Malachi 1:2–3, about the nations Israel and Edom, written centuries after the twins died. 🔴
- **"The older shall serve the younger" (9:12).** From Genesis 25:23, where Rebekah is told "two nations are in your womb." Esau the man never served Jacob; Edom the nation did. 🔴
- **Paul voices the objection himself (9:19).** "Why does He still find fault? For who resists His will?" He knew people would ask it. 🔴
- **The potter (9:20–21).** Paul doesn't invent this picture. It's in Isaiah 29:16, 45:9 and Jeremiah 18. 🔴
- **"Endured with much patience" (9:22).** The vessels of wrath were put up with, not rushed to destruction. 🔴
- **"Not from among Jews only, but also from among Gentiles" (9:24).** The potter's new vessel is a mixed people. 🔴
- **Hosea's "not My people" (9:25–26).** In Hosea it's about unfaithful northern Israel. Paul uses it for Gentiles too. 🔴
- **The stumbling stone (9:32–33).** Isaiah 28:16 and 8:14 fused. Israel's problem was the stone, Christ, not a lack of effort. 🔴

## Read it like AD 57, not 2026
- **Paul talks like Moses.** "I could wish that I myself were accursed" echoes Moses after the golden calf: "blot me out from Your book" (Exodus 32:32). The intercessor offers himself for the people. 🔴
- **"The glory" (9:4).** God's visible presence that filled the tabernacle and temple, later called the Shekinah. 🔴
- **Love and hate as choosing.** In Hebrew idiom "love" and "hate" can mean choose and not choose. Genesis 29:31 calls Leah "unloved" (literally "hated") when Jacob simply loved Rachel more. Malachi 1 is about God's covenant choice of Israel over Edom. 🔴
- **Nations as well as people.** Jacob is Israel and Esau is Edom. In Genesis 25:23 the twins are two nations. Most Jewish readers heard 9:10–13 as a story about which people carries the promise. 🔴 for Genesis; 🟡 for how Paul's readers heard it.
- **The potter in Jeremiah 18 is conditional.** God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter rework spoiled clay, then says: if a nation turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster I planned; if it does evil, I will relent of the good (18:7–10). The picture is about how God deals with nations who turn or don't. 🔴
- **Pharaoh and the gods of Egypt.** In Exodus the plagues are judgment "against all the gods of Egypt" (Exodus 12:12). God raises Pharaoh up so "My name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth" (9:17). Heiser reads it as Yahweh beating the gods behind Pharaoh. 🔴 for Exodus 12:12; 🟡 for Heiser's frame.
- **Israel as God's portion.** Deuteronomy 32:9 says Yahweh's portion is his people, Jacob his allotted inheritance, while the nations went to others. Romans 9–11 is Paul working out how God keeps his portion and gets the nations back. 🟡
- **"Sons of the living God" and the "Lord of Sabaoth" (9:26, 29).** Paul quotes Hosea on outsiders becoming sons of the living God, and Isaiah's "Lord of Sabaoth," the Lord of hosts, the commander of heaven's armies. 🔴

## My notes
- **My thesis, posted on X:** every predestination debate ends up in Romans 9 and almost none of them read it as a chapter about Israel. Paul is answering "has God's word failed" about his own people, not settling Geneva vs. Rome. My position is text-driven, not system-driven. I don't want to be read as a straightforward Calvinist.
- **What I saw in the Bignon and D'Souza debate transcript:** all of Bignon's Romans 9 was verses 14–23, and nobody read past verse 23. Israel never came up. D'Souza's complaint about God making defective clay is the exact objection Paul puts in the critic's mouth at 9:19.
- **The potter isn't Paul's image.** It comes from Jeremiah 18, where the logic is conditional, national relenting: a nation turns and God relents. That's the opposite of a fixed decree about individuals. 🔴 for Jeremiah; 🟡 for how it shapes Romans 9.
- **Both sides are in the text.** Isaiah 10:5–19: Assyria is the rod of God's anger, and then God punishes it for the arrogance of its heart (10:12) and asks whether the axe boasts against the one who swings it (10:15). Genesis 50:20 uses the same Hebrew verb (*chashav*) for the brothers' intent and God's. Acts 2:23 has God's definite plan and lawless men in one verse. Scripture keeps both and doesn't resolve it the way either camp wants. 🔴
- **Decree is not inspiration.** God governing an event doesn't make every word about it Scripture. Pharaoh's speeches are inside God's plan; only one of the two is "God-breathed."
- **Wright** (my vault summary, still to verify against *Paul for Everyone*): a defense of covenant faithfulness, not a treatise on individual destiny. Israel had the map and missed the destination. "Grace, not race." The potter reworking a rebellious Israel into a family of many nations. 🔵 until I check the wording.
- **Heiser** (my vault notes): election here is vocational, a role and a lineage (Jacob as the line to the Messiah), not a list of who gets eternal life. Inside the Deuteronomy 32 worldview, God took Israel as his portion to reclaim the nations. Pharaoh's existing rebellion steered into a win over the gods of Egypt. A remnant of faith inside the chosen nation. 🟡
- **Greek:** *eklogē*, election, selection for a purpose (from *ek* + *legō*). *Eleos*, mercy, behind Hebrew *hesed*. *Sklērunō*, to harden.
- **Method rule:** for a hot-button passage like this, my Logos pull has to ask for the Reformed, Arminian and Catholic/Orthodox readings, each at its strongest.
- **Divine council:** Pharaoh and the gods of Egypt, Israel as God's portion, the Lord of hosts. The council is the backdrop for chapters 9–11.

## META: the book of Ruth
- **Where it sits.** Set "in the days when the judges judged" (1:1), the same era where everyone did what was right in his own eyes. In Christian Bibles it sits between Judges and Samuel, a bridge from the judges to David. In the Hebrew Bible it's in the Writings, one of the five Megilloth, read at the feast of Weeks (Shavuot). 🔴
- **The question the whole book is asking:** can covenant faithfulness, *hesed*, show up in ordinary people in a dark time, and what does God do with it?
- **Who wrote it.** Nobody knows. The Talmud (*Bava Batra*) credits Samuel, but the book names no author, and the genealogy at the end runs to David, so it was written down in David's time or later. ⬜
- **When.** The story is set in the judges period, likely the late 12th century BC. When it was written is open: some evidence from the Hebrew points before the exile, some arguments from its themes point later. ⬜
- **The text is clean.** Ruth has almost no serious text problems. The one real puzzle is the end of 2:7. 🔴
- **Named for a foreigner.** It's the only Old Testament book named for a non-Israelite, and a Moabite at that. 🔴
- **Four movements:**
  - Ch. 1: emptiness. Famine, Moab, three funerals, "call me Mara."
  - Ch. 2: first fullness. Gleaning in Boaz's field.
  - Ch. 3: the threshing floor and the proposal.
  - Ch. 4: the town gate, the marriage, and the line to David.
- **Things to track the whole way through:**
  - *Hesed*, loyal covenant love that goes past what's owed.
  - The *go'el*, the family redeemer.
  - God's hidden hand: he is the subject of a verb only twice (1:6 and 4:13), and his work hides in what looks like chance.
  - Empty to full. Naomi's "empty" (1:21) is what the whole book answers.
  - A Moabite outsider becomes the model Israelite and the great-grandmother of David.

## What the chapter is doing
- A famine drives Elimelech of Bethlehem, his wife Naomi and their two sons to Moab. Elimelech dies. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and about ten years later both sons die too (1:1–5).
- Naomi hears Yahweh has given his people food and heads home. She tells her daughters-in-law three times to go back. Orpah kisses her and goes. Ruth clings to her (1:6–14).
- Ruth's vow: "where you go, I will go ... Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God" (1:16–17).
- In Bethlehem the women ask, "Is this Naomi?" She says call me Mara, bitter: "I went out full, but Yahweh has caused me to return empty." They arrive at the beginning of barley harvest (1:19–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **Famine in the "house of bread."** Bethlehem means house of bread. 🔴 for the name, 🟡 for the irony as intended.
- **The names tell the story.** Elimelech, "my God is king," leaves the promised land. Naomi means pleasant. Mahlon and Chilion sound like "sickness" and "wasting." Mara means bitter. 🔴 for the meanings.
- **Elimelech dies first (1:3).** Before the sons marry. Then about ten years pass, then the sons die (1:4–5). It's easy to read past. 🔴
- **Three pushes (1:8–15).** Naomi sends them home with a blessing and a prayer for "rest" in new husbands (1:8–9). Then the hard math: no more sons in her womb for them to marry (1:11–13). Then she tells Ruth to follow Orpah back "to her people and her gods" (1:15). 🔴
- **Orpah isn't the villain.** She does the sensible thing. She's there so Ruth's choice stands out. 🟡
- **Ruth "clung" to her (1:14).** The verb is *davaq*, the word in Genesis 2:24 for a man clinging to his wife. 🔴
- **Ruth's vow is a conversion (1:16–17).** Land, people, God, and grave, sealed with an oath in Yahweh's own name. 🔴
- **Naomi takes God to court (1:20–21).** "Yahweh has answered against me": *'anah be*, legal language for testifying against someone. Block notes she puts "I" and "Yahweh" at opposite ends of her lines. 🔴 for the words, 🟡 for Block's reading of the order.
- **She says "empty" with Ruth standing right next to her.** 🔴
- **The last line turns it (1:22).** "The beginning of barley harvest." Naomi sees empty; the narrator already shows food coming. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Moab was a loaded place.** Born of Lot's incest (Genesis 19), the people who hired Balaam (Numbers 22–24), barred from Israel's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3). Going there to survive was going to the wrong side of the river. 🔴
- **A widow with no sons had no future.** A woman's living and standing ran through a husband or sons. Three widows and no men means the family line is one step from ending. 🔴
- **"Rest" meant a husband's house (1:9).** *Menuchah*, security in marriage, was what Naomi could still pray for them. 🔴
- **The levirate logic (1:11–13).** A dead man's brother was to marry his widow and raise a son in his name (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). Naomi has no sons left to give. 🔴
- **Gods belonged to lands.** Orpah goes back to "her people and her gods" (1:15), meaning Chemosh, the god of Moab. To switch peoples was to switch gods. Ruth swears by Yahweh, the God of the land she's walking into. 🔴
- **Burial meant belonging.** Being buried with your people was the last mark of who you were. "There I will be buried" gives up Moab for good. 🔴
- **Divine council: Shaddai.** Naomi uses *Shaddai*, "the Almighty," in her bitterest lines (1:20–21). In the Deir Alla texts *shdyn* stands next to *'lhn*, "gods," and some scholars read *Shaddai* as a title of the high God over the council. Naomi uses the high title for the God she thinks has ruled against her. 🟡, a flag, not a load-bearing claim.

## What the chapter is doing
- Before Ruth meets him, the narrator introduces Boaz: a relative of Elimelech, "a mighty man of excellence" (2:1).
- Ruth goes out to glean behind the reapers, and "it so happened" she lands in Boaz's part of the field (2:2–3).
- Boaz notices her, tells her to stay in his field, orders his men not to touch her, gives her water and a meal, and has his workers pull grain out of the bundles for her on purpose (2:8–16).
- She comes home with an ephah of barley. When Naomi hears the name Boaz she blesses Yahweh, "who has not forsaken his lovingkindness to the living and to the dead," and says Boaz is one of their kinsman redeemers (2:17–23).

## Pay attention to this
- **The chapter is a sandwich.** Home, field, home. Naomi and Ruth at the start, the long Boaz scene in the middle, Naomi and Ruth at the end. 🔴
- **"A mighty man of excellence" (2:1).** The Hebrew, *'ish gibbor hayil*, is the title the angel gives Gideon, "mighty warrior" (Judges 6:12). Boaz never fights. The narrator gives him the warrior's title and fills it with character. 🔴 for the phrase, 🟡 for the redefinition.
- **The matching woman.** Boaz later calls Ruth an *'eshet hayil*, "a woman of excellence" (3:11), the same phrase as Proverbs 31:10. 🔴
- **"It so happened that she happened" (2:3).** Literally, "her chance chanced upon" the field. Block calls it the narrator's wink. It looks like luck. 🔴 for the wording, 🟡 for the wink.
- **Boaz's first words are a blessing (2:4).** "May Yahweh be with you." And the reapers answer in kind. In the judges era, a field where people talk like that is news. 🔴
- **The men are ordered not to touch her (2:9).** That tells you the danger was real for a foreign woman alone in the fields. 🔴
- **"Notice" and "foreigner" (2:10).** *Hakkir* and *nokriyyah* share a root, *nkr*. "Why have you noticed me, the unnoticeable?" 🔴
- **"Under whose wings you have come to seek refuge" (2:12).** The word is *kanaph*, wing. Ruth will ask Boaz to spread his *kanaph* over her in 3:9. He becomes the answer to his own prayer. 🔴
- **An ephah of barley (2:17).** Block puts it at about 29–50 pounds, roughly half a month's food from one day. 🔴
- **Naomi's faith comes back online (2:20).** She praises God's *hesed* and names Boaz a *go'el*. 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **Gleaning was law, not charity.** Leviticus 19:9–10, 23:22 and Deuteronomy 24:19–21 told landowners to leave the edges and the dropped grain for the poor and the sojourner. Ruth is both. 🔴
- **It was dangerous work.** An unattached foreign woman among male harvesters had no protection but the owner's word. Block calls Boaz's order the first anti-harassment policy recorded in the Bible. 🔴
- **Water was the workers' right.** Letting Ruth drink from what the young men drew (2:9) puts her with the hired hands, not the gleaners. 🟡
- **Barley harvest came first.** Barley ripened in spring, about April, and wheat a few weeks later (2:23). Ruth gleans through both, about seven weeks. 🔴
- **The *go'el*.** The family redeemer had the right and duty to buy back land (Leviticus 25:25), redeem a relative sold into slavery (25:47–55), and avenge blood (Numbers 35). Naomi naming Boaz a *go'el* turns the story from surviving to being redeemed. 🔴
- **Divine council: refuge under wings.** The picture of God's wings belongs to his protection over his people (Psalm 91:4). Ruth has left Moab and its god for the shelter of Yahweh. The 02-BIBLE templated note ties *kanaph* to the cherubim; I haven't verified that, so it stays out. No council scene in the chapter.

Boaz tells his people not to give her a rough time and drops grain for her on purpose. "Boaz knows that Ruth is Naomi's daughter, and he knows the story, and he's impressed that even though she's a foreigner, she's doing what a good Israelite daughter would do."

- **Boaz and Gideon.** The warrior title gets handed to a man who never fights. Coming right out of Judges, where the "mighty men" were moral disasters, that's the point. 🟡 My Judges 6 note has the Gideon side.

## What the chapter is doing
- Naomi wants "a state of rest" for Ruth. She tells her to wash, anoint herself, put on her best clothes, go to the threshing floor at night, wait until Boaz has eaten and drunk, then uncover his feet and lie down (3:1–4).
- At midnight Boaz wakes startled and finds a woman at his feet. Ruth says, "spread your wing over your maidservant, for you are a kinsman redeemer" (3:9).
- Boaz blesses her, promises to do all she asks, calls her "a woman of excellence," and then names the snag: there's a redeemer closer than he is (3:10–13).
- She stays till just before dawn and leaves unrecognized, carrying six measures of barley, because Boaz said, "Do not go to your mother-in-law empty." Naomi says the man won't rest until it's settled today (3:14–18).

## Pay attention to this
- **The goal is "rest" (3:1).** *Manoach*, the same idea as Naomi's prayer in 1:9: a husband's house. Naomi is after marriage. 🔴
- **The scene is loaded on purpose.** Night, a man whose "heart was merry" after eating and drinking (3:7), uncovered feet, lying down. The words "feet" (*regel*), "lie down" (*shakab*) and "know" can all carry sexual meaning in Hebrew. The narrator builds the tension so the way it resolves shows who these two are. 🔴 for the double meanings, 🟡 for the purpose.
- **Nothing happens.** Boaz wakes startled and asks, "Who are you?" (3:8–9). He doesn't reach for her. 🔴
- **"Spread your wing" (3:9).** *Kanaph* is wing and the corner of a garment. Spreading it over a woman was a betrothal act (Ezekiel 16:8). Ruth asks Boaz to be the answer to his own prayer in 2:12, "under whose wings you have come to seek refuge." 🔴
- **She proposes using the law.** "For you are a kinsman redeemer." It's a legal request, not a come-on. 🔴
- **The roles flip.** Naomi told her Boaz would tell her what to do (3:4). Instead Ruth tells Boaz his duty, and he answers "all that you say, I will do" (3:11). 🔴
- **"A woman of excellence" (3:11).** *'Eshet hayil*, the match for Boaz's own title in 2:1, and the phrase of Proverbs 31:10. 🔴
- **"Stay this night" (3:13).** The verb is *lin*, lodge, the same word as Ruth's vow ("where you lodge, I will lodge," 1:16), not *shakab*. 🔴
- **He guards her name (3:14).** She leaves before anyone can recognize anyone. "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor." 🔴
- **"Do not go ... empty" (3:17).** That undoes Naomi's "Yahweh has caused me to return empty" (1:21). 🔴

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **The threshing floor.** At harvest's end men winnowed at night when the wind came up and slept by the grain to guard it. Threshing floors also had a reputation for loose living (Hosea 9:1). 🔴
- **Garment over a woman meant marriage.** Covering a woman with your cloak was a known sign of taking her as wife. Ezekiel 16:8 uses it for Yahweh and Israel. 🔴
- **It isn't strictly the levirate law.** Deuteronomy 25 binds a dead man's brother. Boaz is a clan relative, so nothing legally forces him. He acts on moral obligation. Block: "The lives of genuinely good people are not governed by laws but character." 🔴 for the law, 🟡 for Block's reading.
- **Six measures of barley (3:15).** Likely a *mohar*, a betrothal pledge, and a message to Naomi. 🟡
- **Honor and shame.** A woman found at a man's feet at night could lose her name for good. Boaz protecting her reputation is as much a part of his *hesed* as the barley. 🔴
- **No divine council material here.** The book's unseen-realm touch is Naomi's use of *Shaddai* in 1:20–21. The wings in this chapter are a picture of shelter.

## My notes
- I stopped a few verses in. Naomi tells Ruth to go lie at Boaz's feet. I'd picked up the clue: "feet" has a sexual sense, and I tied it to Zipporah touching Moses' feet with the cut foreskin (Exodus 4:25).
- Then I sharpened my own question: "my question was did Ruth go have sex? Was Naomi telling her to? Big difference in that wording." And: "you have to admit, if a guy's been drinking and a woman comes, uncovers his bed and lays down by his feet."
- **Where it landed.** Did it happen? No, and the way the text says no is the meaning. Was Naomi telling her to? Her aim is marriage-rest. But she's a grown woman who knows exactly what that setup looks like, and she stages it on purpose as pressure to force a proposal, betting everything on Boaz's character. 🟡
- **A pattern I noticed:** "those Hebrews are pretty sneaky about adding sex to it. The Scriptures, and you read right past it." *Yada* (know), *regel* (feet), *shakab* (lie down). They wrote for the ear, and the first audience caught it. I want this tracked across the whole canon.

## What the chapter is doing
- Boaz sits at the town gate, stops the nearer redeemer as he passes, and seats ten elders as witnesses (4:1–2).
- He offers the man Elimelech's field, and the man says he'll redeem it. Then Boaz adds that whoever takes the field takes Ruth the Moabitess too, to raise up the dead man's name. The man backs out, "lest I ruin my own inheritance," and hands over his sandal (4:3–8).
- Boaz buys it all in front of the witnesses, and the town blesses the marriage by Rachel, Leah, and Perez (4:9–12).
- Yahweh gives Ruth a son. The women tell Naomi this child is her redeemer and Ruth is better to her than seven sons. Naomi holds him. They name him Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David, and the genealogy runs from Perez to David (4:13–22).

## Pay attention to this
- **The man with no name (4:1).** Boaz calls him "my fellow," in Hebrew *peloni almoni*, "Mr. So-and-So." The narrator names everybody else. The man who put himself before his family loses his name. 🔴 for the phrase, 🟡 for reading it as judgment.
- **Land first, then Ruth (4:3–5).** The field is an easy yes. The catch is that Ruth's son would carry Elimelech's line, so the money spent goes out of the buyer's own family. 🔴
- **"Lest I ruin my own inheritance" (4:6).** He protects what's his. Boaz takes the loss. 🔴
- **The narrator explains the sandal (4:7).** "This was the custom in former times." By the writer's day people had forgotten it. That's a clue the book was written well after the events. 🔴 for the note, 🟡 for the dating clue.
- **Perez in the blessing (4:12).** Perez was the son of Tamar and Judah (Genesis 38), another widow, another levirate story, another child in Judah's line. 🔴
- **"Yahweh granted her conception" (4:13).** Only the second time in the book God is the direct subject of an action. The first was ending the famine (1:6). After ten childless years with Mahlon, this is the miracle. 🔴
- **"Better to you than seven sons" (4:15).** Seven sons was the perfect family. A Moabite daughter-in-law beats it. 🔴
- **Naomi holds the child and says nothing (4:16).** The woman who called herself Bitter has her arms full. 🔴
- **Obed, Jesse, David (4:17).** The whole book turns out to be David's family history. 🔴
- **Boaz is seventh of ten (4:18–22).** The honored slot in a ten-name list. And the list names Boaz as Obed's father, not Mahlon, even though the custom made Obed Mahlon's heir. 🔴 for the list, 🟡 for the seventh slot meaning something.

## Read it like 1100 BC, not 2026
- **The gate was the courthouse.** Elders sat at the town gate to settle legal business in public. Ten elders made it binding. 🔴
- **Redeeming land kept it in the family.** Land belonged to God and to the clan (Leviticus 25:23–25). When someone had to sell, the nearest relative had the right to buy it back. 🔴
- **The sandal sealed the deal.** Walking on land claimed it, so handing over a sandal handed over the right to it. Deuteronomy 25:9 has a related but harsher sandal rite for a brother who refuses levirate duty. 🔴 for the texts, 🟡 for the walking-on-land logic.
- **Redeemer and levirate joined by custom.** The *go'el* law (buying land and kin back) and the levirate law (raising a son for a dead brother) are separate in the Torah. Ruth fuses them by custom, not statute. 🔴
- **A Moabite in the royal line.** Deuteronomy 23:3 bars Moabites from Israel's assembly, and here a Moabite becomes David's great-grandmother. Matthew 1:5 names her in the line of Jesus. 🔴
- **No divine council scene.** God's hand in Ruth is hidden, not staged. The one unseen-realm touch in the book is Naomi's *Shaddai* in 1:20–21.

- I didn't write my own retelling of this chapter. My notes here are where the whole-book study landed.
- **Where the study closed:**
  - *Hesed*, the thing the judges era lacked, is the heartbeat of the book.
  - The *go'el* across Leviticus 25, Numbers 35 and Numbers 5, joined to the levirate by custom. Boaz redeems by choice and character, not because a law forces him.
  - Ruth is the quiet answer to Judges: the royal line runs through a foreign widow instead of any of Judges' deliverers.

## What the chapter is doing
- Zechariah's fourth night vision. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of Yahweh, and the satan stands at his right hand to accuse him (3:1).
- Yahweh rebukes the accuser: "Yahweh rebuke you, Satan!" Joshua is "a brand delivered from the fire" (3:2).
- Joshua is in filthy clothes. The angel orders those standing there to strip them off and dress him in festal robes, and Zechariah speaks up: put a clean turban on his head (3:3–5).
- The angel gives Joshua a charge: walk in my ways and you'll run my house and have access among those standing here (3:6–7).
- God promises to bring "My servant the Branch," sets a stone with seven eyes before Joshua, and says he will remove the land's guilt in one day. Everyone will invite his neighbor under his vine and fig tree (3:8–10).

## Pay attention to this
- **It's a courtroom.** A defendant (Joshua), a judge (the angel of Yahweh), a prosecutor standing at the right hand (the satan), and others standing by. 🔴
- **"Satan" has the article.** *Ha-satan*, the accuser, same as Job 1–2. "To accuse him" is the verb form of the same word: the satan stands there to *satan* him. 🔴
- **"Yahweh said... 'Yahweh rebuke you'" (3:2).** Yahweh speaks of Yahweh in the third person. Verse 1 put the angel of Yahweh in the judge's seat, and verse 2 calls the speaker Yahweh. 🔴
- **The accuser loses (3:2).** God doesn't answer the charge. He rebukes the one bringing it. 🔴
- **"A brand delivered from the fire."** A burning stick pulled out of the fire before it's gone. Joshua and the people he stands for just came out of exile. 🔴
- **Filthy clothes (3:3).** The word is strong, close to "excrement-covered." A high priest in that state could not serve. 🔴
- **The angel takes away his iniquity (3:4).** "I have made your iniquity pass away from you." 🔴
- **Zechariah speaks in the vision (3:5).** He calls out for the clean turban, and they do it. 🔴
- **"Access to walk among these who are standing here" (3:7).** The "standing ones" are the heavenly attendants in the court. A human priest is promised a place among them. 🔴
- **"My servant the Branch" (3:8).** *Tsemach*, a title for the coming son of David (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15; Zechariah 6:12). 🔴
- **Vine and fig tree (3:10).** The picture of peace from Micah 4:4 and Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:25). 🔴

## Read it like 519 BC, not 2026
- **Back from exile, temple half-built.** The exiles returned under Cyrus. Zechariah's visions are dated to the second year of Darius (1:7, early 519 BC), while the temple was being rebuilt. The question in the air was whether a priesthood just back from an unclean land could serve God at all. 🔴
- **This is the divine council in session.** The angel of Yahweh presides. Attendants stand before him and take orders (3:4). The accuser is a member of the court with a job to do. Zechariah's night visions are council scenes one after another: horsemen report back (1:10–11), messengers talk to messengers (2:3–4). 🔴
- **The satan is a prosecutor, and he loses.** He's in the court, but God rejects his charge and rebukes him instead (Merrill; Newsom, as pulled). In Job and here, Yahweh and the accuser hold opposite views. 🔴
- **Standing at the right hand.** In an ancient court the accuser stood at the right hand of the accused (Psalm 109:6). 🔴
- **The angel of Yahweh is Yahweh and not Yahweh.** He's distinct from Yahweh, and he speaks and acts as Yahweh: he forgives iniquity (3:4), which only God does. Heiser counts this among the "Two Powers" texts, with Genesis 19:24 and Daniel 7. 🔴 for the text; 🟡 for the Two Powers frame.
- **A human in God's council.** Prophets stood in Yahweh's council to hear (Jeremiah 23:18, 22). Here a priest is promised access among the heavenly standing ones. That's a remarkable promise for a man who was in filthy clothes four verses earlier. 🔴 for the promise; 🟡 for how far to take it.
- **Clean garments and a turban.** The high priest's turban carried the plate "Holy to Yahweh" (Exodus 28:36–38). Putting it back on means the priesthood is restored. 🔴
- **Jude borrows the line.** Jude 9 has Michael, disputing with the devil over Moses' body, say "The Lord rebuke you." Same words, from a Second Temple story (the Assumption of Moses, according to early church writers). 🔴

## My notes
- ***Ha-satan* with the article.** As in Job 1–2, the figure is *the* satan. Hebrew doesn't put the article on a personal name, so it's a title or office, "the accuser." 🔴 This is one of the three test cases (Job, Zechariah, 1 Chronicles 21) for the word before it settles into a name.
- **3:2, the rebuke.** God rejects the accuser's charge and rebukes the accuser (Merrill, *Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi* 120; Newsom). In Job and Zechariah Yahweh and the accuser hold opposing views. The critical "externalization" frame and Heiser's developing-revelation frame look at the same data and come to opposite conclusions about whether the satan is real.
- **A different figure from the Eden rebel.** In my Fact Book work: the satan stands at Joshua's right hand and gets rebuked by Yahweh's messenger, a different figure again from the serpent in Eden. DDD notes Numbers 22 and Zechariah 3 show different divine beings in different and even opposed roles.
- **My X replies on the satan as a title.** I built them on the Greek Old Testament evidence, Joüon-Muraoka's grammar, Ryan Stokes (*JBL* 128.1, 2009), and a real question about 3:2. On the second pass I added the scholarly line before Heiser (Peggy Day, Mullen, Mark Smith) so Heiser isn't treated as the last word.
- **Two Powers.** The angel of Yahweh in Zechariah 3 speaks as God and is still distinct from God.
- My work is on 3:1–2 and the word, not the whole chapter yet.

## Quiz
Take it before you read and again after.

1. Who is standing on trial in this vision?
2. Who is standing at his right hand, and why?
3. True or false: in Hebrew, "satan" in Zechariah 3 has "the" in front of it.
4. Finish 3:2: "Yahweh ______ you, Satan!"
5. What does God call Joshua in 3:2?
   a) A lamp on a stand
   b) A brand delivered from the fire
   c) A rock in the sea
   d) A shepherd of the flock
6. What was Joshua wearing at first?
7. What did they put on him instead?
8. What does the angel promise Joshua if he walks in God's ways (3:7)?
9. What title does God use for the coming servant in 3:8?
10. Which New Testament book repeats "The Lord rebuke you"?

### Answer key
1. Joshua the high priest (3:1).
2. Satan, the accuser, to accuse him (3:1).
3. True. *Ha-satan*, "the accuser."
4. Rebuke (3:2).
5. b. A brand delivered from the fire (3:2).
6. Filthy garments (3:3).
7. Festal robes and a clean turban (3:4–5).
8. He will render justice in God's house, keep his courts, and have access to walk among those standing there (3:7).
9. "My servant the Branch" (3:8).
10. Jude (verse 9).
